{ "H": { "symbol": "H", "name": "Hydrogen", "atomic": 1, "category": "diatomic nonmetal", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 1 (H)", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">Hydrogen<\/a><\/b> is the universe's ultimate building block. Sitting at the very beginning of the periodic table with atomic number 1, it is the lightest, simplest, and most abundant element in existence. In fact, it makes up about 75% of all normal matter! Most of the <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> in our universe was forged just minutes after the Big Bang, meaning the <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> atoms in your body are nearly 13.8 billion years old. On Earth, hydrogen is almost never found floating freely as a gas. Instead, it loves to team up with other elements, most famously bonding with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> to create the water (H<sub>2<\/sub>O) that covers our blue planet. In its pure form, hydrogen is a colorless, odorless, non-toxic, and highly flammable gas. Across cultures, its life-giving nature is recognized: in several Indian languages, it is called \"Jala-janaka\" or \"Udajani,\" which beautifully mirrors its Greek name by also meaning \"the creator of water.\"<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/d\/d9\/Hydrogenglow.jpg", "atomic_mass": 1.008, "density": 0.08988, "melt": 13.99, "boil": 20.271, "phase": "Gas", "discovered_by": "Henry Cavendish", "electron_configuration": "1s1", "electronegativity_pauling": 2.2, "electron_affinity": 72.769, "ionization_energies": [ 1312 ], "sections": { "Isotopes": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">Hydrogen<\/a> is unique among the elements because its three naturally occurring isotopes have their own special names! The most common is <b>Protium<\/b> (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">Hydrogen<\/a>-1), which accounts for over 99.98% of all <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a>. Its nucleus is incredibly simple: just a single proton and no neutrons. The second isotope is <b>Deuterium<\/b> (Hydrogen-2). It has one proton and one neutron. Most of the universe's deuterium was created during the Big Bang. When deuterium replaces protium in water molecules, it forms what scientists call \"heavy water,\" which is commonly used in modern nuclear reactors\u2014like those operating in India's Kalpakkam facility. The third isotope, <b>Tritium<\/b> (Hydrogen-3), has one proton and two neutrons. Tritium is radioactive and glows in the dark! While rare, it is used in self-powered lighting devices like the glowing dials on high-end watches and in cutting-edge nuclear fusion research.<\/p>", "History": "<p>The discovery of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> is a fascinating tale spanning both ancient philosophy and modern chemistry. Long before modern science, ancient Indian philosophers like Kanada developed sophisticated theories of <i>paramanu<\/i> (indivisible atoms). Some modern interpretations of ancient Indian texts, like the <i>Agastya Samhita<\/i>, even point to descriptions of early battery-like setups using <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> that could theoretically split water into <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> gases! In Western science, the Swiss-German alchemist Paracelsus noticed a highly flammable gas bubbling from metals in acids during the 1500s. Fast forward to 1766, and British scientist <b>Henry Cavendish<\/b> officially isolated the gas by mixing <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> with hydrochloric acid, calling it \"flammable air\" and proving it created water when burned. In 1788, the French chemist Antoine Lavoisier gave it the modern name, <b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">Hydrogen<\/a><\/b>, combining the Greek words <i>hydro<\/i> (water) and <i>genes<\/i> (creator).<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>In the vastness of space, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> is the undisputed king. It fuels the stars, including our Sun, where it constantly undergoes nuclear fusion to create <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">helium<\/a>, radiating the light and heat that makes life on Earth possible. It also forms the massive swirling clouds of gas deep in space and makes up the bulk of giant planets like Jupiter and Saturn. But on Earth, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> tells a different story. Because it is so wonderfully light, any unattached <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> gas floated away into space billions of years ago. Today, almost all the hydrogen on our planet is locked away in chemical partnerships. It is a vital part of water, fossil fuels, and every living organism. Interestingly, geologists are now discovering rare pockets of \"white hydrogen\" trapped deep underground, naturally created when water reacts with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>-rich rocks or radioactive minerals!<\/p>", "Applications": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">Hydrogen<\/a> is rapidly becoming a superstar in the global quest for clean, green energy. While traditionally used to refine petroleum and manufacture fertilizers, its future lies in saving the planet. Because <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> only produces water when burned or used in a fuel cell, it is the ultimate zero-emission energy carrier. Today, <b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> fuel cells<\/b> are powering buses, long-haul trucks, and even trains\u2014in fact, Indian Railways is actively testing hydrogen-powered passenger coaches! India is aggressively pursuing this frontier through the <b>National Green Hydrogen Mission<\/b>, aiming for energy independence by 2070. Breakthroughs are happening fast: institutions like the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) are turning biomass into green hydrogen, while IIT Guwahati and the Centre for Nano and Soft Matter Sciences (CeNS) are perfecting ways to split water directly using just sunlight. From powering NASA rocket engines to flying pollution-free airplanes of the future, hydrogen is truly the fuel of tomorrow.<\/p>" } }, "He": { "symbol": "He", "name": "Helium", "atomic": 2, "category": "noble gas", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 2 (He)", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">Helium<\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>He<\/b>, atomic number 2) is a fascinating, colorless, and odorless gas in the noble gas family. It is the second-lightest and second-most abundant element in the universe (after <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a>), making up about 24% of all elemental mass. Though it is constantly created in stars like our Sun through nuclear fusion, it is surprisingly rare on Earth, where it mostly forms from the slow radioactive decay of heavy elements deep underground. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">Helium<\/a> is famously known for its extreme resistance to cold: it has the lowest boiling point of any known element and is the only element that refuses to freeze into a solid under normal atmospheric pressure, no matter how chilly it gets!<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/0\/00\/Helium-glow.jpg", "atomic_mass": 4.0026022, "density": 0.1786, "melt": 0.95, "boil": 4.222, "phase": "Gas", "discovered_by": "Pierre Janssen", "electron_configuration": "1s2", "electronegativity_pauling": null, "electron_affinity": -48, "ionization_energies": [ 2372.3, 5250.5 ], "sections": { "History": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">Helium<\/a> has a truly out-of-this-world origin story! It is famously the first element to be discovered in space before it was found on Earth. This historic breakthrough happened in India during the total solar eclipse of August 18, 1868. French astronomer Pierre Janssen was observing the eclipse from Guntur, Andhra Pradesh, when he spotted a mysterious bright yellow line in the Sun's light spectrum. Soon after, English astronomer Joseph Norman Lockyer independently confirmed it and named the unknown element after <i>Helios<\/i>, the Greek god of the sun. It wasn't until nearly thirty years later, in 1895, that Scottish chemist Sir William Ramsay finally isolated <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">helium<\/a> on Earth by treating a <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/U\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Uranium (U)\">uranium<\/a>-bearing mineral with acid. Later in 1905, massive amounts of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">helium<\/a> were unexpectedly found in natural gas fields in Kansas, USA, which is still the primary way we harvest it today.<\/p>", "Characteristics": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">Helium<\/a> is a true rebel in the world of physics and chemistry. It is the only element that cannot be solidified just by dropping the temperature at standard pressure; it remains a liquid all the way down to absolute zero and requires extreme pressure to freeze! When cooled near absolute zero, liquid <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">helium<\/a> transforms into a bizarre state of matter called a 'superfluid.' In this state, it has absolutely zero friction or viscosity, allowing it to practically defy gravity as it spontaneously creeps up and over the walls of its container! As an inert noble gas, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">helium<\/a> almost never reacts or bonds with other elements, which makes it incredibly stable, non-toxic, and perfectly safe to handle.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">Helium<\/a> exists mainly as two stable forms, or isotopes: <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">helium<\/a>-4 and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">helium<\/a>-3. Helium-4 is incredibly stable and by far the most common. The vast majority of the universe's helium-4 was forged during the fiery beginnings of the Big Bang, while on Earth, it bubbles up from the underground radioactive decay of heavy elements like <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/U\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Uranium (U)\">uranium<\/a>. Helium-3, on the other hand, is extremely rare on our planet but quite abundant in space and solar winds. Because our Moon has been bombarded by these solar winds for billions of years, its surface is rich in helium-3. Scientists are incredibly excited about the prospect of mining the Moon for helium-3 one day, as it could serve as the perfect, clean fuel for future nuclear fusion reactors!<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>While you might first think of party balloons and floating blimps, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">helium<\/a> is a critical resource that powers modern technology. Because of its unmatched cooling abilities, its biggest use is in the medical field, where liquid <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">helium<\/a> supercools the powerful superconducting magnets inside MRI scanners. Without it, modern life-saving medical imaging would be nearly impossible! It is also vital for high-tech manufacturing, like making semiconductor chips for electronics and optical fibers for high-speed internet. In space exploration, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">helium<\/a> is used to pressurize fuel tanks in massive rockets, and deep-sea divers breathe a mixture of helium and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> to avoid 'the bends.' Today, India continues its historic connection with helium by making significant strides in modern research and technology. Institutions like the Raja Ramanna Centre for Advanced Technology (RRCAT) have developed indigenous helium liquefiers, and a major Liquid Helium Cryogenic facility was recently inaugurated at IIT Bombay to support deep-tech research in quantum sensing. Indian astronomers at the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA) are pioneering new methods to estimate helium abundance in the Sun, while researchers at NIT Durgapur are actively exploring ways to extract domestic helium from India's geothermal hot springs!<\/p>" } }, "Li": { "symbol": "Li", "name": "Lithium", "atomic": 3, "category": "alkali metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><strong><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">Lithium<\/a><\/strong> (from the Greek word <em>lithos<\/em>, meaning &quot;stone&quot;) is a fascinating chemical element with the symbol <strong>Li<\/strong> and atomic number 3. As a soft, silvery-white metal belonging to the alkali metal group, it holds the remarkable title of being the lightest metal and the least dense solid element on Earth. Because it is highly reactive, you will never find it freely in nature; instead, it is always locked away in minerals and salts. Today, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a> is a critical resource for the modern world, powering everything from smartphones to electric vehicles and driving global efforts toward clean energy and technological self-reliance.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/e\/e2\/0.5_grams_lithium_under_argon.jpg", "atomic_mass": 6.94, "density": 0.534, "melt": 453.65, "boil": 1603, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Johan August Arfwedson", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s1", "electronegativity_pauling": 0.98, "electron_affinity": 59.6326, "ionization_energies": [ 520.2, 7298.1, 11815 ], "sections": { "Isotopes": "<p>In nature, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a> comes in two stable forms, or isotopes: <sup>6<\/sup>Li and <sup>7<\/sup>Li. The vast majority (about 95.15%) is <sup>7<\/sup>Li. Interestingly, these natural isotopes have unusually low nuclear binding energy compared to their neighbors, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">helium<\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Be\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Beryllium (Be)\">beryllium<\/a>. In fact, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a> is the only light element that can produce net energy through nuclear fission! Because of this unique trait, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a> is surprisingly less common in our Solar System than 28 of the first 34 chemical elements, despite being incredibly light.<\/p><p>Scientists have also discovered seven radioactive isotopes of lithium, though they are highly unstable. The longest-lived is <sup>8<\/sup>Li, with a half-life of just 838 milliseconds, while the shortest-lived vanishes in a tiny fraction of a second. Lithium's isotopes behave differently during natural processes, meaning they naturally separate over time. This separation is also done artificially; for example, the lighter <sup>6<\/sup>Li isotope has been heavily used in nuclear physics and weapons manufacturing. This has slightly altered the natural ratio of lithium isotopes on Earth, making its standard atomic weight a bit tricky to pin down!<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>Because <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a> is highly reactive, it never exists as a pure metal in nature. Instead, it is found hidden in mineral-rich rocks and brines. Historically, the primary sources have been pegmatite minerals, such as spodumene, and massive salt flats like the &quot;<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">Lithium<\/a> Triangle&quot; spanning the Andes mountains in Argentina, Bolivia, and Chile, where <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a>-rich brine is evaporated in large solar ponds.<\/p><p>Recently, India made a massive leap onto the global lithium map. In February 2023, the Geological Survey of India (GSI) announced the landmark discovery of 5.9 million tonnes of inferred lithium resources in the Salal-Haimana area of the Reasi district in Jammu &amp; Kashmir. This high-quality deposit\u2014grading at 500 parts per million or higher\u2014marks the country's first major lithium find. It strategically positions India as a potential powerhouse in global lithium resources, crucial for its &quot;Aatmanirbhar Bharat&quot; (self-reliant India) initiative to reduce dependence on imports for electric vehicle manufacturing and green energy.<\/p>", "History": "<p>The story of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a> begins in 1800 when Brazilian scientist Jos\u00e9 Bonif\u00e1cio de Andrada e Silva discovered the mineral petalite in a Swedish mine. But it wasn't until 1817 that Johan August Arfwedson, working in the lab of famous chemist J\u00f6ns Jakob Berzelius, realized this ore contained an entirely new element. Berzelius named the new substance &quot;lithion&quot; (from <em>lithos<\/em>, Greek for &quot;stone&quot;) because it was discovered in a rock, unlike <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> which were found in plants and animal blood. The element was officially named <strong><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a><\/strong>.<\/p><p>Although early scientists knew <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a> was there (noticing its bright red flame), they couldn't easily separate the pure metal. It was finally isolated in 1821 by British chemist William Thomas Brande using a process called electrolysis. Throughout the 20th century, lithium found unexpected uses, from a revolutionary psychiatric treatment for bipolar disorder (discovered by John Cade in 1949) to the production of tritium for nuclear weapons during the Cold War. Today, its history is being written by the clean energy revolution.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">Lithium<\/a> is often called the &quot;white <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\">gold<\/a>&quot; of the modern world because it is absolutely essential to today's technology and the global energy transition. Its most famous application is in <strong><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a>-ion batteries<\/strong>. Because <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a> is extremely light and holds a massive electrical charge, these batteries are perfect for powering smartphones, laptops, and electric vehicles (EVs), as well as storing energy from renewable sources like solar and wind.<\/p><p>India is rapidly advancing its own indigenous lithium technologies to support this transition. For instance, the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) has developed high-reliability, space-grade lithium-ion cells\u2014including innovative <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">Silicon<\/a>-Graphite anode-based high-energy density cells\u2014and transferred this technology to Indian industries for commercial production. Similarly, the Council of Scientific &amp; Industrial Research's Central Electrochemical Research Institute (CSIR-CECRI) has established India's first pilot plant for manufacturing 18650-type Li-ion cells, driving local innovation.<\/p><p>Beyond batteries, lithium has several other critical industrial uses. It is added to glass and ceramics to make them resistant to sudden temperature changes. In aviation, it is mixed with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a> to create super-strong, lightweight alloys for aircraft. Finally, lithium carbonate continues to be a life-changing pharmaceutical, remaining one of the most effective treatments for bipolar disorder.<\/p>" } }, "Be": { "symbol": "Be", "name": "Beryllium", "atomic": 4, "category": "alkaline earth metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Be\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Beryllium (Be)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Be\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Beryllium (Be)\">Beryllium<\/a><\/a> (symbol <strong>Be<\/strong>, atomic number 4) is a stiff, lightweight, and fascinating metal. Born from the collision of cosmic rays in deep space, it is relatively rare in the universe. On Earth, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Be\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Beryllium (Be)\">beryllium<\/a> is too reactive to exist on its own. Instead, it hides inside beautiful and colorful minerals, such as beryl and emerald, which have been prized for thousands of years.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/e\/e2\/Beryllium_%28Be%29.jpg", "atomic_mass": 9.01218315, "density": 1.85, "melt": 1560, "boil": 2742, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Louis Nicolas Vauquelin", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.57, "electron_affinity": -48, "ionization_energies": [ 899.5, 1757.1, 14848.7, 21006.6 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Be\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Beryllium (Be)\">Beryllium<\/a> possesses remarkable physical and chemical traits that make it stand out among metals, combining extreme lightness with surprising strength and heat resistance.<\/p>", "Physical properties": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Be\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Beryllium (Be)\">Beryllium<\/a> is a hard, steel-gray metal that is brittle at room temperature. It boasts a close-packed hexagonal crystal structure and an exceptional stiffness\u2014making it about 35% stiffer than steel! Despite this incredible rigidity, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Be\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Beryllium (Be)\">beryllium<\/a> is remarkably lightweight. This unique combination of stiffness and low density allows sound to travel through it at a staggering speed of 12.9 kilometers per second under normal conditions.<\/p><p>When it comes to handling heat, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Be\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Beryllium (Be)\">beryllium<\/a> is unmatched. It dissipates the most heat per unit weight of any metal, thanks to its high specific heat and excellent thermal conductivity. Furthermore, it barely expands or contracts when heated or cooled. This means that even under extreme temperature changes, beryllium won't easily warp or change shape, making it incredibly stable.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Be\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Beryllium (Be)\">Beryllium<\/a> is hidden within more than 100 different minerals, though most are quite rare. The most famous is beryl, which includes beloved gemstones like aquamarine and the stunning green emerald. The signature green of an emerald is actually caused by a tiny dash of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a> mixed into the beryl crystal.<\/p><p>Historically and today, India has been a significant source of beryl. In ancient Indian texts like the <em>Arthashastra<\/em> (4th century BCE) and the <em>Puranas<\/em>, beryl was known as <em>vaidurya<\/em> and emerald as <em>marakata<\/em>. These stones were highly prized in the <em>Navaratna<\/em> (nine gems) tradition, symbolizing the planet <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\">Mercury<\/a> and believed to bring protection and fortune.<\/p><p>Today, the primary ores mined for <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Be\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Beryllium (Be)\">beryllium<\/a> are beryl and bertrandite, found in countries like India, the United States, Brazil, and Madagascar. Across the cosmos, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Be\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Beryllium (Be)\">beryllium<\/a> is quite rare; the Sun contains only tiny traces of it. On Earth, it is the 47th most abundant element in the crust, typically concentrated in soils and almost entirely absent from ocean waters.<\/p>", "Chemical properties": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Be\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Beryllium (Be)\">Beryllium<\/a> atoms are incredibly small and hold onto their outer electrons very tightly. Because of this, it doesn't form simple ions easily; instead, it forms strong chemical bonds and links together into long chain-like structures. Interestingly, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Be\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Beryllium (Be)\">beryllium<\/a> behaves very similarly to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a>, sharing what chemists call a \"diagonal relationship\" on the periodic table.<\/p><p>In everyday conditions, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Be\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Beryllium (Be)\">beryllium<\/a> protects itself from the air by instantly forming a microscopic, invisible shield of beryllium oxide on its surface. This armor prevents it from reacting further. However, if heated to extreme temperatures, beryllium will burst into a brilliant flame. Like <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a>, it dissolves easily in certain acids and alkaline solutions, but it shrugs off water thanks to its protective oxide shield.<\/p><p>Beryllium combines with other elements to form a wide variety of fascinating compounds, from heat-resistant white solids like beryllium oxide to striking brick-red compounds like beryllium carbide, which reacts with water to produce methane gas.<\/p>", "History": "<p>Humans have prized <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Be\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Beryllium (Be)\">beryllium<\/a>-containing minerals for thousands of years. As far back as ancient Egypt and ancient India, people treasured beryl and emeralds. Ancient Indian alchemical and gemological texts detailed sophisticated methods for testing and valuing these stones. For a long time, early scientists believed these gems were simply forms of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a> silicate.<\/p><p>In 1798, French chemist Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin discovered a brand new element hidden inside emeralds. At first, it was named \"glucine\" because some of its compounds tasted sweet\u2014though we now know <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Be\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Beryllium (Be)\">beryllium<\/a> is highly toxic! The name <em><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Be\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Beryllium (Be)\">beryllium<\/a><\/em> was introduced in 1828, but both names were used interchangeably until 1949.<\/p><p>The pure metal was finally isolated in 1828 by two scientists, Friedrich W\u00f6hler and Antoine Bussy, working entirely independently. One of beryllium's most famous historical moments occurred in 1932: when scientist James Chadwick bombarded a sample of beryllium with alpha particles, he observed a strange new radiation. This led directly to his Nobel Prize-winning discovery of the neutron!<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Although you rarely see pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Be\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Beryllium (Be)\">beryllium<\/a> in everyday life, it is a critical \"behind-the-scenes\" material in modern technology. It is most commonly mixed with metals like <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a> to create specialized alloys. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Be\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Beryllium (Be)\">Beryllium<\/a>-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a> is highly conductive, incredibly strong, and uniquely \"non-sparking\"\u2014making it essential for heavy-duty industrial tools used in explosive environments like oil rigs.<\/p><p>Because it is so stiff, lightweight, and stable across wild temperature changes, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Be\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Beryllium (Be)\">beryllium<\/a> is a superstar in the aerospace and defense sectors. It is heavily used in supersonic aircraft, military sensors, and satellites. Most famously, the breathtaking golden mirrors of the <strong>James Webb Space Telescope<\/strong> are carved from solid beryllium, allowing them to remain perfectly rigid and functional in the freezing vacuum of deep space.<\/p><p>In India, modern research into beryllium is driven by the nation's strategic space, defense, and nuclear sectors. The Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) has developed specialized processes to extract beryllium from domestic Indian beryl ores, producing high-tech alloys for satellites and nuclear reactors. Furthermore, because beryllium is nearly transparent to X-rays, it is the perfect window material for medical imaging equipment, allowing rays to pass through clearly.<\/p>" } }, "B": { "symbol": "B", "name": "Boron", "atomic": 5, "category": "metalloid", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\">Boron<\/a><\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>B<\/b>, atomic number 5) is an incredibly versatile and fascinating metalloid. Unlike most elements, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\">boron<\/a> was not forged in the fiery cores of stars. Instead, it was born in the extreme environment of deep space, created when high-energy cosmic rays smashed into heavier matter. Because of this unique origin, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\">boron<\/a> is relatively rare in the universe and the Earth's crust. However, because its most common forms\u2014minerals called borates\u2014dissolve easily in water, it can be found in highly concentrated deposits here on Earth. Often described as a \"schizophrenic\" element, it confusingly blends the properties of both metals and non-metals. Today, boron is essential in everything from building ultra-strong aerospace parts to, possibly, the very origin of life.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/a\/a2\/Boron.jpg", "atomic_mass": 10.81, "density": 2.08, "melt": 2349, "boil": 4200, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p1", "electronegativity_pauling": 2.04, "electron_affinity": 26.989, "ionization_energies": [ 800.6, 2427.1, 3659.7, 25025.8, 32826.7 ], "sections": { "History": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/775a874aadfdc99e73b765138414711a.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"250\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"1632\" data-file-height=\"1632\" \/><figcaption>Amorphous <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\">boron<\/a><\/a> powder<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p>The name <i><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\">boron<\/a><\/i> stems from <i>borax<\/i>, the mineral from which it was first extracted, and its ending reflects its chemical similarity to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a><\/a>. Long before it was known as a unique element, early civilizations prized borate minerals. Over 4,000 years ago, ancient societies used them for metalworking. In ancient India, naturally occurring borax was well-known and called <i>Tankana<\/i> or <i>tincal<\/i>\u2014a word that became the root for many modern names for the mineral. Harvested from the Himalayas and Tibet, it was widely used in traditional Ayurvedic medicine as <i>Tankana Bhasma<\/i> for treating ailments, and served as a crucial flux for purifying <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\">gold<\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ag\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silver (Ag)\">silver<\/a>. Around 300 AD, China began using borax for specialized ceramic glazes, which Marco Polo later introduced to Italy.<\/p>\n<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-left\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/f04a847929d002552be76a1b1bd7b74e.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"190\" height=\"181\" style=\"--mw-file-upright: 0.75\" class=\"mw-file-element mw-file-upright\" data-file-width=\"535\" data-file-height=\"510\" \/><figcaption>Sassolite<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\">Boron<\/a> was not officially recognized as a distinct element until 1808. It was discovered independently by French chemists Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis Jacques Th\u00e9nard, and British chemist Sir Humphry Davy. Davy, who playfully named the substance <i>boracium<\/i>, extracted it by applying electric currents and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a><\/a> to boric acid. However, completely pure boron proved extremely stubborn to isolate. It took until 1909 for American chemist Ezekiel Weintraub to finally produce the first genuinely pure sample of the element.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">", "Isotopes": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">Main article: Isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\">boron<\/a><\/a><\/div>\n<p>In nature, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\">boron<\/a> exists mainly as two stable varieties, or isotopes: <sup>11<\/sup>B (which makes up about 80.1% of natural <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\">boron<\/a>) and <sup>10<\/sup>B (the remaining 19.9%). Scientists have created 11 other isotopes in laboratories, but they are all incredibly unstable. For instance, <sup>7<\/sup>B exists for only 3.5\u00d710<sup>\u221222<\/sup> seconds before falling apart!<\/p><p>The two stable isotopes are incredibly useful to researchers. When dissolved in water, <sup>10<\/sup>B and <sup>11<\/sup>B behave slightly differently. Because ocean water holds more <sup>11<\/sup>B compared to rocks on land, geologists can use this unique \"isotopic signature\" to track the history of ancient environments. In medicine, <sup>10<\/sup>B is a lifesaver. It is the key ingredient in Boron Neutron Capture Therapy (BNCT), a cutting-edge cancer treatment that uses targeted neutron beams to destroy brain tumors from the inside out, without harming healthy tissue.<\/p><p>Physicists are also captivated by a highly unstable isotope, <sup>17<\/sup>B. It possesses a bizarre \"nuclear halo,\" meaning the atom is noticeably larger and more spread out than traditional rules of physics say it should be.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading4\">", "Occurrence": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">Main article: Borate minerals<\/div>\n<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-right\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/86ee14d71e196a043c9b9bb83312e342.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"195\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"1024\" data-file-height=\"800\" \/><figcaption>Borax crystals<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p>On a cosmic scale, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\">boron<\/a> is quite rare. Very little of it was made during the Big Bang. Unlike heavier elements like <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\">boron<\/a> is actually destroyed by the intense heat inside stars rather than created there. Instead, the universe makes <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\">boron<\/a> through a dramatic process called \"spallation,\" where high-speed cosmic rays crash into heavier atoms in deep space, shattering them into lighter pieces like boron.<\/p><p>Here on Earth, you will never find pure elemental boron out in nature. It is highly reactive with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a>, meaning it prefers to form borate compounds. (However, scientists were amazed to find tiny flecks of pure boron in dirt brought back from the Moon!) Even though boron makes up a minuscule 0.001% of the Earth's crust, it is easy to mine because many borate minerals\u2014like borax and boric acid\u2014dissolve in water. Over millions of years, water has pooled these minerals together into large, rich deposits, especially in ancient, dried-up lakes and volcanic hot springs.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">", "Applications": "<p>Though rarely discussed, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\">boron<\/a> is an unsung hero of the modern world. Most of the <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\">boron<\/a> mined today is turned into boric acid or borax (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a> tetraborate). In the United States, roughly 70% of this supply is used to make specialized glass and ceramics. If you have ever baked with a Pyrex dish, peered through a telescope lens, or used laboratory beakers, you have relied on borosilicate glass. This special glass uses <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\">boron<\/a> to endure sudden, extreme temperature changes without shattering.<\/p><p>Worldwide, boron's biggest job is in the production of fiberglass. Adding boron makes glass fibers tougher and easier to shape, which is vital for building home insulation and sturdy construction materials. Beyond glass, boron helps create incredibly tough ceramics and advanced materials. Boron fibers are exceptionally lightweight yet incredibly strong, making them ideal for high-tech aerospace parts and even bulletproof vests. You can also find boron silently working in automotive fluids to boost efficiency, in household detergents and bleaches, and in the manufacturing of modern computer semiconductors.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Biological role": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">See also: <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\">Boron<\/a><\/a> deficiency (plant disorder)<\/div>\n<p>For the plant kingdom, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\">boron<\/a> is non-negotiable. It acts as a critical micronutrient that builds and strengthens plant cell walls, ensuring healthy crops and abundant harvests. However, it walks a fine line: while plants need <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\">boron<\/a> to thrive, soils with too much of it (anything above 1.8 parts per million) become toxic, causing leaves to wither and stunt growth.<\/p><p>In the microscopic world, nature uses boron to create unique antibiotics. Scientists discovered the first of these, boromycin, in the 1960s, followed by tartrolons in the 1990s. In modern laboratories, synthetic boron compounds called \"BODIPYs\" are incredibly popular. These brightly glowing fluorescent tags help scientists track and visualize hidden processes inside living cells.<\/p><p>Perhaps most mind-blowing of all is boron's potential link to our origins. Prominent scientists, such as chemist Steve Benner, suspect that ancient borate minerals played a vital role in the origin of life by stabilizing ribose, the fragile sugar backbone of RNA. In 2013, Benner even suggested that ancient Mars had better conditions for this boron-assisted RNA formation than Earth. This fascinating theory hints that primitive life might have actually started on Mars before meteorites carried it to our planet!<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">" } }, "C": { "symbol": "C", "name": "Carbon", "atomic": 6, "category": "polyatomic nonmetal", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 6 (C)", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">Carbon<\/a><\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>C<\/b>, atomic number 6) is a versatile polyatomic nonmetal in group 14 of the periodic table. Known since antiquity in forms like charcoal and diamond, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> is the undisputed chemical backbone of all known life on Earth. Because each <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> atom has four outer electrons, it is \"tetravalent\"\u2014capable of forming four strong covalent bonds with other atoms, including long chains and rings of carbon itself. Carbon makes up about 0.025 percent of Earth's crust. It occurs naturally in three isotopes: stable <sup>12<\/sup>C (98.93%) and <sup>13<\/sup>C (1.07%), alongside the radioactive isotope <sup>14<\/sup>C, which decays with a half-life of about 5,700 years and allows scientists to date ancient organic artifacts.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/6\/68\/Pure_Carbon.png", "atomic_mass": 12.011, "density": 1.821, "melt": null, "boil": null, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Ancient Egypt", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p2", "electronegativity_pauling": 2.55, "electron_affinity": 121.7763, "ionization_energies": [ 1086.5, 2352.6, 4620.5, 6222.7, 37831, 47277 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-left\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/9a6aeb6acca784b59e2b574971aee376.png\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"330\" height=\"282\" style=\"--mw-file-upright: 1.3\" class=\"mw-file-element mw-file-upright\" data-file-width=\"2397\" data-file-height=\"2049\" \/><figcaption>Phase diagram showing <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a>'s extreme sublimation point and liquid phase boundaries<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">Carbon<\/a> is famous for taking on astonishingly different physical personalities\u2014called allotropes\u2014depending on how its atoms are arranged. In graphite, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> atoms bond in flat, hexagonal sheets that easily slide past one another, making it soft, black, and slippery enough to write with. In diamond, carbon atoms form a rigid, three-dimensional lattice where every atom is locked in a tight pyramid structure, creating the hardest naturally occurring substance known. Modern science has unveiled even more exotic carbon structures, such as buckyballs (fullerenes), carbon nanotubes, and one-atom-thick graphene. Renowned Indian scientists, such as Bharat Ratna Prof. C.N.R. Rao, have led pioneering global research into synthesising and understanding these remarkable carbon nanomaterials.<\/p><p>Chemically, carbon possesses an extraordinary property known as catenation\u2014the ability to form stable, endless chains and rings by bonding with itself and other elements. Because of this, carbon is part of roughly 200 million distinct chemical compounds documented in scientific literature, far surpassing all other elements combined! Carbon also holds the highest sublimation temperature of all elements: at normal sea-level atmospheric pressure, solid carbon does not melt into a liquid when heated. Instead, it turns directly into a gas (sublimes) at an incredible 3,900 K (3,630 \u00b0C or 6,560 \u00b0F). Liquid carbon is extremely difficult to study because it can only exist under extreme pressures exceeding 100 atmospheres (10.8 megapascals) and temperatures above 4,000 K (3,730 \u00b0C). In its gaseous vapor state, excited diatomic carbon molecules (C<sub>2<\/sub>) produce a striking green glow.<\/p><p>At the atomic level, carbon is element number 6 with a ground-state electron configuration of 1s<sup>2<\/sup> 2s<sup>2<\/sup> 2p<sup>2<\/sup>, featuring 4 valence electrons in its outer shell. Its first four ionization energies are 1086.5, 2352.6, 4620.5, and 6222.7 kJ\/mol\u2014significantly higher than heavier elements in group 14. Carbon has an electronegativity of 2.55 on the Pauling scale, balancing well with neighboring nonmetals. Its covalent bonding radius shrinks as bond strength increases, measuring 77.2 pm for single bonds (C\u2212C), 66.7 pm for double bonds (C=C), and 60.3 pm for triple bonds (C\u2261C).<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Isotopes": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">Main article: Isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a><\/a><\/div>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">Carbon<\/a> nuclei always contain 6 protons, but their neutron count can range from 2 to 16 across 15 known isotopes. Earth's natural <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> consists almost entirely of two stable isotopes: carbon-12 (<sup>12<\/sup>C), which accounts for 98.93%, and carbon-13 (<sup>13<\/sup>C), which makes up the remaining 1.07%. Biological systems naturally prefer <sup>12<\/sup>C during photosynthesis and metabolism, leaving living organisms slightly enriched in <sup>12<\/sup>C. In 1961, the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) designated carbon-12 as the official universal standard for defining atomic weights. Meanwhile, carbon-13 plays a vital role in chemistry and medicine as the active nucleus used in carbon-13 Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy to map organic molecular structures.<\/p><p>Carbon-14 (<sup>14<\/sup>C) is a famous natural radioactive isotope produced continuously in Earth's upper atmosphere (between 9 and 15 km altitude). High-energy cosmic rays strike atmospheric atoms, creating thermal neutrons that collide with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a>-14 nuclei to yield carbon-14 and a proton. Carbon-14 exists in trace amounts\u2014about 1 part per trillion (1.5 \u00d7 10<sup>\u221210<\/sup> of atmospheric carbon dioxide). It decays by releasing a 0.158 MeV beta particle (\u03b2<sup>\u2212<\/sup>) with a half-life of 5,700 \u00b1 30 years. Because living organisms absorb carbon dioxide throughout their lives, their carbon-14 ratio matches the atmosphere; after death, <sup>14<\/sup>C decays predictably without being replenished. Invented in 1949, radiocarbon dating measures this decay to accurately date ancient organic materials, wood, and archaeological relics up to 40,000 years old.<\/p><p>Among carbon's synthetic isotopes, carbon-8 is the shortest-lived, decaying via proton emission with a fleeting half-life of just 3.5 \u00d7 10<sup>\u221221<\/sup> seconds. On the exotic extreme, carbon-19 exhibits a loose \"nuclear halo,\" where its outer neutron orbits far outside the central core, giving the atom an unusually large nuclear radius.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">", "Occurrence": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/176f8bf3f36d7ce0366de1ebe2fd0ba4.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"188\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"600\" data-file-height=\"451\" \/><figcaption>Natural graphite ore<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<figure class=\"mw-default-size\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/d06ef40b45f5946fe7cf3582d5ac905e.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"188\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"360\" data-file-height=\"271\" \/><figcaption>Raw octahedral diamond crystal<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<figure class=\"mw-default-size\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/fa3ee3e851d8076d00f381063dc87600.png\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"168\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"1687\" data-file-height=\"1133\" \/><figcaption>Global distribution of dissolved inorganic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> in ocean waters<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">Carbon<\/a> is the fourth most abundant element in the observable universe by mass, trailing only <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">helium<\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a>. It is abundant in the Sun, distant stars, comets, and planetary atmospheres. Over 20% of all cosmic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> is bound in complex ring structures called Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons (PAHs). According to the PAH world hypothesis, these space-borne carbon molecules formed roughly two billion years after the Big Bang and may have helped seed the chemical origins of life. Microscopic diamonds also form naturally inside meteorites and at cosmic impact craters, while carbon-rich asteroids in the outer asteroid belt are eyed as potential targets for futuristic space mining.<\/p><p>Across planet Earth (mass 5.972 \u00d7 10<sup>24<\/sup> kg), carbon averages about 730 parts per million (ppm), with roughly 2,000 ppm locked in Earth's metallic core and 120 ppm spread through the mantle and crust\u2014totalling an estimated 4,360 million gigatonnes (Gt) of carbon. Earth's atmosphere contains around 900 Gt of carbon as carbon dioxide (where 1 ppm equals 2.13 Gt). Since 1750, human burning of fossil fuels has added between 347 and 879 Gt of carbon to the atmosphere, contributing to a total of nearly 2,000 Gt absorbed across the atmosphere, oceans, and land peat bogs. World oceans hold approximately 36,000 Gt of dissolved carbon, while the living biosphere accounts for roughly 550 Gt. Vast icy deposits of methane hydrates beneath polar seabed sediments contain another 500 to 3,000 Gt of carbon.<\/p><p>Geologically, carbon makes up about 12% of massive carbonate rock formations such as limestone, dolomite, and marble. Fossil fuels represent massive mineralized carbon deposits: global coal reserves contain about 900 Gt of carbon (out of 18,000 Gt of total resources), with high-grade anthracite coal consisting of 92% to 98% pure carbon. Proven crude oil reserves hold about 150 Gt, while natural gas reserves hold 105 Gt (175 \u00d7 10<sup>12<\/sup> m<sup>3<\/sup>), with an estimated 540 Gt (900 \u00d7 10<sup>12<\/sup> m<sup>3<\/sup>) trapped in shale gas formations.<\/p><p>Natural graphite is mined globally in major deposits across China, Russia, Mexico, Canada, and India (with prominent Indian reserves in states like Odisha, Jharkhand, Tamil Nadu, and Arunachal Pradesh). Natural diamonds originate deep within Earth's mantle and reach the surface through ancient volcanic kimberlite pipes found in South Africa, Botswana, Namibia, the DRC, Angola, Brazil, Australia, Russia, Canada, and Arkansas, USA. Historically, India's legendary Golconda mines (in modern Telangana and Andhra Pradesh) were the world's primary source of extraordinary diamonds\u2014including the famous Koh-i-Noor and Hope Diamond. Ancient Indian gemological treatises (<i>Ratna\u015b\u0101stra<\/i>) and medieval alchemical texts like the <i>Rasa Ratna Samuccaya<\/i> by V\u0101gbha\u1e6da accurately documented the diamond's unmatched hardness (<i>Vajra<\/i>) and chemical invulnerability. In modern Indian science, Birbal Sahni (1891\u20131949), the pioneer of Indian paleobotany, conducted foundational studies on fossilized plant carbon and Indian coal beds, illuminating how ancient plant matter transformed into carbon rich geological formations over millions of years.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Applications": "<style data-file-height=\"500\" \/><\/span><\/div>\n\t\t\t<div class=\"gallerytext\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/W\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tungsten (W)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/W\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tungsten (W)\">Tungsten<\/a><\/a> carbide endmills<\/div>\n\t\t<\/li>\n<\/ul><\/div><\/div><\/div>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">Carbon<\/a> is the chemical basis for all known life, forming the structural foundation of proteins, DNA, carbohydrates, and fats. Beyond food and wood, carbon's largest economic role is in energy and materials. Hydrocarbons like natural gas (methane) and crude oil (petroleum) are refined in petrochemical plants to produce gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and synthetic polymers (plastics). In nature, plants produce cellulose\u2014a natural carbon polymer forming wood, cotton, linen, and hemp\u2014while animals yield natural carbon fibers like wool, silk, and cashmere.<\/p><p>Carbon is vital across metallurgy and heavy industry. When added to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>, carbon forms steel\u2014the world's premier structural alloy. Historically, ancient Indian metallurgists used charcoal (pure carbon) to smelt <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> and forge famous high-carbon Wootz steel (the original Damascus steel), renowned for its strength and wavy patterns. Today, coke (processed coal) acts as a reducing agent in blast furnaces to extract pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> from ore. Carbides formed with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/W\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tungsten (W)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/W\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tungsten (W)\">tungsten<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\">boron<\/a><\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a><\/a> are among the hardest materials on Earth, used in industrial cutting, grinding, and metalworking tools.<\/p><p>Graphite mixed with clay forms pencil leads, while pure graphite serves as a high-temperature lubricant, battery electrode material, motor brush, and neutron moderator in nuclear reactors. Charcoal is widely used in sketching, barbecue grilling, and water filtration. Activated charcoal features a porous surface that traps impurities, making it essential in gas masks, air purifiers, water treatment, and emergency medicine to absorb ingested toxins from the stomach.<\/p><p>Carbon black\u2014a fine powder of elemental carbon\u2014serves as the dark pigment in printing inks, India ink, oil paints, laser printer toners, and automotive finishes, as well as a reinforcing filler in rubber tires. High-performance carbon fiber, produced by heating synthetic polyacrylonitrile (PAN) or polyester fibers until only carbon atoms remain, creates ultra-strong, lightweight composite materials with a higher tensile strength than steel. Carbon fiber composite structures are critical in aerospace, high-end automotive engineering, and space technology\u2014such as payload fairings and rocket casings engineered by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) for PSLV and GSLV rockets.<\/p>\n<div style=\"clear:both;\" class=\"\"><\/div>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">" } }, "N": { "symbol": "N", "name": "Nitrogen", "atomic": 7, "category": "diatomic nonmetal", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 7 (N)", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">Nitrogen<\/a><\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>N<\/b>, atomic number 7) is the invisible titan of Earth's air. As the lightest member of Group 15 on the periodic table (the pnictogens), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a> is a nonmetal that ranks as the seventh most abundant element in both the Milky Way galaxy and our Solar System. Under normal conditions, two <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a> atoms lock together in a nearly unbreakable chemical bond to form dinitrogen (N<sub>2<\/sub>)\u2014a colorless, odorless, and harmless gas that makes up roughly 78% of the air we breathe. Despite completely dominating our atmosphere, nitrogen is surprisingly rare in solid rocks and Earth's crust because its compounds vaporize and dissolve easily. Yet, without nitrogen, life could not exist: it forms the fundamental backbone of proteins, DNA, and the fertilizers that feed billions of people across the globe.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/2\/2d\/Nitrogen-glow.jpg", "atomic_mass": 14.007, "density": 1.251, "melt": 63.15, "boil": 77.355, "phase": "Gas", "discovered_by": "Daniel Rutherford", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p3", "electronegativity_pauling": 3.04, "electron_affinity": -6.8, "ionization_energies": [ 1402.3, 2856, 4578.1, 7475, 9444.9, 53266.6, 64360 ], "sections": { "History": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-left\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/584551aab23bdc952ef7ba9d56495f38.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"293\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"416\" data-file-height=\"487\" \/><figcaption>Daniel Rutherford, discoverer of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a><\/a><\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">Nitrogen<\/a><\/a> compounds have a long and rich history. As far back as antiquity, ammonium chloride was recorded by the Greek historian Herodotus. By the Middle Ages, alchemists routinely worked with powerful <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a> chemicals. They referred to nitric acid as <i>aqua fortis<\/i> (\"strong water\") and created <i>aqua regia<\/i> (\"royal water\")\u2014a fierce mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids famous for its unique ability to dissolve <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\">gold<\/a><\/a>, the king of metals.<\/p>\n<p>In ancient and medieval India, nitrogen compounds played a central role in metallurgy, medicine, and warfare. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">Potassium<\/a> nitrate was known in Sanskrit texts as <i>Suryakshar<\/i> or <i>Saurkshar<\/i> (and <i>Suvarchika<\/i>), and in regional dialects as <i>Shora<\/i> or <i>Shora Qalmi<\/i>. Seminal alchemical and medicinal treatises such as the 13th-century CE <i>Rasaratnasamuccaya<\/i> (authored by V\u0101gbha\u1e6da) and the <i>Rasarnava<\/i> document the extraction and purification of <i>Shora<\/i> from nitrate-rich soils for use in <i>Rasa\u015b\u0101stra<\/i> (Ayurvedic mineral alchemy). By the medieval era, the fertile plains of Bihar became the undisputed global hub for saltpetre production. Specialized communities known as the <i>Nuniahs<\/i> (or <i>Luniahs<\/i>) scraped, leached, and crystallized this \"white <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\">gold<\/a>.\" Because saltpetre was the indispensable oxidizer in gunpowder, control over Bihar's saltpetre trade sparked intense commercial and military conflicts between the Dutch, French, and British East India Companies throughout the 17th to 19th centuries.<\/p>\n<p>The formal discovery of elemental nitrogen took place in 1772 when Scottish physician Daniel Rutherford isolated it and called it \"noxious air.\" Rutherford recognized that this portion of air would not support combustion or animal life, though he distinguished it from Joseph Black's \"fixed air\" (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a><\/a> dioxide). Around the same time, scientists Carl Wilhelm Scheele, Henry Cavendish, and Joseph Priestley independently studied the gas, calling it \"burnt air\" or \"phlogisticated air.\" French chemist Antoine Lavoisier termed it \"mephitic air\" or <i>azote<\/i> (from the Greek <i>azotikos<\/i>, meaning \"no life\"), reflecting how animals suffocated in pure nitrogen. While English speakers preferred the name nitrogen, Lavoisier's root lives on in many languages\u2014such as French, Italian, Russian, German (<i>Stickstoff<\/i>, meaning \"suffocating matter\"), and Dutch (<i>stikstof<\/i>)\u2014as well as in chemical terms like hydrazine, azides, and the group name \"pnictogens\" (from Greek <i>pnigein<\/i>, \"to choke\").<\/p>\n<p>The modern English word <i>nitrogen<\/i> (1794) entered the language from the French <i>nitrog\u00e8ne<\/i>, coined in 1790 by French chemist Jean-Antoine Chaptal from <i>nitre<\/i> (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> nitrate) and the suffix <i>-g\u00e8ne<\/i> (\"producing\"), meaning \"nitric acid producer.\" (Historically, nitre was sometimes confused with Egyptian <i>natron<\/i>, a <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a> carbonate mineral containing no nitrogen). In 1910, Lord Rayleigh discovered that passing an electrical discharge through nitrogen gas created \"active nitrogen\"\u2014a reactive single-atom allotrope that produced a brilliant yellow cloud of light and reacted with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\">mercury<\/a><\/a> to yield explosive <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\">mercury<\/a> nitride.<\/p>\n<p>Modern Indian chemistry made groundbreaking contributions to nitrogen science through Acharya Prafulla Chandra Ray (1861\u20131944), widely celebrated as the \"Father of Indian Chemistry\" and dubbed the \"Master of Nitrites.\" In 1895\u20131896, Ray synthesized mercurous nitrite (Hg<sub>2<\/sub>(NO<sub>2<\/sub>)<sub>2<\/sub>), opening a whole new chapter in inorganic chemistry. In 1912, Ray achieved another major scientific milestone by isolating pure ammonium nitrite (NH<sub>4<\/sub>NO<sub>2<\/sub>), proving for the first time that it could be sublimed at 60\u00b0C without decomposing and disproving long-standing misconceptions in global chemistry. Ray also authored the landmark treatise <i>A History of Hindu Chemistry<\/i> (1902) and established Bengal Chemicals & Pharmaceuticals, India's first pharmaceutical company.<\/p>\n<p>For centuries, human access to nitrogen compounds was strictly limited to natural manure and saltpetre deposits. This changed dramatically in the early 20th century with industrial nitrogen fixation techniques like the Frank\u2013Caro process (1895\u20131899) and the Haber\u2013Bosch process (1908\u20131913). Today, synthetic nitrogen fertilizers produced via the Haber process sustain roughly half of global food production. Concurrently, the Ostwald process (1902) allowed large-scale conversion of synthetic ammonia into nitric acid, providing the essential raw material for industrial explosives during the World Wars of the 20th century.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">", "Isotopes": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">Main article: Isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a><\/a><\/div>\n<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-right\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/d4da30989f947cf5db8f2348f03da869.png\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"580\" height=\"121\" style=\"--mw-file-upright: 2.3\" class=\"mw-file-element mw-file-upright\" data-file-width=\"1552\" data-file-height=\"324\" \/><figcaption>Table of nuclides (Segr\u00e8 chart) from <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a><\/a> to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a><\/a> (including <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a><\/a>). Orange indicates proton emission (nuclides outside the proton drip line); pink for positron emission (inverse beta decay); black for stable nuclides; blue for electron emission (beta decay); and violet for neutron emission (nuclides outside the neutron drip line). Proton number increases going up the vertical axis and neutron number going to the right on the horizontal axis.<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p>Natural <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a> is composed of two stable isotopes: nitrogen-14 (<sup>14<\/sup>N) and nitrogen-15 (<sup>15<\/sup>N). The lighter <sup>14<\/sup>N isotope is overwhelmingly dominant, making up 99.634% of naturally occurring nitrogen, while the slightly heavier <sup>15<\/sup>N makes up the remaining 0.366%, resulting in an average atomic weight of approximately 14.007 u. Both isotopes are forged inside stars during the CNO (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">Carbon<\/a>-Nitrogen-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">Oxygen<\/a>) fusion cycle, but <sup>14<\/sup>N is far more abundant because its formation step involves slow proton capture, causing it to accumulate in greater quantities. Notably, <sup>14<\/sup>N is one of only five stable \"odd\u2013odd\" atomic nuclei in nature (containing an odd number of both protons and neutrons), alongside deuterium (<sup>2<\/sup>H), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a>-6 (<sup>6<\/sup>Li), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\">boron<\/a>-10 (<sup>10<\/sup>B), and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ta\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tantalum (Ta)\">tantalum<\/a>-180m (<sup>180m<\/sup>Ta).<\/p>\n<p>While the ratio of <sup>14<\/sup>N to <sup>15<\/sup>N remains remarkably constant in the open air, it varies in soils, rocks, and water due to isotopic fractionation caused by biological processes (such as nitrogen uptake, nitrification, and denitrification) and chemical evaporation. Biological reactions naturally favor the lighter <sup>14<\/sup>N isotope for chemical reactions, leaving the remaining soil or water substrate enriched in <sup>15<\/sup>N.<\/p>\n<p>In modern scientific research, isotope ratio analysis\u2014expressed as <i>\u03b4<\/i><sup>15<\/sup>N\u2014is a powerful tool across ecology, geology, and climate science. Indian researchers at premier institutions like the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR), and national oceanographic centers extensively analyze <i>\u03b4<\/i><sup>15<\/sup>N signatures in monsoonal ocean sediment cores, Himalayan ice proxies, and agricultural watersheds. These isotopic ratio studies help reconstruct ancient Indian monsoonal climate variations, trace agricultural nitrogen runoff in major river basins, and evaluate soil health across rural landscapes.<\/p>\n<p>The heavy isotope <sup>15<\/sup>N was discovered in 1929 by South African physicist S. M. Naud\u00e9. Because <sup>15<\/sup>N has a fractional nuclear spin of one-half, it produces sharp, narrow spectral lines in Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, making it exceptionally valuable for determining the intricate structures of proteins and complex organic molecules. In contrast, <sup>14<\/sup>N has an integer nuclear spin of one, creating an electric quadrupole moment that causes broader, less defined NMR spectra. Although <sup>15<\/sup>N NMR faces sensitivity challenges due to its low natural abundance (0.366%) and low gyromagnetic ratio (only 10.14% that of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a><\/a>-1, making <sup>1<\/sup>H signal-to-noise about 300 times stronger), scientists overcome this by enriching samples with <sup>15<\/sup>N via chemical exchange or fractional distillation. Crucially, <sup>15<\/sup>N-labeled compounds do not easily swap their nitrogen atoms with the surrounding air, keeping labeled biological samples stable during experiments.<\/p>\n<p>Beyond its two stable forms, scientists have artificially created 13 radioactive isotopes of nitrogen, ranging from <sup>9<\/sup>N to <sup>23<\/sup>N. Most of these radioisotopes decay in a fraction of a second, but nitrogen-13 (<sup>13<\/sup>N) has a half-life of about 10 minutes. This makes <sup>13<\/sup>N indispensable in medicine for Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scanning, where it is generated on-site using medical cyclotrons (by bombarding <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a>-16 with protons) to map blood flow and metabolic activity in real time.<\/p>\n<p>In nuclear power engineering, nitrogen-16 (<sup>16<\/sup>N) plays a critical safety role. Formed inside pressurized and boiling water nuclear reactors when fast neutrons hit <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a>-16 in cooling water via an (n,p) reaction, <sup>16<\/sup>N has a brief half-life of 7.1 seconds. However, as it decays back to <sup>16<\/sup>O, it emits intensely powerful gamma rays (5 to 7 MeV). This requires heavy radiation shielding around primary cooling pipes during reactor operation and acts as an ultra-sensitive, real-time indicator for detecting tiny leaks between primary coolant pipes and secondary steam cycles.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Occurrence": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-right\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/8ff0c78907028408a980966c2edd18ad.png\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"450\" height=\"338\" style=\"--mw-file-upright: 1.8\" class=\"mw-file-element mw-file-upright\" data-file-width=\"800\" data-file-height=\"600\" \/><figcaption>Schematic representation of the flow of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a><\/a> compounds through a land environment<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">See also: <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">Nitrogen<\/a><\/a> cycle<\/div>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">Nitrogen<\/a><\/a> is the most abundant uncombined element on Earth, making up 78.1% of our atmosphere by volume (75.5% by mass)\u2014a colossal reservoir weighing roughly 3.89 million gigatonnes (3.89\u00d710<sup>18<\/sup> kg). In contrast, nitrogen is relatively sparse in Earth's solid crust, averaging just 19 parts per million (similar in abundance to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Nb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Niobium (Nb)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Nb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Niobium (Nb)\">niobium<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">gallium<\/a><\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a><\/a>). Natural nitrate minerals are rare, existing primarily as nitre (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> nitrate, saltpetre) and soda nitre (Chilean saltpetre, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a> nitrate), though mining these minerals was largely rendered obsolete by synthetic chemical processes in the 1920s.<\/p>\n<p>Earth's biosphere relies on a continuous global nitrogen cycle. Although nitrogen gas is all around us, plants cannot absorb atmospheric N<sub>2<\/sub> directly because its double-atom triple bond is extremely tough to break. To become biologically active, nitrogen must be \"fixed\" into reactive compounds like ammonia. Nature accomplishes this through high-energy lightning strikes\u2014which combine nitrogen and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> into nitrogen oxides\u2014and primarily through specialized diazotrophic soil bacteria that use enzymes called nitrogenases.<\/p>\n<p>In traditional Indian farming practices, sustainable nitrogen fixation has been practiced for millennia through legume crop rotation (such as growing pulses like chickpea, pigeon pea\/arhar, and lentils). These crops host symbiotic <i>Rhizobium<\/i> bacteria in their root nodules, naturally enriching the soil with bio-available nitrogen. Today, the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) promotes bio-fertilizers to harness these natural microbial allies.<\/p>\n<p>Once fixed, plants absorb ammonia and nitrogen compounds to synthesize essential proteins. Animals eat these plants to construct their own proteins and eventually excrete nitrogenous waste (such as urea and uric acid). When organisms die, decomposers break down their biological matter, releasing nitrogen back into the environment where denitrifying bacteria complete the cycle by converting nitrates back into N<sub>2<\/sub> gas.<\/p>\n<p>However, human industrial nitrogen fixation (via synthetic urea fertilizers) now rivals natural biological fixation.
