Overuse of chemical nitrogen fertilizers can cause excessive agricultural runoff into rivers and lakes, triggering eutrophication and severe aquatic \"dead zones\" where <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> depletion suffocates fish. Furthermore, denitrification releases nitrous oxide (N<sub>2<\/sub>O)\u2014a greenhouse gas nearly 300 times more potent than <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> dioxide that also degrades the atmospheric ozone layer. To solve this ecological challenge in Indian agriculture, scientists at IFFCO developed revolutionary <b>Liquid Nano Urea<\/b>. By delivering nanoscale nitrogen particles directly onto crop leaves via foliar spray, Nano Urea boosts nutrient uptake efficiency, drastically reducing chemical leaching into groundwater and major river systems like the Ganga and Yamuna.<\/p>\n<p>Nitrogen chemistry also governs fascinating animal adaptations. Deep-sea saltwater fish produce large amounts of trimethylamine oxide to balance osmotic pressure under intense ocean depth; its conversion into dimethylamine creates the characteristic scent of aging seafood. In mammals, tiny amounts of free-radical nitric oxide (NO) serve as a crucial chemical messenger that relaxes blood vessels and regulates blood circulation. As proteins decay after death, biological enzymes break down amino acids (like ornithine and lysine) into long-chain nitrogen-containing amines called putrescine and cadaverine, which produce the characteristic odor of biological decay.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">", "Applications": "<p>Industrial applications of elemental <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a><\/a> are vast and essential to modern manufacturing and technology. Globally, about two-thirds (2\/3) of manufactured <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a> gas is sold in gaseous form, while the remaining one-third (1\/3) is distributed as a super-chilled liquid.<\/p>\n<p>As a gas, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a>'s unreactive, inert nature makes it the ultimate shield against fire, explosion, and decay. Industrial facilities use nitrogen gas to purge fuel tanks, blanket sensitive chemical reactions, and protect delicate microchips during semiconductor fabrication. In the food industry, modified atmosphere packaging (MAP) replaces reactive <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> gas with pure nitrogen in snack bags and food containers, preventing food spoilage, oil rancidity, and stale textures without artificial preservatives.<\/p>\n<p>In its liquid state\u2014boiling at a frigid \u2212196\u00b0C (77.36 K)\u2014liquid nitrogen (LN<sub>2<\/sub>) is a powerhouse of cryogenics. It is widely used for flash-freezing foods, medical cryosurgery (removing skin lesions), and cryo-preserving biological materials such as blood, stem cells, reproductive cells, and genetic banks. Liquid nitrogen also cools high-field superconducting electromagnets used in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) body scanners and particle physics laboratories.<\/p>\n<p>In India's high-tech and space sectors, nitrogen plays an indispensable role. The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) uses massive liquid nitrogen systems at facilities like the UR Rao Satellite Centre (URSC) in Bengaluru and the Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC) in Sriharikota. ISRO employs liquid nitrogen inside giant thermal vacuum chambers to simulate the brutal cryogenic cold of outer space, rigorously testing Indian satellites and rocket engine systems before blastoff. On the agricultural and industrial front, massive fertilizer complexes across India (such as IFFCO, KRIBHCO, and National Fertilizers Limited) process atmospheric nitrogen into millions of tonnes of urea to guarantee food security for 1.4 billion people. Looking to the future, under the National Green <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">Hydrogen<\/a> Mission, India is pioneering <b>Green Ammonia<\/b> production\u2014using solar and wind energy to harvest atmospheric nitrogen and convert it into zero-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> fertilizers and green maritime fuels.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">" } }, "O": { "symbol": "O", "name": "Oxygen", "atomic": 8, "category": "diatomic nonmetal", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 8 (O)", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">Oxygen<\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>O<\/b>, atomic number 8) is the breath of life itself! Sitting in Group 16 (the chalcogens) of the periodic table, this non-metallic gas is famously reactive, eagerly pairing up with almost every other element to form compounds called oxides. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">Oxygen<\/a> is the most abundant element in Earth's crust, making up nearly half (49.2%) of its total weight in the form of water, silicates, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> dioxide, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> ores. Across the cosmos, it reigns as the third most abundant element in the universe, right after <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">helium<\/a>. On Earth, it makes up about 20.8% of the air we breathe. In ancient Indian philosophy, this invisible, life-giving gas was described as <i>Pranavayu<\/i> (\u092a\u094d\u0930\u093e\u0923\u0935\u093e\u092f\u0941)\u2014the vital breath that kindles our internal metabolic fire and sustains every living soul.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/a\/a0\/Liquid_oxygen_in_a_beaker_%28cropped_and_retouched%29.jpg", "atomic_mass": 15.999, "density": 1.429, "melt": 54.36, "boil": 90.188, "phase": "Gas", "discovered_by": "Carl Wilhelm Scheele", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p4", "electronegativity_pauling": 3.44, "electron_affinity": 140.976, "ionization_energies": [ 1313.9, 3388.3, 5300.5, 7469.2, 10989.5, 13326.5, 71330, 84078 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">Oxygen<\/a> is a chemical powerhouse. Because its outer shell needs just two more electrons to become completely stable, an <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> atom will aggressively react with metals, nonmetals, and organic molecules alike\u2014a process known as oxidation. This intense reactivity is why <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> rusts, wood burns, and our bodies are able to extract energy from the food we eat. In its most common atmospheric form, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> atoms link up in pairs to create diatomic oxygen gas (O<sub>2<\/sub>). While pure oxygen gas is completely colorless, odorless, and tasteless at room temperature, it transforms into a striking, light sky-blue substance when cooled into a liquid or frozen into a solid!<\/p><p>Oxygen also exists in another famous form called <b>ozone<\/b> (O<sub>3<\/sub>), which consists of three oxygen atoms bonded together. While ozone gas high up in the stratosphere forms a crucial protective shield that blocks harmful solar ultraviolet radiation, oxygen molecules at high altitudes exhibit fascinating quantum spectroscopy. UV absorption in the Herzberg continuum and Schumann\u2013Runge bands splits O<sub>2<\/sub> into atomic oxygen, driving middle-atmosphere chemistry and high-altitude airglow, while excited singlet molecular oxygen can emit a vibrant red chemiluminescent glow in solution.<\/p>", "Physical properties": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">Oxygen<\/a> possesses several surprising physical traits that shape life on Earth. At standard atmospheric pressure, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> gas condenses into a liquid at a chilly 90.20 K (\u2212182.95 \u00b0C or \u2212297.31 \u00b0F) and freezes solid at 54.36 K (\u2212218.79 \u00b0C or \u2212361.82 \u00b0F). High-purity liquid <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> is typically harvested through the fractional distillation of liquefied air or by cooling air with liquid <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a>. In both liquid and solid states, oxygen displays a faint, beautiful sky-blue hue. This color comes from the molecule absorbing light in the red spectrum\u2014unlike the blue sky above us, which gets its color from Rayleigh scattering of blue sunlight!<\/p><p>Oxygen also dissolves in water much better than <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a> gas does. In air-water equilibrium, there is roughly 1 molecule of dissolved oxygen for every 2 molecules of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a> (a 1:2 ratio), compared to the 1:4 ratio in the atmosphere. Water solubility is strongly temperature-dependent: cold water holds almost twice as much oxygen (14.6 mg\/L at 0 \u00b0C) as warm water (7.6 mg\/L at 20 \u00b0C). At standard sea-level pressure (25 \u00b0C), freshwater holds about 6.04 mL of oxygen per liter, while denser seawater holds 4.95 mL\/L. When chilled to 5 \u00b0C, freshwater solubility jumps by 50% to 9.00 mL\/L, and seawater solubility increases by 45% to 7.20 mL\/L. Liquid oxygen is also extremely reactive and must be kept strictly segregated from flammable materials to prevent explosive combustion.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">Oxygen<\/a> is widespread throughout the universe and our planet. In outer space, it is the third most abundant element by mass\u2014making up roughly 10,400 parts per million of the Milky Way Galaxy and about 0.9% of our Sun's total mass. On Earth, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> is everywhere: it constitutes 88.8% of the mass of the oceans and 49.2% of Earth's solid crust, locked inside quartz, clays, and mineral oxides. In our atmosphere, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> gas accounts for 20.8% of air by volume and 23.1% by mass, totaling an astounding 1 quadrillion (10<sup>15<\/sup>) tonnes!<\/p><p>Earth's high concentration of atmospheric oxygen is unique in the Solar System. Neighboring planets like Mars (which has only 0.1% O<sub>2<\/sub>) and Venus have virtually no free oxygen gas, as theirs is produced only by solar UV rays breaking down <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> dioxide. Earth owes its oxygen abundance to the <b>oxygen cycle<\/b>, driven by plant photosynthesis. Photosynthesis constantly replenishes oxygen, while animal respiration, organic decay, and combustion consume it. Because cold water retains more dissolved oxygen, Earth's polar oceans support thriving, high-density marine ecosystems. Scientists measure water quality using <i>Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD)<\/i> to ensure aquatic life has enough oxygen. However, global atmospheric oxygen levels are slightly dropping due to fossil fuel burning, and warming tropical oceans face deoxygenation risks. Locally, the lush tropical rainforests of India's <b>Western Ghats<\/b> serve as a massive natural 'oxygen factory,' generating vital oxygen and preserving river ecosystems across the subcontinent.<\/p>", "History": "<p>The story of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> bridges ancient philosophy and modern science. Centuries before modern chemistry, ancient Indian thinkers explored the vital nature of air. In classical Ayurvedic texts like the <i>Charaka Samhita<\/i>, <i>Sushruta Samhita<\/i>, and <i>Sharangadhara Samhita<\/i>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> was conceptualized as <b>Prana Vayu<\/b> (\u092a\u094d\u0930\u093e\u0923\u0935\u093e\u092f\u0941)\u2014the life-giving breath drawn into the chest and head to nourish the body's tissues (<i>dhatus<\/i>) and kindle <i>Jatharagni<\/i> (the internal metabolic fire). Ancient texts also recognized <i>Vyana Vayu<\/i> as the internal force circulating this life energy throughout the bloodstream.<\/p><p>In Western chemistry, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> was independently isolated in the 1770s by Swedish-German apothecary <b>Carl Wilhelm Scheele<\/b> (who called it 'fire air') and British scientist <b>Joseph Priestley<\/b> (who called it 'dephlogisticated air'). In 1777, French chemist <b>Antoine Lavoisier<\/b> correctly identified it as a distinct chemical element that powers combustion and respiration. Lavoisier coined the name <b>Oxygen<\/b> from the Greek words <i>oxys<\/i> (sharp or acid) and <i>genes<\/i> (creator or producer), incorrectly believing it was an essential component of all acids. In modern Hindi and Sanskrit science, it is also referred to as <i>Jaranada<\/i> (\u091c\u0930\u093e\u0923\u0926\u093e) or <i>Jaranavayu<\/i> (combustion-supporting air).<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>In nature, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> exists as three stable isotopes: <b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">Oxygen<\/a>-16<\/b> (<sup>16<\/sup>O), <b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">Oxygen<\/a>-17<\/b> (<sup>17<\/sup>O), and <b>Oxygen-18<\/b> (<sup>18<\/sup>O). Oxygen-16 is by far the most abundant, making up an overwhelming 99.76% of all natural oxygen on Earth. It is forged deep inside massive stars during nuclear fusion through the 'triple-alpha process' and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> burning. Oxygen-17 (0.04%) and Oxygen-18 (0.20%) are much rarer but incredibly valuable to science.<\/p><p>Scientists have also produced 10 short-lived radioactive isotopes of oxygen in laboratories, ranging from Oxygen-11 to Oxygen-26, all of which decay in fractions of a second. The stable isotopes <sup>16<\/sup>O and <sup>18<\/sup>O play a starring role in climate science: because water molecules containing lighter <sup>16<\/sup>O evaporate more easily than those with heavier <sup>18<\/sup>O, climate scientists measure the ratio of these isotopes trapped in ancient polar ice cores and ocean sediments to reconstruct Earth's temperature history over hundreds of thousands of years!<\/p>", "Applications": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">Oxygen<\/a> is indispensable to modern industry, medicine, and space exploration. Industrially, the vast majority of commercial <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> is used in steelmaking, where high-purity <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> is blasted into molten <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> to burn away <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> impurities. It is also essential for manufacturing chemicals like ethylene oxide, oxy-acetylene welding of metals, and rocket propulsion, where liquid oxygen (LOX) acts as the powerful oxidizer that launches space rockets.<\/p><p>In medicine, oxygen is the ultimate life-saver. India has made groundbreaking technological contributions to oxygen production and deployment. During healthcare emergencies, organizations like <b>ISRO<\/b> (Indian Space Research Organisation) developed <b>SHWAAS<\/b> (Space Hospital-based Oxygen Aided System), an indigenous medical oxygen concentrator delivering >95% pure oxygen, alongside <b>PRANA<\/b> ventilators. India's Defence Research and Development Organisation (<b>DRDO<\/b>) adapted its high-altitude <b>On-Board Oxygen Generation System (OBOGS)<\/b>\u2014originally built for <b>LCA Tejas<\/b> fighter jets\u2014into heavy-duty hospital Medical Oxygen Plants (MOPs). DRDO's DIPAS institute also created specialized oxygen-enriched chambers for soldiers stationed at the freezing, low-oxygen heights of the <b>Siachen Glacier<\/b>. CSIR laboratories engineered Pressure Vacuum Swing Adsorption (PVSA) systems for local hospitals, while <b>Indian Railways<\/b> operated the historic <b>'Oxygen Express'<\/b> network\u2014running cryogenic tank trains along fast-tracked 'Green Corridors' to deliver tens of thousands of tonnes of Liquid Medical Oxygen across the nation.<\/p>" } }, "F": { "symbol": "F", "name": "Fluorine", "atomic": 9, "category": "diatomic nonmetal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">Fluorine<\/a><\/a> (symbol <strong>F<\/strong>, atomic number 9) is the lightest of the halogens and holds the title as the most chemically reactive and electronegative element on the periodic table. At standard conditions, it exists as an extremely toxic, pale yellow-green diatomic gas (F<sub>2<\/sub>). Because of its relentless appetite for electrons, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a> reacts violently with almost all other elements\u2014including water, glass, metals, and even noble gases like <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Xe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Xenon (Xe)\">xenon<\/a>. While pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a> gas is dangerous, its compounds play essential roles in modern society, ranging from tooth-protecting fluoride in toothpaste to non-stick cookware and life-saving pharmaceuticals.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/2\/2c\/Fluoro_liquido_a_-196%C2%B0C_1.jpg", "atomic_mass": 18.9984031636, "density": 1.696, "melt": 53.48, "boil": 85.03, "phase": "Gas", "discovered_by": "Andr\u00e9-Marie Amp\u00e8re", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p5", "electronegativity_pauling": 3.98, "electron_affinity": 328.1649, "ionization_energies": [ 1681, 3374.2, 6050.4, 8407.7, 11022.7, 15164.1, 17868, 92038.1, 106434.3 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">Fluorine<\/a> is a fierce chemical performer with an electron configuration of [He] 2s<sup>2<\/sup> 2p<sup>5<\/sup>. Needing only one additional electron to complete its outer valence shell, it attracts electrons more strongly than any other element, possessing a top-of-the-scale Pauling electronegativity of 3.98. In its elemental form, two <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a> atoms pair up into a diatomic gas molecule (F<sub>2<\/sub>) with a pale yellow tint and a pungent, choking smell. The bond holding F<sub>2<\/sub> together is surprisingly weak, while the bonds <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a> forms with other elements are exceptionally strong. As a result, fluorine gas reacts rapidly and exothermically upon contact with almost all organic materials, metals, and ceramics.<\/p>", "Physical properties": "<p>At standard temperature and pressure, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a> gas has a density of 1.696 g\/L, making it slightly denser than air. When cooled to an extreme \u2212188.12 \u00b0C (85.03 K), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a> condenses into a bright yellow liquid. Upon further cooling to \u2212219.67 \u00b0C (53.48 K), it freezes into a pale yellow solid. Below \u2212227.6 \u00b0C, solid <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a> shifts between two crystal structure phases (alpha and beta forms). Fluorine has an electron affinity of 328.16 kJ\/mol and extremely high ionization energies, beginning at 1,681 kJ\/mol for the first electron and reaching over 106,434 kJ\/mol for its inner shell electrons.<\/p>", "Chemical properties": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">Fluorine<\/a>'s unmatched electronegativity allows it to form compounds with almost every element, including heavy noble gases such as <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Xe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Xenon (Xe)\">xenon<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Kr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Krypton (Kr)\">krypton<\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Rn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Radon (Rn)\">radon<\/a>. It reacts explosively with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> gas even in pitch darkness at sub-zero temperatures. Water burns in a stream of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a> gas, producing hydrofluoric acid (HF) and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> gas or ozone. Despite its destructive nature toward most metals, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a> can be safely stored in containers made of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a>, or steel because the initial reaction creates a microscopic, protective layer of metal fluoride on the container's inner surface (passivation) that halts further corrosion.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Natural <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a> consists entirely of a single stable isotope, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a>-19 (<sup>19<\/sup>F). With a nuclear spin of 1\/2 and a exceptionally high magnetogyric ratio, <sup>19<\/sup>F is extremely sensitive to magnetic fields, making it an invaluable tool in Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and medical magnetic imaging.<\/p><p>Scientists have synthesized 18 radioactive isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a> with mass numbers ranging from <sup>13<\/sup>F to <sup>31<\/sup>F. Among these, fluorine-18 (<sup>18<\/sup>F) is by far the most important, with a half-life of 109.734 minutes. Fluorine-18 decays via positron emission (\u03b2<sup>+<\/sup>) and electron capture into <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a>-18, making it a crucial radiotracer in Positron Emission Tomography (PET) medical imaging scans to detect cancers and study brain function. In nature, trace amounts of <sup>18<\/sup>F are continuously produced in the atmosphere when cosmic rays hit <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a> atoms, or through natural proton collisions with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> (<sup>18<\/sup>O + p \u2192 <sup>18<\/sup>F + n). Synthetic radioisotopes lighter than <sup>19<\/sup>F decay by proton emission or \u03b2<sup>+<\/sup> decay (such as <sup>17<\/sup>F), while those heavier than <sup>19<\/sup>F undergo \u03b2<sup>\u2212<\/sup> decay, with the heaviest isotopes emitting delayed neutrons. Two nuclear isomers, <sup>18m<\/sup>F (half-life of 162 nanoseconds) and <sup>26m<\/sup>F (half-life of 2.2 milliseconds), have also been documented.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>Because <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a> is so fiercely reactive, it never occurs as a free element in nature. Instead, it ranks as the 24th most abundant element in the Earth's crust, bound tightly within minerals such as fluorite or fluorspar (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a> fluoride, CaF<sub>2<\/sub>), cryolite (Na<sub>3<\/sub>AlF<sub>6<\/sub>), and fluorapatite.<\/p><p>India boasts significant geological deposits of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a>-bearing minerals. The most famous is the <strong>Ambadungar Carbonatite Complex<\/strong> in the Chhota Udepur district of Gujarat. Created around 65 million years ago by alkaline-carbonatite volcanic activity linked to the Deccan Traps, Ambadungar contains extensive reserves of vibrant purple, green, and yellow fluorite crystals. Managed by the Gujarat Mineral Development Corporation (GMDC), fluorspar from Ambadungar has historically served as an indispensable metallurgical flux in Indian steel plants and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a> refineries. Notable occurrences of fluorite are also found in the rocks of Rajasthan (such as the Jalore region) and Maharashtra (Dongargaon).<\/p>", "History": "<p>The mineral fluorspar has been utilized since antiquity; 16th-century German mineralogist Georgius Agricola described its ability to act as a \"flux\" that melted stubborn metal ores. In 1810, French scientist Andr\u00e9-Marie Amp\u00e8re recognized that fluorspar contained a new element analogous to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a> and coined the name \"<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a>.\"<\/p><p>However, isolating elemental <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a> proved to be one of the most hazardous endeavors in chemical history. Early researchers\u2014dubbed the \"<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a> martyrs\"\u2014suffered blindness, severe burns, and fatal poisoning from toxic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> fluoride and fluorine gas. The mystery was finally conquered in 1886 by French chemist Henri Moissan, who successfully isolated fluorine gas by electrolyzing a cold liquid solution of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> fluoride in anhydrous liquid <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> fluoride using <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pt\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Platinum (Pt)\">platinum<\/a> electrodes. Moissan's groundbreaking feat earned him the 1906 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.<\/p>", "Biological role": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">Fluorine<\/a> is not an essential element for mammalian life, but small amounts of fluoride ions significantly benefit skeletal and dental health. Fluoride incorporates into teeth to turn hydroxyapatite enamel into fluorapatite, which is far more resistant to decay caused by acid-producing mouth bacteria. Organofluorine compounds also exist naturally in nature; plants such as <em>Gastrolobium<\/em> produce fluoroacetate to deter herbivores, while other organisms produce fluoroacetone and 2-fluorocitrate. In 2002, scientists discovered the enzyme 5'-fluoro-5'-deoxyadenosine synthase, which enables bacteria to forge <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a>-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a> bonds naturally.<\/p><p>However, excessive intake of fluoride leads to a serious health condition known as <strong>fluorosis<\/strong>, causing enamel mottling (dental fluorosis) and painful bone calcification (skeletal fluorosis). Over 17 states in India\u2014including Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan, and Gujarat\u2014fall within a global natural \"fluoride belt,\" where groundwater leaching through <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a>-rich rocks affects over 60 million people.<\/p><p>To combat this severe public health challenge, Indian scientists achieved a major global breakthrough in 1974: the creation of the <strong>Nalgonda Technique<\/strong> by the National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (NEERI) in Nagpur. Named after the severely affected Nalgonda district in Telangana, this ingenious, low-cost defluoridation method uses sequential treatment with alum, lime, and bleaching powder to remove toxic excess fluoride from drinking water, saving communities across India and developing nations worldwide.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">Fluorine<\/a> is a cornerstone of modern chemical technology and manufacturing:<\/p><ul><li><strong>Fluoropolymers:<\/strong> Strong <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a>-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a> bonds create non-stick, heat-resistant materials like Teflon (polytetrafluoroethylene or PTFE), used in cookware, waterproof Gore-Tex fabric, and industrial seals.<\/li><li><strong>Pharmaceuticals:<\/strong> Substituting <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a> into drug molecules increases their stability and biological absorption. Over 20% of commercial pharmaceuticals\u2014including antibiotics, antidepressants, and anti-cancer drugs\u2014contain fluorine.<\/li><li><strong>Electronics & Semiconductors:<\/strong> High-purity fluorine gas and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a> trifluoride (NF<sub>3<\/sub>) are essential for plasma etching and cleaning semiconductor wafers during <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a> microchip manufacturing.<\/li><li><strong>Nuclear & Energy:<\/strong> <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/U\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Uranium (U)\">Uranium<\/a> enrichment relies on volatile <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/U\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Uranium (U)\">uranium<\/a> hexafluoride (UF<sub>6<\/sub>) gas to separate <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/U\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Uranium (U)\">uranium<\/a> isotopes for nuclear reactors. Advanced molten-salt nuclear reactors also utilize liquid fluoride salts.<\/li><li><strong>Refrigeration:<\/strong> Modern hydrofluoroolefins (HFOs) and hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) serve as eco-friendly refrigerants with low ozone depletion potential.<\/li><\/ul>" } }, "Ne": { "symbol": "Ne", "name": "Neon", "atomic": 10, "category": "noble gas", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\">Neon<\/a><\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>Ne<\/b>, atomic number 10) is a famous noble gas best known for its vivid, electric red-orange glow. Colorless, odorless, and completely tasteless under ordinary conditions, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\">neon<\/a> is a monatomic gas that is about two-thirds as dense as air. Positioned in Group 18 of the periodic table, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\">neon<\/a> is the fifth most abundant element in the universe, forged deep inside giant stars. Yet on Earth, it is extraordinarily rare, making up just 18.2 parts per million of our atmosphere. Known to theoretical chemists as the most inert and chemically aloof of all elements, neon refuses to form stable compounds under any known conditions. From illuminating iconic city skylines with glowing signage to driving ultra-precise microchip lasers and deep-space rock dating, neon is a tiny atom with a brilliant impact.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/f\/f8\/Neon-glow.jpg", "atomic_mass": 20.17976, "density": 0.9002, "melt": 24.56, "boil": 27.104, "phase": "Gas", "discovered_by": "Morris Travers", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6", "electronegativity_pauling": null, "electron_affinity": -116, "ionization_energies": [ 2080.7, 3952.3, 6122, 9371, 12177, 15238, 19999, 23069.5, 115379.5, 131432 ], "sections": { "History": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\">Neon<\/a><\/a> was discovered in London in June 1898 by British chemists Sir William Ramsay and Morris Travers. The duo isolated it by chilling samples of atmospheric air until it turned into a liquid, then carefully warming the liquid to capture different gases as they boiled off at distinct temperatures. After separating <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a><\/a>, and the newly found <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Kr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Krypton (Kr)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Kr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Krypton (Kr)\">krypton<\/a><\/a>, they electrified the remaining trapped gas inside a vacuum tube. Immediately, the gas burst into an unforgettably intense, brilliant crimson-red light. Travers later fondly recalled, <i>\"the blaze of crimson light from the tube told its own story and was a sight to dwell upon and never forget.\"<\/i> Ramsay's young son suggested naming the element \"<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\">neon<\/a>,\" derived from <i>neos<\/i>, the Greek word for \"new\" (analogous to the Latin <i>novum<\/i>). During their search, the team also briefly reported a gas named <i>metargon<\/i>, which was later revealed to be <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a> mixed with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a><\/a> monoxide, before going on to discover <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Xe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Xenon (Xe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Xe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Xenon (Xe)\">xenon<\/a><\/a> in September 1898.<\/p>\n<p>Co-discoverer Morris Travers shares a momentous historical link with India. In 1906, known in scientific circles as \"Rare Gas Travers,\" he moved to India to serve as the founding Director of the prestigious Indian Institute of Science (IISc) in Bangalore. Working alongside the vision of industrialist Jamsetji Tata and the Maharaja of Mysore, Travers spent nearly a decade building IISc's original campus, setting up its premier chemistry laboratories, and establishing the groundwork for modern scientific and cryogenic research in India.<\/p>\n<p>Because <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\">neon<\/a> is so sparse in the atmosphere, it could not be immediately used for lighting like earlier <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a>-filled Moore tubes. However, in 1902, French engineer Georges Claude began producing industrial quantities of neon as a byproduct of his air-liquefaction company, Air Liquide. Claude patented the sealed neon light tube in December 1910. While his attempt to sell neon for home indoor lighting failed because people found the intense red color overwhelming, his business partner realized its potential for eye-catching outdoor advertising in 1912. Neon signs debuted in the United States in 1923 when a Packard car dealership in Los Angeles bought two glowing signs. The mesmerizing red glow captured the public imagination, transforming 20th-century cityscapes into dazzling displays of \"electro-graphic architecture.\"<\/p>\n<p>Neon also played a monumental role in unveiling the hidden structure of atoms. In 1913, legendary physicist J. J. Thomson funneled ionized neon beams through electric and magnetic fields toward a photographic plate. Instead of a single curve, he observed two distinct parabolic patches of light. Thomson realized that neon gas contained atoms of two different masses\u2014specifically neon-20 and neon-22. This historic experiment provided the very first evidence that stable chemical elements exist as different isotopes, and Thomson's setup served as the direct forerunner to the modern mass spectrometer.<\/p>", "Characteristics": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\">Neon<\/a><\/a> is the second-lightest noble gas, positioned between <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">helium<\/a><\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a><\/a>. In its natural state, it is completely colorless, odorless, and non-toxic. However, when placed inside an evacuated tube and excited by an electric voltage, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\">neon<\/a> plasma produces the most intense light discharge of all noble gases. To the human eye, this light glows a vivid red-orange due to strong emission lines in that region, though spectroscopic analysis reveals a hidden green emission line buried within its spectrum.<\/p>\n<p>From a chemical standpoint, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\">neon<\/a> holds the title of the least reactive element in the entire periodic table. While <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">helium<\/a> has a higher ionization energy, quantum mechanical calculations show that <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">helium<\/a> can form exotic species under extreme pressures\u2014such as the helium hydride ion (HeH\u207a), solid Na\u2082He, and theoretical helium hydride fluoride (HHeF). By contrast, equivalent neon molecules like HNeF are completely unbound and unstable. While chemists have theoretically proposed a complex neon anion [B\u2081\u2082(CN)\u2081\u2081Ne]\u207b, no stable neutral or covalent neon compound has ever been synthesized or observed in a laboratory under any temperature or pressure. Neon stands alone as the only noble gas with zero confirmed chemical compounds.<\/p>\n<p>In cryogenic applications, liquid neon is an extraordinary refrigerant. On a volume basis, liquid neon has over 40 times the cooling capacity of liquid helium and three times that of liquid <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a><\/a>. Because it boils at 27.104 K (\u2212246.046 \u00b0C) and melts at 24.56 K (\u2212248.59 \u00b0C), liquid neon provides intense cooling power in a compact range where liquid helium would be far more expensive and prone to rapid evaporation.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\">Neon<\/a><\/a> possesses three stable natural isotopes: <sup>20<\/sup>Ne (90.48%), <sup>21<\/sup>Ne (0.27%), and <sup>22<\/sup>Ne (9.25%). The vast majority of <sup>20<\/sup>Ne is primordial material forged in ancient stars. By contrast, <sup>21<\/sup>Ne and <sup>22<\/sup>Ne are partly primordial and partly \"nucleogenic,\" created inside rocks when alpha particles and neutrons from decaying <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/U\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Uranium (U)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/U\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Uranium (U)\">uranium<\/a><\/a> collide with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a><\/a> atoms (<sup>24<\/sup>Mg and <sup>25<\/sup>Mg). Because of this reaction, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/U\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Uranium (U)\">uranium<\/a>-rich rocks like granites exhibit lower <sup>20<\/sup>Ne\/<sup>22<\/sup>Ne ratios and elevated <sup>21<\/sup>Ne\/<sup>22<\/sup>Ne signatures.<\/p>\n<p>High-energy cosmic rays hitting exposed surface rocks also create \"cosmogenic\" <sup>21<\/sup>Ne through spallation reactions on <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a><\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a> atoms. In India, planetary scientists at the Physical Research Laboratory (PRL) in Ahmedabad utilize high-precision Noble Gas Mass Spectrometry to measure cosmogenic <sup>21<\/sup>Ne trapped inside meteorites that fall across the Indian subcontinent (such as the Kamargaon and Rantila meteorites). By measuring these <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\">neon<\/a> isotopes, PRL researchers accurately calculate the cosmic ray exposure (CRE) age of the meteorites, revealing how many millions of years they drifted through open space before crashing to Earth.<\/p>\n<p>Isotopic signatures also offer clues about the solar system's origins. Solar wind <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\">neon<\/a> is exceptionally rich in <sup>20<\/sup>Ne compared to Earth sources. Because volcanic gases and deep mantle diamonds on Earth are also enriched in <sup>20<\/sup>Ne, geologists suspect that trapped primordial solar gas was locked inside Earth's deep interior during its formation. Except for extremely rare cluster decays of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Th\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Thorium (Th)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Th\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Thorium (Th)\">thorium<\/a><\/a>-228 that produce <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a>-20 (which decays into <sup>20<\/sup>Ne), <sup>20<\/sup>Ne is not produced by radioactive decay, making its distribution across Earth a subject of lively scientific study.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\">Neon<\/a><\/a> is created in massive stars (greater than 8 solar masses) during the <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a>-burning phase of stellar evolution. When core temperatures exceed 500 million kelvins (500 megakelvins), two <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a><\/a> nuclei fuse together to produce <sup>20<\/sup>Ne. Across the cosmos, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\">neon<\/a> is the fifth most abundant chemical element by mass\u2014behind <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">helium<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a>\u2014making up about 1 part in 750 of all universal mass (and 1 part in 600 in the Sun).<\/p>\n<p>Despite its cosmic abundance, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\">neon<\/a> is surprisingly scarce on Earth, comprising only 18.2 parts per million (1 in 55,000) of Earth's atmosphere by volume, or 1 part in 79,000 by mass. Because neon is a light, single-atom gas with high vapor pressure at low temperatures, most of the primordial neon escaped into space while the warm, solid Earth was forming. However, because a single neon atom is lighter than diatomic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a><\/a> (N\u2082) and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> (O\u2082) molecules, a balloon filled with neon will float in air, though more slowly than a <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">helium<\/a> balloon.<\/p>\n<p>Beyond Earth, NASA's LADEE spacecraft confirmed in August 2015 that neon exists in the thin exosphere of the Moon. Meanwhile, the Galileo probe revealed that Jupiter's upper atmosphere is strangely depleted of neon (only 1 part in 6,000 by mass, about one-tenth of solar levels). Planetary scientists hypothesize that neon either dissolved into deep metallic liquid <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> drops inside Jupiter or that the icy planetesimals that built Jupiter formed in regions too warm to trap neon.<\/p>\n<p>On Earth, neon is harvested industrially through the cryogenic fractional distillation of liquid air. Large-scale air separation plants across India\u2014such as those operated by INOX Air Products and Linde India\u2014chill atmospheric air down to liquid temperatures, separating high-purity neon alongside industrial <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a>.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\">Neon<\/a><\/a> is famous for its glowing orange-red advertising signs, high-voltage test indicators, surge arresters, and plasma display panels. However, its most critical modern role is in advanced laser technology. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">Helium<\/a>-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\">Neon<\/a> (He-Ne) gas lasers emit a highly stable red beam at 632.8 nanometers. Pioneered in India by institutions like Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) and the Raja Ramanna Centre for Advanced Technology (RRCAT) in Indore, He-Ne lasers are widely used for precision optical alignment, metrology, biological research, and laboratory education.<\/p>\n<p>In global high-tech manufacturing, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\">neon<\/a> plays an indispensable behind-the-scenes role in microchip production. Semiconductor fabrication relies heavily on excimer lasers (such as <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">Argon<\/a>-Fluoride and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Kr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Krypton (Kr)\">Krypton<\/a>-Fluoride lasers), which use high-purity neon as a buffer gas. These lasers generate deep ultraviolet light to etch microscopic circuitry onto <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a> wafers. As India expands its domestic semiconductor ecosystem under the India Semiconductor Mission, securing high-purity neon gas from cryogenic air separation units has become a vital strategic focus.<\/p>\n<p>In cryogenic engineering, liquid neon offers extraordinary compact cooling power for specialized scientific sensors, superconducting equipment, and aerospace instruments. In deep-sea diving, neon-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> gas mixtures are sometimes used in experimental breathing blends to reduce the narcotic effects caused by <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a> under high pressure. Combining vivid aesthetic beauty with cutting-edge physics, neon remains a silent titan of modern technology.<\/p>" } }, "Na": { "symbol": "Na", "name": "Sodium", "atomic": 11, "category": "alkali metal", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 11 (Na)", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">Sodium<\/a><\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>Na<\/b>, atomic number 11) is a remarkably soft, silvery-white, and highly reactive alkali metal in Group 1 of the periodic table. Soft enough to cut with a butter knife, free <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a> metal is so chemically energetic that it never exists naturally on Earth; it must be manufactured through electrolysis from its mineral salts. As the sixth most abundant element in Earth's crust, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a> makes up about 2.27% of planet Earth, found across minerals like feldspars, sodalite, and halite (common rock salt, NaCl). Over eons of geological time, liquid water has leached soluble sodium ions from surface rocks, carrying them into rivers and oceans. Today, sodium ions and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a><\/a> ions reign as the most abundant dissolved minerals by weight in world oceans. Featuring a single stable isotope (<sup>23<\/sup>Na), sodium powers human nerve signals, illuminates night highways with golden streetlamps, cools advanced nuclear reactors, and drives next-generation sodium-ion energy storage batteries.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/2\/27\/Na_%28Sodium%29.jpg", "atomic_mass": 22.989769282, "density": 0.968, "melt": 370.944, "boil": 1156.09, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Humphry Davy", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1", "electronegativity_pauling": 0.93, "electron_affinity": 52.867, "ionization_energies": [ 495.8, 4562, 6910.3, 9543, 13354, 16613, 20117, 25496, 28932, 141362, 159076 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p>Pure metallic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a> is a soft, bright, silvery metal with a low melting point of 370.944 K (97.79 \u00b0C \/ 208.02 \u00b0F) and a boiling point of 1156.09 K (882.94 \u00b0C \/ 1621.3 \u00b0F). With a density of only 0.968 g\/cm\u00b3, pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a> is actually lighter than water! If placed on water, a piece of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a> floats\u2014though not for long, because it reacts explosively! Sodium is so soft at room temperature that it can easily be cut with a butter knife or squeezed into ribbons. When freshly cut, it exhibits a brilliant metallic sheen, but within seconds of exposure to moist air, it rapidly tarnishes into a dull grey coat of sodium oxide, sodium hydroxide, and sodium carbonate.<\/p>\n<p>Chemically, sodium is a quintessential alkali metal sitting in Group 1 with an electron configuration of [Ne] 3s\u00b9 (or 1s\u00b2 2s\u00b2 2p\u2076 3s\u00b9). Holding a single, loosely bound valence electron in its outermost shell, sodium has a low Pauling electronegativity of 0.93 and a low first ionization energy of 495.8 kJ\/mol. Because it eagerly sheds this outer electron to achieve the ultra-stable closed-shell configuration of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\">neon<\/a><\/a>, sodium forms the single-charged sodium cation (Na\u207a) in nearly all its compounds. Sodium reacts violently with liquid water, releasing flammable <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a><\/a> gas and forming caustic sodium hydroxide (2 Na + 2 H\u2082O \u2192 2 NaOH + H\u2082\u2191). The intense heat generated by this reaction frequently ignites the escaping <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> gas, producing a dramatic, fiery yellow flame.<\/p>\n<p>Sodium metal also exhibits fascinating behavior when dissolved in non-water solvents. Dissolved in liquid ammonia, sodium loses its valence electrons into the solution to form solvated electrons, producing an extraordinary deep-blue conducting liquid that acts as a powerful reducing agent in organic chemistry. Under extremely dry conditions, when metallic sodium is reacted with benzophenone in organic solvents like tetrahydrofuran, it generates an intense indigo-blue ketyl radical color that serves as a visual indicator confirming the total absence of moisture.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Nuclear physicists have identified 20 known isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a>, ranging from <sup>18<\/sup>Na to <sup>37<\/sup>Na. However, virtually all <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a> found on Earth and across the universe consists of a single stable, primordial isotope: <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a>-23 (<sup>23<\/sup>Na). In deep space, <sup>23<\/sup>Na is forged inside massive stars (at least 3 solar masses) during stellar <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a>-burning. When core temperatures reach a searing 600 megakelvins (600 million degrees Celsius), two <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a><\/a> nuclei fuse together to produce sodium-23 along with a proton.<\/p>\n<p>All other sodium isotopes are radioactive with relatively short half-lives. The two most notable naturally occurring radioactive isotopes are cosmogenic nucleomaterials created when high-energy cosmic rays strike atmospheric atoms: sodium-22 (<sup>22<\/sup>Na) with a half-life of 2.602 years, and sodium-24 (<sup>24<\/sup>Na) with a half-life of 14.96 hours. All other radioisotopes of sodium have half-lives of less than one single minute! Scientists have also discovered two metastable nuclear isomers, the longest-lived being <sup>24m<\/sup>Na with a fleeting half-life of 20.2 milliseconds.<\/p>\n<p>Sodium isotopes play a crucial role in emergency nuclear medicine and radiation safety. If a person is exposed to acute neutron radiation\u2014such as during a nuclear criticality accident\u2014thermal neutrons strike the stable <sup>23<\/sup>Na atoms flowing in human blood plasma, converting some of them into radioactive <sup>24<\/sup>Na through neutron activation (<sup>23<\/sup>Na + n \u2192 <sup>24<\/sup>Na). By measuring the precise concentration of <sup>24<\/sup>Na relative to <sup>23<\/sup>Na in a patient's blood sample, medical physicists can calculate the exact absorbed dose of neutron radiation received by the victim, enabling rapid life-saving medical treatment.<\/p>", "History": "<p>Because common salt (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a> chloride) is an absolute necessity for human survival, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a> compounds have been cherished commodities since the dawn of civilization. In medieval Europe, an alkaline <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a> compound known as <i>sodanum<\/i> was widely prescribed as a soothing headache remedy. The word <i>sodium<\/i> itself traces back to the Arabic word <i>suda<\/i>, meaning \"headache,\" reflecting ancient medicinal recognition of soda's pain-alleviating qualities.<\/p>\n<p>In ancient India, sodium chemistry flourished through the practice of Ayurveda and <i>Rasa\u015b\u0101stra<\/i> (iatrochemistry). Classical treatises like the <i>Su\u015bruta Sa\u1e41hit\u0101<\/i> and <i>Rasatara\u1e45gi\u1e47\u012b<\/i> describe an essential plant-derived alkaline medicine called <i>Swarjik\u0101 K\u1e63\u0101ra<\/i> (also known as <i>Sajjik\u1e63\u0101ra<\/i> or <i>Sarjika Kshara<\/i>). Ancient Indian physicians prepared this potent alkali by burning halophytic (salt-loving) desert plants like <i>Fagonia cretica<\/i> (Ushtrapriya) and <i>Cressa cretica<\/i> (Rudanti). Chemically dominated by sodium carbonate (Na\u2082CO\u2083) and sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO\u2083), <i>Sajjik\u1e63\u0101ra<\/i> was classified as a vital <i>P\u0101n\u012bya K\u1e63\u0101ra<\/i> (internal alkaline medicine) used to soothe hyperacidity, dissolve digestive blockages (<i>Gulma<\/i>), and treat abdominal colic and skin conditions. Ancient texts like the <i>Caraka Sa\u1e41hit\u0101<\/i> also carefully categorized <i>Saindhava Lava\u1e47a<\/i> (pure mineral rock salt) and <i>Samudra Lava\u1e47a<\/i> (sea salt) for their therapeutic, preservation, and culinary properties.<\/p>\n<p>In global scientific history, although sodium compounds like soda ash and saltpetre were used for centuries, pure metallic sodium remained hidden because of its intense chemical reactivity. In 1807, legendary English chemist Sir Humphry Davy achieved a historic breakthrough by passing an electric current through molten sodium hydroxide (caustic soda)\u2014a process called electrolysis\u2014to isolate tiny, gleaming spheres of pure sodium metal for the very first time. In 1809, German chemist Ludwig Wilhelm Gilbert proposed the name <i>Natronium<\/i> for Davy's new metal. Later in 1814, Swedish chemist J\u00f6ns Jakob Berzelius selected the official chemical symbol <b>Na<\/b> from the Neo-Latin name <i>natrium<\/i>, derived from <i>natron<\/i>\u2014the natural hydrated sodium carbonate salt mined by ancient Egyptians for mummification, cleansing, and glassmaking.<\/p>\n<p>Sodium played a legendary role in the birth of modern spectroscopy. In 1860, pioneering German scientists Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen discovered that burning sodium compounds imparts a bright, unmistakable yellow light to flames. In a famous demonstration published in <i>Annalen der Physik und Chemie<\/i>, Kirchhoff and Bunsen detonated just 3 milligrams of sodium chlorate in the far corner of a huge 60-cubic-meter lecture hall. The sodium flame test proved so sensitive that it instantly lit up the room's spectroscope, revealing that scientists could detect as little as 1\/20-millionth of a milligram of sodium in a single unit of air!<\/p>\n<p>In 20th-century history, common sodium chloride became a world-changing symbol of freedom. On March 12, 1930, Mahatma Gandhi launched the historic 388-kilometer Dandi Salt March to coastal Gujarat. By picking up a pinch of natural sea salt on the shores of Dandi, Gandhi broke the tyrannical British salt monopoly, transforming simple sodium chloride into the moral spark for India's independence movement.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>Making up 2.27% of Earth's crust, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a> is the sixth most abundant element in the crust and the fourth most abundant metal\u2014ranking behind <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a><\/a>, and just ahead of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a><\/a>. Across the wider cosmos, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a> ranks as the 15th most abundant element by mass, accounting for roughly 0.002% of all universal atoms (20,000 parts per billion). Because pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a> metal reacts instantly with air and water, it is never found uncombined in nature.<\/p>\n<p>Instead, sodium occurs in a wide variety of minerals. Highly soluble mineral salts include halite (rock salt, NaCl) and natron (hydrated sodium carbonate). Less soluble minerals include silicate minerals like amphibole and zeolites, while completely insoluble sodium minerals include cryolite (Na\u2083AlF\u2086) and sodium feldspars (such as albite, NaAlSi\u2083O\u2088), whose insolubility stems from their complex, interconnected polysilicate polymeric anion networks.<\/p>\n<p>Because many sodium salts dissolve readily in liquid water, rainfall has washed sodium ions from continental rocks into surface rivers and oceans over billions of years. Ocean water contains an impressive average sodium concentration of 10.8 grams per liter (about 1.08% by weight), making sodium and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a><\/a> the primary dissolved ions in seawater.<\/p>\n<p>In India, geographical sites showcase immense natural sodium wealth. Rajasthan's iconic <b>Sambhar Salt Lake<\/b>\u2014India's largest inland saltwater lake\u2014is a vital ecological Ramsar wetland and a historic inland salt production basin. Mentioned in ancient epics like the <i>Mah\u0101bh\u0101rata<\/i> (associated with King Vrishparva) and revered as the domain of Goddess Shakambhari of the Chauhan Rajputs, Sambhar Lake yields thousands of tonnes of sodium chloride and sodium sulfate annually. Furthermore, India's extensive salt pans across coastal Gujarat (the vast saline marshlands of the Rann of Kutch) and Tuticorin in Tamil Nadu make India the third-largest producer of salt in the world.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>While free metallic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a> has specialized industrial roles, the vast majority of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a> is consumed in the form of its chemical compounds. Tens of millions of tonnes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a> salts are produced globally each year for heavy industry, food, and manufacturing:<\/p>\n<ul>\n <li><b>Sodium Chloride (NaCl):<\/b> Common table salt is vital for food preservation, culinary seasoning, and winter road anti-icing. It serves as the primary chemical feedstock for the chlor-alkali industry to produce <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a> gas and sodium hydroxide.<\/li>\n <li><b>Sodium Carbonate (Na\u2082CO\u2083):<\/b> Known as soda ash, it is essential for glass manufacturing, detergent formulations, and water softening.<\/li>\n <li><b>Sodium Bicarbonate (NaHCO\u2083):<\/b> Popularly known as baking soda, it acts as a leavening agent in cooking, an antacid, and a mild abrasive in sodablasting.<\/li>\n <li><b>Sodium Hydroxide (NaOH):<\/b> Known as caustic soda, it is a key industrial base used in soap making, paper pulp production, textile treatment, and chemical drain cleaners.<\/li>\n<\/ul>\n<p>In pharmaceuticals, many active drugs are formulated as sodium salts\u2014such as sodium naproxen, diclofenac sodium, and sodium ampicillin\u2014because sodium ions dramatically enhance water solubility and drug bioavailability in the human body at a far lower cost and lighter atomic weight than <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a><\/a>.<\/p>\n<p>Pure metallic sodium is utilized industrially to synthesize specialized chemical compounds like sodium borohydride (NaBH\u2084, a powerful reducing agent), sodium azide (NaN\u2083, used in automobile airbags), indigo dye for blue jeans, and triphenylphosphine. Historically, vast quantities of sodium metal were used to manufacture tetraethyllead (an anti-knock gasoline additive) and isolate pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a><\/a> metal via the Hunter process; though production declined after 1970 as leaded gasoline was phased out worldwide. In organic laboratory synthesis, sodium metal drives famous organic reactions such as the Birch reduction, the sodium fusion test for qualitative element analysis, and the preparation of sodium alkoxides from alcohols. Dissolved in liquid ammonia, sodium reduces alkynes to <i>trans<\/i>-alkenes.<\/p>\n<p>In modern high-tech engineering and optics, sodium plays astounding roles. High-pressure and low-pressure sodium vapor lamps emit an efficient yellow-orange to peach-amber glow, illuminating city streets and highways worldwide. In astronomy, ground-based observatories shine powerful yellow lasers tuned to the sodium D-line (589 nm) into the upper atmosphere (~90 km altitude), exciting mesospheric sodium atoms to create an \"artificial laser guide star.\" This technique allows adaptive optics systems to compensate for atmospheric turbulence, producing ultra-sharp space imagery.<\/p>\n<p><b>Modern Indian Scientific Contributions:<\/b><\/p>\n<p>India is a global leader in utilizing sodium for nuclear power, advanced energy storage, and public health science:<\/p>\n<ul>\n <li><b>Nuclear Energy (IGCAR Kalpakkam):<\/b> At the Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR) in Kalpakkam, Tamil Nadu, Indian nuclear scientists have mastered the engineering of high-temperature liquid sodium metal as a coolant for Fast Breeder Reactors. Used in the Fast Breeder Test Reactor (FBTR) and the 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR), liquid sodium offers superior thermal conductivity and low neutron absorption. IGCAR scientists engineered specialized electromagnetic sodium pumps, safety rigs like SADHANA and SOWART, and under-sodium ultrasonic vision systems to safely navigate high-temperature liquid sodium pools.<\/li>\n <li><b>Sodium-Ion Battery Tech (CSIR-CECRI):<\/b> To drive India's clean energy transition and achieve self-reliance (<i>\u0100tmanirbhar Bh\u0101rat<\/i>), researchers at the CSIR-Central Electrochemical Research Institute (CECRI) in Karaikudi, alongside premier IITs and IISc, are pioneering indigenous <b>Sodium-Ion Batteries (SIBs)<\/b>. Utilizing abundant local sodium resources, CECRI has fabricated 18650 cylindrical cells using NASICON-type cathode materials and hard <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> anodes, delivering a sustainable, affordable, and safe alternative to imported <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a>-ion batteries for electric vehicles and power grids.<\/li>\n <li><b>Food Science & Public Health (CSIR-CFTRI):<\/b> Scientists at the CSIR-Central Food Technological Research Institute (CFTRI) in Mysuru conduct cutting-edge food technology research focused on \"sodium reduction\" in traditional Indian packaged foods, striking a scientific balance between reducing dietary sodium to combat hypertension and preserving authentic traditional flavors.<\/li>\n<\/ul>", "Biological role": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">Sodium<\/a><\/a> is an essential mineral nutrient and the dominant positively charged ion (cation) in the extracellular fluids of all animals, including humans. Together with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a><\/a> ions (Cl\u207b) and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a><\/a> ions (K\u207a), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a> maintains osmotic pressure, regulates fluid balance across cell membranes, and controls blood volume and blood pressure.<\/p>\n<p>At the cellular level, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a> ions are vital for nerve signal transmission and muscle contraction. Cells utilize a specialized membrane-bound protein enzyme called the sodium-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> pump (Na\u207a\/K\u207a-ATPase) to actively pump three sodium ions out of the cell for every two <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> ions pumped in. This process generates an electrical potential gradient across cell membranes. When a nerve cell fires, sodium channels open instantly, allowing Na\u207a ions to rush into the cell and create an electrical action potential that travels rapidly down nerve pathways to command heartbeats, muscle movements, and brain thoughts.<\/p>\n<p>While most plants require very little sodium (unlike potassium), sodium is an essential micronutrient for C4 plants\u2014such as sugarcane, maize (corn), and salt-tolerant desert halophytes\u2014which use sodium ions to regenerate phosphoenolpyruvate during specialized <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> fixation.<\/p>\n<p>In human health, maintaining the right sodium balance is critical. While a minimum amount of sodium is mandatory to sustain life, modern diets frequently contain excessive dietary salt. Modern medical studies show that chronic high sodium intake stresses the kidneys and elevates blood pressure, increasing the risk of hypertension and cardiovascular disease. Balanced sodium intake remains a cornerstone of modern preventive medicine.<\/p>" } }, "Mg": { "symbol": "Mg", "name": "Magnesium", "atomic": 12, "category": "alkaline earth metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">Magnesium<\/a><\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>Mg<\/b>, atomic number 12) is a lightweight, silvery-white alkaline earth metal in Group 2 of the periodic table. Sharing a matching outer electron configuration with its five group siblings, it exhibits similar crystal structure and chemical reactivity. It is the ninth most abundant element in the universe, the eighth most abundant element in Earth's crust, and the second most abundant positive ion in seawater. Indispensable to life, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a> rests at the heart of green chlorophyll molecules in plants to drive photosynthesis and serves as an essential spark for hundreds of metabolic enzymes in humans and animals.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/3\/3f\/Magnesium_crystals.jpg", "atomic_mass": 24.305, "density": 1.738, "melt": 923, "boil": 1363, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Joseph Black", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.31, "electron_affinity": -40, "ionization_energies": [ 737.7, 1450.7, 7732.7, 10542.5, 13630, 18020, 21711, 25661, 31653, 35458, 169988, 189368 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p>As an alkaline earth metal in Group 2 of the periodic table, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a><\/a> has an atomic number of 12 and a ground-state electron configuration of 1s<sup>2<\/sup> 2s<sup>2<\/sup> 2p<sup>6<\/sup> 3s<sup>2<\/sup>. It possesses two valence electrons in its outermost shell, which it easily gives up to achieve a stable, noble-gas electronic structure. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">Magnesium<\/a> is a shiny, silvery-gray solid that bears a striking physical resemblance to its five group siblings\u2014<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Be\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Beryllium (Be)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Be\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Beryllium (Be)\">beryllium<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Strontium (Sr)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Strontium (Sr)\">strontium<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ba\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Barium (Ba)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ba\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Barium (Ba)\">barium<\/a><\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ra\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Radium (Ra)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ra\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Radium (Ra)\">radium<\/a><\/a>. Because of its high chemical reactivity, pure metallic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a> never exists naturally in its uncombined elemental state on Earth; instead, it is found locked inside rock minerals, ocean brines, and living organisms.<\/p><p>Magnesium is famous for being remarkably lightweight\u2014with a density of only 1.738 g\/cm\u00b3, it is just two-thirds the density of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminium (Al)\">aluminium<\/a>. Despite its light weight, magnesium forms exceptionally strong, durable structural alloys when combined with small amounts of other metals, making it a cornerstone element for lightweight engineering in modern transportation, consumer electronics, and space exploration.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Physical properties": "<p>Elemental <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a><\/a> is a gray-white metal with an excellent strength-to-weight ratio. It boasts the lowest melting point (923 K or 650 \u00b0C) and the lowest boiling point (1,363 K or 1,090 \u00b0C) among all the alkaline earth metals.
