Its low melting point makes it relatively easy to cast and shape into intricate mechanical parts.<\/p><p>In its pure polycrystalline form, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a> is somewhat brittle and tends to fracture easily along mechanical shear bands under stress. However, its malleability and ductility can be dramatically improved in two ways: by alloying it with tiny amounts of other elements (such as just 1% <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminium (Al)\">aluminium<\/a>) or by refining its microscopic crystal grain size down to about 1 micrometre (\u03bcm) or less. These grain-refinement techniques allow engineers to transform brittle raw <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a> into flexible, high-toughness sheets and structural components.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Chemical properties": "<p>The chemical behavior of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a><\/a> is defined by its willingness to donate its two 3s outer electrons, forming stable divalent cations (Mg<sup>2+<\/sup>). It has a Pauling electronegativity of 1.31, with a first ionization energy of 737.7 kJ\/mol and a second ionization energy of 1450.7 kJ\/mol. Exposed to air at room temperature, solid <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a> tarnishes slightly as it forms a thin, protective surface film of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a> oxide (MgO) that passivates the metal and slows down further atmospheric corrosion.<\/p><p>When heated in air, magnesium ignites readily and burns with an intensely dazzling, brilliant white flame that reaches temperatures around 3,100 \u00b0C (5,610 \u00b0F). This intense combustion converts the metal into white magnesium oxide powder (MgO) alongside a small amount of magnesium nitride (Mg<sub>3<\/sub>N<sub>2<\/sub>). Magnesium burns so aggressively with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> that it can even continue burning inside an atmosphere of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> dioxide (CO<sub>2<\/sub>), stripping <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> atoms from CO<sub>2<\/sub> molecules to leave behind solid <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> soot and magnesium oxide! Because of this property, conventional water or CO<sub>2<\/sub> fire extinguishers cannot extinguish a magnesium fire; specialized Class D dry powder extinguishers or dry sand must be used instead.<\/p><p>Magnesium reacts slowly with cold water, but reacts rapidly with boiling water or steam to release bubbles of flammable <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a><\/a> gas and form magnesium hydroxide: Mg + 2 H<sub>2<\/sub>O \u2192 Mg(OH)<sub>2<\/sub> + H<sub>2<\/sub>. It also dissolves vigorously in dilute aqueous acids (such as hydrochloric acid), rapidly producing magnesium salts and abundant <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> gas. Magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)<sub>2<\/sub> (famously known as Milk of Magnesia), is poorly soluble in water and acts as a mild, non-toxic alkaline base.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Isotopes": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">Main article: Isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a><\/a><\/div>\n<p>Natural <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a><\/a> is composed of three stable isotopes: <sup>24<\/sup>Mg, <sup>25<\/sup>Mg, and <sup>26<\/sup>Mg. All three are present in substantial quantities in nature. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">Magnesium<\/a>-24 is the most abundant by far, making up about 78.99% (roughly 79%) of natural magnesium, while <sup>25<\/sup>Mg accounts for 10.00% and <sup>26<\/sup>Mg makes up 11.01%. Among synthetic radioisotopes, <sup>28<\/sup>Mg is noteworthy; produced in nuclear reactors from the 1950s through the 1970s for biological and physical experiments, its short half-life of 21 hours meant its scientific utility was severely restricted by rapid shipping decay.<\/p><p>The stable isotope <sup>26<\/sup>Mg plays a pivotal role in planetary science and isotopic geology. It is the radiogenic daughter product of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a>-26 (<sup>26<\/sup>Al), a extinct radioactive isotope that decays with a half-life of 717,000 years. Geochemists have discovered excessive, anomalous amounts of stable <sup>26<\/sup>Mg inside <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">Calcium<\/a>-Aluminium-rich inclusions (CAIs) found within carbonaceous chondrite meteorites. Scientists concluded that these meteorites condensed in the early solar nebula before the parent <sup>26<\/sup>Al had time to decay. Because CAIs represent the oldest solid objects in our Solar System (~4.567 billion years old), tracking their <sup>26<\/sup>Mg abundance offers an invaluable cosmic clock to reconstruct the earliest high-temperature events in solar system history.<\/p><p>In isotopic geology, researchers plot the ratio of <sup>26<\/sup>Mg\/<sup>24<\/sup>Mg against the <sup>27<\/sup>Al\/<sup>24<\/sup>Mg ratio on an isochron plot. While the slope of this isochron line does not directly measure elapsed time, it precisely reveals the initial ratio of <sup>26<\/sup>Al\/<sup>27<\/sup>Al present in the original solar reservoir when the meteorite system sealed itself off.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Occurrence": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable selfref\">See also: Category:<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">Magnesium<\/a><\/a> minerals<\/div>\n<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">See also: Boninite<\/div>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">Magnesium<\/a><\/a> is the ninth most abundant element in the observable universe by mass, created during fusion reactions in massive stars. On Earth, it is the eighth most abundant element in the crust by mass (constituting about 2.1% of the crust) and is tied in seventh place with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a> in terms of molar abundance. Although <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a> is present in over 60 distinct minerals, only six are of major commercial importance: magnesite (MgCO<sub>3<\/sub>), dolomite (CaMg(CO<sub>3<\/sub>)<sub>2<\/sub>), brucite (Mg(OH)<sub>2<\/sub>), carnallite (KMgCl<sub>3<\/sub>\u00b76H<sub>2<\/sub>O), talc (Mg<sub>3<\/sub>Si<sub>4<\/sub>O<sub>10<\/sub>(OH)<sub>2<\/sub>), and olivine ((Mg,Fe)<sub>2<\/sub>SiO<sub>4<\/sub>). It is also found in boninite igneous rocks and natural mineral springs.<\/p><p>Dissolved magnesium ions (Mg<sup>2+<\/sup>) represent the second most abundant positive ion in Earth's oceans (after <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a>), with a concentration of about 1.3 g\/kg\u2014roughly one-eighth the mass of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a> ions in seawater. This vast oceanic reservoir, alongside natural salt lakes and subterranean brine wells, makes seawater one of the most attractive and sustainable commercial sources for extracting pure magnesium metal through electrolysis.<\/p><p>Geographically, India possesses world-renowned reserves of high-grade magnesite and dolomite. The most famous Indian deposit is located in the **Salem district of Tamil Nadu** (the famous \"Chalk Hills\"), earning Salem the historical distinction of being India's **\"Steel and Magnesite City.\"** Commercial magnesite mining began here in 1890 under Henry Turner, establishing the foundation for India's high-temperature refractory brick industry. Significant magnesite belts also stretch across the Himalayan terrain of **Uttarakhand** (in Almora and Pithoragarh districts), Karnataka (Mysore), and Rajasthan, while vast dolomite formations across Chhattisgarh, Odisha, and Madhya Pradesh supply essential fluxes to India's major steel plants.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "History": "<p>The name <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a><\/a> originates from the ancient Greek region of Magnesia (either in Thessaly or Magnesia ad Sipylum, now in modern Turkey), named after the Magnetes tribe. The region yielded three distinct minerals that took centuries to differentiate: magnetite (magnetic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> ore), pyrolusite (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">manganese<\/a><\/a> dioxide), and magnesia (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a> oxide).<\/p><p>In 1618, a farmer named Henry Wicker at Epsom in Surrey, England, attempted to water his cows from a local well during a drought. The cows refused to drink the bitter-tasting water, but Wicker observed that the mineral water remarkably accelerated the healing of cuts, rashes, and scratches on skin. Upon evaporating the spring water, he obtained white mineral crystals known worldwide as \"Epsom salts\"\u2014eventually identified as hydrated <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a> sulfate, MgSO<sub>4<\/sub>\u00b77H<sub>2<\/sub>O. Epsom salts quickly gained international fame as a medicinal laxative and soothing bath salt.<\/p><p>Pure metallic magnesium was first isolated in 1808 by Sir Humphry Davy in London. Davy performed electrolysis on a moist paste of magnesia (MgO) and mercuric oxide (HgO) using a powerful battery, forming a magnesium-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\">mercury<\/a> amalgam from which he distilled away the <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\">mercury<\/a>. Davy originally suggested the name <i>magnium<\/i>, but <i>magnesium<\/i> was ultimately adopted. In 1831, French chemist Antoine Bussy prepared the metal in coherent metallic form by heating anhydrous magnesium chloride with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> vapor. Later, the father of physical chemistry in Imperial Russia, Nikolai Beketov (1827\u20131911), proved that magnesium and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a><\/a> displace other metals from their salt solutions at high temperatures, establishing early metal reactivity concepts.<\/p><p>In ancient Indian history and classical Ayurvedic texts on <i>Rasashastra<\/i> (iatrochemistry), magnesium minerals were recognized and utilized for their therapeutic properties centuries before Western chemistry isolated the pure metal. Magnesite (magnesium carbonate) was known in South Indian tradition as <b><i>Garudapacha<\/i><\/b> (or <i>Palgarudapacha<\/i>) and was formulated to treat bone loss (<i>asthishosha<\/i>), bodily weakness, and eye afflictions. Hydrous magnesium silicate (talc) was studied as <b><i>Nagapashana<\/i><\/b>; through traditional <i>Shodhana<\/i> (purification) and <i>Marana<\/i> (calcination), ancient practitioners transformed these minerals into bioavailable <i>Bhasmas<\/i> used as cardiac tonics and tissue restorers. Furthermore, natural bitter mineral waters (*Khar*) were prescribed in Ayurvedic medicine for their gentle digestive and laxative benefits.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Uses": "<p>As the lightest structural metal available, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a><\/a> is vital across modern metallurgy, aerospace, consumer electronics, and green energy. When alloyed with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminium (Al)\">aluminium<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">manganese<\/a><\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a> creates ultra-light, high-strength alloys used in aircraft structures, automotive engine blocks, transmission cases, steering wheels, laptop casings, and high-performance power tools. In heavy industry, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a> acts as a desulfurizer and deoxidizer in steelmaking, and serves as a reducing agent in the Kroll process to extract pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zirconium (Zr)\">zirconium<\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hf\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hafnium (Hf)\">hafnium<\/a> from their chloride ores. Attached to underground steel pipelines, water heaters, and ship hulls, magnesium blocks act as sacrificial anodes, corroding preferentially to protect steel structures from rust.<\/p><p>Because magnesium burns with an intensely brilliant white light, powdered magnesium is used in emergency signal flares, military tracer ammunition, fireworks, theatrical pyrotechnics, and vintage camera flashbulbs. In refractory applications, calcined magnesite (MgO) is crafted into heat-resistant bricks that line steel-smelting furnaces capable of enduring temperatures above 2,000 \u00b0C.<\/p><p>Biologically, magnesium is indispensable to life on Earth. It sits at the exact center of the <b>chlorophyll<\/b> molecule\u2014the green pigment in plants that absorbs solar energy to power photosynthesis, producing the <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a> we breathe and the food we eat. In humans, the Mg<sup>2+<\/sup> ion is essential for over 300 enzymatic reactions, regulating ATP energy transfer, DNA synthesis, nerve impulse transmission, and muscle contraction. Milk of Magnesia, Mg(OH)<sub>2<\/sub>, is widely used as a gentle antacid and laxative, while Epsom salt baths soothe sore muscles.<\/p><p>In modern Indian science and technology, magnesium plays a crucial role across space, medicine, and clean energy. The <b>Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)<\/b>, working alongside <b>CSIR-NIIST<\/b> (Thiruvananthapuram) and <b>CSIR-CECRI<\/b> (Karaikudi), has pioneered lightweight Aluminium-Magnesium-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Scandium (Sc)\">Scandium<\/a> (Al-Mg-Sc) and specialized magnesium alloy castings. These advanced materials reduce structural weight in satellite frames, launch vehicles (PSLV and GSLV), and liquid propulsion engine systems (LPSC). At <b>IIT Madras<\/b>, researchers have engineered cutting-edge bioresorbable magnesium alloy orthopedic implants coated with nano-hydroxyapatite. These implants provide structural support for broken bones and then dissolve harmlessly inside the body as natural bone heals, eliminating the need for painful secondary removal surgeries. Furthermore, scientists at <b>IIT Madras<\/b> and <b>IISc Bangalore<\/b> are developing solid-state <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> storage systems using <b>magnesium hydride (MgH<sub>2<\/sub>)<\/b>, designing specialized heat-exchanger reactors to safely store green <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> for future clean energy grids. Finally, in the world-famous tea plantations of <b>Assam and the Nilgiris<\/b>, agricultural application of Epsom salt (MgSO<sub>4<\/sub>\u00b77H<sub>2<\/sub>O) corrects soil magnesium deficiency, boosting chlorophyll production and enhancing the yield and flavor profile of Indian tea.<\/p>\n<div style=\"clear:both;\" class=\"\"><\/div>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">" } }, "Al": { "symbol": "Al", "name": "Aluminum", "atomic": 13, "category": "post-transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">Aluminum<\/a><\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>Al<\/b>, atomic number 13) is the lightweight champion of the metal world. Sitting in Group 13 of the periodic table, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a> is a silvery-white, soft, non-magnetic, and remarkably flexible metal. It holds the proud title of being the third most abundant chemical element in Earth's crust\u2014surpassed only by <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a><\/a>\u2014and the single most abundant metal on our planet, making up roughly 8.1% of Earth's solid surface. Weighing only one-third as much as steel, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a> instantly forms a microscopic, self-healing shield of oxide when exposed to air, making it virtually immune to rust. From ancient Indian Ayurvedic remedies and vibrant textile dyes to high-speed trains, beverage cans, and ISRO space rockets, aluminum is an indispensable pillar of modern civilization.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/3\/3e\/Aluminium.jpg", "atomic_mass": 26.98153857, "density": 2.7, "melt": 933.47, "boil": 2743, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": null, "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p1", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.61, "electron_affinity": 41.762, "ionization_energies": [ 577.5, 1816.7, 2744.8, 11577, 14842, 18379, 23326, 27465, 31853, 38473, 42647, 201266, 222316 ], "sections": { "History": "<p>While metallic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a><\/a> is a relatively modern discovery, human civilization has relied on natural <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a> compounds for thousands of years. In ancient India, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a> sulfate\u2014commonly known as alum\u2014held a revered position in science, medicine, and industry. Ancient Sanskrit texts, including classical <i>Rasa\u015b\u0101stra<\/i> (Ayurvedic mineral alchemy) treatises such as the 13th-century <i>Rasaratnasamuccaya<\/i> and the <i>Rasarnava<\/i>, refer to alum by names such as <i>Sphatika<\/i>, <i>Tuvari<\/i>, <i>Shubhra<\/i>, <i>Kankshi<\/i>, and <i>Saurashtri<\/i> (named after the mineral-rich clay deposits of Saurashtra in Gujarat). Alum was classified under the <i>Uparasa<\/i> category of vital minerals. Ayurvedic physicians processed raw alum through <i>\u015aodhana<\/i> (purification in organic liquids) and <i>M\u0101ra\u1e47a<\/i> (calcination) to drive out its 24 molecules of crystallization water, creating a light, snow-white medicinal ash known as <i>Sphatika Bhasma<\/i>. Valued for its powerful <i>Raktastambhaka<\/i> (hemostatic) and astringent properties, <i>Sphatika Bhasma<\/i> was prescribed for stopping internal and external bleeding, healing stubborn wounds, and treating respiratory ailments. Across Indian households, alum (known locally as <i>Phitkari<\/i>) has also been used for centuries as a natural water clarifier\u2014coagulating suspended silt particles in river water\u2014and as an antiseptic facial splash after shaving.<\/p>\n\n<p>Alum also drove ancient India's world-renowned textile empire. Ancient Indian dyers utilized <i>Saurashtri<\/i> (alum) as a critical chemical mordant\u2014a substance that forms a molecular bridge between plant fibers and natural dyes. By treating cotton and silk with alum solutions, Indian artisans permanently fixed bright vegetable colors like <i>Manjistha<\/i> (Indian madder red) into fabrics, creating colorfast textiles that were prized from Rome to East Asia. In the Western world, alum was similarly cherished by ancient Egyptians, Greeks, and Romans for medicine and leather tanning. In 1787, French chemist Antoine Lavoisier deduced that alum's oxide base, alumina, contained a previously unknown metal with an intense grip on <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a>.<\/p>\n\n<p>In the early 19th century, English chemist Sir Humphry Davy named the elusive element <i>alumium<\/i> (later adjusting it to <i>aluminum<\/i> and <i>aluminium<\/i>). However, isolating pure metallic aluminum proved extraordinarily difficult because it binds far more tightly to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> than <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a> or <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a><\/a>. Danish scientist Hans Christian \u00d8rsted finally succeeded in isolating impure metallic aluminum in 1825 by reacting aluminum chloride with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a><\/a> amalgam, and German chemist Friedrich W\u00f6hler refined the process in 1827 to obtain pure metallic globules.<\/p>\n\n<p>Because early chemical extraction required costly metallic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a>, aluminum was initially far more valuable than <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\">gold<\/a><\/a> or <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ag\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silver (Ag)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ag\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silver (Ag)\">silver<\/a><\/a>. Emperor Napoleon III of France hosted state banquets where elite guests were given aluminum forks and spoons while lesser nobility ate with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\">gold<\/a> cutlery! In 1884, a 100-ounce pyramid of solid aluminum was placed atop the Washington Monument in the United States as a supreme symbol of industrial luxury and engineering prowess.<\/p>\n\n<p>The aluminum age truly exploded in 1886 when American inventor Charles Martin Hall and French engineer Paul H\u00e9roult independently discovered that electrolyzing alumina dissolved in a molten salt bath of cryolite (Na\u2083AlF\u2086) yielded pure aluminum metal efficiently. Three years later, in 1889, Austrian chemist Carl Josef Bayer invented the Bayer process to economically extract pure alumina from raw bauxite ore. Together, the Bayer and Hall-H\u00e9roult processes slashed the price of aluminum overnight, converting a precious royal curiosity into the cornerstone of modern transportation, architecture, and flight.<\/p>", "Characteristics": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">Aluminum<\/a><\/a> is a post-transition metal characterized by an astonishing combination of lightness, flexibility, and strength. With a density of just 2.70 grams per cubic centimeter, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a> weighs approximately one-third as much as <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a> or <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a><\/a>. In its purest state, it is soft, silvery-white, non-magnetic, and non-sparking. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">Aluminum<\/a> is extraordinarily ductile and malleable, allowing it to be drawn into fine electrical wires or flattened into thin kitchen foils just 0.004 millimeters thick without tearing.<\/p>\n\n<p>From an electrical and thermal perspective, aluminum is a stellar performer. Although its electrical conductivity is about 62% that of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a> by volume, aluminum's low density means that a kilogram of aluminum conducts twice as much electricity as a kilogram of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a>. This exceptional strength-to-weight efficiency makes aluminum the material of choice for high-voltage overhead power grids across the globe. Aluminum also conducts heat rapidly (thermal conductivity of 237 W\/m\u00b7K), which is why it is used in everything from household cookware to heat sinks inside computers and electronic devices.<\/p>\n\n<p>Chemically, an isolated <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a> atom has the electron configuration [Ne] 3s\u00b2 3p\u00b9, readily relinquishing its three outer electrons to adopt a stable +3 oxidation state. Aluminum has a fierce chemical appetite for <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a>. When fresh aluminum metal is exposed to air, it reacts instantly to form an invisible, dense layer of aluminum oxide (Al\u2082O\u2083) only a few nanometers thick. This oxide film acts as a permanent, self-healing armor that seals the metal beneath, preventing <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> and moisture from causing rust or deep corrosion. If the surface is scratched, the oxide layer instantly reforms in milliseconds.<\/p>\n\n<p>Aluminum is amphoteric, meaning it reacts with both strong acids and strong bases. In acidic solutions, it dissolves to form aluminum salts while releasing <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a><\/a> gas; in strong alkaline solutions (such as caustic soda), it forms soluble aluminate complexes like [Al(OH)\u2084]\u207b. While pure aluminum metal is relatively soft, alloying it with tiny amounts of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a><\/a>, or <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a><\/a> dramatically increases its tensile strength to rival structural steel while preserving its lightweight advantage.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Naturally occurring <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a><\/a> is a monoisotopic and mononuclidic element. Virtually 100% of all <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a> found in Earth's rocks, soils, and oceans consists of a single stable isotope: <b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a>-27 (\u00b2\u2077Al)<\/b>. Containing 13 protons and 14 neutrons, aluminum-27 was forged in the hearts of dying giant stars through proton-capture fusion cycles before being scattered across the cosmos in ancient supernova explosions.<\/p>\n\n<p>In addition to stable \u00b2\u2077Al, nature contains trace amounts of an extraordinarily important radioactive isotope: <b>aluminum-26 (\u00b2\u2076Al)<\/b>. With a half-life of roughly 717,000 years, \u00b2\u2076Al decays by positron emission or electron capture into stable <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a><\/a>-26 (\u00b2\u2076Mg). On Earth, tiny amounts of \u00b2\u2076Al are continuously produced in the upper atmosphere when energetic cosmic rays bombard <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a><\/a> atoms, making it a valuable tracer for cosmic ray exposure and geological dating.<\/p>\n\n<p>In planetary science and astrophysics, aluminum-26 plays a starring historical role. When our solar system formed 4.56 billion years ago, live \u00b2\u2076Al was abundant in the protoplanetary disk. As this radioactive isotope decayed, it released immense thermal energy\u2014acting as the primary heat engine that melted the interiors of early asteroids and planetesimals. This internal heating allowed heavy metals like <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a> to sink to the center while lighter silicate minerals floated to the top, driving planetary differentiation across the early solar system.<\/p>\n\n<p>In India, planetary scientists at the Physical Research Laboratory (PRL) in Ahmedabad utilize advanced high-precision mass spectrometry to measure excess \u00b2\u2076Mg produced by the decay of \u00b2\u2076Al inside primitive meteorites that fall across the Indian subcontinent. By studying <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">Calcium<\/a>-Aluminum-rich Inclusions (CAIs) in meteorites like the Efremovka and Kamargaon falls, Indian researchers calculate the precise timing of early solar system events down to a resolution of a few hundred thousand years, shedding light on the birth of planets.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">Aluminum<\/a><\/a> is the third most abundant element in Earth's crust (comprising roughly 8.1% by mass), surpassed only by <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a> (46.6%) and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a><\/a> (27.7%). Because <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a> has an intense chemical affinity for <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a>, it never occurs naturally as a free native metal under normal conditions. Instead, it is locked inside hundreds of widespread minerals, including feldspars, micas, garnets, and clay minerals like kaolinite.<\/p>\n\n<p>The primary commercial ore for <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a> extraction is <b>bauxite<\/b>\u2014a clay-like sedimentary rock formed by millions of years of intense tropical weathering of aluminous rocks under humid monsoonal climates. Bauxite consists primarily of aluminum hydroxide minerals such as gibbsite [Al(OH)\u2083], boehmite [\u03b3-AlO(OH)], and diaspore [\u03b1-AlO(OH)], mixed with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> oxides, silica, and titania.<\/p>\n\n<p>India is blessed with vast, high-grade bauxite reserves, ranking fifth globally in total bauxite resources. The state of <b>Odisha<\/b> is the unquestioned heartland of Indian aluminum, holding over half of the country's total bauxite deposits. The majestic <b>Panchpatmali hills<\/b> in Koraput district, Odisha, contain one of the largest contiguous plateau bauxite deposits in the world. Operations at Panchpatmali are managed by the National Aluminium Company Limited (NALCO), a premier Navratna public sector enterprise that extracts bauxite to feed its massive alumina refinery at Damanjodi and smelter at Angul. Other major bauxite-rich regions in India include the East Coast bauxite belt spanning Odisha and Andhra Pradesh, the Maikala hill range in Chhattisgarh and Madhya Pradesh, the Ranchi plateau in Jharkhand, and coastal belts in Gujarat and Maharashtra.<\/p>\n\n<p>Extracting pure aluminum metal requires a two-step industrial process: first, bauxite is refined into pure alumina (Al\u2082O\u2083) using hot caustic soda via the Bayer process; second, alumina is dissolved in molten cryolite at 950\u00b0C and electrolyzed using massive electric currents via the Hall-H\u00e9roult process. Because primary aluminum smelting demands substantial electrical energy (~13\u201315 kilowatt-hours per kilogram), recycling aluminum offers incredible environmental benefits. Recycling aluminum requires only <b>5% of the energy<\/b> needed to extract new metal from bauxite ore and produces zero loss in metal quality, making aluminum one of the most sustainable and infinitely recyclable materials on Earth.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">Aluminum<\/a><\/a> is the world's most widely used non-ferrous metal, serving as an essential building block across modern transportation, energy, architecture, packaging, and aerospace. In everyday life, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a> foil seals food freshness, beverage cans offer lightweight recyclability, and sleek <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a> window frames provide structural durability without rusting. In the electrical sector, Aluminum Conductor Steel Reinforced (ACSR) cables form the backbone of national power distribution grids, carrying high-voltage electricity across thousands of kilometers.<\/p>\n\n<p>In modern transportation and defense, aluminum's lightweight strength drives energy efficiency. Indian Railways is undergoing a major technological transformation with the introduction of indigenous <b>aluminum Vande Bharat trainsets<\/b>. Engineered with lightweight aluminum alloy bodies, these modern trains reduce overall vehicle weight by 20% to 30% compared to traditional steel coaches. This weight reduction leads to faster acceleration, lower energy consumption, reduced track wear, and complete freedom from rust during heavy monsoons.<\/p>\n\n<p>India's high-tech aerospace sector relies heavily on advanced aluminum metallurgy. The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) uses specialized high-strength aluminum alloys\u2014such as AA2219, 2000-series, 7000-series, and advanced aluminum-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a> (Al-Li) alloys\u2014developed by the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC) in Thiruvananthapuram and the Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC) in Valiamala, fabricated in partnership with Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL). These cryogenic-tolerant alloys form the massive liquid propellant tanks and structural fuselages for ISRO's PSLV, GSLV Mark III (LVM3), and the Next Generation Launch Vehicle (NGLV), carrying Indian satellites and scientific payloads into orbit.<\/p>\n\n<p>Scientific innovation in aluminum is led by institutions like the <b>Jawaharlal Nehru Aluminium Research Development and Design Centre (JNARDDC)<\/b> in Nagpur\u2014an autonomous Centre of Excellence under the Ministry of Mines that pioneers bauxite beneficiation, advanced alloy development, and eco-friendly utilization of \"red mud\" (bauxite byproduct) into green building materials. Simultaneously, CSIR-Advanced Materials and Processes Research Institute (CSIR-AMPRI) in Bhopal develops ultra-light aluminum matrix composites and metallic foams for structural noise damping and defense armor. Combining ancient roots in Indian medicine and crafts with cutting-edge space technology, aluminum continues to shape the future of human innovation.<\/p>" } }, "Si": { "symbol": "Si", "name": "Silicon", "atomic": 14, "category": "metalloid", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 14 (Si)", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">Silicon<\/a><\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>Si<\/b>, atomic number 14) is a shiny, dark blue-grey metalloid and semiconductor that forms the bedrock of both modern electronics and Earth's geology. Positioned in group 14 of the periodic table directly below <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a><\/a> and above <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">germanium<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tin (Sn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tin (Sn)\">tin<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a><\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Flerovium (Fl)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Flerovium (Fl)\">flerovium<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a> is a tetravalent element that readily shares electrons to construct strong covalent networks. It is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust (27.2% by mass), surpassed only by <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a>. From ancient Harappan silica beads and sacred Indian <i>Sphatika<\/i> quartz crystals to structural plant cell walls and microprocessors powering global supercomputers, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a> spans the bridge between natural history and futuristic human technology.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/2\/2c\/Silicon.jpg", "atomic_mass": 28.085, "density": 2.329, "melt": 1687, "boil": 3538, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "J\u00f6ns Jacob Berzelius", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p2", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.9, "electron_affinity": 134.0684, "ionization_energies": [ 786.5, 1577.1, 3231.6, 4355.5, 16091, 19805, 23780, 29287, 33878, 38726, 45962, 50502, 235196, 257923 ], "sections": { "History": "<p>Because <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a><\/a> is so abundant across the Earth's surface, natural <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a> compounds like quartz, sand, and silicate minerals have been shaped by human hands for thousands of years. Early civilizations recognized the durability and beauty of silica rock crystals. Predynastic Egyptians fashioned ornamental beads and small vases from quartz, while ancient Chinese artisans carved delicate vessels out of rock crystal. By around 1500 BC, Egyptian and Phoenician glassmakers had learned to fuse silica sand with alkali plant ash to manufacture translucent glass containers, while early builders combined natural silicate clays with lime to create durable construction mortars.<\/p>\n<p>In ancient India, silica-based minerals formed the backbone of a sophisticated lapidary and metallurgical tradition. During the Indus Valley Civilization (2600\u20131900 BC), master craftsmen at sites such as Lothal, Chanhu-daro, and Rakhigarhi excelled in working silica stones including quartz, agate, jasper, and chalcedony. Harappan bead-makers developed an advanced heat-treatment technique\u2014baking <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>-rich agates in specialized clay kilns to transform them into deep orange-red carnelian beads that were traded across Ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt. The Harappans also synthesized <i>faience<\/i>, an early artificial ceramic made by crushing quartz sand, mixing it with an alkali binder, and firing it at high temperatures to yield turquoise-glazed ornaments.<\/p>\n<p>Pure, transparent quartz crystal holds a profound place in classical Indian literature, where it is known as <i>Sphatika<\/i> (\u0938\u094d\u092b\u091f\u093f\u0915). Mentioned in foundational texts such as the <i>Rigveda<\/i>, Varahamihira's <i>Brihat Samhita<\/i>, the <i>Garuda Purana<\/i>, and various Saiva Agamas, <i>Sphatika<\/i> was revered as a material of absolute clarity and divine energy. Associated with Lord Shiva in the form of carved <i>Sphatika Lingams<\/i> and with Goddess Lakshmi, quartz rosaries (<i>Sphatika malas<\/i>) were prized in traditional Indian medicine and spiritual practice for their soothing, cooling (<i>sheeta<\/i>) physical and mental properties. The town of Khambhat (Cambay) in Gujarat has maintained an unbroken four-thousand-year heritage as a world capital for lapidary agate and quartz craft.<\/p>\n<p>In Western scientific history, 18th-century chemists suspected that silica (flint) was the oxide of an undiscovered element. Antoine Lavoisier listed silica among the elementary earths in 1789. In 1811, French chemists Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis Jacques Th\u00e9nard produced crude, impure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a> by heating silicon tetrafluoride with metallic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a><\/a>. However, it was Swedish chemist J\u00f6ns Jacob Berzelius who isolated pure elemental silicon in 1824 by heating <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> fluorosilicate with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> metal and thoroughly washing away the residual fluorides. English chemist Thomas Thomson coined the name <i>silicon<\/i> in 1817, combining the Latin word <i>silex<\/i> (meaning 'flint') with the suffix <i>-on<\/i> to highlight its chemical structural kinship with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a><\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\">boron<\/a><\/a>.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Characteristics": "<p>In its elemental form, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a><\/a> is a hard, brittle crystalline solid featuring a distinct dark blue-grey metallic lustre. It crystallizes in a face-centered diamond cubic lattice structure\u2014identical to that of diamond\u2014where each <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a> atom is bonded covalently to four neighboring atoms in a rigid tetrahedral symmetry. Pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a> has a density of 2.329 g\/cm\u00b3, a high melting point of 1687 K (1414 \u00b0C), and a boiling point of 3538 K (3265 \u00b0C). Notably, silicon exhibits an unusual physical density anomaly shared with water: it expands by approximately 9% as it transitions from a liquid state into a solid crystal lattice upon freezing.<\/p>\n<p>Electrically, silicon is a classic semiconductor with an indirect energy bandgap of 1.12 electron-volts (eV) at room temperature. At absolute zero temperature, pure silicon acts as a complete electrical insulator because all of its valence electrons are locked tight within covalent bonds. As the temperature rises, ambient thermal energy excites a small fraction of electrons across the bandgap into the conduction band, allowing electrical current to flow. The electrical conductivity of silicon can be precisely engineered over several orders of magnitude through a process called <i>doping<\/i>\u2014deliberately introducing microscopic trace amounts of electron-rich elements like <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a><\/a> (to create n-type semiconductors) or electron-deficient elements like <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\">boron<\/a><\/a> (to create p-type semiconductors).<\/p>\n<p>Chemically, silicon is relatively unreactive at ambient room temperatures. When exposed to air, its surface immediately reacts with atmospheric <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a> to construct a transparent, microscopically thin layer of silicon dioxide (SiO\u2082). This passive oxide skin shields the underlying bulk crystal from further corrosion or chemical attack. Silicon does not react with water or most acids under normal conditions, though it dissolves readily in hot concentrated aqueous alkalis (such as <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a> hydroxide) to produce silicates and release <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a><\/a> gas. At elevated temperatures (> 900 \u00b0C), silicon reacts vigorously with halogens (forming volatile tetrahalides like SiF\u2084 and SiCl\u2084), burns in <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> to yield silica, and reacts with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> to form high-strength ceramics like silicon nitride (Si\u2083N\u2084) and silicon carbide (SiC).<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Isotopes": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">Main article: Isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a><\/a><\/div>\n<p>Naturally occurring <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a><\/a> consists of three stable isotopes: <sup>28<\/sup>Si (making up 92.24% of natural abundance), <sup>29<\/sup>Si (4.67%), and <sup>30<\/sup>Si (3.07%). Among these stable forms, <sup>28<\/sup>Si is the most dominant because it is created directly during stellar fusion through the alpha process (sequential addition of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">helium<\/a> nuclei). The odd-mass isotope <sup>29<\/sup>Si possesses a nuclear spin of I = 1\/2, making it the only natural <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a> isotope usable in Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) and Electron Paramagnetic Resonance (EPR) spectroscopy to analyze molecular structures in chemistry and material science.<\/p>\n<p>In cosmic astrophysics, <sup>28<\/sup>Si plays a central role in stellar evolution through the <i>silicon-burning process<\/i>. During the final, violent stages of nuclear fusion inside massive stars (greater than 8 to 11 times the mass of our Sun), extreme temperatures exceed 3 billion Kelvin. Under these conditions, photodisintegration breaks down nuclei while alpha particles fuse with <sup>28<\/sup>Si to synthesize heavier elements such as <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a><\/a>, and ultimately <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a><\/a>-56 (which decays into <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a>-56). The silicon-burning phase represents the ultimate nuclear fuel stage of a star before its core collapses, resulting in a cataclysmic Type II supernova explosion.<\/p>\n<p>Scientists have characterized 22 radioactive isotopes of silicon, spanning mass numbers from 22 to 45 (with ultrashort-lived <sup>46<\/sup>Si observed in laboratory collisions of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a>-70 with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Be\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Beryllium (Be)\">beryllium<\/a> at particle accelerator facilities). The two longest-lived radioisotopes are <sup>32<\/sup>Si, with a half-life of roughly 157 years, and <sup>31<\/sup>Si, with a half-life of 2.62 hours. All other radioisotopes have half-lives shorter than seven seconds, with the vast majority decaying in less than one-tenth of a second. <sup>32<\/sup>Si undergoes low-energy beta decay into <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a><\/a>-32 and eventually stable <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a><\/a>-32. <sup>31<\/sup>Si is easily generated by exposing natural silicon to neutron bombardment in nuclear reactors, making it a valuable tracer in quantitative activation analysis as it decays via beta emission carrying up to 1.48 MeV of energy to stable <sup>31<\/sup>P.<\/p>\n<p>Silicon isotopes serve as valuable tools in oceanography and climate science. Dissolved silicon enters the oceans through river transport, continental rock weathering, aeolian windblown dust, and deep hydrothermal vents. Because river inputs and deep groundwater flows have distinct <sup>30<\/sup>Si to <sup>28<\/sup>Si isotopic signatures, oceanographers trace variations in marine <sup>30<\/sup>Si levels to reconstruct ancient ocean circulation currents and biological productivity. A distinct deep-water <sup>30<\/sup>Si gradient of over 0.3 parts per thousand exists between the Atlantic and Pacific ocean basins, reflecting the long-term biological removal of silicon by marine plankton.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Occurrence": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/39de794f99d69d9ba4e2e332d2457efd.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"190\" height=\"232\" style=\"--mw-file-upright: 0.75\" class=\"mw-file-element mw-file-upright\" data-file-width=\"327\" data-file-height=\"400\" \/><figcaption>Olivine<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">Silicon<\/a><\/a> is the eighth most abundant element in the cosmos by mass, behind <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">helium<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\">neon<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a><\/a>. On Earth, however, planetary differentiation concentrated <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a> heavily in the outer rocky layers. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">Silicon<\/a> makes up 27.2% of Earth's crust by weight, ranking second only to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> (45.5%), with which it is almost universally bound as silica (SiO\u2082) or complex silicate minerals. Earth's metallic core (comprising ~31.5% of the planet's mass) is composed mostly of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a> alloys (Fe\u2082\u2085Ni\u2082Co\u2080.\u2081S\u2083), whereas the thick mantle (68.1% of Earth's mass) is rich in dense <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a>-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> silicates such as olivine, (Mg,Fe)\u2082SiO\u2084. Lighter siliceous minerals floated to the surface to create the crust (0.4% of Earth's mass).<\/p>\n<p>As molten magma cools and crystallizes within the crust, silicate minerals form in a predictable sequence known as Bowen's reaction series. Dense olivine crystallizes first, followed progressively by pyroxene, amphibole, biotite mica, orthoclase feldspar, muscovite mica, and finally quartz. This sequence reflects a trend toward increasingly complex, interconnected silicon-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> tetrahedra. Over geological timescales, rain and atmosphere weather these igneous rocks, producing sedimentary deposits of clay, shale, and sandstone, while regional metamorphism under heat and pressure creates an immense array of crystalline metamorphic minerals.<\/p>\n<p>Silicon continuously cycles between land and sea through four major oceanic fluxes: continental weathering, riverine transport, dissolution of windborne terrigenous silicates, and hydrothermal reactions along submarine mid-ocean basalts. Every year, windstorms lift between 300 and 900 million tonnes of aeolian dust into Earth's atmosphere, delivering 80 to 240 million tonnes of particulate silicon into the oceans. Massive dust plumes from the Sahara and Gobi deserts supply critical silicon inputs into the North Atlantic and Pacific Oceans respectively, fueling marine biological growth.<\/p>\n<p>India is endowed with vast high-grade silica sand and quartz reserves distributed across major geological formations. The state of <b>Rajasthan<\/b> (with extensive mining belts in Ajmer, Bhilwara, Udaipur, and Alwar) is a leading domestic producer of high-purity quartz and quartzite. <b>Gujarat<\/b> holds immense silica sand deposits in Kutch and Bharuch, supplying raw materials for chemical and glass manufacturing. High-purity silica sand is also mined extensively in Prakasam and Nellore in Andhra Pradesh, while <b>Sankargarh<\/b> near Prayagraj (Uttar Pradesh) stands as one of India's historically premier hubs for glass-grade silica sand, powering the glass, ceramic, and construction industries of South Asia.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Applications": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">Silicon<\/a><\/a> is the indispensable foundation of modern microelectronics and digital computing. Ultra-pure monocrystalline <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a>\u2014refined to an astounding 'nine-nines' purity (99.9999999%) using the Czochralski crystal growth process\u2014is sliced into paper-thin semiconductor wafers. These wafers are etched to create billions of microscopic transistors, microprocessors, memory chips, integrated circuits, and light-emitting diodes that power smartphones, computers, industrial robotics, and internet infrastructure. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">Silicon<\/a> solar photovoltaic (PV) cells convert sunlight directly into clean electricity, driving global renewable energy transformation.<\/p>\n<p>Beyond electronics, silicon is essential in heavy metallurgy and chemical manufacturing. Elemental silicon is alloyed with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a> to produce ferrosilicon, which acts as a powerful deoxidizer and strengthening agent in steelmaking. Silicon-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a> alloys (such as Silumin) exhibit exceptional fluid castability and wear resistance, making them ideal for automotive engine blocks, cylinder heads, and aerospace structures. In organic chemistry, synthetic silicon-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> polymers called <i>silicones<\/i> yield versatile, heat-resistant sealants, lubricants, medical implants, flexible cookware, and cosmetics.<\/p>\n<p>Silica sand and silicates remain fundamental to global infrastructure. Pure quartz sand is melted to make container glass, flat window glass, and ultra-transparent optical fiber cables for high-speed telecommunications. Silicate minerals are essential raw materials for clay pottery, fine porcelain, bricks, and Portland cement\u2014the primary binder in concrete. Industrial synthetic silicon compounds like silicon carbide (carborundum, SiC) serve as super-hard abrasives, cutting tools, bulletproof ceramic armor, and high-power high-temperature semiconductor components.<\/p>\n<p>India is currently advancing its technological leadership through the national <b>India Semiconductor Mission (ISM)<\/b>, an ambitious government initiative designed to establish commercial silicon wafer fabrication facilities, compound semiconductor foundries, and advanced chip packaging (OSAT) hubs nationwide. India's premier scientific institutions contribute significantly to space-grade and defense microelectronics: the <b>Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)<\/b>, through its Semiconductor Laboratory (SCL Mohali), fabricates indigenous space-hardened microprocessors like the 32-bit <i>Vikram<\/i> processor and collaborates with IIT Madras to develop the <i>IRIS<\/i> RISC-V controller chip for satellite navigation and launch vehicles. Meanwhile, researchers at the <b>Indian Institute of Science (IISc, Bengaluru)<\/b> <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a> world-class innovation in silicon photonics, silicon-on-insulator (SOI) microchips, and on-chip electrostatic discharge (ESD) protection for next-generation global microelectronics.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Biological role": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/249d6d32cf723b1a83d4ac06e47996c2.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"190\" height=\"190\" style=\"--mw-file-upright: 0.75\" class=\"mw-file-element mw-file-upright\" data-file-width=\"1600\" data-file-height=\"1600\" \/><figcaption>A diatom, enclosed in a silica cell wall<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p>Although <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a><\/a> is abundant in rocks and sand, very few organisms can metabolize it directly. Marine organisms such as diatoms, radiolarians, and siliceous glass sponges extract soluble orthosilicic acid (H\u2084SiO\u2084) from seawater to construct intricate, jewel-like microscopic cell walls and skeletons composed of biogenic amorphous silica (SiO\u2082\u00b7nH\u2082O). Diatoms alone generate over 20% of Earth's <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> and form the biological foundation of marine food webs; when they die, their silica frustules sink to the ocean seabed, creating thick deposits of diatomaceous earth used industrially in filtration, agriculture, and thermal insulation.<\/p>\n<p>In terrestrial biology, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a> is a vital beneficial nutrient for many plants, particularly monocots like grasses, sugarcane, bamboo, and rice. Roots absorb orthosilicic acid from soil water and transport it through xylem vessels. Within plant tissues, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a> precipitates into rigid cell wall complexes and microscopic opal deposits known as <i>phytoliths<\/i>. This structural reinforcement stiffens plant stems, keeping leaves positioned to capture sunlight and preventing crop lodging (falling over during storms). Silicon also functions as an active biochemical defense: high silica content wears down the mouthparts of herbivorous insects, creates a physical barrier against fungal pathogens like rice blast disease (<i>Magnaporthe oryzae<\/i>), and triggers plant defense signaling pathways that produce protective phytoalexins and volatile organic compounds.<\/p>\n<p>In Indian agriculture, silicon plays an indispensable role in maintaining paddy (rice) crop productivity. India is the world's second-largest producer of rice, a crop that absorbs more silicon than almost any other cultivated plant. Agricultural research by the Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI) and ICAR has demonstrated that applying silicon fertilizers to Indian paddy soils dramatically increases grain yield, enhances climate resilience against severe monsoon winds, reduces dependence on chemical fungicides, and neutralizes soil toxicities caused by excess heavy metals like <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminium (Al)\">aluminium<\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">arsenic<\/a>.<\/p>\n<p>In human health, trace amounts of silicon are necessary for optimal bone mineralization, cartilage synthesis, and maintaining structural elasticity in skin, hair, nails, and blood vessel walls. In astrobiology, silicon is widely studied as the most plausible alternative to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a><\/a> for hypothetical extraterrestrial life. Because silicon sits directly below <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> in group 14, it shares the ability to form four covalent bonds and create complex chains and rings (such as silanes and silicones), offering a theoretical chemical framework for life under extreme extra-terrestrial environments.<\/p>" } }, "P": { "symbol": "P", "name": "Phosphorus", "atomic": 15, "category": "polyatomic nonmetal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">Phosphorus<\/a><\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>P<\/b>, atomic number 15) is a highly reactive polyatomic nonmetal essential to all living things. Named from the Greek word for \"light-bearer,\" <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a> glows faintly in the dark when exposed to air due to slow oxidation. Because it reacts so readily with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> and other elements, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a> is never found as a free element on Earth; instead, it is mined from abundant phosphate rocks. Phosphorus exists in several distinct forms (allotropes), including hyper-reactive white phosphorus, stable red phosphorus used in safety matches, and semiconducting black phosphorus. From forming the structural backbone of DNA and powering cellular energy to nourishing agricultural crops worldwide, phosphorus is a fundamental building block of life.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/6\/6d\/Phosphorus-purple.jpg", "atomic_mass": 30.9737619985, "density": 1.823, "melt": null, "boil": null, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Hennig Brand", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p3", "electronegativity_pauling": 2.19, "electron_affinity": 72.037, "ionization_energies": [ 1011.8, 1907, 2914.1, 4963.6, 6273.9, 21267, 25431, 29872, 35905, 40950, 46261, 54110, 59024, 271791, 296195 ], "sections": { "History": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-left\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/abc53f207a48982969e0a6955319a7e9.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"190\" height=\"246\" style=\"--mw-file-upright: 0.75\" class=\"mw-file-element mw-file-upright\" data-file-width=\"4724\" data-file-height=\"6126\" \/><figcaption><i>The Alchemist in Search of the Philosophers Stone<\/i> (1771), by Joseph Wright, depicting Hennig Brand discovering <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a><\/a>.<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">Phosphorus<\/a><\/a> holds a special place in chemical history as the very first element discovered whose existence was unknown to ancient civilizations. Its discovery is credited to the Hamburg alchemist Hennig Brand in 1669. Brand was attempting to create the legendary Philosopher's Stone\u2014a mythical substance believed to turn base metals into <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\">gold<\/a>. Reasoning that human urine contained secret life-giving properties, he collected large quantities, allowed it to rot, boiled it down to a thick paste, and distilled it at intense heat. When he cooled the resulting vapors under water, he obtained a white, waxy substance that glowed mysteriously in the dark and burst into brilliant white flames when exposed to air. He named it <i><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a> mirabilis<\/i>, Latin for 'miraculous bearer of light'. The word itself traces back to Ancient Greek <i>Ph\u014dsphoros<\/i> ('light-bearer'), which originally referred to the god of the morning star, the planet Venus.<\/p>\n<p>Brand kept his recipe secret at first, but later sold it for 200 thalers to Johann Daniel Kraft of Dresden. Kraft toured Europe demonstrating the glowing miracle, eventually visiting London where he met the pioneering natural philosopher Robert Boyle. News of the mysterious source leaked out, enabling German chemist Johann Kunckel to reproduce phosphorus in Sweden in 1678. By 1680, Robert Boyle independently perfected its manufacture, using sand in the reaction to react with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a> metaphosphate and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a>: 4 NaPO<sub>3<\/sub> + 2 SiO<sub>2<\/sub> + 10 C \u2192 2 Na<sub>2<\/sub>SiO<sub>3<\/sub> + 10 CO + P<sub>4<\/sub>. Boyle used phosphorus to ignite <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a><\/a>-tipped wooden splints\u2014the direct predecessors of modern matches. His assistant, Ambrose Godfrey-Hanckwitz, turned phosphorus production into a profitable commercial business.<\/p>\n<p>In 1769, Swedish chemists Johan Gottlieb Gahn and Carl Wilhelm Scheele discovered that bones are rich in <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a><\/a> phosphate. By treating bone ash with sulfuric acid, dehydrating the product, and distilling it with charcoal, they produced elemental white phosphorus on a larger scale. In 1777, Antoine Lavoisier officially recognized phosphorus as a distinct chemical element. Bone ash remained the world's main industrial source of phosphorus until the mid-19th century.<\/p>\n<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-left\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/032507c794ce8faa1bd8550962815850.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"190\" height=\"249\" style=\"--mw-file-upright: 0.75\" class=\"mw-file-element mw-file-upright\" data-file-width=\"558\" data-file-height=\"730\" \/><figcaption>Guano mining in the Central Chincha Islands, c. 1860<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-left\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/86214456f0feaae5939ea9b41eb0307f.JPG\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"167\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"5472\" data-file-height=\"3648\" \/><figcaption>Matches from 1828. The <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a><\/a>-tipped match is dipped into liquid containing white phosphorus, and ignites as it is pulled out of the bottle.<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-left\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/f2528328539af0f023a5ff1363c4ec59.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"194\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"8310\" data-file-height=\"6436\" \/><figcaption>A worker tends an electric phosphate smelting furnace in Muscle Shoals, Alabama, 1942<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-left\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/133086dfa508ea4c29f769f08fc8c414.gif\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"188\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"2956\" data-file-height=\"2224\" \/><figcaption>White phosphorus shell explosion in France during the First World War (1918)<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p>Agriculture took a giant leap forward through phosphorus history. In 1609, Inca Garcilaso de la Vega described how indigenous South American civilizations harvested guano (accumulated seabird droppings) as an extraordinarily rich crop fertilizer. In the early 1800s, explorer Alexander von Humboldt introduced guano to Europe, kicking off a global fertilizer boom. By the late 19th century, guano reserves were heavily depleted, paving the way for mineral phosphate rock mining and superphosphate chemical fertilizers.<\/p>\n<p>Early friction matches, invented by Charles Sauria in 1830, contained white phosphorus. However, these matches were notoriously dangerous. Match factory workers suffered from severe industrial poisoning known as \"phossy jaw\"\u2014a painful necrosis of the jawbone caused by inhaling white phosphorus fumes. Public outrage over these conditions led to famous labor protests, including the 1888 London Matchgirls' strike. The discovery of non-toxic red phosphorus allowed safety matches to be developed. In 1900, French chemists Henri S\u00e9v\u00e8ne and Emile David Cahen introduced phosphorus sesquisulfide (P<sub>4<\/sub>S<sub>3<\/sub>) for safe strike-anywhere matches. By 1906, international treaties under the Berne Convention banned white phosphorus in matches worldwide.<\/p>\n<p>In 1888, James Burgess Readman patented the submerged-arc electric furnace, enabling large-scale industrial production of white phosphorus directly from phosphate rock. Sadly, this high volume also made phosphorus a terrifying weapon of war.
