In World War I, white phosphorus was used in incendiary bullets to shoot down <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a><\/a>-filled Zeppelins, as well as in smoke screens and tracer rounds. In World War II, white phosphorus hand grenades (M15, M34, No 77) and incendiary bombs were deployed on a massive scale, including the destructive bombing of Hamburg\u2014ironically the very city where Brand had discovered phosphorus three centuries earlier.<\/p>\n<p>Ancient Indian literature poetically captured humanity's wonder with luminescent materials. Treatises on gemology (<i>Ratna Shastra<\/i>) and texts like the <i>Garuda Purana<\/i> described self-illuminating gems called <i>Jyotirmani<\/i> that glowed in the dark. In modern Indian history, the matchstick industry established deep roots in the 1920s with Wimco in Maharashtra and transformed into a thriving national industry clustered around Kovilpatti and Sivakasi in Tamil Nadu, which pioneered safe red-phosphorus match manufacturing for millions of homes across India.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">", "Characteristics": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">Phosphorus<\/a><\/a> is a nonmetal located in Group 15 (the pnictogens) and Period 3 of the periodic table, with an atomic number of 15 and ground-state electron configuration 1s<sup>2<\/sup> 2s<sup>2<\/sup> 2p<sup>6<\/sup> 3s<sup>2<\/sup> 3p<sup>3<\/sup>. Having five valence electrons, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a> forms diverse chemical bonds and exhibits oxidation states ranging from \u22123 in phosphine gas (PH<sub>3<\/sub>) to +5 in phosphoric acid (H<sub>3<\/sub>PO<sub>4<\/sub>) and inorganic phosphate rocks.<\/p>\n<p>Because <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a> reacts so vigorously with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a>, it never occurs as a free element in nature. Instead, pure phosphorus exists in several dramatically different physical forms, called allotropes:<\/p>\n<p><b>White Phosphorus (P<sub>4<\/sub>):<\/b> Composed of tetrahedral molecules where four phosphorus atoms form a tight, strained pyramid. It is a soft, translucent, waxy solid that is extremely toxic and volatile. White phosphorus spontaneously catches fire in air at room temperature (around 30 \u00b0C), making it pyrophoric. Because of this high reactivity, it must be stored under water. In the dark, white phosphorus glows with an eerie greenish light due to chemiluminescence\u2014a faint light produced as it slowly reacts with atmospheric <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a>.<\/p>\n<p><b>Red Phosphorus:<\/b> Formed by heating white phosphorus to 250 \u00b0C in the absence of air. Red phosphorus forms a complex polymeric chain structure. It is non-toxic, far less reactive, stable in air, and does not catch fire spontaneously. It is the safe red material used on the striking strips of modern matchboxes.<\/p>\n<p><b>Black Phosphorus & Phosphorene:<\/b> Created by heating white phosphorus under high pressure, black phosphorus is the thermodynamically most stable allotrope. It features a puckered, honeycomb-like layered lattice resembling graphite and conducts electricity as a semiconductor. When isolated into single-atom-thick two-dimensional sheets, it forms <i>phosphorene<\/i>. Unlike graphene, which lacks an intrinsic bandgap, phosphorene possesses a direct, tunable bandgap and high charge carrier mobility, making it a superstar candidate for futuristic nanoelectronics and flexible light sensors.<\/p>\n<p><b>Violet (Hittorf's) Phosphorus:<\/b> A complex monoclinic crystal structure produced by dissolving red phosphorus in molten <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a><\/a> and cooling it slowly.<\/p>\n<p>In modern Indian science, premier research institutions such as the Indian Institute of Science (IISc, Bengaluru), IIT Delhi, and CSIR laboratories (like CSIR-CECRI in Karaikudi) are leading advanced studies on phosphorene nanomaterials. Indian researchers are developing protective polymer coatings to prevent phosphorene from degrading in ambient air and engineering phosphorus-based nanocomposites as high-capacity anodes for next-generation <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a>-ion and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a>-ion batteries.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Isotopes": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">Main article: Isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a><\/a><\/div>\n<p>Scientists have identified 22 isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a><\/a>, ranging from <sup>26<\/sup>P to <sup>47<\/sup>P. However, naturally occurring <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a> consists entirely of a single stable isotope: <b>phosphorus-31 (<sup>31<\/sup>P)<\/b>, giving it a 100% natural abundance. Because <sup>31<\/sup>P has a nuclear spin of 1\/2 and high abundance, <sup>31<\/sup>P Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is a powerful analytical technique used by chemists worldwide to determine the structure of phosphorus-bearing organic and inorganic compounds.<\/p>\n<p>Among its synthetic radioactive isotopes, two hold immense importance in biological research and medical diagnostics:<\/p>\n<p><b>Phosphorus-32 (<sup>32<\/sup>P):<\/b> A strong beta-particle emitter (1.71 MeV energy) with a half-life of 14.3 days. In life science laboratories, <sup>32<\/sup>P is routinely incorporated into nucleic acids to create radiolabeled DNA and RNA probes for Northern and Southern blot analyses. Because its high-energy beta rays can penetrate skin and eyes, laboratory workers must wear protective gear and work behind low-density plastic or acrylic shields. Dense shielding materials like <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a><\/a> are avoided because high-energy beta particles striking heavy atoms produce secondary X-rays known as Bremsstrahlung (\"braking radiation\").<\/p>\n<p><b>Phosphorus-33 (<sup>33<\/sup>P):<\/b> A gentler beta emitter (0.25 MeV energy) with a half-life of 25.4 days. Its lower energy emissions make it ideal for delicate applications such as high-resolution DNA sequencing.<\/p>\n<p>In India, nuclear and agricultural scientists at the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) in Mumbai work alongside researchers at the Indian Agricultural Research Institute (ICAR-IARI, New Delhi) using <sup>32<\/sup>P radiotracers. By injecting <sup>32<\/sup>P-labeled fertilizers into experimental soils, Indian scientists precisely track how plant roots absorb phosphorus, enabling farmers across India to maximize Phosphorus Use Efficiency (PUE) and boost agricultural productivity.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Biological role": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">Phosphorus<\/a><\/a> is an absolute necessity for life on Earth. An adult human body contains roughly 700 grams of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a>, making it one of the most abundant minerals in human biology. It plays critical structural, energy, and genetic roles across every living cell:<\/p>\n<p><b>DNA and RNA Backbone:<\/b> Phosphate groups (PO<sub>4<\/sub><sup>3\u2212<\/sup>) form the rigid sugar-phosphate side-chains that link genetic building blocks together, creating the famous double-helix structure of DNA and RNA that stores and executes genetic instructions.<\/p>\n<p><b>Cellular Energy Currency:<\/b> Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP) is the universal energy molecule used by all living organisms. When cells break one of ATP's high-energy phosphate bonds to form ADP (adenosine diphosphate), energy is released to power muscle contractions, nerve signals, protein synthesis, and cellular transport.<\/p>\n<p><b>Cell Membranes:<\/b> Phospholipids\u2014molecules with a water-loving phosphate head and oil-loving fatty acid tail\u2014assemble into double-layered membranes (bilayers) that wrap around every cell, regulating what enters and leaves.<\/p>\n<p><b>Bones and Teeth:<\/b> Approximately 85% of body <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a> combines with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a><\/a> to form <i>hydroxyapatite<\/i> [Ca<sub>10<\/sub>(PO<sub>4<\/sub>)<sub>6<\/sub>(OH)<sub>2<\/sub>], the hard mineral matrix that gives structural rigidity to skeletons and teeth enamel.<\/p>\n<p><b>Plant Growth & Agriculture:<\/b> In plants, phosphorus is one of the three primary macronutrients (N-P-K), essential for vigorous root development, photosynthesis, early flowering, seed production, and crop maturation.<\/p>\n<p>In Indian agriculture, soil health is a primary national focus. Many Indian soils, particularly acidic red soils and alkaline calcareous soils, tend to bind added phosphorus into insoluble compounds of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a>, or <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a>, making it difficult for crops to absorb. Under India's national Soil Health Card initiative, agricultural scientists at ICAR recommend using Phosphate Solubilizing Bacteria (PSB) such as <i>Pseudomonas<\/i> and <i>Bacillus<\/i> species alongside bio-fertilizers. These friendly microbes release natural organic acids that dissolve fixed soil phosphorus, restoring soil fertility for Indian farmers growing staple crops like paddy, wheat, and pulses.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Applications": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">This section is about the applications of elemental <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a><\/a>. For the applications of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a><\/a> compounds, see <a class=\"mw-selflink-fragment\" href=\"#Compounds\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">Phosphorus<\/a><\/a> \u00a7 Compounds<\/a>.<\/div>\n<p>Elemental <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a> and its chemical compounds are vital to modern industry, agriculture, and high technology:<\/p>\n<p><b>Agricultural Fertilizers:<\/b> Over 90% of all mined phosphate rock is converted into agricultural fertilizers. Primary phosphatic fertilizers include Single Superphosphate (SSP), Di-ammonium Phosphate (DAP), and Mono-ammonium Phosphate (MAP), which replenish soil phosphorus and feed billions of people across the globe.<\/p>\n<p><b>Matches and Pyrotechnics:<\/b> Red phosphorus is a vital ingredient on the friction striking surface of safety matchboxes, reacting with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a><\/a> chlorate on match heads to ignite safely. Phosphorus sesquisulfide (P<sub>4<\/sub>S<sub>3<\/sub>) is used in strike-anywhere matches, while elemental phosphorus powers military smoke screens and signaling flares.<\/p>\n<p><b>Food & Industrial Chemistry:<\/b> Phosphoric acid (H<sub>3<\/sub>PO<sub>4<\/sub>) gives cola soft drinks their characteristic sharp, tangy flavor and acts as a rust converter on steel. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">Sodium<\/a> tripolyphosphate (STPP) is used in water softening and detergent formulations, while <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a> phosphates act as leavening agents in baking powder and polishing agents in toothpaste.<\/p>\n<p><b>Metallurgy & Semiconductors:<\/b> Phosphorus serves as a deoxidizer in <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a> and bronze alloys, producing durable <i>phosphor bronze<\/i> used in heavy-duty springs, bearings, and musical instruments. In electronics, tiny amounts of high-purity phosphorus are added as an n-type dopant to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a> wafers to create microprocessors and solar cells.<\/p>\n<p><b>Geographical & Industrial Significance in India:<\/b><\/p>\n<p>India plays a major role in the global phosphorus economy. The <b>Jhamarkotra Rock Phosphate Mine<\/b>, located near Udaipur in Rajasthan and operated by Rajasthan State Mines and Minerals Limited (RSMML), is India's largest indigenous commercial deposit of rock phosphate. It yields high-grade stromatolitic phosphorite (+30% to 34% P<sub>2<\/sub>O<sub>5<\/sub>) crucial for domestic fertilizer production.<\/p>\n<p>To support India's Green Revolution and ensure national food security, domestic fertilizer giants like <b>IFFCO<\/b> (Indian Farmers Fertiliser Cooperative), <b>Coromandel International<\/b>, and <b>GSFC<\/b> process millions of tonnes of phosphate rock into DAP and SSP fertilizers every year. Meanwhile, the industrial cluster around <b>Sivakasi<\/b> and <b>Kovilpatti<\/b> in Tamil Nadu forms India's matchstick and safety pyrotechnics capital, producing safety matches using red phosphorus formulations for consumers across South Asia.<\/p>\n<div style=\"clear:both;\" class=\"\"><\/div>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">" } }, "S": { "symbol": "S", "name": "Sulfur", "atomic": 16, "category": "polyatomic nonmetal", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 16 (S)", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">Sulfur<\/a><\/a><\/b> (also spelled <b>sulphur<\/b>) is a nonmetallic chemical element with symbol <b>S<\/b> and atomic number 16. Recognized by its brilliant lemon-yellow color, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a> is one of nature's most abundant and versatile elements. At room temperature, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a> atoms group together into crown-shaped octatomic rings with the chemical formula S<sub>8<\/sub>. Known since antiquity as <i>brimstone<\/i> (or <i>Gandhak<\/i> in ancient India), sulfur plays a crucial role in modern life\u2014from fertilizing crops and manufacturing rubber to powering advanced batteries. In August 2023, India's historic <b>Chandrayaan-3<\/b> mission made international headlines by confirming the unambiguous presence of sulfur on the surface of the Moon's South Pole.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/2\/23\/Native_sulfur_%28Vodinskoe_Deposit%3B_quarry_near_Samara%2C_Russia%29_9.jpg", "atomic_mass": 32.06, "density": 2.07, "melt": 388.36, "boil": 717.8, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Ancient china", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p4", "electronegativity_pauling": 2.58, "electron_affinity": 200.4101, "ionization_energies": [ 999.6, 2252, 3357, 4556, 7004.3, 8495.8, 27107, 31719, 36621, 43177, 48710, 54460, 62930, 68216, 311048, 337138 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p>Located in Group 16 of the periodic table directly below <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a><\/a> is a polyatomic nonmetal prized for its remarkable chemical versatility. In its pure elemental form at room temperature, it exists as a soft, crystalline solid with a vivid lemon-yellow hue. Pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a> is completely odorless; the pungent 'rotten egg' odor often associated with it comes from <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> sulfide gas (H<sub>2<\/sub>S) or organic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a> compounds rather than the element itself.<\/p>\n<p>Sulfur is multivalent, meaning its atoms can share or gain different numbers of electrons depending on what they react with. This allows sulfur to form a vast array of chemical compounds, ranging from volcanic gases and mineral sulfides to essential biological proteins. Its ability to bond with nearly every other element on the periodic table makes it an indispensable pillar of both geology and biochemistry.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Physical properties": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-left\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/fbeef40435b8c6e1d603791874012321.png\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"190\" height=\"228\" style=\"--mw-file-upright: 0.75\" class=\"mw-file-element mw-file-upright\" data-file-width=\"440\" data-file-height=\"528\" \/><figcaption>As a solid, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a><\/a> is a characteristic lemon yellow; when burned, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a><\/a> melts into a blood-red liquid and emits a blue flame.<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">Sulfur<\/a><\/a> is famous for taking on several distinct physical forms, known as allotropes. The most famous and stable allotrope at room temperature is octasulfur (cyclo-S<sub>8<\/sub>), where eight sulfur atoms interlock to form a puckered, crown-like ring. This ring structure possesses high symmetry (point group D<sub>4d<\/sub>) and zero electric dipole moment (0 D). Solid octasulfur is soft, bright yellow, odorless, and has a density of roughly 2 g\/cm\u00b3. All stable solid allotropes of sulfur are excellent electrical insulators.<\/p>\n<p>When heated, sulfur undergoes fascinating phase changes. At room temperature, it exists as &alpha;-octasulfur. When warmed to 95.2 &deg;C (203.4 &deg;F)\u2014well below its melting point\u2014it slowly transforms into &beta;-octasulfur. This phase change alters how the S<sub>8<\/sub> rings pack together without breaking the rings themselves. Pure sulfur melts at 115.21 &deg;C (239.38 &deg;F) into a mobile, pale-yellow liquid consisting mostly of &beta;-S<sub>8<\/sub> molecules. When cooled, molten sulfur freezes at 119.6 &deg;C (247.3 &deg;F).<\/p>\n<p>As liquid sulfur is heated further between its melting point and boiling point (444.6 &deg;C \/ 832.3 &deg;F), it transforms into &gamma;-sulfur. Uniquely, as the temperature rises past 160 &deg;C, the liquid grows thicker and more viscous instead of becoming runnier. This occurs because the S<sub>8<\/sub> rings snap open and link together into long, tangled polymer chains. Above 200 &deg;C (392 &deg;F), the liquid turns a dark blood-red color, and at even higher temperatures, extreme heat breaks these long chains apart (depolymerization), causing the liquid to become thin and fluid once again. When ignited in air, sulfur melts into a dark red liquid and burns with a striking blue flame, releasing sulfur dioxide gas.<\/p>\n<p>Sulfur also undergoes noticeable sublimation (evaporating directly from a solid to a gas) at temperatures between 20 &deg;C (68 &deg;F) and 50 &deg;C (122 &deg;F), and sublimates rapidly in boiling water at 100 &deg;C (212 &deg;F). Elemental sulfur is completely insoluble in water, but it dissolves readily in nonpolar solvents such as <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> disulfide (CS<sub>2<\/sub>), benzene, toluene, and supercritical <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> dioxide (CO<sub>2<\/sub>).<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Chemical properties": "<p>Under normal conditions, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a><\/a> reacts very slowly with water through a process called hydrolysis. Water protons adsorb onto S<sub>8<\/sub> molecular clusters, causing the <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a> to undergo disproportionation (simultaneously oxidizing and reducing) into <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> sulfide (H<sub>2<\/sub>S) gas and sulfuric acid (H<sub>2<\/sub>SO<sub>4<\/sub>):<\/p>\n<div class=\"block-indent\"><span class=\"frac\"><span class=\"num\">1<\/span>&#8260;<span class=\"den\">2<\/span><\/span> S<sub>8<\/sub> + 4 H<sub>2<\/sub>O &rarr; 3 H<sub>2<\/sub>S + H<sub>2<\/sub>SO<sub>4<\/sub><\/div>\n<div class=\"thumb tmulti floatleft\"><div class=\"thumbinner multiimageinner\" style=\"width:100px;max-width:100px\"><div class=\"trow\"><div class=\"tsingle\" style=\"width:90px;max-width:90px\"><div class=\"thumbimage\" style=\"height:167px;overflow:hidden\"><span typeof=\"mw:File\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/73838df46d65b602ab6e53372fcdc274.png\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"88\" height=\"167\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"426\" data-file-height=\"810\" \/><\/span><\/div><\/div><\/div><div class=\"trow\"><div class=\"tsingle\" style=\"width:90px;max-width:90px\"><div class=\"thumbimage\" style=\"height:124px;overflow:hidden\"><span typeof=\"mw:File\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/ecb9ac1c35c77f87ea9dbed7a17397e7.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"88\" height=\"124\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"660\" data-file-height=\"932\" \/><\/span><\/div><\/div><\/div><div class=\"trow\" style=\"display:flex\"><div class=\"thumbcaption\">Top: Liquid <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a><\/a> sulfide inside a test tube. Bottom: A bottle of sulfuric acid.<\/div><\/div><\/div><\/div>\n<p>The chemical behavior and oxidation states of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a> depend heavily on temperature, energy input, and catalysts. Its second, fourth, and sixth ionization energies are 2,252 kJ\/mol, 4,556 kJ\/mol, and 8,495.8 kJ\/mol, respectively. When sulfur burns in air under normal conditions, it reacts with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a> to form sulfur dioxide (SO<sub>2<\/sub>), where sulfur has an oxidation state of +4. To reach its maximum oxidation state of +6 and form sulfur trioxide (SO<sub>3<\/sub>), temperatures must be raised to 400\u2013600 &deg;C (750\u20131,100 &deg;F) in the presence of a catalyst like <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">vanadium<\/a> pentoxide.<\/p>\n<p>When sulfur reacts with elements less electronegative than itself\u2014such as metals or <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a><\/a>\u2014it acts as an oxidizing agent, gaining electrons to adopt an oxidation state of \u22122 and forming sulfides. Sulfur is extremely reactive overall, forming compounds with almost every element on the periodic table except noble gases. It even reacts at elevated temperatures with notoriously unreactive noble metals like <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ir\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iridium (Ir)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ir\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iridium (Ir)\">iridium<\/a><\/a> to yield <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ir\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iridium (Ir)\">iridium<\/a> disulfide (IrS<sub>2<\/sub>).<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Isotopes": "<div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">Main article: Isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a><\/a><\/div>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">Sulfur<\/a><\/a> has 23 known isotopes, four of which are stable: <sup>32<\/sup>S (94.99% &plusmn; 0.26%), <sup>33<\/sup>S (0.75% &plusmn; 0.02%), <sup>34<\/sup>S (4.25% &plusmn; 0.24%), and <sup>36<\/sup>S (0.01% &plusmn; 0.01%). The overwhelming dominance of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a>-32 (<sup>32<\/sup>S) is due to cosmic nucleosynthesis: it is forged in massive exploding stars (supernovae) during alpha-process fusion reactions. Other stable isotopes like <sup>33<\/sup>S and <sup>34<\/sup>S are formed in secondary stellar bypass processes, with novae explosions contributing a higher proportion of <sup>33<\/sup>S than supernovae.<\/p>\n<p>The ratio between the two most abundant stable isotopes\u2014sulfur-32 and sulfur-34 (expressed as &delta;<sup>34<\/sup>S)\u2014varies noticeably across different geological and environmental samples. Measuring this isotope ratio provides scientists with a powerful chemical clock and environmental tracer. It allows geologists to age-date mineral ores, estimate temperatures of ancient ore-water reactions, determine pH and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> fugacity during ore formation, and trace sulfate-reducing bacteria in marine sediments. Microbes in ocean sediments take in sulfate and process lighter <sup>32<\/sup>S faster than <sup>34<\/sup>S, fractionating sulfur isotopes by up to 66 permil (66&permil;).<\/p>\n<p>In ecology, sulfur isotope signatures help track environmental pollution and water cycles. In forest ecosystems, atmospheric rainfall and rock weathering contribute distinct sulfur signatures. For instance, isotope measurements in Rocky Mountain lakes have enabled researchers to distinguish atmospheric pollution sources from natural watershed runoff.<\/p>\n<p>Among radioactive isotopes, sulfur-35 (<sup>35<\/sup>S) is the most significant, with a half-life of 87.37 days. All other radioisotopes of sulfur decay in under 3 hours. Natural <sup>35<\/sup>S is formed in trace amounts when high-energy cosmic rays strike atmospheric <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a><\/a> (<sup>40<\/sup>Ar). In laboratories, <sup>35<\/sup>S is produced by neutron bombardment of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a><\/a> chloride (<sup>35<\/sup>Cl + n &rarr; <sup>35<\/sup>S + p). Because <sup>35<\/sup>S emits low-energy beta radiation, it served as a crucial radioactive tracer in molecular biology\u2014most notably in the famous 1952 Hershey-Chase experiment that definitively proved DNA, not protein, carries genetic information. Its low radiation energy makes compounds containing <sup>35<\/sup>S relatively safe to handle with standard laboratory precautions.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "History": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">Sulfur<\/a><\/a> is one of the few chemical elements that has been known and utilized since prehistoric times. Because it naturally occurs as bright yellow mineral deposits around active volcanoes and hot springs, ancient civilizations across the globe gathered and experimented with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a> long before modern chemistry emerged. In ancient Germanic and English traditions, it was named <i>brimstone<\/i> (literally \"burning stone\"). The ancient Egyptian Ebers Papyrus (c. 1500 BC) described <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a> ointments for treating eyelid inflammation, while the ancient Greek poet Homer documented its use as a medicinal fumigant.<\/p>\n<p>In ancient India, sulfur held a sacred and medical status, known in Sanskrit as <b>Gandhak<\/b> (\u0917\u0928\u094d\u0927\u0915, meaning \"the odorous one\"). In the classical Indian alchemical tradition of <b>Rasa Shastra<\/b> (iatrochemistry), sulfur was classified as a paramount <i>Uparasa<\/i> (vital mineral secondary to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\">mercury<\/a>). Ancient Indian alchemists discovered that combining purified sulfur with liquid <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\">mercury<\/a><\/a> (<i>Parada<\/i>) created <i>Kajjali<\/i> (black <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\">mercury<\/a> sulfide)\u2014a fundamental matrix used to formulate celebrated Ayurvedic medicines such as <i>Gandhak Rasayan<\/i>, <i>Rasa-Sindoor<\/i>, and <i>Makardhwaj<\/i>. To ensure safety and medicinal efficacy, ancient texts mandated a rigorous purification ritual called <i>Shodhana<\/i>, where raw sulfur was melted and repeatedly poured into warm cow's milk or herbal juices (such as <i>Bhringraj<\/i>) to eliminate impurities before compounding.<\/p>\n<p>In ancient China (3rd century BC), sulfur was called <i>Liuhuang<\/i>. By the 9th century AD, Chinese alchemists combined sulfur, charcoal (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a><\/a>), and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> nitrate (saltpeter) to invent gunpowder (<i>huoyao<\/i>), a breakthrough that permanently altered human history and warfare. In 1777, French chemist Antoine Lavoisier performed rigorous combustion experiments that proved sulfur was an elemental substance rather than a compound containing phlogiston. Industrial sulfur mining exploded in 1894 when German-American engineer Herman Frasch invented the Frasch process, which injected superheated water underground to melt sulfur deposits and pump pure liquid sulfur to the surface.<\/p>\n<p>In August 2023, sulfur added a monumental new chapter to space exploration. India's <b>Chandrayaan-3<\/b> mission landed on the Moon, and its <i>Pragyan<\/i> rover used Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy (LIBS) and Alpha Particle X-ray Spectroscope (APXS) instruments to achieve the world's first in-situ confirmation of sulfur at the lunar South Pole. This landmark discovery provides deep clues about lunar volcanic history and offers critical raw materials for building future human bases on the Moon.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Applications": "<p>Elemental <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a><\/a> is one of the most vital raw materials driving global industry. Over 85% of all harvested <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a> is converted into sulfuric acid (H<sub>2<\/sub>SO<sub>4<\/sub>)\u2014often nicknamed the \"king of chemicals.\" Sulfuric acid is the single most produced industrial chemical worldwide, serving as the essential catalyst and ingredient for manufacturing superphosphate and ammonium sulfate fertilizers, which nourish agricultural crops that feed billions of people across the globe.<\/p>\n<p>Another major industrial application of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a> is the vulcanization of rubber, discovered by Charles Goodyear in 1839. By heating raw sticky rubber with sulfur, sulfur atoms form durable chemical cross-links between polymer chains. This turns soft rubber into tough, elastic, heat-resistant vulcanized rubber, which is used to produce vehicle tires, conveyor belts, shoe soles, and industrial hoses.<\/p>\n<p>In energy storage and green technology, sulfur is spearheading next-generation battery development. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">Lithium<\/a>-Sulfur (Li-S) batteries offer theoretical energy densities up to five times higher than current <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a>-ion batteries at a fraction of the cost and weight. Premier Indian research institutions like CSIR, IISc, and IITs, alongside ISRO space scientists, are actively pioneering advanced Li-S battery technologies to power electric vehicles, renewable energy grids, and space exploration missions.<\/p>\n<p>Sulfur also plays prominent roles in agriculture, medicine, and consumer products. Powdered sulfur is applied directly to crops as an organic fungicide and pesticide to combat mildew, as well as a soil amendment to lower the pH of alkaline soils. In medicine, sulfur's antimicrobial and antifungal properties make it a popular active ingredient in acne treatments, medicated soaps, and anti-dandruff shampoos. It is also used in manufacturing matches, fireworks, black powder, synthetic detergents, pulp and paper bleaching, and pharmaceuticals.<\/p>\n<p>Following ISRO's Chandrayaan-3 discovery of sulfur at the lunar south pole, space scientists are designing methods to use lunar sulfur as a localized building block. By mixing sulfur with lunar regolith (soil), astronaut engineers can produce \"sulfur concrete\"\u2014a water-free, durable construction material ideally suited for building radiation-shielded habitats and landing pads on the Moon without transporting heavy materials from Earth.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Biological role": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">Sulfur<\/a><\/a> is an essential element required by every living organism on Earth. In the human body, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a> ranks as the eighth most abundant element by mass. An average 70 kg (150 lb) adult body contains about 140 grams (4.9 oz) of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a>\u2014roughly equal to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a><\/a> and slightly more than <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a> or <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a><\/a>.<\/p>\n<p>Humans obtain sulfur primarily through dietary proteins containing sulfur-bearing amino acids: <b>methionine<\/b> and <b>cysteine<\/b>. Methionine is an essential amino acid that initiates protein synthesis, while cysteine contains reactive thiol (-SH) groups that form strong disulfide bridges between protein chains. These disulfide bonds act as structural staples, providing strength and elasticity to tough structural proteins like keratin in human hair, skin, and nails, as well as maintaining the 3D folded shapes of enzymes and antibodies.<\/p>\n<p>Sulfur is also an essential component of vital vitamins and coenzymes, including thiamine (vitamin B<sub>1<\/sub>), biotin (vitamin B<sub>7<\/sub>), and Coenzyme A. Furthermore, sulfur forms part of <b>glutathione<\/b>\u2014the body's master antioxidant\u2014which neutralizes toxic free radicals and protects cellular DNA from oxidative damage. In plants, sulfur is indispensable for synthesizing chlorophyll and plant proteins; sulfur-deficient plants develop yellowing leaves and stunted growth, underscoring its crucial role in agricultural food chains.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">" } }, "Cl": { "symbol": "Cl", "name": "Chlorine", "atomic": 17, "category": "diatomic nonmetal", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 17 (Cl)", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">Chlorine<\/a><\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>Cl<\/b>, atomic number 17) is a yellow-green, highly reactive gas at room temperature and the second-lightest member of the halogen family, sitting right between <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a><\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Br\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Bromine (Br)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Br\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Bromine (Br)\">bromine<\/a><\/a> on the periodic table. Known for its sharp, suffocating odor reminiscent of household bleach and swimming pool purifiers, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a> is a powerhouse oxidizing agent. It boasts the single highest electron affinity of all chemical elements (348.575 kJ\/mol) and holds the third-highest electronegativity (3.16 on the Pauling scale), ranking just behind <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a><\/a>. Because it eagerly snatches electrons from other substances, pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a> gas never exists free in nature; instead, it is bound up in vast salt deposits and ocean waters\u2014most famously in common table salt (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a> chloride, NaCl)\u2014which has sustained human life, ancient medicine, and global industry for thousands of years.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/9\/9a\/Chlorine-sample-flip.jpg", "atomic_mass": 35.45, "density": 3.2, "melt": 171.6, "boil": 239.11, "phase": "Gas", "discovered_by": "Carl Wilhelm Scheele", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p5", "electronegativity_pauling": 3.16, "electron_affinity": 348.575, "ionization_energies": [ 1251.2, 2298, 3822, 5158.6, 6542, 9362, 11018, 33604, 38600, 43961, 51068, 57119, 63363, 72341, 78095, 352994, 380760 ], "sections": { "History": "<p>The history of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a> begins long before it was isolated as a gas, inextricably linked with its most famous compound: <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a> chloride (common salt). Archaeological discoveries show that humans harvested natural rock salt as early as 3000 BC and evaporated brine to extract salt as early as 6000 BC. In ancient India, salt held immense medical, dietary, and cultural significance. The classic Ayurvedic treatises of the <i>Brihat-trayi<\/i>\u2014the <i>Charaka Samhita<\/i>, <i>Sushruta Samhita<\/i>, and <i>Ashtanga Hridaya<\/i>\u2014detailed <i>Pancha Lavana<\/i> (the Five Sacred Salts). Among these, <i>Saindhava Lavana<\/i> (rock salt from the Salt Range) was revered as the finest, cooling, and most balanced salt (<i>uttama<\/i>), used in over 60 therapeutic formulations for digestion, eye health, and respiratory strength, alongside <i>Samudra Lavana<\/i> (sea salt) and <i>Sauvarchala Lavana<\/i> (black salt).<\/p>\n<p>Centuries later, medieval Indian alchemists practicing <i>Rasa Shastra<\/i> (iatrochemistry) distilled mineral salts and alkalis using specialized apparatus (<i>Tiryakpatana<\/i>) to prepare acidic liquids known as <i>Dravaka Kalpana<\/i>. Formulations like <i>Shankha Dravaka<\/i> and <i>Lavanamla<\/i> contained crude hydrochloric acid (HCl)\u2014the primary acid of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a>\u2014which alchemists utilized for dissolving tough minerals, refining metals, and treating severe digestive disorders.<\/p>\n<p>Elemental <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a> gas was first prepared in 1774 by Swedish-German chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele. He produced a pale green gas by reacting hydrochloric acid (then called spirit of salt) or a mixture of dilute sulfuric acid and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a> chloride with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">manganese<\/a><\/a> dioxide. However, Scheele mistakenly believed the suffocating gas was a compound containing <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a> (\"dephlogisticated muriatic acid\"). It was not until 1810 that English chemist Sir Humphry Davy proved that the gas was a fundamental chemical element, naming it <i>chlorine<\/i> after the Ancient Greek word <i>khloros<\/i>, meaning \"pale green\" or \"yellowish-green\". Later in the 19th century, industrial processes like the Leblanc process produced massive quantities of byproduct hydrochloric acid, which was converted back into chlorine using <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">manganese<\/a><\/a> dioxide recycled by the Weldon process.<\/p>\n<p>In modern history, common salt\u2014chlorine's universal source\u2014became the supreme symbol of India's freedom struggle. In March 1930, Mahatma Gandhi led the legendary 241-mile Dandi March (Salt Satyagraha) to the coastal village of Dandi in Gujarat to harvest salt illegally in defiance of the oppressive British colonial salt tax. Gandhi's simple act of picking up a handful of natural salt boiled from sea brine ignited nationwide civil disobedience, proving how this humble chlorine compound could shake an empire and lay the groundwork for Indian independence.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Isotopes": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">Main article: Isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a><\/a><\/div>\n<p>Natural <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a> consists of two stable isotopes: <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a>-35 (<sup>35<\/sup>Cl), which makes up approximately 76% (75.76%) of Earth's chlorine, and chlorine-37 (<sup>37<\/sup>Cl), which accounts for the remaining 24% (24.24%). Both stable isotopes are forged in giant stars during cosmic stellar evolution through <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a>-burning and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a><\/a>-burning nuclear fusion processes. Both <sup>35<\/sup>Cl and <sup>37<\/sup>Cl possess a nuclear spin of 3\/2+. While this allows chlorine to be studied using Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, their non-spherical nuclear charge distribution produces a non-zero nuclear quadrupole moment. This causes rapid quadrupolar relaxation, which broadens NMR spectral lines.<\/p>\n<p>All other chlorine isotopes are radioactive, with half-lives too short to have survived since the formation of planet Earth. In laboratory research, the two most commonly used synthetic radioisotopes are chlorine-36 (<sup>36<\/sup>Cl, half-life <i>t<\/i><sub>1\/2<\/sub> = 3.0 \u00d7 10<sup>5<\/sup> years) and chlorine-38 (<sup>38<\/sup>Cl, half-life <i>t<\/i><sub>1\/2<\/sub> = 37.2 minutes), both produced through neutron activation of natural chlorine in nuclear reactors.<\/p>\n<p>Chlorine-36 (<sup>36<\/sup>Cl) is by far the most stable radioisotope of chlorine. Radioisotopes lighter than <sup>35<\/sup>Cl decay primarily by electron capture into isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a><\/a>, whereas radioisotopes heavier than <sup>37<\/sup>Cl decay via beta (\u03b2<sup>\u2212<\/sup>) decay into isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a><\/a>. Chlorine-36 is unique because it can decay by either pathway\u2014decaying into stable <sup>36<\/sup>S via electron capture or into stable <sup>36<\/sup>Ar via beta emission. In nature, trace amounts of cosmogenic <sup>36<\/sup>Cl exist at a tiny ratio of about (7\u201310) \u00d7 10<sup>\u221213<\/sup> to 1 relative to stable chlorine. It forms in Earth's atmosphere when cosmic ray protons smash into <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a>-36 (spallation). In the upper meter of the Earth's crust (lithosphere), <sup>36<\/sup>Cl is generated primarily by thermal neutron activation of <sup>35<\/sup>Cl and spallation of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a><\/a>-39 (<sup>39<\/sup>K) and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a><\/a>-40 (<sup>40<\/sup>Ca). Deeper underground, muon capture by <sup>40<\/sup>Ca becomes the main mechanism for creating <sup>36<\/sup>Cl.<\/p>\n<p>In modern Indian science and hydrology, cosmic <sup>36<\/sup>Cl serves as an invaluable geochemical clock. Hydrogeologists from institutions like the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) and the Physical Research Laboratory (PRL) use <sup>36<\/sup>Cl isotope tracing to accurately age ancient underground aquifers and measure groundwater recharge rates in hyper-arid regions such as Rajasthan's Thar Desert and Gujarat's Rann of Kutch, ensuring sustainable water resource management for farming and rural communities.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">", "Occurrence": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/e249e1ca85c3039b85abd7e65e64c7aa.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"190\" height=\"399\" style=\"--mw-file-upright: 0.75\" class=\"mw-file-element mw-file-upright\" data-file-width=\"787\" data-file-height=\"1653\" \/><figcaption>Liquid <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a><\/a> analysis<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p>Because <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a> is far too chemically reactive to exist as a free element in nature, it is found entirely in the form of chloride salts. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">Chlorine<\/a> is the 20th most abundant element in Earth's crust, averaging about 126 parts per million (ppm) by weight in rock minerals like halite (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a> chloride), sylvite (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a><\/a> chloride), and carnallite. However, continental rocks pale in comparison to Earth's oceans, which hold an immense reservoir of dissolved chloride ions (making up nearly 1.9% of total ocean mass). Inland salt lakes and underground brine wells\u2014such as the Dead Sea in Israel and the Great Salt Lake in Utah\u2014contain even higher concentrations of chloride.<\/p>\n<p>India possesses vast natural salt reserves and is the world's 3rd largest producer of common salt (NaCl), generating over 30 million tonnes annually. India's major salt harvesting hubs include the vast white salt flats of the Rann of Kutch and Bhavnagar in Gujarat, the Sambhar Salt Lake in Rajasthan, the coastal salt pans of Tuticorin (Thoothukudi) in Tamil Nadu, and Chilika Lake in Odisha. Over 70% of India's total salt production comes from Gujarat alone.<\/p>\n<p>While small laboratory batches of chlorine gas can be prepared by combining hydrochloric acid with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">manganese<\/a><\/a> dioxide (MnO<sub>2<\/sub>), the gas is readily available in pressurized steel cylinders. Industrially, elemental chlorine is manufactured on a massive scale by the electrolysis of aqueous <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a> chloride (saltwater brine). Known as the chloralkali process (industrialized in 1892), this electrochemical reaction generates chlorine gas at the anode, while yielding <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a><\/a> gas and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a> hydroxide (NaOH, or caustic soda\u2014the most valuable co-product) at the cathode according to the stoichiometric equation:<\/p>\n<dl><dd>2 NaCl + 2 H<sub>2<\/sub>O \u2192 Cl<sub>2<\/sub> + H<sub>2<\/sub> + 2 NaOH<\/dd><\/dl>\n<p>In India, modern scientific leadership for salt and chlor-alkali technology is anchored by the CSIR-Central Salt & Marine Chemicals Research Institute (CSIR-CSMCRI) in Bhavnagar, Gujarat. CSMCRI develops advanced solar salt crystallization techniques, brine purification technologies, and zero-liquid discharge systems. Major Indian industrial conglomerates\u2014such as Gujarat Alkalies and Chemicals Limited (GACL), DCM Shriram (with major plants in Kota, Rajasthan and Jhagadia, Gujarat), DCW Ltd, and Grasim Industries\u2014operate giant membrane-cell chlor-alkali facilities that produce millions of tonnes of chlorine and caustic soda annually to fuel India's rapidly expanding chemical sector.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">", "Applications": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/4e88489a3b6b6b193c8281926bc337c4.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"188\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"4032\" data-file-height=\"3024\" \/><figcaption>A railway tank car carrying <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a><\/a>, displaying hazardous materials information including a diamond-shaped U.S. DOT placard showing a UN number<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p>Common salt (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a> chloride) is the ultimate starting raw material for nearly all commercial <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a> production. Worldwide, about 15,000 distinct <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a>-containing chemical compounds are commercially traded. Quantitatively, roughly 63% of all elemental chlorine gas produced is used to synthesize organic chemical compounds, 18% is dedicated to manufacturing inorganic chlorine chemicals, and the remaining 19% is used directly for household bleaches, industrial bleaching of paper pulp, and public water disinfection.<\/p>\n<p>The single largest organic consumer of chlorine by volume is 1,2-dichloroethane, which is converted into vinyl chloride monomer\u2014the essential building block for polyvinyl chloride (PVC) plastic. PVC is one of the world's most widely manufactured polymers, vital for producing durable water pipes, electrical wire insulation, window frames, blood bags, and medical tubing. In India, PVC pipe manufacturing plays a transformational role in national agricultural irrigation networks and drinking water infrastructure under rural development programs. Other major industrial organochlorines include methyl chloride, methylene chloride, chloroform, vinylidene chloride, trichloroethylene, perchloroethylene (used in dry cleaning), allyl chloride, epichlorohydrin (for epoxy resins), chlorobenzene, dichlorobenzenes, and trichlorobenzenes.<\/p>\n<p>Key inorganic chlorine compounds include hydrochloric acid (HCl), dichlorine monoxide (Cl<sub>2<\/sub>O), hypochlorous acid (HOCl), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a> chlorate (NaClO<sub>3<\/sub>), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminium (Al)\">aluminium<\/a> trichloride (AlCl<sub>3<\/sub>, an essential industrial catalyst), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a><\/a> tetrachloride (SiCl<sub>4<\/sub>, used to manufacture ultra-pure solar <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a> and fiber-optic glass), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tin (Sn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tin (Sn)\">tin<\/a><\/a> tetrachloride (SnCl<sub>4<\/sub>), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a><\/a> trichloride (PCl<sub>3<\/sub>), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a><\/a> pentachloride (PCl<sub>5<\/sub>), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a> oxychloride (POCl<sub>3<\/sub>), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">arsenic<\/a><\/a> trichloride (AsCl<sub>3<\/sub>), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Antimony (Sb)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Antimony (Sb)\">antimony<\/a><\/a> trichloride (SbCl<sub>3<\/sub>), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Antimony (Sb)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Antimony (Sb)\">antimony<\/a><\/a> pentachloride (SbCl<sub>5<\/sub>), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Bi\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Bismuth (Bi)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Bi\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Bismuth (Bi)\">bismuth<\/a><\/a> trichloride (BiCl<sub>3<\/sub>), and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a><\/a> chloride (ZnCl<sub>2<\/sub>). Metal chlorides are also crucial metallurgical intermediates for extracting pure metals: for instance, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a><\/a> chloride, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a><\/a> tetrachloride (TiCl<sub>4<\/sub> in the Kroll process), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zirconium (Zr)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zirconium (Zr)\">zirconium<\/a><\/a> tetrachloride, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hf\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hafnium (Hf)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hf\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hafnium (Hf)\">hafnium<\/a><\/a> tetrachloride serve as indispensable precursors for producing pure metal sponges.<\/p>\n<p>Chlorine is universally famous as a life-saving water disinfectant. Treating drinking water with chlorine gas, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a> hypochlorite (liquid bleach), or <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a><\/a> hypochlorite (bleaching powder) kills deadly waterborne pathogens like cholera, typhoid, and dysentery. In India, public health chlorination is the backbone of urban municipal water treatment plants and rural drinking water schemes like the Jal Jeevan Mission. To protect flood-affected communities during natural disasters, scientists at the CSIR-National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (CSIR-NEERI) in Nagpur developed <i>NEERI-ZAR<\/i>\u2014a portable, gravity-based water purification system that uses controlled chemical chlorination to deliver clean drinking water to disaster relief camps across India without requiring electricity.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Biological role": "<p>The chloride anion (Cl<sup>\u2212<\/sup>) is an indispensable macro-nutrient and major extracellular electrolyte required for human life and animal metabolism. In the human body, chloride ions play a pivotal role in maintaining fluid balance, regulating osmotic pressure, preserving proper blood pH, and conducting nerve impulses across cell membranes. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">Chlorine<\/a> is also essential for digestion: specialised parietal cells in the stomach lining pump chloride and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a><\/a> ions into gastric juice to form hydrochloric acid (HCl), which creates an acidic environment (pH 1.5 to 3.5) necessary to activate digestive enzymes like pepsin and kill ingested bacteria. The primary dietary source of chloride is common table salt (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a> chloride), alongside sea salt, tomatoes, celery, and olives.<\/p>\n<p>Disruptions in blood chloride concentration <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a> to significant electrolyte imbalances:<\/p>\n<p><b>Hypochloremia<\/b> (abnormally low blood chloride concentration) rarely occurs on its own and is typically accompanied by other metabolic disturbances. It can result from prolonged vomiting, severe sweating, kidney disease, or chronic hypoventilation, and is often linked with chronic respiratory acidosis.<\/p>\n<p><b>Hyperchloremia<\/b> (abnormally high blood chloride concentration) usually produces no obvious symptoms by itself, but when symptoms occur, they closely resemble hypernatremia (excessive <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a> levels), including extreme thirst, confusion, muscle twitching, and high blood pressure. Severe hyperchloremia can impair <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a> transport in red blood cells. A sudden drop in blood chloride can cause cerebral dehydration (brain cell shrinkage), whereas overly rapid fluid rehydration to treat it can trigger dangerous cerebral edema (brain swelling).<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">" } }, "Ar": { "symbol": "Ar", "name": "Argon", "atomic": 18, "category": "noble gas", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">Argon<\/a><\/a><\/b> is a chemical element with the symbol <b>Ar<\/b> and atomic number <b>18<\/b>. Located in Group 18 of the periodic table, it is a noble gas\u2014a family of elements famous for being exceptionally calm, stable, and chemically unreactive. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">Argon<\/a> is the third most common gas floating in Earth's atmosphere, making up about 0.934% (9,340 parts per million by volume) of the air we breathe. That makes <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a> more than twice as abundant as atmospheric water vapor (which averages around 4,000 ppmv), 23 times more abundant than <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> dioxide (400 ppmv), and over 500 times more plentiful than <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\">neon<\/a> (18 ppmv). Though completely invisible and odorless, this \"lazy gas\" shields high-tech industrial manufacturing on Earth and serves as a cosmic tracer studied by space missions\u2014such as India's Chandrayaan-2\u2014to unlock the secrets of our Moon and Solar System.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/5\/53\/Argon-glow.jpg", "atomic_mass": 39.9481, "density": 1.784, "melt": 83.81, "boil": 87.302, "phase": "Gas", "discovered_by": "Lord Rayleigh", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6", "electronegativity_pauling": null, "electron_affinity": -96, "ionization_energies": [ 1520.6, 2665.8, 3931, 5771, 7238, 8781, 11995, 13842, 40760, 46186, 52002, 59653, 66199, 72918, 82473, 88576, 397605, 427066 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-left\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/48c81740be01773b2c506fd01ba9ed98.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"190\" height=\"170\" style=\"--mw-file-upright: 0.75\" class=\"mw-file-element mw-file-upright\" data-file-width=\"1829\" data-file-height=\"1632\" \/><figcaption>A small piece of rapidly melting solid <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a><\/a><\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">Argon<\/a><\/a> is completely colorless, odorless, nonflammable, and non-toxic whether it exists as a solid, liquid, or gas. In water, it dissolves about as easily as <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a> gas and is roughly 2.5 times more soluble than <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a><\/a>. Under normal everyday conditions, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a> is chemically inert, meaning its atoms have a full outer shell of electrons and refuse to bond with other elements to form stable chemical compounds at room temperature.<\/p><p>However, under extreme laboratory conditions, scientists have nudged argon into making rare, temporary chemical bonds. For example, argon fluorohydride (HArF)\u2014a compound made of argon, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a><\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a><\/a>\u2014can exist, but only at ultracold temperatures below 17 K (\u2212256.1 \u00b0C; \u2212429.1 \u00b0F). Argon can also form physical traps called clathrates, where individual argon atoms become locked inside frozen water-ice cages without forming chemical bonds. Researchers have also created short-lived charged ions such as <span class=\"chemf nowrap\">ArH<span class=\"nowrap\"><span style=\"display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left\"><sup style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\">+<\/sup><br \/><sub style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\"><\/sub><\/span><\/span><\/span> (argononium) and high-energy excimer molecules like ArF. Theoretical supercomputer calculations predict that several other stable argon compounds might be possible, though chemists have not yet synthesized them in the lab.<\/p><p>Because argon ions can be energized and focused easily, modern laboratories\u2014such as the Inter-University Accelerator Centre (IUAC) in New Delhi and the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) in Mumbai\u2014frequently use ionized argon streams for high-precision ion-beam etching, surface modification, and advanced materials analysis.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">", "History": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-left\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/04c9a83c83b980a29499cb4f0b024f32.png\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"150\" height=\"338\" style=\"--mw-file-upright: 0.6\" class=\"mw-file-element mw-file-upright\" data-file-width=\"357\" data-file-height=\"804\" \/><figcaption>A: test-tube, B: dilute alkali, C: U-shaped glass tube, D: <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pt\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Platinum (Pt)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pt\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Platinum (Pt)\">platinum<\/a><\/a> electrode<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p>The name <i><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a><\/a><\/i> comes from the Ancient Greek word <span title=\"Ancient Greek (to 1453)-language text\"><span lang=\"grc\">\u1f00\u03c1\u03b3\u03cc\u03bd<\/span><\/span> (the neuter form of <span title=\"Ancient Greek (to 1453)-language text\"><span lang=\"grc\">\u1f00\u03c1\u03b3\u03cc\u03c2<\/span><\/span>), which literally means \"lazy\" or \"inactive.\" Its discoverers chose this name because the gas stubbornly refused to undergo chemical reactions with any other element. Long before its actual discovery, English scientist Henry Cavendish suspected in 1785 that an unreactive gas was hiding inside air, but he was unable to isolate it.<\/p><p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">Argon<\/a> was finally isolated from air in 1894 by Scottish chemist Sir William Ramsay and English physicist Lord Rayleigh at University College London. They noticed a tantalizing mystery: <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a> gas extracted from chemical compounds was 0.5% lighter than <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a> isolated directly from atmospheric air. This tiny discrepancy led them to suspect that air contained an undiscovered, heavier gas. To capture it, Rayleigh and Ramsay replicated Cavendish's classic experiment. They sealed air and extra <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a> inside an inverted test tube (A) over a solution of dilute alkali (B, originally <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a><\/a> hydroxide). Using U-shaped glass tubes (CC) to insulate <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pt\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Platinum (Pt)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pt\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Platinum (Pt)\">platinum<\/a><\/a> electrodes (DD), they powered a high-voltage electrical arc with Grove batteries and a Ruhmkorff induction coil. The electric spark forced <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> to react into nitrogen oxides, which were absorbed by the alkali along with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a><\/a> dioxide. After sparking until the gas volume stopped shrinking and nitrogen spectral lines vanished, they soaked up remaining <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> using alkaline pyrogallate. What remained was a dense, inert gas that they named <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a>.<\/p>\n<figure typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/77827d9e81d7c304cf0aca426132cb79.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"160\" height=\"258\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"2046\" data-file-height=\"3293\" \/><figcaption>Captioned \"Argon\", caricature of Lord Rayleigh in <i>Vanity Fair<\/i>, 1899<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p>Independently in 1882, scientists H. F. Newall and W. N. Hartley had caught glimpses of argon when analyzing the light spectrum of air, noting unexplained glowing lines that didn't belong to any known element.<\/p><p>For decades after its discovery, argon was assigned the chemical symbol \"A\". In 1957, the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) officially changed its standard symbol to \"Ar\".<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">", "Occurrence": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">Argon<\/a><\/a> is surprisingly abundant in our atmosphere, constituting 0.934% of air by volume and 1.288% by total mass. By comparison, Earth's solid crust contains about 1.2 parts per million (ppm) of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a>, while seawater contains roughly 0.45 ppm. Because air is by far the richest source on Earth, virtually all commercial <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a> is collected directly from the atmosphere.<\/p><p>Industrially, argon is captured using cryogenic air separation\u2014a process where clean air is chilled to extreme sub-zero temperatures until it turns liquid, then distilled fractionally. This process separates argon alongside pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\">neon<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Kr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Krypton (Kr)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Kr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Krypton (Kr)\">krypton<\/a><\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Xe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Xenon (Xe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Xe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Xenon (Xe)\">xenon<\/a><\/a>. Major industrial gas production facilities across India\u2014such as those run by Inox Air Products and Linde India\u2014harvest thousands of tons of argon from atmospheric air each year to supply Indian steelmakers, electronics plants, and fabrication workshops.<\/p><p>Beyond Earth, argon has been detected in planetary atmospheres across the Solar System. The thin atmospheres of Mars, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\">Mercury<\/a><\/a>, and Titan (Saturn's largest moon) all contain measurable amounts of argon, dominated by its radiogenic isotope, argon-40.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">", "Isotopes": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">Main article: Isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a><\/a><\/div>\n<p>On Earth, natural <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a><\/a> consists of three stable isotopes: <span class=\"chemf nowrap\"><span class=\"nowrap\"><span style=\"display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.5em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left\"><sup
