style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\">40<\/sup><br \/><sub style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\"><\/sub><\/span><\/span>Ar<\/span> (making up 99.6% of terrestrial <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a>), <span class=\"chemf nowrap\"><span class=\"nowrap\"><span style=\"display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.5em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left\"><sup style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\">36<\/sup><br \/><sub style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\"><\/sub><\/span><\/span>Ar<\/span> (0.34%), and <span class=\"chemf nowrap\"><span class=\"nowrap\"><span style=\"display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.5em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left\"><sup style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\">38<\/sup><br \/><sub style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\"><\/sub><\/span><\/span>Ar<\/span> (0.06%). Almost all of Earth's argon-40 comes from the radioactive decay of <span class=\"chemf nowrap\"><span class=\"nowrap\"><span style=\"display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.5em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left\"><sup style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\">40<\/sup><br \/><sub style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\"><\/sub><\/span><\/span>K<\/span> (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a>-40), a naturally occurring radioisotope with a half-life of 1.25 billion years. Over geologic time, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a>-40 slowly decays: about 11.2% transforms into stable <span class=\"chemf nowrap\"><span class=\"nowrap\"><span style=\"display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.5em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left\"><sup style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\">40<\/sup><br \/><sub style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\"><\/sub><\/span><\/span>Ar<\/span> via electron capture or positron emission, while 88.8% decays into stable <span class=\"chemf nowrap\"><span class=\"nowrap\"><span style=\"display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.5em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left\"><sup style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\">40<\/sup><br \/><sub style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\"><\/sub><\/span><\/span>Ca<\/span> (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a>-40) via beta decay. Geologists rely on this decay ratio for <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">Potassium<\/a>\u2013Argon (K\u2013Ar) dating to determine the exact age of ancient rocks and volcanic formations.<\/p><p>Radioactive argon isotopes also exist in smaller amounts. In the upper atmosphere, cosmic rays striking <span class=\"chemf nowrap\"><span class=\"nowrap\"><span style=\"display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.5em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left\"><sup style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\">40<\/sup><br \/><sub style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\"><\/sub><\/span><\/span>Ar<\/span> create radioactive <span class=\"chemf nowrap\"><span class=\"nowrap\"><span style=\"display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.5em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left\"><sup style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\">39<\/sup><br \/><sub style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\"><\/sub><\/span><\/span>Ar<\/span>, which is also produced underground when neutrons hit potassium. Another isotope, <span class=\"chemf nowrap\"><span class=\"nowrap\"><span style=\"display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.5em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left\"><sup style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\">37<\/sup><br \/><sub style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\"><\/sub><\/span><\/span>Ar<\/span> (half-life of 35 days), is created underground when neutrons strike <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a> during subsurface nuclear detonations.<\/p><p>Across the cosmos, argon's isotopic recipe is dramatically different from Earth's. In burning stars, stellar nucleosynthesis produces mostly primordial <span class=\"chemf nowrap\"><span class=\"nowrap\"><span style=\"display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.5em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left\"><sup style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\">36<\/sup><br \/><sub style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\"><\/sub><\/span><\/span>Ar<\/span> through the alpha-process. Measurements of solar wind show that solar argon is 84.6% <span class=\"chemf nowrap\"><span class=\"nowrap\"><span style=\"display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.5em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left\"><sup style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\">36<\/sup><br \/><sub style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\"><\/sub><\/span><\/span>Ar<\/span>, and the outer gas giant planets have a <sup>36<\/sup>Ar : <sup>38<\/sup>Ar : <sup>40<\/sup>Ar ratio of 8400 : 1600 : 1. On Earth, primordial <span class=\"chemf nowrap\"><span class=\"nowrap\"><span style=\"display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.5em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left\"><sup style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\">36<\/sup><br \/><sub style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\"><\/sub><\/span><\/span>Ar<\/span> makes up only 31.5 ppmv (= 9,340 ppmv \u00d7 0.337%) of the atmosphere\u2014similar to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\">neon<\/a><\/a> (18.18 ppmv).<\/p><p>This heavy concentration of radiogenic argon-40 on Earth created a famous puzzle in chemistry. Standard Earth argon has an atomic mass of 39.948\u2014making it heavier than the next element on the table, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> (39.098). When Dmitri Mendeleev first built the periodic table by atomic weight, putting heavier argon before lighter potassium seemed wrong. Physicist Henry Moseley eventually solved the riddle by proving that the periodic table is actually arranged by atomic number (argon has 18 protons, potassium has 19), confirming argon's proper spot.<\/p><p>In space exploration, argon isotopes are a vital key to understanding planetary geology. Notably, the Indian Space Research Organisation's (ISRO) <b>Chandrayaan-2<\/b> lunar orbiter carried the <b>CHACE-2<\/b> payload (Chandra's Atmospheric Composition Explorer-2), which successfully detected and mapped <span class=\"chemf nowrap\"><span class=\"nowrap\"><span style=\"display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.5em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left\"><sup style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\">40<\/sup><br \/><sub style=\"font-size:inherit;line-height:inherit;vertical-align:baseline\"><\/sub><\/span><\/span>Ar<\/span> in the Moon's tenuous exosphere. By tracking how argon-40 seeps out from radioactive potassium decay deep inside the lunar crust, Indian scientists gained groundbreaking insights into lunar interior dynamics and volcanic degassing processes.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">", "Applications": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-right\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/e67e83cba340b4c2218f602e0a37cb3b.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"200\" height=\"300\" style=\"--mw-file-upright: 0.8\" class=\"mw-file-element mw-file-upright\" data-file-width=\"512\" data-file-height=\"768\" \/><figcaption>Cylinders containing <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a><\/a> gas for use in extinguishing fire without damaging server equipment<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">Argon<\/a><\/a> is prized in industry and technology because of several unique features:<\/p>\n<ul><li>It is chemically completely inert and non-reactive.<\/li><li>It is the most affordable alternative when <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a><\/a> is not inert enough for high-temperature chemical reactions.<\/li><li>It has exceptionally low thermal conductivity, making it an excellent heat insulator.<\/li><li>It has unique electronic properties, including distinct ionization energy and light emission spectrum.<\/li><\/ul>\n<p>While other noble gases could theoretically do many of these jobs, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a> is by far the cheapest because it is harvested on a massive scale as a byproduct during liquid <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a> and liquid <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a><\/a> production in cryogenic air separation plants. Except for <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">helium<\/a><\/a>, argon is the most plentiful noble gas by far.<\/p><p>Its inert nature makes argon essential for arc welding (such as TIG and MIG welding), where it creates a protective gas shield around white-hot metal joints to stop <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> and moisture from weakening the weld. In metallurgy, argon is blown through molten steel in the Argon <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">Oxygen<\/a> Decarburization (AOD) process to refine high-purity stainless steel\u2014a vital technique used heavily in Indian steel mills. It is also used as a protective atmosphere when growing ultra-pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a> crystals for solar panels and microchips, and when refining reactive metals like <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a><\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zirconium (Zr)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zirconium (Zr)\">zirconium<\/a><\/a>.<\/p><p>Thanks to its low thermal conductivity, argon is injected between the double glass panes of modern insulated energy-efficient windows to block heat transfer. In lighting, it fills incandescent lightbulbs to preserve <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/W\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tungsten (W)\">tungsten<\/a> filaments from burning up, and glows with a distinct blue-violet light in <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\">neon<\/a>-style discharge tubes. Argon gas is also installed in automatic fire suppression systems in server rooms and data centers, snuffing out blazes without leaving water or chemical residues that could ruin sensitive computers.<\/p><p>In advanced research, Argon Fluoride (ArF) excimer lasers emit ultra-short ultraviolet light used in semiconductor photolithography to print nanometer-scale circuits on microchips. In India's nuclear and physical science centers\u2014including the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) and the Inter-University Accelerator Centre (IUAC)\u2014argon serves as a cover gas for nuclear reactors, a plasma medium for material etching, and an ion source in particle accelerators for cutting-edge materials research.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">" } }, "K": { "symbol": "K", "name": "Potassium", "atomic": 19, "category": "alkali metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">Potassium<\/a><\/a> (symbol K, derived from Neo-Latin <i>kalium<\/i>, atomic number 19) is a soft, silvery-white alkali metal that is essential for life on Earth. So soft that it can easily be cut with a butter knife, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> reacts violently with water, bursting into a striking lilac flame. It is the seventh most abundant element in Earth's crust and serves as the primary electrolyte inside living cells, powering nerve signals, muscle contractions, and heart rhythms across the biological world.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/b\/b3\/Potassium.JPG", "atomic_mass": 39.09831, "density": 0.862, "melt": 336.7, "boil": 1032, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Humphry Davy", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s1", "electronegativity_pauling": 0.82, "electron_affinity": 48.383, "ionization_energies": [ 418.8, 3052, 4420, 5877, 7975, 9590, 11343, 14944, 16963.7, 48610, 54490, 60730, 68950, 75900, 83080, 93400, 99710, 444880, 476063 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">Potassium<\/a><\/a> is a classic Group 1 alkali metal with an atomic number of 19. It possesses a single valence electron in its outermost shell (electron configuration [Ar] 4s\u00b9), which it readily sheds to form a positively charged cation (K\u207a). Because of this outer electron structure, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> is exceptionally reactive and electropositive, with a Pauling electronegativity of just 0.82.<\/p><p>In its pure elemental form, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> is a soft, light, silvery metal. It is so soft that it can be effortlessly carved with a knife at room temperature. Freshly cut potassium shines brightly, but within seconds of exposure to air, it tarnishes to a dull grey as it reacts with atmospheric <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> and moisture to form a coating of potassium oxide, hydroxide, and carbonate. To prevent rapid oxidation, pure potassium metal must be stored under mineral oil or kerosene.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Physical properties": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">Potassium<\/a><\/a> has a density of 0.862 g\/cm\u00b3, making it the second-least dense metal after <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a><\/a>. Because it is less dense than water (1.0 g\/cm\u00b3), pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> metal actually floats on water while undergoing an intense chemical reaction.<\/p><p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">Potassium<\/a> has a remarkably low melting point of 63.5 \u00b0C (336.7 K), meaning a piece of potassium metal would melt in warm water, and a boiling point of 759 \u00b0C (1,032 K). Like other alkali metals, when heated in a flame, potassium ions emit a characteristic light: a soft violet or lilac flame color caused by electron excitation at a wavelength of 766.5 nanometers. This unique flame test signature allows scientists to easily identify potassium in chemical samples.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Chemical properties": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">Potassium<\/a><\/a> is even more chemically reactive than its neighbor <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a>. When dropped into water, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> reacts exothermically to produce <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> hydroxide (KOH) solution and liberating <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> gas (H\u2082). The heat released by this reaction is so intense that it instantly ignites the escaping <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> gas, creating a bright lilac-colored flame that often ends with a sharp miniature explosion.<\/p><p>Potassium reacts spontaneously with all halogens\u2014<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Br\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Bromine (Br)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Br\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Bromine (Br)\">bromine<\/a><\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/I\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iodine (I)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/I\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iodine (I)\">iodine<\/a><\/a>\u2014to form white crystalline salts such as potassium chloride (KCl). It also reacts with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> to form oxides, peroxides, and a deep orange-colored potassium superoxide (KO\u2082). Potassium superoxide is particularly valuable because it absorbs <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> dioxide while releasing pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> gas, making it useful in self-contained breathing rebreathers for firefighters, submarines, and spacecraft.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Isotopes": "<p>There are 25 known isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a><\/a>, ranging from <sup>32<\/sup>K to <sup>57<\/sup>K, but natural <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> consists of a mixture of just three isotopes: stable <sup>39<\/sup>K (93.26%), stable <sup>41<\/sup>K (6.73%), and long-lived radioactive <sup>40<\/sup>K (0.0117%).<\/p><p>The primordial radioisotope <sup>40<\/sup>K has an extraordinarily long half-life of 1.25 billion years (1.25 \u00d7 10\u2079 years). It decays through two separate nuclear pathways: 88.8% of the time it undergoes beta decay into stable <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a>-40 (<sup>40<\/sup>Ca), and 11.2% of the time it undergoes electron capture or positron emission to turn into stable <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a>-40 (<sup>40<\/sup>Ar). Because <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a> is a noble gas that escapes molten lava but stays trapped inside solidifying rock, the buildup of <sup>40<\/sup>Ar from <sup>40<\/sup>K decay provides the foundation for <b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a>-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a> (K\u2013Ar) dating<\/b>. Geologists and archeologists use K\u2013Ar dating to determine the age of ancient volcanic rocks, fossil-bearing geological layers, and lunar samples.<\/p><p>Potassium-40 (<sup>40<\/sup>K) is also the single largest source of natural internal radioactivity in the human body and animal life. In a healthy 70 kg human, approximately 4,400 atomic nuclei of <sup>40<\/sup>K decay every single second, producing around 31 Becquerels of activity per gram of natural potassium. Bags of potassium-rich salt substitutes (potassium chloride) are so naturally radioactive that science educators frequently use them for classroom demonstrations with Geiger counters.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "History": "<p>Human utilization of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a><\/a> compounds dates back thousands of years, long before the element itself was isolated in pure metallic form. The English name <i><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a><\/i> comes from <i>potash<\/i>, referring to the traditional practice of leaching wood ashes in <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> pots to obtain <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> carbonate. The chemical symbol <b>K<\/b> comes from the Neo-Latin name <i>kalium<\/i>, which originates from the Arabic word <i>al-qalyah<\/i>, meaning \"alkali\" or \"plant ashes\".<\/p><p>In ancient India, knowledge of potassium alkalis and salts was highly developed within traditional medicine and metallurgy. Ancient Ayurvedic texts like the <i>Charaka Samhita<\/i> and <i>Sushruta Samhita<\/i> describe <b>Kshara<\/b> (alkaline ash preparations). A prime example is <i>Yava Kshara<\/i>, prepared by burning dried barley stalks (*Hordeum vulgare*), dissolving the ash in water, filtering it multiple times, and evaporating the liquid to yield purified potassium carbonate (K\u2082CO\u2083). Ayurvedic physicians utilized <i>Yava Kshara<\/i> for its *Lekhana* (scraping\/cleansing) and *Mutrala* (diuretic) properties to treat kidney stones, urinary disorders, and abdominal ailments.<\/p><p>Ancient Indian texts also recorded potassium nitrate (KNO\u2083) under the Sanskrit names <i>Suryakshar<\/i>, <i>Saurkshar<\/i>, or <i>Suvarchika<\/i>, known regionally as <i>Shora<\/i> or <i>Kalmi Shora<\/i>. Medieval alchemical and medical treatises like the 13th-century <i>Rasaratnasamuccaya<\/i> detailed the extraction and crystallization of <i>Shora<\/i> from soil enriched with organic matter. By the medieval and early modern eras, the fertile plains of Bihar became the global hub for saltpetre harvesting, managed by the traditional <i>Nuniah<\/i> community. Because saltpetre was the primary oxidizer in gunpowder, control over Bihar's <i>Shora<\/i> trade became a major strategic driver for European colonial powers like the Dutch, French, and British East India Companies.<\/p><p>In modern chemistry, pure elemental potassium was first isolated in 1807 by English chemist Sir Humphry Davy in London. Davy achieved this by passing an electric current through molten caustic potash (KOH)\u2014making potassium the very first chemical element ever isolated using electrolysis. When Davy saw the tiny, silvery droplets of pure potassium metal burst into purple flames as they touched the air, he reportedly danced around the room in delight.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Occurrence": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">Potassium<\/a><\/a> is created in the universe during explosive stellar events known as Type II supernovae, through <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a>-burning and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ne\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neon (Ne)\">neon<\/a>-burning nuclear fusion processes, as well as s-process nucleosynthesis. It ranks as the 20th most abundant element in the Solar System and the 17th most abundant element by mass on Earth.<\/p><p>Making up about 2.6% of Earth's crust by weight, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> is the seventh most abundant element in the crust. Because of its extreme chemical reactivity, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> is never found as a free metal in nature. Instead, it occurs in widespread minerals such as orthoclase feldspar, muscovite mica, sylvite (potassium chloride, KCl), carnallite, and polyhalite. Dissolved in ocean water, potassium has a concentration of about 0.39 g\/L\u2014roughly one twenty-seventh the concentration of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a>. Potassium ions are less abundant in seawater than <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a> because plant roots absorb potassium rapidly and clay minerals in soil trap potassium ions tightly.<\/p><p>Geographically in India, while the nation has historically relied on imports for its potash needs, extensive deep-seated potash deposits have been identified in the <b>Nagaur-Ganganagar basin of Rajasthan<\/b>, particularly in Bikaner (Lakhasar) and Hanumangarh (Satipura) at depths of 500 to 750 meters. India has launched historic domestic mining projects in these Rajasthan blocks to extract sylvite and polyhalite minerals, advancing national agricultural self-reliance under the *Atmanirbhar Bharat* initiative.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Biological role": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">Potassium<\/a><\/a> is an essential macronutrient and the primary intracellular cation (positively charged ion) in all living animal cells. While <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a> is concentrated in fluids outside cells, over 98% of the human body's total <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> resides inside cellular walls.<\/p><p>The fundamental mechanism sustaining cellular life is the <b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a>-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> pump (Na\u207a\/K\u207a-ATPase)<\/b>, a vital cell membrane enzyme. Powered by ATP energy, this pump continuously moves three <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a> ions (Na\u207a) out of the cell for every two potassium ions (K\u207a) it pumps inside. This active transport creates an electrochemical gradient across cell membranes known as the resting membrane potential. This electrical voltage powers nerve impulse transmission, regulates heartbeats, enables muscle contraction, and maintains cell volume and fluid balance.<\/p><p>An adult human body contains approximately 120 to 140 grams of potassium. Humans require about 3.5 to 4.7 grams of dietary potassium daily, obtained from foods like bananas, tender coconut water, potatoes, leafy green vegetables, pulses, and milk. Adequate potassium intake helps offset excess dietary sodium, lowering blood pressure and reducing cardiovascular risks. Severe potassium deficiency (hypokalemia) or excess (hyperkalemia) can cause dangerous muscle weakness and cardiac arrhythmias.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Applications": "<p>Over 93% of the world's harvested <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a><\/a> is used in global agriculture as <b>potash fertilizers<\/b>, primarily <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> chloride (KCl), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> sulfate (K\u2082SO\u2084), and potassium nitrate (KNO\u2083). Potassium fertilizer boosts plant growth, strengthens crop disease resistance, improves water retention, and increases agricultural yield.<\/p><p>In industrial chemistry, potassium hydroxide (KOH, caustic potash) is widely used to manufacture liquid soaps, detergents, and industrial cleaners. Potassium carbonate (K\u2082CO\u2083) is essential in producing specialty television and optical glasses, ceramics, and chemical catalysts. Potassium nitrate (KNO\u2083) serves in fireworks, black powder, and food curing. Potassium superoxide (KO\u2082) is utilized as an <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> generator in closed-circuit breathing apparatuses. Additionally, a liquid alloy of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a> and potassium called <b>NaK<\/b> remains liquid at room temperature and is used as an efficient high-temperature heat-transfer coolant in specialized nuclear reactors and scientific equipment.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">" } }, "Ca": { "symbol": "Ca", "name": "Calcium", "atomic": 20, "category": "alkaline earth metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">Calcium<\/a><\/a> (symbol Ca, atomic number 20) is a soft, silvery-gray alkaline earth metal that plays a vital role in both Earth's geology and biological life. It is the fifth most abundant element by mass in Earth's crust and the fifth most abundant dissolved ion in the oceans. From building strong bones and teeth in living organisms to forming giant limestone mountains, ancient temple plasters, and modern concrete, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a> is one of nature's most indispensable building blocks.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/7\/72\/Calcium.jpg", "atomic_mass": 40.0784, "density": 1.55, "melt": 1115, "boil": 1757, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Humphry Davy", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2", "electronegativity_pauling": 1, "electron_affinity": 2.37, "ionization_energies": [ 589.8, 1145.4, 4912.4, 6491, 8153, 10496, 12270, 14206, 18191, 20385, 57110, 63410, 70110, 78890, 86310, 94000, 104900, 111711, 494850, 527762 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p>As a group 2 alkaline earth metal, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a><\/a> is highly reactive and never found in its pure metallic form in nature. Instead, it readily binds with other elements to form rich minerals like limestone, marble, chalk, and gypsum. In pure form, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a> is light and silvery, but it quickly tarnishes in air, forming a dark protective layer of oxide and nitride.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Physical properties": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">Calcium<\/a><\/a> melts at 842 \u00b0C (1,115 K) and boils at 1,494 \u00b0C (1,757 K)\u2014significantly higher temperatures than its group neighbors <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a><\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Strontium (Sr)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Strontium (Sr)\">strontium<\/a><\/a>. With a density of only 1.526 g\/cm\u00b3 (or 1.55 g\/cm\u00b3 in bulk), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a> is the lightest metal in its group. Although it is harder than <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a><\/a>, it is soft enough to be cut with a sharp knife with some effort.<\/p><p>At room temperature, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a> atoms crystallize in a face-centered cubic structure, but when heated above 443 \u00b0C (716 K), its crystal arrangement shifts to body-centered cubic. While <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a> are better electrical conductors than calcium by volume, calcium is actually a superior conductor by mass because of its remarkably low density. Because calcium reacts quickly with air on Earth, it is impractical for terrestrial wiring, but scientists have considered using it as an ultra-lightweight electrical conductor in outer space.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Chemical properties": "<p>The chemical behavior of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a><\/a> is typical for heavy alkaline earth metals. It reacts spontaneously with water\u2014faster than <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a><\/a> but slower than <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Strontium (Sr)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Strontium (Sr)\">strontium<\/a><\/a>\u2014producing <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a> hydroxide solution and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> gas bubbles. Exposed to room air, it combines with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a><\/a> to form <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a> oxide (CaO) and calcium nitride (Ca3N2). Fine calcium dust burns spontaneously in air to yield nitride. However, bulk chunks of calcium form a protective hydration film in moist air, and can be stored indefinitely at room temperature if humidity remains below 30%.<\/p><p>Calcium forms several oxides, including quicklime (CaO), calcium peroxide (CaO2) under high <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> pressure, and a yellow superoxide Ca(O2)2. Its hydroxide, Ca(OH)2 (slaked lime), is a strong base. Calcium forms all four standard dihalides and produces exceptionally abundant natural minerals such as calcium carbonate (CaCO3) and calcium sulfate (CaSO4). Like alkali metals and heavy alkaline earth metals (as well as <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Eu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Europium (Eu)\">europium<\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Yb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Ytterbium (Yb)\">ytterbium<\/a>), pure calcium metal dissolves directly in liquid ammonia to form a striking, deep-blue conducting solution.<\/p><p>Because the calcium ion (Ca<sup>2+<\/sup>) is relatively large, it can surround itself with many neighboring atoms, achieving high coordination numbers up to 24 in intermetallic compounds like CaZn13. In analytical chemistry and water treatment, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a>-based chelating agents like EDTA and polyphosphates readily bind calcium ions, effectively softening hard water by removing excess calcium.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Isotopes": "<p>Natural <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a><\/a> consists of a mixture of five stable isotopes (<sup>40<\/sup>Ca, <sup>42<\/sup>Ca, <sup>43<\/sup>Ca, <sup>44<\/sup>Ca, and <sup>46<\/sup>Ca) plus one extremely long-lived radioactive isotope, <sup>48<\/sup>Ca. With a half-life of 4.3 \u00d7 10<sup>19<\/sup> years (trillions of times longer than the age of the universe), <sup>48<\/sup>Ca is considered stable for all practical purposes. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">Calcium<\/a> is the lightest element in the periodic table to possess six naturally occurring isotopes.<\/p><p>The overwhelming majority of natural <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a>\u201496.941%\u2014is <sup>40<\/sup>Ca. Created inside massive stars during the <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a>-burning phase through alpha particle fusion, <sup>40<\/sup>Ca is the heaviest stable atomic nucleus with equal numbers of protons and neutrons (20 of each). Its abundance on Earth is also continuously supplemented by the extremely slow decay of primordial <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a>-40 (<sup>40<\/sup>K). The second most common isotope, <sup>44<\/sup>Ca (2.806%), forms when unstable <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a>-44 (<sup>44<\/sup>Ti) decays via double electron capture. The remaining natural isotopes (<sup>42<\/sup>Ca, <sup>43<\/sup>Ca, <sup>46<\/sup>Ca, and <sup>48<\/sup>Ca) are rare, each making up less than 1% of natural calcium. <sup>46<\/sup>Ca is produced in hot stellar s-processes, while <sup>48<\/sup>Ca is formed by r-process neutron capture in Type Ia supernovae.<\/p><p>Both <sup>40<\/sup>Ca and <sup>48<\/sup>Ca are notable because they are 'doubly magic' nuclei\u2014having completely filled proton and neutron energy shells (20 protons with 20 or 28 neutrons). Calcium is the only chemical element with two primordial doubly magic isotopes. Because <sup>48<\/sup>Ca is doubly magic, its beta decay is blocked by a severe nuclear spin mismatch, forcing it to undergo double beta decay into <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a>-48\u2014making it the lightest known nucleus to undergo double beta decay. Synthetic radioisotopes of calcium range from <sup>35<\/sup>Ca to <sup>60<\/sup>Ca. Among these, <sup>41<\/sup>Ca (half-life of ~100,000 years) is a cosmogenic nuclide created by cosmic ray neutron activation of <sup>40<\/sup>Ca, serving as an important cosmic clock.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "History": "<p>Humans have utilized <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a><\/a> compounds for thousands of years. Lime plaster was used as early as 7000 BC to craft statues in the ancient Near East ('Ain Ghazal), and the earliest recorded lime kiln dates back to 2500 BC in Khafajah, Mesopotamia. Ancient Egyptians used dehydrated gypsum plaster (CaSO4\u00b72H2O) in constructing the Great Pyramid of Giza and royal tombs like Tutankhamun's, while ancient Romans heated limestone (CaCO3) to produce lime mortars for iconic aqueducts and monuments. The word <i><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a><\/i> comes from the Latin <i>calx<\/i>, meaning 'lime'.<\/p><p>In ancient India, builders mastered <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a> chemistry to create exceptionally durable architectural monuments. Known as traditional lime mortar (*Chunam*), builders blended quicklime\/slaked lime with rich organic additives such as jaggery (unrefined palm sugar), curd (casein binder), fenugreek, and fruit extracts like *haritaki* (chebulic myrobalan) and bael. This yielded an extraordinarily strong, flexible, and self-healing plaster that endured centuries of monsoons across ancient rock-cut temples, South Indian monuments like Thanjavur Palace, and Rajasthan's mirror-smooth *Araish* wall plaster. Simultaneously, ancient Ayurvedic texts on *Rasashastra* (iatrochemistry) developed a dedicated calcium mineral branch known as *Sudha Varga*. Ayurvedic physicians processed marine calcium sources like red coral (*Praval*) and conch shells (*Shankha*) through rigorous purification (*Shodhana*) and high-temperature calcination (*Marana*) to create bioavailable remedies like *Praval Bhasma* and *Shankha Bhasma*\u2014fine calcium micro\/nanoparticles used to strengthen bones, treat osteoporosis, and soothe digestive acidity.<\/p><p>In European scientific history, Roman writer Vitruvius noted that burned lime became lighter than the original limestone. In 1755, Scottish chemist Joseph Black proved that this weight loss was caused by the liberation of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> dioxide gas. In 1789, Antoine Lavoisier listed lime (*chaux*) among five un-reducible 'salifiable earths', suspecting that all earths were actually metallic oxides. Finally, in 1808, Sir Humphry Davy isolated pure calcium metal in London by electrolyzing a mixture of lime and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\">mercury<\/a> oxide on a <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pt\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Platinum (Pt)\">platinum<\/a> electrode, building on pioneering work by J\u00f6ns Jakob Berzelius and Magnus Martin of Pontin.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Applications": "<p>Metallic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a><\/a> plays a critical role in heavy metallurgy. Its largest single industrial application is in steelmaking, where <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a> acts as a powerful deoxidizer and desulfurizer. Added to liquid steel, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a> forms floating liquid lime aluminates and sulfide inclusions that float to the top or disperse into microscopic spheres, dramatically improving the steel's castability, cleanliness, and mechanical strength. Small amounts of calcium (0.1%) are alloyed with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a> to create maintenance-free automotive batteries that reduce water loss and self-discharge compared to traditional <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Antimony (Sb)\">antimony<\/a>-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a> batteries. Calcium is also used to strengthen <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a> bearing alloys, control graphitic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> in cast <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>, remove <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Bi\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Bismuth (Bi)\">bismuth<\/a> impurities from <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a>, and serve as a reducing agent in isolating pure metals like <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zirconium (Zr)\">zirconium<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Th\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Thorium (Th)\">thorium<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">vanadium<\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/U\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Uranium (U)\">uranium<\/a>. Household drain cleaners also use calcium metal to generate intense heat and strong calcium hydroxide base to saponify oils and liquefy hair clogs. Furthermore, calcium reacts with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> to form solid calcium hydride (CaH2), providing a safe, portable medium for <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> gas storage.<\/p><p>In modern medicine and oceanography, calcium isotope ratios offer groundbreaking analytical tools. Because lighter calcium isotopes (<sup>40<\/sup>Ca) precipitate slightly faster than heavier ones (<sup>44<\/sup>Ca) when building mineral skeletons, tracking the <sup>44<\/sup>Ca\/<sup>40<\/sup>Ca ratio in human blood or urine reveals the real-time balance between bone formation and bone resorption, enabling early diagnosis of metabolic bone diseases like osteoporosis. In oceanography, changes in marine <sup>44<\/sup>Ca\/<sup>40<\/sup>Ca ratios over geological time demonstrate that ocean calcium concentrations fluctuate rather than remaining constant, shedding light on ancient oceanic climate changes and global <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> cycles.<\/p><p>Calcium compounds are vital across the food, medical, and pharmaceutical sectors. Calcium lactate, calcium diphosphate, and tricalcium phosphate are widely used to fortify foods (calcium supplements are featured on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines). Tricalcium phosphate also serves as a polishing agent in toothpaste and antacids, while calcium lactobionate acts as a pharmaceutical suspending agent, and calcium phosphate serves as a baking leavening agent. Industrial applications include calcium sulfite as a paper bleach and disinfectant, calcium silicate as a rubber reinforcer, and calcium acetate in metallic soaps and synthetic resins.<\/p><p>Geographically, India possesses vast natural deposits of limestone (calcium carbonate) estimated in tens of billions of tonnes across key mineral-producing states such as Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan, Gujarat, Chhattisgarh, and Madhya Pradesh. These massive resources feed India's position as the world's second-largest cement industry, driving modern global infrastructure development.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">" } }, "Sc": { "symbol": "Sc", "name": "Scandium", "atomic": 21, "category": "transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Scandium (Sc)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Scandium (Sc)\">Scandium<\/a><\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>Sc<\/b>, atomic number <b>21<\/b>) is a lightweight, silvery-white transition metal. Although chemically similar to transition metals, it is historically classified as a rare earth element alongside <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Y\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Yttrium (Y)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Y\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Yttrium (Y)\">yttrium<\/a><\/a> and the lanthanoids because it naturally occurs in the same mineral deposits. Discovered in 1879 through spectral analysis of Scandinavian minerals like <i>euxenite<\/i> and <i>gadolinite<\/i>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Scandium (Sc)\">scandium<\/a> is remarkable for giving ordinary metals extraordinary strength, heat tolerance, and crack-free weldability when added in tiny amounts. Today, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Scandium (Sc)\">scandium<\/a> plays a pivotal role in advanced aerospace alloys, high-intensity stadium lighting, clean energy fuel cells, and next-generation green mineral extraction in India.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/f\/f5\/Scandium%2C_Sc.jpg", "atomic_mass": 44.9559085, "density": 2.985, "melt": 1814, "boil": 3109, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Lars Fredrik Nilson", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d1", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.36, "electron_affinity": 18, "ionization_energies": [ 633.1, 1235, 2388.6, 7090.6, 8843, 10679, 13310, 15250, 17370, 21726, 24102, 66320, 73010, 80160, 89490, 97400, 105600, 117000, 124270, 547530, 582163 ], "sections": { "Isotopes": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">Main article: Isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Scandium (Sc)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Scandium (Sc)\">scandium<\/a><\/a><\/div>\n<p>In nature, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Scandium (Sc)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Scandium (Sc)\">scandium<\/a><\/a> is mono-isotopic, existing exclusively as a single stable isotope: <b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Scandium (Sc)\">scandium<\/a>-45 (<sup>45<\/sup>Sc)<\/b>, which has a nuclear spin of 7\/2. All natural scandium atoms on Earth consist of 21 protons, 21 electrons, and 24 neutrons.<\/p>\n<p>Nuclear scientists have synthesized 26 radioactive isotopes of scandium, ranging from <sup>37<\/sup>Sc to <sup>63<\/sup>Sc. Among these synthetic radioisotopes, the most stable and useful are:<\/p>\n<ul>\n <li><b><sup>46<\/sup>Sc<\/b> (half-life of 83.76 days): Used as an industrial radioactive tracer in underground pipeline flow monitoring and oil well tracking.<\/li>\n <li><b><sup>47<\/sup>Sc<\/b> (half-life of 3.35 days): A promising medical radioisotope undergoing intense research for targeted cancer therapy and diagnostic nuclear medicine.<\/li>\n <li><b><sup>48<\/sup>Sc<\/b> (half-life of 43.67 hours), <b><sup>44<\/sup>Sc<\/b> (half-life of 4.04 hours), and <b><sup>43<\/sup>Sc<\/b> (half-life of 3.89 hours).<\/li>\n<\/ul>\n<p>All remaining radioisotopes have half-lives under an hour, with the majority decaying in less than 15 seconds. Scandium also forms several nuclear isomers (excited nuclear states), the most stable of which is <b><sup>44m3<\/sup>Sc<\/b> with a half-life of 58.6 hours. Remarkably, <sup>44m3<\/sup>Sc holds the record as the lightest atomic nucleus to possess a long-lived nuclear isomer.<\/p>\n<p>Lightweight scandium isotopes with masses below <sup>45<\/sup>Sc (such as <sup>37<\/sup>Sc to <sup>44<\/sup>Sc) decay primarily by electron capture or positron emission into isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a><\/a> (with the ultra-light <sup>37<\/sup>Sc\u2013<sup>39<\/sup>Sc decaying by proton emission, and initial detections characterizing their mass excess). Heavier isotopes above <sup>45<\/sup>Sc decay via beta emission into isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a><\/a>. In Indian nuclear research institutions like BARC (Bhabha Atomic Research Centre), radioisotopes like <sup>46<\/sup>Sc are produced in research reactors for agricultural tracer studies and industrial hydrology applications.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Occurrence": "<p>Contrary to its historical label as a \"rare earth,\" <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Scandium (Sc)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Scandium (Sc)\">scandium<\/a><\/a> is actually relatively abundant in Earth's crust\u2014averaging 18 to 25 parts per million (ppm), which is comparable to the abundance of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a><\/a> (20\u201330 ppm). <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Scandium (Sc)\">Scandium<\/a> ranks as the 50th most abundant element overall on Earth (and 35th in the crust). Beyond Earth, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Scandium (Sc)\">scandium<\/a> is much more widespread: it is the 23rd most common element in the Sun and the 26th most abundant element in distant stars.<\/p>\n<p>In cosmic origins, stable scandium is forged deep inside massive exploding stars (supernovae) through rapid neutron capture (the <i>r-process<\/i>), such as reactions combining <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a><\/a>-28 with neutrons (<sup>28<\/sup>Si + 17n \u2192 <sup>45<\/sup>Sc). Cosmic rays speeding through space also create scandium by smashing into heavier <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a>-group atomic nuclei in interstellar space\u2014a process known as cosmic ray spallation (<sup>56<\/sup>Fe + p \u2192 <sup>45<\/sup>Sc + <sup>11<\/sup>C + n).<\/p>\n<p>Despite its presence across Earth's crust, scandium rarely concentrates into rich ore deposits because its ionic radius closely resembles that of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a><\/a>, and aluminium, causing it to disperse in tiny trace amounts inside over 800 common rock-forming minerals. Only a handful of ultra-rare Scandinavian and Malagasy minerals\u2014such as <i>thortveitite<\/i>, <i>euxenite<\/i>, and <i>gadolinite<\/i>\u2014contain high concentrations. Thortveitite is the richest mineral source, containing up to 45% scandium oxide (Sc<sub>2<\/sub>O<sub>3<\/sub>).<\/p>\n<p>In India, scandium occurs naturally in trace amounts within the heavy mineral beach sands of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and Odisha, where state enterprise IREL (India) Limited processes monazite and ilmenite deposits. Additionally, India's vast reserves of bauxite ore mined for aluminium production contain valuable hidden concentrations of scandium. When bauxite is refined into alumina, scandium accumulates in the byproduct known as \"red mud\" (bauxite residue). To turn this industrial byproduct into strategic national wealth, Indian research bodies like the Jawaharlal Nehru Aluminium Research Development & Design Centre (JNARDDC) in Nagpur, CSIR-IMMT in Bhubaneswar, and NITI Aayog are developing pilot plants with major producers like Hindalco, NALCO, and Vedanta to sustainably extract pure scandium oxide from Indian red mud.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">", "History": "<p>The story of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Scandium (Sc)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Scandium (Sc)\">scandium<\/a><\/a> begins in 1869 when the famous Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev, creator of the periodic table, noticed a gap in his table. He mathematically predicted that an unknown element\u2014which he named <i>ekaboron<\/i>\u2014must exist with an atomic weight between 40 and 48. Ten years later, in 1879, Swedish chemist Lars Fredrik Nilson and his team isolated a new oxide while analyzing rare minerals (<i>euxenite<\/i> and <i>gadolinite<\/i>) found in Scandinavia. Nilson isolated about two grams of highly pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Scandium (Sc)\">scandium<\/a> oxide and named the element <i><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Scandium (Sc)\">scandium<\/a><\/i> after the Latin word <i>Scandia<\/i> (Scandinavia). Although Nilson did not initially connect his discovery to Mendeleev's prediction, Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve recognized that scandium was indeed Mendeleev's missing <i>ekaboron<\/i>.<\/p>\n<p>Isolating pure metallic scandium proved extremely difficult because of its strong affinity for <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a>. It was not until 1937 that scientists produced tiny amounts of pure scandium metal through the high-temperature electrolysis of a molten salt mixture of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a><\/a>, and scandium chlorides at 700\u2013800 \u00b0C. The world's first full pound (0.45 kg) of 99% pure scandium metal was only manufactured in 1960.<\/p>\n<p>Industrial interest skyrocketed in 1971 when researchers in the United States and the USSR independently patented <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminium (Al)\">aluminium<\/a>-scandium alloys, discovering that trace amounts of scandium made aluminium immensely stronger and crack-resistant during welding. During the Cold War in the 1980s and 1990s, laser crystals made of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Gd\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gadolinium (Gd)\">gadolinium<\/a>-scandium-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">gallium<\/a> garnet (GSGG) were developed for cutting-edge military lasers under the U.S. Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI).<\/p>\n<p>In India's scientific and historical narrative, while scandium was identified during modern European mineral exploration, India's deep traditional expertise in extraction chemistry (<i>Rasashastra<\/i>) has evolved into 21st-century strategic metallurgy. Recognizing scandium as a vital critical mineral for national sovereignty and high-technology growth, leading Indian scientific institutions\u2014including CSIR laboratories, DRDO, and JNARDDC\u2014are actively writing the next chapter of scandium history by pioneering self-reliant green extraction technologies.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">", "Applications": "<p>Although world production of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Scandium (Sc)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Scandium (Sc)\">scandium<\/a><\/a> is small\u2014only a few tonnes annually\u2014it is considered a super-element because of its transformative impact when added in tiny quantities to other materials.<\/p>\n<p><b>1. Super-Alloys for Aerospace and Sports:<\/b> The single largest application of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Scandium (Sc)\">scandium<\/a> is in high-performance <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminium (Al)\">aluminium<\/a>-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Scandium (Sc)\">scandium<\/a> (Al-Sc) alloys. Adding just 0.1% to 0.5% scandium by weight to aluminium creates micro-precipitates of Al<sub>3<\/sub>Sc. These tiny structures prevent recrystallization and grain growth when the metal is heated, dramatically boosting tensile strength by up to 50%, improving heat resistance, and eliminating hot-cracking during welding. This allows aircraft and rocket components to be welded rather than riveted, saving 4\u20135% in overall structural weight.<\/p>\n<p>In Indian science and space technology, CSIR-NIIST (National Institute for Interdisciplinary Science and Technology, Thiruvananthapuram) and DRDO's Defence Metallurgical Research Laboratory (DMRL) are actively developing indigenous Al-Mg-Sc alloy sheets, plates, and extrusions. These lightweight, high-strength scandium alloys are being evaluated for rocket motor casings and propulsion structures at ISRO's Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC) and aircraft nacelle cowlings at CSIR-NAL, driving India's self-reliance (<i>Atmanirbhar Bharat<\/i>) in strategic aerospace materials.<\/p>\n<p>In consumer products, Al-Sc alloys are used to manufacture ultra-lightweight, durable sports equipment including premium bicycle frames, baseball bats, lacrosse sticks, tent poles, and high-end firearm frames.<\/p>\n<p><b>2. High-Intensity Lighting:<\/b> When scandium iodide (ScI<sub>3<\/sub>) is added to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\">mercury<\/a> vapor lamps, it produces a brilliant white light that closely mimics natural sunlight. These high-intensity discharge lamps feature exceptional color rendering and are widely used in major sports stadiums, arena illumination, and movie set lighting.<\/p>\n<p><b>3. Clean Energy and Solid Oxide Fuel Cells (SOFCs):<\/b> Scandium oxide (scandia, Sc<sub>2<\/sub>O<sub>3<\/sub>) is a critical material in solid oxide fuel cells. Adding scandium to zirconia creates scandia-stabilized zirconia (SSZ), a high-performance ceramic electrolyte. SSZ conducts <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> ions efficiently at lower operating temperatures than traditional materials, significantly enhancing the efficiency, durability, and lifespan of clean fuel cells for green energy generation.<\/p>\n<p><b>4. Advanced Lasers and Defense Technologies:<\/b> Crystals composed of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Gd\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gadolinium (Gd)\">gadolinium<\/a>-scandium-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">gallium<\/a> garnet (GSGG) are twice as efficient as standard Nd:YAG laser crystals. They are utilized in high-power industrial cutting lasers, rangefinders, and strategic defense technologies.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">" } }, "Ti": { "symbol": "Ti", "name": "Titanium", "atomic": 22, "category": "transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">Titanium<\/a><\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>Ti<\/b>, atomic number <b>22<\/b>) is a lustrous, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ag\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silver (Ag)\">silver<\/a>-colored transition metal famous for its unbelievable strength, light weight, and legendary resistance to rust and chemical attack. Named after the mighty Titans of Greek mythology, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a> is as strong as steel yet nearly 45% lighter, and it is virtually immune to corrosion by seawater, acid, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a><\/a>. From space rockets like ISRO's Chandrayaan missions to artificial hip implants and super-bright white paint, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a> is a modern super-metal that powers human technology in the sky, in the oceans, and inside the human body.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/e\/ec\/Titanium.jpg", "atomic_mass": 47.8671, "density": 4.506, "melt": 1941, "boil": 3560, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "William Gregor", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d2", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.54, "electron_affinity": 7.289, "ionization_energies": [ 658.8, 1309.8, 2652.5, 4174.6, 9581, 11533, 13590, 16440, 18530, 20833, 25575, 28125, 76015, 83280, 90880, 100700, 109100, 117800, 129900, 137530, 602930, 639294 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Physical properties": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">Titanium<\/a> is celebrated worldwide for its exceptional <b>strength-to-weight ratio<\/b>. It is a shiny, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ag\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silver (Ag)\">silver<\/a>-white metal that possesses the strength of common structural steel while being nearly 45% lighter. Compared to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminium (Al)\">aluminium<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a> is 60% denser but more than twice as strong as standard aerospace aluminium alloys (such as 6061-T6). Advanced <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a> alloys (like Beta C) can reach extraordinary tensile strengths exceeding 1,400 megapascals (MPa), making them tough enough to withstand severe structural stresses.<\/p>\n<p>Despite its strength, titanium has a relatively high melting point of 1,668 \u00b0C (3,034 \u00b0F). While sometimes mistaken for a refractory metal, it is technically categorized as a transition metal. Pure titanium is quite ductile\u2014meaning it can be drawn into thin wires or hammered into sheets without snapping\u2014especially when kept free of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a> contamination. It is paramagnetic (only weakly attracted to magnetic fields), non-magnetic, and is a relatively poor conductor of heat and electricity compared to metals like <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a><\/a> or <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ag\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silver (Ag)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ag\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silver (Ag)\">silver<\/a><\/a>. When cooled to ultra-low temperatures near absolute zero (below its critical temperature of 0.49 K), titanium becomes a superconductor, carrying electricity with zero electrical resistance.<\/p>\n<p>While remarkably strong, titanium is not as hard as specialized heat-treated tool steel, and it tends to lose its mechanical strength when heated above 430 \u00b0C (806 \u00b0F). Machining and shaping titanium requires specialized techniques and liquid coolants, because the metal tends to stick or \"gall\" against cutting tools. However, like high-grade steel, titanium structures possess a natural <b>fatigue limit<\/b>, meaning they can endure billions of repeating stress cycles without structural failure, guaranteeing decades of reliable service in aircraft and engines.<\/p>\n<p>At the microscopic atomic level, titanium exhibits two different crystalline structures (allotropes). At room temperature, it exists in a hexagonal close-packed pattern known as the <b>alpha (\u03b1) form<\/b>. When heated above 882 \u00b0C (1,620 \u00b0F), its atoms rearrange into a body-centered cubic lattice known as the <b>beta (\u03b2) form<\/b>. The metal's heat capacity spikes dramatically right at this transition temperature before leveling off in the beta phase.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Chemical properties": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img alt=\"Graph showing the Pourbaix diagram of titanium\" src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/b18691045050a72c44658072535d14bf.png\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"257\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"497\" data-file-height=\"511\" \/><figcaption>Pourbaix diagram for <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a><\/a> in pure water, perchloric acid, or <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a> hydroxide<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">Titanium<\/a>'s most legendary feature is its extreme resistance to corrosion, caused by a clever natural phenomenon called <b>passivation<\/b>. The instant fresh <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a> metal is exposed to air or moisture, it reacts with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a> to form an invisible, non-porous protective skin of titanium dioxide (TiO<sub>2<\/sub>). Although this self-healing shield starts out only 1 to 2 nanometers thick, it thickens over several years to about 25 nanometers, completely sealing the metal underneath. Because of this oxide armor, titanium refuses to rust or corrode in ocean seawater, salt spray, harsh organic acids, and corrosive chemicals like <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a><\/a> or aqua regia (a powerful mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acid that dissolves <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\">gold<\/a>).<\/p>\n<p>At room temperature, titanium easily resists dilute hydrochloric and sulfuric acids as well as chloride solutions. However, it can be attacked and dissolved by concentrated hot acids, or by hydrofluoric acid (which destroys the oxide film). While chemically calm under normal conditions, titanium becomes fiercely reactive at elevated temperatures. If heated in open air, titanium will catch fire and burn brightly at temperatures below its melting point. For this reason, titanium melting and welding must always be conducted in a vacuum or under an inert gas shield such as <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ar\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Argon (Ar)\">argon<\/a>.<\/p>\n<p>When heated to 550 \u00b0C (1,022 \u00b0F), titanium reacts vigorously with halogens like <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a><\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Br\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Bromine (Br)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Br\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Bromine (Br)\">bromine<\/a><\/a> to form titanium tetrachloride (TiCl<sub>4<\/sub>) and titanium tetrabromide (TiBr<sub>4<\/sub>). At 1,200 \u00b0C in air (or 610 \u00b0C in pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a>), it burns to produce pure titanium dioxide. Interestingly, titanium is one of the very few chemical elements that can burn in an atmosphere of pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a><\/a> gas; at 800 \u00b0C, it reacts with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a> to form golden titanium nitride (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tin (Sn)\">TiN<\/a>), a glass-hard compound that causes the metal to become brittle if uncontrolled, but serves as a super-tough protective coating on drill bits when applied intentionally.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Occurrence": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">Titanium<\/a><\/a> is surprisingly plentiful on Earth. It is the <b>ninth-most abundant element<\/b> in Earth's crust (making up about 0.63% of the crust by mass) and the seventh-most abundant structural metal. It is present in almost all igneous rocks\u2014the U.S. Geological Survey found <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a> in 784 out of 801 rock types analyzed\u2014as well as in soils (0.5% to 1.5%), living plants, animals, and natural bodies of water. The ocean contains dissolved <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a> at a tiny concentration of about 4 picomolar.<\/p>\n<p>In nature, titanium is never found lying around as a free shiny metal because it binds tightly with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a>. Instead, it occurs in minerals such as <b>ilmenite<\/b> (FeTiO<sub>3<\/sub>), <b>rutile<\/b> (TiO<sub>2<\/sub>), anatase, brookite, perovskite, titanite (sphene), and the ultra-rare mineral akaogiite. Among these, ilmenite and rutile are the primary commercial ores mined worldwide, with total global mineral reserves exceeding 2 billion tonnes.<\/p>\n<p><b>Indian Mineral Wealth & Coastline Geography:<\/b> India holds some of the world's richest and highest-grade reserves of heavy mineral beach sands containing ilmenite and rutile. These prized black sand deposits stretch across five major coastal zones: the famous <b>Chavara coastal belt in Kollam, Kerala<\/b>, the beaches of <b>Manavalakurichi in Tamil Nadu<\/b>, <b>Chatrapur (Ganjam)<\/b> and <b>Brahmagiri in Odisha<\/b>, and <b>Bhavanapadu in Andhra Pradesh<\/b>. The government-owned <i>Kerala Minerals and Metals Limited (KMML)<\/i> operates an integrated mining and processing facility at Chavara, extracting ilmenite directly from Kerala's golden coast. Additionally, inland geological formations such as the vanadiferous titaniferous magnetite deposits in <b>Mayurbhanj (Odisha)<\/b> contain significant amounts of titanium dioxide alongside <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">vanadium<\/a>.<\/p>\n<p>Beyond Earth, titanium has a rich cosmic footprint. It is present in meteorites, in the fiery atmosphere of the Sun, and in cool M-type stars (surfacing at 3,200 \u00b0C). Moon rocks retrieved during NASA's Apollo 17 lunar mission revealed an astonishing 12.1% titanium dioxide (TiO<sub>2<\/sub>) content. While native metallic titanium requires extreme deep-Earth mantle pressures (2.8 to 4.0 gigapascals) to form naturally on Earth, lunar soil samples have revealed tiny microscopic nanocrystals of pure native titanium created by meteoroid impacts in the vacuum of space.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Isotopes": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">Main article: Isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a><\/a><\/div>\n<p>Natural <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a> found across Earth is a mixture of <b>five stable isotopes<\/b>: <sup>46<\/sup>Ti, <sup>47<\/sup>Ti, <sup>48<\/sup>Ti, <sup>49<\/sup>Ti, and <sup>50<\/sup>Ti. By far the most common of these is <b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a>-48 (<sup>48<\/sup>Ti)<\/b>, which makes up about 73.8% of all titanium atoms in existence.<\/p>\n<p>Nuclear scientists have also created 23 synthetic radioactive isotopes of titanium, ranging from light <sup>39<\/sup>Ti to ultra-heavy <sup>66<\/sup>Ti. Most of these radioisotopes are extremely fleeting, decaying in less than half a second.
