However, a few have measurable lives: <b>titanium-44 (<sup>44<\/sup>Ti)<\/b> has a half-life of 63 years and is used by astrophysicists to trace stellar explosions (supernovae), while <sup>45<\/sup>Ti lasts 184.8 minutes, <sup>51<\/sup>Ti lasts 5.76 minutes, and <sup>52<\/sup>Ti lasts 1.7 minutes.<\/p>\n<p>Titanium isotopes lighter than <sup>46<\/sup>Ti decay primarily through positron emission (or electron capture in <sup>44<\/sup>Ti) to transform into isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Scandium (Sc)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Scandium (Sc)\">scandium<\/a><\/a>. Conversely, isotopes heavier than <sup>50<\/sup>Ti decay by emitting beta particles to become isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">vanadium<\/a><\/a>. When bombarded with high-energy deuteron beams in particle accelerators, titanium becomes radioactive, releasing energetic positrons and hard gamma rays.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">", "History": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img alt=\"Engraved profile image of a mid-age male with high forehead. The person is wearing a coat and a neckerchief.\" src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/90fa4620e90102e415814b1cf7c8af2a.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"190\" height=\"248\" style=\"--mw-file-upright: 0.75\" class=\"mw-file-element mw-file-upright\" data-file-width=\"848\" data-file-height=\"1108\" \/><figcaption>Martin Heinrich Klaproth named <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a><\/a> for the Titans of Greek mythology.<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">Titanium<\/a> was first discovered in <b>1791<\/b> by an English clergyman and amateur geologist named <b>William Gregor<\/b> in Cornwall, England. While walking near a stream in the parish of Manaccan, Gregor noticed unusual black magnetic sand (which we now know as ilmenite). Analyzing the sand, he separated <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> oxide from an unknown white metallic oxide, which he realized contained a completely new element. He published his discovery in scientific journals and named the new oxide <i>manaccanite<\/i>.<\/p>\n<p>Four years later, in 1795, Prussian chemist <b>Martin Heinrich Klaproth<\/b> independently rediscovered the same element in a mineral called rutile from Hungary (modern Slovakia). Unaware of Gregor's earlier work, Klaproth named the element <b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">Titanium<\/a><\/b> after the Titans\u2014the legendary giants of Greek mythology known for their immense power. When Klaproth later learned of Gregor's work, he tested a sample of manaccanite and graciously confirmed that Gregor had indeed discovered titanium first.<\/p>\n<p>Unlocking pure titanium metal from its ore proved to be a daunting challenge that stumped scientists for over a century. Unlike <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>, titanium cannot be smelted by heating its ore with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a><\/a>, because titanium greedily reacts with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> to form brittle titanium carbide. In 1887, Swedish chemists Lars Fredrik Nilson and Otto Pettersson produced 95% pure metal by reacting titanium oxide with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a><\/a> gas and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a>. In 1910, American scientist Matthew A. Hunter developed the <b>Hunter process<\/b> at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, producing 99.9% pure metal by heating titanium tetrachloride (TiCl<sub>4<\/sub>) with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a> under extreme pressure.<\/p>\n<p>The true commercial breakthrough arrived in the 1930s when Luxembourgish metallurgist <b>William Justin Kroll<\/b> reduced TiCl<sub>4<\/sub> using <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a><\/a>, and later refined the technique in 1940 using <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a><\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a>. Known as the <b>Kroll process<\/b>, this multi-step chemical reaction produces porous chunks of pure metal called <b>titanium sponge<\/b> and remains the dominant industrial manufacturing method today. Highly pure laboratory titanium was also achieved in 1925 by Anton Eduard van Arkel and Jan Hendrik de Boer using the iodide vapor process.<\/p>\n<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-right\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img alt=\"Rough pieces of shiny metal\" src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/59886db42b86e4860718d9c720d6d638.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"188\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"600\" data-file-height=\"451\" \/><figcaption>Titanium \"sponge\", made by the Kroll process<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p>During the Cold War in the 1950s and 1960s, titanium became a crucial strategic defense material. The Soviet Union built titanium-hulled military submarines (such as the Alfa, Mike, and Sierra II classes) capable of diving to extreme depths, while the United States used massive quantities of titanium to build record-breaking supersonic aircraft like the SR-71 Blackbird, Lockheed A-12, and F-100 Super Sabre. The U.S. maintained strategic stockpiles of titanium sponge (over 15,000 metric tons allocated annually).<\/p>\n<p><b>Modern Indian Scientific Leadership:<\/b> For decades, aerospace-grade titanium sponge technology was tightly guarded by a handful of nations. To achieve complete self-reliance (<i>Aatmanirbhar Bharat<\/i>) in high-tech space and defense applications, India's <b>Defence Metallurgical Research Laboratory (DMRL)<\/b> under DRDO spent over two decades pioneering indigenous technology to manufacture aerospace-grade titanium sponge using the Kroll process. Sponsored and funded by the <b>Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC)<\/b> of the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), a state-of-the-art commercial <b>Titanium Sponge Plant (TSP)<\/b> was established at KMML in Chavara, Kerala, and fully commissioned in 2015. This landmark achievement made India one of only a select few nations in the world capable of producing high-purity aerospace titanium from raw coastal sand under one roof, providing critical titanium alloy components for ISRO's rocket engines, satellite propellant tanks (including those on <b>Chandrayaan-3<\/b>), and naval defense platforms.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">", "Applications": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-right\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img alt=\"A hand holding a cylinder of reflective silvery metal\" src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/7f7f0a2f6fdef6c39103614bdbdd4711.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"167\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"2160\" data-file-height=\"1440\" \/><figcaption>A <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a><\/a> cylinder<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">Titanium<\/a><\/a> plays an irreplaceable role across aerospace, medicine, heavy industry, and everyday consumer products:<\/p>\n<ul>\n<li><b>Aerospace & Space Exploration:<\/b> Because of its immense strength and low weight, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a> is widely alloyed with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminium (Al)\">aluminium<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">vanadium<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mo\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Molybdenum (Mo)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mo\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Molybdenum (Mo)\">molybdenum<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">manganese<\/a><\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a> (such as the famous Ti-6Al-4V alloy). It is used for jet engine fan blades, airframe structural parts, rocket motor casings, and high-pressure propellant tanks for spacecraft\u2014including ISRO's PSLV, GSLV, and Moon missions. Mill products include sheet, plate, bar, wire, forgings, and castings.<\/li>\n<li><b>Medical Implants & Prosthetics:<\/b> Titanium is uniquely <i>biocompatible<\/i>\u2014the human body does not reject it, and bone tissue actually grows directly onto titanium surfaces in a process called <i>osseointegration<\/i>. It is the material of choice for artificial hip and knee joints, dental implants, skull plates, pacemakers, and bone fixation screws.<\/li>\n<li><b>Industrial & Chemical Processing:<\/b> Because seawater and harsh chemicals cannot corrode titanium, it is heavily used in coastal power stations, desalinization plants (converting sea water into drinking water), naval warships, submarine hulls, chemical reactors, heat exchangers, and oil drilling rigs.<\/li>\n<li><b>Metallurgy & Steel Production:<\/b> Added to steel as ferro-titanium, titanium refines grain size, acts as a deoxidizer, and prevents carbide precipitation in stainless steel, preserving strength and rust resistance.<\/li>\n<li><b>Everyday White Pigment:<\/b> Over 95% of all mined titanium ore is turned into <b>titanium dioxide (TiO<sub>2<\/sub>)<\/b>, an intensely white, non-toxic pigment with an ultra-high refractive index. It gives supreme brightness and opacity to white paint, sunscreen, paper, plastics, toothpaste, food coloring, and cosmetics.<\/li>\n<li><b>Pyrotechnics & Recreation:<\/b> Finely powdered titanium metal burns with blinding white sparks, adding dramatic effects to fireworks and stage pyrotechnics. In sporting equipment, titanium produces lightweight premium golf clubs, bicycle frames, tennis rackets, and lightweight camping gear.<\/li>\n<\/ul>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">" } }, "V": { "symbol": "V", "name": "Vanadium", "atomic": 23, "category": "transition metal", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 23 (V)", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">Vanadium<\/a><\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>V<\/b>, atomic number 23) is a hard, silvery-grey, ductile transition metal celebrated for its extraordinary strength-enhancing abilities and vibrant chemical versatility. Rarely found as a free metal in nature, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">vanadium<\/a> forms a protective oxide surface layer (passivation) that shields it against corrosion by air, water, and acids. Though named after <i>Vanad\u00eds<\/i>, the Norse goddess of beauty and fertility, due to the dazzling colors of its chemical compounds, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">vanadium<\/a> has a rich heritage in metallurgy\u2014from trace inclusions in ancient Indian crucible Wootz steel to modern superalloys in supersonic aircraft, industrial catalysts, and long-duration vanadium flow batteries storing clean renewable energy.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/0\/0a\/Vanadium-pieces.jpg", "atomic_mass": 50.94151, "density": 6, "melt": 2183, "boil": 3680, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Andr\u00e9s Manuel del R\u00edo", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d3", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.63, "electron_affinity": 50.911, "ionization_energies": [ 650.9, 1414, 2830, 4507, 6298.7, 12363, 14530, 16730, 19860, 22240, 24670, 29730, 32446, 86450, 94170, 102300, 112700, 121600, 130700, 143400, 151440, 661050, 699144 ], "sections": { "History": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">Vanadium<\/a><\/a> has a colorful discovery history filled with mistaken identities, scientific rivalry, and ancient metallurgical mastery. The element was first discovered in 1801 by Spanish mineralogist Andr\u00e9s Manuel del R\u00edo while working in Mexico City. Del R\u00edo extracted the element from a sample of Mexican \"brown <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a>\" ore (now known as vanadinite, Pb\u2085(VO\u2084)\u2083Cl). Intrigued by the brilliant red, yellow, and blue colors of its chemical salts, he initially named the element <i>panchromium<\/i> (Greek for \"all colors\") and later renamed it <i>erythronium<\/i> (Greek for \"red\") because its salts turned bright red upon heating. However, in 1805, French chemist Hippolyte Victor Collet-Descotils\u2014supported by del R\u00edo's close friend, the famous explorer Baron Alexander von Humboldt\u2014incorrectly claimed that del R\u00edo's discovery was merely an impure sample of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a><\/a>. Doubting his own work, del R\u00edo accepted their verdict and withdrew his claim.<\/p>\n<p>Thirty years later, in 1831, Swedish chemist Nils Gabriel Sefstr\u00f6m rediscovered the mysterious metal inside a newly analyzed sample of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> ore from Taberg, Sweden. Wanting a name starting with the letter V, Sefstr\u00f6m named the element <i><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">vanadium<\/a><\/i> after <i>Vanad\u00eds<\/i>, an Old Norse name for Freyja, the Scandinavian goddess of beauty and fertility, inspired by the gorgeous colors of its chemical compounds. Later that same year, German chemist Friedrich W\u00f6hler rigorously analyzed both samples and conclusively proved that Sefstr\u00f6m's <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">vanadium<\/a> was identical to del R\u00edo's erythronium. Although geologist George William Featherstonhaugh suggested renaming the element <i>rionium<\/i> to honor del R\u00edo's original discovery, the name vanadium stuck worldwide.<\/p>\n<p>Isolating pure metallic vanadium proved exceptionally difficult because vanadium eagerly reacts with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a> at high temperatures. In 1831, Swedish chemist J\u00f6ns Jakob Berzelius believed he had isolated pure vanadium metal, but British chemist Sir Henry Enfield Roscoe demonstrated in 1867 that Berzelius had actually produced vanadium nitride (VN). Roscoe became the first scientist to isolate relatively pure vanadium metal by reducing vanadium(II) chloride (VCl\u2082) with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a><\/a> gas. In 1927, American chemists J. W. Marden and M. N. Rich achieved high-purity (99.9%) metallic vanadium by reducing vanadium pentoxide (V\u2082O\u2085) with metallic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a><\/a> inside a sealed steel bomb.<\/p>\n<p>The industrial revolution transformed vanadium into a strategic commodity. In 1905, after studying high-strength French racing cars, American automotive pioneer Henry Ford adopted vanadium steel for the chassis and crankshafts of the iconic Ford Model T automobile. Adding just a tiny fraction of vanadium doubled the steel's tensile strength while significantly reducing vehicle weight, making cars durable enough to handle rugged country roads. In the early 20th century, most of the world's vanadium was mined from the remote Minas Ragra patr\u00f3nite deposit in Peru by the American Vanadium Company. Later, during the 1910s and 1920s, vanadium became widely available as a valuable byproduct during the extraction of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/U\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Uranium (U)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/U\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Uranium (U)\">uranium<\/a><\/a> from carnotite ore.<\/p>\n<p>In biological history, German chemist Martin Henze made a startling discovery in 1911: he found that marine sea squirts (Ascidiacea) concentrate extraordinary amounts of vanadium in specialized blood cells called vanadocytes, unveiling vanadium's unique role in marine biochemistry.<\/p>\n<p><b>Ancient Indian Crucible Steel (Wootz Steel):<\/b><\/p>\n<p>Long before European chemists isolated vanadium, ancient Indian metallurgists unknowingly harnessed its power to forge the world's finest steel. From the 1st millennium BCE, ironsmiths in South India (across present-day Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, and Karnataka) crafted high-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> crucible steel known as <i>Wootz steel<\/i> (the precursor to legendary Damascus swords). Modern microscopic and chemical analyses by materials scientists have revealed that the local <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> ores mined by ancient Indian smiths contained natural trace impurities of vanadium, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a><\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mo\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Molybdenum (Mo)\">molybdenum<\/a>. During specialized high-temperature crucible smelting and repeated thermal forging, these vanadium trace atoms segregated into microscopic layers, forming submicroscopic networks of ultra-hard vanadium carbides embedded within the <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> matrix. These vanadium carbide bands gave Wootz blades their legendary combination of extreme razor sharpness, flexibility, and their iconic \"watered silk\" wavy surface patterns (<i>Jauhar<\/i>). When the specific vanadium-bearing iron ore veins in South India were exhausted in the 19th century, the traditional secret of manufacturing authentic Damascus blades was temporarily lost to history.<\/p>", "Characteristics": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/422c3b92c058c6ab86577238508cabb3.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"167\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"800\" data-file-height=\"534\" \/><figcaption>Polycrystalline high-purity (99.95%) <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">vanadium<\/a><\/a> cuboids, ebeam remelted and macro-etched<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">Vanadium<\/a><\/a> is a medium-hard, ductile, malleable transition metal with a lustrous steel-blue appearance. With a density of 6.11 g\/cm\u00b3, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">vanadium<\/a> is significantly lighter than <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a> (7.87 g\/cm\u00b3) yet remarkably hard and resistant to wear. It possesses a very high melting point of 2183 K (1910 \u00b0C \/ 3470 \u00b0F) and a boiling point of 3680 K (3407 \u00b0C \/ 6165 \u00b0F), classifying it as a refractory metal along with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Nb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Niobium (Nb)\">niobium<\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ta\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tantalum (Ta)\">tantalum<\/a>.<\/p>\n<p>Chemically, pure vanadium metal exhibits excellent resistance to corrosion. At room temperature, exposure to air causes vanadium to instantly form a thin, protective oxide passivation layer that prevents deeper oxidation. Vanadium resists attack by alkalis, saltwater, hydrofluoric acid, cold hydrochloric acid, and dilute sulfuric acid, though it dissolves in hot concentrated nitric acid, aqua regia, and concentrated sulfuric acid. When heated in air above 933 K (660 \u00b0C \/ 1220 \u00b0F), vanadium oxidizes rapidly into yellow-orange vanadium pentoxide (V\u2082O\u2085). Vanadium also absorbs <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a><\/a> gas readily at high temperatures, forming brittle vanadium hydrides.<\/p>\n<p><b>The Chameleon of Chemistry: Four Vivid Colors:<\/b><\/p>\n<p>Vanadium is world-famous in chemistry education as the \"chameleon metal\" because it exhibits four distinct, beautifully colored oxidation states in aqueous solution, corresponding to four consecutive electronic configurations:<\/p>\n<ul>\n <li><b>+5 Oxidation State (Yellow\/Orange):<\/b> Found in dioxovanadium(V) cations (VO\u2082\u207a) and vanadate ions (VO\u2084\u00b3\u207b). This is vanadium's most stable and highest oxidation state.<\/li>\n <li><b>+4 Oxidation State (Bright Blue):<\/b> Present as the oxovanadium(IV) or vanadyl ion (VO\u00b2\u207a). The vanadyl ion is exceptionally stable and forms numerous coordination complexes.<\/li>\n <li><b>+3 Oxidation State (Emerald Green):<\/b> Occurs as the hydrated vanadium(III) ion (V\u00b3\u207a).<\/li>\n <li><b>+2 Oxidation State (Lavender\/Violet):<\/b> Formed by the hydrated vanadium(II) ion (V\u00b2\u207a).<\/li>\n<\/ul>\n<p>In a famous classroom chemistry demonstration, adding metallic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a><\/a> and acid to a yellow vanadate (+5) solution causes a spectacular rainbow reaction: as <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> gradually reduces vanadium, the solution transitions step-by-step from vibrant yellow (+5) to deep blue (+4), brilliant green (+3), and finally soft lavender-violet (+2)!<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">Main article: Isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">vanadium<\/a><\/a><\/div>\n<p>Naturally occurring <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">vanadium<\/a><\/a> found on Earth consists of two primary isotopes: one stable isotope, <b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">vanadium<\/a>-51 (\u2075\u00b9V)<\/b>, which accounts for 99.75% of natural abundance, and one primordial radioactive isotope, <b>vanadium-50 (\u2075\u2070V)<\/b>, which makes up the remaining 0.25%.<\/p>\n<p>Vanadium-50 is a fascinating nuclear anomaly. It has an extraordinarily long half-life of 2.71 \u00d7 10\u00b9\u2077 years (271 quadrillion years)\u2014a duration more than 19 million times longer than the age of the universe itself! Because it decays so incredibly slowly via electron capture (decaying into stable <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a><\/a>-50) and beta decay (decaying into stable <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a><\/a>-50), vanadium-50 poses zero radiation hazard and behaves as an effectively stable isotope in practical everyday applications.<\/p>\n<p>The dominant stable isotope, vanadium-51 (\u2075\u00b9V), possesses a nuclear spin of 7\/2. Because of its favorable nuclear properties, \u2075\u00b9V is widely utilized in Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy to investigate the structural geometry, active sites, and chemical bonding of complex vanadium catalysts and biological metalloproteins.<\/p>\n<p>Nuclear scientists have artificially synthesized 25 radioactive isotopes of vanadium in particle accelerators, ranging in mass number from \u2074\u00b2V to \u2076\u2078V. Among these synthetic radioisotopes, the longest-lived are <b>vanadium-49 (\u2074\u2079V)<\/b> with a half-life of 330 days, and <b>vanadium-48 (\u2074\u2078V)<\/b> with a half-life of 15.97 days. All other artificial radioisotopes have half-lives shorter than one hour, with most decaying in under ten seconds. For vanadium isotopes lighter than \u2075\u00b9V, the primary decay pathway is electron capture into <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a>; for isotopes heavier than \u2075\u00b9V, the main pathway is beta emission into <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a>.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/b42ae57c240be596583327492a7369d7.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"166\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"2240\" data-file-height=\"1488\" \/><figcaption>Vanadinite<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">Vanadium<\/a><\/a> is the 19th most abundant element in Earth's crust, with an average crustal concentration of roughly 120 parts per million (0.012% by weight)\u2014making it nearly as common as <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a><\/a> or <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a><\/a>. Across the wider universe, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">vanadium<\/a> accounts for about 0.0001% of cosmic matter and has been detected spectroscopically in the light from the Sun and cool M-type red giant stars. Ocean water contains dissolved vanadyl ions at an average concentration of 30 nanomolar (1.5 mg\/m\u00b3), while certain volcanic mineral springs\u2014such as those surrounding Mount Fuji in Japan\u2014contain up to 54 micrograms of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">vanadium<\/a> per liter.<\/p>\n<p>Uncombined metallic vanadium (known as <i>native vanadium<\/i>) is exceptionally rare in nature, discovered only in volcanic gas vents (fumaroles) at the active Colima Volcano in Mexico, alongside rare minerals like shcherbinaite (V\u2082O\u2085) and colimaite (K\u2083VS\u2084). Instead, vanadium compounds are broadly distributed across more than 65 different minerals. Major vanadium-bearing minerals include vanadinite (Pb\u2085(VO\u2084)\u2083Cl), carnotite (K\u2082(UO\u2082)\u2082(VO\u2084)\u2082\u00b73H\u2082O), patr\u00f3nite (VS\u2084), and roscoelite (a vanadium-rich mica).<\/p>\n<p>Despite its mineral diversity, primary mining of pure vanadium ores is rare. Today, roughly 90% of global vanadium production is recovered as a high-value byproduct from leftover slag during steel manufacturing! Most commercial vanadium originates from vanadium-bearing titanomagnetite (titaniferous <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> ores) found in layered igneous rock formations (gabbros). When these ores are smelted in blast furnaces to produce <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a>, vanadium concentrates in the molten slag, which is then processed with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a> salts to extract pure vanadium pentoxide (V\u2082O\u2085). The world's top vanadium producers are China (which accounts for over 70% of global output), South Africa, and Russia.<\/p>\n<p>Significant quantities of vanadium are also present in fossil fuel deposits, including crude oil, coal, oil shale, and tar sands. Crude oils from Venezuela and the Middle East report vanadium concentrations as high as 1200 ppm. When vanadium-rich heavy oils are burned in industrial boilers and marine engines, vanadium residues can cause high-temperature ash corrosion on boiler tubes and engine valves. Globally, fossil fuel combustion releases an estimated 110,000 tonnes of vanadium into the atmosphere every year.<\/p>\n<p><b>Indian Geological Reserves & Resources:<\/b><\/p>\n<p>India possesses substantial resources of vanadium, estimated at over 24 million tonnes of vanadium-bearing ore (containing over 64,000 tonnes of V\u2082O\u2085 equivalent). Geologically, India's vanadium wealth occurs in two distinct environments:<\/p>\n<ul>\n <li><b>Titaniferous Magnetite in Odisha & Peninsular India:<\/b> Extensive vanadiferous titanomagnetite (VTM) deposits occur hosted within the <b>Mayurbhanj Basic Igneous Complex<\/b> in Mayurbhanj district, Odisha (stretching 15 km from Kumhardubi to Hatichhar), as well as in Karnataka and Maharashtra. These ores contain between 0.28% and 1.38% V\u2082O\u2083 and serve as vital domestic feedstocks for steel slag extraction.<\/li>\n <li><b>Carbonaceous Phyllites in Arunachal Pradesh:<\/b> In a groundbreaking discovery, the Geological Survey of India (GSI) identified primary vanadium mineralization in Palaeo-proterozoic carbonaceous phyllite rocks of the Khetabari Formation in the Papum Pare district of <b>Arunachal Pradesh<\/b> (notably in the Depo and Tamang areas). Similar to China's famed \"stone coal\" deposits, this discovery marks India's first major primary sediment-hosted vanadium deposit, promising strategic self-reliance in critical energy minerals.<\/li>\n<\/ul>", "Applications": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-right\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/bf3bed4784c2c4f29fcec26b0d1b3607.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"190\" height=\"188\" style=\"--mw-file-upright: 0.75\" class=\"mw-file-element mw-file-upright\" data-file-width=\"2304\" data-file-height=\"2275\" \/><figcaption>Tool made from <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">vanadium<\/a><\/a> steel<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p>Though hidden from plain sight, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">vanadium<\/a><\/a> is an indispensable workhorse of modern metallurgy, aerospace engineering, industrial chemistry, and green energy technology:<\/p>\n<ul>\n <li><b>Steel Alloys & Ferrovanadium:<\/b> Approximately 85% to 90% of all <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">vanadium<\/a> produced worldwide is consumed in the steel industry in the form of <i>ferrovanadium<\/i> (an alloy containing 35%\u201380% vanadium). Adding as little as 0.05% to 0.15% vanadium to molten steel refines grain size, binds excess <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> into stable micro-carbides, and dramatically enhances tensile strength, hardness, and thermal resistance. Vanadium steel is essential for earthquake-resistant building rebar, high-span bridges, oil pipelines, automotive axles, railway tracks, and high-speed cutting tools (wrenches, drill bits, and knives).<\/li>\n <li><b>Aerospace <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">Titanium<\/a> Alloys (Ti-6Al-4V):<\/b> Vanadium is a critical alloying element in high-performance <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a> alloys, most notably <b>Ti-6Al-4V<\/b> (Grade 5 <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a>), which consists of 90% titanium, 6% <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a><\/a>, and 4% vanadium. Vanadium acts as a beta-phase stabilizer, giving the alloy superior strength-to-weight ratio, high temperature tolerance, and exceptional corrosion resistance. Ti-6Al-4V is extensively used in jet engine compressor blades, supersonic airframes, rocket motor casings, and surgical implants.<\/li>\n <li><b>Industrial Chemical Catalysts:<\/b> Vanadium pentoxide (V\u2082O\u2085) is the core chemical catalyst used in the industrial Contact Process to oxidize <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a> dioxide into <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a> trioxide for manufacturing <b>sulfuric acid<\/b>\u2014the world's most widely produced industrial chemical. Vanadium catalysts are also essential in producing maleic anhydride (for plastics), phthalic anhydride, and selective catalytic reduction (SCR) systems that remove harmful <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a> oxide (NOx) pollutants from power plant smokestacks.<\/li>\n <li><b>Vanadium Redox Flow Batteries (VRFB):<\/b> Vanadium is revolutionary for renewable energy storage! Unlike <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a>-ion batteries, a <i>Vanadium Redox Flow Battery<\/i> uses liquid vanadium electrolytes stored in large external tanks, taking advantage of vanadium's four consecutive oxidation states (+2, +3, +4, +5) to store and release electrical energy. VRFBs offer non-flammable, long-duration energy storage (over 20 years of continuous use with zero capacity degradation), making them ideal for backing up solar and wind power grids.<\/li>\n<\/ul>\n<p><b>Modern Indian Scientific & Industrial Contributions:<\/b><\/p>\n<p>India is actively harnessing vanadium across defense, nuclear metallurgy, green energy, and sustainable waste recycling:<\/p>\n<ul>\n <li><b>Indigenous Aerospace Alloys (MIDHANI & HAL Tejas):<\/b> State-owned metallurgy giant <b>Mishra Dhatu Nigam Limited (MIDHANI)<\/b> in Hyderabad indigenously manufactures high-purity <b>Ti-6Al-4V<\/b> titanium-vanadium alloy products for Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL). These strategic alloys form critical airframe structures, wing fittings, and gas turbine components for India's <b>HAL Tejas<\/b> light combat aircraft (Tejas Mk1A and Mk2) as well as launch vehicle components for the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO).<\/li>\n <li><b>Grid-Scale Flow Battery Innovation (CSIR-CECRI, IIT Madras & NTPC):<\/b> Premier Indian institutions are pioneering indigenous VRFB technology for national grid stability. Researchers at <b>CSIR-Central Electrochemical Research Institute (CSIR-CECRI)<\/b> in Karaikudi and <b>IIT Madras<\/b> have engineered indigenous VRFB stack architectures and cost-effective ion-exchange membranes. In a historic milestone for Indian green energy, India's first grid-scale 3 MWh Vanadium Redox Flow Battery system was commissioned at NTPC's NETRA facility in Greater Noida, establishing a national benchmark for long-duration renewable storage.<\/li>\n <li><b>Sustainable Metallurgical Recovery (CSIR-NML):<\/b> Scientists at the <b>CSIR-National Metallurgical Laboratory (CSIR-NML)<\/b> in Jamshedpur have developed eco-friendly hydrometallurgical extraction processes to recover strategic vanadium pentoxide (V\u2082O\u2085) and ammonium metavanadate from secondary resources\u2014including spent sulfuric acid catalysts and titaniferous steel slag\u2014supporting India's <i>Aatmanirbhar Bharat<\/i> mission for critical mineral independence.<\/li>\n<\/ul>", "Biological role": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">Vanadium<\/a><\/a> plays a far more prominent biological role in marine life and specialized microorganisms than in higher land animals. Although present in trace amounts in the human body (totaling about 100 to 200 micrograms), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">vanadium<\/a> is not officially classified as an essential micronutrient for humans, though it is required in micro-gram amounts by rats and chickens for normal growth and lipid metabolism.<\/p>\n<figure class=\"mw-default-size\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/0a0f58ef80f4951652ad63dba7b315b9.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"200\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"2415\" data-file-height=\"1932\" \/><figcaption>Tunicates such as this bluebell tunicate contain <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">vanadium<\/a><\/a> as vanabins.<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<figure class=\"mw-default-size\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/b1e44ba7081cce0e32ff477d96f66575.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"188\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"3072\" data-file-height=\"2304\" \/><figcaption><i>Amanita muscaria<\/i> contains amavadin.<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p><b>Marine Biochemistry & Specialized Organisms:<\/b><\/p>\n<ul>\n <li><b>Tunicates (Sea Squirts):<\/b> Certain marine tunicates (such as the bluebell tunicate) absorb vanadyl ions from seawater and accumulate vanadium in specialized blood cells called <i>vanadocytes<\/i> at concentrations up to 1,000,000 times higher than surrounding ocean water! They bind the metal using specialized vanadium-binding proteins called <i>vanabins<\/i>. While their exact biological function remains an intriguing mystery, vanabins are believed to play roles in defense against predators or <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> metabolism.<\/li>\n <li><b>Fungi (Fly Agaric):<\/b> The famous red-and-white spotted toadstool mushroom, <i>Amanita muscaria<\/i> (Fly Agaric), accumulates vanadium to form a unique organic coordination complex called <i>amavadin<\/i>.<\/li>\n <li><b>Bacterial & Algal Enzymes:<\/b> Certain <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a>-fixing soil bacteria (such as <i>Azotobacter vinelandii<\/i>) express alternative <i>vanadium nitrogenase<\/i> enzymes that allow them to convert atmospheric <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a> gas into ammonia when environmental <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mo\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Molybdenum (Mo)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mo\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Molybdenum (Mo)\">molybdenum<\/a><\/a> is scarce. Additionally, marine brown algae and fungi utilize vanadium haloperoxidase enzymes to synthesize halogenated organic compounds.<\/li>\n<\/ul>\n<p><b>Medicinal Chemistry & Indian Insulin-Mimetic Research:<\/b><\/p>\n<p>In pharmacology, vanadium compounds exhibit powerful <b>insulin-mimetic<\/b> (insulin-like) properties. Vanadate (VO\u2084\u00b3\u207b) and vanadyl (VO\u00b2\u207a) ions structurally resemble phosphate ions, allowing them to inhibit protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTPase) enzymes in the human body. By blocking PTPases, vanadium complexes keep insulin receptors active, stimulating glucose uptake into cells and lowering blood sugar levels independently of insulin.<\/p>\n<p>To overcome the mild gastrointestinal toxicity of inorganic vanadium salts, bioinorganic chemists across premier Indian institutions\u2014including the Indian Institute of Science (IISc Bengaluru), IIT Bombay, IIT Madras, and CSIR laboratories\u2014are synthesizing novel organic vanadium complexes (such as vanadyl picolinate, acetylacetonates, and Schiff-base derivatives). These Indian research groups are designing bio-compatible, low-toxicity vanadium metallopharmaceuticals aimed at developing affordable oral therapeutics for managing type-2 diabetes.<\/p>" } }, "Cr": { "symbol": "Cr", "name": "Chromium", "atomic": 24, "category": "transition metal", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 24 (Cr)", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">Chromium<\/a><\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>Cr<\/b>, atomic number 24) is a lustrous, steely-grey transition metal renowned for its extraordinary hardness, polished shine, and vivid array of colorful chemical compounds. Positioned in Group 6 of the periodic table, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a> derives its name from the Greek word <i>chroma<\/i>, meaning color, because its diverse chemical states produce a spectacular spectrum of brilliant hues\u2014ranging from deep emerald greens and ruby reds to sunny yellows and intense oranges. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">Chromium<\/a> is the essential shield behind modern stainless steel, forming an invisible, self-healing oxide barrier that defends <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> against rust and corrosion. Beyond its industrial dominance in chrome plating and high-strength alloys, chromium holds deep geographical and cultural significance in India: the mineral-rich <b>Sukinda Valley<\/b> in Odisha harbors nearly all of India's vast chromite reserves, while trace chromium ions are the hidden natural artists responsible for the captivating green of emeralds (<i>Marakata<\/i>) and the radiant crimson of rubies (<i>Padmaraga<\/i>) celebrated in ancient Indian texts.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/a\/a1\/Chromium.jpg", "atomic_mass": 51.99616, "density": 7.19, "melt": 2180, "boil": 2944, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Louis Nicolas Vauquelin", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s1 3d5", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.66, "electron_affinity": 65.21, "ionization_energies": [ 652.9, 1590.6, 2987, 4743, 6702, 8744.9, 15455, 17820, 20190, 23580, 26130, 28750, 34230, 37066, 97510, 105800, 114300, 125300, 134700, 144300, 157700, 166090, 721870, 761733 ], "sections": { "Physical properties": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">Chromium<\/a><\/a> is a hard, brittle transition metal with a polished silvery-grey luster and a high resistance to tarnishing. With a density of 7.19 grams per cubic centimeter, a melting point of 2,180&#160;\u00b0C (3,956&#160;\u00b0F), and a boiling point of 2,944&#160;\u00b0C (5,331&#160;\u00b0F), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a> withstands extreme thermal and physical environments. On the Mohs scale of mineral hardness, pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a> scores an impressive 8.5 to 9, making it one of the hardest pure metallic elements known.<\/p>\n<p>A key chemical superpower of chromium is its ability to undergo <b>passivation<\/b>. When exposed to ambient air or <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a>, chromium instantly forms a microscopic, transparent layer of chromium(III) oxide (Cr<sub>2<\/sub>O<sub>3<\/sub>) just a few atoms thick. This oxide film acts as an impenetrable armor that seals the metal beneath, rendering chromium highly resistant to further oxidation, rust, and attack by many acids. If the surface is scratched, the protective oxide film heals itself within milliseconds in the presence of air.<\/p>\n<p>In quantum chemistry, chromium is famous for its unique electron configuration: [Ar] 4s<sup>1<\/sup> 3d<sup>5<\/sup>. Instead of filling its outer 4s subshell with two electrons as expected, chromium promotes one electron into its 3d orbital to create a half-filled, highly stable 3d<sup>5<\/sup> configuration. This special arrangement accounts for its strong metallic bonding, high melting point, and fascinating magnetic properties\u2014chromium is the only elemental solid that exhibits antiferromagnetic ordering at room temperature (below its N\u00e9el temperature of about 312 K or 39 \u00b0C).<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Isotopes": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">Main article: Isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a><\/a><\/div>\n<p>Naturally occurring <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a><\/a> is composed of four stable isotopes: <sup>50<\/sup>Cr, <sup>52<\/sup>Cr, <sup>53<\/sup>Cr, and <sup>54<\/sup>Cr. Among these, <b><sup>52<\/sup>Cr<\/b> is by far the most abundant, constituting 83.789% of all natural <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a>. The remaining stable isotopes make up 4.345% (<sup>50<\/sup>Cr), 9.501% (<sup>53<\/sup>Cr), and 2.365% (<sup>54<\/sup>Cr). Scientists have also synthesized 25 radioactive isotopes ranging from <sup>42<\/sup>Cr to <sup>70<\/sup>Cr, alongside two metastable nuclear isomers. The most stable radioisotope is <b><sup>51<\/sup>Cr<\/b>, which has a half-life of 27.70 days and is widely used in biomedical research to label red blood cells and measure blood volume.<\/p>\n<p>In nuclear physics, isotopes lighter than <sup>52<\/sup>Cr decay primarily through electron capture into isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">vanadium<\/a><\/a> or <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a><\/a>, while heavier isotopes decay via beta emission into isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">manganese<\/a><\/a>.<\/p>\n<p>Chromium isotopes play a crucial role in planetary science and isotope geology. The isotope <b><sup>53<\/sup>Cr<\/b> is the radiogenic decay product of extinct <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">manganese<\/a>-53 (<sup>53<\/sup>Mn, half-life of 3.7 million years). Because <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">manganese<\/a> and chromium are often concentrated together in planetary rocks, the ratio of <sup>53<\/sup>Cr to <sup>52<\/sup>Cr paired with Mn\/Cr ratios in ancient meteorites provides astronomers with a high-precision chemical clock. This Mn\u2013Cr isotopic system reinforces evidence from <sup>26<\/sup>Al and <sup>107<\/sup>Pd, proving that distinct planetary bodies differentiated within the first few million years of the Solar System's birth.<\/p>\n<p>Furthermore, variations in chromium isotope ratios (<sup>53<\/sup>Cr\/<sup>52<\/sup>Cr) trapped in ancient marine sediments serve as a sensitive proxy for historical atmospheric <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a> concentrations, allowing geologists to reconstruct how Earth's atmosphere became <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a>-rich over billions of years.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">", "Occurrence": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable selfref\">See also: Category:<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">Chromium<\/a><\/a> minerals<\/div>\n<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-left\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/f430d9fdf335cdfbb9bc7a1e7ba47dad.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"190\" height=\"126\" style=\"--mw-file-upright: 0.75\" class=\"mw-file-element mw-file-upright\" data-file-width=\"3008\" data-file-height=\"2000\" \/><figcaption>Crocoite (PbCrO<sub>4<\/sub>)<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-left\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/94e898e6707d6456d3354fb68d0b8e58.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"190\" height=\"152\" style=\"--mw-file-upright: 0.75\" class=\"mw-file-element mw-file-upright\" data-file-width=\"1837\" data-file-height=\"1469\" \/><figcaption>Chromite ore<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">Chromium<\/a><\/a> is the 21st most abundant element in Earth's crust, with an average concentration of roughly 100 parts per million (ppm). Natural erosion of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a>-bearing rocks and volcanic eruptions constantly redistribute trace amounts into the environment. Typical background concentrations are under 10 ng\/m<sup>3<\/sup> in the atmosphere, under 500 mg\/kg in soils, under 0.5 mg\/kg in vegetation, under 10 &#181;g\/L in freshwater, and under 1 &#181;g\/L in seawater. Virtually all commercial chromium is extracted from <b>chromite ore<\/b> (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> chromium oxide, FeCr<sub>2<\/sub>O<sub>4<\/sub>). Pure native elemental chromium metal is exceptionally rare in nature, found only in unusual reducing environments such as the diamond-rich Udachnaya kimberlite pipe in Russia.<\/p>\n<p>Globally, chromite deposits are concentrated in a few key nations. South Africa produces roughly two-fifths of the world's chromite ores and concentrates, Kazakhstan produces about one-third, while India, Russia, and Turkey are major global suppliers.<\/p>\n<p><b>India's Geographical & Geological Hub:<\/b> India holds world-class chromite reserves, with the state of <b>Odisha<\/b> serving as the country's unquestioned chromite capital. The famous <b>Sukinda Valley<\/b> in Jajpur district, nestled between the Daitari and Mahagiri hill ranges, contains an astounding <b>95% to 98% of India's total chromite deposits<\/b>. Geological formations in the Sukinda Ultramafic Complex feature serpentinized peridotites and host the world's thickest known single chromite seam, measuring up to 40 meters across! Major mining companies such as Tata Steel, Odisha Mining Corporation (OMC), and FACOR operate extensive open-cast mines in Sukinda, producing high-grade ore for domestic ferrochrome smelting and global export.<\/p>\n<p>In natural water systems, chromium exists primarily as non-toxic trivalent Cr(III) or toxic hexavalent Cr(VI), depending on soil pH and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> levels. While Cr(III) predominates in most natural soils, certain mineral-rich groundwaters can accumulate total chromium levels up to 39 &#181;g\/L, of which up to 30 &#181;g\/L may be present as hexavalent Cr(VI).<\/p>\n<div style=\"clear:left;\" class=\"\"><\/div>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">", "History": "<p>Long before <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a> was isolated as a chemical element in Western laboratories, its dramatic colors captivated ancient civilizations. In ancient India, gemology (<i>Ratna Shastra<\/i>) flourished as a precise art and science. Sanskrit encyclopedias such as the 6th-century <i>Brihat Samhita<\/i> by Varahamihira and medieval alchemical texts like the 13th-century <i>Rasaratnasamuccaya<\/i> cataloged precious gems with meticulous detail. They celebrated the serene green emerald (<i>Marakata<\/i>) and the fiery red ruby (<i>Padmaraga<\/i> or <i>Manikya<\/i>). Modern spectroscopy later revealed that both of these prized <i>Navaratnas<\/i> (nine sacred gemstones) owe their vivid colors to the exact same element: trace trivalent <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a> (Cr<sup>3+<\/sup>) ions substituting for <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a><\/a> in their crystal lattices!<\/p>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">Chromium<\/a> also played a silent protective role in ancient Chinese metallurgy. Over 2,000 years ago during the Qin Dynasty, weapon smiths treated bronze swords, spears, and arrowheads buried with the famous Terracotta Army with a thin chromium oxide coating, leaving these ancient weapons remarkably shiny and rust-free when excavated in modern times.<\/p>\n<p>The Western scientific discovery of chromium began in 1761 when German mineralogist Johann Gottlob Lehmann discovered a vibrant orange-red mineral in Siberia's Ural Mountains, which he named \"Siberian red <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a>\" (now known as crocoite, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a> chromate, PbCrO<sub>4<\/sub>). In 1797, French chemist <b>Louis Nicolas Vauquelin<\/b> analyzed samples of crocoite ore. Vauquelin produced chromium trioxide and successfully isolated pure metallic chromium by reducing the oxide with charcoal in a high-temperature furnace. Intrigued by the brilliant red, yellow, and green colors of its chemical compounds, Vauquelin named the new element <i>chromium<\/i>, from the Greek word <i>chroma<\/i> (color).<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">", "Applications": "<p>About <b>85% of all <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a> consumed globally<\/b> is used in metal alloys, with the remainder powering the chemical, refractory ceramic, and foundry industries. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">Chromium<\/a>'s primary application is the manufacture of <b>stainless steel<\/b>. Adding at least 10.5% <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a> to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a> creates an alloy that is practically immune to rust, because chromium forms an invisible, self-healing oxide passivation layer on the steel surface. Stainless steel is essential for modern kitchen cutlery, medical surgical instruments, food processing plants, chemical storage tanks, and architectural skyscrapers.<\/p>\n<p>In India, Sukinda's rich chromite ore is converted into ferrochrome and charge-chrome inside heavy industrial furnaces. This domestic ferrochrome powers India's booming steel industry, supplying high-performance stainless steel for structural infrastructure, heavy machinery, defense armor, and lightweight passenger coaches like the Indian Railways' high-speed <b>Vande Bharat Express<\/b> trains.<\/p>\n<p>Chromium is also famous for <b>chrome plating<\/b>. Through electroplating, a paper-thin layer of chromium is deposited onto metal or plastic surfaces, providing a bright, mirror-like finish that resists tarnishing, scratches, and corrosion. Shiny chrome trims are ubiquitous on automobiles, motorcycles, bathroom faucets, hand tools, and commercial machinery. Beyond metals, chromium compounds serve as high-temperature refractory bricks to line blast furnaces, as specialized foundry sand, and as vivid industrial pigments (such as chrome yellow and chrome green).<\/p>\n<p><b>Indian Scientific Innovation in Leather Processing:<\/b> Historically, chromium salts (specifically trivalent chromium sulfate) have been the world's primary agent for tanning animal hides into durable leather. However, traditional chrome tanning discharged large amounts of chromium-laden wastewater. To solve this environmental challenge, scientists at the <b>CSIR-Central Leather Research Institute (CSIR-CLRI)<\/b> in Chennai developed revolutionary <b>Waterless Chrome Tanning Technology (WCTT)<\/b>. This indigenous Indian breakthrough completely eliminates water from the chrome tanning step, cuts salt usage by 20%, saves millions of liters of freshwater, and eliminates chromium discharge into rivers, setting a global benchmark for eco-friendly industrial chemistry.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Biological role": "<p>The biological role of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a><\/a> depends entirely on its chemical oxidation state. Trivalent <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a> (<b>Cr(III)<\/b> or Cr<sup>3+<\/sup>) is considered a trace dietary element. For decades, scientists hypothesized that Cr(III) assisted insulin in regulating carbohydrate, fat, and protein metabolism through an oligopeptide molecule known as chromodulin (low-molecular-weight <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a>-binding substance). However, modern medical research has not conclusively established an essential biochemical pathway, and \"chromium deficiency\" is not recognized as a formal medical condition because healthy individuals do not require dietary chromium supplements. Common foods contain small amounts of chromium (1 to 13 micrograms per serving). Trace amounts of chromium (and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a><\/a>) can also leach into food when acidic dishes are cooked for extended periods in stainless steel cookware, particularly when the cookware is brand new.<\/p>\n<p>In sharp contrast, hexavalent chromium (<b>Cr(VI)<\/b> or Cr<sup>6+<\/sup>) is a severe toxin, mutagen, and known human carcinogen. Ingesting Cr(VI) through contaminated drinking water has been linked to stomach tumors, liver damage, and severe allergic contact dermatitis, while inhaling Cr(VI) dust causes lung cancer and nasal ulcers.<\/p>\n<p><b>Modern Indian Remediation Science:<\/b> Environmental contamination from open-cast chromite mining in regions like the Sukinda Valley in Odisha has historically led to hexavalent Cr(VI) leaching into local water bodies like the Damsala Nallah and the Brahmani River basin. To combat this public health risk, Indian scientists at the <b>CSIR-Institute of Minerals and Materials Technology (CSIR-IMMT)<\/b> in Bhubaneswar, along with researchers at the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) and leading Indian universities, have developed cutting-edge remediation technologies. They isolate indigenous, chromium-tolerant bacteria (such as <i>Bacillus<\/i> and <i>Pseudomonas<\/i> species) and native fungi from Sukinda soils capable of bio-reducing toxic Cr(VI) into non-toxic, insoluble Cr(III). Coupled with phytoremediation using local metallophyte plants, these innovative bio-cleanup methods neutralize chromium pollution, protecting ecosystems and communities across India.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">" } }, "Mn": { "symbol": "Mn", "name": "Manganese", "atomic": 25, "category": "transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">Manganese<\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>Mn<\/b>, atomic number 25) is a hard, brittle, silvery-gray transition metal that closely resembles <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>. Named from the ancient region of Magnesia, it is never found as a pure metal in nature but occurs abundantly in minerals like pyrolusite (MnO<sub>2<\/sub>). <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">Manganese<\/a> is the essential powerhouse of modern metallurgy\u2014adding strength, toughness, and rust-resistance to steel\u2014and plays a vital role in household batteries, agricultural nutrients, and chemical oxidizers. India has deep historical and scientific ties to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">manganese<\/a>, spanning ancient <i>Wootz steel<\/i> crucible metallurgy, <i>Rasa Shastra<\/i> texts (where it was recognized as <i>Vaikrant<\/i>), Asia's deepest underground manganese mine at Balaghat, deep-sea mining in the Indian Ocean, and cutting-edge battery recycling research.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/6\/64\/Manganese_element.jpg", "atomic_mass": 54.9380443, "density": 7.21, "melt": 1519, "boil": 2334, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Torbern Olof Bergman", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d5", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.55, "electron_affinity": -50, "ionization_energies": [ 717.3, 1509, 3248, 4940, 6990, 9220, 11500, 18770, 21400, 23960, 27590, 30330, 33150, 38880, 41987, 109480, 118100, 127100, 138600, 148500, 158600, 172500, 181380, 785450, 827067 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">Manganese<\/a><\/b> is a versatile transition metal located in Group 7 and Period 4 of the periodic table. Its electron configuration is [Ar] 3d<sup>5<\/sup> 4s<sup>2<\/sup>. With five unpaired electrons in its 3d subshell, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">manganese<\/a> exhibits rich chemical reactivity and forms a wide array of colourful compounds.<\/p>\n\n<h3>Chemical Reactivity and Oxidation States<\/h3>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">Manganese<\/a> is chemically active and reacts readily with air, water, and acids. When exposed to moist air, it slowly tarnishes, forming a protective oxide layer. In water containing dissolved <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a>, it oxidizes (\"rusts\") much like <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>. In its pure elemental form, manganese is far too brittle to be used alone, but it excels when alloyed with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a>, and other metals.<\/p>\n\n<p>Manganese displays a wide range of oxidation states from -3 to +7, making it a chameleon of transition metal chemistry. Its key oxidation states include:<\/p>\n<ul>\n <li><b>+2 (Manganese II):<\/b> Pale pink in color, found in manganese sulfate (MnSO<sub>4<\/sub>) and rhodochrosite. This is the most chemically stable ion in aqueous solutions and plays a vital role as a plant biological cofactor.<\/li>\n <li><b>+3 (Manganese III):<\/b> Found in braunite and intermediate biological catalytic complexes.<\/li>\n <li><b>+4 (Manganese IV):<\/b> Found in dark brown or black pyrolusite (MnO<sub>2<\/sub>), a strong oxidizing agent used in glassmaking, chemical synthesis, and dry-cell batteries.<\/li>\n <li><b>+7 (Manganese VII):<\/b> Famous for intense purple <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> permanganate (KMnO<sub>4<\/sub>), a powerful oxidizer used in water purification, laboratory titrations, and medical disinfectants.<\/li>\n<\/ul>\n\n<h3><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">Sulfur<\/a>-Fixing and Deoxidizing Power<\/h3>\n<p>In chemical and metallurgical processing, manganese has a powerful chemical affinity for <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a>. During steelmaking, manganese acts as a scavenger: it binds with unwanted <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a> to form manganese sulfide (MnS), preventing brittle <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> sulfide from causing cracks when hot steel is shaped. It also reacts with dissolved <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> to form manganese oxides, purifying the molten metal.<\/p>\n\n<h3>Magnetic & Green Chemistry Behavior<\/h3>\n<p>Because of its unpaired d-electrons, manganese metal and its common ions are <b>paramagnetic<\/b>\u2014meaning they are weakly attracted to external magnetic fields, although elemental manganese is not permanently magnetic. In modern green chemistry, non-toxic manganese complexes are actively studied as eco-friendly catalysts to replace expensive, scarce noble metals in industrial organic synthesis.<\/p>", "Physical properties": "<p>In its pure metallic state, <b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">manganese<\/a><\/b> is a hard, brittle, silvery-gray metal with a distinct luster, visually resembling <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>. However, unlike <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>, pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">manganese<\/a> is extremely brittle and cannot be easily hammered, bent, or machined without fracturing.<\/p>\n\n<h3>Key Physical Constants<\/h3>\n<ul>\n <li><b>Density:<\/b> 7.21 g\/cm\u00b3 (slightly lighter than <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>).<\/li>\n <li><b>Melting Point:<\/b> 1,519 K (1,246 \u00b0C or 2,275 \u00b0F).<\/li>\n <li><b>Boiling Point:<\/b> 2,334 K (2,061 \u00b0C or 3,742 \u00b0F).<\/li>\n <li><b>Phase:<\/b> Solid at room temperature.<\/li>\n <li><b>Hardness & Texture:<\/b> Hard and brittle; shatters easily under high impact when unalloyed.<\/li>\n<\/ul>\n\n<h3>Thermal and Oxidation Behavior<\/h3>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">Manganese<\/a> has a high melting point and requires substantial thermal energy to melt. At room temperature, manganese tarnishes slowly in air, acquiring a dull oxide film. In water containing dissolved <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a>, it gradually oxidizes or \"rusts\", breaking down in a process similar to iron corrosion. When heated to high temperatures in air, it burns to form manganese tetroxide (Mn<sub>3<\/sub>O<sub>4<\/sub>).<\/p>\n\n<h3>Magnetic Behavior and Allotropes<\/h3>\n<p>Neither elemental manganese metal nor its common ores are ferromagnetic (permanently magnetic like lodestone). Instead, manganese metal and its simple ions exhibit <b>paramagnetism<\/b>, responding weakly to external magnetic fields. Solid manganese exists in four distinct crystal structures (allotropes\u2014alpha, beta, gamma, and delta) depending on temperature, with the complex cubic alpha-phase being stable at room temperature.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Naturally occurring <b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">manganese<\/a><\/b> consists of a single stable isotope, <b><sup>55<\/sup>Mn<\/b> (100% natural abundance). Because it has only one stable isotope, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">manganese<\/a> is classified as a monoisotopic element.<\/p>\n\n<h3>Radioisotopes and Decay Modes<\/h3>\n<p>Synthetic nuclear research has isolated 25 radioisotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">manganese<\/a>, ranging from <sup>46<\/sup>Mn to <sup>72<\/sup>Mn, along with 3 nuclear isomers (meta states). The most stable radioactive isotopes are:<\/p>\n<ul>\n <li><b><sup>53<\/sup>Mn:<\/b> Half-life of 3.7 million years.<\/li>\n <li><b><sup>54<\/sup>Mn:<\/b> Half-life of 312.08 days.<\/li>\n <li><b><sup>52<\/sup>Mn:<\/b> Half-life of 5.591 days.<\/li>\n<\/ul>\n<p>All other radioisotopes have half-lives shorter than 3 hours, and the majority decay in less than 1 minute. For isotopes lighter than stable <sup>55<\/sup>Mn, the primary decay mode is electron capture. For heavier isotopes, the primary decay mode is beta decay.<\/p>\n\n<h3>Stellar Origin and Supernova Nucleosynthesis<\/h3>\n<p>Manganese is part of the \"<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> group\" of cosmic elements. Astrophysicists believe these elements were synthesized in massive stars shortly before catastrophic supernova explosions. Minute quantities of radioactive <sup>53<\/sup>Mn are continually formed on meteorites and Earth through cosmic ray impacts (spallation) on <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> atoms.<\/p>\n\n<h3>Isotope Geology and Solar System Dating<\/h3>\n<p>Because radioactive <sup>53<\/sup>Mn decays into <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a>-53 (<sup>53<\/sup>Cr) with a 3.7-million-year half-life, the ratio of manganese to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a> (Mn\/Cr) acts as a cosmic clock in isotope geology. By measuring variations in <sup>53<\/sup>Cr\/<sup>52<\/sup>Cr and Mn\/Cr ratios in ancient meteorites, scientists confirmed a non-zero initial <sup>53<\/sup>Mn\/<sup>55<\/sup>Mn ratio in early solar matter. Along with isotopic evidence from <sup>26<\/sup>Al and <sup>107<\/sup>Pd, this proves that <sup>53<\/sup>Mn decayed <i>in situ<\/i> inside early planetary bodies, confirming nucleosynthetic processes right before the coalescence of the Solar System over 4.5 billion years ago.<\/p>", "History": "<p>The history of <b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">manganese<\/a><\/b> is a fascinating journey spanning tens of thousands of years, linking cave art pigments, alchemical glassmaking, ancient Indian metallurgy, and modern battery technology.<\/p>\n\n<h3>Etymology: The Tale of Two Magnesias<\/h3>\n<p>The name <i><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">manganese<\/a><\/i> comes from the ancient region of Magnesia (located in modern Greece or Turkey). In antiquity, two distinct black minerals were discovered there, both named <i>magnes<\/i>:<\/p>\n<ul>\n <li><b>Male magnes:<\/b> Magnetic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> ore (magnetite or lodestone), which attracted <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> and gave us the word <i>magnet<\/i>.<\/li>\n <li><b>Female magnes:<\/b> Non-magnetic black mineral (pyrolusite or <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">manganese<\/a> dioxide, MnO<sub>2<\/sub>), which did not attract <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> but decolorized green glass.<\/li>\n<\/ul>\n<p>By the 16th century, glassmakers and alchemists referred to manganese dioxide as <i>manganesum<\/i> to distinguish black <i>magnesia nigra<\/i> from white <i>magnesia alba<\/i> (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a> oxide). Italian physician Michele Mercati called the black mineral <i>manganesa<\/i>, which evolved into <i>manganese<\/i> (and German <i>Mangan<\/i>), while white magnesia eventually yielded the name <i><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a><\/i>.<\/p>\n\n<h3>Prehistoric Pigments and Ancient Glass<\/h3>\n<p>Natural manganese dioxide is abundant and was used as an ancient pigment. Black drawings in France's Gargas and Lascaux caves, created 24,000 to 30,000 years ago, were made using mineral MnO<sub>2<\/sub>. Ancient Egyptian, Roman, and 14th-century Venetian glassmakers added manganese compounds to glass as \"glassmaker's soap\" to clarify green iron impurities or tint glass purple.<\/p>\n\n<h3>Ancient Indian Context: Rasa Shastra & Wootz Steel Metallurgy<\/h3>\n<p>India possesses a rich ancient heritage in manganese science. In <b>Rasa Shastra<\/b> (the Ayurvedic alchemy of metals and minerals), manganese ores were identified as <b>Vaikrant<\/b> and classified among the prestigious <i>Maharasas<\/i> (eight primary minerals) in classic texts such as the <i>Rasa Ratna Samuchaya<\/i>. Traditional scholars performed meticulous <i>Shodhana<\/i> (purification) and <i>Marana<\/i> (calcination) processes to make therapeutic mineral ashes (<i>Bhasma<\/i>).<\/p>\n\n<p>In metallurgy, ancient Indian artisans as early as 300 BCE forged world-renowned <b>Wootz steel<\/b>\u2014a high-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> crucible steel made at ancient production sites like Kodumanal (Tamil Nadu) and exported worldwide. Indian metalsmiths empirically selected manganese-rich iron ores and pyrolusite fluxes to deoxidize molten steel, remove <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a>, and boost toughness. Archaeological studies of the 1,600-year-old <b>Delhi Iron Pillar<\/b> reveal trace manganese (~0.05%), contributing to its legendary corrosion resistance.<\/p>\n\n<h3>Alchemical Experiments and Chemical Isolation<\/h3>\n<p>In the 17th and 18th centuries, chemists utilized manganese dioxide in pioneering experiments. Johann Glauber (17th c.) and Ignatius Gottfried Kaim (1770) discovered that heating MnO<sub>2<\/sub> with alkalis yielded purple permanganate salts. In the mid-18th century, Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele reacted MnO<sub>2<\/sub> with acids to discover <b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a> gas<\/b> (later commercialized via the Leblanc and Weldon processes).<\/p>\n<p>Scheele recognized that pyrolusite contained an unknown metal element. In <b>1774<\/b>, Swedish chemist <b>Johan Gottlieb Gahn<\/b> officially isolated an impure sample of manganese metal by reducing manganese dioxide with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> in a crucible.
