(Kaim may also have isolated a metal sample around 1770).<\/p>\n\n<h3>Steel Revolutions, Manganism Warning, and Batteries<\/h3>\n<p>Historians speculated that Spartan sword steel gained extraordinary hardness from manganese-bearing Greek iron ores. In 1816, manganese was proven to harden iron without increasing brittleness. In 1856, British metallurgist Robert Forester Mushet introduced <i>spiegeleisen<\/i> (a 15% manganese iron alloy) into Bessemer steelmaking, enabling mass steel production.<\/p>\n<p>In 1837, British scholar James Couper first documented that heavy occupational exposure among manganese miners triggered a severe Parkinson's-like movement disorder, now known as <i>manganism<\/i>. In 1866, Georges Leclanch\u00e9 invented the Leclanch\u00e9 dry cell battery using MnO<sub>2<\/sub> as a cathode depolarizer, establishing manganese's role in 20th-century <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a>-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> and alkaline dry batteries. In 1912, manganese phosphate conversion coatings (Parkerizing) were patented to rust-proof firearms.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">Manganese<\/a><\/b> is the 12th most abundant element in the Earth's crust, constituting approximately 1,000 parts per million (0.1%) of crustal material. It is widely distributed across land, soil, atmosphere, and oceans.<\/p>\n\n<h3>Environmental Distribution and Key Ores<\/h3>\n<ul>\n <li><b>Soil:<\/b> Contains 7 to 9,000 ppm of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">manganese<\/a>, with a global average of 440 ppm.<\/li>\n <li><b>Atmosphere:<\/b> Present in trace concentrations averaging 0.01 \u00b5g\/m\u00b3.<\/li>\n <li><b>Primary Minerals:<\/b> <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">Manganese<\/a> never occurs naturally as a pure native metal. Its chief economic minerals are <b>pyrolusite<\/b> (MnO<sub>2<\/sub>), <b>braunite<\/b> (Mn<sup>2+<\/sup>Mn<sup>3+<\/sup><sub>6<\/sub>SiO<sub>12<\/sub>), <b>psilomelane<\/b> ((Ba,H<sub>2<\/sub>O)<sub>2<\/sub>Mn<sub>5<\/sub>O<sub>10<\/sub>), and <b>rhodochrosite<\/b> (manganese carbonate, MnCO<sub>3<\/sub>). Manganese ores usually occur in close proximity to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> ores like sphalerite.<\/li>\n<\/ul>\n\n<h3>Global Reserves and Mining Leaders<\/h3>\n<p>Land-based manganese resources are massive but unevenly distributed. About <b>80% of known global reserves<\/b> are located in South Africa, mainly in the Kalahari manganese fields near Hotazel (estimated at 15 billion tons). In 2011, South Africa led world production with 3.4 million tons. Other major manganese mining nations include Australia, China, Gabon, Brazil, India, Kazakhstan, Ghana, Ukraine, and Malaysia.<\/p>\n\n<h3>Indian Geography: MOIL and Asia's Deepest Mine<\/h3>\n<p>India is one of the world's leading producers of manganese ore. State-run central public enterprise <b>MOIL Limited<\/b> (formerly Manganese Ore India Limited) operates 11 major mines in Central India. Notably, the <b>Balaghat Mine<\/b> in Madhya Pradesh is recognized as the largest and deepest underground manganese mine in Asia. Other vital Indian mines operate in Nagpur and Bhandara districts (Maharashtra) and Keonjhar and Sundargarh districts (Odisha).<\/p>\n\n<h3>Indian Ocean Deep-Sea Manganese Nodules<\/h3>\n<p>In addition to terrestrial mines, huge deposits of manganese cover the abyssal ocean floor in the form of <b>polymetallic nodules<\/b> (manganese nodules). Under India's national <i>Deep Ocean Mission<\/i>, the National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT) and the Ministry of Earth Sciences are developing deep-sea mining technology. India holds exclusive rights granted by the International Seabed Authority (ISA) to explore 75,000 square kilometers in the Central Indian Ocean Basin, harvesting manganese-rich seabed nodules using submersibles like <i>MATSYA 6000<\/i>.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>From strengthening skyscraper steel and powering consumer electronics to supporting crop growth and advancing clean energy, <b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">manganese<\/a><\/b> is an indispensable element in modern industry and daily life.<\/p>\n\n<h3>1. Steelmaking and Metallurgy (85\u201390% of Global Use)<\/h3>\n<p>The overwhelming majority of global <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">manganese<\/a> production is consumed by the <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> and steel industry. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">Manganese<\/a> serves three vital roles: deoxidizing molten <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>, removing <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a> impurities, and forming high-strength alloys.<\/p>\n<ul>\n <li><b>Ferro-Manganese & Silico-Manganese:<\/b> Essential master alloys added to molten <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> during steel production.<\/li>\n <li><b>High-Strength Steel:<\/b> Manganese enhances hardness, tensile strength, toughness, workability, and wear resistance. Tough Hadfield steel (containing 12\u201314% Mn) is used in rail tracks, rock crushers, excavator buckets, and bank vaults.<\/li>\n<\/ul>\n\n<h3>2. Household Dry Batteries<\/h3>\n<p>Manganese dioxide (MnO<sub>2<\/sub>) has served as the cathode depolarizer in standard disposable dry batteries\u2014such as <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a>-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> and long-lasting alkaline batteries\u2014for over a century, providing reliable portable power.<\/p>\n\n<h3>3. Rust Protection & Chemical Oxidizers<\/h3>\n<ul>\n <li><b>Rust-Proof Coatings:<\/b> Electrochemical manganese phosphate coatings (Parkerizing) protect steel firearms, tools, and auto parts against rust and wear.<\/li>\n <li><b>Water Purification:<\/b> <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">Potassium<\/a> permanganate (KMnO<sub>4<\/sub>) is an intense oxidizer used to purify drinking water, disinfect municipal wastewater, and act as a medical antiseptic.<\/li>\n <li><b>Glass, Ceramics & Rubber:<\/b> MnO<sub>2<\/sub> clarifies green glass, pigments ceramics purple\/brown, and accelerates rubber processing.<\/li>\n<\/ul>\n\n<h3>4. Agriculture and Nutrition<\/h3>\n<p>Manganese sulfate (MnSO<sub>4<\/sub>) is added to agricultural fertilizers and animal feeds as an essential micronutrient, supporting plant photosynthesis and enzyme activity while functioning as a crop fungicide.<\/p>\n\n<h3>5. Modern Indian Scientific Research: Green Energy & Recycling<\/h3>\n<p>Indian scientific institutions are driving innovation in manganese-based green chemistry and clean energy:<\/p>\n<ul>\n <li><b>Battery Recycling (CSIR-NML):<\/b> The CSIR-National Metallurgical Laboratory in Jamshedpur has commissioned pilot hydrometallurgical recycling facilities to extract high-purity manganese, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a> from spent electric vehicle and electronic batteries, fostering a circular economy.<\/li>\n <li><b>Advanced Energy Storage (CSIR-CECRI & IITs):<\/b> Researchers at CSIR-CECRI (Karaikudi) and IITs (such as IIT Madras and IIT Bombay) are developing eco-friendly manganese-based <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a>-ion and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a>-manganese oxide (LMO) battery cathodes, as well as manganese catalysts for sustainable green chemistry.<\/li>\n<\/ul>" } }, "Fe": { "symbol": "Fe", "name": "Iron", "atomic": 26, "category": "transition metal", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 26 (Fe)", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">Iron<\/a><\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>Fe<\/b>, from Latin <i>ferrum<\/i>, atomic number 26) is a vital transition metal located in group 8 and period 4 of the periodic table. It is the most abundant chemical element on Earth by total mass, forming much of our planet's liquid outer core and solid inner core, and ranking as the fourth most abundant element in Earth's crust (about 5%). From the <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>-rich core of distant supergiant stars to the red hemoglobin carrying <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> in our blood, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> is the master element of cosmic architecture and human civilization. In ancient India, iron metallurgy reached legendary heights with the invention of high-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> <i>Wootz<\/i> crucible steel and rust-resistant monuments like the famous 4th-century Iron Pillar of Delhi. Today, iron alloyed with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a><\/a> forms steel\u2014the indispensable foundation of modern skyscrapers, bridges, railways, and space rockets.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/images-of-elements.com\/iron-2.jpg", "atomic_mass": 55.8452, "density": 7.874, "melt": 1811, "boil": 3134, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "5000 BC", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d6", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.83, "electron_affinity": 14.785, "ionization_energies": [ 762.5, 1561.9, 2957, 5290, 7240, 9560, 12060, 14580, 22540, 25290, 28000, 31920, 34830, 37840, 44100, 47206, 122200, 131000, 140500, 152600, 163000, 173600, 188100, 195200, 851800, 895161 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">Iron<\/a> is a lustrous, silvery-white transition metal with a density of 7.874 g\/cm\u00b3. Under normal atmospheric conditions, pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> melts at 1,811 K (1,538 \u00b0C or 2,800 \u00b0F) and boils at 3,134 K (2,861 \u00b0C or 5,182 \u00b0F). At the atomic level, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> has an atomic number of 26 and a ground-state electron configuration of 1s<sup>2<\/sup> 2s<sup>2<\/sup> 2p<sup>6<\/sup> 3s<sup>2<\/sup> 3p<sup>6<\/sup> 4s<sup>2<\/sup> 3d<sup>6<\/sup> (or [Ar] 3d<sup>6<\/sup> 4s<sup>2<\/sup>). Its valence electrons allow it to adopt multiple oxidation states, most commonly +2 (ferrous, Fe<sup>2+<\/sup>) and +3 (ferric, Fe<sup>3+<\/sup>). Iron has a Pauling electronegativity of 1.83, an electron affinity of 14.785 kJ\/mol, and a first ionization energy of 762.5 kJ\/mol followed by higher ionization steps (1,561.9, 2,957, 5,290, 7,240, 9,560, and up to 895,161 kJ\/mol for its 26th electron).<\/p><p>Iron is famous for its ferromagnetism\u2014it is strongly attracted to magnets and can be permanently magnetized at room temperature. However, when heated above its Curie temperature of 1,043 K (770 \u00b0C), iron loses its permanent magnetism and becomes paramagnetic. Pure elemental iron is relatively soft and malleable, but its mechanical properties transform dramatically when combined with minute amounts of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a><\/a> and other metals. For instance, while pure single-crystal iron has a modest tensile strength of only 10 MPa and a Brinell hardness of 3, cold-worked iron reaches 690 MPa (hardness 200), pearlitic steel achieves 1,200 MPa (hardness 350), martensitic steel reaches 2,070 MPa (hardness 600), ausformed hardened steel reaches an impressive 2,930 MPa (hardness 850\u20131,200), and microscopic iron \"whiskers\" exhibit a mind-boggling tensile strength of 11,000 MPa!<\/p><p>Unlike metals such as <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a><\/a> or <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a><\/a>, which form a protective oxide shield when exposed to air, ordinary iron rusts continuously in the presence of moisture and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a>. Rust (hydrated iron oxide) is flaky and porous, flaking off to continuously expose fresh underlying metal to further oxidation. However, under special metallurgical conditions\u2014such as the high-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a> forge-welding techniques developed in ancient India\u2014iron can form a non-porous passive layer that halts corrosion completely.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">Main article: Isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a><\/div><p>Natural <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> on Earth is composed of four stable isotopes: <sup>56<\/sup>Fe (the most abundant at 91.754%), <sup>54<\/sup>Fe (5.845%), <sup>57<\/sup>Fe (2.119%), and <sup>58<\/sup>Fe (0.282%). Scientists have also synthesized 24 artificial radioactive isotopes in nuclear laboratories. Among the stable isotopes, <sup>57<\/sup>Fe is uniquely important in physics and chemistry because it is the only stable <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> isotope with a nuclear spin (\u22121\/2). This nuclear spin makes <sup>57<\/sup>Fe the primary core isotope used in M\u00f6ssbauer spectroscopy, an ultra-precise analytical technique used to study electronic structures, magnetic properties, and chemical bonding in materials and biological proteins. Theoretically, <sup>54<\/sup>Fe can undergo double electron capture to form <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a><\/a>-54 (<sup>54<\/sup>Cr), but this extremely rare event has never been observed in experiment, establishing a lower half-life limit of 4.4 \u00d7 10<sup>20<\/sup> years (trillions of times longer than the age of the universe!).<\/p><p>Iron-60 (<sup>60<\/sup>Fe) is an extinct radioactive isotope with a half-life of 2.6 million years. Although no original <sup>60<\/sup>Fe remains from Earth's formation, its decay product\u2014its granddaughter nuclide stable <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a><\/a>-60 (<sup>60<\/sup>Ni)\u2014serves as a cosmic clock. By measuring <sup>60<\/sup>Ni concentrations in primitive meteorites such as <i>Semarkona<\/i> and <i>Chervony Kut<\/i>, planetary scientists proved that <sup>60<\/sup>Fe was active during the early formation of the Solar System 4.6 billion years ago. The heat released by decaying <sup>60<\/sup>Fe, alongside <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a><\/a>-26 (<sup>26<\/sup>Al), helped melt and differentiate early asteroids into metallic cores and rocky mantles.<\/p><p>In stellar astrophysics, <sup>56<\/sup>Fe holds a monumental place as the ultimate endpoint of nuclear fusion inside massive stars. During the <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a>-burning phase inside supergiant stars, lighter nuclei fuse into radioactive <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a><\/a>-56 (<sup>56<\/sup>Ni, made of 14 alpha particles). Inside stars, intense gamma radiation causes photodisintegration, preventing fusion from efficiently building heavier elements beyond <sup>56<\/sup>Ni. With a half-life of about 6 days, <sup>56<\/sup>Ni rapidly decays into radioactive <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a><\/a>-56 (<sup>56<\/sup>Co), which then decays into stable <sup>56<\/sup>Fe. Although <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a><\/a>-62 (<sup>62<\/sup>Ni) has a marginally higher binding energy per nucleon than <sup>56<\/sup>Fe, stellar conditions strongly favor producing <sup>56<\/sup>Fe because <sup>56<\/sup>Fe has a lower mass per nucleon due to its higher fraction of lighter protons. Elements heavier than iron cannot form via normal fusion; they require the extreme neutron-burst environment of a supernova via rapid neutron capture (the r-process).<\/p><p>Theoretical cosmologists speculate that in the extremely distant future of the universe\u2014trillions upon trillions of years from now, assuming protons do not decay\u2014cold quantum tunnelling will allow light atomic nuclei to fuse into <sup>56<\/sup>Fe, while heavy elements decay into iron. In this hypothetical epoch, all stellar-mass objects across the cosmos will eventually condense into cold, dead spheres of pure iron.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">Iron<\/a> is the sixth most abundant element in the universe and the single most abundant refractory element in space. On Earth, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> accounts for roughly 32.1% of our planet's total mass, making it Earth's most abundant element by mass. The vast majority of Earth's <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> resides deep below our feet, concentrated in the liquid outer core and solid inner core (alloyed with about 5% to 10% <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a><\/a>). In the Earth's crust, iron ranks as the fourth most abundant element (about 5% by mass), trailing only <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a><\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a><\/a>. Native metallic iron is rare on Earth's surface except when delivered by iron-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a> meteorites.<\/p><p>In nature, iron occurs primarily in mineral ores as oxides, carbonates, and sulfides. The most important commercial iron ores are hematite (Fe<sub>2<\/sub>O<sub>3<\/sub>, rich red ore), magnetite (Fe<sub>3<\/sub>O<sub>4<\/sub>, magnetic black ore), goethite, limonite, and siderite (FeCO<sub>3<\/sub>), as well as iron pyrite (FeS<sub>2<\/sub>, known as \"fool's <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\">gold<\/a>\").<\/p><p>India is blessed with some of the world's largest and highest-grade iron ore deposits, primarily located in ancient Precambrian rock formations across peninsular India. The country's iron ore geography is centered around major mineral belts:<\/p><ul><li><b>Odisha\u2013Jharkhand Belt:<\/b> India's richest iron ore region, producing high-grade hematite. Major mining centers include Keonjhar, Sundargarh, Mayurbhanj, and Jajpur in Odisha, alongside the Singhbhum district in Jharkhand. The historic Noamundi and Joda mines in this belt have supplied Tata Steel for over a century.<\/li><li><b>Durg\u2013Bastar\u2013Chandrapur Belt:<\/b> Spanning Chhattisgarh and Maharashtra, this belt contains the famous <b>Bailadila<\/b> iron ore range in Dantewada district\u2014renowned for producing some of the highest-purity hematite ore in the world\u2014and the Dalli-Rajhara mines that supply the Bhilai Steel Plant.<\/li><li><b>Bellary\u2013Chitradurga\u2013Chikkamagaluru\u2013Tumakuru Belt:<\/b> Located in Karnataka, this region is a major hub for high-grade hematite and magnetite ores (such as Hospet-Bellary and the Kudremukh magnetite deposits).<\/li><li><b>Maharashtra\u2013Goa Belt:<\/b> Coastal iron ore reserves that support major domestic steel mills and international export shipments.<\/li><\/ul>", "History": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">Main article: History of ferrous metallurgy<\/div><p>Human interaction with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> began thousands of years ago with meteorites\u2014ancient Sumerians and Egyptians called <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> \"metal from heaven\" (<i>an-bar<\/i> in Sumerian, <i>bij-n-pt<\/i> in Egyptian). The transition from bronze to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> tools around 1200 BCE marked the dawn of the Iron Age across the ancient world.<\/p><p>In ancient India, iron technology developed independently as early as the 2nd millennium BCE. Early literary references appear in the <i>Rigveda<\/i>, which uses the term <i>ayas<\/i> for metal, while later Vedic texts (the <i>Yajurveda<\/i> and <i>Atharvaveda<\/i>) explicitly distinguish <i>krishna-ayas<\/i> or <i>syama-ayas<\/i> (\"black metal,\" meaning iron) from <i>loha-ayas<\/i> (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a>). Classic Indian medical treatises such as the <i>Sushruta Samhita<\/i> (c. 600 BCE) detailed the fabrication of over 100 specialized surgical instruments (<i>sastra<\/i>) made of tempered iron-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> alloys, emphasizing controlled quenching in water, oil, or milk to obtain razor-sharp surgical blades.<\/p><p>By the 6th century BCE, South Indian metallurgists (in present-day Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana, and Andhra Pradesh) pioneered one of the greatest innovations in world metallurgical history: <b>Wootz Steel<\/b> (known locally as <i>Ukku<\/i> or <i>Urukku<\/i>, meaning \"melted steel\"). Artisans placed high-purity iron ore together with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a>-rich organic plant matter (such as <i>Cassia auriculata<\/i> leaves and wood) inside sealed clay crucibles, heating them in high-temperature bloomery furnaces. This process produced ultra-high-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> crucible steel containing microscopic cementite nanostructures. Exported across ancient maritime trade routes to the Middle East, Wootz steel was forged into legendary Damascus blades, famed worldwide for their razor sharpness and flowing water-like surface patterns.<\/p><p>Ancient India also mastered forge-welding massive iron structures with exceptional corrosion resistance. The world-famous <b>Iron Pillar of Delhi<\/b>, erected in the 4th\u20135th century CE during the reign of King Chandragupta II Vikramaditya (currently at the Qutb complex), stands 7.2 meters tall and weighs over 6 tonnes. Despite exposure to Delhi's monsoon rains and seasonal sun for over 1,600 years, the pillar remains virtually rust-free! Landmark research led by Indian metallurgist <b>Prof. R. Balasubramaniam<\/b> of IIT Kanpur revealed the scientific secret: ancient Indian blacksmiths used charcoal smelting, leaving a high concentration of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a> (~0.25%) in the wrought iron. The <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a> acts as a catalyst, inducing the formation of an ultra-thin protective passive layer composed of crystalline iron <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> phosphate hydrate (FePO<sub>4<\/sub>\u00b7H<sub>3<\/sub>PO<sub>4<\/sub>\u00b74H<sub>2<\/sub>O), magnetite (Fe<sub>3<\/sub>O<sub>4<\/sub>), and amorphous misawite (\u03b4-FeOOH). This self-healing passive film seals the metal surface and prevents further oxidation. Similar rust-resistant iron structures include the massive iron beams of the Konark Sun Temple in Odisha and the Dhar Iron Pillar in Madhya Pradesh.<\/p><p>In the alchemical tradition of <i>Rasa Shastra<\/i> (recorded in classical texts like the <i>Rasaratnasamuchchaya<\/i>), Indian scholar-chemists classified iron into categories such as <i>munda<\/i> (wrought\/cast iron), <i>tiksna<\/i> (hard crucible steel), and <i>kanta<\/i> (magnetic iron). They prepared <i>Lauha Bhasma<\/i>\u2014micro-calcined nano-iron ash\u2014used in Ayurvedic medicine to treat <i>pandu roga<\/i> (anemia) and boost cellular vitality.<\/p><p>In modern times, India's industrial iron revolution was spearheaded by visionary industrialist <b>Jamsetji Nusserwanji Tata<\/b>, who laid the foundation for Tata Iron and Steel Company (Tata Steel) in 1907 at Sakchi (now Jamshedpur, Jharkhand), creating Asia's first integrated steel city. Today, modern scientific advancements are driven by premier research institutes such as the <b>CSIR-National Metallurgical Laboratory (NML)<\/b> in Jamshedpur, which pioneers eco-friendly mineral beneficiation and iron ore pelletization, and the <b>Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL)<\/b>, keeping India among the top global producers of steel.<\/p>", "Applications": "<table class=\"wikitable floatright\"><caption>Characteristic values of tensile strength (TS) and Brinell hardness (BH) of various forms of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a>.<\/caption><tbody><tr><th>Material<\/th><th>TS <br \/>(MPa)<\/th><th>BH <br \/>(Brinell)<\/th><\/tr><tr><td><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">Iron<\/a><\/a> whiskers<\/td><td>11000<\/td><td><\/td><\/tr><tr><td>Ausformed (hardened) <br \/>steel<\/td><td>2930<\/td><td>850\u20131200<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>Martensitic steel<\/td><td>2070<\/td><td>600<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>Bainitic steel<\/td><td>1380<\/td><td>400<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>Pearlitic steel<\/td><td>1200<\/td><td>350<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>Cold-worked <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a><\/td><td>690<\/td><td>200<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>Small-grain iron<\/td><td>340<\/td><td>100<\/td><\/tr><tr><td><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">Carbon<\/a><\/a>-containing iron<\/td><td>140<\/td><td>40<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>Pure, single-crystal iron<\/td><td>10<\/td><td>3<\/td><\/tr><\/tbody><\/table><p>Iron is by far the most widely used of all metals, accounting for over 90% of global metal production. Its immense strength, abundance, and low cost make it the undisputed backbone of modern engineering and construction. Because pure iron is relatively soft, almost all industrial iron is converted into alloys\u2014primarily steel. Steel is produced by combining iron with small amounts of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> (0.002% to 2.1%) along with alloying elements like <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">manganese<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mo\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Molybdenum (Mo)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mo\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Molybdenum (Mo)\">molybdenum<\/a><\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/V\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Vanadium (V)\">vanadium<\/a><\/a>.<\/p><p>Major applications of iron and steel include:<\/p><ul><li><b>Structural Construction:<\/b> Reinforcing steel bars (rebar), structural I-beams, girders, bridges, skyscrapers, concrete foundations, and roofing sheets.<\/li><li><b>Transportation & Heavy Industry:<\/b> Automotive chassis, engine blocks, railway tracks, train locomotives, cargo ships, container vessels, heavy mining machinery, and agricultural tractors.<\/li><li><b>Specialty Alloys & High-Tech Defense:<\/b> Stainless steel (containing at least 10.5% <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a>) resists rust and is used in kitchenware, cutlery, surgical instruments, and food processing plants. Ultra-high-strength maraging steels and iron-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a>-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a> superalloys are engineered by organizations like <b>ISRO<\/b> (Indian Space Research Organisation) and <b>DRDO<\/b> for rocket motor casings, missile bodies, and aerospace turbines.<\/li><li><b>Magnetism & Electrical Machinery:<\/b> <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">Silicon<\/a>-steel laminations are used in electric transformer cores, electric motors, power generators, and electromagnets due to their high magnetic permeability and low hysteresis loss.<\/li><li><b>Chemical Catalysis & Pigments:<\/b> Iron compounds act as critical industrial catalysts, most notably in the Haber-Bosch process to synthesize ammonia fertilizer from <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a>. Iron oxide pigments provide durable red, yellow, and black colors in paints, brick masonry, and ceramics.<\/li><li><b>Biological Necessity & Medicine:<\/b> Iron is an essential trace nutrient for almost all living organisms. In human physiology, iron forms the active core of <b>hemoglobin<\/b> in red blood cells, which binds and carries <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> from our lungs to every tissue in the body, and <b>myoglobin<\/b> in muscle tissue. Iron deficiency leads to anemia, causing fatigue and weakness. In traditional Indian medicine (Ayurveda), micro-calcined iron preparations known as <i>Lauha Bhasma<\/i> have been used for centuries to treat anemia and restore vitality.<\/li><\/ul>" } }, "Co": { "symbol": "Co", "name": "Cobalt", "atomic": 27, "category": "transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">Cobalt<\/a><\/a><\/b> is a hard, lustrous, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ag\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silver (Ag)\">silver<\/a>-gray transition metal with the symbol <b>Co<\/b> and atomic number <b>27<\/b>. Named after legendary German mountain goblins called <i>kobolds<\/i>, pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a> is ferromagnetic\u2014meaning it is strongly attracted to magnets\u2014and remains magnetic up to an extraordinarily high temperature. In the Earth's crust, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a> is rarely found as a free metal; it occurs almost exclusively bound inside mineral compounds alongside <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a><\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a><\/a>, with rare uncombined natural metal found only inside ancient meteoric <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a> alloys. Famous across human history for giving a breathtaking deep blue color to glass and ceramics\u2014such as India's world-renowned Jaipur Blue Pottery\u2014cobalt has evolved into a vital modern material that powers electric vehicle batteries, aerospace superalloys, and life-saving nuclear cancer therapy developed by Indian scientists at BARC.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/6\/62\/Cobalt_ore_2.jpg", "atomic_mass": 58.9331944, "density": 8.9, "melt": 1768, "boil": 3200, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Georg Brandt", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d7", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.88, "electron_affinity": 63.898, "ionization_energies": [ 760.4, 1648, 3232, 4950, 7670, 9840, 12440, 15230, 17959, 26570, 29400, 32400, 36600, 39700, 42800, 49396, 52737, 134810, 145170, 154700, 167400, 178100, 189300, 204500, 214100, 920870, 966023 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-left\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img alt=\"a sample of pure cobalt\" src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/909af75d84e779f8fd4e4cb9f07b2661.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"227\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"649\" data-file-height=\"589\" \/><figcaption>A block of electrolytically refined <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a><\/a> (99.9% purity) cut from a large plate<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">Cobalt<\/a><\/a> is a tough, ferromagnetic metal with a density (specific gravity) of 8.9 grams per cubic centimeter. Among all ferromagnetic elements, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a> holds its magnetism up to the highest temperature known: its Curie temperature is a scorching 1,115 \u00b0C (2,039 \u00b0F), above which it loses its permanent magnetic properties. Its intrinsic magnetic moment measures between 1.6 and 1.7 Bohr magnetons per atom, and its ability to channel magnetic fields (relative permeability) is about two-thirds that of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a>. Metallic cobalt can freeze into two different crystal patterns: hexagonal close-packed (hcp) at lower temperatures and face-centered cubic (fcc) at higher temperatures. The theoretical transition temperature between these two crystal structures is 450 \u00b0C (842 \u00b0F), but because the energy difference between them is tiny, pure cobalt samples often feature a random mixing or intergrowth of both structures.<\/p>\n<p>Chemically, cobalt is a weakly reducing metal that resists everyday corrosion because it naturally forms a thin, protective oxide skin (passivation film) on its surface. However, it reacts readily when heated with halogens and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a><\/a>. Burning cobalt in <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a> forms cobalt(II,III) oxide (Co<sub>3<\/sub>O<sub>4<\/sub>), which sheds <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a> at 900 \u00b0C (1,650 \u00b0F) to yield cobalt monoxide (CoO). Cobalt reacts directly with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/F\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Fluorine (F)\">fluorine<\/a><\/a> gas (F<sub>2<\/sub>) at 520 K (247 \u00b0C) to form cobalt trifluoride (CoF<sub>3<\/sub>), and bonds with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a><\/a> (Cl<sub>2<\/sub>), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Br\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Bromine (Br)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Br\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Bromine (Br)\">bromine<\/a><\/a> (Br<sub>2<\/sub>), and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/I\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iodine (I)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/I\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iodine (I)\">iodine<\/a><\/a> (I<sub>2<\/sub>) to produce binary halides. While cobalt refuses to react with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a><\/a> gas (H<sub>2<\/sub>) or <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/N\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nitrogen (N)\">nitrogen<\/a><\/a> gas (N<sub>2<\/sub>) even when strongly heated, it combines with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\">boron<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">arsenic<\/a><\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a><\/a>. At room temperature, it dissolves slowly in mineral acids and oxidizes very gradually in moist air, but remains untarnished in completely dry air.<\/p>\n<p>These remarkable thermal and magnetic properties make cobalt alloys essential for high-temperature engineering. In India, research institutes such as the Defence Metallurgical Research Laboratory (DMRL) in Hyderabad utilize cobalt-base alloys to fabricate high-strength, heat-resistant components capable of enduring extreme operational stresses.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">", "Isotopes": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">Main article: Isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a><\/a><\/div>\n<p>Natural <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a> on Earth consists entirely of a single stable isotope: <b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a>-59 (<sup>59<\/sup>Co)<\/b>. Beyond this stable form, scientists have created and characterized 22 radioactive isotopes ranging from <sup>50<\/sup>Co to <sup>78<\/sup>Co, along with 4 nuclear isomers (meta states) that all decay in under 15 minutes. Among the radioisotopes, the most stable and famous is <b>cobalt-60 (<sup>60<\/sup>Co)<\/b>, which has a half-life of 5.2714 years. Other notable radioisotopes include <sup>57<\/sup>Co (half-life of 271.81 days), <sup>56<\/sup>Co (77.24 days), and <sup>58<\/sup>Co (70.84 days). All other cobalt radioisotopes have half-lives shorter than 18 hours, and most break down in less than a single second.<\/p>\n<p>The decay pathways of cobalt isotopes depend on their mass relative to stable <sup>59<\/sup>Co. Isotopes lighter than <sup>59<\/sup>Co primarily decay via electron capture into isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a> (element 26). Conversely, heavier isotopes decay via beta emission into isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a><\/a> (element 28). The stable <sup>59<\/sup>Co nucleus possesses a magnetic quadrupole moment and can be detected using Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. In fact, <sup>59<\/sup>Co features the broadest chemical shift range of any NMR-active nucleus\u2014spanning over 20,000 parts per million (ppm) with signal widths reaching up to 20 kHz! Chemists frequently use <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> hexacyanocobaltate (0.1M K<sub>3<\/sub>Co(CN)<sub>6<\/sub> in D<sub>2<\/sub>O) as an NMR reference standard because its highly symmetrical structure produces sharp, clear spectral lines.<\/p>\n<p>Synthetic <b>cobalt-60<\/b> plays a vital, life-saving role in modern medicine and industry in India. India is one of the world's leading producers of industrial cobalt-60, creating the isotope by irradiating cobalt-59 target absorber rods inside Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs) at the <b>Rajasthan Atomic Power Station (RAPS)<\/b> in Rawatbhata. The irradiated sources are processed at the Rajasthan Atomic Power Project Cobalt Facility (RAPPCOF) in Kota and distributed by the Board of Radiation & Isotope Technology (BRIT). Crucially, scientists at the <b>Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC)<\/b> developed the <b>Bhabhatron<\/b>\u2014an indigenous, highly affordable Cobalt-60 teletherapy machine. The Bhabhatron uses high-energy gamma rays emitted by <sup>60<\/sup>Co to destroy cancer tumors, bringing accessible radiation therapy to hospitals across India and being donated to developing nations across Africa and Asia.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">", "History": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-left\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img alt=\"cobalt blue Chinese porcelain\" src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/1b6a8b8e40ffc886e2e3eb9177330acb.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"190\" height=\"236\" style=\"--mw-file-upright: 0.75\" class=\"mw-file-element mw-file-upright\" data-file-width=\"2206\" data-file-height=\"2735\" \/><figcaption>Early Chinese blue and white porcelain, manufactured <abbr title=\"circa\">c.<\/abbr><span style=\"white-space:nowrap;\">&#8201;1335<\/span><\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p>For thousands of years, human civilizations have prized <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a><\/a> compounds for their ability to impart an intense, mesmerizing blue color to glass, glazes, and ceramics. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">Cobalt<\/a> pigments have been detected in ancient Egyptian statues, Persian jewelry dating to the 3rd millennium BC, Roman glass ruins at Pompeii destroyed in 79 AD, and legendary Chinese porcelain from the Tang (618\u2013907 AD) and Ming (1368\u20131644 AD) dynasties. Bronze Age artisans cast blue <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a> glass as early as the 14th century BC, evidenced by a glass ingot recovered from the Uluburun shipwreck off the Turkish coast. Ancient Egyptians obtained cobalt colorants from cobalt-bearing alum deposits in their Western Oases to decorate 18th-Dynasty glassware (1550\u20131292 BC).<\/p>\n<p>In India, cobalt blue glazes established a celebrated artistic lineage. During the Mughal period, Turko-Persian artistic influences brought blue ceramic techniques into the subcontinent, where cobalt glazes adorned architectural tiles and pottery. This craft evolved into <b>Jaipur Blue Pottery<\/b>, which received grand royal patronage in the 19th century from Maharaja Sawai Ram Singh II of Jaipur. Unlike traditional ceramics, Jaipur Blue Pottery uses no clay; artisans craft a dough from powdered quartz, glass powder, Fuller's earth (<i>multani mitti<\/i>), borax, and gum, painting it with cobalt oxide glaze. Because cobalt oxide maintains its rich color without degrading under intense kiln temperatures, it produces the stunning blue designs famous worldwide today. Historical research shows that Indian painters and artisans sourced cobalt glazes both through vibrant overland trade routes (such as Kashan in Persia) and regional mineral preparations.<\/p>\n<p>The name <i>cobalt<\/i> originates from the 16th-century German word <i>kobald<\/i>, referring to troublesome mountain goblins or earth spirits. Medieval miners in Saxony struggled to extract <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a><\/a> or <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ag\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silver (Ag)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ag\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silver (Ag)\">silver<\/a><\/a> from cobalt ores; instead of metal, smelting produced useless dark powders (cobalt oxide) and released foul, poisonous fumes of volatile <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">arsenic<\/a><\/a> oxide. Believing mischievous spirits had cursed the ore, miners dubbed it \"cobalt\"\u2014a term recorded by Renaissance alchemists Paracelsus, Georgius Agricola, and Basil Valentine.<\/p>\n<p>Swedish chemist <b>Georg Brandt<\/b> discovered cobalt as a distinct new element around 1735. Brandt demonstrated that cobalt was a previously unknown \"semi-metal\"\u2014distinct from <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Bi\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Bismuth (Bi)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Bi\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Bismuth (Bi)\">bismuth<\/a><\/a>\u2014and proved that cobalt compounds were the true source of the blue color in glass (which had previously been misattributed to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Bi\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Bismuth (Bi)\">bismuth<\/a>). Cobalt holds a historic milestone as the very first metal discovered in modern history; all previously known metals (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ag\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silver (Ag)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ag\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silver (Ag)\">silver<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\">gold<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\">mercury<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tin (Sn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tin (Sn)\">tin<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a><\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Bi\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Bismuth (Bi)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Bi\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Bismuth (Bi)\">bismuth<\/a><\/a>) had been used since prehistoric times without recorded discoverers.<\/p>\n<p>During the 19th century, large-scale production of cobalt blue pigment (cobalt oxide combined with alumina) and smalt (powdered cobalt glass used for ceramics) flourished at Norway's Blaafarvev\u00e6rket, following earlier 16th-century smalt mining across Norway, Sweden, Saxony, and Hungary. Global mining shifted to New Caledonia in 1864, Ontario (Canada) in 1904, and the massive <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a>-cobalt deposits of Katanga Province in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 1914. When the 1978 Shaba conflict briefly disrupted Katanga's mines, global markets adapted quickly through recycling and cobalt-free alternatives.<\/p>\n<p>In physics, John Livingood and Glenn T. Seaborg discovered the radioisotope cobalt-60 in 1938. In 1956, physicist Chien-Shiung Wu used cobalt-60 nuclei at Columbia University in her landmark experiment that disproved the law of conservation of parity in weak nuclear beta decay. Following World War II, growing military demand for cobalt in jet engine superalloys led the United States to open major domestic mines at Blackbird Canyon, Idaho. In the 21st century, cobalt has become a vital strategic resource driving rechargeable <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a>-ion batteries, high-temperature superalloys, and green energy technology.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">", "Occurrence": "<p>Stable <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a><\/a> is forged deep inside dying massive stars and supernova explosions through the r-process of nuclear fusion. It makes up approximately 0.0029% (29 parts per million) of the Earth's crust, where it is almost always found in close association with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a><\/a>. Both elements are signature components of meteoric <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a>, where metallic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a>-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> alloys remain shielded from atmospheric <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> and moisture. In Earth's oceans, dissolved <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a> readily reacts with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chlorine (Cl)\">chlorine<\/a><\/a>.<\/p>\n<p>On land, cobalt occurs bound in chemical compounds within <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a><\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a> mineral deposits. Its major natural minerals include the sulfides cobaltite (CoAsS), safflorite (CoAs<sub>2<\/sub>), glaucodot ((Co,Fe)AsS), and skutterudite (CoAs<sub>3<\/sub>). In the rich <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a> beds of Katanga, the mineral cattierite occurs alongside vaesite. When exposed to air and water, these mineral sulfides weather into striking pink erythrite (also known as \"cobalt glance,\" Co<sub>3<\/sub>(AsO<sub>4<\/sub>)<sub>2<\/sub>\u00b78H<sub>2<\/sub>O) and spherocobaltite (CoCO<sub>3<\/sub>). Trace amounts of cobalt compounds exist throughout rocks, soil, plants, and animals worldwide. Pure uncombined natural cobalt metal is exceedingly rare on Earth, but has been reported in rock cores from the Kola Superdeep Borehole and lunar rock samples returned by the Soviet Luna 24 mission, likely formed by high-energy meteorite impacts. Cobalt is also present in tobacco smoke, as tobacco plants absorb heavy metals from soil into their leaves.<\/p>\n<p>In India, cobalt is recognized as a strategic critical mineral essential for clean energy and defense. While primary cobalt deposits are scarce, India possesses significant potential secondary reserves associated with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a> ores. The most prominent occurrence is in the <b>Sukinda Valley of Odisha<\/b>, where cobalt is contained within nickeliferous limonite overburden generated during chromite mining. Cobalt occurrences are also documented in the <b>Khetri Copper Belt of Rajasthan<\/b> (within minerals like cobaltite and cobalt-bearing pentlandite at the Madan-Kudan mine), the <b>Singhbhum Copper Belt of Jharkhand<\/b>, and ultramafic ophiolite rocks in <b>Nagaland<\/b>, which are actively evaluated by the Geological Survey of India (GSI).<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">", "Applications": "<p>Global consumption of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a><\/a> reached 116,000 tonnes in 2016 and continues to expand rapidly. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">Cobalt<\/a>'s unique combination of high melting point, strength at elevated temperatures, and magnetic properties makes it indispensable across modern technology:<\/p>\n<ul>\n<li><b>Rechargeable Batteries:<\/b> <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">Cobalt<\/a> is a core component of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a>-ion battery cathodes (such as <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">Lithium<\/a> Cobalt Oxide, LiCoO<sub>2<\/sub>, and NMC formulations), providing high energy density and thermal stability for smartphones, laptops, and electric vehicles. In India, under the National Mission on Transformative Mobility and Battery Storage, premier institutes like CSIR-CECRI (Central Electrochemical Research Institute) and the IITs are actively researching advanced cobalt cathode chemistry and battery recycling.<\/li>\n<li><b>Superalloys & Aerospace:<\/b> Cobalt-base superalloys maintain exceptional mechanical strength, tough corrosion resistance, and structural stability at temperatures above 1,000 \u00b0C. They are essential for jet engine turbine blades, industrial gas turbines, and rocket thrusters. In India, institutes like DMRL and ISRO utilize cobalt superalloys for aerospace engines and rocket hardware.<\/li>\n<li><b>Permanent Magnets:<\/b> Cobalt is alloyed with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a> to make powerful Alnico magnets, and with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sm\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Samarium (Sm)\">samarium<\/a> to produce high-performance <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sm\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Samarium (Sm)\">Samarium<\/a>-Cobalt (SmCo) magnets used in aerospace sensors, electric motors, and defense electronics.<\/li>\n<li><b>Industrial Catalysts & Pigments:<\/b> Cobalt catalysts are used extensively in petroleum refining (hydrodesulfurization to remove <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a> from fuels) and chemical synthesis. Cobalt oxide continues to power brilliant blue pigments (cobalt blue and smalt) for ceramics, glassmaking, and paints.<\/li>\n<\/ul>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Biological role": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">Cobalt<\/a><\/a> is an essential ultratrace element required for the health and metabolism of humans and animals. Its primary biological function is as the central metal atom in <b>cobalamin<\/b>, universally known as <b>Vitamin B<sub>12<\/sub><\/b>. Neither plants nor animals can synthesize Vitamin B<sub>12<\/sub> on their own; it is produced exclusively by specialized bacteria and archaea. In ruminant animals such as cows, sheep, and buffaloes, microbes residing in the stomach convert dietary <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a> salts into Vitamin B<sub>12<\/sub>. Maintaining a minimum <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a> level in grazing soils (recommending a daily livestock intake of 0.20 mg\/kg) is therefore vital for livestock health.<\/p>\n<p>In cobalamin-based proteins, a ring structure called corrin holds the cobalt atom. Coenzyme B<sub>12<\/sub> features a rare, highly reactive <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a>-cobalt (C\u2013Co) chemical bond that participates directly in enzymatic reactions. In humans, Vitamin B<sub>12<\/sub> operates via two main active forms:<\/p>\n<ul>\n<li><b>Methylcobalamin (MeB<sub>12<\/sub>):<\/b> Facilitates methyl (\u2212CH<sub>3<\/sub>) group transfers essential for DNA synthesis and cellular replication.<\/li>\n<li><b>Adenosylcobalamin:<\/b> Catalyzes molecular rearrangements involving direct <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> transfers. For example, the enzyme methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MUT) relies on adenosylcobalamin to convert methylmalonyl-CoA into succinyl-CoA\u2014a crucial metabolic step for extracting energy from fats and proteins.<\/li>\n<\/ul>\n<p>Beyond Vitamin B<sub>12<\/sub>, biological systems utilize other non-corrin cobaltoproteins where cobalt binds directly to the protein structure. These include <i>methionine aminopeptidase 2<\/i> (an essential human and mammalian enzyme) and <i>nitrile hydratase<\/i> (a bacterial enzyme that metabolizes nitriles).<\/p>\n<p>In India, where a large population follows a traditional vegetarian diet, Vitamin B<sub>12<\/sub> nutrition is a significant focus of public health research supported by ICMR (Indian Council of Medical Research). Because plants do not produce cobalamin, dairy products derived from ruminant livestock\u2014whose gut bacteria process cobalt\u2014serve as a principal dietary source of Vitamin B<sub>12<\/sub> for millions across the nation.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">" } }, "Ni": { "symbol": "Ni", "name": "Nickel", "atomic": 28, "category": "transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">Nickel<\/a><\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>Ni<\/b>, atomic number 28) is a lustrous, silvery-white transition metal with a subtle, warm golden tinge. Renowned for its exceptional hardness, ductility, and remarkable ability to resist heat and corrosion, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a> is an unsung hero of chemistry and modern technology. Locked deep within Earth's metallic core alongside <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a>, it is also a centerpiece of cosmic chemistry and ancient history\u2014from 2nd-century BCE Greco-Bactrian cupronickel coins minted in ancient India's northwestern frontier to high-performance superalloys powering ISRO space missions today. Whether protecting household cutlery from rust, energizing electric vehicle batteries, or serving as an essential micro-nutrient for soil microbes, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a> seamlessly bridges Earth's deep geological history with futuristic green technology.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/5\/57\/Nickel_chunk.jpg", "atomic_mass": 58.69344, "density": 8.908, "melt": 1728, "boil": 3003, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Axel Fredrik Cronstedt", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d8", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.91, "electron_affinity": 111.65, "ionization_energies": [ 737.1, 1753, 3395, 5300, 7339, 10400, 12800, 15600, 18600, 21670, 30970, 34000, 37100, 41500, 44800, 48100, 55101, 58570, 148700, 159000, 169400, 182700, 194000, 205600, 221400, 231490, 992718, 1039668 ], "sections": { "Isotopes": "<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">\n\n=== Isotopes ===\n<\/div>\n<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">Main article: Isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a><\/a><\/div>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">Nickel<\/a> isotopes span a wide range of atomic masses, from lightweight <sup>48<\/sup>Ni all the way up to heavy <sup>82<\/sup>Ni. In nature, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a> is composed of five stable isotopes: <sup>58<\/sup>Ni, <sup>60<\/sup>Ni, <sup>61<\/sup>Ni, <sup>62<\/sup>Ni, and <sup>64<\/sup>Ni. The most abundant of these is <b>nickel-58<\/b>, which makes up about 68.077% of all natural nickel on Earth.<\/p><p>Among all atomic nuclei in the universe, <b>nickel-62<\/b> holds a mind-boggling distinction: it possesses the highest nuclear binding energy per nucleon of any known nuclide (8.7946 MeV\/nucleon). Nuclear binding energy is the \"cosmic glue\" that holds an atom's protons and neutrons together, making <sup>62<\/sup>Ni the most tightly bound nucleus in existence! Although popular science often incorrectly gives this crown to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a>-56 or <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>-58, nickel-62 is the true nuclear champion. Despite this, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> remains far more abundant in the universe because extreme heat and high-energy light inside giant stars break nickel apart (a process called photodisintegration) before it can accumulate in large amounts.<\/p><p>Nickel also plays a fascinating role in planetary history. <b>Nickel-60<\/b> is the decay product of the extinct radioactive isotope iron-60 (which had a half-life of 2.6 million years). By measuring tiny variations of <sup>60<\/sup>Ni in meteorites, scientists can peer back 4.5 billion years to reconstruct the birth of our Solar System. In total, nuclear physicists have characterized 26 radioactive nickel isotopes. The longest-lived are <b>nickel-59<\/b> (half-life of 76,000 years), <b>nickel-63<\/b> (100.1 years), and <b>nickel-56<\/b> (6.1 days). Most other radioisotopes fall apart in less than 60 hours, and many in under 30 seconds. Nickel also exhibits one excited metastable state.<\/p><p>In astrophysics, radioactive <b>nickel-56<\/b> is forged during the intense <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a>-burning phase of dying giant stars and released during explosive Type Ia supernovae. As <sup>56<\/sup>Ni decays into <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a><\/a>-56 and eventually stable <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>-56 via electron capture, it releases energy that powers the brilliant glowing light curves of supernovae observed across distant galaxies. Meanwhile, long-lived <sup>59<\/sup>Ni acts as a geological clock: cosmogenic <sup>59<\/sup>Ni created by space radiation helps scientists date how long meteorites have rested on Earth and measure cosmic dust buried in ancient polar ice sheets and ocean sediments.<\/p><p>At the extreme frontiers of nuclear physics lie two \"doubly magic\" isotopes: <b>nickel-48<\/b> (discovered in 1999) and <b>nickel-78<\/b> (half-life 110 milliseconds). Nickel-48 contains 28 protons and 20 neutrons, making it the most proton-rich heavy nucleus known, while <sup>78<\/sup>Ni (28 protons, 50 neutrons) is a vital building block in supernova element creation (r-process). Both isotopes possess filled nuclear shells that make them remarkably stable despite extreme proton-neutron imbalances.<\/p><p>On Earth, <b>nickel-63<\/b> is created in nuclear reactors when <sup>62<\/sup>Ni absorbs neutrons. Because it emits steady streams of high-speed electrons (beta particles), <sup>63<\/sup>Ni is used in specialized high-speed electronic switches called krytrons and is being researched to build long-lasting, miniaturized betavoltaic nuclear batteries for space probes and medical implants.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">\n\n=== Occurrence ===\n<\/div>\n<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">See also: Ore genesis and Category:<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">Nickel<\/a><\/a> minerals<\/div>\n<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-left\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/6ffc41fc5bfe79dfd983b271ad437f91.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"188\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"3264\" data-file-height=\"2448\" \/><figcaption>Widmanst\u00e4tten pattern showing the two forms of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a><\/a>\u2013<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a>, kamacite and taenite, in an octahedrite meteorite<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">Nickel<\/a> is a widespread element on Earth and across the cosmos. Geophysical evidence indicates that the vast majority of Earth's nickel is locked deep inside the planet's liquid outer core and solid inner core, where it exists as an alloy mixed with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a>. In space, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>-nickel alloys are common in metallic meteorites, existing as two primary mineral forms: <b>kamacite<\/b> (containing 5% to 10% nickel) and <b>taenite<\/b> (containing 20% to 65% nickel). When meteorites are polished and etched with acid, these alloys display geometric cross-hatched patterns known as Widmanst\u00e4tten patterns. Nickel in meteorites was first scientifically identified in 1799 by French chemist Joseph-Louis Proust while analyzing a meteorite sample from Campo del Cielo, Argentina.<\/p><p>On Earth's crust, identified land-based nickel resources containing 1% nickel or greater exceed 130 million tonnes\u2014roughly double the current known economic reserves. Geologists classify nickel deposits into two main types: <b>laterites<\/b> (oxides) which make up about 60% of land reserves, and <b>sulfide deposits<\/b> which account for 40%. Oxide ores include nickeliferous limonite, (Fe,Ni)O(OH), and garnierite (a hydrous nickel silicate mixture). Sulfide ores primarily consist of pentlandite and pyrrhotite, (Fe,Ni)<sub>9<\/sub>S<sub>8<\/sub> and (Fe,Ni)<sub>7<\/sub>S<sub>6<\/sub>, along with millerite and the nickel-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">arsenic<\/a> mineral nickeline.<\/p><p>In India, the primary repository of nickel is located in the famous <b>Sukinda Valley<\/b> in the Jajpur district of Odisha. Sukinda holds over 95% of India's nickel resources, primarily stored as nickeliferous laterite and within Chromite Overburden (COB)\u2014waste rock produced during <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Chromium (Cr)\">chromium<\/a> mining containing 0.4% to 0.9% nickel. Nickel deposits are also found alongside <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a><\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/U\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Uranium (U)\">uranium<\/a> mineralization in the historic Singhbhum Shear Zone around Jaduguda and Ghatsila in Jharkhand, as well as in Malanjkhand in Madhya Pradesh.<\/p>", "History": "<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">\n\n=== History ===\n<\/div>\n<p>The human connection with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a> spans thousands of years, starting long before anyone knew <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a> existed as a distinct element. Unintentional use of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a> dates back to at least 3500 BCE, when ancient bronzes from Syria were crafted containing up to 2% nickel. In ancient China, metalworkers produced a prized silvery alloy known as <i>baitong<\/i> (\"white <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a>\") around 1700\u20131400 BCE. Exported to Europe as <i>paktong<\/i> in the 17th century, its true nickel content was not scientifically proved until 1822.<\/p><p>One of the most extraordinary ancient numismatic breakthroughs occurred in the 2nd century BCE in the northwestern region of the Indian subcontinent (ancient Bactria and Gandhara). Greco-Bactrian kings\u2014such as <b>Agathocles<\/b>, <b>Euthydemus II<\/b>, and <b>Pantaleon<\/b>\u2014issued striking coins made from a cupronickel alloy containing approximately 75% <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a><\/a> and 25% nickel. These ancient didrachms and chalkons featured images of Dionysos and panthers, representing the first intentional use of cupronickel coinage in human history\u2014sharing the exact 75:25 <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a>-to-nickel ratio used in modern U.S. nickel coins two millennia later!<\/p>\n<figure class=\"mw-default-size\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/04795ef517c561d3ef96e6c67b2046bc.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"182\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"2452\" data-file-height=\"1789\" \/><figcaption>Nickeline\/niccolite<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p>In medieval Germany, miners working in the Ore Mountains discovered a reddish mineral that looked promisingly like copper ore. However, no matter how hard they tried to smelt it, they could extract no copper at all. Frustrated, the miners blamed a mischievous sprite of German folklore named <i>Nickel<\/i> (similar to \"Old Nick\" or the devil) for cursing the ore, calling it <i>Kupfernickel<\/i> (\"copper-demon\"). Today, this mineral is known as nickeline or niccolite (nickel arsenide, NiAs).<\/p><p>In 1751, Swedish chemist and mineralogist <b>Baron Axel Fredrik Cronstedt<\/b> attempted to extract copper from kupfernickel at a <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a><\/a> mine in Los, Sweden. Instead of copper, he isolated a brand-new silvery-white metal. Cronstedt named the element <b>nickel<\/b> after the mythical mine spirit that gave the mineral its name. Initially, nickel was produced in small quantities as a byproduct of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a> blue pigment manufacturing (starting in 1824). Large-scale industrial smelting began in Norway in 1848, and global demand exploded after 1889 when nickel was added to steel. Major mining booms followed the discovery of laterite ores in New Caledonia (1865), and massive sulfide deposits in Canada's Sudbury Basin (1883), Russia's Norilsk-Talnakh (1920), and South Africa's Merensky Reef (1924).<\/p>", "Applications": "<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">\n\n=== Applications ===\n<\/div>\n<figure class=\"mw-default-size\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/83fbf5ece5398c701713731eb4350bd2.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"453\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"587\" data-file-height=\"1064\" \/><figcaption><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">Nickel<\/a><\/a> foam (top) and its internal structure (bottom)<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">Nickel<\/a> is predominantly an alloying metal. Globally, about 68% of all refined <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a> goes into manufacturing <b>stainless steel<\/b>, 10% into nonferrous alloys, 9% into electroplating, 7% into alloy steel, 3% into foundries, and 4% into other products including rechargeable batteries. Across end-use industries, engineering accounts for 27%, metal goods 20%, transport 14%, tubular products 14%, electronics 11%, building and construction 10%, and miscellaneous uses 5%.<\/p><p>Nickel adds exceptional toughness, tensile strength, and corrosion resistance to metals. It is essential in everyday goods\u2014from stainless steel cookware, coins, and electric guitar strings to microphone capsules, plumbing fixtures, and specialized magnetic alloys like Permalloy, Invar, and Elinvar.
