Historically, nickel was used to forge traditional ceremonial weapons across Southeast Asia (such as ornate <i>Kris<\/i> daggers with patterned <i>pamor<\/i> blades made from meteoric <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>). Because of its corrosion resistance, nickel was also used as a <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ag\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silver (Ag)\">silver<\/a> substitute and cheap coinage metal.<\/p>\n<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-left\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/d8a76ff81251c12a9a4a28cd3c63a5c9.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"255\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"470\" data-file-height=\"480\" \/><figcaption>A \"horseshoe magnet\" made of alnico nickel alloy<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p>In high technology and energy, nickel plays a massive role. <b>Alnico magnets<\/b> (made of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a>, nickel, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a>) create strong permanent magnetic fields. Porous nickel foam and mesh serve as gas diffusion electrodes in alkaline fuel cells. Nickel catalysts, especially finely divided <b>Raney nickel<\/b> (a nickel-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminum (Al)\">aluminum<\/a> alloy), are widely used to hydrogenate unsaturated vegetable oils into margarine. In medicine, studies (such as Forte et al.) have investigated trace nickel levels in human blood (0.89 ng\/mL in type 2 diabetics vs 0.77 ng\/mL in controls). Nickel is also magnetostrictive\u2014contracting slightly by about 50 parts per million when exposed to a magnetic field\u2014and acts as a tough binder (6% to 12% by weight) in cemented <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/W\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tungsten (W)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/W\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tungsten (W)\">tungsten<\/a><\/a> carbide tools.<\/p><p>In mining, nickel acts as an effective fire assay collector for <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pt\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Platinum (Pt)\">Platinum<\/a> Group Elements (PGE: <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pt\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Platinum (Pt)\">platinum<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pd\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Palladium (Pd)\">palladium<\/a>, etc.) and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\">gold<\/a><\/a>. In advanced materials, <b>Nitinol<\/b> (a nickel-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ti\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Titanium (Ti)\">titanium<\/a><\/a> alloy) exhibits incredible shape memory and superelasticity, springing back to its original shape when heated. In 2025, QuesTek Innovations and Stoke Space developed 3D-printed nickel superalloys engineered for reusable spacecraft engines operating in extreme high-pressure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> environments (such as the Zenith full-flow staged combustion engine).<\/p><p>India holds a vital position in nickel science and strategic engineering. Institutions like <b>CSIR-NML<\/b> (National Metallurgical Laboratory, Jamshedpur) and <b>CSIR-IMMT<\/b> (Bhubaneswar) have pioneered indigenous hydrometallurgical leaching, reduction roasting, and bio-metallurgical processes using fungi like <i>Aspergillus niger<\/i> to extract nickel and ferro-nickel from Sukinda's low-grade chromite overburden, transforming mining waste into strategic wealth. Defense public sector enterprise <b>MIDHANI<\/b> (Mishra Dhatu Nigam Limited, Hyderabad) manufactures specialized nickel-based superalloys (such as Superni, Inconel, and Nimonic) crucial for DRDO defense systems, jet engines (LCA Tejas), and ISRO rocket engines (GSLV, Chandrayaan, and Gaganyaan space missions). Furthermore, institutions like <b>IGCAR<\/b> (Kalpakkam) and <b>BARC<\/b> rely on nickel superalloys for structural integrity in India's <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a>-cooled Fast Breeder Reactors.<\/p>", "Biological role": "<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">\n\n=== Biological role ===\n<\/div>\n<p>Although its biological importance was not recognized until the 1970s, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a> is now known to be an essential trace element for plants, bacteria, archaea, and fungi. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">Nickel<\/a> sits at the active core of several critical enzymes. The enzyme <b>urease<\/b> uses <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a> to hydrolyze urea into ammonia and carbamate; in pathogenic bacteria, urease acts as a key virulence factor. <b>NiFe hydrogenases<\/b> use nickel and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> to catalyze the conversion of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> gas (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">H<sub>2<\/sub><\/a>) into protons and electrons (and vice versa).<\/p><p>In methanogenic archaea, a nickel-tetrapyrrole coenzyme known as <b>cofactor F430<\/b> powers the enzyme methyl coenzyme M reductase, which produces methane gas. Other nickel-containing enzymes include <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> monoxide dehydrogenase (featuring an Fe-Ni-S cluster), a rare bacterial class of superoxide dismutase, and glyoxalase I enzymes found in bacteria and trypanosomal parasites (which use Ni<sup>2+<\/sup> instead of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a><\/a>).<\/p><p>In human health, dietary nickel may act as a prebiotic by nourishing beneficial bacteria in the large intestine. The U.S. Institute of Medicine has not established a Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for humans, but sets a tolerable upper intake limit of 1 mg\/day for soluble nickel salts. Typical dietary intake ranges between 70 and 100 \u03bcg\/day, of which less than 10% is absorbed and excreted via urine. Small amounts of nickel leach into food cooked in stainless steel cookware\u2014for example, an acidic serving of tomato sauce leaches an average of 88 \u03bcg of nickel after 10 cooking cycles.<\/p><p>On a planetary scale, nickel played a dramatic role in Earth's worst mass extinction! Massive volcanic eruptions of the Siberian Traps 252 million years ago flooded the oceans with nickel. This sudden nutrient boom triggered an explosive population growth of methane-producing archaea (<i>Methanosarcina<\/i>), releasing vast clouds of methane gas into the atmosphere. This led to extreme global warming and ocean acidification, causing the Permian\u2013Triassic extinction event that wiped out over 90% of all species on Earth.<\/p>" } }, "Cu": { "symbol": "Cu", "name": "Copper", "atomic": 29, "category": "transition metal", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 29 (Cu)", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">Copper<\/a><\/a><\/b> is a chemical element with the symbol <b>Cu<\/b> and atomic number <b>29<\/b>. Known in ancient Sanskrit texts as <i>Tamra<\/i> (\u0924\u093e\u092e\u094d\u0930), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a> is a soft, malleable, and ductile transition metal renowned for its warm reddish-orange metallic luster and exceptional ability to conduct heat and electricity. As one of the very few metals that occurs naturally in pure metallic form, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a> has been shaped by human hands for over 10,000 years\u2014from the ancient Indus Valley Civilization, where it produced bronze artwork and durable <i>Tamra-patra<\/i> (copper plate inscriptions), to the modern world, where it powers electrical grids, microelectronics, and renewable energy. Beyond its industrial brilliance, copper is an essential biological micronutrient for all living organisms and possesses natural antimicrobial properties long celebrated in traditional Ayurvedic practices such as <i>Tamra Jal<\/i>.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/f\/f0\/NatCopper.jpg", "atomic_mass": 63.5463, "density": 8.96, "melt": 1357.77, "boil": 2835, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Middle East", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s1 3d10", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.9, "electron_affinity": 119.235, "ionization_energies": [ 745.5, 1957.9, 3555, 5536, 7700, 9900, 13400, 16000, 19200, 22400, 25600, 35600, 38700, 42000, 46700, 50200, 53700, 61100, 64702, 163700, 174100, 184900, 198800, 210500, 222700, 239100, 249660, 1067358, 1116105 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-left\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/07e0f771ff81abafdfedf01389073169.JPG\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"180\" height=\"178\" style=\"--mw-file-upright: 0.7\" class=\"mw-file-element mw-file-upright\" data-file-width=\"3616\" data-file-height=\"3584\" \/><figcaption>A <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a><\/a> disc (99.95% pure) made by continuous casting; etched to reveal crystallites<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-left\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/743b6be6f1f8c340a6fcf46d8f9f9b75.gif\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"180\" height=\"115\" style=\"--mw-file-upright: 0.7\" class=\"mw-file-element mw-file-upright\" data-file-width=\"306\" data-file-height=\"196\" \/><figcaption><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">Copper<\/a><\/a> just above its melting point keeps its pink luster color when enough light outshines the orange incandescence color.<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">Copper<\/a><\/a> is a soft, highly malleable, and remarkably ductile transition metal with a distinctive pinkish-orange metallic sheen when freshly cut or polished. Along with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\">gold<\/a><\/a>, it is one of the only two non-grey metallic elements in the periodic table. When copper melts at 1084.62 \u00b0C (1357.77 K), it retains its rich pinkish luster provided external light outshines its glowing orange incandescence.<\/p>\n<p>Among non-precious metals, copper boasts unmatched electrical and thermal conductivity, second only to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ag\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silver (Ag)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ag\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silver (Ag)\">silver<\/a><\/a>. This exceptional conductivity arises from its unique electron configuration ([Ar] 3d\u00b9\u2070 4s\u00b9), in which a single electron in the outermost 4s shell can move with extreme ease through the metal's crystal lattice. Pure copper is physically soft and weak under mechanical stress, but its strength and hardness can be dramatically enhanced by mixing it into versatile alloys.<\/p>\n<p>While pure copper does not react with pure water, prolonged exposure to moist atmospheric air causes it to slowly react with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a><\/a> dioxide, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a> compounds. This oxidation process forms a protective, pale-green layer of basic copper carbonate known as a patina or verdigris. This green coating acts as a durable shield, protecting the underlying metal from further corrosion for centuries\u2014a feature visible on historic copper domes, architectural monuments, and ancient Indian statues.<\/p>\n<p>Copper forms several essential metal alloys. Combining copper with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a><\/a> yields brass, while fusing it with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tin (Sn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tin (Sn)\">tin<\/a><\/a> creates bronze. Alloying copper with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a><\/a> produces cupronickel, prized for marine hardware and coinage, as well as constantan, an alloy whose stable electrical resistance across temperature shifts makes it indispensable in thermocouples and strain gauges. Sterling <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ag\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silver (Ag)\">silver<\/a> contains 7.5% copper blended with pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ag\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silver (Ag)\">silver<\/a> to add structural rigidity for jewelry and tableware.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Isotopes": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">Main article: Isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a><\/a><\/div>\n<p>Scientists have identified 29 distinct isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a><\/a>, ranging from mass numbers 52 to 80. Natural <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a> on Earth is composed of two stable isotopes: <b><sup>63<\/sup>Cu<\/b>, which makes up roughly 69.15% of naturally occurring copper, and <b><sup>65<\/sup>Cu<\/b>, which accounts for the remaining 30.85%. Both of these stable nuclei possess a nuclear spin of 3\/2.<\/p>\n<p>The remaining 27 copper isotopes are radioactive. The most stable radioisotope is <b><sup>67<\/sup>Cu<\/b>, with a half-life of 61.83 hours. Researchers have also characterized 10 metastable nuclear isomers, among which <b><sup>68m<\/sup>Cu<\/b> is the longest-lived, boasting a half-life of 3.8 minutes. Radioactive copper isotopes display clear decay patterns based on their mass numbers: isotopes lighter than mass 64 decay via positron emission (\u03b2\u207a) into <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a><\/a>, whereas isotopes heavier than mass 64 undergo electron emission (\u03b2\u207b) into <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a><\/a>. Sitting right in the middle is <b><sup>64<\/sup>Cu<\/b> (half-life of 12.7 hours), which is unique because it decays through both \u03b2\u207a and \u03b2\u207b pathways.<\/p>\n<p>Radioactive copper isotopes play a crucial role in modern nuclear medicine. In particular, <b><sup>62<\/sup>Cu<\/b> (used in the radiopharmaceutical <sup>62<\/sup>Cu-PTSM) and <b><sup>64<\/sup>Cu<\/b> serve as essential positron-emitting tracers in Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scanning, enabling doctors to monitor cardiac blood flow, evaluate brain tissue perfusion, and target cancerous tumors with extreme precision.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Occurrence": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">See also: List of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a><\/a> ores<\/div>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">Copper<\/a><\/a> is forged deep within massive exploding stars (supernovae) and stellar nucleosynthesis. It ranks as the 26th most abundant element in the Earth's crust, occurring at an average concentration of about 50 parts per million (ppm)\u2014making it less abundant than <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a><\/a> (75 ppm) but far more plentiful than <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a><\/a> (14 ppm). Typical background concentrations of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a> are around 1 ng\/m\u00b3 in atmospheric air, 150 mg\/kg in soil, 30 mg\/kg in plant vegetation, 2 \u03bcg\/L in freshwater, and 0.5 \u03bcg\/L in ocean seawater.<\/p>\n<p>In nature, copper occurs both as pure native copper metal and within a rich spectrum of minerals. Major copper-bearing minerals include:<\/p>\n<ul>\n <li><b>Sulfides:<\/b> Chalcopyrite (CuFeS\u2082, the principal commercial ore), bornite (\"peacock ore\"), digenite, covellite, and chalcocite.<\/li>\n <li><b>Sulfosalts:<\/b> Tetrahedrite-tennantite and enargite.<\/li>\n <li><b>Carbonates:<\/b> Azurite (brilliant deep blue) and malachite (vibrant green).<\/li>\n <li><b>Oxides:<\/b> Cuprite (copper(I) oxide, Cu\u2082O) and tenorite (copper(II) oxide, CuO).<\/li>\n<\/ul>\n<p>While native copper usually exists as polycrystalline masses, spectacular individual specimens have been uncovered throughout history. The largest single mass of native elemental copper ever discovered was unearthed in 1857 on the Keweenaw Peninsula in Michigan, USA, weighing an extraordinary 420 tonnes. The largest documented single crystal of native copper measured 4.4 \u00d7 3.2 \u00d7 3.2 cm.<\/p>\n<p>In India, copper mining has a rich geographical and geological significance. The largest single contiguous copper ore deposit in India is the <b>Malanjkhand Copper Belt<\/b>, located in the Balaghat district of Madhya Pradesh. Holding nearly 300 million tonnes of ore reserves, Malanjkhand is operated by the public sector enterprise <b>Hindustan Copper Limited (HCL)<\/b> and accounts for over 70% of India's total indigenous copper ore production. Other historic mining centers include the <b>Khetri Copper Belt<\/b> in Rajasthan and the <b>Singhbhum Copper Belt<\/b> in Jharkhand. To efficiently extract copper from lean Indian ores, premier research institutions like the <b>CSIR-National Metallurgical Laboratory (CSIR-NML)<\/b> in Jamshedpur pioneered advanced mineral flotation flowsheets and eco-friendly bioleaching techniques using thermophilic bacteria.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading2\">", "Biological role": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">Main article: <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">Copper<\/a><\/a> in biology<\/div>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">Copper<\/a><\/a> is an essential trace micronutrient vital for the survival of all living organisms, including plants, animals, fungi, and micro-organisms. In the human body, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a> acts as a non-negotiable cofactor for key enzymes that drive critical biological functions:<\/p>\n<ul>\n <li><b>Cytochrome c oxidase:<\/b> The key enzyme responsible for cellular energy (ATP) production inside mitochondria.<\/li>\n <li><b>Superoxide dismutase:<\/b> A critical antioxidant enzyme that neutralizes toxic free radicals and protects cellular DNA from oxidative damage.<\/li>\n <li><b>Tyrosinase:<\/b> Essential for synthesizing melanin, the pigment responsible for skin, hair, and eye coloration.<\/li>\n <li><b>Ceruloplasmin:<\/b> Transports over 95% of total copper in human blood plasma and regulates body <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a> metabolism.<\/li>\n<\/ul>\n<p>In nature's design, copper plays a breathtaking respiratory role. While humans and mammals rely on <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>-centered hemoglobin to carry <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> in red blood cells, many invertebrates\u2014such as octopuses, snails, spiders, and crustaceans\u2014use copper-based proteins called <b>hemocyanin<\/b>. When bound to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a>, hemocyanin turns a striking royal blue color, giving these creatures true \"blue blood.\"<\/p>\n<p>Copper is also famous for its potent <b>oligodynamic effect<\/b>\u2014a natural antimicrobial phenomenon where trace copper ions dissolve into liquids and rapidly destroy bacteria, viruses, and fungi by rupturing their cell membranes and damaging their nucleic acids. Solid copper surfaces kill over 99.9% of harmful bacteria, including <i>E. coli<\/i>, <i>Salmonella<\/i>, and superbugs like MRSA, within two hours of contact.<\/p>\n<p>This biological purity was recognized thousands of years ago in India. Ancient Ayurvedic treatises, including the <b>Charaka Samhita<\/b> and <b>Sushruta Samhita<\/b>, extolled the virtues of <i>Tamra<\/i> (copper) for purifying water and maintaining health. The classical practice of storing clean water overnight in a pure copper vessel\u2014known as <b>Tamra Jal<\/b>\u2014allows trace copper ions to naturally sterilize the water, boost digestive fire (<i>Agni<\/i>), and balance the body's three doshas (Vata, Pitta, and Kapha). Modern scientific studies confirm that this traditional practice effectively neutralizes waterborne microbial pathogens.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "History": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">Copper<\/a><\/a> holds a legendary place in human history as one of the earliest metals ever mastered by civilization, alongside <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\">gold<\/a><\/a> and meteoritic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a>. Because <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a> occurs naturally in pure metallic form, early humans began fashioning <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a> tools, beads, and ornaments over 10,000 years ago (c. 8000 BCE). The era following the Neolithic period is known as the Chalcolithic Age (or Copper Age), marking humanity's transition from stone tools to metallurgy. Around 3500 BCE, ancient metalsmiths discovered that smelting copper ore with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tin (Sn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tin (Sn)\">tin<\/a><\/a> produced bronze\u2014a much harder alloy that ushered in the Bronze Age and transformed tools, armor, and architecture.<\/p>\n<p>The English word <i>copper<\/i> stems from the Old English <i>coper<\/i>, which derives from the Latin <i>cuprum<\/i>\u2014a shortened form of <i>aes cyprium<\/i> (\"metal of Cyprus\"). The Romans mined vast quantities of high-grade copper on the Mediterranean island of Cyprus, establishing it as the primary supplier of the ancient Western world.<\/p>\n<p>In India, copper has an ancient metallurgical heritage spanning over five millennia:<\/p>\n<ul>\n <li><b>Harappan Metallurgy (c. 3300\u20131300 BCE):<\/b> Artisans of the Indus Valley (Harappan) Civilization extracted copper ore from the ancient <b>Khetri mines<\/b> in Rajasthan to craft weapons, household utensils, and artistic masterpieces. They perfected the <i>cire perdue<\/i> (lost-wax) casting technique, creating world-famous artifacts such as the 4,500-year-old bronze statuette of the <i>Dancing Girl of Mohenjo-daro<\/i>.<\/li>\n <li><b>Tamra-patra (Copper Plate Inscriptions):<\/b> For over two thousand years across ancient and medieval India, kings from the Maurya, Gupta, and Chola empires recorded royal decrees, land grants, and legal contracts on durable copper plates known as <i>Tamra-patra<\/i> (or <i>Tamra-shasana<\/i>). Indian rulers chose copper because it resists rusting and atmospheric decay, ensuring that historical records survived intact for centuries (such as the Maurya-era Sohgaura copper plate).<\/li>\n <li><b>The Sultanganj Buddha:<\/b> Cast during the Gupta-Pala transitional period (c. 500\u2013700 CE) in Bihar, the magnificent <b>Sultanganj Buddha<\/b> stands 2.3 meters tall and weighs over 500 kg. It remains the largest complete ancient pure-copper statue in the world, representing an extraordinary pinnacle of ancient Indian metallurgical engineering and lost-wax metal casting.<\/li>\n<\/ul>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">", "Applications": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">See also: <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">Copper<\/a><\/a> in renewable energy<\/div>\n<figure class=\"mw-default-size\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/00f8286e62f90b3ab06dac437ce33ea5.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"167\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"1200\" data-file-height=\"800\" \/><figcaption><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">Copper<\/a><\/a> fittings for soldered plumbing joints<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">Copper<\/a><\/a> is an indispensable material in modern industry, architecture, and technology. Its global consumption is divided among four main sectors:<\/p>\n<ul>\n <li><b>Electrical Wire & Electronics (60%):<\/b> Power distribution grids, household wiring, electric motor windings, transformers, and printed circuit board traces rely heavily on copper's supreme electrical conductivity.<\/li>\n <li><b>Roofing & Plumbing (20%):<\/b> Corrosion-resistant copper pipes, fittings, flashing, and architectural cladding provide durable, leak-free water supply systems and timeless building exteriors.<\/li>\n <li><b>Industrial Machinery (15%):<\/b> Heat exchangers, industrial boilers, hydraulic lines, and radiator cores utilize copper's outstanding thermal conductivity.<\/li>\n <li><b>Alloys & Specialty Uses (5%):<\/b> Brass, bronze, cupronickel, and coinage metals.<\/li>\n<\/ul>\n<p>For over two centuries, copper-based anti-fouling paints have been applied to marine boat hulls to suppress the growth of algae, barnacles, and shellfish. In agriculture, copper compounds such as copper sulfate (Bordeaux mixture) serve as essential fungicides and soil nutritional supplements. In culinary arts, copper cookware is prized by chefs for its fast, uniform heat distribution (such as whipping egg whites into voluminous peaks), though copper pots are usually lined with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tin (Sn)\">tin<\/a> or stainless steel to prevent reacting with acidic foods.<\/p>\n<p>Because pure copper is soft and ductile, machining pure copper can be tricky as copper shavings stick to cutting tools; hence, free-machining brass and copper alloys are preferred for precision machined components.<\/p>\n<p>In modern high-tech and scientific frontiers, copper plays a central role. In the clean energy transition, electric vehicles (EVs) require up to four times more copper than conventional internal combustion cars for electric motors, battery interconnects, and charging infrastructure. In physics and material science, copper oxides form the foundation of high-temperature <b>cuprate superconductors<\/b>, such as <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Y\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Yttrium (Y)\">Yttrium<\/a> <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ba\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Barium (Ba)\">Barium<\/a> Copper Oxide (YBCO). Premier Indian research organizations\u2014including the <b>Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR)<\/b>, <b>Indian Institute of Science (IISc) Bangalore<\/b>, and <b>Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC)<\/b>\u2014conduct cutting-edge research on cuprate superconductors that conduct electricity with zero energy loss. Additionally, Indian scientists at IITs and CSIR laboratories are developing eco-friendly copper nanoparticle catalysts for antimicrobial surface coatings and advanced wastewater purification systems.<\/p>\n<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">" } }, "Zn": { "symbol": "Zn", "name": "Zinc", "atomic": 30, "category": "transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">Zinc<\/a><\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>Zn<\/b>, atomic number 30), historically known in commerce as <i>spelter<\/i>, is a versatile, bluish-white metal located in Group 12 of the periodic table. Chemically, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> shares a close kinship with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a><\/a>, forming stable ions in the +2 oxidation state with a very similar ionic size. Best known for its remarkable ability to shield steel from rust through galvanization, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> is also a critical biological element essential for all living creatures. India holds a monumental place in zinc's story: ancient Indian metallurgists at Zawar in Rajasthan pioneered the world's very first industrial-scale zinc smelting and downward distillation process over two thousand years ago, earning India historic recognition as the birthplace of pure metallic zinc extraction.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/b\/ba\/Zinc_%2830_Zn%29.jpg", "atomic_mass": 65.382, "density": 7.14, "melt": 692.68, "boil": 1180, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "India", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.65, "electron_affinity": -58, "ionization_energies": [ 906.4, 1733.3, 3833, 5731, 7970, 10400, 12900, 16800, 19600, 23000, 26400, 29990, 40490, 43800, 47300, 52300, 55900, 59700, 67300, 71200, 179100 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-left\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/11c864b33d62911a360d5512c7839d82.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"250\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"1032\" data-file-height=\"1032\" \/><figcaption>Piece of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a><\/a> sheet<\/figcaption><\/figure><p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">Zinc<\/a> is a lustrous, bluish-white metal with diamagnetic magnetic properties. When exposed to moist air, its shiny surface gradually reacts to form a dull, protective layer of basic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> carbonate that prevents deeper corrosion. Zinc is somewhat less dense than <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a> (7.14 g\/cm\u00b3) and crystallizes in a distorted hexagonal close-packed (hcp) crystal lattice, where each zinc atom has six nearest neighbors in its own plane at 265.9 pm and six others at a distance of 290.6 pm.<\/p><p>Zinc exhibits fascinating temperature-dependent mechanical properties. At room temperature, it is relatively hard and brittle. However, when warmed to between 100 \u00b0C and 150 \u00b0C, zinc undergoes a transformation, becoming remarkably malleable and ductile so that it can easily be rolled into thin sheets or shaped into complex forms. If heated further above 210 \u00b0C, it becomes extremely brittle once again and can be crushed into a fine powder simply by hammering!<\/p><p>As an electrical conductor, zinc performs moderately well. Unusually for a metal, zinc has a relatively low melting point of 419.53 \u00b0C (692.68 K) and a boiling point of 907 \u00b0C (1180 K). Its melting point is lower than any other d-block transition metal except <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\">mercury<\/a><\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cd\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cadmium (Cd)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cd\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cadmium (Cd)\">cadmium<\/a><\/a>. Because of their completely filled d-electron shells (3d<sup>10<\/sup>) and low melting points, zinc, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cd\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cadmium (Cd)\">cadmium<\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\">mercury<\/a> are frequently set apart from typical transition metals in detailed chemical classifications.<\/p><p>Zinc readily forms alloys with a vast array of metals, most famously creating brass when combined with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a><\/a>. It also forms binary alloys with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminium (Al)\">aluminium<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Antimony (Sb)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Antimony (Sb)\">antimony<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Bi\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Bismuth (Bi)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Bi\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Bismuth (Bi)\">bismuth<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\">gold<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\">mercury<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ag\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silver (Ag)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ag\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silver (Ag)\">silver<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tin (Sn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tin (Sn)\">tin<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Te\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tellurium (Te)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Te\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tellurium (Te)\">tellurium<\/a><\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a><\/a>. Interestingly, while neither zinc nor <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zirconium (Zr)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zirconium (Zr)\">zirconium<\/a><\/a> is magnetic on its own, their intermetallic compound <b>ZrZn<sub>2<\/sub><\/b> unexpectedly becomes ferromagnetic when cooled below 35 K!<\/p>", "Physical properties": "<p>In its physical state, elemental <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> is a solid metal with a density of 7.14 g\/cm\u00b3 at room temperature, making it moderately heavy yet easy to work with in structural applications. Pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> displays a shiny, metallic, bluish-gray surface when freshly cut. It melts at 419.53 \u00b0C (692.68 K) and boils at 907 \u00b0C (1180 K). Its heat of fusion is 7.32 kJ\/mol, and its heat of vaporization is 115 kJ\/mol, reflecting the relatively weak metallic bonding caused by its completely filled 3d<sup>10<\/sup> electron subshell.<\/p><p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">Zinc<\/a>'s electrical conductivity is roughly 27% that of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a>, allowing it to function effectively in electrical groundings, battery anodes, and protective coatings. Sound waves travel through solid zinc at approximately 3,850 m\/s. Its thermal expansion coefficient is 30.2 \u00b5m\/(m\u00b7K), meaning it expands predictably under heating. When alloyed, zinc dramatically lowers the melting point of companion metals, which makes zinc alloys like Zamak ideal for precision die-casting of complex shapes with tight tolerances.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img alt=\"A black shiny lump of solid with uneven surface\" src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/cfb2b830fafbcfc1ee570ba132180147.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"231\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"372\" data-file-height=\"343\" \/><figcaption>Sphalerite (ZnS)<\/figcaption><\/figure><p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">Zinc<\/a> makes up approximately 70 parts per million (0.007%) of Earth's continental crust by mass, ranking as the 24th most abundant crustal element. Across the Solar System, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> is the 22nd most abundant element, averaging 312 ppm. Background environmental concentrations of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> typically do not exceed 1 \u00b5g\/m\u00b3 in air, 300 mg\/kg in soil, 100 mg\/kg in vegetation, 20 \u00b5g\/L in freshwater, and 5 \u00b5g\/L in seawater.<\/p><p>Geochemically, zinc is classified as a <i>chalcophile<\/i> element\u2014meaning it prefers to pair up with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a><\/a> and heavy chalcogens rather than <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a><\/a> or halogens. The principal commercial ore of zinc is <b>sphalerite<\/b> (zinc sulfide, ZnS), which contains 60% to 62% zinc by mass and crystallized under reducing conditions in Earth's early crust. Other important zinc minerals include smithsonite (zinc carbonate, ZnCO<sub>3<\/sub>), hemimorphite (zinc silicate), wurtzite (a hexagonal crystal form of ZnS), and hydrozincite. Most of these non-sulfide minerals were formed by long-term weathering of primordial sphalerite deposits.<\/p><p>Globally identified zinc resources total between 1.9 and 2.8 billion tonnes, with major mining reserves located in Australia, China, Canada, the United States, and Iran. Up to 2002, approximately 346 million tonnes of zinc had been mined throughout human history, with an estimated 109 to 305 million tonnes currently in active use. Data from the United States Geological Survey (USGS) shows that even though global zinc production grew by over 80% in recent decades, ongoing exploration continuously discovers new reserves, maintaining a stable supply lifespan for future generations.<\/p><p><b>India's Geographical Relevance:<\/b> India is home to some of the richest zinc deposits in the world, concentrated overwhelmingly in the state of <b>Rajasthan<\/b>. The <b>Rampura Agucha mine<\/b> in Bhilwara district, operated by Hindustan Zinc Limited (HZL, a Vedanta company), is celebrated as the world's largest underground zinc-producing mine! Other major operating mines in Rajasthan include Zawar, Sindesar Khurd, Rajpura Dariba, and Kayad. Hindustan Zinc controls roughly 77% of India's primary zinc market, making India a global powerhouse in primary zinc production and metallurgy.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Naturally occurring <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> on Earth consists of five stable isotopes: <sup>64<\/sup>Zn (49.17% natural abundance), <sup>66<\/sup>Zn (27.73%), <sup>68<\/sup>Zn (18.45%), <sup>67<\/sup>Zn (4.04%), and <sup>70<\/sup>Zn (0.61%). Among these, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a>-64 is by far the most abundant in nature.<\/p><p>Nuclear scientists have synthesized several dozen radioisotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a>. The most stable radioactive isotope is <b><sup>65<\/sup>Zn<\/b>, which has a half-life of 243.66 days, followed by <sup>72<\/sup>Zn with a half-life of 46.5 hours. Zinc also features 10 nuclear isomers\u2014metastable excited states of the atomic nucleus\u2014led by <sup>69m<\/sup>Zn with a half-life of 13.75 hours. The superscript <i>m<\/i> signifies a metastable state that eventually drops to the ground state by emitting high-energy gamma ray photons.<\/p><p>The decay pathways of zinc radioisotopes follow clear rules based on atomic mass:<\/p><p>Zinc radioisotopes lighter than mass 66 decay primarily via <b>electron capture<\/b>, absorbing an inner shell electron to transform into an isotope of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a><\/a>:<\/p><p style=\"text-align:center;\">\\( \\text{}^{n}_{30}\\text{Zn} + e^{-} \\rightarrow \\text{}^{n}_{29}\\text{Cu} + \\nu_e \\)<\/p><p>Conversely, zinc radioisotopes heavier than mass 66 decay primarily via <b>beta-minus emission (\u03b2<sup>\u2212<\/sup>)<\/b>, ejecting an electron and an electron antineutrino to form an isotope of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">gallium<\/a><\/a>:<\/p><p style=\"text-align:center;\">\\( \\text{}^{n}_{30}\\text{Zn} \\rightarrow \\text{}^{n}_{31}\\text{Ga} + e^{-} + \\bar{\\nu}_e \\)<\/p>", "History": "<p>India holds a preeminent place in the global history of science as the undisputed birthplace of pure metallic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> production. While ancient civilizations in the Mediterranean and China knew how to make brass by smelting <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a> ores together with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a>-rich minerals, isolating pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> metal was an extraordinary technical challenge. Because zinc metal boils at 907 \u00b0C\u2014a temperature lower than what is required to reduce zinc ore\u2014in conventional top-heated furnaces, zinc vapor instantly rises, reacts with atmospheric <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a>, and escapes as zinc oxide smoke.<\/p><p><b>The Zawar Distillation Revolution:<\/b> Ancient Indian metallurgists at <b>Zawar<\/b>, near Udaipur in Rajasthan, solved this ancient conundrum as early as 750 BCE by inventing a revolutionary <b>downward distillation<\/b> process (known in Sanskrit alchemical texts as <i>tiryakpatana yantra<\/i>). They packed brinjal-shaped (eggplant-shaped) clay retorts with zinc ore (sphalerite), charcoal, and organic reagents. These retorts were inverted over open furnace hearths with clay tubes extending downward into water-cooled collection vessels below. When heated from above, the zinc ore reduced to zinc vapor, which traveled downward away from the fire, condensing into droplets of pure metallic zinc!<\/p><p>By the 12th century CE, Zawar had grown into the world's first industrial-scale zinc refinery, operating hundreds of distillation furnaces simultaneously. This pioneering technology flourished in India centuries before Western Europe managed to produce metallic zinc.<\/p><p><b>Ancient Indian Texts &amp; Terminology:<\/b> In ancient Sanskrit, zinc was known as <i>Rasaka<\/i>, <i>Jasada<\/i>, or <b>Yashada<\/b>. Famous alchemical and medical treatises documented its production and properties:<\/p><ul><li><b>Rasa Ratnakara<\/b>, authored by the legendary sage and chemist <b>Nagarjuna<\/b> (c. 9th\u201310th century CE), contains detailed descriptions of extracting metallic zinc (<i>rasaka<\/i>) and preparing brass (<i>pittala<\/i>).<\/li><li><b>Rasa Ratna Samuccaya<\/b> (13th century) provides intricate engineering details and drawings of the <i>tiryakpatana yantra<\/i> furnace used for downward zinc distillation.<\/li><li>Ayurvedic medicine developed <b>Yashada Bhasma<\/b> (calcined zinc oxide ash), a revered traditional formulation used for centuries to treat eye disorders, promote skin healing, and boost immunity.<\/li><\/ul><p><b>Transmission to Europe:<\/b> In 1738, English metallurgist William Champion patented a downward zinc distillation method in Bristol that was virtually identical to the Zawar technique long practiced in Rajasthan. European chemists like Paracelsus introduced the name <i>zincum<\/i> in the 16th century (derived from German <i>Zinke<\/i>, meaning 'jagged teeth', describing zinc crystals in furnaces), and German chemist Andreas Sigismund Marggraf isolated pure metallic zinc in 1746.<\/p>", "Applications": "<ol><li><b>Galvanizing (55%):<\/b> Coating <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> and steel with a thin layer of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> to shield them from atmospheric rust. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">Zinc<\/a> acts as a sacrificial anode (cathodic protection)\u2014even if the outer surface is scratched, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> corrodes first to preserve the <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> beneath. Galvanized <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> (GI) sheets, guardrails, utility poles, bridges, and automobile bodies rely heavily on zinc.<\/li><li><b>Brass and Bronze (16%):<\/b> Brass (an alloy of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a> and zinc) is prized for its golden appearance, acoustic resonance, and low friction, making it essential for musical instruments, plumbing valves, decorative artifacts, and door locks.<\/li><li><b>Die-Casting Alloys (21%):<\/b> High-purity zinc alloys like <b>Zamak<\/b> (zinc, aluminium, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Magnesium (Mg)\">magnesium<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a>) are die-cast into precision components for automobiles, electrical housings, toys, and door handles.<\/li><li><b>Chemicals and Healthcare (8%):<\/b> Zinc oxide (ZnO) is a vital ingredient in sunscreens (reflecting harmful UV rays), rubber tire manufacturing (vulcanization), calamine lotion, diaper rash ointments, white pigments, and dietary supplements.<\/li><\/ol><p><b>Batteries &amp; Indian Energy Innovations:<\/b> Zinc has long powered dry-cell batteries (zinc-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> and alkaline batteries) due to its favorable electrochemical potential. Today, as the world moves toward renewable energy storage, <b>zinc-air batteries<\/b> are emerging as a safe, eco-friendly, and cost-effective alternative to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a>-ion batteries. In India, <b>Hindustan Zinc Limited<\/b> partnered with <b>IIT Madras<\/b> to successfully build a 1 kWh rechargeable zinc-air battery prototype for grid storage. Meanwhile, Indian researchers at <b>SASTRA Deemed University<\/b> (supported by DST) developed innovative silica-ZnO nanofluid electrolytes to suppress zinc corrosion, while institutes like <b>CSIR-NCL<\/b> and <b>IISc Bangalore<\/b> are actively advancing next-generation zinc-ion energy storage systems.<\/p>", "Biological role": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">Zinc<\/a> is an indispensable trace element for all forms of life\u2014humans, animals, plants, and microorganisms. It is the second most abundant trace metal in the human body after <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a><\/a>, and holds the unique distinction of being the <b>only metal present in all six enzyme classes<\/b>!<\/p><p>More than 300 enzymes and 1,000 transcription factors depend on <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> ions for structural stability and catalytic activity. Approximately 10% of all human proteins (~3,000 proteins) bind <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a>. It is stored and transported inside cells by proteins called metallothioneins, usually coordinated to the amino acid side chains of cysteine, histidine, aspartic acid, and glutamic acid. Zinc plays crucial roles in DNA synthesis, cell division, immune function, wound healing, and gene expression.<\/p><p>An adult human body contains roughly 2 to 4 grams of zinc, distributed mainly in skeletal muscle, bone, brain, liver, kidneys, skin, and retina. The prostate gland and seminal fluid contain extraordinarily high zinc concentrations, vital for prostate health and reproductive fertility. Intestinal absorption of dietary zinc is carefully regulated by transporter proteins such as ZIP4 and TRPM7.<\/p><p>In the brain, zinc is stored within synaptic vesicles of glutamatergic neurons and released during nerve transmission, regulating synaptic plasticity, learning, and memory. The transporter SLC30A3 regulates cerebral zinc levels. Maintaining proper zinc balance is critical: excess synaptic zinc can trigger neurotoxicity and oxidative stress, while zinc deficiency impairs cognitive development.<\/p><p><b>Agricultural Importance in India:<\/b> Zinc is equally vital for plant growth, building cell walls and activating growth hormones. However, zinc deficiency is widespread in Indian agricultural soils, affecting <b>35% to 50% of Indian soils<\/b> (and projected to reach 63%). Soil zinc deficiency reduces crop yields and leads to \"hidden hunger\" in humans\u2014causing childhood stunting and weakened immunity. To combat this, the <b>Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR)<\/b> and Indian agricultural universities promote zinc-fortified fertilizers (zinc-coated urea) and biofortified crop varieties like zinc-dense rice (<i>CR Dhan 315<\/i>) and wheat (<i>WB 02<\/i>), ensuring nutritional security across the nation.<\/p>" } }, "Ga": { "symbol": "Ga", "name": "Gallium", "atomic": 31, "category": "post-transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">Gallium<\/a><\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>Ga<\/b>, atomic number 31) is a remarkable post-transition metal in Group 13 of the periodic table, situated directly below <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminium (Al)\">aluminium<\/a>. Famous for its captivating physical trick, pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">gallium<\/a> is a soft, silvery-blue metal with an extraordinarily low melting point of 29.76 \u00b0C (85.57 \u00b0F)\u2014meaning a solid crystal of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">gallium<\/a> will literally melt into a mirror-like liquid puddle right in the warmth of your hand! Elemental gallium does not occur freely in nature; instead, it is hidden as a trace passenger inside <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a><\/a> ores and bauxite (aluminium ore). Once considered a rare chemical curiosity, gallium has become indispensable to modern technology, driving ultra-fast microchips, 5G cellular networks, high-efficiency solar cells, and energy-saving LED lights. India holds strategic importance in the global gallium landscape, featuring pioneering extraction initiatives at National Aluminium Company (<b>NALCO<\/b>) in Odisha using indigenous technology developed with the <b>Bhabha Atomic Research Centre<\/b> (<b>BARC<\/b>), alongside world-class Gallium Nitride (<b>GaN<\/b>) semiconductor research spearheaded by the <b>Indian Institute of Science (IISc)<\/b> and <b>DRDO<\/b>.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/b\/b1\/Solid_gallium_%28Ga%29.jpg", "atomic_mass": 69.7231, "density": 5.91, "melt": 302.9146, "boil": 2673, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Lecoq de Boisbaudran", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p1", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.81, "electron_affinity": 41, "ionization_energies": [ 578.8, 1979.3, 2963, 6180 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">Gallium<\/a> is a soft, silvery metal with a subtle bluish luster when pure. In its solid state, it is brittle enough to fracture like glass if struck, but soft enough to be cut with a knife. What makes <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">gallium<\/a> world-famous is its astonishing thermal behavior: it melts at just 29.76 \u00b0C (85.57 \u00b0F), slightly above standard room temperature. Unlike <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\">mercury<\/a><\/a>, which is a liquid metal that poses severe toxic risks, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">gallium<\/a> is low in toxicity and safe to hold in an open hand, where body heat quickly turns it into a shimmering liquid pool.<\/p><p>Gallium possesses one of the widest liquid temperature spans of any element on the periodic table. While it melts at ~30 \u00b0C, it does not boil until it reaches an extraordinary 2,673 \u00b0C (4,843 \u00b0F)! This gives liquid gallium a staggering liquid range of over 2,640 \u00b0C, making it ideal for high-temperature thermometers and extreme thermal applications where other liquids would instantly vaporize.<\/p><p>Another fascinating quirk of gallium is its behavior upon freezing. Like water, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">germanium<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Bi\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Bismuth (Bi)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Bi\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Bismuth (Bi)\">bismuth<\/a><\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Antimony (Sb)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Antimony (Sb)\">antimony<\/a><\/a>, gallium expands by 3.1% when it solidifies from a liquid. Because of this expansion, solidifying gallium can exert immense mechanical pressure. Scientists and jewelers learn early never to store liquid gallium in rigid glass or metal containers, because as it freezes, it will burst the container wide open!<\/p><p>Liquid gallium easily \"wets\" surfaces such as glass, porcelain, and human skin, leaving behind a fine dark-gray metallic residue. Furthermore, liquid gallium readily diffuses into the microscopic grain boundaries of other metals\u2014most notably <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminium (Al)\">aluminium<\/a>, aluminium-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a><\/a> alloys, and structural steel. This causes a dramatic loss of ductility known as <i>liquid metal embrittlement<\/i>. A single drop of liquid gallium placed on a sturdy aluminium girder slowly seeps into its molecular lattice, rendering the solid metal so brittle that it can be crumbled into dust by hand!<\/p>", "Physical properties": "<ul style=\"text-align:left\" class=\"gallery mw-gallery-packed\"><li class=\"gallerybox\" style=\"width: 202px\"><div class=\"thumb\" style=\"width: 200px;\"><span typeof=\"mw:File\"><img alt=\"Crystalline (orthorhomobic) gallium\" src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/abd1a895bc3f449408869ef5adfb1b76.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" (Ga)\">gallium<\/a><\/a><\/div><\/li><li class=\"gallerybox\" style=\"width: 186px\"><div class=\"thumb\" style=\"width: 184px;\"><span typeof=\"mw:File\"><img alt=\"Crystallization of gallium from the liquid\" src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/34ca1a35f5191b75800b23801a5ae55d.JPG\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"184\" height=\"150\" class=\"mw-file-element\" (Ga)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">gallium<\/a><\/a> from liquid<\/div><\/li><li class=\"gallerybox\" style=\"width: 208.66666666667px\"><div class=\"thumb\" style=\"width: 206.66666666667px;\"><span typeof=\"mw:File\"><img alt=\"Liquid gallium at 86 \u00b0F (30 \u00b0C)\" src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/d1943d0f4fb5edd0e9bb0e41cd94eeb7.png\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"207\" height=\"150\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"1443\" data-file-height=\"1049\" \/><\/span><\/div><div class=\"gallerytext\">Liquid <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">gallium<\/a><\/a> at 30 \u00b0C<\/div><\/li><\/ul><p>Elemental gallium exhibits a density of 5.91 g\/cm\u00b3 in its solid state at 20 \u00b0C. Unusually for most substances, liquid gallium is denser than solid gallium (liquid density is ~6.095 g\/cm\u00b3 at its melting point), which is why solid gallium crystals float on liquid gallium just as ice cubes float on liquid water.<\/p><p>Under ambient conditions, gallium does not adopt simple metallic structures like face-centered cubic or body-centered cubic packing. Instead, its room-temperature stable crystal phase (known as Ga-I) forms a complex orthorhombic lattice containing eight atoms per conventional unit cell. Within this unit cell, each gallium atom has only one nearest neighbor at a close distance of 244 pm, while its remaining six unit-cell neighbors are spaced 27 to 39 pm farther away. The two closest atoms form covalently bonded <b>Ga<sub>2<\/sub> dimers<\/b>, which serve as the fundamental structural building blocks of the crystal. Because strong covalent bonds bind the pairs internally while weaker forces hold the dimers together in the lattice, relatively little thermal energy is needed to melt the crystal\u2014explaining why gallium melts at such a remarkably low temperature compared to neighboring elements like <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminium (Al)\">aluminium<\/a> (660.32 \u00b0C) and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/In\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Indium (In)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/In\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Indium (In)\">indium<\/a><\/a> (156.6 \u00b0C).<\/p><p>This crystal arrangement is strikingly similar to that of diatomic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/I\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iodine (I)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/I\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iodine (I)\">iodine<\/a><\/a>. It arises because gallium's outer 4p electron extends beyond the core nucleus and [Ar]3d<sup>10<\/sup> electron shell. Because filled 3d<sup>10<\/sup> orbitals shield the positive nuclear charge poorly, gallium's outer electron is held tightly, giving gallium a higher first ionization energy (578.8 kJ\/mol) than aluminium (577.5 kJ\/mol).<\/p><p>Gallium's physical properties are highly <i>anisotropic<\/i>\u2014meaning their values vary significantly along its three main crystal axes (<i>a<\/i>, <i>b<\/i>, and <i>c<\/i>):<\/p><table class=\"wikitable\"><caption>Properties of gallium along different crystal axes<\/caption><tbody><tr><th>Property<\/th><th><i>a<\/i><\/th><th><i>b<\/i><\/th><th><i>c<\/i><\/th><\/tr><tr><td>Linear thermal expansion \u03b1 (~25 \u00b0C, \u00b5m\/(m\u00b7K))<\/td><td>16<\/td><td>11<\/td><td>31<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>Electrical resistivity \u03c1 (29.7 \u00b0C, n\u03a9\u00b7m)<\/td><td>543<\/td><td>174<\/td><td>81<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>Electrical resistivity \u03c1 (0 \u00b0C, n\u03a9\u00b7m)<\/td><td>480<\/td><td>154<\/td><td>71.6<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>Electrical resistivity \u03c1 (77 K, n\u03a9\u00b7m)<\/td><td>101<\/td><td>30.8<\/td><td>14.3<\/td><\/tr><tr><td>Electrical resistivity \u03c1 (4.2 K, p\u03a9\u00b7m)<\/td><td>13.8<\/td><td>6.8<\/td><td>1.6<\/td><\/tr><\/tbody><\/table><p>As shown above, electrical resistivity along the <i>a<\/i>-axis is nearly seven times higher than along the <i>c<\/i>-axis at room temperature. Furthermore, upon melting, gallium's coefficient of thermal expansion increases dramatically by several hundred percent.<\/p>", "Chemical properties": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">Gallium<\/a> belongs to Group 13 (the <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\">boron<\/a> family) and exhibits electron configuration [Ar] 3d<sup>10<\/sup> 4s<sup>2<\/sup> 4p<sup>1<\/sup>. Its chemistry is dominated by the <b>+3 oxidation state<\/b> (trivalent <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">gallium<\/a>), where it sheds its three valence electrons (4s<sup>2<\/sup> 4p<sup>1<\/sup>) to form stable Ga<sup>3+<\/sup> ions.<\/p><p>Like aluminium, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">gallium<\/a> forms <b>amphoteric<\/b> oxides and hydroxides\u2014meaning they react readily with both acids and bases. Gallium oxide (Ga<sub>2<\/sub>O<sub>3<\/sub>) and gallium hydroxide (Ga(OH)<sub>3<\/sub>) dissolve in strong acids to produce trivalent gallium salts such as gallium nitrate [Ga(NO<sub>3<\/sub>)<sub>3<\/sub>] or gallium chloride [GaCl<sub>3<\/sub>]:<\/p><p style=\"text-align:center;\">\\( \\text{Ga(OH)}_3 + 3\\text{HCl} \\rightarrow \\text{GaCl}_3 + 3\\text{H}_2\\text{O} \\)<\/p><p>When treated with strong alkalis like <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a> hydroxide (NaOH), gallium oxide and hydroxide dissolve to form soluble gallate complex ions [Ga(OH)<sub>4<\/sub>]<sup>\u2212<\/sup>:<\/p><p style=\"text-align:center;\">\\( \\text{Ga(OH)}_3 + \\text{NaOH} \\rightarrow \\text{Na}[\\text{Ga(OH)}_4] \\)<\/p><p>Gallium also exhibits lower oxidation states, though less frequently than heavier group members <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/In\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Indium (In)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/In\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Indium (In)\">indium<\/a><\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Tl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Thallium (Tl)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Tl\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Thallium (Tl)\">thallium<\/a><\/a>. The +1 oxidation state occurs in specialized compounds: for example, gallium dichloride (GaCl<sub>2<\/sub>) is actually a mixed-valence compound composed of equal parts gallium(I) and gallium(III), accurately written as Ga<sup>I<\/sup>[Ga<sup>III<\/sup>Cl<sub>4<\/sub>]. Simple monohalides like GaCl are unstable above 0 \u00b0C, spontaneously disproportionating into elemental gallium metal and gallium trichloride (GaCl<sub>3<\/sub>). True +2 oxidation states feature direct Ga\u2013Ga metal-metal bonds, as found in gallium monosulfide (GaS, formulated as Ga<sub>2<\/sub><sup>4+<\/sup>(S<sup>2\u2212<\/sup>)<sub>2<\/sub>) and the dioxane complex Ga<sub>2<\/sub>Cl<sub>4<\/sub>(C<sub>4<\/sub>H<sub>8<\/sub>O<sub>2<\/sub>)<sub>2<\/sub>.<\/p><p>At ambient temperatures, metallic gallium does not tarnish in dry air because it rapidly coats itself with a microscopic, protective passivating film of gallium oxide. However, when heated to high temperatures, it burns brilliantly in pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> to yield white Ga<sub>2<\/sub>O<sub>3<\/sub> powder. Gallium reacts slowly with water at room temperature, but dissolves smoothly in non-oxidizing mineral acids (like HCl or H<sub>2<\/sub>SO<sub>4<\/sub>) and alkalis, evolving <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a><\/a> gas.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">Gallium<\/a> is not found in its free elemental state anywhere in Earth's crust. It has an average crustal abundance of approximately 16.9 parts per million (ppm), ranking as the 34th most abundant element in Earth's crust\u2014comparable in overall abundance to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a><\/a> (14 ppm), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a><\/a> (25 ppm), and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Nb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Niobium (Nb)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Nb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Niobium (Nb)\">niobium<\/a><\/a> (20 ppm).<\/p><p>However, unlike <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a> or <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">gallium<\/a> is geochemically <i>dispersed<\/i>. Because Ga<sup>3+<\/sup> (ionic radius 62 pm) closely matches Al<sup>3+<\/sup> (53 pm) and Zn<sup>2+<\/sup> (74 pm) in size and charge, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">gallium<\/a> replaces aluminium in bauxite minerals and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> in sulfide ores rather than forming concentrated deposits of its own. Rare independent gallium minerals do exist\u2014such as gallite (CuGaS<sub>2<\/sub>) and germanite\u2014but they are far too scarce to serve as economic sources of the metal. Consequently, virtually all global gallium is produced as a valuable by-product during the industrial refining of bauxite (which typically contains ~50 ppm gallium) and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> sphalerite ores.<\/p><p>The United States Geological Survey (USGS) estimates that world reserves of bauxite and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> ores contain over 1 million tonnes of gallium. Additional small quantities exist in coal flue dusts (<1% by mass). Global annual refinery production of primary gallium passed 100 tonnes in 2010 and accelerated to approximately 450 tonnes per year in recent years.<\/p><p><b>India's Geographical Relevance & Extraction Initiatives:<\/b> India holds vast reserves of bauxite across major mining belts in Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Jharkhand, and Chhattisgarh. The <b>National Aluminium Company Limited (NALCO)<\/b>, operating one of Asia's largest integrated alumina refineries at <b>Damanjodi in Koraput district, Odisha<\/b>, is at the forefront of securing India's domestic gallium supply.<\/p><p>To reduce dependence on foreign imports of this critical strategic mineral, NALCO collaborated with premier national laboratories\u2014including the <b>Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC)<\/b> and the <b>Heavy Water Board (HWB)<\/b>\u2014to develop indigenous solvent extraction technology for recovering high-purity gallium directly from Bayer process alumina liquor and red mud residue. NALCO established a 10-tonne per year pilot extraction facility at Damanjodi. Simultaneously, the <b>Jawaharlal Nehru Aluminium Research Development and Design Centre (JNARDDC)<\/b> in Nagpur leads nationwide research on recovering strategic metals like gallium and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Scandium (Sc)\">scandium<\/a> from bauxite tailings. Furthermore, India's major zinc mining hubs in Rajasthan (such as the world-class Rampura Agucha and Zawar mines operated by Hindustan Zinc) process sphalerite ores containing trace gallium, reinforcing India's potential for mineral self-reliance.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">Gallium<\/a> possesses 30 known isotopes, spanning atomic mass numbers from 60 to 89. Naturally occurring <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">gallium<\/a> on Earth is composed of two stable, non-radioactive isotopes:<\/p><ul><li><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">Gallium<\/a>-69 (<sup>69<\/sup>Ga):<\/b> Makes up 60.11% of natural gallium.<\/li><li><b>Gallium-71 (<sup>71<\/sup>Ga):<\/b> Makes up the remaining 39.89% of natural gallium.<\/li><\/ul><p>All other 28 isotopes are synthetic radioisotopes. Among these, the longest-lived radioisotope is <b>gallium-67 (<sup>67<\/sup>Ga)<\/b>, with a half-life of 3.2617 days. Gallium-67 decays by electron capture into stable <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a><\/a>-67 while emitting diagnostic gamma rays. In nuclear medicine, <sup>67<\/sup>Ga-citrate injections are widely utilized in <b>gallium scans<\/b> to locate medical infections, chronic inflammatory foci, and specific cancers like Hodgkin's lymphoma.<\/p><p>Another vital medical radioisotope is <b>gallium-68 (<sup>68<\/sup>Ga)<\/b>, which has a short half-life of 67.84 minutes. Produced conveniently on-site in hospital radioisotope generators from parent <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">germanium<\/a>-68 (<sup>68<\/sup>Ge), gallium-68 decays via positron emission (\u03b2<sup>+<\/sup>) to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a>-68. When attached to targeting molecules like DOTA-TATE, gallium-68 is a premier agent for <b>Positron Emission Tomography (PET)<\/b> scanning, enabling high-resolution imaging of neuroendocrine tumors.<\/p><p>Gallium radioisotopes display clear decay patterns based on atomic mass:<\/p><p>Isotopes lighter than stable <sup>69<\/sup>Ga decay predominantly through positron emission (\u03b2<sup>+<\/sup>) or electron capture, converting into isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a><\/a>:<\/p><p style=\"text-align:center;\">\\( \\text{}^{n}_{31}\\text{Ga} + e^{-} \\rightarrow \\text{}^{n}_{30}\\text{Zn} + \\nu_e \\)<\/p><p>Isotopes heavier than stable <sup>71<\/sup>Ga decay primarily via beta-minus emission (\u03b2<sup>\u2212<\/sup>), turning into isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">germanium<\/a><\/a>:<\/p><p style=\"text-align:center;\">\\( \\text{}^{n}_{31}\\text{Ga} \\rightarrow \\text{}^{n}_{32}\\text{Ge} + e^{-} + \\bar{\\nu}_e \\)<\/p><p>Gallium-70 (half-life 21.1 minutes) is a fascinating crossover case that decays through both pathways\u2014either shedding an electron to form <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">germanium<\/a><\/a>-70 or capturing an electron to form <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a>-70.<\/p>", "History": poster=\"\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/thumb\/e\/e4\/Gallium_drops.ogv\/250px--Gallium_drops.ogv.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser\" controls=\"\" resource=\"\/wiki\/File:Gallium_drops.ogv\"><source src=\"\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/transcoded\/e\/e4\/Gallium_drops.ogv\/Gallium_drops.ogv.480p.vp9.webm\" type=\"video\/webm; vorbis&quot;\" data-width=\"1920\" data-height=\"1080\" \/><source src=\"\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/transcoded\/e\/e4\/Gallium_drops.ogv\/Gallium_drops.ogv.240p.vp9.webm\" type=\"video\/webm; codecs=&quot;vp9, opus&quot;\" data-transcodekey=\"240p.vp9.webm\" data-width=\"426\" data-height=\"240\" \/><\/video><\/span><figcaption>Small <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">gallium<\/a><\/a> droplets fusing together<\/figcaption><\/figure><p>The history of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">gallium<\/a> is one of the most famous scientific triumphs in the development of chemistry. In 1871, Russian chemist <b>Dmitri Mendeleev<\/b> created his landmark Periodic Table. Spotting an empty gap directly below <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Al\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Aluminium (Al)\">aluminium<\/a>, Mendeleev boldly predicted the existence of an undiscovered element he provisionally named <b>eka-aluminium<\/b> (symbol <i>Ea<\/i>, meaning 'one step beyond aluminium' in Sanskrit prefix terminology).<\/p><p>Mendeleev did not merely guess its existence\u2014he calculated its specific physical and chemical properties using the trend laws of his periodic table.
