Four years later, in 1875, French chemist <b>Paul-\u00c9mile Lecoq de Boisbaudran<\/b> discovered the element in a sample of sphalerite mineral from the Pyrenees using spectrographic analysis, recognizing its two characteristic violet emission lines. Later that year, Lecoq isolated pure metallic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">gallium<\/a> by electrolyzing gallium hydroxide dissolved in <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> hydroxide (KOH).<\/p><p>Mendeleev's predictions matched the actual properties of gallium with astonishing precision:<\/p><table class=\"wikitable\"><caption>Comparison between Mendeleev's 1871 predictions and actual properties of gallium<\/caption><tbody><tr><th>Property<\/th><th>Mendeleev's Prediction (1871)<\/th><th>Actual Properties<\/th><\/tr><tr><th>Atomic weight<\/th><td>~68<\/td><td>69.723<\/td><\/tr><tr><th>Density<\/th><td>5.9 g\/cm\u00b3<\/td><td>5.904 g\/cm\u00b3<\/td><\/tr><tr><th>Melting point<\/th><td>Low<\/td><td>29.767 \u00b0C<\/td><\/tr><tr><th>Formula of oxide<\/th><td>M<sub>2<\/sub>O<sub>3<\/sub><\/td><td>Ga<sub>2<\/sub>O<sub>3<\/sub><\/td><\/tr><tr><th>Density of oxide<\/th><td>5.5 g\/cm\u00b3<\/td><td>5.88 g\/cm\u00b3<\/td><\/tr><tr><th>Nature of hydroxide<\/th><td>Amphoteric<\/td><td>Amphoteric<\/td><\/tr><\/tbody><\/table><p>Remarkably, when Lecoq de Boisbaudran first measured the density of his new element as 4.7 g\/cm\u00b3, Mendeleev wrote him a letter suggesting he re-purify his sample and re-measure it. Upon doing so, de Boisbaudran obtained the correct value of 5.904 g\/cm\u00b3\u2014exactly as Mendeleev had calculated! This historic validation established the Periodic Law as a true predictive science.<\/p><p>Lecoq named the element <i>Gallia<\/i>, after Latin <i>Gallia<\/i> (meaning 'Gaul', the historical region of France). Contemporary chemists suspected a clever multilingual pun: <i>Le coq<\/i> is French for 'the rooster', and the Latin word for rooster is <i>gallus<\/i>! Although Lecoq publicly denied this in an 1877 article, the double meaning remains a famous piece of science folklore.<\/p><p><b>Ancient Indian Metallurgical Connections:<\/b> While isolated metallic gallium was unknown in antiquity due to its low concentration in ores, its host minerals\u2014sphalerite (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> sulfide) and bauxite clays\u2014were mined and processed in ancient India. In classical Indian alchemical texts like <i>Rasa Ratnakara<\/i> (authored by chemist Nagarjuna c. 9th\u201310th century CE) and <i>Rasa Ratna Samuccaya<\/i> (13th century CE), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> ores were classified under <i>Rasaka<\/i> and refined at <b>Zawar in Rajasthan<\/b> using revolutionary downward distillation furnaces (<i>tiryakpatana yantra<\/i>). Modern geochemical analyses of Zawar <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> tailings reveal trace concentrations of gallium, showing that gallium compounds passed through ancient Indian furnaces over 2,000 years ago as silent partners in early zinc extraction!<\/p><p><b>The Semiconductor & LED Revolution:<\/b> For nearly a century after its discovery, gallium was used primarily in high-temperature thermometers and low-melting alloys. The era of modern electronics transformed gallium in the 1960s with the synthesis of <b>Gallium Arsenide (GaAs)<\/b>, a compound semiconductor with superior electron speed compared to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a>. In the early 1990s, Japanese researchers Shuji Nakamura, Isamu Akasaki, and Hiroshi Amano developed high-brightness blue Light-Emitting Diodes (LEDs) using <b>Gallium Nitride (GaN)<\/b> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/In\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Indium (In)\">Indium<\/a> Gallium Nitride (InGaN), earning the <b>2014 Nobel Prize in Physics<\/b>. Today, blue GaN LEDs form the heart of energy-saving white LED lightbulbs worldwide.<\/p>", "Applications": "<ol><li><b>Semiconductors & Microchips (98% of world demand):<\/b> <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">Gallium<\/a> is dominated by compound semiconductors:<ul><li><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">Gallium<\/a> Arsenide (GaAs):<\/b> Features electron mobility up to six times faster than <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a><\/a>. GaAs integrated circuits power high-frequency radio-frequency (RF) power amplifiers in 5G smartphones, radar systems, satellite communications, and ultra-high-efficiency multi-junction solar panels used in space exploration.<\/li><li><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">Gallium<\/a> Nitride (GaN):<\/b> A wide-bandgap semiconductor capable of handling high power, extreme voltages, and high temperatures. GaN is replacing <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a> in electric vehicle (EV) fast chargers, 5G cellular base stations, high-performance power adapters, and blue\/ultraviolet laser diodes (used in Blu-ray players and optical projection).<\/li><\/ul><\/li><li><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Gd\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gadolinium (Gd)\">Gadolinium<\/a> Gallium Garnet (GGG):<\/b> Synthetic single-crystal GGG substrates are used in magneto-optical devices, bubble memory research, and specialized laser optics (~2% of market).<\/li><li><b>Liquid Metal Alloys & Galinstan:<\/b> Gallium forms non-toxic eutectic alloys with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/In\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Indium (In)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/In\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Indium (In)\">indium<\/a><\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tin (Sn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tin (Sn)\">tin<\/a><\/a>. The most famous is <b>Galinstan<\/b> (68.5% Ga, 21.5% In, 10% Sn), which remains liquid down to \u221219 \u00b0C (\u22122 \u00b0F). Galinstan has successfully replaced toxic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\">mercury<\/a><\/a> in medical thermometers, high-performance computer liquid cooling systems, flexible electronic circuits, and soft robotics.<\/li><li><b>Permanent Magnets & Solar Energy:<\/b> Adding trace amounts of gallium to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Nd\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neodymium (Nd)\">neodymium<\/a>-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/B\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Boron (B)\">boron<\/a> (NdFeB) permanent magnets enhances their thermal stability and coercivity in electric vehicle motors. Gallium is also a key component in CIGS (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a><\/a> <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/In\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Indium (In)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/In\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Indium (In)\">indium<\/a><\/a> gallium selenide) thin-film solar panels.<\/li><\/ol><p><b>India's Strategic Semiconductor Ecosystem (GAETEC & IISc):<\/b> India has designated gallium as a critical strategic mineral for defense, aerospace, and telecommunications self-reliance (<i>Atmanirbhar Bharat<\/i>):<\/p><ul><li><b>GAETEC (Gallium Arsenide Enabling Technology Centre), Hyderabad:<\/b> Established in 1996 as a specialized compound semiconductor foundry under DRDO\/SITAR, GAETEC manufactures indigenous GaAs Monolithic Microwave Integrated Circuits (MMICs) and High Electron Mobility Transistors (HEMTs). These components power India's defense AESA radars, electronic warfare platforms, missile seekers, and ISRO satellite missions (such as the radar imaging satellite EOS-04).<\/li><li><b>IISc CeNSE & GaN Semiconductor Hub:<\/b> At the <b>Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru<\/b>, researchers at the Centre for Nano Science and Engineering (<b>CeNSE<\/b>), in collaboration with DRDO's Solid State Physics Laboratory (<b>SSPL<\/b>, Delhi), established India's first sovereign <b>GaN-on-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">Silicon<\/a> and GaN-on-SiC semiconductor process foundry<\/b>. They developed India's first indigenous GaN power transistors (e-mode HEMTs). To bring this technology to market, IISc researchers launched deep-tech startup <b>AGNIT Semiconductors<\/b>, manufacturing commercial GaN components for 5G telecommunications, green energy electronics, and national defense radar systems.<\/li><\/ul>", "Biological role": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">Gallium<\/a> has no known natural biological role in humans, animals, plants, or microorganisms. Because elemental <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">gallium<\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">gallium<\/a> salts are not readily absorbed by the body, metallic gallium is low in toxicity and considered safe to handle in small quantities, though it leaves gray smudges on skin.<\/p><p><b>The \"Trojan Horse\" Mechanism in Medicine:<\/b> Trivalent gallium ions (Ga<sup>3+<\/sup>) possess an ionic radius (62 pm) and electrical charge nearly identical to ferric <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> ions (Fe<sup>3+<\/sup>, 64 pm). Because of this remarkable physical resemblance, biological transport mechanisms inside bacteria and rapidly dividing human cancer cells mistake Ga<sup>3+<\/sup> for Fe<sup>3+<\/sup> and actively absorb it.<\/p><p>However, unlike <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>, gallium cannot be reduced to a +2 oxidation state under physiological conditions. Once inside a cell, Ga<sup>3+<\/sup> substitutes for Fe<sup>3+<\/sup> in key metabolic enzymes (such as ribonucleotide reductase) but fails to carry out electron transfer reactions. This effectively shuts down cellular respiration, DNA replication, and protein synthesis\u2014acting like a cellular <b>Trojan Horse<\/b> that starves disease-causing bacteria and tumor cells of essential <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>!<\/p><p><b>Medical Therapies & Antimicrobial Research:<\/b><\/p><ul><li><b>Gallium Nitrate (Ganite):<\/b> An FDA-approved intravenous medication used to treat cancer-related hypercalcemia (dangerously elevated blood <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a> levels). It inhibits bone breakdown while stifling tumor growth.<\/li><li><b>Antimicrobial & Anti-biofilm Treatments:<\/b> Gallium compounds are actively researched as novel treatments for multidrug-resistant \"superbug\" infections (such as <i>Pseudomonas aeruginosa<\/i> in cystic fibrosis patients), where gallium disrupts bacterial iron uptake and destroys protective bacterial biofilms.<\/li><li><b>Nuclear Medicine Diagnostics:<\/b> Radiopharmaceuticals containing <sup>67<\/sup>Ga and <sup>68<\/sup>Ga play vital roles in hospital PET scans and diagnostic imaging worldwide.<\/li><\/ul>" } }, "Ge": { "symbol": "Ge", "name": "Germanium", "atomic": 32, "category": "metalloid", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">Germanium<\/a><\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>Ge<\/b>, atomic number <b>32<\/b>) is a lustrous, hard, grayish-white metalloid that sits in the <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> family of the periodic table, right between <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a><\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tin (Sn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tin (Sn)\">tin<\/a><\/a>. In its pure form, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">germanium<\/a> looks almost identical to shiny crystalline <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a>, behaving as a remarkable semiconductor that paved the way for modern electronics. While it was once the king of early transistors, today <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">germanium<\/a> plays a critical role in high-speed optical fiber communications, infrared night-vision technology, and ultra-efficient space solar panels. Though germanium does not naturally exist as a free metal, its history reaches from ancient <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> smelting techniques in India to outer space. Today, the Government of India classifies germanium as one of its 30 strategic <b>Critical Minerals<\/b> vital for high-tech self-reliance (<i>Atmanirbhar Bharat<\/i>), while Indian astronomers continue to uncover its cosmic origins in distant stars.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/0\/08\/Polycrystalline-germanium.jpg", "atomic_mass": 72.6308, "density": 5.323, "melt": 1211.4, "boil": 3106, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Clemens Winkler", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p2", "electronegativity_pauling": 2.01, "electron_affinity": 118.9352, "ionization_energies": [ 762, 1537.5, 3302.1, 4411, 9020 ], "sections": { "History": "<p>The story of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">germanium<\/a> is one of the most famous triumphs in the history of chemistry. In 1869, when Russian chemist <b>Dmitri Mendeleev<\/b> created his landmark periodic table, he noticed a gap in the <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> family between <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a><\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tin (Sn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tin (Sn)\">tin<\/a><\/a>. Confident in his periodic law, Mendeleev predicted that an undiscovered element existed to fill this spot. He named this missing element <i>ekasilicon<\/i> (meaning \"beyond <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a>,\" given the symbol Es) and calculated its atomic mass, density, and chemical behavior with astonishing accuracy.<\/p>\n<p>Sixteen years later, in mid-1885, miners working at the Himmelsf\u00fcrst mine near Freiberg, Saxony (in modern Germany) discovered an unusually <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ag\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silver (Ag)\">silver<\/a>-rich mineral named <b>argyrodite<\/b>. German chemist <b>Clemens Winkler<\/b> analyzed the ore in 1886 and realized it contained <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ag\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silver (Ag)\">silver<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a>, and an unknown element. Winkler initially considered naming his new discovery <i><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Np\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Neptunium (Np)\">neptunium<\/a><\/i> after the newly discovered planet Neptune (found mathematically in 1846). However, because that name had been briefly used for another proposed substance, he named it <b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">Germanium<\/a><\/b> (from <i>Germania<\/i>, the Latin name for Germany) to honor his homeland. Winkler analyzed 500 kilograms of argyrodite ore in 1887, isolating pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">germanium<\/a> tetrachloride (GeCl<sub>4<\/sub>) to measure its atomic mass at 72.32, which French chemist Paul-\u00c9mile Lecoq de Boisbaudran corroborated via spark spectroscopy at 72.3.<\/p>\n<p>Winkler synthesized key compounds including fluorides, chlorides, oxides (GeO<sub>2<\/sub>), sulfides, and tetraethylgermane (Ge(C<sub>2<\/sub>H<sub>5<\/sub>)<sub>4<\/sub>)\u2014the very first organogermane compound. When Winkler compared his measurements to Mendeleev's predictions from 1871, the results matched almost perfectly, providing overwhelming proof for Mendeleev's periodic law:<\/p>\n<div style=\"margin: 10px auto; overflow-x: auto;\">\n<table class=\"wikitable\">\n<caption>Comparison between Mendeleev's 1871 Predictions and Winkler's 1887 Discovery<\/caption><tbody>\n<tr><th>Property<\/th><th>Mendeleev's Prediction (1871)<\/th><th>Winkler's Actual Measurement (1887)<\/th><\/tr>\n<tr><td>Atomic Mass<\/td><td>72.64<\/td><td>72.63<\/td><\/tr>\n<tr><td>Density<\/td><td>5.5 g\/cm<sup>3<\/sup><\/td><td>5.35 g\/cm<sup>3<\/sup><\/td><\/tr>\n<tr><td>Melting Point<\/td><td>High<\/td><td>947 \u00b0C<\/td><\/tr>\n<tr><td>Color<\/td><td>Gray<\/td><td>Gray<\/td><\/tr>\n<tr><td>Oxide Type<\/td><td>Refractory dioxide<\/td><td>Refractory dioxide (GeO<sub>2<\/sub>)<\/td><\/tr>\n<tr><td>Oxide Density<\/td><td>4.7 g\/cm<sup>3<\/sup><\/td><td>4.7 g\/cm<sup>3<\/sup><\/td><\/tr>\n<tr><td>Oxide Character<\/td><td>Feebly basic<\/td><td>Feebly basic<\/td><\/tr>\n<tr><td>Chloride Boiling Point<\/td><td>Under 100 \u00b0C<\/td><td>86 \u00b0C (GeCl<sub>4<\/sub>)<\/td><\/tr>\n<tr><td>Chloride Density<\/td><td>1.9 g\/cm<sup>3<\/sup><\/td><td>1.9 g\/cm<sup>3<\/sup><\/td><\/tr>\n<\/tbody>\n<\/table>\n<\/div>\n<p>For decades after its discovery, germanium remained a scientific curiosity produced in tiny quantities of only a few hundred kilograms per year. That changed dramatically during World War II, when germanium point-contact Schottky diodes were developed for radar pulse detection. Then in 1948, the invention of the <b>germanium transistor<\/b> revolutionized technology, igniting the solid-state electronics era. World production skyrocketed to 40 metric tons by the late 1950s, and the first <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a>-germanium (Si-Ge) alloys were created in 1955.<\/p>\n<p>Between 1950 and the early 1970s, germanium dominated electronics. However, as semiconductor refining advanced, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a> gradually replaced germanium in transistors and microchips\u2014a transition spearheaded by companies like Fairchild Semiconductor (founded in 1957). Silicon was far more abundant in common sand and quartz, making it drastically cheaper ($10 per kg in 1998 compared to $800 per kg for germanium). Nevertheless, demand for germanium rebounded in the late 20th century for fiber optics, infrared night vision, and solar power. In 1987, the U.S. designated germanium a strategic national defense stockpile material.<\/p>\n<p>India shares a rich historical connection with germanium's host ores and modern strategic relevance. Long before western chemistry isolated the element, ancient Indian metallurgists pioneered high-temperature <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> distillation at <b>Zawar, Rajasthan<\/b> over 2,000 years ago\u2014the world's oldest known industrial <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> smelting site. The <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> blende (sphalerite) processed at Zawar naturally contained trace amounts of germanium! In the 21st century, recognizing germanium's strategic role in defense optics and microelectronics, India's Ministry of Mines officially declared germanium as one of its <b>30 Critical Minerals<\/b> essential for national security and technological self-reliance under the <i>Atmanirbhar Bharat<\/i> initiative.<\/p>", "Characteristics": "<p>Under room temperature and standard atmospheric pressure, pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">germanium<\/a> is a hard, brittle, lustrous metalloid with a distinctive grayish-white metallic sheen. It crystallizes in a face-centered diamond cubic structure\u2014the exact same crystal structure found in <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a><\/a> and diamond\u2014known as <b>\u03b1-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">germanium<\/a><\/b>. In this form, it exhibits a threshold displacement energy of 19.7 (+0.6\/-0.5) eV. Under intense hydrostatic pressure exceeding 120 kilobars (nearly 120,000 times atmospheric pressure), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">germanium<\/a> undergoes a dramatic structural transition into a metallic allotrope called <b>\u03b2-germanium<\/b>, which mirrors the crystal structure of \u03b2-<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tin (Sn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tin (Sn)\">tin<\/a><\/a>.<\/p>\n<p>One of germanium's most remarkable physical quirks is that it expands as it freezes! When liquid germanium solidifies from a molten state at its melting point of 1,211.4 K (938.25 \u00b0C), its volume expands\u2014a rare trait shared by only a handful of substances, including water, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">gallium<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Bi\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Bismuth (Bi)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Bi\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Bismuth (Bi)\">bismuth<\/a><\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Antimony (Sb)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Antimony (Sb)\">antimony<\/a><\/a>.<\/p>\n<p>Electrically, pure germanium is an indirect bandgap semiconductor. Thanks to ultra-precise metallurgical techniques known as <b>zone refining<\/b>\u2014where a narrow molten zone moves slowly along an ingot to sweep away impurities\u2014scientists can produce crystalline germanium with an impurity level of just 1 part in 10<sup>10<\/sup> (one atom of impurity per 10 billion germanium atoms). This makes hyper-pure germanium one of the purest materials ever created by humankind. In 2005, scientists discovered that a semi-metallic alloy of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/U\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Uranium (U)\">uranium<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Rh\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Rhodium (Rh)\">rhodium<\/a>, and germanium (U-Rh-Ge) becomes a superconductor in the presence of extremely powerful electromagnetic fields.<\/p>\n<p>However, pure germanium possesses a curious defect mechanism: under certain conditions, it spontaneously extrudes tiny, elongated single-crystal filaments known as <b>germanium whiskers<\/b>. In early electronic components, these microscopic whiskers could bridge electrical gaps and touch adjacent circuits, causing mysterious short circuits and device failures.<\/p>\n<p>Modern Indian scientific institutions are at the forefront of researching germanium's advanced characteristics. Researchers at the <b>Indian Institute of Science (IISc, Bengaluru)<\/b> Centre for Nano Science and Engineering (CeNSE), the <b>Indian Institutes of Technology (IIT Bombay, IIT Delhi)<\/b>, and the <b>Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC)<\/b> Technical Physics Division are investigating <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">Silicon<\/a>-Germanium (SiGe) heterostructures. By straining SiGe crystal layers, Indian scientists enhance electron and hole mobility, enabling ultra-fast microprocessors, high-frequency radio-frequency (RF) communication chips, and emerging spin-qubit quantum computing processors.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Natural <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">germanium<\/a> found on Earth is composed of five stable and long-lived isotopes: <sup>70<\/sup>Ge, <sup>72<\/sup>Ge, <sup>73<\/sup>Ge, <sup>74<\/sup>Ge, and <sup>76<\/sup>Ge. Among these, <b><sup>74<\/sup>Ge<\/b> is the most abundant, making up about 36.52% of all natural <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">germanium<\/a>. It is followed by <sup>72<\/sup>Ge (27.45%), <sup>70<\/sup>Ge (20.57%), <sup>73<\/sup>Ge (7.76%), and <sup>76<\/sup>Ge, which is the least abundant natural isotope at 7.75%.<\/p>\n<p>While four of these isotopes are completely stable, <b><sup>76<\/sup>Ge<\/b> is slightly radioactive. It undergoes a rare nuclear decay process called double beta decay, emitting two electrons and two antineutrinos to transform into stable <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">selenium<\/a>-76. Because this decay is extremely improbable, <sup>76<\/sup>Ge has an astounding half-life of 2.02 \u00d7 10<sup>21<\/sup> years\u2014a timeframe more than 100 billion times longer than the age of the universe!<\/p>\n<p>Beyond these five natural forms, nuclear physicists have synthesized at least 27 artificial radioactive isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">germanium<\/a>, with atomic masses ranging from 58 to 89. The most stable synthetic radioisotope is <b><sup>68<\/sup>Ge<\/b>, which decays by electron capture with a half-life of 270.95 days into <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">gallium<\/a>-68 (a vital radioisotope used in medical PET scans). The second longest-lived is <b><sup>71<\/sup>Ge<\/b>, which also decays via electron capture with a half-life of 11.468 days. All other synthetic germanium isotopes have half-lives shorter than two days, and most vanish in under two hours.<\/p>\n<p>High-purity isotopic germanium plays a crucial role in cutting-edge Indian and international research. Indian nuclear physicists at institutions like BARC and the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) utilize detectors enriched with <sup>76<\/sup>Ge for deep underground experiments searching for neutrinoless double beta decay\u2014a groundbreaking phenomenon that could explain why matter dominates antimatter in our universe. Furthermore, Indian material scientists explore isotopically pure germanium to minimize lattice thermal vibrations (phonons), improving heat dissipation in next-generation microchips.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>In the cosmos, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">germanium<\/a> is forged deep inside evolving stars through stellar nucleosynthesis. It is produced primarily via the <b>s-process<\/b> (slow neutron capture), where lighter atomic nuclei inside pulsating red giant stars slowly absorb neutrons over thousands of years. Spectroscopic observations have detected <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">germanium<\/a> in distant stars across our galaxy as well as in the atmosphere of Jupiter.<\/p>\n<p>In June 2025, astronomers from the <b>Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA), Bengaluru<\/b> made a groundbreaking astronomical discovery using the 2-meter Himalayan Chandra Telescope (HCT) situated high in the Himalayas at Hanle, Ladakh. Led by researcher Ajay Kumar Saini and Professor Gajendra Pandey, the team used the Hanle Echelle Spectrograph (HESP) to capture the first-ever spectrum of singly-ionized <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">germanium<\/a> (Ge II) in a rare Extreme <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/He\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Helium (He)\">Helium<\/a> (EHe) star named <b>A980<\/b>, located 25,800 light-years away in the constellation Ophiuchus. Remarkably, they discovered that germanium levels in star A980 were <b>eight times higher<\/b> than in our Sun! This extraordinary discovery provided direct observational evidence that the star formed from the merger of two white dwarf stars, shedding new light on cosmic nucleosynthesis.<\/p>\n<p>On Earth, germanium is relatively rare, making up approximately 1.6 parts per million (ppm) of the Earth's crust\u2014ranking as the 34th most abundant element. It is roughly as common as <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Co\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cobalt (Co)\">cobalt<\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Nb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Niobium (Nb)\">niobium<\/a>, but unlike those metals, germanium rarely forms concentrated mineral deposits of its own. Rare germanium-bearing minerals include <b>argyrodite<\/b> (Ag<sub>8<\/sub>GeS<sub>6<\/sub>), <b>briartite<\/b>, <b>germanite<\/b>, and <b>renierite<\/b>, but only germanite is ever found in mineable quantities.<\/p>\n<p>Instead of dedicated mines, commercial germanium is recovered almost exclusively as a by-product during the industrial smelting of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a> ores (specifically from <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a> blende, or sphalerite). Additionally, an unusual geochemical process causes germanium to accumulate in certain coal seams\u2014a phenomenon first discovered by geochemist Victor Moritz Goldschmidt. For instance, Hartley coal ash in England contains up to 1.6% germanium, and massive coal deposits in Xilinhaote, Inner Mongolia hold an estimated 1,600 tonnes of germanium.<\/p>\n<p>Because India currently has no active commercial germanium mines and imports 100% of its supply, domestic institutions are aggressively exploring sustainable recovery methods. Scientists at India's <b>National Metallurgical Laboratory (NML)<\/b> and industrial giants like <b>Hindustan <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">Zinc<\/a><\/b> are researching hydrometallurgical techniques to extract trace germanium from zinc oxide smelting flue dust and coal fly ash generated by thermal power plants, supported by government initiatives under <b>KABIL<\/b> (Khanij Bidesh India Ltd) and the Geological Survey of India (GSI).<\/p>", "Applications": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">Germanium<\/a>'s unique optical and electronic properties make it indispensable for modern technology. According to global consumption data, its applications are distributed across key high-tech industries:<\/p>\n<div class=\"pie-thumb thumb tright\"><div class=\"thumbinner\"><div class=\"smooth-pie-container\" style=\"\">\n<div class=\"smooth-pie-legend-container\"><div class=\"smooth-pie-caption\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">Germanium<\/a><\/a> Usage Breakdown (2023)<\/div>\n<ol class=\"smooth-pie-legend\">\n<li><span class=\"l-color\" style=\"-webkit-print-color-adjust: exact; print-color-adjust: exact;background:#0b88d4;color:#000\"><\/span><span class=\"l-label\">Fiber Optics (26.0%)<\/span><\/li>\n<li><span class=\"l-color\" style=\"-webkit-print-color-adjust: exact; print-color-adjust: exact;background:#0b6d3a;color:#000\"><\/span><span class=\"l-label\">Infrared Optics (22.0%)<\/span><\/li>\n<li><span class=\"l-color\" style=\"-webkit-print-color-adjust: exact; print-color-adjust: exact;background:#0a4777;color:#000\"><\/span><span class=\"l-label\">PET Catalyst (20.0%)<\/span><\/li>\n<li><span class=\"l-color\" style=\"-webkit-print-color-adjust: exact; print-color-adjust: exact;background:#7fba39;color:#000\"><\/span><span class=\"l-label\">Electronics (12.0%)<\/span><\/li>\n<li><span class=\"l-color\" style=\"-webkit-print-color-adjust: exact; print-color-adjust: exact;background:#c8b89b;color:#000\"><\/span><span class=\"l-label\">Solar Power (10.0%)<\/span><\/li>\n<li><span class=\"l-color\" style=\"-webkit-print-color-adjust: exact; print-color-adjust: exact;background:#48c1b5;color:#000\"><\/span><span class=\"l-label\">Gamma-Ray Detectors (5.0%)<\/span><\/li>\n<li><span class=\"l-color\" style=\"-webkit-print-color-adjust: exact; print-color-adjust: exact;background:#cfd2d4;color:#000\"><\/span><span class=\"l-label\">Other Uses (5.0%)<\/span><\/li>\n<\/ol>\n<\/div>\n<\/div><\/div><\/div>\n<p><b>Fiber Optic Communications (26%):<\/b> <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">Germanium<\/a> dioxide (GeO<sub>2<\/sub>) is added as a dopant to the glass core of optical fiber cables. This increases the core's refractive index, enabling light signals to bounce cleanly inside the cable via total internal reflection without signal degradation. In India, germanium-doped fiber optic cables form the backbone of the nation's 5G telecom expansion and the <b>BharatNet project<\/b>, bringing high-speed broadband internet to hundreds of thousands of rural villages.<\/p>\n<p><b>Infrared Optics & Defense (22%):<\/b> Unlike ordinary glass, germanium metal is completely transparent to long-wave infrared light (8 to 14 micrometers). It can be polished into lenses and windows for thermal imaging cameras, night-vision sights, and missile guidance systems. The <b>Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO)<\/b> and Indian defense manufacturers rely heavily on germanium optics for thermal imaging units used by the Indian Armed Forces. To bypass supply dependencies, Indian defense researchers are also innovating germanium-free thermal imaging sensors for military drones.<\/p>\n<p><b>PET Polymerization Catalysts (20%):<\/b> Germanium dioxide serves as a premier catalyst in producing polyethylene terephthalate (PET) plastic. PET synthesized with germanium catalysts boasts exceptional clarity and brilliance, making it highly favored for food-grade plastic bottles, synthetic polyester textiles, and optical films.<\/p>\n<p><b>Electronics & Microchips (12%):<\/b> While <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a> dominates standard computer chips, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">Silicon<\/a>-Germanium (SiGe) alloys are essential for ultra-high-speed integrated circuits. SiGe transistors operate at microwave and millimeter-wave frequencies, powering wireless communications, automotive radar, and satellite transceivers.<\/p>\n<p><b>Space Solar Energy (10%):<\/b> Multi-junction solar cells built on germanium crystal wafers offer highest energy conversion efficiency (>30%). These solar panels power space satellites, deep-space probes, and missions developed by the <b>Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)<\/b>.<\/p>\n<p><b>Radiation Detectors & Other Uses (10%):<\/b> High-Purity Germanium (HPGe) single crystals serve as the <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\">gold<\/a> standard for gamma-ray spectroscopy detectors used in nuclear power stations, radiation monitoring, and airport security. Smaller applications include chemotherapy research (such as spirogermanium), metallurgy alloys, and phosphors for fluorescent lighting.<\/p>" } }, "As": { "symbol": "As", "name": "Arsenic", "atomic": 33, "category": "metalloid", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">Arsenic<\/a><\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>As<\/b>, atomic number 33) is a versatile metalloid positioned in Group 15 of the periodic table, right beneath <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a><\/a>. Infamous throughout history as the \"king of poisons\" and the \"inheritance powder,\" <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">arsenic<\/a> displays a dark, double-edged personality: while its volatile compounds were once the covert weapon of Renaissance poisoners, its crystalline forms are essential for modern high-speed microchips and life-saving leukemia treatments. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">Arsenic<\/a> exists in several distinct forms (allotropes), most notably a brittle, metallic steel-grey crystal that sublimates directly into gas when heated. Arsenic holds profound historical and contemporary significance in India: ancient Ayurvedic scholars cataloged its mineral ores\u2014<b>Haritala<\/b> (yellow orpiment) and <b>Manashila<\/b> (red realgar)\u2014in texts like the <i>Rasa Ratna Samuccaya<\/i>, developing sophisticated multi-step purification (<i>Shodhana<\/i>) methods to turn these toxic minerals into therapeutic medicines. In modern times, while geogenic arsenic leaching into the shallow tubewells of the Ganga-Brahmaputra alluvial plain presents a major public health challenge, pioneering Indian scientists\u2014such as <b>Prof. T. Pradeep<\/b> of IIT Madras with his award-winning <b>AMRIT<\/b> filter and researchers at CSIR-CGCRI\u2014have developed world-leading nanotechnology and ceramic membrane filtration systems to bring safe drinking water to millions of affected citizens.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/3\/3b\/Arsenic_%2833_As%29.jpg", "atomic_mass": 74.9215956, "density": 5.727, "melt": null, "boil": null, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Bronze Age", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p3", "electronegativity_pauling": 2.18, "electron_affinity": 77.65, "ionization_energies": [ 947, 1798, 2735, 4837, 6043, 12310 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-left\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/3b87ee37111120b5516225ea62790257.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"230\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"400\" data-file-height=\"368\" \/><figcaption>Metallic grey <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">arsenic<\/a><\/a> crystal<\/figcaption><\/figure><p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">Arsenic<\/a><\/a><\/b> is a chemical element classified as a metalloid\u2014an element that exhibits physical and chemical properties intermediate between true metals and non-metals. Positioned in Group 15 (the pnictogens) directly below <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a><\/a> and above <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Antimony (Sb)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Antimony (Sb)\">antimony<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">arsenic<\/a> shares structural and chemical similarities with both of its periodic neighbors.<\/p><p>Arsenic occurs in three major elemental allotropes (different structural forms of the same element):<\/p><ul><li><b>Grey Metallic Arsenic:<\/b> The most common, stable, and chemically reactive allotrope at ambient conditions. It forms a brittle, steel-grey crystalline solid with a density of 5.727 g\/cm\u00b3. Its crystal structure consists of layered rhombohedral sheets of six-membered rings. Because its electrons can move across these sheets, grey metallic arsenic conducts electricity moderately well, though not as efficiently as true metals like <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a><\/a> or <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ag\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silver (Ag)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ag\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silver (Ag)\">silver<\/a><\/a>.<\/li><li><b>Yellow Arsenic:<\/b> A soft, waxy molecular solid created by rapidly cooling arsenic vapor. Composed of tetrahedral \\(\\text{As}_4\\) units held together by weak van der Waals forces (analogous to white <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a>), yellow arsenic has a low density of 1.97 g\/cm\u00b3. It is volatile, extraordinarily toxic, and light-sensitive\u2014exposing yellow arsenic to room light causes it to rapidly transform back into grey arsenic.<\/li><li><b>Black Arsenic:<\/b> An amorphous form structurally similar to black <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/P\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Phosphorus (P)\">phosphorus<\/a>, synthesized by condensing arsenic vapor onto surfaces kept between 100 \u00b0C and 280 \u00b0C. It is glassy, brittle, and a poor electrical conductor.<\/li><\/ul><p>An extraordinary physical property of arsenic is its behavior when heated under normal atmospheric pressure. Unlike most elements, solid arsenic does not melt when heated at 1 atm; instead, it undergoes <b>sublimation<\/b>, transforming directly from a solid into a dense, yellowish gas at 615 \u00b0C (888 K or 1,139 \u00b0F). Arsenic can only be forced to melt into a liquid state under high pressure (28 atmospheres), reaching its liquid melting point at 817 \u00b0C (1,090 K).<\/p><p>Chemically, arsenic exhibits principal oxidation states of <b>\u22123<\/b>, <b>+3<\/b>, and <b>+5<\/b>. When heated in open air, arsenic burns with a faint bluish flame, producing toxic white clouds of arsenic trioxide (\\(\\text{As}_2\\text{O}_3\\)) accompanied by a characteristic garlic-like odor:<\/p><p style=\"text-align:center;\">\\( 4\\text{As} + 3\\text{O}_2 \\rightarrow 2\\text{As}_2\\text{O}_3 \\)<\/p><p>Arsenic trioxide is weakly acidic (amphoteric), dissolving in water to form arsenious acid (\\(\\text{H}_3\\text{AsO}_3\\)). Arsenic reacts readily with halogens to form trihalides and pentahalides, such as arsenic pentafluoride (\\(\\text{AsF}_5\\)), and reacts with electropositive metals to form binary compounds called arsenides (such as <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">gallium<\/a> arsenide, \\(\\text{GaAs}\\)).<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">Main article: Isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">arsenic<\/a><\/a><\/div><p>Naturally occurring <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">arsenic<\/a><\/a> is a monoisotopic element, consisting entirely of a single stable isotope: <b><sup>75<\/sup>As<\/b> (100% natural abundance). Because it has only one stable nuclide, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">arsenic<\/a> is also classified as a mononuclidic element, which allows its standard atomic weight to be determined with extreme precision (74.9215956 u).<\/p><p>Nuclear physicists have synthesized 32 radioactive isotopes of arsenic, spanning atomic mass numbers from <sup>64<\/sup>As up to <sup>95<\/sup>As, along with at least 11 metastable nuclear isomers. Most of these synthetic radioisotopes are highly unstable, with half-lives measuring under 100 minutes, and many decaying in less than a single minute.<\/p><p>Among the radioactive isotopes, the longest-lived and most scientifically notable include:<\/p><ul><li><b><sup>73<\/sup>As:<\/b> Half-life of 80.30 days (decays via electron capture to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">germanium<\/a>-73).<\/li><li><b><sup>74<\/sup>As:<\/b> Half-life of 17.77 days.<\/li><li><b><sup>71<\/sup>As:<\/b> Half-life of 65.30 hours.<\/li><li><b><sup>77<\/sup>As:<\/b> Half-life of 38.79 hours.<\/li><li><b><sup>76<\/sup>As:<\/b> Half-life of 26.24 hours.<\/li><li><b><sup>72<\/sup>As:<\/b> Half-life of 26.0 hours.<\/li><\/ul><p>The radioactive decay pathways of arsenic radioisotopes follow distinct patterns determined by their atomic mass relative to stable <sup>75<\/sup>As:<\/p><p>Isotopes lighter than stable <sup>75<\/sup>As decay primarily via <b>positron emission (\u03b2<sup>+<\/sup>)<\/b> or <b>electron capture<\/b> to form stable or long-lived isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">germanium<\/a><\/a>:<\/p><p style=\"text-align:center;\">\\( \\text{}^{n}_{33}\\text{As} + e^{-} \\rightarrow \\text{}^{n}_{32}\\text{Ge} + \\nu_e \\)<\/p><p>Isotopes heavier than stable <sup>75<\/sup>As decay primarily via <b>beta-minus emission (\u03b2<sup>\u2212<\/sup>)<\/b>, transforming into isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">selenium<\/a><\/a>:<\/p><p style=\"text-align:center;\">\\( \\text{}^{n}_{33}\\text{As} \\rightarrow \\text{}^{n}_{34}\\text{Se} + e^{-} + \\bar{\\nu}_e \\)<\/p><p>A fascinating nuclear exception is <b><sup>74<\/sup>As<\/b>, which undergoes dual decay pathways! It decays simultaneously by electron capture (66%) into <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ge\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Germanium (Ge)\">germanium<\/a>-74 and by beta-minus emission (34%) into <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">selenium<\/a>-74. Because of its positron-emitting properties, <sup>74<\/sup>As and <sup>72<\/sup>As have been utilized in medical physics as positron emitters for Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scanning to locate and map tumor growth in human tissue.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-left\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/832cf4ba22be943345fbeae61306e529.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"147\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"340\" data-file-height=\"200\" \/><figcaption>Vibrant red realgar (As<sub>4<\/sub>S<sub>4<\/sub>) crystal<\/figcaption><\/figure><figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-left\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/4593131df3d024fd9c8e5d0abded2a60.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"179\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"640\" data-file-height=\"458\" \/><figcaption>The historical <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">arsenic<\/a> labyrinth at Botallack Mine, Cornwall<\/figcaption><\/figure><p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">Arsenic<\/a><\/a><\/b> is the 53rd most abundant element in Earth's crust, with an average background concentration of roughly 1.5 to 1.8 parts per million (ppm). Native elemental <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">arsenic<\/a> crystals occur in nature, but they are exceptionally rare. Instead, arsenic is geochemically classified as a <i>chalcophile<\/i> element, meaning it has a strong affinity for binding with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a><\/a> and heavy metals in hydrothermal ore veins.<\/p><p>Arsenic is found in over 500 distinct mineral species. The most abundant commercial arsenic minerals include:<\/p><ul><li><b>Arsenopyrite (FeAsS):<\/b> Also known as mispickel, a steel-grey to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ag\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silver (Ag)\">silver<\/a> <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> arsenic sulfide mineral that serves as the world's chief commercial source of arsenic.<\/li><li><b>Realgar (As<sub>4<\/sub>S<sub>4<\/sub> or AsS):<\/b> A striking, ruby-red to orange-red arsenic disulfide mineral.<\/li><li><b>Orpiment (As<sub>2<\/sub>S<sub>3<\/sub>):<\/b> A brilliant, canary-yellow arsenic trisulfide mineral with a pearly luster.<\/li><li><b>Arsenolite and Claudetite (As<sub>2<\/sub>O<sub>3<\/sub>):<\/b> Secondary natural oxide minerals formed by the weathering of arsenic sulfides.<\/li><li><b>Enargite (Cu<sub>3<\/sub>AsS<sub>4<\/sub>) and Tennantite:<\/b> Important <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a>-arsenic minerals mined primarily for <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a> extraction.<\/li><\/ul><p>Most industrial arsenic is not mined directly, but is recovered as a byproduct during the roasting and smelting of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\">gold<\/a><\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Zn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Zinc (Zn)\">zinc<\/a><\/a> ores. Major global producers of arsenic trioxide include China, Morocco, Russia, and Chile.<\/p><p><b>Geographical &amp; Hydro-Geological Context in India:<\/b> In India, arsenic presents a profound geographical and environmental story. The vast <b>Ganga-Brahmaputra alluvial plains<\/b>\u2014spanning West Bengal, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand, and Assam\u2014contain deep layers of river sediments eroded over millions of years from the Himalayan mountains. These sediments naturally contain trace amounts of arsenopyrite and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> oxides.<\/p><p>Under anaerobic (reducing) underground conditions in shallow alluvial aquifers, naturally occurring micro-organisms metabolize organic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> and dissolve <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> oxy-hydroxides. This natural biogeochemical process releases inorganic arsenic ions (toxic arsenite \\(\\text{As}^{3+}\\) and arsenate \\(\\text{As}^{5+}\\)) directly into shallow groundwater. As a result, millions of shallow tubewells drilled across rural West Bengal (such as in Murshidabad, Nadia, North and South 24 Parganas) and neighboring states draw groundwater with arsenic levels exceeding the World Health Organization (WHO) safety limit of 10 ppb (10 \u03bcg\/L), creating one of the largest geogenic water quality challenges in human history.<\/p>", "History": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-left\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/8d827f8f3782b2b722dcf109a28da7df.png\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"90\" height=\"90\" style=\"--mw-file-upright: 0.35\" class=\"mw-file-element mw-file-upright\" data-file-width=\"16\" data-file-height=\"16\" \/><figcaption>Alchemical symbol for <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">arsenic<\/a><\/a><\/figcaption><\/figure><p>The name <i><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">arsenic<\/a><\/a><\/i> traces a rich linguistic journey across ancient languages. It originated from the Syriac word <i>zarnika<\/i> and the Arabic <i>al-zarn\u012bkh<\/i> (meaning \"the orpiment\"), rooted in the ancient Persian word <i>zar<\/i> (\"<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\">gold<\/a>\") and <i>zarnikh<\/i> (\"yellow\" or \"<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\">gold<\/a>-colored\"). The Greeks adopted the word as <i>arsenikon<\/i> (\u1f00\u03c1\u03c3\u03b5\u03bd\u03b9\u03ba\u03cc\u03bd), playfully connecting it via folk etymology to the Greek adjective <i>arsenikos<\/i> (\u1f00\u03c1\u03c3\u03b5\u03bd\u03b9\u03ba\u03cc\u03c2), meaning \"male\" or \"virile,\" due to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">arsenic<\/a>'s potent chemical reactivity. This entered Latin as <i>arsenicum<\/i>, evolved into Old French <i>arsenic<\/i>, and entered the English language as <i>arsenic<\/i>.<\/p><p>Arsenic minerals were used by ancient civilizations thousands of years ago. During the Bronze Age, ancient smiths melted arsenic minerals together with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a><\/a> to forge <b>arsenical bronze<\/b>\u2014an alloy harder and easier to cast than pure <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a>, widely used before <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tin (Sn)\">tin<\/a> bronze became dominant.<\/p><p><b>Ancient Indian History &amp; Rasashastra Knowledge:<\/b> In ancient India, arsenic minerals played a central role in <b>Ayurveda<\/b> and the specialized alchemical discipline of <b>Rasashastra<\/b> (iatrochemistry or mineral-based medicine), which developed between the 1st millennium BCE and the 12th century CE. Classical texts such as the <i>Charaka Samhita<\/i>, <i>Sushruta Samhita<\/i>, <i>Rasa Ratna Samuccaya<\/i> (by Vagbhata), <i>Rasarnava<\/i>, and <i>Rasa Hridaya Tantra<\/i> cataloged three primary arsenic minerals:<\/p><ul><li><b>Haritala (Orpiment, As<sub>2<\/sub>S<sub>3<\/sub>):<\/b> A golden-yellow mineral classified as an <i>Uparasa<\/i> (secondary mineral). Ancient scholars recognized two varieties: <i>Patra Haritala<\/i> (foliated or layered, highly prized) and <i>Pinda Haritala<\/i> (lumpy).<\/li><li><b>Manashila (Realgar, As<sub>4<\/sub>S<sub>4<\/sub>):<\/b> A vivid red to orange-red mineral, valued in traditional formulations for treating respiratory conditions, asthma, and chronic skin disorders.<\/li><li><b>Somala or Gauripashana (White Arsenic, As<sub>2<\/sub>O<sub>3<\/sub>):<\/b> Arsenic trioxide, recognized as extraordinarily potent and toxic.<\/li><\/ul><p>Because raw arsenic compounds are inherently toxic, Rasashastra scholars developed sophisticated pharmaceutical protocols known as <b>Shodhana<\/b> (purification and detoxification). Minerals like <i>Haritala<\/i> were wrapped in cloth and suspended in specialized boiling apparatuses called <b>Dolayantra<\/b>, where they were detoxified by steaming them in herbal media such as <i>Kushmanda<\/i> (ash gourd) juice, lime water, or plant decoctions. This was followed by <b>Marana<\/b> (calcination), where the purified mineral was ground with herbal extracts and roasted in sealed clay retorts (<i>Puta<\/i>) to create bio-compatible micro-crystalline ashes known as <b>Haritala Bhasma<\/b> and <b>Manashila Bhasma<\/b>. These <i>Rasaushadhis<\/i> were meticulously prepared for treating severe skin ailments (like psoriasis), stubborn fevers, and pulmonary conditions, serving the twin alchemical goals of <i>Dhatuvada<\/i> (transmutation of metals) and <i>Dehavada<\/i> (body rejuvenation and longevity).<\/p><p><b>Greco-Egyptian &amp; Islamic Alchemy:<\/b> In the Western world, Greco-Egyptian alchemist Zosimos of Panopolis (c. 300 AD) described roasting <i>sandarach<\/i> (realgar) to produce \"cloud of arsenic\" (arsenic trioxide), which he reduced to grey metallic arsenic. Islamic polymath <b>Jabir ibn Hayyan<\/b> (Geber) described isolating arsenic prior to 815 AD. Later in Europe, Albertus Magnus (Albert the Great, 1193\u20131280) isolated elemental arsenic in 1250 by heating soap together with arsenic trisulfide. In 1649, German chemist Johann Schr\u00f6der published two reliable methods for isolating pure arsenic metal.<\/p><p><b>The \"King of Poisons\" &amp; Forensic Science:<\/b> Because arsenic trioxide is odorless, tasteless, and easily mixed into food or drink, producing symptoms that mimicked natural intestinal illnesses (like cholera), it became the secret weapon of choice for political assassinations and family poisonings during the Renaissance. It earned nicknames such as the \"poison of kings,\" the \"king of poisons,\" and \"inheritance powder.\" This reign of undetected murder came to an abrupt end in 1836 when English chemist James Marsh invented the <b>Marsh test<\/b>\u2014a highly sensitive chemical procedure capable of detecting microscopic traces of arsenic in human tissue. (Another sensitive technique, the Reinsch test, was introduced shortly after.)<\/p><p><b>18th to 20th Century Uses &amp; Pigments:<\/b> In 1760, French chemist Louis Claude Cadet de Gassicourt synthesized <i>Cadet's fuming liquid<\/i> (impure cacodyl) by reacting <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a><\/a> acetate with arsenic trioxide\u2014widely considered the very first synthetic organometallic compound in chemical history!<\/p><p>During the 18th and 19th centuries, arsenic compounds entered everyday life in bizarre ways. Victorian women consumed \"white arsenic\" mixed with vinegar and chalk to produce a fashionable pale complexion. In 1858, accidental food adulteration with arsenic led to the tragic Bradford sweet poisoning in England, resulting in 21 deaths. Brilliant green arsenic pigments\u2014such as <b>Scheele's Green<\/b> (<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a> arsenite, invented in 1775 by Carl Wilhelm Scheele) and <b>Paris Green<\/b> (copper acetoarsenite, 1814)\u2014became immensely popular in dyed clothing, toys, and printed floral wallpapers. Historians suggest that damp wallpaper releasing toxic arsenic gas (trimethylarsine) contributed to Napoleon Bonaparte's illness and death on Saint Helena in 1821!<\/p><p>In the 1860s, an industrial byproduct called <b>London Purple<\/b> (a mixture of arsenic trioxide, aniline, lime, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> oxide) was used as an agricultural insecticide, later superseded by Paris Green, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a> arsenate, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a> arsenite, which dominated farming until DDT was discovered in 1942.<\/p><p>In medicine, small diluted doses of arsenic were prescribed as general tonics. <b>Fowler's Solution<\/b> (1% <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/K\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Potassium (K)\">potassium<\/a> arsenite solution) was widely used from 1786 into the mid-20th century to treat skin diseases, anemia, and even performance issues in racehorses and work dogs. In 1932, the legendary Australian racehorse <i>Phar Lap<\/i> died suddenly; a 2006 forensic analysis of his preserved hair proved he died of an accidental massive arsenic overdose. As Sydney veterinarian Percy Sykes recalled: <i>\"In those days, arsenic was quite a common tonic... I'd reckon 90 per cent of the horses had arsenic in their system.\"<\/i><\/p>", "Applications": "<ol><li><b>High-Tech Semiconductors &amp; Optoelectronics:<\/b> The single most important modern technological use of high-purity <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">arsenic<\/a> is in the compound semiconductor <b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">Gallium<\/a> Arsenide (GaAs)<\/b> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/In\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Indium (In)\">Indium<\/a> Arsenide (InAs). <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">Gallium<\/a> arsenide possesses a wider bandgap and significantly higher electron mobility than <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a>, allowing electronic transistors to operate at ultra-high microwave frequencies. GaAs microchips power 5G smartphone radio-frequency modules, radar systems, satellite communications, high-efficiency solar cells for space probes, infrared LEDs, and semiconductor laser diodes used in fiber-optic communications. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">Arsenic<\/a> is also used as an n-type dopant in traditional <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a><\/a> semiconductor manufacturing.<\/li><li><b>Metallurgy &amp; Alloys:<\/b> Adding tiny amounts of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">arsenic<\/a> (0.5% to 2%) to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a><\/a> improves the sphericity of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a> shot during manufacturing and significantly increases the mechanical hardness and grid strength of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a>-acid automotive batteries. Small amounts of arsenic are also added to brass alloys to prevent dezincification (corrosion) in plumbing fittings.<\/li><li><b>Modern Pharmaceuticals &amp; Oncology:<\/b> In a remarkable medical comeback, arsenic trioxide (marketed under the brand name <i>Trisenox<\/i>) is an FDA-approved first-line chemotherapy medication used globally to treat <b>Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL)<\/b>. It works by targeting and degrading the PML-RARA fusion protein, inducing apoptosis (programmed cell death) in cancer cells and restoring healthy blood cell production.<\/li><li><b>Wood Preservation &amp; Specialty Glass:<\/b> Historically, Chromated <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">Copper<\/a> Arsenate (CCA) was applied to millions of cubic meters of structural lumber to protect wood against termites and fungal rot (though its residential use has been restricted due to environmental concerns). In glassmaking, small amounts of arsenic trioxide act as a clarifying agent to eliminate tiny air bubbles from optical lenses.<\/li><\/ol>", "Biological role": "<p>While trace amounts of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">arsenic<\/a> have been shown to be essential in the diets of certain animals (such as chicks, rats, and goats), <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">arsenic<\/a> has no known beneficial biological role in human physiology. On the contrary, inorganic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">arsenic<\/a> compounds are potent toxicants, cellular poisons, and confirmed Class 1 human carcinogens.<\/p><p><b>Biochemical Toxicity Mechanism:<\/b> Arsenic toxicity operates through two primary biochemical pathways depending on its oxidation state:<\/p><ul><li><b>Trivalent Arsenic (Arsenite, As<sup>3+<\/sup>):<\/b> Soft electrophilic arsenite ions avidly bind to vicinal sulfhydryl (-SH) thiol groups on cysteine amino acid residues within critical enzymes. In particular, arsenite inhibits the pyruvate dehydrogenase multi-enzyme complex, disrupting the citric acid (Krebs) cycle and halting the production of cellular adenosine triphosphate (ATP). This triggers severe oxidative stress, cellular damage, and tissue necrosis.<\/li><li><b>Pentavalent Arsenic (Arsenate, As<sup>5+<\/sup>):<\/b> Pentavalent arsenate acts as a structural mimic of inorganic phosphate (\\(\\text{PO}_4^{3-}\\)). It substitutes for phosphate in biochemical reactions, forming unstable arsenate esters that spontaneously hydrolyze\u2014a process known as <b>arsenolysis<\/b>. This uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, preventing cells from synthesizing ATP energy molecules.<\/li><\/ul><p><b>Groundwater Public Health Crisis in India:<\/b> In the Ganga-Brahmaputra alluvial basin of India (covering rural districts in West Bengal, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand, and Assam), long-term consumption of groundwater containing high levels of geogenic arsenic causes chronic <b>arsenicosis<\/b>. Clinical symptoms include hyperpigmentation (dark rain-drop spots on the skin), palmoplantar keratosis (painful nodular thickening of the skin on palms and soles), peripheral vascular disease (blackfoot disease), and elevated incidence of skin, bladder, lung, and liver cancers.<\/p><p><b>Pioneering Indian Scientific Innovations in Remediation:<\/b> To tackle this mass health crisis, Indian scientists and institutions have pioneered world-leading, low-cost water purification technologies:<\/p><ul><li><b>Prof. T. Pradeep &amp; the AMRIT Filter (IIT Madras):<\/b> A research team led by <b>Professor Thalappil Pradeep<\/b> at the Indian Institute of Technology Madras developed <b>AMRIT<\/b> (<i>Arsenic and Metal Removal by Indian Technology<\/i>). This revolutionary filter utilizes nanoscale <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> oxy-hydroxide held within biopolymer cages to selectively adsorb arsenite and arsenate ions from contaminated water. AMRIT consistently reduces arsenic levels from 200\u2013500 ppb down to well below the WHO safe limit of 10 ppb, operating without electricity or releasing nanoparticles, at an ultra-affordable cost of less than 5 paise per liter! Deployed in thousands of rural villages across West Bengal, Bihar, and Uttar Pradesh, this life-saving technology earned Prof. Pradeep the prestigious <b>Padma Shri<\/b> national honor and the global <b>Eni Award<\/b>.<\/li><li><b>CSIR-CGCRI Ceramic Membrane Technology (Kolkata):<\/b> Scientists at the <b>CSIR-Central Glass and Ceramic Research Institute<\/b> in Kolkata developed modular hybrid ceramic microfiltration membrane systems. By combining colloidal adsorbents with robust ceramic membranes, CSIR-CGCRI community plants purify up to 100,000 liters of groundwater per day, removing both arsenic and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> for rural populations.<\/li><li><b>CSIR-NEERI &amp; Academic Research:<\/b> Indian institutes like CSIR-NEERI, CSIR-CMERI (Durgapur), IISc Bengaluru, and IIT Kharagpur continue to advance phytoremediation (using hyperaccumulating ferns like <i>Pteris vittata<\/i> to extract arsenic from soils) and microbial bioremediation, demonstrating India's leadership in environmental protection and clean water technology.<\/li><\/ul>" } }, "Se": { "symbol": "Se", "name": "Selenium", "atomic": 34, "category": "polyatomic nonmetal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">Selenium<\/a><\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>Se<\/b>, atomic number <b>34<\/b>) is a remarkable non-metallic element with a captivating dual personality. Belonging to the chalcogen family (Group 16) alongside <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a><\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Te\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tellurium (Te)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Te\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tellurium (Te)\">tellurium<\/a><\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">selenium<\/a> sits right between them on the periodic table. In its pure form, it can exist as a dark glass-like solid, a vibrant brick-red powder, or a lustrous silvery-gray semiconductor crystal that possesses the extraordinary ability to convert light directly into electricity (photoconductivity). In nature, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">selenium<\/a> rarely occurs as a pure element; instead, it hides as a trace mineral in sulfide ores and soils. For living organisms, selenium operates on a razor's edge: in microscopic trace amounts, it is an essential micronutrient vital for immune defense, thyroid health, and cell protection, yet in larger doses, it becomes toxic. In India, selenium has profound agricultural and scientific significance\u2014from the unique high-selenium (\"seleniferous\") soils of Punjab's Shivalik foothills to cutting-edge biomedical research at the <b>Indian Institute of Science (IISc)<\/b>, where scientists design artificial selenium enzymes to fight disease.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/7\/7f\/Selenium.jpg", "atomic_mass": 78.9718, "density": 4.81, "melt": 494, "boil": 958, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "J\u00f6ns Jakob Berzelius", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p4", "electronegativity_pauling": 2.55, "electron_affinity": 194.9587, "ionization_energies": [ 941, 2045, 2973.7, 4144, 6590, 7880, 14990 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">Selenium<\/a><\/a><\/b> is a chemical element in Group 16 of the periodic table, placing it in the chalcogen family right between <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a><\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Te\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tellurium (Te)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Te\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tellurium (Te)\">tellurium<\/a><\/a>. Classified as a polyatomic nonmetal (sometimes described as a metalloid due to its intermediate semiconductor properties), its chemical behavior bridges the light, reactive nonmetal <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a> and the heavier, more metallic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Te\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tellurium (Te)\">tellurium<\/a>.<\/p>\n<p>Chemically, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">selenium<\/a> has an electron configuration of <code>[Ar] 3d\u00b9\u2070 4s\u00b2 4p\u2074<\/code> and a Pauling electronegativity of 2.55. It forms compounds in several oxidation states, most commonly -2, +4, and +6. <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">Selenium<\/a> burns in air with a blue flame to form selenium dioxide (SeO\u2082), which dissolves in water to produce selenious acid (H\u2082SeO\u2083). When reacted with metals, selenium forms selenides containing the Se\u00b2\u207b ion, behaving similarly to sulfides. It also reacts with halogens to form halides like selenium tetrafluoride (SeF\u2084) and selenium dichloride (SeCl\u2082), and with strong reducing agents to form colorful polyselenide chains (Se\u2099\u00b2\u207b). Unlike its neighbor <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a>, liquid selenium does not exhibit dramatic viscosity increases when heated. It strongly resists oxidation by ordinary air and is not attacked by non-oxidizing acids like hydrochloric acid.<\/p>", "Physical properties": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size mw-halign-left\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/95a9307846eda7bc0e55fa8962bb8206.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"190\" height=\"148\" style=\"--mw-file-upright: 0.75\" class=\"mw-file-element mw-file-upright\" data-file-width=\"704\" data-file-height=\"547\" \/><figcaption>Structure of hexagonal (gray) <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">selenium<\/a><\/a><\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">Selenium<\/a><\/a><\/b> is famous for its structural diversity, existing in several distinct allotropes (different physical forms) that transform depending on temperature and how quickly it is heated or cooled:<\/p>\n<ul>\n <li><b>Gray (Hexagonal) <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">Selenium<\/a>:<\/b> The most stable, dense, and commercially important form of selenium has a density of 4.81 g\/cm\u00b3. It features a chiral hexagonal crystal lattice (space group 152 or 154 depending on chirality) made up of long, helical polymeric chains. Within each chain, Se\u2013Se covalent bonds measure 237.3 pm with a bond angle of 103.1\u00b0, while adjacent chains sit 343.6 pm apart. Gray selenium melts at 221 \u00b0C (494 K) and boils at 685 \u00b0C (958 K). Unlike all other allotropes, gray selenium is insoluble in <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/C\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Carbon (C)\">carbon<\/a> disulfide (CS\u2082) and acts as a semiconductor with notable <b>photoconductivity<\/b>\u2014meaning its electrical conductivity increases significantly when exposed to light!<\/li>\n <li><b>Red Amorphous Selenium:<\/b> When selenium is precipitated during chemical reactions, it usually forms a fine, brick-red powder with a density of about 4.28 g\/cm\u00b3.<\/li>\n <li><b>Black Vitreous Selenium:<\/b> Produced when molten selenium is rapidly quenched, this shiny, black, glass-like solid is brittle and slightly soluble in CS\u2082. Its structure consists of complex, irregular polymeric rings containing up to 1,000 selenium atoms. Upon heating, black selenium softens at 50 \u00b0C and converts into stable gray selenium at 180 \u00b0C (a transformation accelerated by trace halogens or amines).<\/li>\n <li><b>Red Monoclinic Selenium (\u03b1, \u03b2, and \u03b3 forms):<\/b> When black selenium is dissolved in CS\u2082 and the solvent is evaporated at controlled rates, three distinct red monoclinic crystalline forms appear (all belonging to space group 14). These forms are built from puckered cyclooctaselenium (Se\u222f \/ Se\u2088) rings, very similar to S\u2088 rings in <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a>. In these Se\u2088 rings, the Se\u2013Se bond length averages 233.5 pm with a bond angle of 105.7\u00b0. The \u03b1-form represents the most densely packed arrangement, while in the \u03b3-form, half the rings are oriented in one configuration and half in its mirror image. Other minor allotropes can also contain Se\u2086 or Se\u2087 rings.<\/li>\n<\/ul>", "Isotopes": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">Main article: Isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">selenium<\/a><\/a><\/div>\n<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">Selenium<\/a><\/a><\/b> has seven naturally occurring isotopes. Five of these are completely stable: <sup>74<\/sup>Se, <sup>76<\/sup>Se, <sup>77<\/sup>Se, <sup>78<\/sup>Se, and <sup>80<\/sup>Se, with <b><sup>80<\/sup>Se<\/b> being the most abundant in nature at 49.6%. Naturally occurring <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">selenium<\/a> also contains a long-lived primordial radioisotope, <b><sup>82<\/sup>Se<\/b>, which undergoes double beta decay with an astronomical half-life of 8.76 \u00d7 10\u00b9\u2079 years (nearly 6 billion times the age of the Universe!). Additionally, minute traces of <b><sup>79<\/sup>Se<\/b> (half-life of 327,000 years) occur naturally in <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/U\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Uranium (U)\">uranium<\/a> ores as a product of nuclear fission.<\/p>\n<p>Beyond natural forms, scientists have synthesized numerous unstable radioisotopes ranging from <sup>64<\/sup>Se to <sup>95<\/sup>Se.
