The most useful synthetic radioisotope is <b><sup>75<\/sup>Se<\/b>, which has a half-life of 119.78 days and emits gamma rays widely used in industrial non-destructive testing (radiography) and nuclear medical imaging. Another long-lived synthetic isotope is <sup>72<\/sup>Se, with a half-life of 8.4 days. Radioactive isotopes lighter than the stable range primarily decay by beta-plus decay (positron emission) into isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/As\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Arsenic (As)\">arsenic<\/a><\/a>, while those heavier than the stable range undergo beta-minus decay into isotopes of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Br\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Bromine (Br)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Br\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Bromine (Br)\">bromine<\/a><\/a>.<\/p>\n\n<table class=\"wikitable\">\n <caption><b>Key Selenium Isotopes<\/b><\/caption>\n <thead>\n <tr>\n <th>Isotope<\/th>\n <th>Natural Abundance \/ Type<\/th>\n <th>Half-life<\/th>\n <th>Decay Mode<\/th>\n <\/tr>\n <\/thead>\n <tbody>\n <tr><td><b><sup>74<\/sup>Se<\/b><\/td><td>0.89% (Primordial)<\/td><td>Stable<\/td><td>None<\/td><\/tr>\n <tr><td><b><sup>75<\/sup>Se<\/b><\/td><td>Synthetic (Radioisotope)<\/td><td>119.78 days<\/td><td>Electron Capture \u2192 <sup>75<\/sup>As<\/td><\/tr>\n <tr><td><b><sup>76<\/sup>Se<\/b><\/td><td>9.37% (Primordial)<\/td><td>Stable<\/td><td>None<\/td><\/tr>\n <tr><td><b><sup>77<\/sup>Se<\/b><\/td><td>7.63% (Primordial)<\/td><td>Stable<\/td><td>None<\/td><\/tr>\n <tr><td><b><sup>78<\/sup>Se<\/b><\/td><td>23.77% (Primordial)<\/td><td>Stable<\/td><td>None<\/td><\/tr>\n <tr><td><b><sup>79<\/sup>Se<\/b><\/td><td>Trace (Fission Product)<\/td><td>327,000 years<\/td><td>Beta-minus \u2192 <sup>79<\/sup>Br<\/td><\/tr>\n <tr><td><b><sup>80<\/sup>Se<\/b><\/td><td>49.61% (Primordial)<\/td><td>Stable<\/td><td>None<\/td><\/tr>\n "History": "<figure class=\"mw-default-size\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/ac3e0d52a7c9d8e3d16d03132a8a711e.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"190\" height=\"253\" style=\"--mw-file-upright: 0.75\" class=\"mw-file-element mw-file-upright\" data-file-width=\"1200\" data-file-height=\"1600\" \/><figcaption><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">Selenium<\/a><\/a> is named after Selene, the Greek Goddess of the Moon<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">Selenium<\/a><\/a><\/b> was discovered in 1817 by famous Swedish chemists J\u00f6ns Jacob Berzelius and Johan Gottlieb Gahn. While analyzing a reddish-brown sediment left behind in the <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a> chambers of a sulfuric acid plant in Gripsholm, Sweden, they initially suspected the substance was the known element <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Te\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tellurium (Te)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Te\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tellurium (Te)\">tellurium<\/a><\/a> (named after <i>Tellus<\/i>, the Roman goddess of the Earth). However, after careful isolation, Berzelius realized he had found a completely new element. To complement <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Te\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Tellurium (Te)\">tellurium<\/a>, he named the new element <i><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">selenium<\/a><\/i>, after <b>Selene<\/b>, the Greek goddess of the Moon.<\/p>\n\n<p>In 1873, English electrical engineer Willoughby Smith made a groundbreaking discovery: the electrical resistance of gray selenium drops sharply when exposed to light! This phenomenon of <b>photoconductivity<\/b> sparked an industrial revolution in light sensing. In the mid-1870s, Werner von Siemens built the first commercial selenium photoelectric sensors, and in 1879, Alexander Graham Bell utilized a selenium photodetector to build the <b>photophone<\/b>\u2014the world's first device to transmit spoken voice wirelessly on a beam of light. By the 1930s, selenium rectifiers were developed to convert alternating current (AC) into direct current (DC), becoming the backbone of power electronics until <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Si\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silicon (Si)\">silicon<\/a> rectifiers replaced them in the 1970s. Selenium also revolutionized office work as the photoreceptor coating on light-sensitive drums in early xerographic photocopiers.<\/p>\n\n<p>Selenium's biological mystery took longer to solve. For over a century, selenium was known only as a potent toxin that poisoned livestock eating accumulator weeds on Western ranges. In 1954, biochemist Jane Pinsent found the first hints of selenium's biological role in microorganisms. In 1957, Klaus Schwarz and Walter Mertz proved that selenium is an indispensable trace element for mammals. During the 1970s, researchers discovered selenium at the active heart of the vital antioxidant enzyme glutathione peroxidase, and in the 1980s, scientists revealed that selenium is incorporated into proteins as <b>selenocysteine<\/b>\u2014the 21st amino acid of life, uniquely encoded by the UGA codon through a specialized SECIS RNA element.<\/p>\n\n<p><b>Indian Historical & Alchemical Connections:<\/b> In classical Indian alchemy and Ayurveda (<i>Rasashastra<\/i>), ancient metallurgists studied mineral classifications known as <i>Maharasas<\/i> in texts like <i>Rasa Ratna Samuccaya<\/i>. Among these minerals, the mysterious substance <b>Chapala<\/b> has been identified by several historians of Indian science and modern researchers as selenium-containing ores or <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Bi\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Bismuth (Bi)\">bismuth<\/a> compounds. Through traditional multi-step purification (<i>Shodhana<\/i>) and high-temperature furnace incineration (<i>Bhasmikarana<\/i>), ancient practitioners converted mineral complexes into bio-compatible <i>Bhasmas<\/i> (ash preparations)\u2014an early precursor to modern nano-medicine!<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable selfref\">See also: Category:Selenide minerals<\/div>\n<figure class=\"mw-default-size\" typeof=\"mw:File\/Thumb\"><img src=\"\/school1\/ptable\/theme-assets\/default\/images\/inline\/c46db06e7c0d96e4ffb280f36d1860c8.jpg\" decoding=\"async\" width=\"250\" height=\"185\" class=\"mw-file-element\" data-file-width=\"2236\" data-file-height=\"1658\" \/><figcaption>Native <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">selenium<\/a><\/a> in sandstone, from a <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/U\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Uranium (U)\">uranium<\/a> mine near Grants, New Mexico<\/figcaption><\/figure>\n<p>Native (pure elemental) <b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">selenium<\/a><\/a><\/b> is an extremely rare natural mineral, occasionally forming steep rhombohedra or microscopic, hair-like (acicular) crystals. In minerals, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">selenium<\/a> occurs in inorganic forms such as selenides, selenates, and selenites, but dedicated selenium ores are exceptionally scarce. <i>(Note: The common decorative mineral named \"selenite\" is actually a transparent variety of gypsum\u2014<a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ca\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Calcium (Ca)\">calcium<\/a> sulfate hydrate\u2014named after the Moon long before selenium was discovered, and contains no selenium at all!)<\/i><\/p>\n\n<p>Instead of forming its own rich mines, selenium occurs primarily as an impurity replacing <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a><\/a> in sulfide ores of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ni\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Nickel (Ni)\">nickel<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a>, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>. Consequently, virtually all commercial selenium is recovered as a valuable byproduct during the electrolytic refining of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a> anodic slimes. Selenium ranks 44th in crustal abundance at approximately 0.05 to 0.09 mg\/kg (ppm). Average concentrations in the atmosphere are under 1 ng\/m\u00b3, while freshwater and seawater hold around 0.5 \u00b5g\/L.<\/p>\n\n<p>In ecology, certain plants known as <i>selenium accumulators<\/i> or <i>indicator plants<\/i> thrive in selenium-rich soils by absorbing high concentrations of selenate. Key species include <i>Astragalus<\/i> (locoweeds), prince's plume (<i>Stanleya<\/i>), woody asters (<i>Xylorhiza<\/i>), and false goldenweed (<i>Oonopsis<\/i>). Animals eating these plants can suffer severe selenium poisoning.<\/p>\n\n<p><b>Indian Geographical & Agricultural Context (The Seleniferous Belt of Punjab):<\/b> In India, selenium exhibits a dramatic local geographical story. In the northeastern foothill region of Punjab\u2014specifically across pockets in the <b>Nawanshahr (Shahid Bhagat Singh Nagar)<\/b> and <b>Hoshiarpur<\/b> districts near the Shivalik mountain range\u2014the soil is naturally enriched with high levels of selenium. Rainwater streams washing down from the Shivalik hills carry selenium-dense sediments into agricultural fields, while intensive groundwater irrigation concentrates soluble selenate in topsoil. In these \"seleniferous soils,\" crops such as wheat and rice absorb excessive selenium, exhibiting characteristic \"snow-white\" leaf chlorosis and stunting. Consuming fodder and grain from these areas leads to selenium toxicity (selenosis) in local livestock (causing hoof deformation and hair loss) and humans (causing nail cracking and hair thinning). Institutions like <b>Punjab Agricultural University (PAU)<\/b> and the <b>Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)<\/b> have conducted extensive soil mapping and mitigation research to safeguard Indian agriculture and public health in these pockets.<\/p>", "Applications": "<div class=\"mw-heading mw-heading3\">\n<p>A broad spectrum of technological, industrial, and health applications rely on <b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">selenium<\/a><\/a><\/b> and its chemical compounds:<\/p>\n<ul>\n <li><b>Glassmaking & Ceramics:<\/b> <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">Selenium<\/a> is widely used in glass manufacturing. Adding tiny amounts neutralizes the pale green tint caused by <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> impurities in clear glass bottles and windows. Larger quantities impart a brilliant ruby-red color to decorative glass, traffic signals, and artistic ceramics.<\/li>\n <li><b>Electronics, Photovoltaics & Copiers:<\/b> Due to its photoconductivity, gray <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">selenium<\/a> was historically used in light meters, photocells, exposure meters, and selenium rectifiers. In modern green energy, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a> <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/In\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Indium (In)\">indium<\/a> <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ga\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gallium (Ga)\">gallium<\/a> selenide (<b>CIGS<\/b>) thin-film solar cells deliver high efficiency in flexible photovoltaic panels. Selenium photoconductive drums were also fundamental to xerographic copiers.<\/li>\n <li><b>Pigments & Paints:<\/b> <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cd\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cadmium (Cd)\">Cadmium<\/a> sulfoselenide compounds produce intensely bright, heat-resistant red, orange, and maroon pigments used in plastics, industrial coatings, artists' paints, and enamels.<\/li>\n <li><b>Metallurgy:<\/b> Adding selenium to brass and stainless steel improves machinability while allowing manufacturers to replace toxic <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a> in plumbing fixtures and hardware.<\/li>\n <li><b>Healthcare & Consumer Products:<\/b> Selenium disulfide (<b>SeS\u2082<\/b>) is the active ingredient in medical anti-dandruff shampoos, killing scalp fungi and slowing skin cell shedding. Selenium supplements and fortified livestock feed prevent deficiency diseases.<\/li>\n <li><b>Modern Indian Scientific Research & Nuclear Applications:<\/b>\n <ul>\n <li><b>BARC & Industrial Radiography:<\/b> Scientists at the <b>Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC)<\/b> in Mumbai utilize the synthetic radioisotope <b>Selenium-75 (<sup>75<\/sup>Se)<\/b> as an effective gamma-ray source for non-destructive testing (NDT). Gamma cameras powered by <sup>75<\/sup>Se inspect weld integrity in heavy gas pipelines, boilers, and structural steel across India's industrial sector.<\/li>\n <li><b>Nanotechnology & Energy Storage:<\/b> Research teams across <b>Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs)<\/b> and CSIR laboratories actively develop selenium quantum dots, biosensors, and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Na\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sodium (Na)\">sodium<\/a>-selenium \/ <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Li\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lithium (Li)\">lithium<\/a>-selenium battery technologies for next-generation energy storage.<\/li>\n <\/ul>\n <\/li>\n<\/ul>", "Biological role": "<link rel=\"mw-deduplicated-inline-style\" href=\"mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237\" \/><div role=\"note\" class=\"hatnote navigation-not-searchable\">Main article: <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">Selenium<\/a><\/a> in biology<\/div>\n<style E.g. chloroform\" class=\"notheme mw-no-invert\">2<\/span><\/div><div class=\"nfpa-704-diamond-code nfpa-704-diamond-red\">\n<span title=\"Flammability 0: Will not burn. E.g. water\" class=\"notheme mw-no-invert\">0<\/span><\/div><div class=\"nfpa-704-diamond-code nfpa-704-diamond-yellow\">\n<span title=\"Instability 0: Normally stable, even under fire exposure conditions, and is not reactive with water. E.g. liquid nitrogen\" class=\"notheme mw-no-invert\">0<\/span><\/div><\/div><\/div><\/div>\n<\/td><\/tr>\n<\/tbody><\/table>\n\n<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">Selenium<\/a><\/a><\/b> is an essential trace element nutrient for human and animal life, though the adult human body contains only about 13 to 20 mg of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Se\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Selenium (Se)\">selenium<\/a> in total. Selenium walks a tightrope in biology: human dietary needs require roughly 55 micrograms per day, but intakes exceeding 400 micrograms per day cause chronic selenium toxicity (selenosis).<\/p>\n\n<p>In living organisms, selenium is incorporated into two unusual amino acids: <b>selenocysteine<\/b> (often called the 21st amino acid of life) and <b>selenomethionine<\/b>. In selenocysteine, a selenium atom replaces the <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/S\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Sulfur (S)\">sulfur<\/a> atom of cysteine. Selenocysteine is built into vital proteins known as <i>selenoenzymes<\/i> through a unique biological genetic mechanism, where the UGA stop codon is recoded by a SECIS (Selenocysteine Insertion Sequence) RNA element.<\/p>\n\n<p>Key selenoenzymes in the body include:<\/p>\n<ul>\n <li><b>Glutathione Peroxidases (GSH-Px):<\/b> A family of powerful antioxidant enzymes that use selenium to neutralize harmful reactive <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> species (ROS)\u2014such as <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/H\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Hydrogen (H)\">hydrogen<\/a> peroxide (H\u2082O\u2082) and organic hydroperoxides\u2014protecting cell membranes and DNA from oxidative destruction.<\/li>\n <li><b>Thioredoxin Reductases:<\/b> Essential selenoenzymes found across animal cells that regulate cell growth, redox balance, and DNA synthesis.<\/li>\n <li><b>Iodothyronine Deiodinases:<\/b> Three selenium-dependent enzymes located in the thyroid gland and peripheral tissues that activate inactive thyroid hormone (T\u2084) into active thyroid hormone (T\u2083) and deactivate hormone metabolites, regulating body metabolism.<\/li>\n<\/ul>\n\n<p>Dietary selenium also provides protective benefits against heavy metal toxicity, particularly <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\"><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\">mercury<\/a><\/a> toxicity. Selenium binds to <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\">mercury<\/a> with extremely high affinity, forming inert <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Hg\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Mercury (Hg)\">mercury<\/a> selenide (HgSe) complexes that prevent mercury from inhibiting vital selenoenzymes in brain and endocrine tissues. Marine animals like bluefin tuna carry the unique selenium compound <i>selenoneine<\/i> in their blood to guard against marine mercury exposure.<\/p>\n\n<p><b>Pioneering Indian Scientific Contributions (Prof. G. Mugesh & IISc Bengaluru):<\/b> India has made world-leading contributions to modern selenium biochemistry. Professor <b>Govindasamy Mugesh<\/b> and his research team at the <b>Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru<\/b>, are international pioneers in synthetic bioinorganic chemistry. The IISc team designed novel organoselenium compounds (such as modified ebselen derivatives and catalytic triad mimics) that functionally mimic natural glutathione peroxidase (GPx) and thyroid deiodinase enzymes. By synthesizing artificial selenoenzymes that neutralize reactive <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/O\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Oxygen (O)\">oxygen<\/a> species and prevent cellular oxidative damage, IISc's groundbreaking work opens promising avenues for treating cardiovascular diseases, neurodegenerative disorders, diabetic nephropathy, and inflammatory conditions.<\/p>" } }, "Br": { "symbol": "Br", "name": "Bromine", "atomic": 35, "category": "diatomic nonmetal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b>Bromine<\/b> (symbol <b>Br<\/b>, atomic number 35) is a fascinating element that stands out on the periodic table as a reddish-brown liquid at room temperature\u2014the only nonmetal to do so. In fact, apart from mercury, it is the only element that naturally exists as a liquid under normal conditions! If left unsealed, this dense liquid quickly evaporates into a pungent, rust-colored gas. Found mostly in the ocean and salt lakes rather than in solid rocks, bromine gets its name from the ancient Greek word <i>bromos<\/i>, meaning 'stench,' thanks to its sharp, bleach-like smell. In India, bromine holds special geographic and economic importance. The Rann of Kutch in Gujarat is one of the world's richest sources of bromine-heavy brine, rivaling even the Dead Sea. Because of this natural abundance, Gujarat has become a major hub for India's booming bromine industry. Although it is toxic in large amounts and highly reactive\u2014making it rare to find on its own in nature\u2014bromine is surprisingly essential for animal life, playing a crucial, recently discovered role in the development of our collagen.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/8\/87\/Bromine-ampoule.jpg", "atomic_mass": 79.904, "density": 3.1028, "melt": 265.8, "boil": 332, "phase": "Liquid", "discovered_by": "Antoine J\u00e9r\u00f4me Balard", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p5", "electronegativity_pauling": 2.96, "electron_affinity": 324.537, "ionization_energies": [ 1139.9, 2103, 3470, 4560, 5760, 8550, 9940, 18600 ], "sections": { "History": "<p>The story of bromine's discovery is a tale of two chemists working completely independently in the 1820s: Antoine Balard in France and Carl Jacob L\u00f6wig in Germany. L\u00f6wig first isolated the smelly red liquid from a local mineral water spring in 1825, while Balard extracted it from the ash of seaweed in 1826. Because Balard published his findings first, he usually receives the primary credit! Even earlier, the famous chemist Justus von Liebig had stumbled upon it but mistakenly thought it was just a mixture of iodine and chlorine. Bromine found its first major role in the 1840s, helping to create some of the world's earliest photographs known as daguerreotypes. Later, during the American Civil War, bromine solutions were used to fight gangrene and infections before modern antiseptics were invented. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, doctors prescribed bromide salts as a popular sedative and anticonvulsant, though these have mostly been replaced by safer modern medicines today. In modern India, the historical use of such salts has transformed into a massive industrial enterprise, with organizations like the India Bromine Platform (IBP) driving its safe application and technological advancement across the country.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Like many elements, bromine comes in a few different 'flavors' called isotopes. These are versions of the atom that have the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons. In nature, you will only find two types: <b>Bromine-79<\/b> and <b>Bromine-81<\/b>. Amazingly, they exist in almost a perfect 50\/50 split on Earth! This nearly even distribution is incredibly handy for scientists when they use machines like mass spectrometers to figure out whether bromine is present in an unknown chemical sample. Scientists have also created several other bromine isotopes in laboratories, but they are radioactive and break down too quickly to be found in nature. Some of these laboratory-made radioactive versions, like Bromine-77 and Bromine-82, are used as valuable tools in specialized scientific and medical research.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Bromine is an incredibly useful tool in modern industry, though its uses have evolved over time. For many years, its biggest claim to fame was in making flame retardants\u2014chemicals added to plastics, furniture, and electronics to stop them from catching fire. However, because some of these chemicals were found to accumulate in the environment and harm the Earth's ozone layer when released into the atmosphere, their use is now more carefully regulated. Today, bromine is still a superstar in many other fields. It is a key ingredient in creating high-density, clear drilling fluids for the oil and gas industry, water treatment chemicals that keep swimming pools and industrial cooling towers safe, and a wide variety of medicines and agricultural products. In India, companies located in the Rann of Kutch harvest naturally occurring brine to produce the liquid bromine that supplies the nation's fast-growing pharmaceutical and agrochemical sectors, making it a true cornerstone of the region's economy.<\/p>" } }, "Kr": { "symbol": "Kr", "name": "Krypton", "atomic": 36, "category": "noble gas", "description": "", "extract_html": "Krypton (symbol: Kr, atomic number: 36) is a hidden treasure of the periodic table. Its name even comes from the ancient Greek word <i>kryptos<\/i>, meaning 'hidden.' Although it is a colorless, odorless, and chemically inactive noble gas, it plays a dazzling role in the modern world. Found in tiny amounts in Earth's atmosphere, krypton is famous for creating bright, white light when an electrical charge passes through it. Today, this 'hidden' gas illuminates our world, powers advanced lasers, and even helps Indian scientists propel satellites through space.", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/9\/9c\/Krypton-glow.jpg", "atomic_mass": 83.7982, "density": 3.749, "melt": 115.78, "boil": 119.93, "phase": "Gas", "discovered_by": "William Ramsay", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6", "electronegativity_pauling": 3, "electron_affinity": -96, "ionization_energies": [ 1350.8, 2350.4, 3565, 5070, 6240, 7570, 10710, 12138, 22274, 25880, 29700, 33800, 37700, 43100, 47500, 52200, 57100, 61800, 75800, 80400, 85300, 90400, 96300, 101400, 111100, 116290, 282500, 296200, 311400, 326200 ], "sections": { "History": "Krypton was discovered in Britain in 1898 by two chemists, William Ramsay (from Scotland) and Morris Travers (from England). They found it in the leftover residue after boiling away almost all the components of liquid air. This remarkable discovery of noble gases eventually earned Ramsay a Nobel Prize in 1904.\n\nFor a time, krypton held a special place in global measurements. From 1960 to 1983, the official length of one meter was defined by the glowing light of a specific krypton isotope (krypton-86). This standard replaced a physical metal bar kept in France and offered an exact, unchangeable measure based on the fabric of the universe, before being eventually replaced by the speed of light.", "Characteristics": "As a noble gas, krypton generally doesn't react with other elements, preferring to stay entirely to itself. But when exposed to electricity, it lights up brilliantly! Krypton is known for producing a number of sharp, bright colors, with its strongest lights being vivid greens and yellows. \n\nWhen cooled down to extreme temperatures to become a solid, it turns white and forms a neat, cube-like crystal structure, which is typical of most noble gases.", "Isotopes": "Naturally occurring krypton is made of five stable forms (called isotopes), along with one type that decays so slowly\u2014over billions of years\u2014that it's considered basically stable. \n\nOne particularly interesting isotope is krypton-81. Since it takes thousands of years to break down, scientists use it to date ancient, underground water sources that have been hidden away for up to 800,000 years. Another version, krypton-85, is a radioactive gas created during nuclear reactions. Because it escapes into the air when nuclear fuel is processed, monitoring krypton-85 helps global authorities detect secret nuclear weapons testing.\n\nIn India, the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) plays a crucial role in studying these isotopes. BARC scientists actively monitor krypton-85 to ensure environmental safety and keep a close watch on nuclear activities. Additionally, researchers at India's Raja Ramanna Centre for Advanced Technology (RRCAT) experiment with trapping and cooling different krypton isotopes using lasers to explore the cutting-edge field of atom optics.", "Applications": "You've likely seen krypton at work without even knowing it! Because its light appears so bright and white, it is widely used in high-speed photography flashes and energy-efficient fluorescent bulbs. When mixed with mercury, it produces the glowing greenish-blue light often seen in luminous neon signs.\n\nBeyond lighting up streets and studios, krypton is a heavyweight in the world of high-tech and space exploration. Powerful krypton lasers are used in light shows and critical nuclear fusion research. In the medical field, special mixtures of krypton gas help doctors capture clearer MRI and CT scans of a patient's lungs.\n\nKrypton has also taken to the stars, especially in India's booming space sector. The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) uses krypton gas as a highly efficient and cost-effective fuel for the electric thrusters that maneuver satellites in orbit. Furthermore, ISRO has utilized specialized krypton lamps to calibrate sensitive scientific instruments on missions like Chandrayaan-3, helping India uncover the secrets of the moon." } }, "Rb": { "symbol": "Rb", "name": "Rubidium", "atomic": 37, "category": "alkali metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p>Rubidium (symbol <strong>Rb<\/strong>, atomic number 37) is a very soft, silvery-white metal that belongs to the alkali metal family. Like its chemical cousins potassium and sodium, it is highly reactive. It is the first alkali metal in its group to be heavier than water. While ancient Indian alchemical texts (<em>Rasashastra<\/em>) intricately described the 'metals of antiquity' such as gold, silver, iron, and mercury, rubidium remained hidden from the world until modern times. Today, however, it plays a starring role in advanced Indian scientific research. For instance, the groundbreaking theories of Indian physicist Satyendra Nath Bose laid the foundation for the Bose-Einstein condensate, a state of matter first achieved using rubidium atoms! On Earth, it exists naturally as two isotopes, one of which is slightly radioactive with a half-life far longer than the age of the universe.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/c\/c9\/Rb5.JPG", "atomic_mass": 85.46783, "density": 1.532, "melt": 312.45, "boil": 961, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Robert Bunsen", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s1", "electronegativity_pauling": 0.82, "electron_affinity": 46.884, "ionization_energies": [ 403, 2633, 3860, 5080, 6850, 8140, 9570, 13120, 14500, 26740 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "Rubidium is a fascinating element with extreme behaviors, known for its softness, vivid color in a flame, and intense reactivity. It shares many characteristics with other alkali metals like potassium and caesium.", "Physical properties": "Rubidium is a very soft, ductile, silvery-white metal that you could easily cut with a butter knife. It melts at just 39.3 \u00b0C (102.7 \u00b0F), which means it would melt on a hot summer day in many parts of India! When heated to 688 \u00b0C (1,270 \u00b0F), it boils into a vapor. It easily forms mixtures, called amalgams or alloys, with metals like mercury, gold, iron, sodium, and potassium. When you put a tiny amount of rubidium in a flame, it produces a beautiful, bright purple-red color. This color is very similar to potassium's flame, so scientists use advanced tools like spectroscopes to tell them apart.", "Chemical properties": "Chemically, rubidium is incredibly eager to react with other elements. It is the second most electropositive (electron-donating) of the stable alkali metals. Because of this strong desire to react, dropping rubidium into water causes an explosive chemical reaction! It reacts violently, sinking in the water while producing hydrogen gas and rubidium hydroxide. The reaction is so vigorous that it usually bursts into flames, igniting the escaping hydrogen gas. Rubidium is so reactive that it can even catch fire spontaneously just by being exposed to the air. Therefore, it must be carefully stored in special mineral oils or in a vacuum to prevent it from reacting.", "Isotopes": "In nature, rubidium is found in two forms, called isotopes. About 72% of it is rubidium-85, which is perfectly stable. The remaining 28% is rubidium-87, which is slightly radioactive. However, you don't need to worry about its radioactivity! Rubidium-87 decays incredibly slowly, with a 'half-life' of 48.8 billion years\u2014that's more than three times the estimated age of the entire universe! Because it decays at such a steady, slow rate into an element called strontium, geologists around the world (and in institutions like the Geological Survey of India) use rubidium to figure out the age of ancient rocks. By measuring the ratio of rubidium to strontium in a rock, they can trace the tectonic and geological history of places like the Peninsular Indian shield. Other artificial, highly radioactive isotopes of rubidium have been created in labs, but they last for only minutes or days.", "Occurrence": "Rubidium isn't the most abundant element, but it is more common in the Earth's crust than metals like copper or zinc. It is naturally found mixed into minerals like leucite, pollucite, and lepidolite. Lepidolite, a type of lithium-rich mica, is the main commercial source for rubidium. In India, geological explorations in regions such as the Govindpal area of Chhattisgarh's Bastar district have revealed lepidolite deposits with notable concentrations of rubidium. Furthermore, researchers are actively exploring geothermal systems, such as those in the Puga Valley of Eastern Ladakh, for potential rare metal enrichment, including rubidium. In the oceans, seawater contains a tiny but measurable amount of rubidium as well.", "History": "Rubidium was discovered in 1861 by two brilliant German scientists, Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff. They found it using a brand-new tool they had just invented: the spectroscope, which identifies elements based on the unique colors of light they emit. When they analyzed the mineral lepidolite, they noticed striking deep red lines in the spectrum. Because of these bright red lines, they named the new element 'rubidium,' from the Latin word <em>rubidus<\/em>, meaning 'deep red'. They went to great lengths to study it, processing 150 kilograms of ore just to get a tiny pinch of rubidium salts! For many decades, rubidium remained a scientific curiosity with few practical uses. But its true potential was unlocked in the modern era of quantum physics. In 1995, rubidium-87 was cooled to near absolute zero to create a 'Bose-Einstein condensate'\u2014a bizarre state of matter predicted decades earlier by Albert Einstein and Indian physicist Satyendra Nath Bose. This incredible achievement earned its creators the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2001, cementing Bose's and rubidium's intertwined legacy in the history of science.", "Applications": "Today, rubidium is a superstar in high-tech research and electronics. Because it is easily turned into a vapor and interacts perfectly with lasers, it is one of the most popular elements for laser cooling and studying quantum mechanics. Recently, researchers at the Raman Research Institute (RRI) in Bengaluru, India, have conducted groundbreaking experiments using ultra-cooled rubidium atoms to study 'Rydberg states,' which is crucial for building future quantum computers and advanced sensors. Rubidium is also used in atomic clocks, which are incredibly precise timekeepers essential for GPS satellites and telecommunications networks. It helps polarize gases for medical imaging, acts as a 'getter' to remove unwanted gases in vacuum tubes, and is used in special types of glass. In medicine, a short-lived isotope called rubidium-82 acts very much like potassium in the human body, allowing doctors to use it in PET scans to safely image the heart's blood flow and locate brain tumors. There has even been research into using rubidium supplements to help treat conditions like depression, showing just how versatile this 'deep red' element truly is." } }, "Sr": { "symbol": "Sr", "name": "Strontium", "atomic": 38, "category": "alkaline earth metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Sr\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Strontium (Sr)\">Strontium<\/a><\/b> is a soft, silvery metal with a pale yellow tint. If you've ever watched a spectacular red firework light up the night sky, you've seen strontium in action! In its pure form, this element is highly reactive and must be stored in mineral oil to keep it from turning into a powder when it meets the air.<\/p>\n<p>Beyond making fireworks and emergency flares burn crimson red, strontium has some amazing connections to our world and history. In India, it was recently declared one of the nation's 30 \"critical minerals.\" Exciting new deposits were just discovered in the coal mines of Telangana! It also helps us solve ancient mysteries: Indian archaeologists use \"strontium isotope analysis\" on ancient teeth and bones to trace the movement of early humans and trade goods\u2014like proving that ancient cotton found in Arabia originally came from India.<\/p>\n<p>Strontium even has a place in medicine. Because it is chemically similar to calcium, our bodies absorb it into our bones. In modern Indian healthcare and homeopathy (where it's known as <i>Strontium carbonicum<\/i>), specialized strontium compounds are used to treat bone pain and manage osteoporosis. From dazzling fireworks to cutting-edge science and ancient history, strontium is truly a remarkable element!<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/8\/84\/Strontium-1.jpg", "atomic_mass": 87.621, "density": 2.64, "melt": 1050, "boil": 1650, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "William Cruickshank (chemist)", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2", "electronegativity_pauling": 0.95, "electron_affinity": 5.023, "ionization_energies": [ 549.5, 1064.2, 4138, 5500, 6910, 8760, 10230, 11800, 15600, 17100, 31270 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "Strontium is a soft, shiny metal with a yellowish hue. It is highly reactive, meaning it easily undergoes chemical changes when exposed to things like air or water. Because it reacts so quickly with oxygen and moisture, it must be stored in special liquids like mineral oil. In nature, you won't find pure strontium lying around; it's always bonded to other elements.", "Isotopes": "An atom's identity is determined by how many protons it has, but the number of neutrons can vary. These variations are called \"isotopes.\" Strontium has four naturally occurring isotopes. Scientists can look at the ratios of these isotopes\u2014especially in a technique called \"strontium isotope analysis.\" In India, archaeologists use this fascinating method on ancient teeth and artifacts to trace the ancient trade routes and movements of early human populations.", "History": "Strontium's story began in 1790 near a Scottish village called Strontian, where it was first identified in a mineral. It was later isolated as a pure element by Sir Humphry Davy in 1808. Today, its historical significance has expanded. For example, recent discoveries of strontium deposits in the coal mines of Telangana mark an important chapter for modern India's resource independence, leading to its classification as a critical mineral for the nation.", "Occurrence": "You typically find strontium in minerals like celestine and strontianite. While major deposits have traditionally been found in places like China and Spain, India has recently made significant strides by discovering strontium within coal mining waste in the Telangana region. Recognizing its value for modern industries, India now lists strontium as one of its 30 critical minerals, aiming to tap into these domestic sources.", "Applications": "If you enjoy the bright red bursts in fireworks or the red glow of emergency road flares, you are admiring strontium at work! Besides its starring role in pyrotechnics, strontium is used to make special types of glass and magnets. In modern times, it is also being researched for new industrial applications as part of India's push to secure essential resources for future technologies.", "Biological role": "Strontium behaves a lot like calcium in the human body, meaning our bodies will happily absorb it into our bones. This unique trait makes it very useful in medicine. In Indian healthcare and homeopathy (known as <i>Strontium carbonicum<\/i>), specific strontium compounds are used to treat bone pain and help manage diseases like osteoporosis by making bones stronger. However, radioactive forms of strontium can be dangerous because they can also settle into bones and cause harm." } }, "Y": { "symbol": "Y", "name": "Yttrium", "atomic": 39, "category": "transition metal", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 39 (Y)", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Y\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Yttrium (Y)\">Yttrium<\/a><\/b> is a silvery-white transition metal that is often grouped with rare-earth elements. It was first discovered in a quarry in Ytterby, Sweden, in 1787. Even though it is called a \"rare earth\" element, it is actually quite abundant in the Earth's crust! In modern India, yttrium plays a crucial role in advancing clean energy and new technologies. Scientists at Indian institutions like the Centre for Nano and Soft Matter Sciences (CeNS) are exploring yttrium compounds to build high-performance supercapacitors and advanced energy storage systems. India also holds significant deposits of rare-earth minerals like monazite and xenotime, found in coastal beach sands across Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and Odisha, making it an important player in the future of critical minerals.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/9\/90\/Piece_of_Yttrium.jpg", "atomic_mass": 88.905842, "density": 4.472, "melt": 1799, "boil": 3203, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Johan Gadolin", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d1", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.22, "electron_affinity": 29.6, "ionization_energies": [ 600, 1180, 1980, 5847, 7430, 8970, 11190, 12450, 14110, 18400, 19900, 36090 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p>Yttrium is a soft, silver-metallic element that is highly crystalline. In its pure form, it is relatively stable in air because it forms a protective oxide layer on its surface, much like aluminum. If you turn it into fine turnings or powder, however, it can easily ignite! It is chemically very similar to the lanthanides (the top row of elements at the bottom of the periodic table) and is almost always found alongside them in nature. One of its most famous characteristics is its use in creating high-temperature superconductors, which can carry electricity with zero resistance at temperatures above the boiling point of liquid nitrogen.<\/p>", "History": "<p>The story of yttrium begins in 1787, when a part-time chemist named Carl Axel Arrhenius found an unusual black rock in a quarry near the Swedish village of Ytterby. He sent it to various chemists, and in 1789, Johan Gadolin identified a new \"earth\" (oxide) within it, which was later named yttria. This rock eventually led to the discovery of several new elements! The pure metal was finally isolated by Friedrich W\u00f6hler in 1828.<\/p>\n<p>While yttrium doesn't have an ancient history in India, it is becoming a vital part of the nation's modern scientific journey. With the launch of initiatives like the National Critical Mineral Mission, India is increasingly focusing on elements like yttrium to build a self-reliant supply chain for aerospace, defense, and renewable energy sectors. Today, researchers in India are using green chemistry to synthesize yttrium nanoparticles for antibacterial applications and quantum research.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>Yttrium is found in most rare-earth minerals and uranium ores, but it is never found in nature as a free element. Interestingly, lunar rocks brought back by the Apollo missions contain high levels of yttrium! On Earth, it is commercially extracted from minerals like monazite and xenotime.<\/p>\n<p>In India, yttrium is geologically significant. The country has vast reserves of monazite-bearing beach sands along the coasts of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Gujarat. Additionally, xenotime, a phosphate mineral rich in yttrium, is found in the riverine placer deposits of Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand. Through exploratory projects like SHORE (Shallow Subsurface Imaging of India for Resource Exploration), scientists at the CSIR-National Geophysical Research Institute continue to map and discover these vital rare-earth deposits across the Indian subcontinent.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Yttrium has many fascinating applications! Its most important use is in making phosphors, which are materials that emit light. These are used in LEDs and were crucial for creating the red color in older cathode-ray tube (CRT) televisions. Yttrium is also a key ingredient in YAG (yttrium aluminum garnet) lasers, which are used in everything from medical surgeries to metal cutting.<\/p>\n<p>It is added to alloys to increase their strength and is used in spark plugs and microwave filters. Recently, Indian scientists have been harnessing yttrium's unique properties to develop advanced energy storage solutions, such as supercapacitors, and exploring its potential in next-generation quantum and spintronic devices. Because of its strategic importance, yttrium is a critical building block for the technologies of tomorrow.<\/p>" } }, "Zr": { "symbol": "Zr", "name": "Zirconium", "atomic": 40, "category": "transition metal", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 40 (Zr)", "extract_html": "<p><b>Zirconium<\/b> (symbol <b>Zr<\/b>, atomic number 40) is a silvery-white, strong, and corrosion-resistant metal that looks a bit like titanium. Long before it was used in modern science, zirconium was known in ancient times in the form of zircon crystals, which were prized as colorful gemstones. In fact, the name <i>zirconium<\/i> comes from the Persian word <i>zargun<\/i>, meaning &quot;gold-like.&quot; While you might know it best from its use in cubic zirconia\u2014a popular diamond substitute\u2014zirconium is incredibly important in modern technology. It is highly heat-resistant and doesn\\'t absorb neutrons, making it essential for nuclear power plants. It is also used in spacecraft, medical implants, and everyday products like deodorants. Zirconium is abundant in nature, and India holds some of the world\\'s most significant deposits along its beautiful coastal beaches.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/1\/1d\/Zirconium-pieces.jpg", "atomic_mass": 91.2242, "density": 6.52, "melt": 2128, "boil": 4650, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Martin Heinrich Klaproth", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d2", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.33, "electron_affinity": 41.806, "ionization_energies": [ 640.1, 1270, 2218, 3313, 7752, 9500 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p>Zirconium is a tough, silvery metal that refuses to rust or corrode easily, even when exposed to harsh chemicals like acids or saltwater. Because it is highly resistant to heat, it is considered a &quot;refractory&quot; metal, meaning it can withstand extreme temperatures without melting or breaking down. At room temperature, it is solid, bendable, and easy to shape. Interestingly, while solid zirconium is very safe and stable, zirconium powder can easily catch fire if it isn\\'t handled carefully!<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>In nature, zirconium is found as a mix of five different types, called isotopes. Four of these are completely stable, meaning they don\\'t break down over time. The fifth one is mildly radioactive, but it takes an incredibly long time to decay\u2014more than 20 quintillion years! Scientists also use synthetic (man-made) isotopes of zirconium in medical research, especially for tracking how well certain medicines work inside the body.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>Zirconium is quite common in the Earth\\'s crust, but you won\\'t find it just lying around as a pure metal. Instead, it is locked inside minerals, most famously <b>zircon<\/b>. These zircon crystals are incredibly durable; in fact, some zircon grains found on Earth are billions of years old, acting as tiny &quot;time capsules&quot; that help scientists understand the early history of our planet.<\/p> <p><b>Indian Geographical Relevance:<\/b> India is incredibly rich in zirconium resources, with over 30 million tonnes of zircon reserves. These are mostly found in the heavy mineral sands along the coastlines of Odisha (like the Chhatrapur coast), Tamil Nadu (Manavalakurichi region), and Kerala (Kollam district). Over millions of years, ocean waves and winds naturally concentrated these minerals on the beaches, creating some of the most economically valuable &quot;placer deposits&quot; in the world.<\/p>", "History": "<p>The story of zirconium begins long before modern chemistry. Ancient people cherished zircon crystals as beautiful gemstones, calling them names like jargon, jacinth, or hyacinth.<\/p> <p><b>Indian Historical and Cultural Context:<\/b> In ancient Indian texts and Hindu mythology, zircon holds a special place; legends even describe a magical, jewel-encrusted Kalpavriksha (wish-fulfilling tree) that had vibrant green zircon leaves. Throughout the Middle Ages, people believed these stones could bring wealth, promote wisdom, and ensure a peaceful night\\'s sleep.<\/p> <p>It wasn\\'t until 1789 that a German chemist named Martin Heinrich Klaproth realized that zircon contained a brand new element. A few decades later, in 1824, the Swedish chemist J\u00f6ns Jacob Berzelius finally managed to extract zirconium in its metal form.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Today, zirconium is a superstar in both industry and everyday life. Because it doesn\\'t absorb the neutrons flying around inside a nuclear reactor, it is the perfect material for building the tubes that hold nuclear fuel.<\/p> <p><b>Modern Indian Scientific Contributions:<\/b> India\u2019s own <b>Nuclear Fuel Complex (NFC)<\/b> plays a major role here, producing specialized zirconium sponge and zirconium alloys to power the country\\'s expanding nuclear energy program.<\/p> <p>Beyond nuclear power, zirconium is used to make strong, heat-resistant parts for space vehicles and jet engines. In the medical field, zirconium compounds (like zirconia) are used to make incredibly strong and safe dental implants and artificial joints, because the human body naturally accepts them. You can even find zirconium in everyday items, like antiperspirant deodorants and the water purifiers used in homes!<\/p>" } }, "Nb": { "symbol": "Nb", "name": "Niobium", "atomic": 41, "category": "transition metal", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 41 (Nb)", "extract_html": "<p><b>Niobium<\/b> is a shiny, light gray metal that plays a silent but essential role in our modern world. Though you might not hear about it every day, it is a superstar in high-tech industries. When mixed with other metals, it creates super-strong alloys used in everything from jet engines to rockets. It is also famous for its superconducting abilities, meaning it can carry electricity without any resistance when cooled down. In India, niobium is recognized as a strategic and critical mineral, playing a crucial part in the nation's <i>Atmanirbhar Bharat<\/i> (self-reliant India) initiative to develop advanced materials for space and nuclear energy right at home.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/c\/c2\/Niobium_strips.JPG", "atomic_mass": 92.906372, "density": 8.57, "melt": 2750, "boil": 5017, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Charles Hatchett", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s1 4d4", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.6, "electron_affinity": 88.516, "ionization_energies": [ 652.1, 1380, 2416, 3700, 4877, 9847, 12100 ], "sections": { "History": "<p>Niobium's story began in 1801 when English chemist Charles Hatchett discovered it in a mineral sample and originally named it \"columbium.\" For decades, it was confused with another very similar element called tantalum. It was not until 1846 that German chemist Heinrich Rose realized they were two distinct elements and renamed it \"niobium\"\u2014inspired by Niobe, the daughter of Tantalus in Greek mythology. Historically in India, the strategic importance of niobium became prominent in the mid-20th century as the country expanded its nuclear and military capabilities. Today, it remains a focal point for India's push towards self-reliance in critical materials, ensuring a steady domestic supply for next-generation technologies.<\/p>", "Characteristics": "<p>Niobium is a transition metal that is as soft and malleable as pure iron. When exposed to air at room temperature, it takes on a beautiful bluish tinge. One of its most magical properties is superconductivity: at extremely low temperatures, it allows electricity to flow with absolutely zero resistance. This makes it incredibly valuable for making powerful magnets. Indian scientific institutions, such as the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) and the Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research, have made significant breakthroughs in producing high-purity niobium ingots and developing niobium-titanium superconducting alloys indigenously. These advancements are essential for building cutting-edge particle accelerators and advanced nuclear reactors.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>In nature, niobium exists entirely as a single stable isotope, known as Niobium-93. This means that all naturally occurring niobium is made up of atoms with the same mass. Scientists have also created several artificial, radioactive isotopes in laboratories, but they are generally short-lived and used mainly for research purposes. The predictable and stable nature of Niobium-93 is exactly what makes it so dependable when used in precise, high-tech engineering applications and energy research.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>Niobium is never found as a free metal in nature; it prefers to bond with other elements in minerals like columbite and pyrochlore. While Brazil and Canada hold the vast majority of the world's niobium reserves, India has its own notable deposits. Major Indian sources are associated with carbonatite rocks and pegmatite belts. Significant exploration has taken place at Amba Dongar in Gujarat, where niobium is found as pyrochlore. Other important deposits are located in the Sung Valley and Samchampi Complex in the Northeast, Sevathur in Tamil Nadu, and the mica belts of Bihar and Rajasthan. The Geological Survey of India continues to actively explore these regions to secure the country's domestic supply.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Niobium is a true workhorse element. Its biggest job is strengthening steel; adding just a tiny pinch of niobium makes steel significantly stronger and lighter, which is perfect for building cars, bridges, and gas pipelines. In the aerospace industry, niobium alloys are used in jet engines and rocket nozzles because they can withstand extreme heat. Its superconducting magnets are crucial for MRI machines in hospitals. In India, modern research is taking niobium even further. For example, researchers at the Centre for Nano and Soft Matter Sciences (CeNS) in Bengaluru have recently developed innovative niobium-based materials (like lanthanum-doped silver niobate) for supercapacitors. These breakthroughs promise highly efficient energy storage solutions for the future of portable electronics and renewable energy in India.<\/p>" } }, "Mo": { "symbol": "Mo", "name": "Molybdenum", "atomic": 42, "category": "transition metal", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 42 (Mo)", "extract_html": "<p><b>Molybdenum<\/b> (symbol Mo, atomic number 42) is a silvery-gray metal that is incredibly tough and resistant to heat. Although it's not well-known to the general public, it's a silent superhero in both our bodies and modern industry. Nature uses molybdenum in essential enzymes that help plants and animals process nutrients, making life on Earth possible. In fact, modern Ayurvedic researchers in India are increasingly studying its role as a vital trace mineral for human health and detoxification. In the industrial world, molybdenum is famous for making steel stronger and more heat-resistant, which is why it's used in everything from engine parts to armor plating. While India relies mostly on imports for this metal, small amounts are recovered as a by-product of copper and uranium mining in places like Madhya Pradesh, Jharkhand, and Tamil Nadu.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/f\/f0\/Molybdenum.jpg", "atomic_mass": 95.951, "density": 10.28, "melt": 2896, "boil": 4912, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Carl Wilhelm Scheele", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s1 4d5", "electronegativity_pauling": 2.16, "electron_affinity": 72.1, "ionization_energies": [ 684.3, 1560, 2618, 4480, 5257, 6640.8, 12125, 13860, 15835, 17980, 20190, 22219, 26930, 29196, 52490, 55000, 61400, 67700, 74000, 80400, 87000, 93400, 98420, 104400, 121900, 127700, 133800, 139800, 148100, 154500 ], "sections": { "Isotopes": "<p>Molybdenum comes in many different forms, known as isotopes. Think of isotopes as siblings in a family\u2014they share the same identity but have slightly different weights. In nature, we find seven stable \"siblings\" of molybdenum. The most common one is Molybdenum-98. There are also many artificial versions created by scientists. The most famous artificial sibling is Molybdenum-99, which is incredibly important in modern medicine. Hospitals use it to produce a special radioactive tracer that helps doctors safely see inside the human body and diagnose diseases.<\/p>", "History": "<p>For a long time, people didn't know what molybdenum was. Ancient Greeks and early scientists often confused its naturally occurring ore, molybdenite, with lead or graphite\u2014the stuff used in pencils. The name \"molybdenum\" even comes from the Greek word \"molybdos,\" which means \"lead.\" It wasn't until 1778 that the Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele proved it was a completely unique element, and shortly after, Peter Jacob Hjelm successfully isolated the pure metal.<\/p><p>For over a century, the metal sat unused because it was so hard to work with. But during World War I, its true potential was unlocked. When military engineers needed a stronger, lighter armor for their tanks, they turned to molybdenum. It proved to be a fantastic substitute for heavier metals, allowing tanks and artillery to move faster while offering better protection. Since then, it has become a crucial ingredient for building tough, heat-resistant materials. In India, research centers like the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) and the National Metallurgical Laboratory (NML) continue to develop innovative ways to extract this strategic metal from low-grade local ores.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Today, molybdenum is primarily used as a powerful \"vitamin\" for steel. Adding just a little bit of molybdenum makes steel and cast iron incredibly strong, durable, and resistant to rust and extreme heat. You'll find it in car engines, aircraft parts, industrial pipelines, and even drill bits. Beyond metals, it's used in special lubricants that can withstand high temperatures where normal oils would catch fire or burn away. It's also an essential micronutrient in agriculture; studies in states like Tamil Nadu have highlighted its importance in helping crops like green gram thrive in acidic soils.<\/p>", "Biological role": "<p>Despite being found only in tiny amounts in the environment, molybdenum is essential for almost all living things. It sits at the heart of special enzymes\u2014nature's tiny machines\u2014that help break down and process nutrients. One of its most important jobs is \"nitrogen fixation.\" Without molybdenum, bacteria in the soil wouldn't be able to pull nitrogen from the air to feed plants, meaning a massive part of the food chain would collapse. In humans, it helps our bodies break down toxins and process medications. The ancient Indian science of Rasashastra (the Ayurvedic study of minerals) has long recognized the power of trace metals, and modern researchers are actively exploring how small amounts of molybdenum contribute to overall wellness and disease prevention.<\/p>" } }, "Tc": { "symbol": "Tc", "name": "Technetium", "atomic": 43, "category": "transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Tc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Technetium (Tc)\">Technetium<\/a><\/b> is a true trailblazer of the periodic table! Sitting at atomic number 43, it was the very first element to be artificially created by humans, which is exactly why its name comes from the Greek word <i>techn\u0113tos<\/i>, meaning \"artificial.\" Unlike most elements, you will not find technetium naturally hanging out in rocks or oceans; it is a purely synthetic, radioactive metal born in nuclear reactors. It was finally discovered in 1937, long after chemists had predicted a missing element right beneath manganese. In fact, when Dmitri Mendeleev first proposed his periodic table, he used the ancient Sanskrit word <i>eka<\/i> (meaning \"one\") and called the mystery element \"eka-manganese.\" Today, this silvery-gray metal plays an incredibly vital, life-saving role in modern medicine, helping doctors around the world\u2014including across India's vast healthcare networks\u2014diagnose diseases by peering inside the human body.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/a\/ab\/Technetium-sample-cropped.jpg", "atomic_mass": 98, "density": 11, "melt": 2430, "boil": 4538, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Emilio Segr\u00e8", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d5", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.9, "electron_affinity": 53, "ionization_energies": [ 702, 1470, 2850 ], "sections": { "History": "<p>The story of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Tc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Technetium (Tc)\">technetium<\/a> is one of the greatest scavenger hunts in scientific history. Since it does not exist naturally in Earth's crust, early chemists were puzzled by the gaping hole at atomic number 43. Decades before its discovery, the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev predicted its existence. Fascinatingly, Mendeleev used Sanskrit, a classical Indian language, to name his predicted elements, calling this one \"eka-manganese\" (meaning one spot below manganese). For years, researchers mistakenly claimed they had found it, giving it names like \"polonium,\" \"ilmenium,\" and \"masurium.\" It was not until 1937 that Italian scientists Carlo Perrier and Emilio Segr\u00e8 finally proved its existence. They discovered it in a piece of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mo\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Molybdenum (Mo)\">molybdenum<\/a> foil that had been bombarded with atoms in an American cyclotron. Because it was entirely man-made, they named it <b>technetium<\/b>!<\/p>", "Characteristics": "<p>Because <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Tc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Technetium (Tc)\">technetium<\/a> is radioactive, its atoms are fundamentally unstable and break down over time. It is a silvery-gray, shiny metal that looks quite similar to platinum. What makes it incredibly special is its rarity: it is one of the lightest elements that has absolutely no stable isotopes. On Earth, there are virtually no natural deposits of technetium. Any tiny, microscopic traces found in nature only appear when uranium ores spontaneously undergo radioactive decay. Because of its scarcity, all the technetium used today must be carefully produced in nuclear research facilities and reactors.<\/p>", "Physical properties": "<p>If you were to hold a solid chunk of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Tc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Technetium (Tc)\">technetium<\/a> (which you shouldn't do without radiation shielding!), it would feel heavy and dense. It has a high melting point of around 2,157 \u00b0C (3,915 \u00b0F) and boils at an extreme 4,265 \u00b0C (7,709 \u00b0F). Technetium is a transition metal, which means it is a great conductor of electricity. In fact, at extremely cold temperatures (near absolute zero), it turns into a superconductor, meaning electricity can flow through it without any resistance at all!<\/p>", "Chemical properties": "<p>In terms of chemistry, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Tc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Technetium (Tc)\">technetium<\/a> is a bit of a middle child, showing traits of the elements directly above and below it: <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Mn\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Manganese (Mn)\">manganese<\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Re\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Rhenium (Re)\">rhenium<\/a>. It slowly tarnishes when exposed to moist air, turning dull over time. When crushed into a fine powder, it can even catch fire in oxygen! Technetium can form a wide variety of chemical compounds, commonly bonding with oxygen to create technetates. Interestingly, a tiny pinch of pertechnetate added to water is incredibly effective at preventing iron and steel from rusting, though its radioactivity limits this use to closed, highly controlled industrial systems.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Every single isotope (variation) of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Tc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Technetium (Tc)\">technetium<\/a> is radioactive. Some isotopes, like Technetium-97 and Technetium-98, are relatively long-lived, taking millions of years to decay by half. But the real star of the show is <b>Technetium-99m<\/b>. The \"m\" stands for metastable, meaning it is a highly energetic version of the atom that releases gamma rays as it calms down. With a short half-life of just six hours, Technetium-99m vanishes quickly, making it perfectly safe for short-term use in the human body. In India, facilities managed by the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) and the Board of Radiation &amp; Isotope Technology (BRIT) heavily rely on managing and extracting these specific isotopes for critical national applications.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>The most famous and life-changing use of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Tc\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Technetium (Tc)\">technetium<\/a> is in modern healthcare. Technetium-99m is a superhero of nuclear medicine, used in tens of millions of diagnostic procedures worldwide every year. When attached to specific chemicals, it can be injected into the human body to travel to the brain, heart, bones, or kidneys. Doctors then use special cameras to capture the gamma rays it emits, creating detailed, inside-out pictures of the patient's organs. In India, institutions like the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) play a monumental role in indigenously producing and distributing these medical radioisotopes. Through these efforts, Indian hospitals are able to perform advanced, lifesaving diagnostics for cardiology and oncology, proving that this \"artificial\" element has a very real, human impact.<\/p>" } }, "Ru": { "symbol": "Ru", "name": "Ruthenium", "atomic": 44, "category": "transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b>Ruthenium<\/b> is a rare, hard, silvery-white metal. It belongs to the platinum group of elements in the periodic table, meaning it shares many properties with platinum, like being highly resistant to rust and chemical attacks. Because of its toughness and ability to withstand high temperatures and corrosion, it is mostly used in electronics, such as electrical contacts and specialized resistors. It is also used to make metal alloys harder and in chemical processes as a catalyst. Discovered in 1844 by the Russian scientist Karl Ernst Claus, its name comes from \"Ruthenia,\" the Latin word for Russia. While ancient civilizations were unaware of this element, modern science has found incredible uses for it, from advanced electronics to life-saving cancer treatments.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/a\/a8\/Ruthenium_crystal.jpg", "atomic_mass": 101.072, "density": 12.45, "melt": 2607, "boil": 4423, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Karl Ernst Claus", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s1 4d7", "electronegativity_pauling": 2.2, "electron_affinity": 100.96, "ionization_energies": [ 710.2, 1620, 2747 ], "sections": { "Physical properties": "<p>Ruthenium is a solid, hard, and shiny white metal that belongs to the platinum family. In the periodic table, it sits in group 8. It is very special because its outer electron shell only has one electron, unlike other similar metals that usually have two. This quirky arrangement doesn't change how it reacts with other chemicals, but it makes it a fascinating element for scientists to study. Ruthenium is incredibly tough, melting at a very high temperature of 2,334 &deg;C (4,233 &deg;F) and boiling at 4,150 &deg;C (7,502 &deg;F).<\/p>", "Chemical properties": "<p>Like other platinum-group metals, ruthenium is extremely stubborn when it comes to reacting with other chemicals. It doesn't tarnish or rust at room temperature, and it takes extreme heat (about 800 &deg;C) for it to react with oxygen. Normal acids won't melt it, though it can be broken down by certain harsh bleaching chemicals like sodium hypochlorite. When added in small amounts to other metals, such as platinum, palladium, or titanium, ruthenium acts like a super-shield, making the new metal mix much harder and more resistant to rust. Interestingly, ruthenium can hold on to a wide range of electrical charges (oxidation states), making it very versatile for different chemical reactions.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>In nature, ruthenium exists as a mix of seven stable forms, known as isotopes. Scientists have also created over 30 artificial, radioactive isotopes of ruthenium in laboratories. While most of these radioactive versions break down (decay) very quickly&mdash;often in just a few minutes&mdash;some last a bit longer. For example, Ruthenium-106 is a radioactive version created from splitting uranium or plutonium, and it takes about a year to break down by half. This specific isotope has become highly important in the medical field.<\/p>", "Occurrence and Geography": "<p>Ruthenium is one of the rarest elements on Earth, ranking 78th in abundance in the Earth's crust. It is almost always found in tiny amounts mixed with other platinum-group metals in ores. The largest amounts are mined in the Ural Mountains of Russia, as well as in North America (Canada) and South Africa.<\/p><p>In India, there are no major commercial mines for ruthenium. While the Geological Survey of India (GSI) has found promising traces of platinum-group elements in places like Dras in Ladakh, the Baula-Nausahi complex in Odisha, Hanumalpur in Karnataka, and Sittampundi in Tamil Nadu, India still imports most of the ruthenium it needs for its high-tech industries.<\/p>", "History": "<p>For centuries, ancient civilizations, including the pre-Columbian peoples of the Americas, unknowingly used natural mixes of platinum metals. However, identifying ruthenium as a unique, separate element took a long time because it is so rare and hard to isolate. In 1827, scientists J&ouml;ns Berzelius and Gottfried Osann examined leftovers from Russian platinum but couldn't quite prove they had found a new element. Finally, in 1844, the Russian scientist Karl Ernst Claus succeeded. He isolated the metal at Kazan University and named it 'ruthenium' in honor of his homeland, Russia (from 'Ruthenia,' the Latin word for Russia).<\/p><p>Interestingly, while ancient India had a world-renowned metallurgical tradition&mdash;producing marvels like Wootz steel and the rust-resistant Iron Pillar of Delhi, which were well documented in ancient Sanskrit texts&mdash;ruthenium was completely unknown to them. It is a modern discovery that requires advanced chemistry to extract.<\/p>", "Applications and Modern Scientific Contributions": "<p>Today, ruthenium is a star in the electronics and chemical industries. About half of all ruthenium produced is used to make wear-resistant electrical contacts and thick-film resistors found in modern electronics. It is also used to harden the gold used in the tips of expensive fountain pens and is added to special superalloys used in jet engine turbines.<\/p><p>In modern science, particularly in India, ruthenium is making waves. The Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) in India achieved a major medical breakthrough by developing affordable, indigenous Ruthenium-106 (Ru-106) plaques to treat eye cancers, saving many lives and reducing reliance on expensive imports. Furthermore, scientists at Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) and other research centers are actively studying new ruthenium-based drugs as less toxic alternatives to traditional cancer treatments. Indian researchers are also at the forefront of using ruthenium nanoparticles in green chemistry, helping to reduce pollution, and in cutting-edge physics to develop the next generation of electronic devices.<\/p>" } }, "Rh": { "symbol": "Rh", "name": "Rhodium", "atomic": 45, "category": "transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p>Rhodium (Rh) is a rare, silvery-white, and highly reflective transition metal with the atomic number 45. Known as one of the rarest and most valuable precious metals on Earth, it is extremely hard and resistant to corrosion. While it was discovered by William Hyde Wollaston in 1803 in South American platinum ores, its importance has grown globally, including in modern India. Indian scientists and research institutes like the IITs have been actively exploring rhodium-based catalysts\u2014tiny helpers that speed up chemical reactions\u2014for sustainable chemistry and developing advanced nanomaterials. In everyday life, rhodium is famously used in jewelry for a shiny finish and in cars' catalytic converters to clean up exhaust gases, a crucial application for meeting India's modern environmental standards.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/5\/54\/Rhodium_%28Rh%29.jpg", "atomic_mass": 102.905502, "density": 12.41, "melt": 2237, "boil": 3968, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "William Hyde Wollaston", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s1 4d8", "electronegativity_pauling": 2.28, "electron_affinity": 110.27, "ionization_energies": [ 719.7, 1740, 2997 ], "sections": { "History": "Rhodium was discovered in 1803 by the English chemist William Hyde Wollaston, shortly after he found another element, palladium. He extracted rhodium from a crude platinum ore found in South America. By using a series of chemical reactions, Wollaston produced a red powder. He named the new metal \"rhodium\" after the Greek word \"rhodon,\" meaning rose, because of the beautiful rose-red color of this compound. Although ancient India had a rich and famous metallurgical tradition\u2014mastering gold, silver, iron, and steel\u2014rhodium belongs to a group of metals that are incredibly hard to melt and isolate. Thus, it wasn't known in the ancient world. However, in modern times, as Indian science has rapidly advanced, Indian chemists have become deeply involved in studying rhodium and utilizing its unique properties for cutting-edge chemical research.", "Characteristics": "Rhodium is a hard, silvery-white metal that shines brilliantly and does not easily tarnish or rust. It is part of the \"platinum group\" of metals, meaning it shares many traits with platinum, such as a very high melting point and an incredible resistance to corrosion. Even when exposed to air or water, rhodium stays shiny and unchanged. Because it is both durable and beautiful, it is often plated over other jewelry metals, like silver or white gold, to give them a bright, scratch-resistant finish.", "Chemical properties": "Chemically, rhodium is known as a \"noble metal.\" This means it is very stubborn about reacting with other substances\u2014it prefers to stay just as it is! It does not dissolve easily in most acids, not even in the famously strong \"aqua regia\" (a mixture that can dissolve gold) unless it's in a specific powdered form. When it does form compounds, it most commonly takes on a +3 oxidation state, meaning it shares three electrons to bond with other elements. Indian scientific institutions frequently study these rhodium compounds because they are fantastic \"catalysts\"\u2014substances that help chemical reactions happen faster and more efficiently without being used up themselves.", "Isotopes": "Isotopes are different versions of the same element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. In nature, rhodium is as simple as it gets: it has only one stable, naturally occurring isotope, known as Rhodium-103. Scientists have also created several radioactive isotopes of rhodium in laboratories, but these are unstable and break down quickly. Because natural rhodium is 100% Rhodium-103, its atomic weight is very precise and reliable for scientists working with it around the world.", "Occurrence": "Rhodium is incredibly rare\u2014one of the rarest elements in the Earth's crust. You won't find a mine dedicated only to rhodium. Instead, it is usually found mixed in small amounts with other metals like platinum, palladium, nickel, or copper. The majority of the world's rhodium comes from river sands and mineral deposits in South Africa, Russia, and North America. In India, which is a major consumer of precious metals, rhodium isn't mined locally in large quantities, but it is imported and highly valued for its industrial importance, especially in a rapidly growing automotive market.", "Applications": "The most important use for rhodium today is in the automotive industry. It is a key ingredient in the catalytic converters of cars and trucks, where it helps clean up harmful exhaust gases, making the air safer to breathe. This application is incredibly important in modern India, where strict vehicle emission standards are enforced to combat urban air pollution. Beyond cars, rhodium is used to coat jewelry and silverware to keep them brilliantly shiny and scratch-free. Additionally, Indian scientists and global researchers use rhodium to create advanced catalysts for manufacturing essential chemicals, including pharmaceuticals and new eco-friendly nanomaterials." } }, "Pd": { "symbol": "Pd", "name": "Palladium", "atomic": 46, "category": "transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pd\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Palladium (Pd)\">Palladium<\/a><\/b> is a brilliant, silvery-white metal that plays a massive hidden role in our daily lives. Discovered in 1803 by English chemist William Hyde Wollaston and named after the asteroid Pallas, it sits right next to platinum and shares many of its prized qualities. It doesn't tarnish easily, and uniquely, it can soak up 900 times its own volume in hydrogen gas! Palladium is a true superhero of modern industry, mostly famous for its use in cars to clean up toxic exhaust fumes. While major global supplies come from South Africa and Russia, India has recently tapped into this precious resource. Geological surveys have found traces of palladium-bearing platinum group elements in ancient Precambrian rocks in states like Odisha, Tamil Nadu, and Karnataka. In fact, Odisha even started a pilot project in 2026 to extract these valuable metals locally.
