Whether it's shining in fine \"white gold\" jewelry or making our air cleaner, palladium is an incredibly valuable element.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/d\/d7\/Palladium_%2846_Pd%29.jpg", "atomic_mass": 106.421, "density": 12.023, "melt": 1828.05, "boil": 3236, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "William Hyde Wollaston", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 4d10", "electronegativity_pauling": 2.2, "electron_affinity": 54.24, "ionization_energies": [ 804.4, 1870, 3177 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p>Palladium doesn't react with oxygen at room temperature, which means it doesn't tarnish in the air, keeping its beautiful silver-white shine. If you heat it up to a scorching 800 \u00b0C, it will finally start to form a thin brownish layer on the surface, but otherwise, it stays brilliantly clean. One of its most amazing features is that it can act as a superconductor (carrying electricity with zero resistance) when cooled to incredibly low temperatures and bombarded with alpha particles.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>In nature, <b>palladium<\/b> is made up of six stable, unchanging forms called isotopes. However, scientists have discovered dozens of other radioactive versions (radioisotopes) of the metal. The longest-lasting of these, Palladium-107, can survive for 6.5 million years and can even be found in tiny trace amounts in nature! Most of the other radioactive isotopes vanish incredibly quickly, breaking down into neighboring elements like rhodium or silver in just a matter of hours or days. Interestingly, studying these specific isotopes in ancient meteorites helps astronomers understand how our early Solar System and its rocky planets formed billions of years ago. Palladium-107 is also slowly created inside modern nuclear reactors, although it's considered one of the safer, more benign byproducts.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>Mining for <b>palladium<\/b> is a massive global effort, with total production reaching over 210,000 kilograms in 2022! Most of the world's supply currently comes from deep nickel and copper mines in Russia and South Africa, with smaller amounts sourced from Canada, the United States, and Zimbabwe. It's incredibly rare to find free-floating chunks of pure palladium; instead, it usually hides out naturally blended with gold and platinum in riverbeds and deep rock formations.<\/p><p>Interestingly, India is beginning to make its own mark on the palladium map. Geological experts have identified promising reserves of platinum group metals\u2014which include palladium\u2014in ancient, billion-year-old rock formations across the country. In states like Odisha (notably the Baula-Nuasahi and Sukinda areas), Tamil Nadu (the Sittampundi complex), and parts of Karnataka, the metal has been traced in underground chromite ore bodies. Recognizing this hidden potential, India is even exploring new ways to mine and process these local reserves, reducing reliance on global superpowers. Though theoretically, scientists could also extract palladium from spent nuclear fuel, the process is too complex and expensive to be used today, making earthly mining efforts in places like South Africa, Russia, and potentially India, our best source.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Today, the biggest job for <b>palladium<\/b> is cleaning up our environment. It is the key ingredient in the catalytic converters of most gasoline-powered cars, turning toxic exhaust gases into safer substances. In India, the push for cleaner air and the adoption of strict BS-VI emission norms has made palladium more critical than ever. But its talents don't stop there! Because it can absorb huge amounts of hydrogen, it is being researched for hydrogen fuel cells, the clean energy of the future.<\/p><p>Beyond saving the planet, palladium is also highly valued in electronics, dentistry, and even professional concert flutes. In the world of fashion and culture, palladium is a shining star. It is frequently mixed with gold to create gorgeous \"white gold\" jewelry, offering a lighter, tarnish-resistant alternative to platinum that has become increasingly popular with Indian consumers and investors alike. As a highly precious commodity, it is one of only four metals (alongside gold, silver, and platinum) to have its own official currency codes. As demand grows, local efforts like Odisha's pilot project to extract platinum group metals from native chromite ores highlight just how important palladium has become to modern technology and the economy.<\/p>", "History": "<p>In 1802, English chemist William Hyde Wollaston noticed a mysterious new noble metal in his lab. He named it <b>palladium<\/b> in August of that year, inspired by the recently discovered asteroid \"Pallas\" (which astronomers thought was a planet at the time). Wollaston managed to purify some of the metal from crude platinum ore found in South America and famously sold it anonymously in a small London shop in 1803. This sparked drama when another scientist, Richard Chenevix, wrongly claimed it was just a fake alloy of platinum and mercury. Wollaston even offered a \u00a320 reward to anyone who could artificially create it\u2014a prize no one could claim because palladium was indeed a brand-new element! He finally revealed himself as its true discoverer in 1805.<\/p><p>Historically, palladium chloride was actually prescribed to treat tuberculosis, though its side effects soon led doctors to find better medicines. By the 20th and 21st centuries, the metal became incredibly valuable. As countries worldwide\u2014including India, with its strict BS-VI emission standards\u2014demanded cleaner cars, the need for palladium in catalytic converters skyrocketed. Because most of it comes from Russia and South Africa, political events and supply delays have historically caused wild price spikes. To secure their own supplies, countries like India have begun exploring local deposits. Geological surveys have identified potential platinum group element reserves in ancient rock formations, like the Baula-Nuasahi and Sukinda areas in Odisha, and the Sittampundi complex in Tamil Nadu, marking an exciting new chapter in India's hunt for this rare metal.<\/p>" } }, "Ag": { "symbol": "Ag", "name": "Silver", "atomic": 47, "category": "transition metal", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 47 (Ag)", "extract_html": "<p><b>Silver<\/b> is a beautiful, shiny metal with the chemical symbol <b>Ag<\/b> (from the Latin word <i>argentum<\/i>) and atomic number 47. Known for its brilliant white glow, it is the best conductor of heat and electricity of all metals, and it reflects light perfectly. Because it is soft and easy to shape, silver has been used for thousands of years to make coins, jewelry, and beautiful objects. In India, silver holds a special place in history and culture. It is deeply connected to the Moon (<i>Chandra<\/i>), symbolizing coolness and feminine energy. Beyond its beauty, silver is an essential ingredient in modern technology like solar panels and electronics.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/e\/e4\/Silver-nugget.jpg", "atomic_mass": 107.86822, "density": 10.49, "melt": 1234.93, "boil": 2435, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "unknown, before 5000 BC", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s1 4d10", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.93, "electron_affinity": 125.862, "ionization_energies": [ 731, 2070, 3361 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p>Silver is an incredibly special metal because of how it handles heat, electricity, and light. If you were to touch a piece of silver to something warm, the heat would travel through it faster than almost any other material! The same goes for electricity\u2014silver is the undisputed champion of conducting electrical currents, even better than copper.<\/p>\n<p>In addition to its invisible super-powers, silver is famous for its appearance. It is a \"lustrous\" or shiny white metal that reflects light perfectly, which is why it was historically used to make the best mirrors. Silver is also very soft and \"ductile,\" meaning it can be pulled into a wire as thin as a single atom without breaking. Because it is so soft, jewelers often mix (or alloy) silver with a little bit of copper to make it strong enough for everyday wear.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Everything in the universe is made of atoms, and atoms of the same element can sometimes have different weights. These different versions are called \"isotopes.\" In nature, silver comes in two stable, permanent forms that are almost equally common. Both of these stable forms were forged billions of years ago in the intense heat of exploding stars, or supernovas, before becoming part of the Earth.<\/p>\n<p>Scientists can also create other forms of silver in laboratories, but these are \"radioactive\" and unstable. This means they break down over time, turning into other elements like palladium or cadmium. While these unstable forms don't stick around long, they help scientists understand the building blocks of our universe.<\/p>", "History": "<p>Silver has a rich and fascinating history that stretches back thousands of years. It is one of the seven \"metals of antiquity,\" meaning humans have known about and used it since prehistoric times. Because silver is often found mixed with other rocks and metals in the Earth, ancient people had to figure out clever ways to melt and purify it.<\/p>\n<p>In India, silver's history is deeply woven into both science and culture. Over 5,000 years ago, the craftsmen of the Indus Valley Civilization were already creating stunning silver jewelry and utensils. During the 6th century BCE, India introduced <b>silver punch-marked coins<\/b>, which were among the earliest standardized money systems in South Asia. The <b>Zawar mines<\/b> in Rajasthan are celebrated as one of the world's oldest sites for mining silver and zinc.<\/p>\n<p>Silver is also highly valued in traditional Indian medicine, known as <b>Ayurveda<\/b>. In ancient texts related to <i>Rasashastra<\/i> (the science of minerals), experts described how to purify silver and turn it into a medicinal ash called <i>Rajat Bhasma<\/i>. This ash was used to treat neurological and respiratory issues. Long before modern science understood bacteria, Indian traditions encouraged storing water and milk in silver vessels to keep them pure, taking advantage of silver's natural ability to kill germs.<\/p>\n<p>Culturally, silver is linked to the Moon (<i>Chandra<\/i>) in Hindu tradition, symbolizing peace, clarity, and feminine energy. From temple offerings to the bold, beautiful tribal jewelry of Rajasthan and Gujarat, silver continues to be a symbol of purity and prosperity.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Today, silver is used in ways that ancient people could never have imagined. Because it is such a fantastic conductor of electricity, a tiny amount of silver can be found inside almost every electronic device, from smartphones and computers to television screens. It is also a critical component in building solar panels, helping us capture energy from the sun.<\/p>\n<p>Silver's ability to reflect light makes it perfect for creating specialized mirrors and window coatings that keep buildings warm in the winter and cool in the summer. Historically, silver chemicals were the magic behind traditional photography, capturing images on film before the invention of digital cameras.<\/p>\n<p>Beyond technology, silver remains a favorite material for beautiful jewelry and silverware. And, confirming ancient Ayurvedic practices, modern medicine uses silver today for its antimicrobial properties. You can find silver in bandages, medical tools, and special creams to prevent infections and help wounds heal faster.<\/p>" } }, "Cd": { "symbol": "Cd", "name": "Cadmium", "atomic": 48, "category": "transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b>Cadmium<\/b> is a soft, silvery-white metal with the symbol <b>Cd<\/b> and atomic number 48. It looks and acts a lot like zinc, but it is rarer and much more toxic. You'll often find cadmium hiding inside zinc ores rather than on its own. It's famous for its use in rechargeable nickel-cadmium batteries and for making bright yellow, orange, and red paints.<\/p><p>Even though it has been used in many modern products, cadmium is highly toxic to humans and the environment. Because of this, many countries are stepping away from using it. In India, for instance, cadmium isn't naturally mined on its own, but it is extracted as a byproduct of zinc smelting by companies like Hindustan Zinc in Rajasthan. While not a part of traditional Ayurvedic medicine, strict testing is required in India today to ensure herbal remedies aren't accidentally contaminated by this heavy metal.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/images-of-elements.com\/cadmium-4.jpg", "atomic_mass": 112.4144, "density": 8.65, "melt": 594.22, "boil": 1040, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Karl Samuel Leberecht Hermann", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.69, "electron_affinity": -68, "ionization_energies": [ 867.8, 1631.4, 3616 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p>Cadmium is a soft, malleable, and ductile metal that you can almost cut with a knife. It has a beautiful silvery-bluish tint. When you bend a piece of cadmium, it makes a surprising 'crying' or crackling sound, much like tin does! It melts at 321 \u00b0C (610 \u00b0F), which is quite low for a metal. Chemically, Cadmium is very similar to its periodic table neighbor, zinc, but it doesn't rust easily. It resists corrosion well, which is why it has been used to plate other metals to protect them. It doesn't dissolve in water but will react with acids.<\/p>", "History": "<p>Cadmium was discovered in 1817 by German chemist Friedrich Stromeyer. He found it as an impurity in zinc carbonate (calamine). Pharmacists noticed that some calamine turned yellow when heated, which shouldn't happen if it were pure. Stromeyer investigated and discovered a brand new element! He named it 'cadmium' after the Latin word for calamine, <em>cadmia<\/em>.<\/p><p>Before the rise of modern chemistry, elements like cadmium were unknown to ancient civilizations. For example, in ancient Indian texts and Ayurveda, cadmium is completely absent. Its modern presence in some herbal formulations is strictly due to accidental soil or industrial contamination, which today's Indian authorities tightly monitor under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>You won't find solid chunks of pure cadmium lying around in nature. It usually sneaks into zinc ores, like sphalerite. Because it tags along with zinc, it is almost entirely produced as a byproduct of mining and refining zinc.<\/p><p>Geographically, in places like India, cadmium production is closely tied to zinc mining. Hindustan Zinc Limited, based in the mineral-rich state of Rajasthan (operating famous mines like Rampura Agucha and Zawar), is the primary producer of cadmium in India. The metal is recovered during the hydrometallurgical refining processes at their massive zinc smelters.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>For a long time, the biggest use of cadmium was in rechargeable nickel-cadmium (Ni-Cd) batteries. These were the go-to rechargeable batteries for electronics before lithium-ion batteries took over.<\/p><p>Cadmium is also famous in the art world. Cadmium pigments produce brilliant, long-lasting yellows, oranges, and reds. Despite the toxicity, some artists still prefer them because of their vibrant colors. It is also used to coat steel to prevent rust, in some specialized alloys, and in control rods for nuclear reactors because it is great at absorbing neutrons.<\/p>", "Biological role": "<p>Cadmium has almost no known useful biological role in humans or most animals. Instead, it is highly toxic. Over time, cadmium can build up in the body, especially in the kidneys, causing severe health issues and bone softening (a disease historically known as <em>Itai-itai<\/em> in Japan).<\/p><p>In modern India, the Ministry of AYUSH has set strict regulations to ensure that traditional medicines (like Ayurvedic, Siddha, and Unani) are rigorously tested for heavy metals. This ensures that accidental cadmium contamination from soil or water doesn't harm consumers. Because of its toxicity, the world is moving away from cadmium. The European Union and other international bodies have restricted its use in electronics and jewelry to protect human health and the environment.<\/p>" } }, "In": { "symbol": "In", "name": "Indium", "atomic": 49, "category": "post-transition metal", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 49 (In)", "extract_html": "<p><strong>Indium<\/strong> (symbol <strong>In<\/strong>, atomic number 49) is a brilliant, silvery-white metal that is incredibly soft\u2014so soft you can actually bite into it or cut it with a butter knife! When bent, it produces a high-pitched \"squealing\" sound known as a \"tin cry.\"<\/p>\n<p>Though not named after India directly, its name has a deep Indian connection. It comes from the indigo blue line seen in its light spectrum, and the word \"indigo\" is derived from the Latin <em>indicum<\/em>, meaning \"of India\" (referring to the famous indigo dye historically exported from the Indian subcontinent).<\/p>\n<p>Today, indium is the unsung hero of the digital age. In the form of indium tin oxide (ITO), it is a vital, transparent, electrically conductive coating used in almost every flat-screen TV, smartphone touch screen, and solar panel.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/images-of-elements.com\/indium-2.jpg", "atomic_mass": 114.8181, "density": 7.31, "melt": 429.7485, "boil": 2345, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Ferdinand Reich", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p1", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.78, "electron_affinity": 37.043, "ionization_energies": [ 558.3, 1820.7, 2704, 5210 ], "sections": { "Isotopes": "<p>In nature, indium is a fascinating anomaly. It is made up almost entirely of a single radioactive isotope, Indium-115, which accounts for about 95.7% of all natural indium. You might wonder why we aren't worried about its radioactivity! The secret lies in its incredibly slow decay: its half-life is 441 trillion years, which is nearly 30,000 times longer than the current age of the universe. The rest of natural indium is made up of the stable isotope Indium-113. It is extremely rare for an element to have a radioactive isotope be far more abundant than its stable one.<\/p>", "History": "<p>Indium was discovered in 1863 in Germany by chemists Ferdinand Reich and Hieronymus Theodor Richter. Reich, who was colorblind, was examining zinc ores and asked Richter to look at the colored lines produced in a spectroscope. Richter spotted a brilliant, never-before-seen blue line. They named the new element <em>indium<\/em> after this indigo-blue spectral line.<\/p>\n<p>The name holds a special historical connection to <strong>India<\/strong>. The word \"indigo\" comes from the Latin word <em>indicum<\/em>, which literally translates to \"of India.\" For centuries, India was the world's primary supplier of the rich indigo dye, cementing the country's legacy in the very name of this vital modern element. Richter successfully isolated the pure metal a year later, but the two scientists eventually had a falling out over who deserved the credit for the discovery!<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>In the cosmos, indium is born in the hearts of low-to-medium mass stars over thousands of years through a process called slow neutron capture (the s-process). On Earth, indium is quite rare\u2014about as scarce as silver\u2014and it never forms its own concentrated minerals or \"indium mines.\"<\/p>\n<p>Instead, indium hides away as a trace element within other mineral deposits, most notably zinc sulfide (sphalerite). Because of this, practically all of the world's indium is extracted as a byproduct of smelting zinc and, to a lesser extent, lead.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Indium's unique properties make it a cornerstone of modern electronics. Its most famous application is as <strong>Indium Tin Oxide (ITO)<\/strong>. This remarkable compound is optically transparent but conducts electricity, making it the perfect coating for the touch screens on our smartphones, tablets, flat-screen televisions, and even solar panels. It's also used in low-melting-point alloys, high-vacuum seals, and to make the semiconductors that power blue and white LED lights.<\/p>\n<p>In <strong>India<\/strong>, the rapidly growing electronics market and the push for technological self-reliance have sparked important scientific research regarding indium. Since India does not possess primary indium mining reserves, modern Indian scientific contributions are heavily focused on sustainability and recovery. Institutions like <strong>IIT Roorkee<\/strong>, supported by India's Ministry of Mines, have pioneered research into recycling electronic waste (e-waste) to recover valuable indium from discarded LCD screens. These domestic innovations are crucial for securing the critical materials needed for India's booming semiconductor and electronics manufacturing industries.<\/p>" } }, "Sn": { "symbol": "Sn", "name": "Tin", "atomic": 50, "category": "post-transition metal", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 50 (Sn)", "extract_html": "<p><b>Tin<\/b> (symbol <b>Sn<\/b>, from Latin <i>stannum<\/i>) is a silvery-white, post-transition metal known for its softness and low melting point. If you bend a bar of tin, you can actually hear a faint, crackling sound called the \"tin cry\" caused by its crystals shifting! Tin has been essential to human civilization for millennia. Historically, it was a critical ingredient in creating bronze, a tough alloy of copper and tin that launched the Bronze Age. In ancient India, it was prized in traditional medicine and metallurgy, famously known as <i>Trapu<\/i>. Today, tin is incredibly important for modern technology, mostly used as solder to glue electronic components together in smartphones, computers, and solar panels. It is also used in the iconic \"tin cans\" to prevent steel from rusting, making it a quiet but essential part of our daily lives.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/6\/6a\/Tin-2.jpg", "atomic_mass": 118.7107, "density": 7.365, "melt": 505.08, "boil": 2875, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "unknown, before 3500 BC", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p2", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.96, "electron_affinity": 107.2984, "ionization_energies": [ 708.6, 1411.8, 2943, 3930.3, 7456 ], "sections": { "History": "<p>The story of tin dates back to the dawn of the Bronze Age, around 3000 BC. Early metalworkers discovered that adding a small amount of tin to copper created a surprisingly hard, durable alloy\u2014bronze\u2014which revolutionized tools, weapons, and art. The ancient world saw massive trade networks built just to transport rare tin ores like cassiterite. In ancient India, tin was highly valued and referred to as <i>Trapu<\/i> in early Vedic texts, and later as <i>Vanga<\/i> in the Puranas. It was famous for making <i>Kansa<\/i> (bronze), which was considered a pure, \"sattvic\" metal perfect for cooking and dining utensils. Traditional Ayurvedic science even used purified tin ashes, known as <i>Vanga Bhasma<\/i>, to treat various ailments. Fast forward to the 20th century, and tin drove the global canning industry, creating immense wealth and trade hubs in countries like Bolivia. Even though its market has shifted over the decades, tin's rich history shows how a simple metal helped shape human progress.<\/p>", "Characteristics": "<p>Tin is a relatively soft metal with a silvery shine. It does not rust or tarnish easily in water or air, making it excellent for protective coatings. An interesting quirk about tin is that it has two main forms, or allotropes. At room temperature, it is a shiny, bendable metal known as \"white tin\" (\u03b2-tin). However, if the temperature drops well below freezing, it slowly transforms into a crumbly, non-metallic gray powder known as \"gray tin\" (\u03b1-tin). This bizarre transformation was historically called \"tin pest,\" and ancient craftsmen had to be careful not to let their tin objects freeze! Tin is also very chemically similar to its neighbors on the periodic table, germanium and lead. It has a low melting point, making it incredibly easy to melt down and mix with other metals to form helpful alloys.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Tin holds a very special record on the periodic table: it has the highest number of stable isotopes of any element! An isotope is just a version of an atom with a different number of neutrons. While most elements have just a few stable versions, tin boasts ten (ranging from Tin-112 to Tin-124). Physicists believe this is because tin's atomic number is 50, a \"magic number\" in nuclear physics that creates highly stable atomic nuclei. Because of this unique stability, tin is incredibly easy to study using advanced lab techniques like NMR spectroscopy. While stable tin is totally safe, scientists have also discovered over 30 unstable, radioactive isotopes of tin, though most of these exist for less than a year before decaying away.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>Like many heavy elements, tin is forged in the fiery cores of low-to-medium mass stars and scattered across the universe. Here on Earth, it ranks as the 49th most abundant element in the crust. You will almost never find pure tin lying around in nature; instead, it is hidden within ores, the most important being a heavy, dark mineral called cassiterite (tin dioxide). A lot of the world's tin is mined from riverbeds and valleys where heavy cassiterite stones settled after washing down from granite mountains. Today, countries like China, Indonesia, and Peru are the top producers of tin. In India, small natural deposits are found in places like the Tosham hills of Haryana, hinting at where ancient Indian metalworkers might have sourced their materials. Because we use so much of it, scientists predict Earth's easily mineable tin could run low in the coming decades, making recycling scrap tin more important than ever.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>In modern times, tin is the unsung hero holding our digital world together. Nearly half of all the tin mined today is used as \"solder\"\u2014a low-melting alloy that acts as the conductive glue for printed circuit boards in smartphones, computers, and electric vehicles. Another major use is \"tinplating,\" where a thin layer of tin is coated over steel to prevent rust, giving us the classic, food-safe \"tin can.\" In India, the push for advanced technology and renewable energy has brought tin back into the spotlight. Premier research institutions like the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) and the IITs are pioneering the use of tin-based perovskites\u2014a non-toxic alternative to lead\u2014to build next-generation, high-efficiency solar cells. Additionally, organizations like ISRO collaborate with academia to develop specialized tin alloys that can endure the harsh environments of space. From preserving our food to powering the solar revolution and exploring the cosmos, tin's uses are endlessly versatile.<\/p>" } }, "Sb": { "symbol": "Sb", "name": "Antimony", "atomic": 51, "category": "metalloid", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p>Antimony is a fascinating chemical element with the symbol <strong>Sb<\/strong> (from its Latin name, <em>stibium<\/em>) and atomic number 51. It is a shiny, silvery-grey metalloid, meaning it has properties of both metals and non-metals. In nature, it is most commonly found as a sulfide mineral called stibnite.<\/p><p>Antimony has a rich history across the world, but it holds a particularly special place in Indian culture and medicine. For thousands of years, stibnite has been known in India as <em>Surma<\/em> or <em>Anjanam<\/em>. It was ground into a fine powder to create traditional eye cosmetics (kohl), believed to protect and cool the eyes in the hot Indian climate. In ancient Indian medical systems like Ayurveda and Unani, specifically in the branch of <em>Rasashastra<\/em>, antimony is carefully processed to create traditional medicines.<\/p><p>Beyond ancient remedies, antimony played a starring role in modern Indian science. In 1920, the brilliant Indian physician Dr. Upendranath Brahmachari, working in Kolkata, synthesized an antimony compound called <em>urea stibamine<\/em>. This groundbreaking discovery became a highly effective cure for kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis), saving millions of lives and earning Dr. Brahmachari multiple Nobel Prize nominations!<\/p><p>Today, China is the world's leading producer of antimony, largely from the Xikuangshan Mine in Hunan. The metal is extracted by heating stibnite and mixing it with carbon or iron. In the modern world, antimony is an unsung hero hiding in everyday items. It is often mixed with lead and tin to make strong alloys used in bullets, solders, and engine bearings. It also strengthens the lead plates inside car batteries, acts as a powerful flame retardant in clothing and plastics, and is even used to make the tiny semiconductors that power our electronics.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/5\/5c\/Antimony-4.jpg", "atomic_mass": 121.7601, "density": 6.697, "melt": 903.78, "boil": 1908, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "unknown, before 3000 BC", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p3", "electronegativity_pauling": 2.05, "electron_affinity": 101.059, "ionization_energies": [ 834, 1594.9, 2440, 4260, 5400, 10400 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p>Antimony is a fascinating metalloid, meaning it shares properties with both metals and non-metals. When pure, it is a shiny, silvery-grey substance that is surprisingly brittle\u2014so brittle that it can be easily crushed into a powder! It does not react with air or water at room temperature, making it quite stable, but it will catch fire if heated strongly, producing a thick white smoke.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Like many elements, antimony comes in different forms called isotopes, which vary slightly in weight. In nature, you will find two stable, naturally occurring isotopes of antimony: <sup>121<\/sup>Sb and <sup>123<\/sup>Sb. Scientists have also created about 37 artificial, radioactive versions in laboratories, but these break down over time.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>Antimony is not very common\u2014it ranks 63rd in abundance in the Earth's crust, making it as rare as silver! Although pure, native antimony is occasionally found in nature, it is almost always discovered locked inside a sulfide mineral called <strong>stibnite<\/strong>. Today, China is the largest miner and producer of this mineral, providing the lion's share of the world's antimony.<\/p>", "History": "<p>Antimony has an incredibly rich and ancient history, especially in places like India, Egypt, and the Middle East. As early as 3100 BC in predynastic Egypt, crushed stibnite was used as an eye cosmetic known as <em>kohl<\/em>.<\/p><p>In <strong>India<\/strong>, this same mineral has been known for millennia as <em>Surma<\/em> or <em>Anjanam<\/em>. Applied to the eyelids, Surma was a traditional staple believed to protect the eyes from the glaring sun and ward off infections. Ancient Indian medicinal practices, such as Ayurveda and Unani (specifically the alchemy-like branch called <em>Rasashastra<\/em>), carefully processed antimony into various therapeutic treatments.<\/p><p>Across the world, ancient scholars like Pliny the Elder and early Arabic alchemists wrote extensively about antimony's unique properties. In 1540, the Italian metallurgist Vannoccio Biringuccio published one of the first detailed guides on how to isolate pure antimony metal.<\/p><p>In modern times, antimony played a starring role in Indian medical history. In 1920, the renowned Indian physician <strong>Dr. Upendranath Brahmachari<\/strong> synthesized an antimony-based drug called <em>urea stibamine<\/em>. This was a miraculous cure for kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis), a deadly tropical disease. His discovery saved millions of lives globally and earned him multiple Nobel Prize nominations!<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Today, antimony is an unsung hero of modern industry. Because it is so brittle on its own, it is almost always mixed (alloyed) with other metals like lead and tin to make them stronger and harder. These alloys are used to make bullets, durable solders, and plain bearings for machinery.<\/p><p>You can also find antimony hard at work inside car batteries (lead-acid batteries), where it helps stiffen the lead plates. Additionally, antimony compounds are heavily used to make flame-retardant materials for clothing, toys, and aircraft, keeping us safe from fires. Finally, highly purified antimony is used in tiny amounts to help create the semiconductors and microchips that power our electronic devices.<\/p>" } }, "Te": { "symbol": "Te", "name": "Tellurium", "atomic": 52, "category": "metalloid", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b>Tellurium<\/b> is a rare, brittle, and silvery-white metalloid that bridges the gap between metals and non-metals. Discovered in 1782 in the mountains of modern-day Romania, this element is actually rarer on Earth than platinum! While tellurium wasn't used by ancient civilizations\u2014including in India, where it has no historical footprint\u2014it has become incredibly important in the modern world. Today, the Government of India classifies tellurium as a \"critical mineral\" because it is a key ingredient in advanced technologies like solar panels and thermoelectric devices. Though toxic in large amounts and known to give a person's breath a distinct garlic-like smell if exposed, tellurium is quietly powering the clean-energy revolution of tomorrow.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/c\/c1\/Tellurium2.jpg", "atomic_mass": 127.603, "density": 6.24, "melt": 722.66, "boil": 1261, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Franz-Joseph M\u00fcller von Reichenstein", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p4", "electronegativity_pauling": 2.1, "electron_affinity": 190.161, "ionization_energies": [ 869.3, 1790, 2698, 3610, 5668, 6820, 13200 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p>Tellurium is a fascinating element that falls into the \"metalloid\" category, meaning it acts a bit like a metal and a bit like a non-metal. It is chemically related to sulfur and selenium. When you find it in its pure, crystalline form, it is silvery-white and shines like a metal, but it is extremely brittle and can be easily crushed into a powder. One of its most unique quirks is that it is far more common out in the wider universe than it is here on Earth. When our planet was forming in the scorching early days of the solar system, tellurium turned into a gas and floated away into space, leaving very little behind in the Earth's crust!<\/p>", "Physical properties": "<p>Tellurium comes in two main forms, or \"allotropes\": a silvery-white crystal and a dark brown-black powder. The crystalline version is a semiconductor, which means it can carry electricity under certain conditions. Interestingly, tellurium conducts electricity slightly better when light shines on it! It has a very high melting point of about 450\u00b0C (841\u00b0F) and boils at nearly 988\u00b0C (1810\u00b0F), making it the most heat-resistant element in its chemical family. If you manage to melt it down, liquid tellurium is surprisingly corrosive and can easily eat through metals like copper, iron, and stainless steel.<\/p>", "Chemical properties": "<p>At the atomic level, crystalline tellurium is built like a spiral staircase. Its atoms form parallel, helical chains with three atoms making up each turn of the spiral. Because of this stable structure, the gray crystalline form of tellurium doesn't react much with the oxygen in the air at room temperature. It also doesn't evaporate easily. When it does form chemical bonds, it prefers to team up with metals, most famously combining with gold in nature to create unique minerals.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Isotopes are variations of an element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Tellurium has eight naturally occurring isotopes. Six of them are completely stable, but two (Tellurium-128 and Tellurium-130) are slightly radioactive. Don't worry, though\u2014Tellurium-128 has a half-life of 2.2 septillion years (that's 2.2 followed by 24 zeros!). This is the longest known half-life of any radioactive isotope, making it about 160 trillion times older than the entire universe! Scientists have also created over 30 artificial, short-lived radioactive versions of tellurium in laboratories to study its atomic behavior.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>Tellurium is one of the rarest solid elements on Earth. To put it in perspective, it is just as scarce in the Earth's crust as platinum! You can occasionally find pure tellurium in nature, but it usually prefers to bond with other metals. It is most famous for bonding with gold to form minerals like <i>calaverite<\/i>. While you won't find large mines dedicated solely to tellurium, it is typically collected as a bonus by-product when mining for copper or lead. In India, geologists have discovered promising tellurium deposits combined with bismuth and gold in the Parsoi area of Uttar Pradesh's Mahakoshal belt. Recognizing its growing importance for the future, the Indian government officially designated tellurium as one of 30 \"critical minerals\" in 2023, and public sector companies like Hindustan Copper Ltd (HCL) have taken steps to recover it during copper processing.<\/p>", "History": "<p>Tellurium was discovered in 1782 by Franz-Joseph M\u00fcller von Reichenstein, an Austrian mining inspector working in Transylvania (modern-day Romania). He was studying a strange gold ore and realized it contained an unknown element. After three years of rigorous testing, he noticed that when heated, this mystery metal gave off a white smoke that smelled strongly of radishes! The element was officially named \"tellurium\" in 1798 by German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth, drawing from the Latin word <i>tellus<\/i>, meaning \"Earth.\" While tellurium doesn't appear in ancient Indian texts or early history, it made a brief splash in the 1920s when scientists tried using it to stop car engines from knocking. The idea was abandoned because it gave the exhaust an unbearable garlic-like stench!<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Today, tellurium is a rising star in green technology. Its biggest modern use is in the manufacturing of high-efficiency cadmium telluride (CdTe) thin-film solar panels. In India, premier scientific institutions like the IITs and the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) are actively researching tellurium nanostructures to create even better solar cells, cutting-edge photodetectors, and thermoelectric devices that can turn waste heat directly into electricity. Aside from renewable energy, tellurium is mixed into copper, iron, and steel to make them easier to machine and cut. It is also added to rubber to help it withstand heat and wear.<\/p>", "Biological role": "<p>Tellurium has no known biological use for humans or animals. In fact, our bodies actively try to get rid of it! If a person is exposed to even small amounts of tellurium, their body converts it into a harmless gas called dimethyl telluride. The only side effect? It gives their breath and sweat an incredibly strong, pungent garlic odor that can last for weeks! However, some simple organisms handle it differently. Certain types of fungi can actually use tellurium as a substitute for sulfur when building proteins, and some bacteria have the fascinating ability to absorb toxic tellurium compounds and turn them into pure, metallic tellurium crystals right inside their cells.<\/p>" } }, "I": { "symbol": "I", "name": "Iodine", "atomic": 53, "category": "diatomic nonmetal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/I\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iodine (I)\">Iodine<\/a><\/b> is a fascinating chemical element, known for being a lustrous, purple-black solid that turns into a beautiful violet gas when heated. Sitting at number 53 on the periodic table, it's the heaviest stable member of the halogen family. While it was officially discovered in 1811 by a French chemist, its impact on human health has been observed for thousands of years. In ancient India, medical texts like the <i>Charaka Samhita<\/i> and <i>Sushruta Samhita<\/i> documented treatments for neck swellings known as <i>Galaganda<\/i> (goiter) using seaweed and burnt sponge\u2014materials we now know are packed with iodine! Today, iodine is famous for its role in keeping our thyroid glands healthy. It's so vital that a lack of it is the world's leading preventable cause of intellectual disabilities, which is why you often see \"iodized salt\" in your grocery store.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/c\/c2\/Iodine-sample.jpg", "atomic_mass": 126.904473, "density": 4.933, "melt": 386.85, "boil": 457.4, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Bernard Courtois", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p5", "electronegativity_pauling": 2.66, "electron_affinity": 295.1531, "ionization_energies": [ 1008.4, 1845.9, 3180 ], "sections": { "History": "<p>The official story of iodine's discovery begins in France in 1811. During the Napoleonic Wars, French chemist Bernard Courtois was working with seaweed ashes to make saltpetre for gunpowder. When he accidentally added too much sulfuric acid to his mixture, a stunning cloud of violet vapor arose and crystallized into dark crystals on cold surfaces. He had discovered a new element! The name \"iodine\" comes from the ancient Greek word <i>iod\u0113s<\/i>, which means \"violet,\" perfectly describing the color of its gas.<\/p><p>However, humanity's relationship with iodine stretches back much further. Long before it was identified as an element, ancient civilizations recognized the health problems caused by its absence. In ancient India, the medical condition we now call goiter (an enlarged thyroid gland) was known as <i>Galaganda<\/i>. Ancient Ayurvedic texts like the <i>Charaka Samhita<\/i> and <i>Sushruta Samhita<\/i> recommended treating it with substances like seaweed, which are naturally rich in iodine. Fast forward to the modern era, India played a pivotal role in the global fight against iodine deficiency. In the 1950s, Indian nutrition scientist <b>Dr. Vulimiri Ramalingaswami<\/b> conducted the famous \"Kangra Valley Experiment\" in Himachal Pradesh. His groundbreaking research proved that goiter was caused by iodine deficiency and could be prevented by simply adding it to salt. Thanks to this, India became the first South Asian country to implement Universal Salt Iodization, with public health leaders like <b>Dr. Chandrakant S. Pandav<\/b> (often called the \"Iodine Man of India\") ensuring its success and saving millions from preventable health issues.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Isotopes are different versions of the same element that have different weights. In nature, almost all iodine exists as a single, stable version called Iodine-127. However, scientists have discovered many radioactive versions, which can be incredibly useful\u2014or sometimes dangerous.<\/p><p>The longest-living radioactive version is iodine-129, which has a half-life of over 16 million years! Most of the iodine-129 on Earth today comes from human nuclear activities. Other radioactive versions, like iodine-123 and iodine-125, have much shorter lives but are everyday superheroes in hospitals. Because our bodies naturally send all the iodine we consume straight to our thyroid gland, doctors can use these slightly radioactive isotopes to take special pictures of the thyroid or to treat conditions like thyroid cancer.<\/p><p>There is also iodine-131, which is often released during nuclear accidents. Because the thyroid quickly absorbs it, it can cause damage and increase the risk of cancer. That's why people living near nuclear accidents are sometimes given regular (stable) iodine tablets\u2014if the thyroid is already full of safe iodine, it won't absorb the dangerous radioactive kind!<\/p>", "Everyday Uses": "<p>While you might know iodine best from the small bottle of brown liquid used to clean scrapes and cuts, it has many other jobs! About half of all the iodine produced in the world is used to make special chemical compounds for industry. It's a key ingredient in animal feed, food stabilizers, dyes, and even in photography. It's also an essential part of the \"radiocontrast\" dyes that doctors inject into the body to make X-ray and CT scans clearer. Because it's generally safe and absorbs X-rays well, it's perfect for helping doctors see inside us. Minor uses include helping clear smog and even \"cloud seeding\" to encourage rain.<\/p>", "Why Our Bodies Need It": "<p>Iodine is absolutely essential for life. In fact, it is the heaviest element that living organisms commonly need! Your body uses iodine to make special thyroid hormones that regulate your growth, metabolism, and development.<\/p><p>If a person doesn't get enough iodine from their diet, their thyroid gland works overtime trying to capture whatever little iodine is available, causing it to swell up into a condition known as a goiter. Historically, India had a famous \"goiter belt\" along the sub-Himalayan and Terai regions because heavy rainfall and flooding washed the natural iodine out of the soil. Later research showed that this soil depletion affected almost all regions of India, making it a nationwide challenge.<\/p><p>Because iodine is so crucial for brain development in babies and children, health organizations worldwide focus on making sure everyone gets enough. This is mostly done by adding a tiny amount of iodine to everyday table salt\u2014a simple trick that has drastically improved global health.<\/p>" } }, "Xe": { "symbol": "Xe", "name": "Xenon", "atomic": 54, "category": "noble gas", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 54 (Xe)", "extract_html": "<p><b>Xenon<\/b> is a chemical element with the symbol <b>Xe<\/b> and atomic number 54. It is a colorless, dense, odorless noble gas found in Earth's atmosphere in trace amounts. Although generally unreactive, xenon can undergo a few chemical reactions such as the formation of xenon hexafluoroplatinate, the first noble gas compound to be synthesized. Known for its beautiful blue glow in electrical discharge tubes, xenon has many modern applications, from lighting to space exploration.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/5\/5d\/Xenon-glow.jpg", "atomic_mass": 131.2936, "density": 5.894, "melt": 161.4, "boil": 165.051, "phase": "Gas", "discovered_by": "William Ramsay", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6", "electronegativity_pauling": 2.6, "electron_affinity": -77, "ionization_energies": [ 1170.4, 2046.4, 3099.4 ], "sections": { "History": "<p>Xenon was discovered in 1898 by Scottish chemist Sir William Ramsay and his assistant, Morris Travers. They found it in the leftover residue after evaporating liquid air. Its name comes from the Greek word <i>x\u00e9nos<\/i>, which means 'stranger' or 'foreigner'\u2014a fitting name for an element that was hiding as a rare guest in the air!<\/p><p>Interestingly, there is a strong historical connection between the discovery of xenon and Indian science. Morris Travers, the co-discoverer of xenon, later traveled to India and became the founding Director of the prestigious <b>Indian Institute of Science (IISc)<\/b> in Bangalore in 1909. His foundational work helped establish one of India's most important scientific research institutions.<\/p>", "Characteristics": "<p>Xenon is a noble gas, meaning it sits in the far-right column of the periodic table. Because its outer electron shell is completely full, xenon is generally very stable and prefers to keep to itself rather than react with other elements. It is colorless, odorless, and heavy. In fact, if you could fill a balloon with xenon, it would drop to the floor like a rock because it is about 4.5 times heavier than Earth's air!<\/p><p>When an electrical current is passed through xenon gas, it emits a brilliant, glowing blue light. For a long time, scientists thought xenon couldn't form chemical compounds at all. However, in 1962, chemists proved that xenon could indeed react with highly reactive elements like fluorine and oxygen, breaking the long-held belief that noble gases were completely inert.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Xenon exists in nature as a mix of several different forms, called isotopes. There are seven stable isotopes of xenon, and a couple of others that are very slightly radioactive but have incredibly long lifespans.<\/p><p>Scientists use xenon isotopes like atomic clocks to study the history of our solar system. By looking at the types of xenon found in meteorites, researchers can learn about the formation of the Earth and the early solar system. In modern research, Indian scientists have also tracked radioactive xenon and krypton isotopes in atmospheric monitoring\u2014for instance, measuring traces of these gases in Jodhpur, India, following global nuclear events to study atmospheric transport.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Because of its unique properties, xenon is used in many incredible ways! Its brilliant light is used in high-intensity photographic flashes, IMAX movie projectors, and even high-end car headlights.<\/p><p>In medicine, xenon is a highly effective, though expensive, anesthetic that is safe for the human body and helps protect the brain and heart during surgeries.<\/p><p>One of the most futuristic uses of xenon is in space exploration. Xenon is the preferred fuel for 'ion thrusters'\u2014advanced engines that push spacecraft through the vacuum of space. The <b>Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)<\/b> actively uses xenon-based stationary plasma thrusters. For example, ISRO's GSAT-9 (South Asia Satellite) utilized a xenon electric propulsion system for maintaining its orbit, making satellites much lighter and more efficient by reducing the need for heavy chemical fuels. Additionally, Indian researchers have utilized xenon in specialized balloon-borne hard X-ray astronomy projects, continuing to prove that this rare 'stranger' gas is essential for exploring the universe!<\/p>" } }, "Cs": { "symbol": "Cs", "name": "Cesium", "atomic": 55, "category": "alkali metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cs\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cesium (Cs)\">Cesium<\/a><\/b> is a rare, soft, silvery-golden alkali metal that holds a special place in the world of chemistry and modern physics. Known for being extremely reactive, it bursts into flames when exposed to air and reacts explosively with water\u2014even at freezing temperatures! Amazingly, it has such a low melting point (28.5 &deg;C or 83.3 &deg;F) that it can literally melt from the warmth of your hand. Because of its extreme reactivity, cesium is never found free in nature. Today, its most famous use is in keeping the world perfectly on time: atomic clocks using cesium are so precise they won't lose a single second in millions of years. In India, cesium's importance is growing rapidly. It has been designated a 'critical mineral' for its role in advanced technology, and India\u2019s Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) has made groundbreaking contributions by successfully isolating radioactive Cesium-137 from nuclear waste for life-saving medical treatments and industrial applications.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/3\/3d\/Cesium.jpg", "atomic_mass": 132.905451966, "density": 1.93, "melt": 301.7, "boil": 944, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Robert Bunsen", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s1", "electronegativity_pauling": 0.79, "electron_affinity": 45.505, "ionization_energies": [ 375.7, 2234.3, 3400 ], "sections": { "History & Discovery": "<p>The story of <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cs\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cesium (Cs)\">cesium<\/a> begins in 1860 with two pioneering German scientists, Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff. Using a newly invented tool called a spectroscope, they examined mineral water from a spring and spotted two bright blue lines that no one had ever seen before. Because of this brilliant sky-blue color, they named the new element \"cesium,\" from the Latin word <i>caesius<\/i>, meaning \"sky blue.\" While ancient Indian texts, such as those detailing traditional <i>Rasayan Shastra<\/i> (alchemy), did not explicitly mention cesium\u2014as it requires highly advanced modern tools to isolate\u2014India has fully embraced the element in modern times. In the 20th and 21st centuries, Indian science institutions built upon these early European discoveries, turning their attention to mastering the complex nuclear physics of cesium isotopes for peaceful and strategic applications.<\/p>", "Properties & Occurrence": "<p>As an alkali metal, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cs\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cesium (Cs)\">cesium<\/a> is famously dramatic. It is the most electropositive and alkaline stable element, boasting the largest atomic radius of any non-radioactive element. This large size makes it highly willing to give away its outermost electron, resulting in violent chemical reactions. Physically, it is one of the very few metals\u2014along with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\">gold<\/a> and <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a>\u2014that has a distinct color, exhibiting a beautiful silvery-gold tint. It is incredibly soft and is one of just five elemental metals that can be liquid at or near room temperature. In nature, it is quite rare and typically found in trace amounts within minerals like pollucite. Excitingly, recent geological explorations in India have uncovered significant rare earth deposits containing cesium in the Jhalda-II block of Purulia, West Bengal. This promising local reserve highlights the geographical potential of the Indian subcontinent to supply essential critical minerals for future technology.<\/p>", "Applications & Indian Contributions": "<p>Beyond its iconic role in atomic clocks that define the modern \"second\" and power GPS systems worldwide, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cs\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cesium (Cs)\">cesium<\/a> is a critical material in the oil industry, where heavy cesium-formate fluids are used in deep drilling. However, some of the most remarkable modern applications come directly from Indian scientific innovation. Scientists at India's Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) achieved a major breakthrough in managing nuclear waste by developing an indigenous process to recover the radioactive isotope <b>Cesium-137<\/b>. Rather than just storing the waste, they brilliantly turned it into a valuable resource by vitrifying it (turning it into a stable glass) inside special \"pencils.\" Today, these Indian-made cesium pencils are deployed commercially in medical irradiators used for blood irradiation, cancer treatment, and sterilizing food or medical supplies. Recognizing its incredible strategic value, the Indian government recently overhauled policies to incentivize the domestic mining of cesium, officially classifying it as a critical mineral to secure the nation's technological independence.<\/p>" } }, "Ba": { "symbol": "Ba", "name": "Barium", "atomic": 56, "category": "alkaline earth metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b>Barium<\/b> is a soft, silvery-white metal that you almost never see in its pure form because it reacts so easily with air! In the modern world, it's famous for giving fireworks a brilliant green color and for its crucial role in the oil and gas industry. Although it wasn't isolated until 1808 by Sir Humphry Davy, Barium holds a massive significance in <b>India's geological landscape<\/b>. The <b>Mangampet deposit<\/b> in Andhra Pradesh, India, is the single largest bedded deposit of baryte (barium sulfate) in the entire world! Today, Barium is a hidden hero in everything from drilling fluids to medical imaging.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/f\/f5\/Barium_%2856_Ba%29.jpg", "atomic_mass": 137.3277, "density": 3.51, "melt": 1000, "boil": 2118, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Carl Wilhelm Scheele", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2", "electronegativity_pauling": 0.89, "electron_affinity": 13.954, "ionization_energies": [ 502.9, 965.2, 3600 ], "sections": { "Characteristics & Physical Properties": "<p>Imagine a metal so soft you can cut it with a knife, yet so reactive it must be stored under oil to prevent it from rapidly tarnishing in the air. That's Barium! When pure, it's a shiny, silvery-white alkaline earth metal, but it eagerly binds with oxygen and water. Because it's so reactive, it never occurs in nature as a free element. Instead, you'll find it locked away in minerals like baryte (barium sulfate) and witherite (barium carbonate).<\/p>", "Geological Significance in India": "<p>While ancient Indian texts like the Ayurveda heavily documented metals like gold and iron, Barium was quietly waiting beneath the earth. Today, India is a powerhouse of Barium production! The <b>Mangampet deposit<\/b> in the Kadapa district of Andhra Pradesh is globally renowned. Discovered in the 1960s, it's the <b>world's largest single deposit of bedded barytes<\/b>. Formed millions of years ago by ancient volcanic activity, this site is so crucial that it was declared a National Geological Monument in 1982. The massive reserves here make India one of the leading global suppliers of this vital mineral.<\/p>", "History": "<p>The story of Barium begins in the 17th century when alchemists in Italy were fascinated by \"Bologna stones\" that glowed in the dark after being heated. However, the elemental form wasn't discovered until 1808, when the brilliant English chemist Sir Humphry Davy managed to isolate it using electricity. As modern science grew in India, pioneering chemists like <b>Prafulla Chandra Ray<\/b> (often called the father of Indian chemistry) studied various complex chemical compounds, connecting traditional Indian metallurgical knowledge with the rigorous modern study of elements like Barium.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Barium is a busy element! Most of the Barium mined in places like Mangampet, India, is used as a \"weighting agent\" in the oil and gas industry to help drill deep wells safely. But Barium has a flashy side too\u2014barium compounds are the secret ingredient that gives fireworks their spectacular green explosions. In the medical world, a chalky \"barium swallow\" drink helps doctors take clear X-ray images of the digestive system. It's also used to remove unwanted gases from vacuum tubes, and in creating special kinds of glass and ceramics.<\/p>" } }, "La": { "symbol": "La", "name": "Lanthanum", "atomic": 57, "category": "lanthanide", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 57 (La)", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/La\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lanthanum (La)\">Lanthanum<\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>La<\/b>, atomic number 57) is a soft, silvery-white metal that gives its name to the entire \"lanthanide\" series of the periodic table. It is highly reactive, meaning it is never found pure in nature, but instead hides within rich mineral sands like monazite and bastn\u00e4site. Lanthanum is a modern technological marvel, secretly powering everything from the high-end camera lenses in our smartphones to the massive batteries in hybrid electric vehicles. In India, lanthanum holds immense strategic importance due to the country's vast coastal reserves of monazite sand, placing it at the heart of the nation's push for self-reliance in rare-earth technologies.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/f\/f7\/Lanthanum.jpg", "atomic_mass": 138.905477, "density": 6.162, "melt": 1193, "boil": 3737, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Carl Gustaf Mosander", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 5d1", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.1, "electron_affinity": 53, "ionization_energies": [ 538.1, 1067, 1850.3, 4819, 5940 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/La\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lanthanum (La)\">Lanthanum<\/a> is the prototype of the lanthanide series. It is a soft, malleable metal\u2014so soft you can easily cut it with a knife! When freshly cut, it shines with a brilliant silvery-white metallic luster, but it quickly tarnishes and oxidizes when exposed to air, turning dark. Because it is highly reactive, it even reacts with water to form lanthanum hydroxide and hydrogen gas. Despite its name being part of the \"rare earth\" elements, lanthanum is actually quite common in the Earth's crust\u2014it is nearly three times as abundant as <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">lead<\/a>. However, it is challenging to separate from its neighboring rare-earth metals.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>In nature, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/La\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lanthanum (La)\">lanthanum<\/a> is primarily made up of two isotopes: stable Lanthanum-139 (which makes up about 99.91% of natural lanthanum) and primordial, long-lived radioactive Lanthanum-138 (making up the remaining 0.09%). Lanthanum-138 has an incredibly long half-life of over 100 billion years\u2014much older than the universe itself! Scientists have also created dozens of artificial, highly radioactive isotopes in laboratories, though most of them decay away in just a few minutes or hours.<\/p>", "History": "<p>The element was discovered in 1839 by the Swedish chemist Carl Gustaf Mosander. While studying a mineral called cerite, Mosander noticed an impurity that he successfully extracted by treating the mineral with dilute nitric acid. He named this new substance <i>lanthana<\/i>, from the Ancient Greek word <i>lanthanein<\/i>, which translates to \"to lie hidden\"\u2014a perfect name for an element so difficult to find and isolate! For many decades, isolating pure lanthanum was incredibly difficult until modern chemical processes were developed.<br><br>In the Indian context, the history of lanthanum is deeply intertwined with the discovery of massive <b>monazite sand<\/b> deposits along the coasts of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and Odisha. In the early 20th century, these rich beach sands drew global attention. Recognizing their strategic value, India established Indian Rare Earths Limited (IREL) in 1950. Operating facilities like the Rare Earth Refining Unit in Aluva, Kerala, India took control of its domestic lanthanum and rare-earth processing, ensuring these \"hidden\" elements played a vital role in national development.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/La\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lanthanum (La)\">Lanthanum<\/a> is the silent engine of modern green technology and high-end optics. Its most famous application is in the massive Nickel-Metal Hydride (NiMH) batteries that power millions of hybrid electric cars worldwide; a single hybrid car battery can contain over 10 kilograms of lanthanum! When added to glass, lanthanum oxide improves the refractive index, which is why it is widely used to manufacture professional camera lenses, telescope optics, and even the glass in modern smartphone cameras.<br><br>In India, lanthanum is critical to the country's <b>\"Mine-to-Magnet\"<\/b> and rare-earth corridor initiatives. Through state-owned IREL's Rare Earth Extraction Plant (REEP) in Odisha, India actively processes lanthanum to reduce dependence on foreign imports. Beyond green tech, lanthanum is famously found in your pocket: it is a key ingredient in <i>mischmetal<\/i>, a special alloy used to make the sparking flints in everyday lighters!<\/p>", "Biological role": "<p>For most of history, scientists believed that <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/La\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lanthanum (La)\">lanthanum<\/a> had absolutely no biological role in any living organism. In human medicine, its main use is actually pharmacological: a compound called lanthanum carbonate is prescribed to patients with severe kidney disease to help absorb excess phosphate from their diet. However, in a surprising recent discovery, scientists found that certain unique bacteria (called methanotrophs) living in extreme volcanic mudpots actually rely on lanthanum as a vital nutrient! These bacteria use lanthanum as a cofactor for an enzyme that helps them consume methane gas, proving that even \"rare earths\" can be the secret to life for some of Earth's most resilient microbes.<\/p>" } }, "Ce": { "symbol": "Ce", "name": "Cerium", "atomic": 58, "category": "lanthanide", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ce\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cerium (Ce)\">Cerium<\/a><\/b> (symbol <b>Ce<\/b>, atomic number 58) is a fascinating, silvery-white rare-earth metal that easily tarnishes in the air. Despite the name \"rare-earth,\" it is actually quite common\u2014about as abundant as <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Cu\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Copper (Cu)\">copper<\/a>! Cerium is incredibly useful in our daily lives, playing a hidden but vital role in everything from the self-cleaning ovens in our kitchens to the catalytic converters that reduce pollution from our cars. In India, cerium holds special geographical significance, as it is found abundantly in the monazite sands along the coastal regions of Kerala and Tamil Nadu, making the country one of the world's significant sources of this crucial element.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/0\/0d\/Cerium2.jpg", "atomic_mass": 140.1161, "density": 6.77, "melt": 1068, "boil": 3716, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Martin Heinrich Klaproth", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 5d1 4f1", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.12, "electron_affinity": 55, "ionization_energies": [ 534.4, 1050, 1949, 3547, 6325, 7490 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p>When freshly cut, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ce\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cerium (Ce)\">cerium<\/a> is a beautiful, shiny metal that looks a bit like <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a>, but it is much softer\u2014so soft you can cut it with a knife! However, it doesn't stay shiny for long. When exposed to air, it quickly reacts with oxygen to form a yellow-gray layer of rust, much like an apple turning brown when left on the counter. Cerium is also pyrophoric, meaning if you scratch or strike it, it can spark and catch fire easily. Because of this exciting property, it is often mixed with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Fe\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Iron (Fe)\">iron<\/a> to make \"flints\" for cigarette lighters and fire starters used by campers.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>In nature, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ce\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cerium (Ce)\">cerium<\/a> comes in a mix of four different versions, called isotopes. These are Cerium-136, Cerium-138, Cerium-140, and Cerium-142. The most common by far is Cerium-140, making up nearly 90% of all natural cerium. Scientists consider these four natural isotopes to be stable, meaning they don't break down quickly over time. In laboratories, scientists have created many other artificial isotopes of cerium, but these are radioactive and break down very fast\u2014some disappearing in just a few minutes! These radioactive forms are usually created as byproducts when heavier elements like <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/U\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Uranium (U)\">uranium<\/a> are split apart in nuclear reactors.<\/p>", "History": "<p><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ce\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cerium (Ce)\">Cerium<\/a> was discovered in 1803 by scientists in Sweden and Germany working independently. The Swedish chemist J\u00f6ns Jakob Berzelius named the new element after Ceres, a dwarf planet in our solar system that had been discovered just two years earlier (which in turn was named after the Roman goddess of agriculture). For many decades, cerium remained a scientific curiosity. However, its story took an interesting turn in India. During the early 20th century, massive deposits of monazite sand were discovered along the coastal tracts of Kerala, particularly the Neendakara\u2013Kayamkulam belt. These golden-yellow sands are rich in rare-earth elements, heavily dominated by cerium (often classified as monazite-(Ce)). Recognizing the strategic importance of these minerals, the Indian government established Indian Rare Earths Limited (IREL) after independence to carefully manage and extract these valuable resources. Today, India\u2019s monazite sands remain a crucial part of the global rare-earth supply chain.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>You might not see it, but <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ce\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Cerium (Ce)\">cerium<\/a> is hard at work all around you! Its most famous job is in your car's catalytic converter, where cerium oxide helps clean up toxic exhaust gases before they leave the tailpipe. It is also the magic ingredient used to polish glass surfaces to a flawless finish, from the screen of your smartphone to giant telescope lenses. When added to glass during manufacturing, cerium can block harmful UV rays and remove unwanted green tints. Modern Indian scientific institutions, such as the CSIR-National Institute for Interdisciplinary Science and Technology (NIIST) in Thiruvananthapuram, have made significant contributions to cerium research. Indian scientists have developed highly efficient methods to extract cerium from local monazite sands and are pioneering new uses for cerium nanoparticles in cutting-edge biomedical applications and environmental protection technologies.<\/p>" } }, "Pr": { "symbol": "Pr", "name": "Praseodymium", "atomic": 59, "category": "lanthanide", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b>Praseodymium<\/b> (symbol <b>Pr<\/b>, atomic number 59) is a soft, silvery, and highly valued rare-earth metal. Known for its magnetic, electrical, and optical magic, it sits in the lanthanide series of the periodic table. While it's too eager to react with its surroundings to be found in its pure form in nature, it is widely used in our modern world. In fact, pure praseodymium slowly develops a cool green oxide coating when exposed to air! Though not known to ancient Indian metallurgists who worked with elements like gold and iron, today it holds immense strategic value. Under India's National Critical Mineral Mission, praseodymium is a key focus for its role in advanced technologies, with vital rare earth corridors being developed across states like Tamil Nadu, Odisha, and Kerala to secure the future of renewable energy and electric vehicles.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/c\/c7\/Praseodymium.jpg", "atomic_mass": 140.907662, "density": 6.77, "melt": 1208, "boil": 3403, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Carl Auer von Welsbach", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f3", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.13, "electron_affinity": 93, "ionization_energies": [ 527, 1020, 2086, 3761, 5551 ], "sections": { "Physical properties": "<p>Praseodymium is a soft, silvery metal that can be easily shaped and stretched. It is paramagnetic at room temperature, which means it is weakly attracted to magnets. Unlike some other rare-earth metals that have complicated magnetic behaviors at freezing temperatures, praseodymium keeps things simple and stays paramagnetic unless it gets extremely cold. It is strong and malleable, making it a wonderful ingredient for specialized metal alloys.<\/p>", "Chemical properties": "<p>When left out in the open air, praseodymium slowly tarnishes. Much like how iron forms rust, praseodymium grows a flaky green oxide crust; a small piece can completely corrode away in about a year! Because of this, it is usually stored in protective oil or sealed glass. It also reacts nicely with hot water to form praseodymium hydroxide, and it readily combines with all halogens (like chlorine and fluorine) to create various interesting salts. Most often, it prefers a '+3' oxidation state, giving its compounds a beautiful yellowish-green color that scientists love using to tint specialized glasses.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>In nature, praseodymium is as pure as it gets: it has only one stable, naturally occurring form, known as praseodymium-141. This makes it what scientists call a 'monoisotopic' element. Its atomic core holds exactly 82 neutrons\u2014a 'magic number' in physics that grants it extra stability. While researchers have created 38 other artificial, radioactive versions of praseodymium in labs, almost all of them break down in less than a minute. The longest-lasting artificial form is praseodymium-143, which sticks around for about 13 and a half days before decaying.<\/p>", "History": "<p>The story of praseodymium begins in the mid-1800s when European chemists were trying to untangle a mysterious earth called 'didymium'. For decades, they thought didymium was a single element. But in 1885, a clever Austrian chemist named Carl Auer von Welsbach managed to split it into two distinct new elements. Because one of them formed bright green salts, he named it 'praseodymium', combining the Greek words 'prasinos' (meaning leek-green) and 'didymos' (meaning twin). Its twin was named neodymium. Historically, ancient Indian alchemists (practitioners of <i>Rasashastra<\/i>) did not know of this element, as their profound metallurgical expertise focused on base and noble metals. However, the legacy of Indian metallurgy has evolved, and today Indian scientists are at the forefront of unlocking the secrets of rare earths like praseodymium.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>Despite being called a 'rare-earth' metal, praseodymium isn't actually that rare! It is more common in the Earth's crust than elements like tin or boron. However, it is never found naturally by itself; it is always mingled with its rare-earth siblings like cerium, lanthanum, and neodymium. For India, this element is of massive geographical and strategic importance. India is home to about 6% of the world's rare earth reserves. Praseodymium is primarily extracted from a mineral called monazite, which is abundantly found in the coastal beach sands of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Odisha, and Andhra Pradesh, as well as in inland deposits in Jharkhand and West Bengal. Recognizing its importance, India is developing 'Rare Earth Corridors' to seamlessly link the mining and processing of these vital sands.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Praseodymium has a colorful resume! In the 1920s, it was first used to give glass and ceramics a vibrant, warm yellow-orange hue known as 'Praseodymium Yellow.' Today, its uses are much more high-tech. Because of its unique light-filtering and glowing properties, it is essential in creating fiber optic cables, lasers, and even the safety goggles worn by welders and glassblowers. But its biggest claim to fame is its partnership with neodymium. Together, they form incredibly strong, durable permanent magnets (NdPr magnets) used in wind turbines, electric vehicle motors, and modern electronics. Indian scientific contributions are heavily focused on these applications. Modern Indian researchers are developing advanced sensors\u2014such as cobalt-doped praseodymium orthoferrite for CO2 sensing\u2014and supercapacitors for energy storage. Additionally, Indian chemical engineers are pioneering advanced solvent extraction techniques to efficiently separate praseodymium from its twin, neodymium, aiming to power the nation's clean energy revolution by 2030.<\/p>" } }, "Nd": { "symbol": "Nd", "name": "Neodymium", "atomic": 60, "category": "lanthanide", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><strong>Neodymium (Nd)<\/strong> is a fascinating, silvery-white metal that belongs to a group of elements known as the rare-earth metals. Despite the name \"rare,\" it is actually fairly common in the Earth's crust\u2014about as common as familiar metals like copper, cobalt, or nickel! When exposed to air, neodymium quickly gets a colorful tarnish, producing pink, purple, and yellow rust-like compounds.<\/p>\n\n<p>Most famously, neodymium is the magic ingredient behind the world's strongest permanent magnets. You can find these powerful magnets in everything from tiny earbuds and smartphone speakers to massive wind turbines and electric vehicle motors. But its talents don't stop there! Neodymium is also used to color glass with a beautiful reddish-purple tint that changes color under different lighting, and it's a key part of powerful lasers used in scientific research.<\/p>\n\n<p>While neodymium was discovered in Austria in 1885, today it has immense global importance, particularly in India. India holds about 6-8% of the world's rare earth reserves, with significant neodymium-bearing monazite sands along the coasts of Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu. Driven by initiatives like the <em>Atmanirbhar Bharat<\/em> (Self-Reliant India) and the National Critical Mineral Mission, India is aggressively scaling up its own neodymium production to power the green energy revolution and secure its future in advanced technologies.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/c\/c9\/Neodymium_%2860_Nd%29.jpg", "atomic_mass": 144.2423, "density": 7.01, "melt": 1297, "boil": 3347, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Carl Auer von Welsbach", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f4", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.14, "electron_affinity": 184.87, "ionization_energies": [ 533.1, 1040, 2130, 3900 ], "sections": { "Physical properties": "\n<h3>Physical Properties<\/h3>\n<p>In its pure form, neodymium is a hard, shiny metal with a bright, silvery luster. Unlike a regular kitchen magnet that sticks to your fridge, pure neodymium is only weakly magnetic at room temperature (a property called paramagnetism). However, when cooled down to extremely low temperatures (below -253 \u00b0C), it reveals complex magnetic behaviors.<\/p>\n<p>To create the super-strong magnets we use every day, neodymium is mixed (or alloyed) with iron and boron. This magical combination creates the legendary \"NdFeB\" magnets, which are incredibly strong for their small size and weight.<\/p>\n", "Chemical properties": "\n<h3>Chemical Properties<\/h3>\n<p>Neodymium is a very active element. If you leave a piece of neodymium metal out in the open air, it will quickly tarnish and rust, much like iron. The rust layer it forms doesn't protect the metal; instead, it flakes off, allowing the rest of the metal to continue corroding until it completely turns into powder.
