Because of this, neodymium is usually stored in mineral oil or sealed tightly away from air and moisture.<\/p>\n<p>When it reacts, neodymium typically forms compounds with a +3 charge, which often have beautiful pastel colors like violet, pink, and lilac. It can react slowly with cold water (or quickly with hot water) to produce hydrogen gas, and it eagerly combines with elements like fluorine, chlorine, bromine, and iodine to form colorful salts.<\/p>\n", "Isotopes": "\n<h3>Isotopes<\/h3>\n<p>Atoms of the same element can have different weights, called isotopes. In nature, neodymium is a mix of five stable isotopes (meaning they don't break down over time) and two very mildly radioactive ones. The most common stable isotope is Neodymium-142.<\/p>\n<p>The two natural radioactive isotopes, Neodymium-144 and Neodymium-150, have half-lives that are unimaginably long\u2014far longer than the age of the universe! Because they decay so incredibly slowly, they are completely safe to be around. Scientists even use the slow decay of other elements into neodymium to figure out the age of ancient rocks and meteorites, a technique known as samarium-neodymium dating.<\/p>\n", "History": "\n<h3>History<\/h3>\n<p>The story of neodymium is a tale of mistaken identity. In 1839, a Swedish chemist named Carl Gustaf Mosander extracted what he thought was a new element called \"didymium\" (meaning \"twin\" in Greek). For over 40 years, scientists believed didymium was a single, pure element.<\/p>\n<p>However, in 1885, an Austrian chemist named Carl Auer von Welsbach realized that didymium was actually a mixture of two different elements hiding together. He successfully separated them, naming the green-colored one praseodymium (\"green twin\") and the pink-colored one neodymium, which means \"new twin.\"<\/p>\n<p>For a long time, purifying neodymium was very difficult. It wasn't until the 1950s, using new techniques developed during World War II, that scientists were able to easily produce high-purity neodymium on a large scale.<\/p>\n", "Occurrence": "\n<h3>Where is it Found?<\/h3>\n<p>Despite being a \"rare-earth\" metal, neodymium is not actually rare\u2014it's widely distributed in the Earth's crust. However, it is never found naturally as a pure metal. Instead, it is locked inside minerals like monazite and bastn\u00e4site, mixed up with several other rare-earth elements.<\/p>\n<p>Today, China produces the vast majority of the world's commercial neodymium, but <strong>India plays a crucial and growing role in the global supply chain<\/strong>. India's coastal beaches, particularly in Andhra Pradesh (which holds about 30% of the country's monazite), Odisha, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu, are incredibly rich in monazite sands. Newer explorations have also found promising inland deposits in states like Arunachal Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh.<\/p>\n<p>Under the guidance of India's National Critical Mineral Mission and companies like IREL (India) Limited, the country is rapidly scaling up its mining and processing capabilities. This push aims to increase India's domestic production of neodymium to over 500 tonnes by 2027, securing a vital resource for the booming electric vehicle and wind energy markets.<\/p>\n", "Applications": "\n<h3>Modern Applications and Scientific Breakthroughs<\/h3>\n<p>Neodymium is the unsung hero of modern technology. Its most famous application is in <strong>neodymium magnets<\/strong> (NdFeB). These are the strongest permanent magnets commercially available. Because they are so powerful, they allow engineers to make electronic devices smaller and lighter. They are essential for smartphone speakers, hard disk drives, cordless tools, electric vehicle motors, and the massive generators inside wind turbines.<\/p>\n<p>In addition to magnets, neodymium is a fantastic glass additive. It gives glass a mesmerizing purple hue that shifts color depending on the lighting. This special glass is also used in powerful <strong>lasers<\/strong>, which are utilized in everything from medical eye surgery to cutting steel and even advanced nuclear fusion experiments.<\/p>\n<p><strong>A Modern Indian Scientific Breakthrough:<\/strong> Neodymium is not just a material for today's technology, but also tomorrow's. In a groundbreaking 2025 discovery, scientists at the <strong>Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research (JNCASR) in Bengaluru, India<\/strong>, unlocked a brand-new form of magnetism in neodymium nitride (NdN) thin films. They discovered that the magnetism in this material is driven by the <em>orbital motion<\/em> of electrons rather than their traditional \"spin.\" This major leap in the field of <strong>\"orbitronics\"<\/strong> paves the way for a future of ultra-fast, highly energy-efficient quantum devices and advanced computer memory, ensuring that neodymium remains at the cutting edge of global scientific innovation!<\/p>\n" } }, "Pm": { "symbol": "Pm", "name": "Promethium", "atomic": 61, "category": "lanthanide", "description": "", "extract_html": "\n <h2>The Stolen Fire of the Atomic Age<\/h2>\n <p><strong>Promethium<\/strong> (atomic number 61) is a rare and highly radioactive metal. In Greek mythology, Prometheus stole fire from the gods to give to humanity. Similarly, promethium offers a kind of \"nuclear fire\" that provides long-lasting power. In a beautiful cross-cultural parallel, the ancient Indian traditions revere <em>Agni<\/em>, the god of fire, who represents the spark of life and the transformative energy of the universe. Just as ancient Vedic texts describe Agni as an eternal flame, the steady radioactive glow of promethium serves as an enduring source of energy for modern technology.<\/p>\n <p>Because it is so radioactive, promethium does not naturally occur on Earth in large amounts\u2014it is constantly glowing and decaying. Instead, it was discovered in the fallout of nuclear reactions in 1945. Today, scientists at institutions like India's Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) study its unique properties, while space agencies around the world, including the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), explore similar radioisotope technologies to keep satellites and space probes powered in the freezing darkness of deep space.<\/p>\n ", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/5\/5b\/Promethium.jpg", "atomic_mass": 145, "density": 7.26, "melt": 1315, "boil": 3273, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Chien Shiung Wu", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f5", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.13, "electron_affinity": 12.45, "ionization_energies": [ 540, 1050, 2150, 3970 ], "sections": { "Physical properties": "\n <h3>A Glowing Metal<\/h3>\n <p>If you could safely hold a piece of promethium, you would see a silvery-white metal. But you wouldn't want to hold it for long! It is intensely radioactive. The radiation it emits causes the air around it to glow with a pale blue or greenish light in the dark. It is a solid metal at room temperature, but it melts at about 1,042 \u00b0C (1,908 \u00b0F).<\/p>\n <p>Like the eternal fires described in ancient Indian <em>Vedas<\/em>, promethium produces its own steady warmth and light as its atoms decay over time.<\/p>\n ", "Isotopes": "\n <h3>Unstable Atoms<\/h3>\n <p>Every element is made of atoms, and atoms have different variations called <em>isotopes<\/em>. Most elements have at least one stable, unchanging isotope. Promethium is an exception\u2014<strong>none of its isotopes are stable<\/strong>. Every single atom of promethium will eventually break apart (decay) into other elements, releasing energy.<\/p>\n <p>Its longest-lived isotope, Promethium-145, lasts for about 17.7 years before half of it disappears. The most useful isotope, Promethium-147, has a half-life of just 2.6 years. This fleeting, temporary nature means promethium is always transforming, echoing the ancient philosophical concepts of impermanence found in early Buddhist and Hindu thought across the Indian subcontinent.<\/p>\n ", "Occurrence": "\n <h3>Rarer Than Gold<\/h3>\n <p>You won't find promethium easily in nature. Because all of it decays so quickly, any promethium that existed when Earth was formed billions of years ago has long since turned into other elements. Today, the only natural promethium on Earth is created in tiny amounts when uranium ores undergo rare natural nuclear reactions.<\/p>\n <p>Scientists estimate there are less than 600 grams (about 1.3 pounds) of natural promethium in Earth's entire crust at any given moment! Almost all the promethium used in science and industry today is artificially created in nuclear reactors, such as those operated by the Department of Atomic Energy in India and similar organizations globally.<\/p>\n ", "History": "\n <h3>The Missing Element<\/h3>\n <p>For decades, scientists knew there had to be an element number 61 to fill a gap in the periodic table, but it was nowhere to be found. Researchers around the world searched for it in minerals and ores, often mistaking other elements for it.<\/p>\n <p>It wasn't until 1945, during the Manhattan Project in the United States, that chemists finally proved its existence by analyzing the radioactive byproducts of a nuclear reactor. Grace Mary Coryell, the wife of one of the discoverers, suggested the name \"promethium\" after the Greek titan Prometheus, signifying the brave new era of nuclear energy.<\/p>\n ", "Applications": "\n <h3>Powering the Future<\/h3>\n <p>Promethium's steady release of energy makes it incredibly useful. When placed inside a special material, its radiation creates a reliable light source that doesn't need electricity. It is also used to make <strong>atomic batteries<\/strong>. Unlike the chemical batteries in your phone, atomic batteries can last for years without needing a charge.<\/p>\n <p>These batteries are perfect for places where it's impossible to change a battery, such as pacemakers inside the human body or remote space probes. In India, modern space exploration spearheaded by ISRO relies on the deep understanding of such nuclear materials to design long-lasting power sources for missions reaching out to the Moon, Mars, and beyond, turning the \"stolen fire\" of promethium into a tool for cosmic discovery.<\/p>\n " } }, "Sm": { "symbol": "Sm", "name": "Samarium", "atomic": 62, "category": "lanthanide", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p>Samarium is a fascinating silvery-white metal with the symbol Sm and atomic number 62. Though it sounds like it might be from another world, samarium is part of the \"rare earth\" family (specifically, the lanthanides) and is found right here on Earth. Discovered in 1879 by French chemist Paul-\u00c9mile Lecoq de Boisbaudran, it was the very first chemical element to be named after a real person\u2014Vassili Samarsky-Bykhovets, a Russian mine official!<\/p>\n<p>Samarium is famous for making incredibly powerful magnets. When combined with cobalt to make \"samarium-cobalt\" magnets, it creates a magnetic force that is not only incredibly strong but can survive blistering temperatures\u2014over 700\u00b0C (1,292\u00b0F)\u2014without losing its power! This makes it a superstar in defense, aerospace, and everyday gadgets.<\/p>\n<p>In the medical world, a radioactive version of samarium (Samarium-153) is a cancer-fighting hero, used in medicines that target and kill cancer cells in bones. Another form (Samarium-149) acts as a safety sponge in nuclear reactors by soaking up stray neutrons.<\/p>\n<p>In India, samarium plays a critical strategic role. Extracted primarily from the rich monazite sands found along the Indian coastline, it is a key focus of India's \"National Critical Mineral Mission.\" Facilities like the Rare Earth Permanent Magnet (REPM) plant in Visakhapatnam are turning domestic samarium into high-tech magnets to build a self-reliant future in advanced technology!<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/8\/88\/Samarium-2.jpg", "atomic_mass": 150.362, "density": 7.52, "melt": 1345, "boil": 2173, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Lecoq de Boisbaudran", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f6", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.17, "electron_affinity": 15.63, "ionization_energies": [ 544.5, 1070, 2260, 3990 ], "sections": { "Physical properties": "<p>If you held a piece of samarium in your hand, it would feel similar to zinc in terms of hardness and weight. When freshly cut, it sparkles with a bright, silvery shine. However, if left out in the open air, it slowly tarnishes and loses its luster.<\/p>\n<p>Samarium loves to change its internal shape depending on the temperature and pressure. At room temperature, its atoms are arranged in one pattern, but if you heat it up to over 700\u00b0C (1,300\u00b0F), the atoms shift into a new arrangement. Heat it even more, and they shift again!<\/p>\n<p>One of the coolest physical quirks of samarium is its magnetic personality. While the metal itself is paramagnetic (weakly attracted to magnets) at room temperature, it becomes uniquely magnetic when chilled to nearly absolute zero. Furthermore, scientists have discovered that mixing a tiny amount of samarium into certain iron-based materials can turn them into \"superconductors\"\u2014materials that conduct electricity with zero resistance\u2014at relatively warm temperatures for superconductors!<\/p>", "Chemical properties": "<p>Samarium is quite a reactive metal. If you leave it exposed to air, it slowly rusts at room temperature. If it gets too hot (around 150\u00b0C or 302\u00b0F), it can even burst into flames! Because it loves reacting with oxygen and moisture, it has to be stored carefully, often sealed tightly under an inert gas like argon or submerged in mineral oil.<\/p>\n<p>When samarium meets water, a chemical dance begins. It reacts slowly with cold water but much more rapidly with hot water, bubbling up as it releases hydrogen gas and forms samarium hydroxide. If you drop it into certain acids, like dilute sulfuric acid, it dissolves easily and creates a beautiful pale-green to yellow liquid!<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>In nature, samarium is a mix of five perfectly stable forms (called isotopes) and two slightly radioactive ones that break down incredibly slowly. The most common form is Samarium-152, making up over a quarter of all natural samarium.<\/p>\n<p>One of its slightly radioactive forms, Samarium-147, decays so slowly\u2014taking over a hundred billion years\u2014that scientists use it as a \"geological clock.\" By measuring how much of it has broken down, geologists can determine the age of ancient rocks and meteorites!<\/p>\n<p>Samarium also has some fascinating artificial forms created in labs. Samarium-149 is famous for its ability to absorb neutrons, making it an essential \"safety net\" to control the reactions in nuclear power plants. On the medical frontier, Samarium-153, which is highly radioactive but short-lived (with a half-life of less than two days), is used in a drug called Quadramet. When injected into patients, it safely travels to the bones and destroys pain-causing cancer cells.<\/p>", "History": "<p>The story of samarium is a tale of international discovery. In the late 19th century, scientists across Europe were racing to discover new elements in strange minerals. French chemist Paul-\u00c9mile Lecoq de Boisbaudran officially discovered samarium in Paris in 1879. He extracted it from a heavy, dark mineral called \"samarskite.\"<\/p>\n<p>Interestingly, samarskite was named after Vassili Samarsky-Bykhovets, a Russian mine official who had allowed scientists to study the mineral samples from the Ural Mountains. Because Boisbaudran named the element after the mineral, Samarium became the very first element on the periodic table to indirectly honor a real person!<\/p>\n<p>For a long time, samarium didn't have many practical uses. But in the 1950s, new technologies allowed scientists to separate it perfectly, and soon they discovered its amazing magnetic properties and nuclear benefits.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Samarium is a true unsung hero of modern technology. Its most famous role is in <strong>Samarium-Cobalt (SmCo) magnets<\/strong>. Unlike regular magnets, which can lose their power when they get too hot, samarium-cobalt magnets stay incredibly strong even at blistering temperatures up to 700\u00b0C (1,292\u00b0F). This makes them essential for things that run hot, like jet engines, military radar systems, and precision aerospace instruments.<\/p>\n<p>Beyond magnets, samarium is a lifesaver. The radioactive isotope Samarium-153 is the active ingredient in specialized cancer medicines that target bone tumors. Meanwhile, Samarium-149 is used to build control rods for nuclear reactors because it acts like a sponge, safely absorbing stray neutrons to keep the nuclear reaction stable.<\/p>\n<p><strong>The Indian Context and Modern Research:<\/strong><\/p>\n<p>In India, samarium holds immense strategic value. The country is home to vast reserves of monazite sands along its coastal regions, which are rich in rare earth elements like samarium. Recognizing its importance for national defense and green technology, the Indian government's <strong>National Critical Mineral Mission<\/strong> focuses on building a self-reliant rare earth supply chain.<\/p>\n<p>A shining example of this is the dedicated Rare Earth Permanent Magnet (REPM) plant in Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh, operated by IREL (India) Limited. This facility takes domestic samarium and turns it into the high-performance SmCo magnets needed for India's defense and space programs.<\/p>\n<p>Indian scientists are also at the cutting edge of samarium research. Institutes like the Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology (IIST) and the Institute of Chemical Technology (ICT) in Mumbai are actively exploring new uses for the element. Modern Indian research includes creating samarium-doped glasses for specialized radiation shielding and developing samarium-based nanomaterials that could one day be used for advanced biological imaging and disease diagnosis. From ancient coastal sands to futuristic space and medical technologies, samarium is a vital part of India's scientific journey!<\/p>" } }, "Eu": { "symbol": "Eu", "name": "Europium", "atomic": 63, "category": "lanthanide", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p>Europium is a chemical element with the symbol <strong>Eu<\/strong> and atomic number 63. It belongs to the lanthanide series of rare-earth elements and is known as the softest, least dense, and most chemically reactive of the group\u2014so soft it can be easily cut with a knife! Its most famous superpower is glowing brightly when used in phosphorescent materials. It is what gave older color televisions their vibrant red colors, and it is even used as an anti-counterfeiting measure in euro banknotes. In India, trace amounts of europium are found in the monazite sands along the coasts of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and Odisha, connecting this fascinating element to local geology and modern Indian scientific research.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/6\/6a\/Europium.jpg", "atomic_mass": 151.9641, "density": 5.264, "melt": 1099, "boil": 1802, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Eug\u00e8ne-Anatole Demar\u00e7ay", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f7", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.2, "electron_affinity": 11.2, "ionization_energies": [ 547.1, 1085, 2404, 4120 ], "sections": { "Physical properties": "<p>Europium is a soft, silvery-white metal. It is about as soft as lead, meaning it can be dented and cut quite easily. It forms a basic \"body-centered cubic\" crystal structure. Among its rare-earth neighbors, europium stands out because its atoms take up a relatively large amount of space. This unusual trait happens because its electrons are arranged in a way that makes it act a bit differently, giving it unique magnetic properties.<\/p>", "Chemical properties": "<p>Europium is the most reactive of all the rare-earth elements. If you leave a shiny piece of europium out in the air, it quickly reacts with oxygen and tarnishes, completely oxidizing in just a few days. It also reacts violently with water\u2014much like calcium does\u2014to produce hydrogen gas. Because it is so eager to react, scientists rarely get to see its pure, shiny metallic form unless it is carefully stored under special mineral oil. If heated to between 150 and 180 \u00b0C, europium will literally catch fire in the air! It also dissolves easily in certain acids, forming beautiful pale pink solutions.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>In nature, europium is mostly made of two main types (or isotopes): Europium-151 and Europium-153. They exist in almost equal amounts. While Europium-153 is perfectly stable, Europium-151 is very slightly radioactive. However, its radioactivity is so weak and slow that it takes billions of years to decay, making it practically harmless. Scientists have also created several artificial, highly radioactive isotopes of europium in laboratories, but these break down very quickly, mostly in a matter of days or minutes.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>You will not find europium sitting freely in nature. Instead, it is locked away in various minerals like bastn\u00e4site and monazite. In <strong>India<\/strong>, monazite is prominently found in the famous coastal beach sands of states like Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, and Odisha. Because these sands contain valuable elements like thorium (crucial for India's nuclear energy program) and rare earths like europium, their mining and processing are carefully managed by the Indian government through IREL (India) Limited.<\/p>\n<p>In geology, scientists study the \"europium anomaly\"\u2014how much europium is in a rock compared to other rare-earth elements\u2014to understand how ancient magmas cooled and formed rocks. Even out in space, astronomers look for the signature of europium in stars to figure out when and how those stars were born!<\/p>", "History": "<p>Because rare-earth elements naturally mix together in rocks and behave very similarly, early scientists had a remarkably tough time telling them apart. In 1885, William Crookes noticed some strange, unknown glowing lines when studying rare-earth minerals. By 1896, French chemist Eug\u00e8ne-Anatole Demar\u00e7ay suspected that samples of a recently discovered element called samarium were actually hiding another unknown element. Demar\u00e7ay finally managed to separate it in 1901 and named it \"europium\" after the continent of Europe.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Europium has some very specialized, brilliant uses\u2014literally! Its most famous application relies on its ability to glow (phosphoresce). It is the magical ingredient that provided the bright red colors in traditional tube televisions and helps create the crisp, white light in modern fluorescent bulbs.<\/p>\n<p>Today, <strong>Indian scientists and research institutions<\/strong> are actively researching europium-doped materials to develop better LEDs, advanced lasers, and cutting-edge tools for bio-imaging. In medicine, europium compounds are used to tag antibodies, helping doctors detect specific diseases with laser-excited fluorescence. Because it glows brightly under UV light, europium is even printed on euro banknotes as a hidden anti-counterfeiting security feature. Furthermore, europium is highly valued in nuclear research for its excellent ability to absorb neutrons, making it useful in the control rods of nuclear reactors.<\/p>" } }, "Gd": { "symbol": "Gd", "name": "Gadolinium", "atomic": 64, "category": "lanthanide", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b>Gadolinium<\/b> (Gd) is a silvery-white metal that belongs to a group of elements called rare earths. Discovered in the late 19th century and named after the Finnish chemist Johan Gadolin, this unique metal has some fascinating magnetic properties. While you might never see it in your daily life, gadolinium plays a crucial role in modern medicine and technology.<\/p>\n<p>In the context of <b>India<\/b>, gadolinium holds special significance. While it is not mined directly on its own, it is extracted from the rich <b>monazite sands<\/b> found abundantly along the Indian coastline, especially in states like Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and Odisha. India's ability to process these sands locally through facilities like IREL (India) Limited ensures the nation remains self-reliant in critical rare earth materials.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/c\/c2\/Gadolinium-2.jpg", "atomic_mass": 157.253, "density": 7.9, "melt": 1585, "boil": 3273, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f7 5d1", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.2, "electron_affinity": 13.22, "ionization_energies": [ 593.4, 1170, 1990, 4250 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p>Gadolinium is a soft, shiny, silvery metal. It is somewhat malleable, meaning it can be shaped without breaking. What makes gadolinium truly special is how it reacts to magnets and temperature. At room temperature or lower, gadolinium becomes strongly magnetic. In fact, if you cool it down, its magnetic pull becomes even stronger!<\/p>", "Physical properties": "<p>When you hold gadolinium, it feels like a typical metal, but its inner workings are quite unique. It has an unusually high ability to capture neutrons, making it very useful in nuclear reactors. In addition, when it is placed in a magnetic field, gadolinium actually changes temperature\u2014a rare property known as the magnetocaloric effect.<\/p>", "Chemical properties": "<p>In the air, gadolinium forms a thin layer of rust (oxidation) that eventually flakes off, exposing more metal to the air. Because of this, it needs to be stored carefully to avoid tarnishing. It reacts slowly with cold water and much faster with hot water, and it easily dissolves in acids to form colorful salts.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Gadolinium in nature is made up of several different versions of the same element, known as isotopes. Some of these are stable and will last forever, while others very slowly break down over billions of years. Scientists can also create artificial isotopes of gadolinium in laboratories for specialized research.<\/p>", "History": "<p>Gadolinium was discovered in 1880 by a Swiss chemist named Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac. He found it in a mineral called gadolinite. Six years later, another scientist managed to separate it into a purer form. The element and the mineral are both named in honor of Johan Gadolin, a pioneering chemist who studied rare earth elements.<\/p>\n<p>Historically, India's involvement with these rare earths began around 1909, when monazite sands were discovered on its beaches. Over the decades, India developed advanced domestic capabilities for separating rare earth elements, allowing the extraction of high-purity gadolinium today.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>You won't find gadolinium lying around as a pure chunk of metal in nature. Instead, it is locked inside minerals like monazite and bastn\u00e4site. <\/p>\n<p>In <b>India<\/b>, vast coastal deposits of monazite sand\u2014particularly in Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, and Odisha\u2014are the primary source of gadolinium. State-run companies carefully process these sands to separate out the valuable rare earth elements. Globally, gadolinium is also mined in countries like China, the United States, and Australia.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Gadolinium's most famous use is in hospitals. It is the key ingredient in MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging) contrast agents. When injected into a patient, gadolinium helps create incredibly clear pictures of the body's internal organs and blood vessels. In <b>India<\/b>, extensive medical research is conducted at top institutions like the IITs, focusing on advanced gadolinium-based nanoparticles for improved tumor imaging and targeted therapies.<\/p>\n<p>Beyond medicine, gadolinium is used in nuclear power plants to control nuclear reactions, thanks to its neutron-absorbing powers. It is also used in creating green phosphors for color TV tubes, and researchers are exploring its use in revolutionary magnetic refrigeration systems that could one day replace traditional, less eco-friendly fridges.<\/p>" } }, "Tb": { "symbol": "Tb", "name": "Terbium", "atomic": 65, "category": "lanthanide", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Tb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Terbium (Tb)\">Terbium<\/a><\/b> is a fascinating and rare silvery-white metal that belongs to a group of elements called the lanthanides. Discovered in 1843 in a Swedish quarry, it is so soft you can cut it with a knife! Even though it might not be a household name, terbium is a hidden superstar in modern technology. It gives the brilliant green colors you see in older color TVs and modern smartphone screens, and it plays a vital role in creating super-strong magnets. In India, the quest for rare earth elements like terbium is an active frontier. While the rich coastal sands of Kerala and Odisha are famous for containing light rare earths, heavy rare earths like terbium are much harder to find in large amounts. Today, leading Indian scientific institutions, such as the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) and Indian Rare Earths Limited (IREL), are working tirelessly to develop advanced technologies to extract and purify these precious elements from domestic minerals, pushing India toward self-reliance in high-tech materials.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/9\/9a\/Terbium-2.jpg", "atomic_mass": 158.925352, "density": 8.23, "melt": 1629, "boil": 3396, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Carl Gustaf Mosander", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f9", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.1, "electron_affinity": 112.4, "ionization_energies": [ 565.8, 1110, 2114, 3839 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "Terbium is a shiny, silvery-white metal that is surprisingly soft\u2014you can actually cut it with a knife! Like its neighbors on the periodic table, it belongs to the rare earth family. It is relatively stable in the air, meaning it doesn't rust or tarnish as quickly as some other metals. However, it can slowly react with water and burns brightly when heated.", "Physical properties": "At room temperature, terbium is a solid metal. One of its most magical physical traits is how it responds to magnets and temperatures. When it gets very cold, it acts like a strong magnet. In everyday conditions, it is weakly magnetic. It also has a special party trick: when mixed into certain materials, it glows with a brilliant, vibrant green light, making it incredibly useful for lighting and displays.", "Chemical properties": "Chemically, terbium is quite friendly and likes to combine with other elements. It is mostly found in a \"+3\" state, which simply means it likes to share three of its electrons when bonding. It dissolves beautifully in acids to form colorful solutions that often look faintly pink or colorless.", "Isotopes": "In nature, terbium is incredibly pure\u2014it exists almost entirely as just one stable version (or \"isotope\") called Terbium-159. Scientists have created other radioactive versions of terbium in laboratories, but they break down quickly and aren't found naturally on Earth.", "History": "Terbium's story began in 1843 when Swedish chemist Carl Gustaf Mosander was studying a strange black rock from a quarry in Ytterby, Sweden. He found that it contained not one, but three new elements! He named them yttrium, erbium, and terbium, all honoring the small town of Ytterby. For a long time, terbium was just a scientific curiosity, but as technology advanced, its glowing and magnetic secrets were unlocked.", "Occurrence": "You won't find terbium lying around on its own in nature. It is always hidden inside complex minerals like monazite and bastn\u00e4site. In India, the beautiful beaches of Kerala (especially the Chavara-Neendakara belt), Tamil Nadu, and Odisha hold massive reserves of monazite sand. However, these sands are mostly rich in \"light\" rare earths. Heavy rare earths like terbium are present in much smaller amounts. Today, Indian institutions like the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) and Indian Rare Earths Limited (IREL) are at the forefront of researching new ways to efficiently extract these vital heavy rare earths from domestic resources, aiming to boost India's technological independence.", "Applications": "Terbium is a modern-day technological hero. Its most famous job is creating the bright green colors in screens, from vintage color televisions to the crisp displays of modern smartphones and tablets. It is also used in energy-saving fluorescent lamps. Beyond lighting, terbium is combined with iron and its sister element, dysprosium, to create \"Terfenol-D,\" a special alloy that physically changes its shape in a magnetic field! This shape-shifting superpower is used in advanced sonar systems, sensors, and special speakers." } }, "Dy": { "symbol": "Dy", "name": "Dysprosium", "atomic": 66, "category": "lanthanide", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 66 (Dy)", "extract_html": "<p><b>Dysprosium<\/b> is a shiny, silvery-white rare earth metal that belongs to the lanthanide series on the periodic table. Its name comes from the Greek word <i>dysprositos<\/i>, meaning \"hard to get,\" which makes perfect sense considering it took scientists over 30 attempts to finally isolate it! While you will never find dysprosium floating around as a free element in nature, it is hidden within minerals like monazite and bastn\u00e4site. It is incredibly magnetic, highly reactive to water and air at room temperature, and easily cuts with a knife. Despite being \"hard to get,\" dysprosium plays a crucial role in the modern world, powering everything from electric vehicles to nuclear reactors.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/5\/55\/Dysprosium-2.jpg", "atomic_mass": 162.5001, "density": 8.54, "melt": 1680, "boil": 2840, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Lecoq de Boisbaudran", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f10", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.22, "electron_affinity": 33.96, "ionization_energies": [ 573, 1130, 2200, 3990 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p>Dysprosium is a soft, highly magnetic metal that glows with a bright, silvery sheen. However, this glow doesn't last long if left out in the open\u2014dysprosium slowly tarnishes in the air and burns readily to form dysprosium oxide. When exposed to water or cold acids, it quickly dissolves and releases hydrogen gas. One of its most fascinating features is its behavior at extremely low temperatures. Below -188\u00b0C, dysprosium is strongly magnetic (ferromagnetic), but as it warms up, it enters a bizarre state called antiferromagnetism, where its magnetic fields cancel each other out. Finally, at room temperature, it becomes paramagnetic, meaning it is only weakly attracted to magnets.<\/p>", "Physical properties": "<p>Dysprosium is a dense, heavy metal that remains solid at room temperature. It melts at a scorching 1,407\u00b0C (2,565\u00b0F) and boils at 2,562\u00b0C (4,653\u00b0F). What makes dysprosium physically remarkable is its ability to shrink and expand when exposed to a magnetic field\u2014a property known as magnetostriction. In fact, an alloy of dysprosium, iron, and terbium (called Terfenol-D) has the highest known magnetostriction of any material, allowing it to change its shape in response to magnetism.<\/p>", "Chemical properties": "<p>Chemically, dysprosium is a very reactive rare earth element. It loves to bond with other elements, particularly halogens like fluorine, chlorine, and bromine, creating brightly colored salts that range from pale yellow to vibrant green. When mixed with water, dysprosium reacts to form dysprosium hydroxide. It is generally found in a +3 oxidation state, which simply means it tends to share three of its electrons when making chemical bonds. While dysprosium itself isn't highly toxic, its soluble salts can be mildly dangerous, so chemists handle it with care!<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>In nature, dysprosium is a blend of seven different stable isotopes (atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons). The most abundant of these is Dysprosium-164, which makes up about 28% of all naturally occurring dysprosium. Scientists have also created over 29 artificial, radioactive isotopes in laboratories. Most of these radioactive versions are very short-lived, decaying in just a few milliseconds or days, though Dysprosium-154 can last for millions of years!<\/p>", "History": "<p>The story of dysprosium began in 1886 when a French chemist named Paul \u00c9mile Lecoq de Boisbaudran was analyzing an ore called erbia. After painstakingly dissolving the ore in acid and adding ammonia over 30 separate times, he finally succeeded in separating a brand-new element! Because it was so incredibly difficult to isolate, he named it dysprosium, meaning \"hard to get.\" It wasn't until the 1950s, when ion-exchange technology was developed, that scientists were finally able to produce pure dysprosium metal in large quantities.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>Dysprosium doesn't exist on its own in nature; it prefers to hide inside complex rare-earth minerals like xenotime, fergusonite, and monazite. It is relatively rare, making up only about 5.2 parts per million of the Earth's crust. For many years, the primary source of dysprosium was the heavy mineral sands of the world. In India, the coastal sands of Kerala\u2014specifically the Chavara-Neendakara-Kayamkulam belt\u2014are incredibly rich in monazite. While Indian monazite is mostly known for lighter rare earths, it also contains trace amounts of dysprosium. To tap into this strategic resource, the state-owned IREL (India) Limited established its Rare Earths Division in Aluva, Kerala, where scientists have developed advanced chemical processes to extract these critical metals from the sands.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Dysprosium is a hidden superhero in today's green technology revolution! Because it can withstand high temperatures without losing its magnetic powers, it is a vital ingredient in the ultra-strong neodymium magnets used in electric vehicle (EV) motors and offshore wind turbines. This makes it a highly strategic metal for countries pushing for clean energy, aligning perfectly with India's modern \"mine-to-magnet\" initiatives. Additionally, because dysprosium is excellent at absorbing neutrons, it is heavily used in control rods to keep nuclear reactors safely balanced. You can also find it in high-intensity commercial lighting, specialized lasers, and data storage devices like computer hard drives.<\/p>" } }, "Ho": { "symbol": "Ho", "name": "Holmium", "atomic": 67, "category": "lanthanide", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><strong>Holmium (Ho)<\/strong> is a silvery-white, relatively soft, and malleable rare earth metal with the atomic number 67. To the naked eye, it might just look like another shiny piece of metal, but holmium has a secret power: it possesses the highest magnetic strength of any naturally occurring element! This extraordinary magnetism makes it incredibly valuable for specialized high-tech applications, from generating the strongest artificial magnetic fields to powering advanced medical lasers.<\/p>\n<p>In the context of India, holmium plays a fascinating role. While India boasts some of the world's largest rare earth reserves\u2014particularly in the monazite sands along the coasts of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and Odisha\u2014these sands are mostly rich in \"light\" rare earths. Because holmium is a \"heavy\" rare earth, extracting it from domestic sands is highly challenging. To secure a steady supply of crucial elements like holmium, India launched the National Critical Mineral Mission in 2025 and established Dedicated Rare Earth Corridors. Meanwhile, premier Indian institutions like the IITs and CSIR are spearheading research into advanced extraction technologies, ensuring that the nation's high-tech and medical sectors continue to thrive.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/0\/0a\/Holmium2.jpg", "atomic_mass": 164.930332, "density": 8.79, "melt": 1734, "boil": 2873, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Marc Delafontaine", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f11", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.23, "electron_affinity": 32.61, "ionization_energies": [ 581, 1140, 2204, 4100 ], "sections": { "Physical properties": "<p>Holmium is a shiny, silvery-white metal that is relatively soft and easy to shape. What truly sets holmium apart is its magnetic properties. It has the highest magnetic strength of any element found in nature! If you cool holmium down to very low temperatures, it becomes powerfully magnetic. Because of this, it is often combined with other metals, like yttrium, to create specialized, highly magnetic compounds used in advanced technology.<\/p>", "Chemical properties": "<p>In dry air, holmium remains shiny and relatively stable. However, when exposed to moisture or higher temperatures, it starts to react. It slowly tarnishes in the air, developing a yellowish crust that looks a bit like iron rust. It also dissolves easily in acids, bubbling up as it releases hydrogen gas and forming bright yellow solutions. Like many rare earth elements, it happily combines with elements like oxygen and halogens (such as fluorine and chlorine) to form beautiful, colorful salts.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>In nature, holmium exists almost entirely as a single stable version, or \"isotope,\" called holmium-165. Scientists have also created several artificial, radioactive versions of holmium in laboratories. One of these, holmium-166, has found an important calling in the medical field. It releases a specific type of energy that makes it incredibly useful for targeted cancer therapies and for calibrating highly sensitive radiation-detecting instruments.<\/p>", "History": "<p>Holmium's story begins in 1878 when Swiss chemists Jacques-Louis Soret and Marc Delafontaine noticed a mysterious, previously unseen light pattern while examining rare earth minerals. Around the same time, Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve independently discovered the element while studying erbium. Cleve managed to separate out a brown substance he called <em>holmia<\/em>, after the Latin name for his hometown of Stockholm. It took several more decades before scientists could completely isolate pure holmium metal, but the name stuck, honoring the Swedish capital where part of its discovery took place.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Holmium is a superstar in both the medical and technological worlds. Its incredible magnetic properties make it ideal for creating the strongest artificial magnetic fields, which are used in scientific research and specialized equipment. One of its most life-changing uses is in medical lasers. Holmium lasers (often called Ho:YAG lasers) emit a very precise type of light that is perfect for delicate surgeries. In India, for example, these lasers have revolutionized urology, offering a highly effective, minimally invasive way to treat kidney stones and prostate conditions, dramatically improving patient recovery times.<\/p>\n<p>Beyond medicine, holmium is used to color glass and cubic zirconia, giving them a beautiful yellow or pink tint. Because it can absorb neutrons, it is also used to safely regulate nuclear reactors. Recently, researchers have even stored data on single atoms of holmium, pointing toward a future where this remarkable element could help build ultra-powerful quantum computers!<\/p>" } }, "Er": { "symbol": "Er", "name": "Erbium", "atomic": 68, "category": "lanthanide", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b>Erbium<\/b> is a fascinating, silvery-white metal belonging to the rare-earth group of elements on the periodic table. While it might not be a household name, you likely interact with erbium's magic every day! It is the secret ingredient that powers global internet communications, acting as a light amplifier in the long fiber-optic cables that send data across oceans. <\/p><p>Discovered in a small Swedish village in the 19th century, erbium has grown into a globally critical material. In <b>India<\/b>, erbium-bearing minerals such as monazite are naturally found in the rich coastal beach sands of states like Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, and Odisha. Today, Indian scientists at premier institutions (like the IITs) are pioneering modern research on erbium-doped nano-materials for next-generation electronics, sensors, and optics. Furthermore, erbium-powered lasers (Er:YAG) are widely utilized in Indian medical research and dermatology, proving highly effective for safely treating acne and post-traumatic scars on diverse Indian skin types.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/2\/2a\/Erbium-2.jpg", "atomic_mass": 167.2593, "density": 9.066, "melt": 1802, "boil": 3141, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Carl Gustaf Mosander", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f12", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.24, "electron_affinity": 30.1, "ionization_energies": [ 589.3, 1150, 2194, 4120 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "Erbium is a soft, malleable metal with a bright, silvery shine. When exposed to air, it is surprisingly stable compared to some of its rare-earth cousins, meaning it doesn't rust or tarnish as quickly. One of erbium's most famous traits is its beautiful pink color. When erbium is mixed with other elements, its salts naturally give off a pastel pink hue, which has historically made it a popular coloring agent for glass and porcelain.", "Physical properties": "As a solid metal, erbium is fairly heavy and dense. It has a high melting point of 1,529 \u00b0C (2,784 \u00b0F), which allows it to withstand extreme environments. What makes erbium truly special physically is how it interacts with light. Erbium atoms can absorb invisible infrared light and emit it in a way that perfectly matches the wavelengths used in optical fibers. This unique optical property is why erbium is completely irreplaceable in modern telecommunications.", "Chemical properties": "Chemically, erbium is part of the lanthanide series. It reacts slowly with water and quickly dissolves in acids to form erbium salts. In its most common chemical form, it loses three of its electrons (known as the +3 oxidation state) to bond with other elements. When it burns, it forms erbium oxide, a stunning pink compound that has been prized by glassmakers and artists for over a century.", "Isotopes": "In nature, erbium is a mix of six different stable isotopes. You can think of isotopes as 'siblings' of the element\u2014they have the same chemical personality but slightly different weights. Erbium-166 is the most abundant of these siblings. Scientists have also created many radioactive, artificial isotopes of erbium in laboratories to study nuclear physics, though these decay very quickly and aren't found in nature.", "History": "Erbium's story begins in 1843 in a tiny Swedish village called Ytterby, a place famous for yielding several new elements. The Swedish chemist Carl Gustaf Mosander discovered erbium while analyzing a strange black rock from a local quarry. For decades, it was difficult to separate erbium from its rare-earth neighbors. It wasn't until 1934 that scientists finally managed to produce pure erbium metal. While its origins are Scandinavian, erbium's impact is now global. In modern India, the historical mapping of monazite sands along the peninsular coasts has shifted erbium from a geological curiosity to a strategic mineral of immense national interest.", "Occurrence": "Like most rare-earth elements, erbium is never found pure in nature. Instead, it is locked inside complex minerals like monazite and bastn\u00e4site. While countries like China and the United States hold major deposits, India boasts significant reserves of rare-earth-bearing beach sands. Specifically, the coastal belts of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and Odisha contain monazite sand rich in these elements. Although extracting heavy rare earths like erbium from these sands requires advanced processing, India's domestic reserves are a vital part of its strategic mineral security.", "Applications": "Erbium's most vital job is keeping the internet running! It is used in erbium-doped fiber amplifiers (EDFAs), which boost light signals traveling through fiber-optic cables so data can cross continents without fading. \n\nBeyond the internet, erbium is used in specialized lasers. The Er:YAG laser is heavily used in dentistry and dermatology because it can cut tissue precisely without generating excess heat. In India, these lasers have been extensively studied and embraced for scar removal and cosmetic skin treatments. Erbium is also added to sunglasses and safety glasses to block harmful laser light, and it is still used today to give glass and cubic zirconia a beautiful, permanent pink tint." } }, "Tm": { "symbol": "Tm", "name": "Thulium", "atomic": 69, "category": "lanthanide", "description": "", "extract_html": "Thulium is a fascinating, silvery-gray metal and a member of the lanthanide series on the periodic table. With the atomic number 69 and the symbol Tm, it is the second-least abundant rare earth element naturally found on Earth (only promethium is rarer). Though soft enough to be cut with a knife, thulium has powerful modern uses. It is prized in advanced medical lasers and portable X-ray devices. Due to its scarcity and high cost, it is considered a highly specialized, niche element rather than a household name.", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/6\/6b\/Thulium-2.jpg", "atomic_mass": 168.934222, "density": 9.32, "melt": 1818, "boil": 2223, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Per Teodor Cleve", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f13", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.25, "electron_affinity": 99, "ionization_energies": [ 596.7, 1160, 2285, 4120 ], "sections": { "Physical properties": "Despite being a metal, pure thulium is surprisingly soft\u2014you can actually slice it with a knife! It boasts a bright, silvery shine, though it will slowly tarnish when exposed to air. Like many metals, it is both malleable (can be hammered into sheets) and ductile (can be drawn into wires). When it comes to its magnetic personality, thulium changes its behavior based on the temperature. Below a chilling -241\u00b0C (32 K), it is ferromagnetic like iron. As it warms up, it becomes antiferromagnetic, and finally, above -217\u00b0C (56 K), it settles into being paramagnetic.", "Chemical properties": "Thulium is fairly well-behaved in the air but will slowly tarnish. If heated to 150\u00b0C, it readily burns to form thulium(III) oxide. It reacts quite slowly with cold water but much more quickly with hot water, releasing hydrogen gas. Thulium also reacts enthusiastically with all halogens\u2014like fluorine and chlorine\u2014especially at higher temperatures. When dissolved in dilute sulfuric acid, it creates a pale green solution. Interestingly, in most of its chemical reactions, thulium forms a +3 oxidation state, and these thulium ions can glow with a beautiful, bright blue luminescence under certain conditions.", "Isotopes": "In nature, thulium exists entirely as a single, stable isotope: thulium-169. However, scientists have created over 30 artificial, radioactive isotopes of thulium in laboratories. The most important of these is thulium-170, which has a half-life of about 128.6 days. When natural thulium-169 is bombarded in a nuclear reactor, it turns into thulium-170, which naturally emits X-rays. This makes it incredibly useful as a portable radiation source. Most other artificial thulium isotopes are short-lived, with half-lives of less than 10 minutes.", "History": "Thulium was discovered in 1879 by Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve. He was studying a rare earth mineral called erbia and realized it contained unknown impurities. By carefully separating them, he found two new materials: holmium and thulium. He named thulium after \"Thule\", the ancient Greek and Roman name for a mythical, icy region in the far north, often associated with Scandinavia or Iceland. Initially given the symbol \"Tu\", it was later changed to \"Tm\". Thulium is so rare that early chemists could not even isolate enough of it to see its green oxide. It wasn't until 1911 that an almost pure sample was finally produced, requiring a grueling 15,000 purification steps!", "Occurrence": "You will never find pure thulium lying around in nature. It is always locked away in minerals alongside other rare earth elements, most notably in monazite, gadolinite, and euxenite. It is incredibly scarce, making up just 0.5 parts per million of the Earth's crust. It is the rarest of all the stable lanthanides! Most of the world's thulium ore is mined in China, but there are also significant reserves in Australia, Brazil, Greenland, the United States, and India. In the Indian context, thulium is found in coastal mineral sands, primarily within monazite deposits along the coasts of Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, and Kerala. It is increasingly viewed as a critical strategic mineral for India's high-tech, green energy, and defense future.", "Applications": "Because it is rare and expensive, thulium is reserved for specialized, high-tech jobs rather than everyday products. One of its most important uses is in the medical field. Thulium-doped lasers are incredibly precise and are used for minimally invasive surgeries, such as prostate procedures and skin treatments. Furthermore, the radioactive isotope thulium-170 is used in portable X-ray machines. Because these devices do not need a heavy electrical power source, they are life-savers in remote areas, field hospitals, and emergency sites. Thulium is also used as an anti-counterfeiting measure in some high-value banknotes (like the Euro) because it glows a brilliant blue under UV light. Finally, it plays a key role in advanced microwave equipment, high-precision optical lenses, and high-temperature superconductors.", "Biological role": "Thulium has no known biological role in humans or any other living organisms. We do consume tiny, trace amounts of it every year through vegetables, but plant roots generally do not absorb much of it. While soluble thulium salts are considered mildly toxic and should be handled with care, insoluble thulium is completely non-toxic. Overall, thulium is regarded as having a very low level of toxicity, meaning it poses virtually no threat to human health." } }, "Yb": { "symbol": "Yb", "name": "Ytterbium", "atomic": 70, "category": "lanthanide", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Yb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Ytterbium (Yb)\">Ytterbium<\/a><\/b> is a silvery-white, soft metal that belongs to a group of elements called the lanthanides, or rare earth metals. Found in trace amounts in the Earth's crust, it is rarely used in its pure form but plays a crucial role in modern technology, from atomic clocks to powerful lasers. Although it's named after a small Swedish village where it was first discovered, Ytterbium is found globally. In India, it can be traced to the rich monazite sands along the coastal beaches of Kerala, an important geological source for rare earth minerals.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/c\/ce\/Ytterbium-3.jpg", "atomic_mass": 173.0451, "density": 6.9, "melt": 1097, "boil": 1469, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.1, "electron_affinity": -1.93, "ionization_energies": [ 603.4, 1174.8, 2417, 4203 ], "sections": { "Physical properties": "<p>Ytterbium is a shiny, soft metal that you could easily shape or bend. It has a silvery-white appearance with a slight pale yellow tint. One of its most unique features is how it reacts to extreme conditions. Under normal room temperature, it conducts electricity like a typical metal. However, if you squeeze it under immense pressure, it changes its behavior and acts more like a semiconductor (similar to the materials used in computer chips). Unlike many of its rare-earth cousins, ytterbium isn't strongly magnetic at low temperatures. It also has an unusually low melting point (824 \u00b0C or 1515 \u00b0F) and boiling point for a metal in its group.<\/p>", "Chemical properties": "<p>When left in the open air, ytterbium slowly loses its shine, taking on a brownish or golden tarnish as it reacts with oxygen. If you grind it into a fine powder, it becomes highly reactive and can even burn with a brilliant, emerald-green flame! It dissolves slowly in water, but if dropped into acidic solutions, it quickly bubbles away as it releases hydrogen gas. When it forms compounds, they are usually colorless or white.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>In nature, ytterbium is a mix of seven stable \"versions,\" known as isotopes. These natural isotopes are perfectly safe and don't break down over time. Scientists have also created over 30 artificial, radioactive isotopes in laboratories. Some of these radioactive versions, especially Ytterbium-169, give off specific types of radiation and are highly useful in medicine, acting like portable X-ray machines to help doctors see inside the human body.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>Ytterbium doesn't exist as a pure nugget in nature. Instead, it hides inside complex rare-earth minerals. One of the most important sources is monazite sand. Interestingly, the beautiful coastal beaches of Kerala in southern India are famous for their rich deposits of monazite sands, which hold a treasure trove of rare-earth elements like ytterbium, alongside thorium. While China, the US, and Brazil are also major producers, the monazite deposits in Kerala represent an important geological and strategic resource for India. Since ytterbium looks and acts so much like the other rare earths mixed with it, scientists had a very hard time figuring out how to separate it until the mid-20th century.<\/p>", "History": "<p>The story of ytterbium starts in 1878 with a Swiss chemist named Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac. He found it hidden inside a mineral from a famous quarry in Ytterby, Sweden\u2014a tiny village that has remarkably lent its name to four different elements on the periodic table! For decades, what chemists thought was just \"ytterbium\" turned out to be a mix of two different elements. In 1907, a French chemist named Georges Urbain finally managed to separate the true ytterbium from a new element, which he called lutetium.<\/p>", "Applications and Modern Research": "<p>Because it is scarce and hard to separate, ytterbium isn't used in everyday items like copper or iron. However, it has some incredible high-tech jobs. It is used to make extremely precise atomic clocks\u2014some of the most accurate timekeepers ever created! It's also used to build powerful solid-state lasers and to strengthen stainless steel. In India, leading scientific institutions like the Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research (JNCASR) conduct cutting-edge research using ytterbium. They study it to develop advanced intermetallic compounds, exploring new quantum materials and their potential for future technologies.<\/p>" } }, "Lu": { "symbol": "Lu", "name": "Lutetium", "atomic": 71, "category": "lanthanide", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p>Lutetium (symbol Lu, atomic number 71) is a silvery-white metal that marks the end of the lanthanide series in the periodic table. Often grouped with rare earth elements, it is known for being the hardest and densest among them. While it doesn't appear in ancient Indian texts like traditional metals (e.g., copper or gold), lutetium has significant modern relevance in India. Today, Indian scientists at institutions like the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) in Mumbai have made critical contributions by indigenously producing Lutetium-177, a vital radioisotope used for advanced cancer treatments. Furthermore, India's rich monazite sand deposits along the coasts of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and Odisha serve as important natural sources for rare earth elements, including lutetium. Though rare and challenging to extract, lutetium is a fascinating element with specialized uses in medical science, radiometric dating, and chemical research.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/e\/e8\/Lutetium.jpg", "atomic_mass": 174.96681, "density": 9.841, "melt": 1925, "boil": 3675, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Georges Urbain", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d1", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.27, "electron_affinity": 33.4, "ionization_energies": [ 523.5, 1340, 2022.3, 4370, 6445 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p>Lutetium is a chemical element with the symbol Lu and atomic number 71. It is a silvery-white metal that resists corrosion in dry air but can tarnish when exposed to moisture. As the final element in the lanthanide series, it is traditionally counted among the rare earth elements, although some scientists classify it as the first element of the sixth-period transition metals. Lutetium is quite rare, though it is more abundant in the Earth's crust than silver. Because of the 'lanthanide contraction'\u2014a phenomenon where atoms get slightly smaller across the series\u2014lutetium is the smallest, densest, and hardest atom among its rare earth peers. Its physical toughness is notable, boasting the highest Brinell hardness (890\u20131300 MPa) of any lanthanide.<\/p>", "Physical properties": "<p>At its core, a lutetium atom contains 71 electrons. In chemical reactions, it typically loses its three outermost electrons, resulting in a +3 oxidation state. What makes lutetium unique among lanthanides is its atomic structure: its 4f electron shell is completely full and highly stabilized, meaning only its outermost electrons are involved in chemical bonding. This behavior makes it act more like a transition metal (such as scandium or yttrium) than a typical rare earth element. Lutetium boasts the highest density and melting point of all the lanthanides, solidifying its reputation as an incredibly dense, tough, and robust metal.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>In nature, lutetium is found as a mix of two isotopes: lutetium-175 and lutetium-176. Lutetium-175 is stable and makes up the vast majority (about 97.4%) of the natural element. The remaining 2.6% is lutetium-176, which is weakly radioactive with an incredibly long half-life of 38 billion years. Because it decays so slowly, scientists use it to determine the age of ancient minerals and meteorites. Beyond these natural forms, scientists have created over 40 synthetic radioisotopes in laboratories. The most important of these in modern times is Lutetium-177. Institutions like India's Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) have pioneered the indigenous production of Lutetium-177. This isotope is revolutionary in 'theranostics' (therapy combined with diagnostics), offering highly targeted and effective treatments for certain types of cancers, such as neuroendocrine tumors.<\/p>", "History": "<p>The discovery of lutetium in 1907 involved a dramatic race between three scientists: Georges Urbain of France, Baron Carl Auer von Welsbach of Austria, and Charles James of the United States. All three independently found lutetium hidden as an impurity in a mineral called ytterbia. Urbain was the first to publish his findings, which led to a bitter dispute with Welsbach over who truly deserved the credit. In 1909, the naming honors were awarded to Urbain, who named the element 'lutecium' (later changed to lutetium) after Lutetia, the ancient Roman name for Paris. Although Welsbach's proposed name, 'cassiopeium,' was popular among German scientists for decades, the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry officially settled on lutetium in 1949. Pure lutetium metal was incredibly difficult to isolate and was not produced until 1953. In a modern context, while lutetium lacks the ancient historical roots of metals like iron or gold in ancient Indian texts, India's geographical history plays a part in its story today; the country's vast coastal monazite deposits represent significant reserves of rare earth elements, from which lutetium can be extracted.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Because it is so rare and difficult to separate from other elements, natural lutetium has very few commercial applications and is used only in small quantities. It is sometimes used as a catalyst in complex chemical reactions, such as cracking petroleum in refineries, or mixed into metal alloys. However, its most profound application is in the field of nuclear medicine. The synthetic radioisotope Lutetium-177 is used globally\u2014and is now produced domestically in India\u2014for targeted radiotherapy. Bound to special molecules like DOTA-TATE, it seeks out and destroys cancer cells with remarkable precision, making lutetium a tiny but mighty weapon in the fight against neuroendocrine tumors and prostate cancer.<\/p>" } }, "Hf": { "symbol": "Hf", "name": "Hafnium", "atomic": 72, "category": "transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><strong>Hafnium<\/strong> (symbol <strong>Hf<\/strong>, atomic number 72) is a shiny, silvery-gray metal that looks and acts a lot like its periodic table neighbor, zirconium. Because they are so similar, hafnium is almost always found hiding inside zirconium minerals, and separating the two is quite a challenge!<\/p>\n<p>Despite being relatively rare, hafnium plays a massive role in high-tech industries. It is incredibly good at absorbing neutrons and can withstand extreme heat, making it a star player in nuclear reactors and aerospace engineering. In India, hafnium is officially recognized as a critical strategic mineral. It is vital for the nation's advanced space missions and nuclear energy programs, with major research driven by institutions like the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) and the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO).<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/1\/17\/Hafnium_%2872_Hf%29.jpg", "atomic_mass": 178.492, "density": 13.31, "melt": 2506, "boil": 4876, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Dirk Coster", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d2", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.3, "electron_affinity": 17.18, "ionization_energies": [ 658.5, 1440, 2250, 3216 ], "sections": [ { "title": "Characteristics", "content": "\n<p>Hafnium is a tough, heavy transition metal that resists corrosion and handles extreme temperatures with ease. One of its most famous features is its ability to swallow up neutrons, a property that makes it incredibly useful in nuclear science. Curiously, while a solid chunk of hafnium is perfectly safe, hafnium in powder form is pyrophoric\u2014meaning it can spontaneously catch fire in the air!<\/p>\n<p>Chemically, it is like a twin to zirconium. The two elements are so identical in their chemical behaviors that early chemists struggled for years to tell them apart. It wasn't until scientists started using X-rays to look at their atomic structures that they could finally separate the two.<\/p>\n" }, { "title": "Isotopes", "content": "\n<p>Hafnium has dozens of different versions, known as isotopes, which vary slightly in their weight. Five of these are stable and make up the hafnium we find in nature.<\/p>\n<p>There is also one very famous (and controversial) radioactive form called a \"nuclear isomer\" (specifically, Hafnium-178m2). For years, scientists debated whether this highly energetic isomer could be triggered to release a massive burst of gamma rays all at once, potentially creating a new kind of weapon. Ultimately, creating this isomer proved far too difficult and expensive, and the idea of a hafnium weapon remains the stuff of science fiction.<\/p>\n" }, { "title": "Occurrence", "content": "\n<p>You won't find pure hafnium sitting around in nature. It prefers to blend in, naturally occurring inside zirconium-rich minerals like zircon. Extracting it requires processing massive amounts of heavy mineral sands.<\/p>\n<p>In India, these heavy mineral sands are found abundantly along the coastal stretches of states like <strong>Kerala, Odisha, and Tamil Nadu<\/strong>. Because hafnium is found within these domestic zircon deposits, India's ability to mine and process it locally is a tremendous advantage for its strategic industries.<\/p>\n" }, { "title": "History", "content": "\n<p>When the famous chemist Dmitri Mendeleev created his early periodic table in 1869, he left a blank space for element 72, predicting that a heavier cousin of titanium and zirconium must exist. For decades, scientists hunted for it. It wasn't until 1923 that Dirk Coster and George de Hevesy finally found it hiding inside a piece of Norwegian zircon.<\/p>\n<p>They made the discovery in Copenhagen, Denmark. To honor the city, they named the new element \"Hafnium,\" derived from <em>Hafnia<\/em>, the Latin name for Copenhagen.<\/p>\n<p>In modern times, India has made significant historical strides in hafnium technology to ensure national self-reliance. Historically dependent on complex foreign supply chains for this critical metal, India established its first indigenous hafnium metal sponge pilot plant at <strong>C-MET (Centre for Materials for Electronics Technology)<\/strong> in Hyderabad. This milestone, achieved in collaboration with ISRO's Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC), marked a major step forward in India's ability to produce space-grade hafnium domestically.<\/p>\n" }, { "title": "Applications", "content": "\n<p>Because hafnium is a master at absorbing neutrons, its most crucial job is inside nuclear reactors. It is used to make control rods that regulate the nuclear fission process\u2014acting like the brakes in a nuclear power plant. In India, the <strong>Nuclear Fuel Complex (NFC)<\/strong> and the <strong>Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC)<\/strong> have pioneered the complex chemical processes needed to completely separate hafnium from zirconium, ensuring both elements can be used safely in the country's nuclear fuel cycle.<\/p>\n<p>Beyond nuclear energy, hafnium's ability to survive blazing temperatures makes it perfect for aerospace alloys, including rocket engines and spacecraft thrusters. It's also found in everyday technology: if you have a modern smartphone or computer, there's a good chance hafnium oxide is inside its tiny microchips, helping the transistors run faster and more efficiently.<\/p>\n" } ] }, "Ta": { "symbol": "Ta", "name": "Tantalum", "atomic": 73, "category": "transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b>Tantalum<\/b> (symbol <b>Ta<\/b>, atomic number 73) is a rare, hard, blue-gray metal that is highly resistant to corrosion and heat. It is a critical mineral in the modern world, essential for making the electronics and semiconductors used in everyday devices like smartphones and laptops. In late 2023, a team of researchers from IIT Ropar made a groundbreaking discovery: they found traces of tantalum in the sands of the Sutlej River in Punjab, India! This remarkable find highlights India's potential to become a significant player in the global supply of this strategic metal. Historically named after Tantalus from Greek mythology, tantalum today sits at the intersection of modern technology and exciting new geological discoveries in India.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/6\/61\/Tantalum.jpg", "atomic_mass": 180.947882, "density": 16.69, "melt": 3290, "boil": 5731, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Anders Gustaf Ekeberg", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d3", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.5, "electron_affinity": 31, "ionization_energies": [ 761, 1500 ], "sections": { "History": "<p>Tantalum was first discovered in 1802 by the Swedish chemist Anders Gustaf Ekeberg. He named the element after Tantalus, a character from Greek mythology who was punished by having water recede whenever he tried to drink. Ekeberg chose this name because tantalum oxide doesn't react or 'drink' acid when placed in it! For a long time, scientists confused tantalum with another element called niobium because they are so similar and often found together. It wasn't until 1846 that Heinrich Rose finally proved they were two distinct elements.<\/p><p>In modern times, the history of tantalum took an exciting turn in India. In 2023, researchers from the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Ropar serendipitously discovered tantalum in the Sutlej River in Punjab. This recent discovery adds a thrilling new chapter to the story of tantalum, showing that this ancient metal is still surprising us today!<\/p>", "Characteristics": "<p>Tantalum is a superhero among metals! It is incredibly dense, hard, and has a beautiful blue-gray color. One of its most amazing superpowers is its ability to resist corrosion\u2014it is almost completely immune to chemical attacks at temperatures below 150\u00b0C. In fact, it is so resistant that it won't even dissolve in strong acids that can melt other metals.<\/p><p>Tantalum is also highly ductile, meaning it can be stretched into very thin wires without breaking. When you combine this with a super high melting point (over 3,000\u00b0C), you get a metal that can survive the most extreme environments imaginable. This makes it a perfect fit for high-tech applications, and its discovery in the Sutlej riverbed means India could soon harness these remarkable characteristics locally.<\/p>", "Physical properties": "<p>Physically, tantalum is heavy and extremely tough. Its melting point is a scorching 3,017 \u00b0C (5,463 \u00b0F)\u2014one of the highest of all elements, surpassed only by metals like tungsten and rhenium! This means it can withstand temperatures that would turn most other metals into puddles.<\/p><p>When exposed to air, it forms a protective oxide layer that makes it even more durable. Because it is so biocompatible (meaning the human body doesn't reject it or react to it negatively), it can even be used safely inside the human body! The physical resilience of tantalum is exactly why its recent discovery in Indian river sands is so valuable for the nation's high-tech manufacturing goals.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>In nature, tantalum comes in two main 'flavors' or isotopes: Tantalum-181 and Tantalum-180m. Tantalum-181 makes up almost all of the naturally occurring tantalum (99.99%). The other one, Tantalum-180m, is incredibly rare and has a fascinating quirk\u2014it exists in an 'excited' state but is remarkably stable, with a half-life so incredibly long that it has never actually been observed to decay!<\/p><p>Scientists have also created several artificial, radioactive isotopes of tantalum in laboratories for research purposes. Understanding these isotopes helps scientists around the world, including those at India's top research institutes, trace the origins of geological samples like the ones found in Punjab.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>Tantalum is quite rare, making up just a tiny fraction of the Earth's crust (about 1 or 2 parts per million). It is typically found in minerals like tantalite and columbite. For many years, countries like Australia, Brazil, and nations in Central Africa (like Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo) have been the main producers of tantalum.<\/p><p>However, the geographic map of tantalum occurrence is shifting. In a landmark discovery in 2023, researchers from IIT Ropar identified the presence of tantalum in the Sutlej River basin in Punjab, India. This was a monumental find, as India traditionally relied on imports for this critical mineral. The Sutlej river discovery suggests that there may be untapped mineral wealth within the country, offering a potential boost to India's self-reliance in critical minerals.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Tantalum is practically everywhere in modern technology! Its biggest use is in electronics. Because it can hold a large electrical charge in a very small volume, it is used to make tiny capacitors found in smartphones, laptops, gaming consoles, and automotive electronics. Beyond gadgets, tantalum's incredibly high melting point makes it ideal for making parts for jet engines, rockets, and chemical manufacturing equipment.<\/p><p>Furthermore, because the human body completely ignores it (it's biocompatible), it is widely used in medicine for surgical instruments, bone implants, and pacemakers. With the burgeoning electronics manufacturing sector in India\u2014such as the 'Make in India' semiconductor push\u2014the newly discovered tantalum deposits in the Sutlej River could provide a vital homegrown supply chain for creating the next generation of electronic devices!<\/p>" } }, "W": { "symbol": "W", "name": "Tungsten", "atomic": 74, "category": "transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b>Tungsten<\/b> (symbol <b>W<\/b>, atomic number 74), also known as wolfram, is a remarkable transition metal famous for having the highest melting point of any element. Its name comes from the Swedish words \"tung sten,\" meaning \"heavy stone.\" It is a grayish-white, lustrous metal that is incredibly hard and dense. Found in minerals like wolframite and scheelite, tungsten is essential for everything from old-school incandescent lightbulb filaments to cutting-edge aerospace engineering. In India, tungsten is classified as a strategic and critical mineral, vital for defense and high-tech industrial growth. The country has historical deposits in places like Degana in Rajasthan, and ongoing exploration by the Geological Survey of India (GSI) continues to secure this precious resource for the nation's future.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/c\/c8\/Tungsten_rod_with_oxidised_surface.jpg", "atomic_mass": 183.841, "density": 19.25, "melt": 3695, "boil": 6203, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Carl Wilhelm Scheele", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d4", "electronegativity_pauling": 2.36, "electron_affinity": 78.76, "ionization_energies": [ 770, 1700 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p>Tungsten is a grayish-white, lustrous metal that shines brightly when polished. Because of its incredible density and hardness, it is not an element you can easily dent or scratch. Its name originally comes from the Swedish words \"tung sten,\" meaning \"heavy stone,\" which perfectly describes its nature. However, it\u2019s most famous symbol, \"W\", actually comes from its other historical name, \"Wolfram\".<\/p>", "Physical properties": "<p>Tungsten is the ultimate heavyweight champion of the periodic table. It holds the record for the highest melting point of all discovered metals\u2014a blistering 3,422 \u00b0C (6,192 \u00b0F)\u2014and also boasts the highest boiling point.
