Its density is almost exactly the same as gold, making it impressively heavy and substantial. When pure, it can be stretched and pulled into incredibly thin wires, but usually, it is hard and brittle.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>In nature, tungsten is a mix of five different isotopes (versions of the element with slightly different weights). Four of these are considered completely stable, while one is technically radioactive\u2014but it decays so unimaginably slowly that its half-life is billions of times longer than the age of the universe! Scientists also study synthetic, short-lived tungsten isotopes in advanced physics labs to better understand nuclear structure.<\/p>", "Chemical properties": "<p>Despite its ruggedness, tungsten is surprisingly well-behaved chemically. It strongly resists corrosion and doesn't easily react with oxygen or water at room temperature. It only begins to oxidize when things get really hot! It also gracefully ignores most acids, though it can be dissolved by a specific mix of nitric and hydrofluoric acids. Its ability to remain stable under extreme conditions makes it incredibly valuable for high-stakes scientific applications, including research conducted by Indian space and nuclear scientists.<\/p>", "History": "<p>Tungsten\u2019s journey is a tale of early chemistry and modern industry. While ancient Indian metallurgists were globally renowned masters of iron and steel (such as the famous Wootz steel), they did not identify tungsten as a distinct element. Instead, tungsten was first hypothesized by Peter Woulfe in 1779 and officially isolated in 1783 by Spanish brothers Juan Jos\u00e9 and Fausto Elhuyar. They extracted it from wolframite, a mineral often found alongside tin ores. The element\u2019s alternative name, \"wolfram\", is the source of its chemical symbol, W. Today, the scientific legacy of tungsten continues robustly in India. Premier institutions like the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) pioneer the development of indigenous tungsten heavy alloys (WHA) and powder metallurgy techniques, cementing India's capabilities in nuclear and aerospace applications.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>In nature, tungsten is never found as a pure, shiny metal but is rather locked away in chemical compounds inside rocks. It is most commonly extracted from minerals like wolframite and scheelite. In India, key tungsten occurrences are mapped in states like Rajasthan (notably the historic Degana mines), Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Maharashtra. Although domestic extraction has faced challenges due to low-grade ores, Indian scientists and the Indian Bureau of Mines are actively developing advanced beneficiation technologies. These physical and chemical processes aim to efficiently extract high-quality tungsten, boosting India's strategic mineral security.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Because of its incredible strength, density, and heat resistance, tungsten is practically everywhere! For over a century, it literally lit up our homes as the glowing wire filament inside incandescent lightbulbs. Today, it is mostly used to manufacture tungsten carbide\u2014an extraordinarily hard material essential for industrial cutting tools, mining drills, and even scratch-resistant jewelry. In the modern Indian context, tungsten is indispensable. It forms the core of specialized heavy alloys used extensively by the defense sector for radiation shielding, missile tips, and armor-piercing ammunition. Its unmatched high-temperature tolerance also makes it a crucial component in India's rapidly growing aerospace sector, electronics manufacturing, and high-performance engineering.<\/p>", "Biological role": "<p>Surprisingly, tungsten holds the record as the heaviest element known to play a functional biological role! While it can be toxic in high concentrations to animals and humans, some ancient species of bacteria and archaea actually rely on tungsten in their enzymes. These microscopic organisms often thrive in extreme environments, like scalding deep-sea hydrothermal vents, where they utilize tungsten much like other lifeforms use molybdenum. While it is not a nutrient for humans, modern environmental science\u2014including research by Indian agricultural and soil scientists\u2014carefully monitors tungsten levels in soil and water. Understanding how tungsten interacts with the ecosystem helps ensure environmental safety and sustainable industrial practices.<\/p>" } }, "Re": { "symbol": "Re", "name": "Rhenium", "atomic": 75, "category": "transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><strong>Rhenium<\/strong> is a silvery-white, exceedingly rare transition metal with the atomic number 75. Discovered in 1925, it was the last stable element to be found. With one of the highest melting points (3,186\u00b0C) and the highest boiling point among stable elements, rhenium is built for extreme environments. Today, this incredibly dense metal plays a critical role in modern technology, from crafting heat-resistant superalloys for jet engines and spacecraft to serving as a catalyst in producing high-octane fuel. Due to its scarcity and immense strategic value, it is considered a critical mineral globally, including in India's rapidly growing aerospace and defense sectors.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/d\/d9\/Pure_rhenium_bead%2C_arc_melted%2C_21_grams._Original_size_in_cm_-_1.5_x_1.7.jpg", "atomic_mass": 186.2071, "density": 21.02, "melt": 3459, "boil": 5869, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Masataka Ogawa", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d5", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.9, "electron_affinity": 5.8273, "ionization_energies": [ 760, 1260, 2510, 3640 ], "sections": { "History": "<p>In 1908, Japanese chemist Masataka Ogawa claimed to have discovered the 43rd element, naming it <em>nipponium<\/em> after Japan. However, modern analysis reveals he had actually discovered element 75 (rhenium) but misinterpreted his findings. The element was officially \"rediscovered\" and named in 1925 by German scientists Walter Noddack, Ida Tacke-Noddack, and Otto Berg. They named it rhenium after the river Rhine (Latin: <em>Rhenus<\/em>).<\/p>\n<p>To obtain a usable sample, they extracted just 1 gram of rhenium by processing a staggering 660 kilograms of molybdenite ore! Rhenium's discovery marked a historical milestone: it was the very last naturally occurring stable element ever discovered on the periodic table.<\/p>", "Characteristics": "<p>Rhenium is a dense, silvery-white metal known for its extreme resilience. It boasts the second-highest melting point of any element (exceeded only by tungsten) and the highest boiling point of all stable elements. It is also remarkably dense\u2014only platinum, iridium, and osmium pack more mass into the same space.<\/p>\n<p>When prepared in its typical solid form, rhenium is highly ductile, meaning it can be easily bent, coiled, or rolled. In addition to its physical toughness, rhenium resists wear and corrosion from harsh chemicals like alkalis and acids. At ultra-low temperatures, certain rhenium alloys, such as those mixed with molybdenum or tungsten, even become superconducting.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Naturally occurring rhenium is made up of just two isotopes. Interestingly, the only stable isotope (rhenium-185) makes up a minority (37.4%) of the natural supply. The remaining 62.6% is rhenium-187, which is technically unstable and radioactive, but its half-life is so incredibly long\u2014over 41 billion years\u2014that it is practically stable on human timescales.<\/p>\n<p>Because of this slow decay, scientists use rhenium-187 to date ancient ores and rocks. In the medical field, synthetic radioactive isotopes like rhenium-186 and rhenium-188 are utilized in targeted radiotherapy for treating bone cancer and relieving pain.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>Rhenium is exceptionally scarce, ranking among the rarest elements in the Earth's crust with an average concentration of just 1 part per billion. It is generally not found as a free metal in nature. Instead, it \"hides\" in trace amounts within the mineral molybdenite, which is its primary commercial source. Chile is currently the world's leading producer, holding the largest reserves within its copper ore deposits.<\/p>\n<p>Interestingly, a natural rhenium mineral called rheniite was only discovered in 1994, condensing from the hot volcanic gases of the Kudriavy volcano in the Kuril Islands. In India, rhenium is recognized as a strategic and critical mineral. With potential traces found in copper belts (like Singhbhum) and coal mines, India is actively exploring domestic sources and recycling technologies to secure its supply for national industries.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Rhenium is a heavy hitter in high-tech industries. The vast majority of the world's rhenium (about 70%) is mixed with nickel to create high-temperature superalloys. These tough materials form the critical turbine blades in jet engines and gas turbines, allowing them to run hotter, longer, and more efficiently.<\/p>\n<p>Another major use is in the petrochemical industry, where platinum-rhenium catalysts help refine crude oil into high-octane, lead-free gasoline. Because it can withstand extreme heat and wear, rhenium is also used in electrical contacts, thermocouples, and spacecraft components. In India, as the aerospace and defense sectors rapidly expand, the demand for rhenium superalloys and advanced metal recovery technologies is higher than ever.<\/p>" } }, "Os": { "symbol": "Os", "name": "Osmium", "atomic": 76, "category": "transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b>Osmium (Os)<\/b> is a fascinating and incredibly dense metal, known for being the heaviest naturally occurring element on Earth. Imagine a block of osmium the size of a milk jug\u2014it would weigh about as much as an adult human! First discovered in 1803 by English chemist Smithson Tennant, it has a beautiful bluish-silver color and is highly prized for its extreme hardness.<\/p><p>While ancient Indian texts like the Vedas and traditional Ayurvedic treatises like the <em>Charaka Samhita<\/em> demonstrate a rich history of metallurgy (focusing on gold, silver, copper, and iron), osmium is notably absent. It requires modern, advanced chemical techniques to extract. Today, osmium plays a role in modern Indian scientific research, such as studying river sediments in the Ganga to understand ancient geological changes, and it is catching the eye of the growing Indian luxury market as a rare, investment-grade precious metal.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/3\/3c\/Osmium-bead.jpg", "atomic_mass": 190.233, "density": 22.59, "melt": 3306, "boil": 5285, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Smithson Tennant", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d6", "electronegativity_pauling": 2.2, "electron_affinity": 103.99, "ionization_energies": [ 840, 1600 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "Osmium is part of the platinum group of metals. It is incredibly hard, brittle, and remains shiny even at very high temperatures. Because it's so dense and tough, it's very difficult to shape or mold. However, these same properties make it an excellent addition to alloys when you need something that won't wear down easily.", "Physical properties": "Osmium holds the title for the densest naturally occurring element\u2014it's about twice as heavy as lead! It has a striking bluish-silver appearance and an incredibly high melting point of over 3,000\u00b0C (5,400\u00b0F). Because it is so hard and brittle, it can easily shatter if struck hard enough, making it challenging to work with in its pure form.", "Chemical properties": "When osmium is exposed to the air, especially in a powdered form, it slowly reacts with oxygen to form osmium tetroxide. This compound has a very strong, sharp smell\u2014in fact, the name 'osmium' comes from the Greek word 'osme', meaning 'odor'. Osmium tetroxide is highly toxic and can cause damage to the eyes, skin, and lungs, which is why scientists handle this element with extreme care.", "Isotopes": "Osmium exists in nature as a mix of seven different versions, called isotopes. Six of these are completely stable, while one is very slightly radioactive, though it breaks down so slowly that it takes billions of years. In India, geologists have analyzed osmium isotopes in the sediments of the mighty Ganga river. By studying these tiny traces, Indian scientists can learn about how the Earth's continents have weathered and changed over millions of years.", "History": "Osmium was discovered in 1803 by Smithson Tennant in London. He found it alongside another metal, iridium, in the leftover residue when platinum was dissolved in powerful acids. Although ancient Indian metallurgy (Rasashastra) was highly advanced, extracting osmium required chemical techniques that were not yet invented. Thus, there are no mentions of osmium in ancient Indian texts. Today, however, osmium is gaining recognition in India's modern technological and luxury sectors.", "Occurrence": "Osmium is one of the rarest elements in the Earth's crust. It is typically found mixed with other precious metals like platinum and iridium in natural river sands and specific rock formations. While India does not have major primary mines for osmium, the metal is sourced globally and brought into the country for specialized scientific and industrial uses. Most of the world's osmium comes from large mining operations in South Africa, Russia, and North America.", "Applications": "Because pure osmium is so hard and brittle, it is usually mixed with other metals to create super-durable alloys. In the past, it was famous for being used in the tough tips of fountain pens and phonograph needles. Today, osmium is used in high-wear electrical contacts and specialized scientific equipment. In modern Indian research labs, osmium compounds like osmium tetroxide are crucial for preparing biological samples for electron microscopes, allowing scientists to see the tiny structures of cells with incredible contrast." } }, "Ir": { "symbol": "Ir", "name": "Iridium", "atomic": 77, "category": "transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><strong>Iridium<\/strong> (symbol <strong>Ir<\/strong>, atomic number 77) is a remarkable transition metal belonging to the platinum group. Known for its extreme durability and silvery-white appearance, it is the most corrosion-resistant metal on Earth. Iridium is so resilient that it remains completely unaffected by air, water, and even highly corrosive acids like aqua regia. Because of its incredible hardness and high melting point, it is challenging to shape but incredibly valuable in high-tech industries.<\/p><p>Interestingly, iridium is exceptionally rare in the Earth's crust but is found in higher concentrations in meteorites. The discovery of an iridium-rich layer of clay across the globe provided key evidence for the asteroid impact that wiped out the dinosaurs 66 million years ago!<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/a\/a8\/Iridium-2.jpg", "atomic_mass": 192.2173, "density": 22.56, "melt": 2719, "boil": 4403, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Smithson Tennant", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d7", "electronegativity_pauling": 2.2, "electron_affinity": 150.94, "ionization_energies": [ 880, 1600 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p>Iridium is a silvery-white, hard, and extremely brittle metal. It belongs to the platinum group and shares a visual resemblance to platinum, though it has a slight yellowish tint. Because it is so stiff and has a very high melting point, working with solid iridium is quite difficult. Instead of traditional metalworking, it is usually processed using powder metallurgy. Amazingly, iridium is the only metal that can maintain excellent mechanical properties in the air at scorching temperatures above 1,600 &deg;C (2,910 &deg;F).<\/p>", "Physical properties": "<p>Iridium is famous for being incredibly dense. In fact, it is the second-densest naturally occurring element, just slightly behind osmium, with a density of 22.56 g\/cm&sup3;. It melts at a staggering 2,446 &deg;C (4,435 &deg;F) and boils at 4,130 &deg;C (7,466 &deg;F). It is also highly resilient to deformation. The stiffness of iridium, measured by its modulus of elasticity, is the second highest of all metals. When cooled to near absolute zero (below 0.14 K), iridium even becomes a superconductor, meaning it can conduct electricity with zero resistance.<\/p>", "Chemical properties": "<p>When it comes to corrosion, iridium is practically invincible. It is the most corrosion-resistant metal known to science. It does not react with standard acids, including the notoriously strong <em>aqua regia<\/em> (a mix of nitric and hydrochloric acids). However, under very specific conditions, it can be dissolved in concentrated hydrochloric acid if sodium perchlorate is present. At high temperatures, it will react with oxygen, halogens, or sulfur, forming compounds like iridium disulfide.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>In nature, iridium is found as a mix of two stable isotopes: <sup>191<\/sup>Ir (about 37.3%) and <sup>193<\/sup>Ir (about 62.7%). Scientists have also discovered or created dozens of radioactive isotopes. The most important of these is Iridium-192, which has a half-life of roughly 74 days. Iridium-192 is highly valued in the medical field for cancer treatments (brachytherapy) and in industrial settings to X-ray and inspect steel welds in oil and gas pipelines.<\/p>", "History": "<p>Iridium was discovered in 1803 by the British chemist Smithson Tennant. While studying platinum ores, he found a residue that would not dissolve in acid. He realized this residue contained two new elements: osmium and iridium. Tennant named iridium after <em>Iris<\/em>, the Greek goddess of the rainbow, because the salts produced by the metal displayed a wide and striking array of colors. A major historical milestone for the metal occurred in 1889, when an alloy of 90% platinum and 10% iridium was used to craft the International Prototype Meter bar, which stood as the global standard for the unit of length for decades.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>On Earth, iridium is one of the rarest elements in the crust&mdash;much rarer than gold or platinum. It is generally found alongside other platinum-group metals in natural alloys or nickel and copper deposits. The largest primary reserves are located in South Africa, Russia, and Canada. However, iridium is surprisingly common in meteorites. During Earth's early, molten history, most of its iridium sank into the planet's core because of its density and tendency to bond with iron. The thin layer of iridium found in the Earth's crust at the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary is what gave scientists the clue that a massive asteroid impact caused the extinction of the dinosaurs.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Today, iridium is essential in modern technology. Its extreme heat resistance makes it perfect for high-grade spark plugs in airplanes and cars, as well as for making crucibles used to grow laser and LED crystals. It is also used in OLED screens and as a catalyst in chemical production. In the push for green energy, iridium electrodes are increasingly important for systems that produce green hydrogen. In the Indian context, iridium plays a role in advanced aerospace research. Institutions like the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR-NIIST) have studied iridium coatings for carbon-carbon composites, developing specialized materials designed to withstand the extreme conditions of space travel.<\/p>" } }, "Pt": { "symbol": "Pt", "name": "Platinum", "atomic": 78, "category": "transition metal", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 78 (Pt)", "extract_html": "Platinum is a chemical element with the symbol Pt and atomic number 78. Known for its brilliant silvery-white luster, it is one of the most precious and versatile metals on Earth. As a transition metal, platinum is dense, malleable, and highly unreactive, earning it the title of a 'noble metal'. Because it does not corrode or tarnish, even at incredibly high temperatures, it has transitioned from an ancient decorative material to a cornerstone of modern industrial and medical technology. Today, its scarcity and unique chemical properties make it highly valuable, playing a critical role in everything from clean energy technologies to life-saving medical devices and luxury jewelry.", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/6\/68\/Platinum_crystals.jpg", "atomic_mass": 195.0849, "density": 21.45, "melt": 2041.4, "boil": 4098, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Antonio de Ulloa", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s1 4f14 5d9", "electronegativity_pauling": 2.28, "electron_affinity": 205.041, "ionization_energies": [ 870, 1791 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "Platinum is renowned for its remarkable physical and chemical properties. It is exceptionally dense\u2014almost twice as dense as lead\u2014and highly malleable, meaning it can be easily shaped into intricate forms or drawn into thin wires. With a staggering melting point of 1,768.3 \u00b0C (3,214.9 \u00b0F), it can withstand extreme heat that would melt most other metals. Chemically, platinum is famous for its resistance to corrosion and tarnishing. It does not react with oxygen in the air, which makes it a 'noble' metal. Despite its unreactive nature, platinum is an extraordinary catalyst, meaning it can speed up chemical reactions without being consumed itself\u2014a property that makes it invaluable in industrial and environmental applications.", "Isotopes": "In nature, platinum exists as a mix of six different isotopes: Platinum-190, 192, 194, 195, 196, and 198. The most abundant of these is Platinum-195, which makes up about 33.8% of all natural platinum. Platinum-195 is particularly important to scientists because its unique atomic properties make it highly useful in Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, a technique used to study molecular structures. While most platinum isotopes are completely stable, Platinum-190 is technically radioactive, though it is incredibly rare (only 0.012% of natural platinum) and decays so slowly (with a half-life of hundreds of billions of years) that its radioactivity is entirely negligible.", "Occurrence": "Platinum is incredibly rare, occurring at a concentration of only 0.005 parts per million in the Earth's crust. It is often found in its uncombined, native form or alloyed with other similar metals in riverbed (alluvial) deposits. Today, the vast majority of the world's platinum comes from the Merensky Reef in South Africa's Bushveld Complex, which accounts for about 75% of known reserves. Other major deposits are found in the Ural Mountains of Russia and the Sudbury Basin in Canada, where platinum was famously deposited by an ancient meteor strike!\n\nIn the context of India, platinum is primarily a strategic import rather than a domestically mined commodity. However, as demand grows for critical minerals, the Geological Survey of India (GSI) has been actively exploring potential deposits. Significant prospects have been identified in the Baula-Nuasahi complex in Odisha, the Sittampundi complex in Tamil Nadu, and recently, promising mineralized zones have been discovered in the Mahasamund district of Chhattisgarh, offering hope for future domestic production.", "History": "While platinum may seem like a modern marvel, its history stretches back thousands of years. As early as 700 BCE, Ancient Egyptian artisans used platinum in decorative objects, such as the famous Casket of Thebes. Over 2,000 years ago, indigenous civilizations in South America were already forging the metal into ceremonial jewelry.\n\nHowever, when Spanish conquistadors encountered the metal in the 16th century while searching for gold, they were less than impressed. Because platinum was so difficult to melt, they viewed it as a nuisance and an 'unripe' impurity. They dismissively named it 'platina', meaning 'little silver', and often threw it back into rivers. It wasn't until the mid-18th century, after Spanish scientist Antonio de Ulloa brought samples back to Europe in 1746, that platinum was finally recognized and studied by the scientific community as a distinct and highly valuable element.", "Applications": "Today, platinum is a 'strategic metal' found in a surprising number of everyday and high-tech applications. Its most significant use is in the automotive industry, where it serves as the crucial catalyst in catalytic converters, transforming toxic engine exhaust fumes into safer emissions. In the chemical industry, it helps refine crude oil and produce fertilizers.\n\nBecause it is completely biocompatible and resists corrosion, platinum is essential in modern medicine. It is used to manufacture pacemakers, artificial heart valves, and dental equipment. Remarkably, platinum-based compounds like cisplatin are among the most effective chemotherapy drugs used to treat certain cancers.\n\nBeyond industry, platinum's rarity and durability make it a highly sought-after status symbol in fine jewelry, notably in India where it is marketed as a 'new-age' luxury metal. Looking to the future, platinum is set to play a major role in the green energy transition, serving as a key component in hydrogen fuel cells that generate clean electricity." } }, "Au": { "symbol": "Au", "name": "Gold", "atomic": 79, "category": "transition metal", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 79 (Au)", "extract_html": "Gold is a fascinating and beautiful chemical element with the symbol Au (from the Latin word *aurum*) and the atomic number 79. It is one of the densest and most malleable metals on Earth, so soft that a single ounce can be beaten into a sheet covering over 300 square feet! Known for its brilliant, warm yellow color and its remarkable resistance to tarnishing or rusting, gold has captivated human beings for thousands of years. From ancient civilizations who worshipped it as the 'flesh of the gods' to modern scientists who use it in cutting-edge space technology, gold is much more than just a pretty metal; it is a vital part of our history, culture, and technological advancement.", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/8\/8a\/Gold_%2879_Au%29.jpg", "atomic_mass": 196.9665695, "density": 19.3, "melt": 1337.33, "boil": 3243, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Middle East", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s1 4f14 5d10", "electronegativity_pauling": 2.54, "electron_affinity": 222.747, "ionization_energies": [ 890.1, 1980 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "Gold is what scientists call a 'noble metal,' meaning it is highly unreactive and won't rust, tarnish, or corrode over time. This incredible stability is why ancient gold coins and jewelry dug out of the ground still look as shiny as the day they were made! It is an excellent conductor of both heat and electricity. Because it is incredibly malleable (easy to press into thin sheets) and ductile (easy to stretch into wires), gold is highly prized in modern electronics. If you crack open a smartphone, computer, or television, you'll find tiny gold components that keep the device running smoothly. Gold also reflects infrared radiation, which makes it perfect for the visors of astronaut space suits and the protective shielding on satellites.", "Isotopes": "In nature, gold only has one stable isotope: Gold-197. This means that all naturally occurring gold is made of atoms with exactly 118 neutrons. However, scientists have been able to create many other radioactive isotopes of gold in laboratories. Among these artificial versions, Gold-198 is the most famous, as it has been used in medical treatments, particularly for targeting certain types of cancer and in medical imaging.", "Occurrence": "Most of the gold found on Earth actually arrived from outer space! Billions of years ago, meteorites containing precious metals bombarded our young planet, seeding the Earth's crust with gold. Today, gold is found in rock veins and deep underground deposits across the world, often alongside quartz or other minerals. It can also be found as small flakes or nuggets in the beds of rivers and streams, which is what triggered the famous gold rushes of the 19th century. Despite humans mining it for millennia, gold is quite rare; it's estimated that all the gold ever mined in human history would fit into just three Olympic-sized swimming pools!", "History": "Gold has a rich and profound history, widely regarded as the first metal ever used by humans. In ancient Egypt, it was heavily tied to the sun god Ra and used for the pharaohs' magnificent death masks. But perhaps nowhere is the history of gold as vibrant and culturally deeply rooted as in India.\n\nAncient Indian texts, including the Rig Veda, celebrate rivers as 'givers of gold.' Over 5,000 years ago, the Indus Valley Civilization was already crafting intricate gold jewelry, a tradition of adornment and spiritual devotion that continues in India today. During times of economic shifts, gold served as a trusted currency and a symbol of power.\n\nIndia is also home to the legendary Kolar Gold Fields (KGF) in Karnataka. Mining in the Kolar region dates back over 2,000 years. During the British era, KGF became one of the world's deepest and most productive gold mines, reaching depths of up to 3,000 meters. The mining town was so advanced and wealthy that it was the first city in India to get electricity, earning it the nickname 'Little England.' Although the mines were closed in 2001, the rich legacy of KGF and India's ancient love affair with gold continues to shine brightly." } }, "Hg": { "symbol": "Hg", "name": "Mercury", "atomic": 80, "category": "transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b>Mercury<\/b> (chemical symbol: <b>Hg<\/b>, atomic number: 80) is a fascinating and unique transition metal. Nicknamed \"quicksilver\" for its heavy, silvery appearance and liquid state at room temperature, it is the only metal with this remarkable property under standard conditions. Mercury is incredibly dense\u2014so dense that materials like lead or iron can float on it. Throughout history, it has captivated alchemists and scientists alike, though today it is most widely known for its high toxicity. Extracted primarily from the striking red mineral called cinnabar, mercury has a complex legacy spanning ancient medicine, medieval alchemy, and modern industry.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/b\/be\/Hydrargyrum_%2880_Hg%29.jpg", "atomic_mass": 200.5923, "density": 13.534, "melt": 234.321, "boil": 629.88, "phase": "Liquid", "discovered_by": "unknown, before 2000 BCE", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10", "electronegativity_pauling": 2, "electron_affinity": -48, "ionization_energies": [ 1007.1, 1810, 3300 ], "sections": { "Physical properties": "<p>Mercury stands out on the periodic table as the only metal that is liquid at room temperature. It has a high density of 13.534 grams per cubic centimeter, meaning a small vial of mercury is surprisingly heavy! It freezes at \u221238.83 \u00b0C and boils at 356.73 \u00b0C, giving it one of the narrowest liquid ranges of any metal. Chemically, it does not react with most acids but can form alloys, known as amalgams, with <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Au\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Gold (Au)\">gold<\/a>, <a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Ag\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Silver (Ag)\">silver<\/a>, and other metals. Its unique electron configuration prevents its atoms from sharing electrons strongly, causing it to act almost like a noble gas and remain a liquid.<\/p>", "History and Indian context": "<p>Mercury has a profound and ancient history, especially in India, where it has been studied for centuries under <b>Rasashastra<\/b>\u2014a specialized branch of Ayurveda often translated as the \"Science of Mercury.\" Ancient Indian alchemists considered mercury (known as <i>Rasa<\/i> or <i>Parada<\/i>) to be a powerful, transformative substance. They believed that through elaborate purification processes (<i>Samskaras<\/i>), mercury's toxicity could be removed, turning it into a potent medicine for rejuvenation and longevity. While modern pseudoscientific myths sometimes claim mercury fueled ancient flying machines (<i>Vimanas<\/i>), historians view these as symbolic alchemical metaphors. Beyond India, mercury was used globally by ancient Chinese, Egyptian, and Greek civilizations, often prized for its mystical properties and used as a brilliant red pigment (vermilion) derived from its ore, cinnabar.<\/p>", "Modern uses and safety": "<p>Today, the practical uses of mercury have sharply declined due to its severe toxicity. Historically, it was essential in thermometers, barometers, blood pressure monitors, and dental amalgams. In India and worldwide, it also saw heavy industrial use, particularly in the chlor-alkali process to manufacture caustic soda. However, mercury is a potent neurotoxin that can cause serious damage to the nervous and immune systems if inhaled, ingested, or absorbed. Because of this, global agreements like the Minamata Convention aim to phase out its use. Now, electronic devices have largely replaced mercury-based instruments, though it still finds limited application in fluorescent lighting and some specialized scientific equipment.<\/p>" } }, "Tl": { "symbol": "Tl", "name": "Thallium", "atomic": 81, "category": "post-transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p>Thallium is a chemical element with the symbol <b>Tl<\/b> and atomic number 81. It is a soft, silvery-white metal that quickly tarnishes to a dull bluish-gray when exposed to air. Although it looks a lot like tin or lead, it hides a deadly secret: thallium is highly toxic and historically infamous as the \"poisoner's poison.\" Discovered in 1861 by its brilliant green spectral line, it is now primarily used in high-tech electronics, specialized optics, and nuclear medicine. Because it is not found free in nature, it is typically gathered as a byproduct of refining other metal ores.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/5\/55\/Thallium_%2881_Tl%29.jpg", "atomic_mass": 204.38, "density": 11.85, "melt": 577, "boil": 1746, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "William Crookes", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p1", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.62, "electron_affinity": 36.4, "ionization_energies": [ 589.4, 1971, 2878 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p>Thallium is a heavy, post-transition metal that is soft enough to be cut with a standard knife at room temperature. Freshly cut thallium shines with a bright, silvery metallic luster, but it rapidly reacts with oxygen in the air, forming a heavy, grayish oxide crust that makes it look like lead. To prevent this, scientists often store it under oil.<\/p><p>Chemically, it behaves in unusual ways. While it shares a group on the periodic table with elements like aluminum and gallium, its chemical bonds are influenced by the \"inert pair effect\"\u2014a phenomenon where its outermost electrons are reluctant to participate in reactions. This makes thallium often act more like potassium or silver in its compounds. When ingested, the human body actually mistakes thallium for potassium, which is one of the reasons it is so devastatingly toxic at a cellular level.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Thallium has 41 known isotopes, but only two of them\u2014Thallium-203 and Thallium-205\u2014are stable and make up all naturally occurring thallium on Earth. The rest are radioactive and generally short-lived.<\/p><p>The most famous of these radioactive forms is Thallium-201. Far from being a poison, this artificially created isotope is a lifesaver in modern medicine. Because it emits low-energy X-rays and gamma rays, it is widely used in nuclear cardiology. During a cardiac stress test, doctors inject a tiny, safe amount of Thallium-201 into a patient's bloodstream to capture highly detailed images of blood flow to the heart muscle, helping diagnose heart disease.<\/p>", "History": "<p>The story of thallium begins in 1861 with a brilliant flash of green light. British chemist William Crookes and French chemist Claude-Auguste Lamy independently discovered the element using a then-revolutionary technique called flame spectroscopy. When analyzing leftover sludge from a sulfuric acid factory, they noticed an unknown, bright green line in the spectrum. Crookes named the new element \"thallium\" after the Greek word <i>thallos<\/i>, meaning a green shoot or twig.<\/p><p>Though both men played crucial roles\u2014Crookes identified it, and Lamy first isolated the solid metal\u2014a bitter rivalry erupted over who deserved the credit.<\/p><p>In the 20th century, thallium gained a dark reputation. Because its soluble salts are colorless, odorless, and nearly tasteless, it became a popular ingredient in rat poisons and insecticides. Unfortunately, these same traits made it the weapon of choice for murderers, earning it the grim nickname of \"the poisoner's poison.\" Today, its use in commercial pesticides has been largely banned worldwide.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>While its days as a household pesticide are long gone, thallium remains valuable in specialized modern industries. It is a critical component in manufacturing high-tech infrared detectors, photoelectric cells, and specialized optical glasses that require a high refractive index.<\/p><p>In India, thallium occasionally makes headlines for different reasons. Due to its historical notoriety, it still surfaces in rare but high-profile homicidal poisonings and domestic disputes. These criminal cases highlight a major challenge in public health: diagnosing thallium poisoning is difficult because early symptoms\u2014such as unexplained nerve pain, gastrointestinal distress, and delayed hair loss (alopecia)\u2014mimic other illnesses. Consequently, Indian medical literature frequently emphasizes the need for heightened clinical awareness to catch and treat exposure early.<\/p><p>Despite its dark side, thallium's contributions to advanced electronics and nuclear medicine make it an irreplaceable, if dangerous, element in the modern world.<\/p>" } }, "Pb": { "symbol": "Pb", "name": "Lead", "atomic": 82, "category": "post-transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b><a href=\"\/school1\/ptable\/element\/Pb\" class=\"wiki-link\" title=\"Lead (Pb)\">Lead<\/a><\/b> is a heavy, soft, and easily shaped metal with a dull gray appearance when exposed to air. Sitting at atomic number 82, it has the highest atomic number of any stable element. Although it is relatively unreactive, lead is highly valued for its high density, low melting point, and resistance to corrosion. Because it is so easy to extract from its ores, humans have used it for thousands of years. In ancient India, lead was known during the Vedic period and later held a special place in Ayurvedic medicine and alchemy (Rasa Shastra). Through a rigorous purification process, raw toxic lead was transformed into <i>Naga Bhasma<\/i>, an ash-like preparation used in traditional remedies. Today, while we still use lead in batteries and radiation shielding, we are much more aware of its toxicity, as it can be harmful to the human nervous system and organs.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/6\/63\/Lead-2.jpg", "atomic_mass": 207.21, "density": 11.34, "melt": 600.61, "boil": 2022, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Middle East", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p2", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.87, "electron_affinity": 34.4204, "ionization_energies": [ 715.6, 1450.5, 3081.5, 4083, 6640 ], "sections": { "Physical properties": "<p>Lead is a heavy, dense metal that feels surprisingly soft\u2014you can even scratch it with your fingernail! When freshly cut, it shines with a bluish-silver gleam, but it quickly turns a dull gray as it reacts with the air. It has a relatively low melting point, which made it incredibly easy for ancient metallurgists to work with and mold into various shapes. It does not conduct electricity as well as metals like copper or silver, but it is highly resistant to corrosion. Because of its density, it acts as an excellent shield against sound and radiation.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>In nature, lead exists as a mix of four stable isotopes (different versions of the same element with varying atomic weights). Interestingly, three of these natural isotopes are the final, stable endpoints of the radioactive decay chains of heavier elements like uranium and thorium. This means that over billions of years, much of the universe\u2019s radioactive elements slowly decay and eventually turn into lead! Because of this unique property, scientists often use the ratio of different lead isotopes in rocks to determine the age of the Earth and even date ancient artifacts.<\/p>", "History": "<p>Lead\u2019s story spans millennia. Its principal ore, galena, usually contains silver, which sparked widespread mining in ancient times, particularly during the Roman Empire where it was used for plumbing (giving us the word \"plumber\" from the Latin <i>plumbum<\/i>). However, India also shares a rich history with lead. Texts from the Vedic period mention the metal, and it was deeply integrated into ancient Indian alchemy and Ayurvedic medicine. Through a complex, fiery purification process known as <i>Rasa Shastra<\/i>, Indian healers neutralized the metal\u2019s toxicity to create <i>Naga Bhasma<\/i>, an herbo-metallic powder historically used to treat ailments like diabetes and digestive issues. During the Industrial Revolution, lead production soared globally, eventually leading to its use in paints and gasoline\u2014before its severe health hazards were widely recognized.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Today, the world produces millions of tons of lead each year, heavily relying on recycling. By far, its most common use is in lead-acid batteries, which are essential for starting everyday cars and providing backup power for computer networks. Because it blocks radiation so effectively, lead is also used to line the protective aprons you wear during dental X-rays and to shield nuclear reactors. It has historical uses in construction, bullets, weights, and solders. However, due to its well-documented toxicity\u2014causing neurological and developmental harm\u2014many everyday uses of lead, such as in paint, pipes, and gasoline, have been strictly phased out to protect public health.<\/p>" } }, "Bi": { "symbol": "Bi", "name": "Bismuth", "atomic": 83, "category": "post-transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "Bismuth (symbol Bi, atomic number 83) is a fascinating heavy metal that stands out in the periodic table for its striking appearance and surprisingly friendly nature. Unlike its toxic heavy metal neighbors like lead and polonium, bismuth is incredibly safe for humans. When freshly produced, it has a silvery-white color, but as it reacts with the air, it develops a dazzling, iridescent, stair-step crystal structure that looks like a miniature, rainbow-colored ancient temple. Because of its safety and unique properties, bismuth has become a modern superhero in replacing lead in everything from plumbing to medicine. In fact, you might have even swallowed some\u2014it is the active ingredient in popular pink stomach medicines!", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/a\/a5\/Bismuth-2.jpg", "atomic_mass": 208.980401, "density": 9.78, "melt": 544.7, "boil": 1837, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Claude Fran\u00e7ois Geoffroy", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p3", "electronegativity_pauling": 2.02, "electron_affinity": 90.924, "ionization_energies": [ 703, 1610, 2466, 4370, 5400, 8520 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "Bismuth has some of the most unusual physical properties of any metal. It is incredibly brittle and has a remarkably low melting point (271.5 \u00b0C or 520.7 \u00b0F), making it easy to melt on an ordinary stovetop. But what truly makes bismuth weird and wonderful is how it behaves when it freezes. Like water turning into ice, liquid bismuth actually expands as it cools and turns into a solid\u2014a very rare trait among metals!\n\nIt is also highly diamagnetic, meaning it actively repels magnetic fields. If you place a piece of bismuth near a strong magnet, it will actually push away. Furthermore, it is one of the worst conductors of both electricity and heat among all metals. Its natural tendency to form intricate, hopper-shaped (stair-step) crystals, combined with the thin layer of oxidation that creates brilliant hues of pink, yellow, blue, and green, makes bismuth a favorite among rock collectors and science enthusiasts.", "Isotopes": "For a long time, scientists believed that natural bismuth (specifically its only primordial isotope, bismuth-209) was completely stable\u2014meaning it would never undergo radioactive decay. However, in 2003, researchers in France discovered that bismuth is actually very, very slightly radioactive.\n\nDon't worry, though! It undergoes alpha decay with a half-life of over 20 quintillion years (2.01 x 10^19 years). To put that into perspective, that is roughly a billion times longer than the estimated age of the entire universe! Because it decays so unfathomably slowly, it is treated as completely stable and safe for all everyday and medical uses. In the medical world, other short-lived isotopes of bismuth (like bismuth-213) are artificially created and used as targeted radiation to hunt down and treat certain cancers like leukemia.", "Applications": "Bismuth may not be as famous as gold or iron, but its unique properties make it incredibly useful. Historically, it was used to treat digestive complaints, and today, it is still the star ingredient in stomach remedies (like bismuth subsalicylate) that soothe indigestion and fight stomach ulcers. In the context of Ayurveda, bismuth is sometimes debated by scholars to be \"Chapala,\" a mineral discussed in ancient Indian texts, though its exact traditional use remains controversial. Recognizing its growing importance, the Indian government in 2023 classified bismuth as one of 30 \"critical minerals\" essential for national security and economic growth.\n\nIn modern industry, bismuth is primarily known as the ultimate \"green\" substitute for lead. Because it is non-toxic, it is replacing lead in drinking water pipes, fishing weights, bullets, and solders. Its low melting point makes it perfect for creating specialized alloys used in fire sprinkler systems and electrical fuses, which are designed to melt and trigger safety mechanisms when they get too hot. It is also highly valued in cosmetics, where bismuth compounds are added to eyeshadows, lipsticks, and nail polishes to give them a luxurious, pearlescent shimmer." } }, "Po": { "symbol": "Po", "name": "Polonium", "atomic": 84, "category": "post-transition metal", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 84 (Po)", "extract_html": "<p><b>Polonium<\/b> (symbol <b>Po<\/b>, atomic number <b>84<\/b>) is a highly radioactive and rare post-transition metal. It was discovered in 1898 by the pioneering scientists Marie and Pierre Curie, who named it after Marie\\'s homeland, Poland. It has the distinction of being the first element discovered solely because of its radioactivity. A remarkably toxic and dangerous element, polonium is famous for its intense radioactive decay, glowing blue in the dark because it constantly excites the surrounding air. Due to its extreme radioactivity, it has a very short lifespan in the environment and must be handled with extraordinary care.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/images-of-elements.com\/polonium.jpg", "atomic_mass": 209, "density": 9.196, "melt": 527, "boil": 1235, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Pierre Curie", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p4", "electronegativity_pauling": 2, "electron_affinity": 136, "ionization_energies": [ 812.1 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p>Polonium is a silvery-grey metal that is incredibly radioactive. One of its most well-known forms, Polonium-210, is 5,000 times more radioactive than radium! In fact, a small piece of polonium emits so many alpha particles that it glows with a bright blue light as it ionizes the surrounding air. This intense radioactivity also generates an enormous amount of heat. A one-gram chunk of Polonium-210 will quickly heat itself to over 500&deg;C (932&deg;F). Because of this intense radiation, polonium is highly toxic\u2014billions of times more dangerous than hydrogen cyanide\u2014and can cause severe damage to living tissues if inhaled or swallowed.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Polonium has 42 known isotopes, all of which are radioactive\u2014meaning there are no stable forms of this element. Its isotopes range in atomic mass from 186 to 227. In nature, it appears only in tiny amounts as part of the natural decay chains of uranium and thorium. Polonium-210 is the most abundant natural isotope and has a half-life of about 138 days, meaning half of it safely decays away into stable lead every few months. Scientists can also create it artificially in nuclear reactors by bombarding bismuth with neutrons. Two other forms, Polonium-209 and Polonium-208, last a bit longer, with half-lives of 124 years and nearly 3 years, respectively.<\/p>", "History": "<p>When Marie and Pierre Curie were studying a uranium-rich ore called pitchblende in 1898, they noticed something strange: the ore was significantly more radioactive than the uranium and thorium inside it. This clue led them to discover polonium! Marie Curie named the newly found element after her native country, Poland (Latin: <i>Polonia<\/i>). At the time, Poland was divided among neighboring empires and didn\\'t exist as an independent nation. Curie hoped that naming the element would draw global attention to Poland\\'s struggle for independence, making polonium one of the first elements ever named to make a political statement.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Because polonium is so dangerously radioactive, many of its past uses have been discontinued. However, it still plays some fascinating roles in modern science and industry. Historically, the immense heat generated by Polonium-210\\'s decay made it an excellent atomic heat source. It was famously used to keep the internal components of Soviet Moon rovers (Lunokhod 1 and 2) warm during freezing lunar nights in the 1970s.<\/p><p>Today, it is mostly used in scientific research as a powerful source of alpha radiation. In specialized industrial settings, it helps neutralize static electricity in devices that manufacture paper, wire, or sheet metal. When mixed with beryllium, it is also used as a portable tool to generate neutrons. In India, researchers at institutions like the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) study polonium carefully for environmental monitoring, particularly tracking its presence in food chains and areas with naturally high background radiation.<\/p>" } }, "At": { "symbol": "At", "name": "Astatine", "atomic": 85, "category": "metalloid", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 85 (At)", "extract_html": "<p><b>Astatine<\/b> (symbol <b>At<\/b>, atomic number 85) is the rarest naturally occurring element in the Earth's crust. It is a highly radioactive element that only appears temporarily as heavier elements decay. Because its most stable isotope only lasts for about 8.1 hours before breaking apart, scientists have never seen a solid piece of it! If you gathered enough to see, its intense radiation would generate so much heat that it would instantly vaporize itself.<\/p><p>Positioned in the halogen group on the periodic table, right below iodine, astatine is predicted to look dark, lustrous, and metallic. Today, it stands at the exciting forefront of cancer research, where its powerful but short-lived radiation is being harnessed for Targeted Alpha Therapy to destroy tumor cells without harming surrounding healthy tissue.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/images-of-elements.com\/astatine.jpg", "atomic_mass": 210, "density": 6.35, "melt": 575, "boil": 610, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Dale R. Corson", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p5", "electronegativity_pauling": 2.2, "electron_affinity": 233, "ionization_energies": [ 899.003 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p>Because astatine is so short-lived and intensely radioactive, its physical traits remain a mystery\u2014scientists simply cannot keep a large enough sample around long enough to weigh or test it! If a visible piece were ever assembled, it would instantly vaporize itself due to the heat generated by its own radiation.<\/p><p>Most of what we know is predicted based on its neighbors in the periodic table. As a heavy halogen, it shares similarities with iodine but also sits on the borderline between metals and nonmetals, showing some metallic behavior. All of its isotopes are incredibly unstable, decaying rapidly into lighter elements like polonium, bismuth, or radon.<\/p>", "History": "<p>When Dmitri Mendeleev created his famous periodic table, he left a blank space below iodine for an undiscovered element, temporarily dubbing it \"eka-iodine.\" Finding this missing puzzle piece became a global quest, leading to several false alarms.<\/p><p>For example, in 1937, Indian chemist Dr. Rajendralal De claimed to have discovered the missing element in monazite sand and named it \"dakin.\" However, his claim was dismissed by the broader scientific community because the sample he described would have been impossibly and dangerously radioactive to handle, and its properties did not match the actual element.<\/p><p>The true breakthrough finally came in 1940 at the University of California, Berkeley. Scientists Dale R. Corson, Kenneth Ross MacKenzie, and Emilio Segr\u00e8 synthesized the element by bombarding bismuth with alpha particles in a cyclotron. They appropriately named it \"astatine,\" drawn from the Ancient Greek word <i>\u00e1statos<\/i>, which perfectly translates to \"unstable.\"<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>There are 41 known isotopes of astatine, and every single one of them is fleeting and radioactive. There are absolutely no stable forms of astatine in existence. The most \"stable\" isotope, astatine-210, boasts a short half-life of just 8.1 hours. On the other end of the spectrum, astatine-213 disappears almost instantaneously, with a half-life of merely 125 nanoseconds!<\/p><p>The incredible, focused energy released when these isotopes decay is exactly what makes astatine so valuable for modern medicine. <b>Astatine-211<\/b> (which has a half-life of 7.2 hours) is currently a rising star in experimental Targeted Alpha Therapy (TAT) for cancers like prostate and thyroid cancer. By attaching astatine-211 to specialized molecules that seek out cancer cells, doctors can deliver potent, localized radiation directly to tumors\u2014destroying the cancer from the inside out while sparing the surrounding healthy tissue.<\/p>" } }, "Rn": { "symbol": "Rn", "name": "Radon", "atomic": 86, "category": "noble gas", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 86 (Rn)", "extract_html": "<p><strong>Radon (Rn)<\/strong> is a fascinating, invisible, and odorless gas. It belongs to a group known as the \"noble gases,\" meaning it typically prefers to be left alone and doesn't easily react with other elements. What makes radon truly unique, however, is that it is radioactive. It's naturally created when heavier elements like uranium and radium slowly break down in the earth's crust.<\/p><p>In the context of India, radon holds significant geographic and scientific interest. The coastal areas of Kerala, particularly places like Panmana, are known as High Background Radiation Areas (HBRAs) due to the presence of radioactive minerals in the soil, which naturally release more radon. Modern Indian scientists, particularly at the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) in Mumbai, have dedicated extensive research to monitoring indoor radon levels across the country to ensure public health and safety. Furthermore, researchers in the Himalayan region have studied fluctuations in radon gas emissions from the earth as potential early warning signs for earthquakes.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/images-of-elements.com\/radon.jpg", "atomic_mass": 222, "density": 9.73, "melt": 202, "boil": 211.5, "phase": "Gas", "discovered_by": "Friedrich Ernst Dorn", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p6", "electronegativity_pauling": 2.2, "electron_affinity": -68, "ionization_energies": [ 1037 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "Radon is a heavy, invisible gas that you cannot see, smell, or taste. Because it is much heavier than the air we breathe, it tends to settle in low-lying areas like basements and ground floors of buildings. It is highly radioactive, meaning it is constantly breaking down and releasing energy. As it breaks down, it turns into other solid radioactive elements known as 'radon daughters' or 'radon progeny', which can attach to dust particles in the air.", "Physical properties": "At room temperature, radon is a colorless gas. However, when it is cooled down to a solid state, it glows with a beautiful, bright yellow color! If it is cooled even further, that glow changes to an orange-red. It is one of the heaviest gases known in nature\u2014about nine times heavier than the air we breathe. It also dissolves in water, which is why it can sometimes be found in groundwater or well water.", "Chemical properties": "As a 'noble gas', radon is incredibly stubborn and rarely reacts with other chemicals. For a long time, scientists believed it was completely unreactive. However, in modern laboratories, chemists have been able to force it to combine with a few other highly reactive elements, like fluorine, to create new compounds. Still, in everyday nature, you will almost always find radon completely by itself as a single, independent atom.", "Isotopes": "An 'isotope' is a version of an element that has a different weight. Radon has many isotopes, but they are all radioactive and unstable. The most common and longest-lasting one is called Radon-222. Even then, its 'half-life' (the time it takes for half of it to break down) is only about 3.8 days. This means radon doesn't stick around for very long; it quickly transforms into other elements like polonium and lead.", "Occurrence": "Radon is born from the natural decay of uranium and radium, which are found in rocks and soils all over the world. It slowly seeps out of the ground and into the air. In the open outdoors, it disperses quickly and is harmless. However, it can become trapped inside buildings, especially in poorly ventilated basements. In India, the geographic distribution of radon is very diverse. Areas with uranium-rich soils, such as parts of Punjab, Rajasthan, and the coastal monazite sands of Kerala, show naturally higher levels of radon. Institutions like Panjab University and BARC have conducted extensive surveys to map these occurrences and help guide safe building practices.", "Applications": "Historically, radon was sometimes used in hospitals to treat certain types of cancer through radiation therapy, though safer alternatives are mostly used today. Today, its most fascinating application is in earth sciences. Because radon is released from rocks, scientists use it to trace how groundwater flows. In India, measuring radon gas escaping from the ground along the Himalayan fault lines is an active area of research for predicting earthquakes! When tectonic plates shift and build up pressure, the rocks crack and release trapped radon, providing a potential clue that an earthquake might be coming." } }, "Fr": { "symbol": "Fr", "name": "Francium", "atomic": 87, "category": "alkali metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><strong>Francium<\/strong> is an incredibly rare, highly radioactive alkali metal with the symbol <strong>Fr<\/strong> and atomic number <strong>87<\/strong>. It holds the fascinating distinction of being the second-rarest naturally occurring element in the Earth's crust, right after astatine. In fact, scientists estimate that there are only about 20 to 30 grams of francium present in the entire Earth's crust at any given time! Due to its extreme radioactivity and incredibly short half-life\u2014its most stable isotope lasts for just 22 minutes\u2014francium is exceedingly difficult to study. If you could somehow gather enough of it to see, it would likely appear as a shiny, silvery-white metal. However, as an alkali metal, it is highly reactive and would vaporize itself almost instantly while reacting explosively with moisture in the air.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/images-of-elements.com\/francium.jpg", "atomic_mass": 223, "density": 1.87, "melt": 300, "boil": 950, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Marguerite Perey", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p6 7s1", "electronegativity_pauling": 0.79, "electron_affinity": 46.89, "ionization_energies": [ 380 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p>Francium is the heaviest known alkali metal. Like other members of its group (such as sodium and potassium), it has a single valence electron, making it extremely reactive. While it has never been collected in a large enough quantity to be seen by the naked eye or weighed on a scale, scientists predict it would be a silvery-white solid at room temperature. Its melting point is estimated to be quite low, around 27 \u00b0C (81 \u00b0F). Chemically, it reacts violently with water and air, much like its lighter cousins, though observing this in a lab is practically impossible because francium decays into other elements far too quickly. Its extreme instability is due to the sheer size of its atomic nucleus, which simply cannot hold itself together.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Francium is notoriously unstable. It has 34 known isotopes, ranging in atomic mass from 199 to 232, and every single one of them is highly radioactive. The most stable isotope is <strong>Francium-223<\/strong>, but even this form has a half-life of just 21.8 minutes. This means that if you had a lump of Francium-223, half of it would decay into radium or astatine in less than 22 minutes! Most other isotopes of francium have half-lives measured in mere seconds or fractions of a second. This rapid decay makes isolating the element practically impossible and presents a major challenge for scientists attempting to study its atomic properties.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Because francium is so incredibly rare and vanishes so quickly due to radioactive decay, it has absolutely no commercial, industrial, or medical applications. You will not find it in any everyday products or technologies. However, it holds significant value in the realm of specialized scientific research. Physicists and chemists synthesize tiny amounts of francium in laboratories using particle accelerators to study atomic structure, quantum mechanics, and the weak nuclear force. For instance, advanced spectroscopy experiments on francium help test theories of quantum electrodynamics (QED) and atomic parity violation. In India, like in the rest of the world, francium is mostly a topic of deep academic interest, taught in chemistry curricula (such as in competitive exams like JEE and NEET) as a prime theoretical example of periodic trends and intense radioactivity.<\/p>", "History": "<p>The discovery of francium is a story of persistence and national pride. For decades, chemists knew there was a missing alkali metal in the periodic table, right below cesium. Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev, the creator of the periodic table, had predicted its existence and temporarily named it 'eka-caesium'. Many scientists claimed to have discovered it in the early 20th century, but all were proven wrong. It wasn't until <strong>1939<\/strong> that French physicist <strong>Marguerite Perey<\/strong> at the Curie Institute in Paris finally discovered the elusive element. She found it while purifying a sample of actinium-227, which decays into francium. Perey proudly named the new element 'francium' in honor of her home country, France. Francium also holds a unique place in history: it was the very last chemical element to be discovered first in nature, rather than being artificially synthesized in a lab.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>Finding francium in nature is like searching for a needle in a planetary haystack. It occurs naturally only in trace amounts in uranium and thorium ores, specifically as a brief intermediate step in the radioactive decay of actinium-227. At any given moment, the entire crust of the Earth contains no more than 20 to 30 grams (about an ounce) of francium! Because it decays so rapidly, any naturally occurring francium is constantly disappearing, only to be replaced by newly formed francium from actinium decay. To study it today, scientists don't bother mining for it; instead, they artificially create it in laboratories by bombarding radium or gold atoms with other particles in high-energy accelerators.<\/p>" } }, "Ra": { "symbol": "Ra", "name": "Radium", "atomic": 88, "category": "alkaline earth metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b>Radium<\/b> is a highly radioactive, silvery-white metal that glows in the dark with a faint blue light. Discovered by Marie and Pierre Curie in 1898, this fascinating element was once hailed as a miracle cure and used in everyday products like toothpaste and glowing watches, before its dangerous radiation was fully understood. In India, the arrival of radium in the 1930s at centers like the Radium Institute in Patna and the Tata Memorial Hospital in Mumbai revolutionized early cancer treatment and laid the foundation for the nation's modern radiological and nuclear safety standards. Though rarely used today due to its extreme radioactivity, radium remains a legendary element that changed our understanding of science and medicine.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/b\/bb\/Radium226.jpg", "atomic_mass": 226, "density": 5.5, "melt": 1233, "boil": 2010, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Pierre Curie", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p6 7s2", "electronegativity_pauling": 0.9, "electron_affinity": 9.6485, "ionization_energies": [ 509.3, 979 ], "sections": { "Isotopes": "<p>All versions of radium\u2014called isotopes\u2014are radioactive, meaning they are unstable and break apart by releasing radiation. There are no stable forms of radium. The most common and longest-lived isotope is Radium-226, which has a 'half-life' of 1,600 years. This means it takes 1,600 years for half of a sample of Radium-226 to decay into another element (specifically, the radioactive gas called radon).<\/p><p>Because it takes so long to break down, Radium-226 is practically the only form of radium found in nature, making up nearly 100% of it. Other isotopes of radium exist, but they break down so quickly\u2014some in a matter of days or even fractions of a second\u2014that they vanish almost as soon as they are created in the natural decay chain of uranium and thorium. Interestingly, scientific experiments, including some using advanced techniques, have revealed that certain radium isotopes like Radium-224 have unique, asymmetrical 'pear-like' shapes in their nucleus.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>Radium does not exist in nature as a stable element; it is highly radioactive and constantly breaking down into other elements. Because of its short lifespan compared to the age of the Earth, any original radium that existed when the planet was formed is long gone.<\/p><p>However, radium is constantly being reborn. It is a natural byproduct of the decay of heavier radioactive elements like uranium and thorium. Wherever these heavy elements are found, tiny traces of radium will be there too.<\/p><h3>Indian Geography and Radium<\/h3><p>In India, you won't find mines dedicated to digging up radium. Instead, its presence is tied to the country's rich deposits of thorium and uranium. For instance, the famous monazite sands along the coasts of Kerala and Tamil Nadu are packed with thorium, which slowly decays to produce minuscule amounts of radium over time. Similarly, uranium-rich regions in Jharkhand and Rajasthan also harbor natural traces of this glowing element. Scientists continually monitor these areas to study natural background radiation, ensuring the safety of the local environment.<\/p>", "History": "<p>Radium was discovered by the famous husband-and-wife team, Marie and Pierre Curie, on December 21, 1898. While studying a radioactive mineral called pitchblende, they managed to separate a tiny amount of this new, highly radioactive element. It was named 'radium' from the Latin word for 'ray' because of the intense energy it emitted.<\/p><p>In the early 20th century, radium was considered a scientific marvel. Because it glowed in the dark and was thought to have health benefits, people added it to everyday items like drinking water, toothpaste, cosmetics, and the dials of clocks and watches. Unfortunately, many of the workers who painted these glowing dials, known as the 'Radium Girls', suffered severe radiation poisoning, revealing the dark and deadly side of this glowing metal.<\/p><h3>Radium in India<\/h3><p>India was remarkably quick to adopt this new wonder-element for medical science. Around 1930, the first stocks of radium were brought to the Radium Institute in Patna. Soon, pioneers of Indian radiotherapy established radium treatment centers across the country. The Tata Memorial Hospital in Mumbai even built a special 'Radon plant' to use the radioactive gas produced by radium for cancer therapy. These early efforts were crucial; they not only helped countless cancer patients but also forced India to develop strict radiation safety rules under the guidance of institutions like the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC). Over time, safer artificial radioactive materials replaced radium, but its legacy as the starting point of India's journey into nuclear medicine and radiation safety remains profoundly important.<\/p>" } }, "Ac": { "symbol": "Ac", "name": "Actinium", "atomic": 89, "category": "actinide", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 89 (Ac)", "extract_html": "<p><b>Actinium<\/b> (symbol <b>Ac<\/b>, atomic number 89) is a highly radioactive and incredibly rare metal that gives its name to the actinide series of the periodic table. Born from the decay of heavier elements like uranium and thorium, actinium is so intensely radioactive that it literally glows with an eerie pale blue light in the dark! Its name is derived from the ancient Greek word <i>aktis<\/i>, meaning \"beam\" or \"ray,\" which perfectly captures its radiant nature. It is about 150 times more radioactive than radium. Because it is so scarce in nature, scientists today produce it synthetically in nuclear reactors. While it has no everyday consumer uses, actinium is stepping into the spotlight as a powerful tool in modern medicine, offering promising new ways to target and destroy cancer cells.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/2\/27\/Actinium_sample_%2831481701837%29.png", "atomic_mass": 227, "density": 10, "melt": 1500, "boil": 3500, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Friedrich Oskar Giesel", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p6 7s2 6d1", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.1, "electron_affinity": 33.77, "ionization_energies": [ 499, 1170 ], "sections": { "History": "<p>The story of <b>Actinium<\/b> begins in 1899 with French chemist Andr\u00e9-Louis Debierne. While working with pitchblende (a uranium-rich ore) left over after Marie and Pierre Curie had extracted radium, Debierne noticed a new, mysterious radioactive substance. Independent of Debierne, German chemist Friedrich Oskar Giesel discovered the same element in 1902. Giesel initially named it \"emanium\" because it emanated such strong radioactivity, but Debierne's earlier discovery was eventually recognized, and the name \"actinium\" became official. Historically, actinium was incredibly difficult to study because its chemical behavior is almost identical to the rare-earth element lanthanum, making the two notoriously hard to separate. It wasn't until 1955 that completely pure actinium metal was finally isolated.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Actinium has absolutely no stable isotopes; every natural or synthetic form of it is radioactive. The most common and longest-lived isotope found in nature is <b>Actinium-227<\/b>, which has a half-life of about 21.77 years. It decays over time, primarily emitting beta particles as it transforms into lighter elements. However, the true star of modern research is <b>Actinium-225<\/b>. With a much shorter half-life of just 10 days, this isotope decays by rapidly firing off powerful alpha particles. In the scientific world, creating and studying these isotopes requires specialized nuclear reactors and particle accelerators, as natural actinium is far too rare to mine directly.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Because of its extreme rarity, high cost, and dangerous radioactivity, <b>actinium<\/b> has no commercial or industrial uses. However, it is a superstar in the field of <b>Targeted Alpha Therapy (TAT)<\/b> for cancer treatment. Scientists attach the isotope Actinium-225 to special targeting molecules (like antibodies) that seek out specific cancer cells. Once attached to the tumor, the actinium acts like a microscopic smart-bomb, blasting the cancer cells with high-energy alpha particles while leaving surrounding healthy tissue largely unharmed! Beyond medicine, Actinium-227 is sometimes combined with beryllium to create reliable neutron sources for scientific experiments and oil well logging. In India, institutions under the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) are actively researching such cutting-edge radiopharmaceuticals, aligning with global efforts to use advanced nuclear technology for life-saving medical treatments and deep radiochemical research.<\/p>" } }, "Th": { "symbol": "Th", "name": "Thorium", "atomic": 90, "category": "actinide", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><strong>Thorium (Th)<\/strong>, atomic number 90, is a weakly radioactive, silvery-white metal that holds incredible promise for the future of clean energy. When exposed to air, it slowly tarnishes to an olive-grey color as it forms thorium dioxide. Despite being a heavy actinide metal, it is surprisingly soft and malleable, and it boasts a very high melting point. If ground into a fine powder, it is reactive enough to ignite spontaneously in the air!<\/p>\n\n<p>Every single isotope of thorium is technically unstable (radioactive), but its most common form, Thorium-232, decays so incredibly slowly that its half-life is 14 billion years\u2014roughly the age of the universe itself. Because it decays so slowly, thorium is still found abundantly in nature today, making it one of the rare \"primordial\" radioactive elements alongside uranium. In fact, thorium is about three times more abundant in the Earth's crust than uranium.<\/p>\n\n<p>Historically, thorium was discovered in 1828 by the Swedish chemist J\u00f6ns Jacob Berzelius, who named it after Thor, the fierce Norse god of thunder. For a long time, it was used in everyday items like gas lantern mantles, camera lenses, and heat-resistant ceramics. However, as people learned more about radioactivity in the 20th century, many of these everyday uses were phased out. Today, its most exciting application lies in the realm of nuclear power. Thorium is famously abundant in India, particularly in the rich monazite sands of the Kerala coastline, setting the stage for India's unique and ambitious thorium-based nuclear energy program.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/f\/f7\/Thorium-1.jpg", "atomic_mass": 232.03774, "density": 11.724, "melt": 2023, "boil": 5061, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "J\u00f6ns Jakob Berzelius", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p6 7s2 6d2", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.3, "electron_affinity": 112.72, "ionization_energies": [ 587, 1110, 1930, 2780 ], "sections": { "Isotopes": "<p>While there are several isotopes of thorium, none of them are perfectly stable. However, <strong>Thorium-232<\/strong> makes up nearly all naturally occurring thorium, and it is a true survivor. With a half-life of 14 billion years, it has been around since the formation of the Earth! It decays by emitting alpha particles, eventually turning into a stable isotope of lead (Lead-208) after a long chain of transformations.<\/p>\n\n<p>What makes Thorium-232 incredibly special is that it is \"fertile.\" While it cannot sustain a nuclear chain reaction on its own, absorbing a neutron transforms it into Uranium-233, an excellent \"fissile\" nuclear fuel. This remarkable property is the foundation of India's long-term energy strategy. By designing special reactors\u2014like the Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR)\u2014scientists can breed fuel from thorium, unlocking a virtually inexhaustible energy source.<\/p>\n\n<p>Other trace isotopes, like Thorium-230, are found in deep ocean waters and are used by scientists to study ancient oceans and date geological events.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>Thorium is surprisingly plentiful, being three to four times more abundant in the Earth's crust than uranium. It is primarily extracted as a by-product from <strong>monazite sands<\/strong>, a reddish-brown phosphate mineral that is also rich in rare-earth elements.<\/p>\n\n<p>India is blessed with some of the largest thorium reserves on the planet, accounting for roughly 25% of the global supply! These massive deposits are largely found along the beautiful coastal regions of <strong>Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Odisha, and Andhra Pradesh<\/strong>. Over millions of years, the weathering of ancient granites and gneisses in the Western Ghats washed these heavy, thorium-rich minerals down rushing rivers, eventually depositing them along the sun-drenched beaches of the Indian peninsula.<\/p>", "History": "<p>The story of thorium began in 1828 when a Norwegian vicar and amateur mineralogist named Morten Thrane Esmark discovered a strange black mineral on the island of L\u00f8v\u00f8ya. He sent it to the renowned Swedish chemist J\u00f6ns Jacob Berzelius, who identified a new element and named it after <strong>Thor<\/strong>, the Norse god of thunder and war.<\/p>\n\n<p>For over a century, thorium's main claim to fame was its use in the glowing mantles of gas lamps and in specialized glass for high-end optics.
