But its true destiny was uncovered in the atomic age. Recognizing that India had vast reserves of thorium but very little uranium, the visionary Indian physicist <strong>Dr. Homi J. Bhabha<\/strong> architected India's ambitious three-stage nuclear power program in the 1950s. Bhabha's genius was to design a series of reactors that would eventually use the country's domestic thorium as their main fuel, bypassing the need for imported uranium and ensuring India's long-term energy independence.<\/p>\n\n<p>Today, Indian scientists at institutions like the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) and the Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR) continue to build on this legacy. With modern advancements in fast breeder reactors and advanced heavy water reactors, Bhabha's dream of a thorium-powered nation is steadily becoming a reality.<\/p>" } }, "Pa": { "symbol": "Pa", "name": "Protactinium", "atomic": 91, "category": "actinide", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><strong>Protactinium<\/strong> (symbol <strong>Pa<\/strong>, atomic number <strong>91<\/strong>) is a dense, silvery-gray actinide metal and one of the rarest and most expensive naturally occurring elements on Earth. Highly radioactive and toxic, it readily reacts with oxygen, water vapor, and inorganic acids. It most commonly forms compounds in a +5 oxidation state, though +4, +3, and +2 states are also possible. It is incredibly scarce, typically found in concentrations of just a few parts per trillion in the Earth's crust. Because of its extreme rarity and dangerous radioactivity, protactinium has no commercial uses outside of specialized scientific research. Notably, it is the only highly radioactive element with only one naturally occurring isotope that isn't monoisotopic\u2014arising almost exclusively from the decay of Uranium-235.<\/p>\n\n<p><strong>Key Scientific Facts:<\/strong><\/p>\n<ul>\n <li><strong>Appearance:<\/strong> Bright, silvery metallic luster<\/li>\n <li><strong>Phase at Room Temperature:<\/strong> Solid (Body-centered tetragonal crystal structure)<\/li>\n <li><strong>Melting Point:<\/strong> 1568 \u00b0C (2854 \u00b0F)<\/li>\n <li><strong>Boiling Point:<\/strong> 4027 \u00b0C (7280 \u00b0F)<\/li>\n <li><strong>Density:<\/strong> 15.43 g\/cm\u00b3<\/li>\n <li><strong>Standard Atomic Weight:<\/strong> 231.03588<\/li>\n <li><strong>Electron Configuration:<\/strong> [Rn] 5f\u00b2 6d\u00b9 7s\u00b2<\/li>\n<\/ul>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/a\/af\/Protactinium-233.jpg", "atomic_mass": 231.035882, "density": 15.37, "melt": 1841, "boil": 4300, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "William Crookes", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p6 7s2 5f2 6d1", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.5, "electron_affinity": 53.03, "ionization_energies": [ 568 ], "sections": { "History": "<p>In 1871, the pioneering chemist Dmitri Mendeleev predicted the existence of an element between thorium and uranium, noting a gap in his famous periodic table. However, it wasn't until 1913 that Kazimierz Fajans and Oswald Helmuth G\u00f6hring first identified a short-lived isotope of the element, initially naming it \"brevium\" because of its brief half-life of just 1.17 minutes. Later, in 1917 and 1918, two separate groups of scientists\u2014Otto Hahn and Lise Meitner in Germany, and Frederick Soddy and John Cranston in Great Britain\u2014independently discovered a much more stable isotope, Protactinium-231. The name was officially changed to \"protactinium\", meaning \"parent of actinium\", because it eventually decays into the element actinium. In 1934, Aristid von Grosse became the first to successfully isolate pure protactinium.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Scientists have discovered thirty radioisotopes of protactinium, ranging from Pa-210 to Pa-239. The most stable isotope is Protactinium-231 (Pa-231), which has a remarkable half-life of 32,650 years. Another important isotope is Pa-233, which has a half-life of about 27 days, and Pa-230, with a half-life of 17.4 days. All the other known isotopes have half-lives of less than two days, and the vast majority decay in under two minutes. Protactinium also has two nuclear isomers, Pa-217m and Pa-234m, with Pa-234m having a short half-life of just 1.17 minutes.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>Protactinium is extremely rare and expensive, making it one of the most elusive natural elements. It naturally occurs in just two isotopes: Pa-231 and Pa-234, though nearly all natural protactinium exists as Pa-231. This isotope is an alpha emitter formed by the radioactive decay of Uranium-235. To put its rarity into perspective, a typical ton of pitchblende (a uranium-rich ore) contains only about 0.1 milligrams of protactinium. Today, rather than mining it from ores, most of the world's very limited supply of protactinium is carefully extracted from the spent nuclear fuel of power plants for advanced scientific research.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Due to its extreme scarcity, high radioactivity, and significant toxicity, protactinium has no commercial, industrial, or everyday uses. Its applications are strictly confined to the realm of scientific research.<\/p><p><strong>Geochemical Tracing:<\/strong> Scientists use Protactinium-231 alongside Thorium-230 as a powerful \"clock\" (known as Pa\/Th dating) to measure historical sedimentation rates in oceans. This helps researchers understand ancient climate changes and ocean current dynamics.<\/p><p><strong>Nuclear Energy and India's Context:<\/strong> Protactinium plays a starring, hidden role in advanced nuclear physics\u2014particularly in thorium-based nuclear reactors. This is deeply relevant to India's Three-Stage Nuclear Power Programme, which aims to harness the country's vast thorium reserves. When Thorium-232 absorbs a neutron, it temporarily becomes Protactinium-233 before decaying into Uranium-233, the actual fissile fuel. Understanding and managing this \"bridge\" isotope is critical for the safety and efficiency of next-generation thorium reactors, making protactinium a key stepping stone in India's quest for long-term energy independence.<\/p>" } }, "U": { "symbol": "U", "name": "Uranium", "atomic": 92, "category": "actinide", "description": "Chemical element with atomic number 92 (U)", "extract_html": "<p><strong>Uranium<\/strong> is a silvery-gray, radioactive metal that has forever changed the course of human history. With an atomic number of 92 (symbol <strong>U<\/strong>), it is one of the heaviest elements found naturally on Earth. While it might look like just another shiny metal, its atomic structure holds an incredible secret: the power of nuclear fission. By splitting its atoms, we can unlock vast amounts of energy, making uranium the undisputed heavyweight champion of modern electricity generation.<\/p><p>Beyond its scientific intrigue, uranium plays a unique role in global energy and geopolitics. It doesn't just fuel nuclear power plants\u2014it also serves as the cornerstone for strategic defense programs and advanced industrial applications. In India, uranium takes on special significance as the starting point for a highly ambitious, self-reliant nuclear program spearheaded by legendary physicist Dr. Homi J. Bhabha.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/b\/b2\/Ames_Process_uranium_biscuit.jpg", "atomic_mass": 238.028913, "density": 19.1, "melt": 1405.3, "boil": 4404, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Martin Heinrich Klaproth", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p6 7s2 5f3 6d1", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.38, "electron_affinity": 50.94, "ionization_energies": [ 597.6, 1420 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p>In its pure form, uranium is a dense, silvery-white metal that is approximately 70% denser than lead. It has a high melting point of 1,132 \u00b0C (2,070 \u00b0F) and a boiling point of 4,131 \u00b0C (7,468 \u00b0F). If you were to leave a piece of uranium exposed to the air, it would slowly tarnish, developing a dark oxide coating.<\/p><p>One of the most defining characteristics of uranium is its radioactivity. It is constantly, albeit slowly, decaying and releasing particles. Because of its massive atomic nucleus, uranium is weakly radioactive and primarily emits alpha particles. Interestingly, uranium is also paramagnetic (weakly attracted to magnets) and happens to be a surprisingly good conductor of heat and electricity.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Uranium is most famous for its role in <strong>nuclear energy<\/strong>. Within the heart of a nuclear reactor, the uranium-235 isotope is bombarded with neutrons, causing it to split (fission) and release an enormous amount of heat. This heat boils water into steam, which spins massive turbines to generate clean, carbon-free electricity.<\/p><p>In the <strong>military and defense<\/strong> sectors, enriched uranium is used to power nuclear submarines, allowing them to stay submerged for years without refueling, and forms the core of nuclear weapons.<\/p><p>Additionally, <strong>depleted uranium<\/strong>\u2014the leftover material after uranium is enriched\u2014is incredibly dense. This makes it highly useful in civilian applications such as radiation shielding in medical therapy machines, as well as counterweights in aircraft wings and industrial machinery.<\/p>", "History": "<p>The story of uranium begins in 1789, when German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth discovered it in a mineral called pitchblende. He named the new element after the recently discovered planet Uranus. For over a century, uranium was mostly used as a colorant, adding brilliant yellow-green hues to ceramic glazes and glass.<\/p><p>Everything changed in 1896 when French physicist Henri Becquerel accidentally discovered radioactivity while working with uranium salts. The world suddenly realized that atoms held hidden, immense energy. This led to the dawn of the atomic age in the mid-20th century, culminating in the first nuclear reactors and, tragically, the atomic bombs of World War II.<\/p><p>In the <strong>Indian context<\/strong>, the history of uranium is deeply tied to the visionary scientist <strong>Dr. Homi J. Bhabha<\/strong>. Known as the father of India's nuclear program, Dr. Bhabha founded the Atomic Energy Establishment, Trombay in 1954 (later renamed the <strong>Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, or BARC<\/strong>, in his honor). Bhabha devised a unique three-stage nuclear power program. Since India had limited high-grade uranium but vast thorium reserves, his brilliant strategy was to use natural uranium in the first stage (Pressurized Heavy Water Reactors) to produce power and plutonium. This plutonium would then fuel the second stage, eventually leading to a third stage powered entirely by India's abundant thorium\u2014a vision that continues to drive the country's energy independence today.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>Uranium is surprisingly common. It is found in trace amounts everywhere\u2014in rocks, soil, and even the oceans. In fact, it is about as abundant in the Earth's crust as tin or tungsten. However, extracting it requires finding concentrated deposits in specific mineral formations.<\/p><p>Globally, countries like Kazakhstan, Canada, and Australia are the heavyweights in uranium mining. In India, domestic uranium reserves are relatively modest but strategically vital. The Uranium Corporation of India Limited (UCIL) manages mining operations primarily in the Singhbhum belt of Jharkhand, as well as in regions like Tummalapalli in Andhra Pradesh, which holds one of the largest low-grade uranium reserves in the world.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Uranium exists in nature primarily as three distinct isotopes: <strong>Uranium-238<\/strong> (which makes up about 99.27% of natural uranium), <strong>Uranium-235<\/strong> (about 0.72%), and a tiny trace of <strong>Uranium-234<\/strong> (0.005%).<\/p><p>The star of the show is <strong>U-235<\/strong>. It is the only naturally occurring isotope that is \"fissile,\" meaning it can easily sustain a nuclear chain reaction. Because natural uranium contains so little U-235, it often has to be \"enriched\"\u2014a complex process that increases the concentration of U-235 so it can be used efficiently in power plants and reactors.<\/p><p>Meanwhile, <strong>U-238<\/strong> is considered \"fertile.\" While it doesn't split easily on its own, it can absorb a neutron and eventually transform into Plutonium-239, another powerful fissile material. This transformation is the exact science underlying the second stage of India's nuclear program, utilizing Fast Breeder Reactors to produce more fuel than they consume.<\/p>" } }, "Np": { "symbol": "Np", "name": "Neptunium", "atomic": 93, "category": "actinide", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b>Neptunium<\/b> is a fascinating synthetic, radioactive metal with the symbol <b>Np<\/b> and atomic number 93. Named after the planet Neptune\u2014following uranium, which was named after Uranus\u2014neptunium was the very first transuranic element to be artificially created. It sits in the actinide series of the periodic table, possessing a silvery metallic appearance when freshly prepared. Although it can be found in vanishingly small trace amounts in natural uranium ores, nearly all of the world's neptunium is produced in nuclear reactors as a byproduct of uranium irradiation.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/e\/e5\/Neptunium2.jpg", "atomic_mass": 237, "density": 20.45, "melt": 912, "boil": 4447, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Edwin McMillan", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p6 7s2 5f4 6d1", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.36, "electron_affinity": 45.85, "ionization_energies": [ 604.5 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "Neptunium is a hard, silvery actinide metal that tarnishes slowly in air. It boasts a notably high density of 20.45 g\/cm\u00b3 and melts at a relatively low 639 \u00b0C (1182 \u00b0F), but it boils at a much higher extrapolated temperature of 4174 \u00b0C (7545 \u00b0F). One of its most intriguing physical properties is its ability to exist in three different crystal structures depending on the temperature (orthorhombic at room temperature, tetragonal, and body-centered cubic at higher temperatures). Chemically, it's quite active, capable of exhibiting oxidation states ranging from +2 to +7, with +5 being the most common in solutions. Because it is radioactive, handling it requires specialized safety equipment.", "Isotopes": "All isotopes of neptunium are radioactive, meaning none are completely stable. The most significant and longest-lived isotope is neptunium-237, which has a staggering half-life of 2.14 million years. It decays mostly by emitting alpha particles. Another important isotope is neptunium-239, which has a much shorter half-life of just 2.4 days. This short-lived isotope was the very first form of neptunium ever synthesized and is an important intermediate step in the creation of plutonium-239 in nuclear reactors.", "Occurrence": "For a long time, neptunium was considered an entirely artificial element. However, trace amounts of neptunium-237 and neptunium-239 do occur naturally in uranium-bearing ores. These tiny traces are created by natural nuclear reactions when uranium atoms capture stray neutrons. Despite this, the natural occurrence is so microscopic that practically all neptunium used in scientific research today is synthetically produced as a byproduct in nuclear power plants, extracted from spent nuclear fuel.", "History": "The story of neptunium is a landmark in nuclear science. It was discovered in 1940 by scientists Edwin McMillan and Philip H. Abelson at the Berkeley Radiation Laboratory in California. By bombarding uranium-238 with slow neutrons using a cyclotron, they successfully created neptunium-239, marking the discovery of the first element heavier than uranium (a transuranic element). Following the planetary naming theme started by uranium (Uranus), they named the new element after the next planet in the solar system, Neptune. McMillan was later awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1951 for this groundbreaking discovery.", "Applications": "While neptunium doesn't have many everyday commercial uses, it plays a vital strategic and scientific role. Its primary application is serving as the raw material to produce plutonium-238, an essential power source used in Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generators (RTGs). These RTGs act as long-lasting nuclear batteries for deep-space missions, powering iconic spacecraft like the Voyager probes and the Curiosity rover. In specialized industrial and research settings, neptunium is also used in instruments designed to detect high-energy neutrons.<br><br><b>The Indian Context:<\/b> In India, neptunium has a special significance within the nation's ambitious Three-Stage Nuclear Power Programme, originally envisioned by Dr. Homi J. Bhabha. In the first stage, Indian Pressurized Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs) use natural uranium as fuel. The neutron irradiation in these reactors naturally produces neptunium and plutonium as byproducts. Managing and processing these transuranic elements is a critical capability developed at institutions like the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC). The mastery over these processes is essential as India transitions toward Fast Breeder Reactors and ultimately a closed nuclear fuel cycle, optimizing energy output and carefully managing nuclear waste." } }, "Pu": { "symbol": "Pu", "name": "Plutonium", "atomic": 94, "category": "actinide", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p>Plutonium (symbol Pu, atomic number 94) is a fascinating, silvery-gray metal that belongs to a group of elements called actinides. When exposed to air, it quickly loses its shine and turns into a dull gray or sometimes greenish-yellow color. It is a radioactive, synthetic (human-made) element, though incredibly tiny trace amounts can be found in nature. Plutonium is famous for being a powerful source of nuclear energy. While it is highly toxic and must be handled with extreme care, it has changed the course of world history and continues to play a vital role in modern science, including space exploration and energy production. In India, plutonium is the cornerstone of the country's ambitious three-stage nuclear power program, envisioned by Dr. Homi Bhabha to achieve long-term energy independence.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/0\/0f\/Plutonium_ring.jpg", "atomic_mass": 244, "density": 19.816, "melt": 912.5, "boil": 3505, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Glenn T. Seaborg", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p6 7s2 5f6", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.28, "electron_affinity": -48.33, "ionization_energies": [ 584.7 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p>Plutonium is a highly unusual metal. It exists in six different solid forms (called allotropes) under normal pressure, and each form behaves differently. Unlike most metals, it is a poor conductor of electricity and heat. Even more strangely, it actually gets denser when it melts into a liquid! Chemically, it readily reacts with elements like carbon, halogens, nitrogen, silicon, and hydrogen. When it comes into contact with moist air, plutonium forms oxides and hydrides that can expand the sample by up to 70% in volume. This can cause it to flake off into a powder that is 'pyrophoric'\u2014meaning it can spontaneously catch fire in the air. Furthermore, handling plutonium is extremely dangerous because it is highly toxic and radioactive; if it enters the body, it can accumulate in the bones.<\/p>", "Physical properties": "<p>Freshly prepared plutonium looks bright and silvery, much like nickel, but it quickly oxidizes in air to a dull gray (though yellow and olive green tarnish have also been reported). At room temperature, its typical form is as hard and brittle as gray cast iron, but when mixed (alloyed) with other metals, it can become soft and ductile. It has a relatively low melting point (640 \u00b0C or 1,184 \u00b0F) but a very high boiling point (3,228 \u00b0C or 5,842 \u00b0F), meaning it stays in a liquid state across a huge range of temperatures. The radiation it naturally emits slowly damages its own crystal structure over time, a process known as self-irradiation. A chunk of the isotope plutonium-238 generates so much heat from its own radioactive decay that it can glow red-hot if not cooled.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>Plutonium is generally considered a human-made element, but incredibly tiny, trace amounts do exist in nature. It is the heaviest element known to occur naturally. These traces are found in natural uranium ores where uranium atoms occasionally absorb neutrons and transform into plutonium. Another form, plutonium-244, has such a long lifespan (a half-life of 80 million years) that it can survive from the ancient cosmic events that created it. Traces of primordial plutonium-244, created by exploding stars (supernovae) and colliding neutron stars long before Earth was formed, have been found in the deep sea floor. Today, minute traces of plutonium also exist in the environment due to atmospheric nuclear weapons testing carried out in the mid-20th century.<\/p>", "History": "<p>Plutonium was first synthesized and isolated in late 1940 and early 1941 by scientists Glenn T. Seaborg, Arthur Wahl, Joseph W. Kennedy, and Edwin McMillan at the University of California, Berkeley. They achieved this by bombarding uranium with deuterons in a cyclotron. Following the tradition of naming elements after planets (uranium after Uranus and neptunium after Neptune), it was named after the dwarf planet Pluto. Because of World War II, its discovery was kept a strict secret until 1948. Producing plutonium was a major part of the Manhattan Project, and it formed the core of the first atomic bombs, including the one detonated in the 1945 Trinity test and the 'Fat Man' bomb dropped on Nagasaki.<\/p><p>In India, plutonium holds immense strategic importance. Following its independence, India established the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) at Trombay. Guided by the visionary Dr. Homi J. Bhabha, India developed research reactors like CIRUS and Dhruva, which successfully produced weapons-grade plutonium. This indigenous capability enabled India's peaceful nuclear explosion in 1974 (Smiling Buddha) and the 1998 Pokhran tests (Shakti). While ancient Indian texts like the Vedas do not mention synthetic elements like plutonium, modern Indian scientific achievements strongly reflect a deep, enduring pursuit of harnessing the fundamental forces of nature.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>The most famous use of plutonium is as a fuel for nuclear reactors and in nuclear weapons. The isotopes plutonium-239 and plutonium-241 are 'fissile', meaning they can easily sustain a nuclear chain reaction to release massive amounts of energy. The percentage of another isotope, plutonium-240, determines the grade of the material, such as weapons-grade or reactor-grade, because of its high rate of spontaneous fission.<\/p><p>In India, plutonium is the absolute key\u2014the 'bridge' fuel\u2014in the nation's unique Three-Stage Nuclear Power Programme. Because India has limited uranium but vast reserves of thorium, the strategy involves extracting plutonium from spent uranium fuel (Stage 1). This plutonium is then used in Fast Breeder Reactors (Stage 2) to generate electricity and convert thorium into usable nuclear material for the final stage. A monumental achievement for Indian science occurred recently when the Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam achieved first criticality in April 2026, marking a massive advancement in commercial fast breeder technology.<\/p><p>Another isotope, plutonium-238, generates a steady supply of heat through natural decay. This heat is converted into electricity in devices called Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generators (RTGs), which are used to power spacecraft like the Voyager probes, the Curiosity and Perseverance Mars rovers, and New Horizons, allowing them to explore deep space where solar panels wouldn't work. On Earth, the disposal of plutonium waste from dismantled weapons and power plants remains a critical environmental and non-proliferation challenge.<\/p>" } }, "Am": { "symbol": "Am", "name": "Americium", "atomic": 95, "category": "actinide", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b>Americium (Am)<\/b> is a fascinating synthetic, radioactive element with the atomic number 95. Part of the actinide series, it sits below europium on the periodic table and was named after the Americas to honor this connection. A silvery-white metal that tarnishes slowly in dry air, americium is unique among synthetic elements because it is widely found in everyday households! Its most famous application is in ionization smoke detectors, where a tiny amount of americium-241 is used to keep us safe from fires. While primarily synthesized in nuclear reactors, americium continues to play a vital role in industry, scientific research, and even deep-space exploration.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/e\/ee\/Americium_microscope.jpg", "atomic_mass": 243, "density": 12, "melt": 1449, "boil": 2880, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Glenn T. Seaborg", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p6 7s2 5f7", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.13, "electron_affinity": 9.93, "ionization_energies": [ 578 ], "sections": { "History": "<p>The story of americium begins during the intense era of the Manhattan Project. In the late autumn of 1944, a team of pioneering scientists\u2014Glenn T. Seaborg, Leon O. Morgan, Ralph A. James, and Albert Ghiorso\u2014first intentionally synthesized and identified americium at the University of California, Berkeley, and the University of Chicago's Metallurgical Laboratory.<\/p><p>They created it by bombarding plutonium with neutrons in a cyclotron. It was the fourth transuranium element (elements beyond uranium) to be discovered. Because it sits directly below europium in the newly restructured periodic table of the time, Seaborg suggested naming it \"americium\" after the Americas. The discovery was kept secret until after World War II, finally being announced to the public in November 1945 by Seaborg on a national radio show!<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>Americium is practically non-existent in nature. While minuscule trace amounts might exist in uranium ores as a result of rare natural nuclear reactions, essentially all americium on Earth today is synthetic. It is produced as a by-product in nuclear reactors when uranium and plutonium absorb neutrons. Over decades of atmospheric nuclear testing and reactor operations, small amounts of americium have been released into the environment, but commercial quantities are strictly synthesized in specialized facilities under heavy regulation.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>All isotopes of americium are radioactive and none are stable. The most important and widely used isotope is <b>Americium-241<\/b>, which has a half-life of 432.2 years. It decays by emitting alpha particles and gamma rays, eventually turning into neptunium-237. Another significant isotope is <b>Americium-243<\/b>, which is the most stable isotope of the element, boasting a half-life of 7,370 years. Scientists use americium-243 for deeper chemical studies and to act as target material for synthesizing even heavier transuranic elements in particle accelerators.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Unlike many synthetic elements that exist only in laboratories, americium has tangible, everyday uses. Its most famous role is in <b>ionization smoke detectors<\/b>. A tiny fraction of a gram of americium-241 emits alpha particles that ionize the air inside the detector, creating a small electric current. When smoke enters the chamber, it disrupts this current, triggering the alarm.<\/p><p>In the industrial sector, americium-241 is used in thickness and density gauges to measure materials like glass, paper, and metal during manufacturing. When mixed with beryllium, it creates a portable neutron source used extensively for oil well logging, geological exploration, and highway construction.<\/p><p><b>Indian Context & Future Horizons:<\/b> In India, americium is utilized within the nation's nuclear research and industrial monitoring sectors. Indian scientific organizations rely on americium-beryllium neutron sources for soil moisture testing, agriculture, and geological surveys. Looking to the future, space agencies worldwide are researching americium-241 as a long-lasting power source (Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generators, or RTGs) for deep-space probes. Because it generates heat through radioactive decay, it could power spacecraft exploring the outer planets where solar energy is insufficient.<\/p>" } }, "Cm": { "symbol": "Cm", "name": "Curium", "atomic": 96, "category": "actinide", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p>Curium (symbol <strong>Cm<\/strong>, atomic number <strong>96<\/strong>) is a fascinating, synthetic, and highly radioactive metal. Named in honor of the pioneering scientists Marie and Pierre Curie, this element is a heavy hitter in the actinide series. It glows with a mesmerizing purple light in the dark because of its intense radioactivity. While you will not find curium naturally on Earth today, scientists have mastered the art of creating it in laboratories and nuclear reactors. It has proven incredibly valuable in space exploration, powering devices that analyze Martian rocks, and remains a proud subject of radiochemistry research around the world, including landmark achievements in India.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/images-of-elements.com\/s\/curium-glow.jpg", "atomic_mass": 247, "density": 13.51, "melt": 1613, "boil": 3383, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Glenn T. Seaborg", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p6 7s2 5f7 6d1", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.28, "electron_affinity": 27.17, "ionization_energies": [ 581 ], "sections": { "History": "<p>Curium's story began in secret during the height of World War II. It was first synthesized in 1944 as part of the Manhattan Project by a team of brilliant scientists: Glenn T. Seaborg, Ralph A. James, and Albert Ghiorso at the University of California, Berkeley. By bombarding plutonium with alpha particles in a cyclotron, they successfully created this new element. Its discovery was closely guarded and only revealed to the public after the war in 1945 - interestingly, Seaborg first let the secret slip on a children's radio show called the <em>Quiz Kids<\/em>! The element was proudly named 'Curium' after Marie and Pierre Curie, matching the naming pattern of gadolinium (named after Johan Gadolin), which sits just above it on the periodic table.<\/p>", "Characteristics": "<p>Curium is a hard, dense, and silvery-white metal. One of its most striking features is that it literally glows purple in the dark due to the sheer intensity of its radiation. It has a melting point of 1,340 deg C (2,444 deg F) and is chemically reactive, easily forming compounds. Curium is electropositive and typically exists in a +3 oxidation state. Because it is highly toxic and radioactive, it poses significant health risks - if absorbed into the body, it tends to accumulate in the bones, disrupting the production of red blood cells.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Curium has no stable forms; all 19 of its known isotopes (from <sup>233<\/sup>Cm to <sup>251<\/sup>Cm) are radioactive. The longest-lived isotope is Curium-247, boasting a half-life of 15.6 million years! Other notable isotopes include Curium-242 and Curium-244, which are more commonly used in research and have shorter half-lives of 162.8 days and 18.1 years, respectively. Curium-250 is particularly unique because it mostly decays by spontaneously splitting apart (spontaneous fission). Many of its isotopes can sustain nuclear chain reactions, meaning they could theoretically be used as nuclear reactor fuel, though their extreme radioactivity and scarcity make this impractical today.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>Because even its longest-lived isotope (Curium-247) has a half-life much shorter than the age of the Earth, any primordial curium that existed when our planet formed has long since decayed away into other elements. Today, curium is almost entirely synthetic, created in small amounts in nuclear reactors or laboratories. It does occasionally appear as a byproduct in spent nuclear fuel. Historically, trace amounts of curium were also detected in the environment following atmospheric nuclear weapons testing, such as the <em>Ivy Mike<\/em> thermonuclear test in 1952. While natural curium does not exist on Earth, scientists believe traces of it may occasionally be brought here by cosmic rays or produced in distant stellar events.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Despite its rarity and hazards, curium has carved out a niche in some truly out-of-this-world applications. Its most famous role is in space exploration. Curium-244 serves as the alpha particle source for Alpha Particle X-ray Spectrometers (APXS). These incredible instruments have been mounted on Mars rovers - like <em>Pathfinder<\/em>, <em>Spirit<\/em>, <em>Opportunity<\/em>, and <em>Curiosity<\/em> - to zap Martian rocks and soil, helping scientists understand their chemical composition. Thanks to the intense heat generated by its radioactivity, curium has also been studied as a power source for radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) in spacecraft. In the past, Curium-242 was even considered for powering long-lasting pacemakers before safer lithium batteries took over. In nuclear research, curium is used as a stepping stone to synthesize even heavier, undiscovered elements.<\/p>", "Indian Context": "<p>India has made significant strides in the complex field of radiochemistry. A major milestone for the country occurred in December 1975, when scientists at the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) in Trombay successfully isolated and purified Curium-242 for the very first time in India. The team achieved this by irradiating indigenously prepared Americium-241 with neutrons in the Cirus reactor. Working with highly radioactive materials required immense skill and the use of specialized glove boxes, marking a proud achievement in India's nuclear research capabilities.<\/p>" } }, "Bk": { "symbol": "Bk", "name": "Berkelium", "atomic": 97, "category": "actinide", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p>Berkelium is a highly radioactive, silvery-white synthetic metal that doesn't exist naturally on Earth. Born in a laboratory in 1949, it was named after Berkeley, California, where it was first created. Because it is so rare and difficult to produce, you won't find berkelium in any everyday items. Instead, this extreme element plays a starring role in advanced scientific research, helping scientists understand the complex behavior of heavy metals and serving as a crucial building block to discover even newer, superheavy elements on the periodic table.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/f\/fc\/Berkelium.jpg", "atomic_mass": 247, "density": 14.78, "melt": 1259, "boil": 2900, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p6 7s2 5f9", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.3, "electron_affinity": -165.24, "ionization_energies": [ 601 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "<p>Berkelium is a soft, silvery-white metal, but its most defining trait is its intense radioactivity. Because it is both extremely rare and highly radioactive, scientists must use specialized, heavily shielded equipment just to study it. The element can exist in two different crystal structures depending on the temperature, and it melts at around 986 &deg;C (1,807 &deg;F).<\/p>\n<p>One of the biggest challenges in studying berkelium is that it decays very quickly. The most common form used in labs, berkelium-249, has a half-life of just 330 days. As it decays, it transforms into another element called californium and emits powerful radiation. This means a piece of berkelium will actually generate its own heat from radiation and slowly contaminate itself over time, making it incredibly tricky to analyze.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Every single form&mdash;or isotope&mdash;of berkelium is radioactive; there are no stable versions. Scientists have discovered over a dozen different isotopes, with atomic weights ranging from 235 to 254.<\/p>\n<p>The longest-lasting isotope is berkelium-247, which takes about 1,380 years for half of it to decay. However, producing it is extremely difficult. Instead, researchers rely on berkelium-249. Even though half of it decays in just 330 days, it emits a \"softer\" type of radiation (beta particles) that is slightly easier to handle safely. Still, because it constantly decays into a more dangerous element, scientists have to work fast!<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>You won't find berkelium anywhere in nature. It is a strictly synthetic (human-made) element. Even if some berkelium had formed when the Earth was born billions of years ago, its short half-life means it would have vanished long before humans existed.<\/p>\n<p>Today, berkelium is born in specialized nuclear reactors, like the ones at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in the US and the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Russia. Making berkelium is a painstakingly slow and expensive process&mdash;in fact, since its discovery, only slightly more than a single gram has ever been produced in the United States! It can take years of careful work to create and purify just a few milligrams of this elusive metal.<\/p>", "History": "<p>The story of berkelium began in December 1949. A team of pioneering scientists&mdash;including Glenn T. Seaborg, Albert Ghiorso, Stanley G. Thompson, and Kenneth Street Jr.&mdash;successfully created the element at the University of California, Berkeley. To do this, they used a cyclotron (a type of particle accelerator) to bombard a smaller element, americium, with helium nuclei.<\/p>\n<p>They named their new discovery \"berkelium\" in honor of the city of Berkeley. This was a clever nod to the periodic table: the element sitting directly above berkelium is terbium, which was named after the Swedish village of Ytterby where it was found.<\/p>\n<p>Since those early days, exploring these heavy elements has become a worldwide effort. Indian nuclear scientists, for example, are active contributors to the global research on the nuclear fuel cycle and the complex chemistry of actinides (the family of elements berkelium belongs to). Their theoretical models and research help international teams better understand these mysterious, heavy elements.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Because it is so incredibly rare, dangerous, and expensive to produce, berkelium has no practical or commercial uses. You won't find it in any gadgets or medical devices.<\/p>\n<p>Instead, berkelium's true value lies in pushing the boundaries of science. Its most famous role is acting as a \"target\" to create even heavier, newer elements. In 2009, a tiny 22-milligram sample of berkelium was created in Tennessee and shipped to Russia. There, scientists bombarded it with calcium atoms for months. This historic international collaboration&mdash;which involved theoretical contributions from scientists across the globe, including Indian physicists&mdash;successfully created the first atoms of a brand new element: tennessine (element 117).<\/p>\n<p>Recently, scientists have also used berkelium to create \"berkelocene,\" a complex molecule that helps researchers finally understand how this mysterious element forms chemical bonds. For now, berkelium remains an invaluable tool for unlocking the deepest secrets of the periodic table.<\/p>" } }, "Cf": { "symbol": "Cf", "name": "Californium", "atomic": 98, "category": "actinide", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b>Californium (Cf)<\/b> is a fascinating, human-made chemical element with the atomic number 98. First created in 1950 at the University of California, Berkeley (which inspired its name), it is a highly radioactive metal belonging to the actinide series. Californium is famous for being one of the heaviest elements ever produced in amounts large enough to see with the naked eye.<\/p>\n<p>Unlike most synthetic elements that exist only in laboratories for fleeting moments, Californium actually has practical, real-world applications. Its most widely used isotope, Californium-252, is an incredibly powerful source of neutrons. Because of this, it is used to kick-start nuclear reactors, scan for precious metals, and even treat certain types of cancers. However, due to its intense radioactivity, it requires highly specialized handling and is exceptionally expensive to produce.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/9\/93\/Californium.jpg", "atomic_mass": 251, "density": 15.1, "melt": 1173, "boil": 1743, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p6 7s2 5f10", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.3, "electron_affinity": -97.31, "ionization_energies": [ 608 ], "sections": { "Physical properties": "Californium is a silvery-white metal that is surprisingly soft\u2014it can easily be sliced with an ordinary knife. In a vacuum, it starts to turn into a gas at temperatures above 300 \u00b0C (570 \u00b0F), but under normal conditions, it melts at around 900 \u00b0C (1,650 \u00b0F). \n\nWhat's especially interesting about Californium is its magnetic personality. When cooled to extremely low temperatures, it can act like a regular magnet, and at slightly warmer temperatures, it responds to external magnetic fields. The metal exists in two distinct crystal shapes depending on the temperature, and it will slowly tarnish if left exposed to room-temperature air.", "Isotopes": "There are 20 known isotopes of Californium, which are different versions of the element that vary in weight. The most stable one is Californium-251, which takes 898 years for half of it to decay away. \n\nHowever, the superstar of the group is Californium-252. Even though its half-life is only about 2.6 years, it is an absolute powerhouse when it comes to emitting neutrons. A single microgram (one-millionth of a gram) of Californium-252 shoots out an astonishing 2.3 million neutrons every single second! Because it throws off so much radiation, it is extremely hazardous but also incredibly useful for specialized scientific and industrial tasks.", "History": "Californium was born in the lab! It was first synthesized on February 9, 1950, by a legendary team of scientists\u2014Stanley G. Thompson, Kenneth Street Jr., Albert Ghiorso, and Glenn T. Seaborg\u2014at the University of California, Berkeley. To create it, they used a particle accelerator called a cyclotron to smash alpha particles (helium ions) into a tiny target made of curium. \n\nThey named the new element \"Californium\" in honor of both the university and the state. At the time, they joked that making the element was just as difficult as it was for early pioneers to travel to California a century earlier. By the 1960s and 70s, specialized reactors began producing small, weighable batches of the element. In the early 1970s, it was sold for a mind-boggling $10 per microgram, making it one of the most expensive materials on Earth!", "Occurrence": "You won't find Californium naturally occurring on Earth today. Because all of its isotopes are radioactive and eventually decay, any Californium that might have existed when our planet formed billions of years ago is long gone. \n\nToday, traces of Californium can only be found in the environment near specialized nuclear facilities or medical centers that use it. Small amounts were also released into the atmosphere during nuclear weapons testing in the mid-20th century. Interestingly, scientists once believed that Californium was created naturally in the explosive deaths of stars (supernovas), but modern astronomy suggests that other elements are responsible for the light we see from those cosmic blasts.", "Applications and Modern Uses": "Californium is one of the few superheavy, synthetic elements with major practical uses, largely thanks to its ability to unleash a massive flood of neutrons. \n\n\u2022 **Nuclear Power:** It is used as a highly reliable \"spark plug\" to start up nuclear reactors.\n\u2022 **Material Scanning:** Industries use it for Prompt Gamma Neutron Activation Analysis (PGNAA), a technique that bombs coal, cement, or minerals with neutrons to instantly analyze their chemical makeup. \n\u2022 **Oil and Gas Exploration:** It is lowered into boreholes to detect water, oil, and gas layers deep underground.\n\u2022 **Medical Treatments:** In specialized radiation therapies, Californium-252 is used to target and shrink certain types of stubborn cancers when traditional treatments fail.\n\u2022 **Scientific Discovery:** It is often used as a target in particle accelerators to help scientists discover even heavier, brand-new elements like Oganesson (element 118).", "Indian Context": "In India, Californium has made headlines in a rather unusual and bizarre way\u2014through high-stakes scams. Over the years, Indian law enforcement agencies have arrested several smuggling gangs trying to sell mysterious \"stones\" or metallic objects for millions of rupees, falsely claiming the material was the ultra-rare Californium. \n\nWhen these seized materials were tested by India's Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) and the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE), they were consistently found to be completely ordinary, non-radioactive fakes. Real Californium is strictly regulated, intensely radioactive, and requires massive lead-lined casks for transport, making it virtually impossible to find on the black market! On the legitimate side, Indian research institutions like BARC have safely used loaned Californium-252 sources for decades to conduct advanced radiological physics training and research." } }, "Es": { "symbol": "Es", "name": "Einsteinium", "atomic": 99, "category": "actinide", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b>Einsteinium<\/b> (symbol <b>Es<\/b>, atomic number <b>99<\/b>) is a fascinating, highly radioactive synthetic metal. Part of the actinide series, it was first discovered in 1952 in the radioactive debris of the world's first hydrogen bomb explosion (\"Ivy Mike\"). It was named in honor of the renowned physicist Albert Einstein.<\/p>\n<p>Because it is highly radioactive and decays quickly, einsteinium is extremely difficult to study. Its most common isotope, einsteinium-253, glows with a mysterious blue light due to its intense radiation, generating so much heat that it can actually damage its own crystalline structure! This element does not exist naturally on Earth and is produced in tiny quantities\u2014about a milligram per year\u2014in specialized nuclear reactors. While einsteinium currently has no everyday practical applications, it represents a remarkable achievement in nuclear chemistry and pushes the boundaries of our understanding of the periodic table.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/5\/55\/Einsteinium.jpg", "atomic_mass": 252, "density": 8.84, "melt": 1133, "boil": 1269, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p6 7s2 5f11", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.3, "electron_affinity": -28.6, "ionization_energies": [ 619 ], "sections": { "History": "<p>The story of einsteinium's discovery is deeply tied to the dawn of the thermonuclear age. It was first identified in December 1952 by a team of scientists led by Albert Ghiorso at the University of California, Berkeley, alongside researchers from the Argonne and Los Alamos National Laboratories. They discovered the new element while analyzing the radioactive fallout from the \"Ivy Mike\" hydrogen bomb test in the Pacific Ocean.<\/p>\n<p>The immense explosion created a massive burst of neutrons, allowing uranium atoms to rapidly absorb multiple neutrons and transform into heavier, entirely new elements. Initially, this groundbreaking discovery was kept a strict military secret due to Cold War tensions, and was only declassified and announced to the public in 1955. The element was officially named <b>einsteinium<\/b> to honor Albert Einstein, while the closely related element 100 was named fermium after Enrico Fermi.<\/p>", "Characteristics": "<p>Einsteinium is a soft, silvery, paramagnetic metal. Its most striking physical feature is its self-luminescence\u2014it emits a visible blue glow in the dark, a direct result of its intense radiation releasing heat (nearly 1,000 watts per gram). This extreme radioactivity makes studying the metal in bulk nearly impossible because the radiation rapidly destroys its own crystal lattice.<\/p>\n<p>Chemically, it typically exhibits a +3 oxidation state, which is standard for late actinides, though a +2 state is also possible. It has a melting point of 860 \u00b0C (1580 \u00b0F) and an estimated boiling point of 996 \u00b0C (1825 \u00b0F). As a synthetic transuranium element, einsteinium is extremely hazardous and toxic. It must be handled with extraordinary caution in specialized, highly controlled facilities.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Einsteinium has 18 known isotopes and four nuclear isomers, with mass numbers ranging from 240 to 257. All of them are highly radioactive and unstable. The most stable isotope is einsteinium-252, which has a half-life of 471.7 days, though it is incredibly difficult to produce. The most commonly used isotope for scientific research, einsteinium-253, has a much shorter half-life of just 20.47 days.<\/p>\n<p>Other notable isotopes include einsteinium-254 (with a half-life of 275.7 days) and einsteinium-255 (39.8 days). Because its isotopes decay so quickly\u2014often transforming into lighter elements like berkelium or californium\u2014studying einsteinium requires scientists to work in a continuous race against time before their samples literally disappear.<\/p>", "Applications": "<p>Due to its scarcity, short half-life, and extreme radioactivity, einsteinium has no everyday commercial or industrial uses. Instead, it is highly valued in basic scientific research, specifically as a stepping stone for synthesizing even heavier, superheavy elements. For example, in 1955, einsteinium was crucially used as a target to discover mendelevium (element 101). Later, researchers used the rare isotope einsteinium-254 to attempt the creation of element 119 (ununennium).<\/p>\n<p>An interesting historical application occurred when einsteinium-254 was used as a calibration marker in the chemical analysis spectrometer aboard the Surveyor 5 lunar probe, helping scientists analyze the surface of the Moon.<\/p>\n<p>In the <b>Indian context<\/b>, while the element is not produced or used locally in industries, einsteinium holds an important place in advanced academic curricula. Students of nuclear physics and chemistry across India study its properties as a prime example of the f-block actinide series. Furthermore, Indian scientific media closely follow global breakthroughs related to this elusive element to keep the nation's robust research community informed about the frontiers of nuclear science.<\/p>" } }, "Fm": { "symbol": "Fm", "name": "Fermium", "atomic": 100, "category": "actinide", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b>Fermium<\/b> (symbol <b>Fm<\/b>, atomic number 100) is a fascinating, highly radioactive synthetic element. It holds a unique place in scientific history as the heaviest element that can be formed by bombarding lighter elements with neutrons. Because of this, it is the last element on the periodic table that can theoretically be prepared in macroscopic (visible) quantities, although pure fermium metal has not yet been produced.<\/p>\n\n<p>Fermium was first discovered in the radioactive debris of the \"Ivy Mike\" nuclear test in 1952\u2014the world's first successful hydrogen bomb explosion. Due to the secrecy of the Cold War, this discovery was kept classified by the U.S. military until 1955. The element was named in honor of Enrico Fermi, the visionary physicist who developed the first artificial nuclear reactor.<\/p>\n\n<p>As a member of the actinide series, fermium does not occur naturally on Earth and must be synthesized in specialized high-flux nuclear reactors. It typically exhibits a +3 oxidation state in chemical compounds. Because only microscopic amounts of fermium can be produced and its isotopes decay quickly, it has no commercial, industrial, or everyday applications. Instead, it is used exclusively for advanced scientific research to help physicists understand the limits of nuclear stability and the behavior of the heaviest elements in the universe.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/upload.wikimedia.org\/wikipedia\/commons\/5\/58\/Ivy_Mike_-_mushroom_cloud.jpg", "atomic_mass": 257, "density": null, "melt": 1800, "boil": null, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p6 7s2 5f12", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.3, "electron_affinity": 33.96, "ionization_energies": [ 627 ], "sections": { "Isotopes": "<p>Fermium has 20 known isotopes, ranging in atomic weight from 241 to 260. All of them are radioactive and relatively short-lived. The most stable isotope is <b>fermium-257<\/b>, which has a half-life of about 100.5 days. Other notable isotopes include fermium-253 (half-life of 3 days) and fermium-255 (20.1 hours). Most other isotopes decay much faster, with half-lives ranging from a few hours to mere milliseconds.<\/p>\n\n<p>An interesting scientific roadblock occurs with heavier fermium isotopes. When fermium-257 captures a neutron to become fermium-258, it undergoes spontaneous fission (splitting apart) in just 370 microseconds. Heavier isotopes like fermium-259 and fermium-260 also undergo rapid spontaneous fission. This phenomenon prevents scientists from creating even heavier elements through standard neutron capture in reactors, creating a barrier known as the \"fermium gap.\" Because of this gap, elements heavier than fermium must be painstakingly synthesized by colliding ions in particle accelerators.<\/p>", "Occurrence": "<p>Fermium does not exist naturally in the Earth's crust. It is a strictly synthetic element that must be artificially created in highly specialized laboratories. Today, it is produced in microscopic quantities by bombarding lighter elements, such as plutonium or curium, with intense neutrons in high-flux nuclear reactors.<\/p>\n\n<p>While India has a robust nuclear research program led by institutions like the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) and the Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR), fermium is not a focus of domestic industrial or energy programs. Indian nuclear research primarily targets energy security, advanced reactor technologies, and the thorium fuel cycle. Since fermium has no commercial or practical applications, it remains a subject of fundamental global physics research and is produced only in a few elite high-flux reactor facilities worldwide.<\/p>" } }, "Md": { "symbol": "Md", "name": "Mendelevium", "atomic": 101, "category": "actinide", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><strong>Mendelevium<\/strong> is a synthetic, highly radioactive metal with the atomic number <strong>101<\/strong> and the symbol <strong>Md<\/strong>. Belonging to the actinide series, it is a transuranic element, which means it exists beyond uranium in the periodic table. Because it doesn't occur naturally on Earth, it must be created artificially in laboratories using particle accelerators. Mendelevium is renowned as a monumental achievement in nuclear chemistry, demonstrating that elements could be synthesized and identified even when produced literally one atom at a time.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/images-of-elements.com\/s\/mendelevium.jpg", "atomic_mass": 258, "density": null, "melt": 1100, "boil": null, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p6 7s2 5f13", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.3, "electron_affinity": 93.91, "ionization_energies": [ 635 ], "sections": { "History and Discovery": "<p>Mendelevium was first synthesized in 1955 by a legendary team of scientists at the University of California, Berkeley, which included Albert Ghiorso, Glenn T. Seaborg, Bernard Harvey, Gregory Choppin, and Stanley G. Thompson. They created the new element by bombarding atoms of einsteinium-253 with alpha particles (helium nuclei) using a cyclotron. The element was proudly named to honor <strong>Dmitri Mendeleev<\/strong>, the famous Russian chemist who created the periodic table of elements, serving as a lasting tribute to his foundational contributions to science.<\/p>", "Scientific Facts and Isotopes": "<p>As a highly radioactive metal, mendelevium typically exhibits a +3 oxidation state, though a +2 state is also accessible in certain aqueous solutions. Mendelevium has seventeen known isotopes, all of which are radioactive and artificially produced. The most stable of these is <strong>mendelevium-258<\/strong>, which has a half-life of approximately 51.5 days. However, scientists often use the shorter-lived mendelevium-256 (with a half-life of about 77 minutes) in experiments because it is easier to produce in somewhat larger quantities. Mendelevium stands out as the heaviest element that still has an isotope with a half-life longer than a single day.<\/p>", "Modern Uses": "<p>Because it can only be produced in incredibly minuscule amounts and has a relatively short half-life, mendelevium currently has <strong>no commercial or industrial applications<\/strong>. Its use is strictly confined to basic scientific research. Today, scientists study mendelevium to better understand the chemical and physical properties of the late actinide elements and to push the boundaries of what we know about atomic structure.<\/p>", "Indian Context": "<p>While there are no specific facilities in India producing mendelevium or unique industrial applications for it within the country, the element holds a special place in the Indian scientific and educational landscape. In Indian academic literature and university curricula, mendelevium is frequently highlighted as a powerful example of human ingenuity in nuclear science. It serves as a key pedagogical tool to illustrate the fascinating history of the periodic table, the successful synthesis of transuranic elements, and the deeply international, collaborative nature of scientific discovery.<\/p>" } }, "No": { "symbol": "No", "name": "Nobelium", "atomic": 102, "category": "actinide", "description": "", "extract_html": "Nobelium (symbol No, atomic number 102) is a synthetic, highly radioactive element in the actinide series. It does not exist naturally on Earth and is created artificially in particle accelerators by bombarding lighter elements like curium or californium with heavy ions. Discovered in the 1960s after a period of intense international competition, nobelium was named after Alfred Nobel. Due to its extreme instability\u2014its longest-lived isotope has a half-life of only about 58 minutes\u2014nobelium is incredibly difficult to study and has no commercial applications, making it exclusively a subject of high-level scientific research.", "local_image": "https:\/\/images-of-elements.com\/nobelium.jpg", "atomic_mass": 259, "density": null, "melt": 1100, "boil": null, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Joint Institute for Nuclear Research", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p6 7s2 5f14", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.3, "electron_affinity": -223.22, "ionization_energies": [ 642 ], "sections": { "Characteristics": "### Physical and Chemical Properties\nNobelium is a heavy, radioactive metal that belongs to the actinide series on the periodic table. While its short half-life makes it challenging to study in large quantities, scientists predict it to be a solid at room temperature with a stable +2 oxidation state. Because it decays so quickly, its chemical behavior is mostly explored \"one atom at a time.\" Modern experimental techniques allow researchers to better understand how it fits into the heavy-element region of the periodic table.\n\n### Discovery and History\nThe discovery of nobelium was highly competitive. In 1957, scientists at the Nobel Institute of Physics in Sweden claimed to have created element 102 and proposed the name 'nobelium'. However, their results couldn't be replicated. Over the next decade, teams at the University of California, Berkeley, and the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna, Russia, engaged in a priority dispute. Ultimately, the international scientific community credited the Soviet team for the definitive synthesis of the element, though the name nobelium was kept to honor Alfred Nobel.\n\n### Modern Uses and Global Context\nNobelium has no commercial, industrial, or medical applications. Its only use is in fundamental scientific research, particularly in nuclear physics and atomic theory, where it helps scientists test the limits of atomic stability. While nobelium is produced in only a few highly specialized accelerator facilities worldwide (such as in the U.S., Germany, Japan, and Russia), the theoretical physics and chemistry behind such heavy elements are studied globally. In India, premier research institutions like the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) contribute to the theoretical models of nuclear physics and heavy-element chemistry. Although India is not directly involved in producing nobelium, the element shares its namesake's legacy with several Indian Nobel laureates who have made landmark contributions to global science.", "Isotopes": "Fourteen isotopes of nobelium have been identified so far, with mass numbers ranging from 248 to 260, as well as 262. Every single one of them is highly radioactive. Additionally, scientists have discovered seventeen nuclear isomers. \n\nThe longest-lived isotope is **nobelium-259**, which has a half-life of just 58 minutes. However, in chemical experiments, researchers often use the shorter-lived **nobelium-255** (half-life of 3.52 minutes) because it can be produced more reliably and in larger quantities by bombarding californium-249 with carbon-12 ions. \n\nMost nobelium isotopes decay extremely rapidly. After nobelium-259 and nobelium-255, the half-lives drop significantly: nobelium-253 lasts for 1.57 minutes, and the rest decay in a matter of seconds or even fractions of a second. The shortest-lived known isotope, nobelium-248, vanishes in less than 2 microseconds. As researchers push to create heavier nobelium isotopes, they find that the intense mutual repulsion of protons makes the nucleus highly prone to spontaneous fission, setting a natural limit on the stability of these super-heavy actinide elements. Still, scientists predict that an undiscovered isotope, nobelium-261, might have an even longer half-life of up to 3 hours, offering an exciting frontier for future research." } }, "Lr": { "symbol": "Lr", "name": "Lawrencium", "atomic": 103, "category": "actinide", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b>Lawrencium<\/b> is a synthetic, highly radioactive chemical element with the symbol <b>Lr<\/b> and atomic number <b>103<\/b>. It is the final member of the actinide series in the periodic table. Because it is not found naturally on Earth, lawrencium must be created in high-energy physics laboratories by bombarding lighter elements with charged particles. Named after Ernest O. Lawrence, the inventor of the cyclotron particle accelerator, this elusive element exists only for fleeting moments. While we cannot observe it in our daily lives, its creation represents a remarkable triumph of modern nuclear physics.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/images-of-elements.com\/lawrencium.jpg", "atomic_mass": 266, "density": null, "melt": 1900, "boil": null, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p6 7s2 5f14 7p1", "electronegativity_pauling": 1.3, "electron_affinity": -30.04, "ionization_energies": [ 470 ], "sections": { "History and Discovery": "<p>Lawrencium was first synthesized in 1961 at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in California by a team of scientists including Albert Ghiorso, Torbj\u00f8rn Sikkeland, Almon E. Larsh, and Robert M. Latimer. The team created the element by bombarding a target containing californium isotopes with boron ions in a particle accelerator. Around the same time, the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna, Russia, also conducted experiments to create element 103. In 1992, the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) officially recognized both teams as co-discoverers. The element was proudly named after Ernest O. Lawrence, paying homage to his groundbreaking invention, the cyclotron, which paved the way for discovering many synthetic elements.<\/p>", "Scientific Characteristics": "<p>As a transuranic synthetic metal, lawrencium is incredibly difficult to study. Its extremely short half-life and the fact that scientists can only produce a few atoms at a time mean that its bulk physical properties are largely theoretical. Scientists predict that if enough lawrencium could be gathered, it would be a dense, silvery metal. In terms of chemistry, it behaves as a trivalent element, comfortably completing the actinide series with the electron configuration [Rn] 5f<sup>14<\/sup> 7s<sup>2<\/sup> 7p<sup>1<\/sup>.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>All known isotopes of lawrencium are radioactive and unstable. Scientists have identified several isotopes, ranging in mass. The most stable one discovered so far is <b>Lawrencium-266<\/b>, which has a half-life of approximately 11 hours. However, much of the chemical research on this element relies on <b>Lawrencium-260<\/b> or <b>Lawrencium-262<\/b> (with a half-life of about 3.6 hours), as they can be produced more reliably in laboratories. The element decays quickly into lighter, more stable elements, leaving researchers with only a brief window to study its fascinating properties.<\/p>", "Modern Uses and Global Context": "<p>Due to its extreme radioactivity and fleeting existence, lawrencium currently has no commercial or practical applications outside of basic scientific research. Its primary use is in expanding our understanding of the universe, specifically the properties of superheavy elements and how relativity affects their atomic structures. Worldwide, including in the <b>Indian context<\/b>, lawrencium is an object of academic fascination. In India, it frequently features in higher education curricula and competitive examinations as a prime example of human ingenuity in the realm of nuclear science and transuranic chemistry, though no dedicated production facilities exist within the country.<\/p>" } }, "Rf": { "symbol": "Rf", "name": "Rutherfordium", "atomic": 104, "category": "transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b>Rutherfordium (Rf)<\/b> is a fascinating synthetic element with atomic number 104, named in honor of the renowned physicist Ernest Rutherford. As a superheavy, man-made element, it does not exist naturally on Earth and can only be created in specialized particle accelerators by smashing lighter atoms together. It is highly radioactive and extremely unstable, with its most stable known isotope surviving for just about 48 minutes before decaying. Because it vanishes so quickly, rutherfordium has no practical or commercial uses outside of scientific research. However, studying it helps scientists understand the complex rules that govern the heaviest elements in our universe. In the periodic table, it proudly takes its place as a transition metal, behaving similarly to its lighter cousin, hafnium.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/images-of-elements.com\/s\/rutherfordium.jpg", "atomic_mass": 267, "density": 23.2, "melt": 2400, "boil": 5800, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Joint Institute for Nuclear Research", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p6 7s2 5f14 6d2", "electronegativity_pauling": null, "electron_affinity": null, "ionization_energies": [ 580 ], "sections": { "History": "<p>The story of rutherfordium is one of scientific rivalry and cutting-edge discovery during the Cold War. In the 1960s, two leading research teams\u2014one at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in the Soviet Union and another at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in California, USA\u2014both claimed to have created the element first. This sparked a decades-long debate over who should get the credit and the right to name it. The Americans proposed the name \"rutherfordium\" after Ernest Rutherford, the father of nuclear physics, while the Soviets suggested \"kurchatovium\" after Igor Kurchatov. It wasn't until 1997 that the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) officially settled the dispute, granting credit to both teams but finalizing the name as rutherfordium.<\/p><p>While rutherfordium cannot be naturally found or routinely handled, it continues to be a subject of global scientific interest, including significant contributions from India. At prominent Indian research institutions like the <b>Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC)<\/b> in Mumbai, scientists have conducted advanced theoretical research on rutherfordium. Indian researchers frequently present at national symposia (such as the DAE-BRNS symposium on nuclear physics), using complex mathematical models and first-principles density functional theory to predict how rutherfordium's structural and electronic properties compare to lighter elements. This Indian theoretical work is vital for understanding superheavy elements that disappear almost as soon as they are created.<\/p>", "Isotopes": "<p>Rutherfordium has no stable or naturally occurring isotopes. In chemistry, isotopes are different versions of an element that have the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons. For rutherfordium, every single isotope is highly radioactive and fleeting. Scientists have managed to synthesize around 17 different isotopes in the laboratory, with atomic masses ranging from 252 to 270.<\/p><p>These isotopes are born through intense atomic collisions and almost immediately begin to fall apart, or \"decay.\" Most rutherfordium isotopes decay through a process called spontaneous fission, where the nucleus simply breaks apart into smaller, lighter elements. Others undergo alpha decay, spitting out energetic particles as they transform. The most \"stable\" of these is rutherfordium-267, but even it has a half-life of only about 48 minutes\u2014meaning half of the material vanishes in less than an hour! Because these isotopes exist for such a short time, studying them requires incredibly precise and fast equipment.<\/p>" } }, "Db": { "symbol": "Db", "name": "Dubnium", "atomic": 105, "category": "transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b>Dubnium<\/b> (symbol <b>Db<\/b>, atomic number 105) is a highly radioactive, human-made element. It does not exist naturally on Earth and is incredibly fleeting. Its most stable form, dubnium-268, survives for only about 16 hours before decaying. This extreme instability makes studying dubnium incredibly challenging, as scientists can only examine a few atoms at a time.<\/p>\n\n<p>The story of dubnium is intertwined with Cold War rivalry. It was first synthesized in 1968 by a Soviet team at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (JINR) in Dubna, Russia, and shortly after in 1970 by an American team at the Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory in California. Both teams fiercely competed to claim the discovery and name the new element, sparking a dispute that lasted over two decades\u2014a period often called the \"Transfermium Wars\". Finally, in 1993, global scientific authorities decided to share the credit between both teams. By 1997, it was officially named <i>dubnium<\/i> to honor the Russian town of Dubna.<\/p>\n\n<p>Chemically, dubnium belongs to group 5 of the periodic table, making it a heavier cousin to familiar metals like vanadium, niobium, and tantalum. Although difficult to study, experiments suggest it shares many properties with these metals, though with a few unexpected quirks caused by its massive, superheavy nature. Currently, dubnium has no commercial or industrial applications; its sole use is in scientific research to better understand the behavior of superheavy elements and to validate quantum mechanical models.<\/p>\n\n<p>While the initial discovery of superheavy elements was driven by researchers in Russia and the United States, the modern quest to understand these colossal atoms is a global effort. Scientists from India have become increasingly prominent in this cutting-edge field. Researchers like Dr. Moumita Maiti (IIT Roorkee) and Dr. Susant Lahiri (Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics) have actively participated in major international collaborations studying superheavy elements. For example, Indian scientists were key contributors in landmark experiments at Germany's GSI facility that discovered new isotopes of neighboring elements like Seaborgium. Their ongoing efforts are crucial in the worldwide search for the theoretical \"island of stability\"\u2014a predicted group of superheavy elements that might live long enough to reveal entirely new realms of physics and chemistry.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/images-of-elements.com\/s\/transactinoid.png", "atomic_mass": 268, "density": 29.3, "melt": null, "boil": null, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Joint Institute for Nuclear Research", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p6 7s2 5f14 6d3", "electronegativity_pauling": null, "electron_affinity": null, "ionization_energies": [], "sections": { "Isotopes": "<p>Because dubnium is a \"superheavy\" element\u2014meaning its nucleus is packed with a massive number of protons and neutrons\u2014it is extremely unstable. There are no naturally occurring or stable isotopes of dubnium. Its longest-lasting isotope, dubnium-268, has a half-life of just around 16 hours. This means that if you had a handful of dubnium-268 atoms, half of them would decay into lighter elements in less than a day.<\/p>\n\n<p>This incredibly short lifespan poses a huge hurdle for scientists. Making things even more difficult is the fact that creating the \"most stable\" forms of dubnium is actually the hardest part. Scientists generally create these superheavy elements by smashing a beam of smaller atoms into a target of larger atoms using high-energy particle accelerators. However, the ingredients available usually don't have enough neutrons to build the most stable version of dubnium. They have to rely on rare and complex reactions to even get close.<\/p>\n\n<p>Usually, an experiment might produce just a few individual atoms of dubnium at a time! For instance, in 2022, using the state-of-the-art Superheavy Element Factory in Dubna, scientists were able to measure the 16-hour lifespan of dubnium-268 more accurately. Another isotope, dubnium-270, has been created in even tinier amounts\u2014just three atoms have ever been recorded, surviving for about an hour each. Interestingly, these heavier versions of dubnium often aren't even made directly; they are caught as the \"leftovers\" when even heavier, newly discovered elements (like moscovium and tennessine) break apart and decay.<\/p>" } }, "Sg": { "symbol": "Sg", "name": "Seaborgium", "atomic": 106, "category": "transition metal", "description": "", "extract_html": "<p><b>Seaborgium<\/b> (symbol <b>Sg<\/b>, atomic number 106) is a synthetic, highly radioactive element in the periodic table. It does not occur naturally and can only be created in laboratories by smashing lighter elements into heavy ones. Named after the legendary American nuclear chemist Glenn T. Seaborg, it holds the distinction of being one of the very few elements named after a living person at the time of its official naming. Because it decays so quickly\u2014its most stable isotope has a half-life of just a few minutes\u2014only tiny amounts of seaborgium have ever been made. It sits in Group 6 of the periodic table, right below tungsten, and scientists predict it behaves as a solid metal at room temperature.<\/p>", "local_image": "https:\/\/images-of-elements.com\/s\/transactinoid.png", "atomic_mass": 269, "density": 35, "melt": null, "boil": null, "phase": "Solid", "discovered_by": "Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory", "electron_configuration": "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d10 5p6 6s2 4f14 5d10 6p6 7s2 5f14 6d4", "electronegativity_pauling": null, "electron_affinity": null, "ionization_energies": [], "sections": { "History": "<p>The story of seaborgium's discovery was full of international competition and controversy. It was first synthesized in 1974, almost simultaneously, by two rival teams: one led by Albert Ghiorso at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in the US, and another at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna, Russia. The American team made it by bombarding a californium-249 target with oxygen-18 ions.<\/p><p>For over two decades, the discovery sparked a fierce \"Transfermium Wars\" naming dispute between the scientific institutions. It wasn't until 1997 that the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) officially approved the name \"seaborgium,\" honoring Glenn T. Seaborg's monumental contributions to discovering numerous transuranium elements.<\/p>", "Isotopes and Modern Uses": "<p>Seaborgium has no stable isotopes; all known forms are highly radioactive. The most stable known isotope is seaborgium-271, with a half-life of roughly 2.4 minutes, though it decays into lighter elements almost immediately. Because of this extreme instability, seaborgium has no commercial, industrial, or everyday uses. Instead, it is highly prized for fundamental scientific research. Studying seaborgium helps physicists verify the trends in the periodic table, understand relativistic effects on superheavy elements, and search for the theoretical \"Island of Stability\" where certain heavy isotopes might last longer.<\/p><p>In recent years, Indian scientists have also made significant contributions to the study of superheavy elements. For instance, researchers such as Prof. M. Maiti from IIT Roorkee collaborated with international teams at the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in Germany to discover a new isotope, seaborgium-257.
